chapters.title: Limits, Continuity and Differentiability

concepts.title: Indeterminate Forms and Why Limits Need Techniques
concepts.quote: Put x = 10.0001 into a function and you can almost feel the limit. Now try doing that in an exam, for every question, without a calculator — you can't, and that is exactly why limits have techniques.
concepts.oneLine: The four indeterminate forms — 0/0, ∞/∞, ∞−∞, 0×∞ — are the signal that a limit needs a technique, and the first, second and fourth are really the same form in disguise.
notes: Start by burning this small chart into your memory: 0/0, ∞/∞, ∞−∞, 0×∞. There are seven indeterminate forms in all, and we will meet the rest slowly, but these four are the ones that show up first.

Now look closer at them. If anything is approaching infinity, its reciprocal must approach 0 — so 0×∞ is just 0/0 or ∞/∞ written differently. Pull the ∞ down to the denominator and it becomes a 0 there; push the 0 down and it becomes an ∞. The first, second and fourth are more or less the same form. Leave the middle one, ∞−∞, aside for now.

So how do we actually find a limit? In the beginning you can cheat a little. For a limit as x approaches 10, put x = 10.0001 and you get a feel for the right hand limit; put x = 9.9999 and you get the left hand limit. Fine — but you cannot do that in every question. With a calculator in your hand it is a different story; in an exam it is not a method.

That is the whole reason techniques exist. Three come first, and honestly the first two are so easy that a student who does not yet know what a limit means can still use them: factorization method, rationalization method, and the ∞/∞ form method. Factorization is the simplest idea of all — wherever the expression can be factorized, factorize it. The next section opens that up with the limit of (x³ − 27)/(x⁴ − 81) as x approaches 3.

quickChecks.q: Direct substitution in a limit gives you 0 × ∞. Which of the four forms can you rewrite it as?
steps: 1. Write it as f·g with f → 0 and g → ∞.
2. Bring g down as 1/g, which approaches 0, giving 0/0.
3. Or bring f down as 1/f, which approaches ∞, giving ∞/∞.
quickChecks.answer: Either 0/0 or ∞/∞ — your choice, pick whichever is easier to simplify.

quickChecks.q: A function g(x) approaches ∞ as x approaches 2. What does 1/g(x) approach?
steps: 1. Anything approaching infinity has a reciprocal approaching zero.

quickChecks.q: To estimate a limit as x approaches 10, which value gives the left hand limit: 9.9999 or 10.0001?
steps: 1. Left hand means approaching from values below 10.
2. 9.9999 is below 10, so it imitates the left hand limit.
3. 10.0001 is above 10, so that one gives the right hand limit.
quickChecks.answer: 9.9999 — and remember, this is only for understanding, not a solving method.

concepts.title: Factorization Method for 0/0
concepts.quote: Put x = 3 in (x³ − 27)/(x⁴ − 81) and you get 0 on top, 0 at the bottom. This is the question that has handed marks to every student — one factorization line and the answer falls out.
concepts.oneLine: When direct substitution gives 0/0, factorize the top and the bottom, cancel the common factor — it is a tiny non-zero quantity, not a zero — and then substitute.
notes: Take limit x → 3 of (x³ − 27)/(x⁴ − 81). Put 3 in the numerator, you get 0. Put 3 in the denominator, you get 0 again. But look carefully — we are not actually allowed to put 3, x is only approaching 3.

So the top is approaching 0 and the bottom is approaching 0. Writing 0/0 is the quick way to record that. In this whole chapter, whenever a 0 appears inside a limit, read it as "tending to 0" — the arrow is not drawn every single time.

Wherever the expression can be factorized, factorize there. On top use a³ − b³ with a = x, b = 3. At the bottom, x⁴ − 81 is a difference of squares: (x² − 9)(x² + 9), and x² − 9 splits once more into (x − 3)(x + 3). Now (x − 3) sits on both sides and goes away.

Now the honest part, because this is where students get scared. We are not cancelling 0 — we are cancelling (x − 3), a very small quantity approaching 0, and it is the exact same quantity on top and at the bottom. If you were allowed to cancel 0, then from 0 = 0 you could write 0 × 5 = 0 × 7, cancel the 0, and claim 5 = 7. That is nonsense. A genuine 0 can never be cancelled; an identical non-zero factor always can. Once it is gone the form is no longer 0/0, so just put x = 3.

quickChecks.q: Evaluate limit x → 2 of (x² − 4)/(x − 2).
steps: 1. At x = 2, top = 0 and bottom = 0, so the form is 0/0.
3. Cancel (x − 2) to get x + 2, then put x = 2.

quickChecks.q: Evaluate limit x → 1 of (x³ − 1)/(x² − 1).
steps: 1. At x = 1 both top and bottom tend to 0.
3. Cancel (x − 1): (x² + x + 1)/(x + 1). Put x = 1 to get 3/2.

quickChecks.q: Evaluate limit x → 2 of (x³ − 8)/(x⁴ − 16).
steps: 1. At x = 2 it is the 0/0 form.

concepts.title: Rationalization Method for 0/0
concepts.oneLine: When a 0/0 limit has square roots, multiply by the conjugate so the surd turns into a²−b², the (x−a) factor cancels, and you can put the value in.
notes: After factorization, the second method you must have ready is rationalization. Look at limit x→2 of (√(x+3) − √5)/(√(x+7) − 3). Put x = 2: the top goes to √5 − √5 = 0, the bottom goes to √9 − 3 = 0. Again 0/0.

The instant you see this, one thing should click in your head: the root has to go, and the only tool that kills a root is a² − b². If a term looks like a − b with roots in it, multiply it by a + b. The roots square away and you are left with plain algebra.

Here the root sits on top and at the bottom, so I multiply by both conjugates. Top: (√(x+3) − √5)(√(x+3) + √5) = x + 3 − 5 = x − 2. Bottom: (√(x+7) − 3)(√(x+7) + 3) = x + 7 − 9 = x − 2. And because the top was multiplied by (√(x+3) + √5), that factor now sits in the denominator; the bottom's (√(x+7) + 3) now sits on top.

Now the (x − 2) above and the (x − 2) below cancel — that is the whole point of the move. What is left is (√(x+7) + 3)/(√(x+3) + √5), and this has no 0/0 problem. Put x = 2: (3 + 3)/(√5 + √5) = 6/(2√5) = 3/√5. Honestly, this is a very simple-level thing once you see it.

quickChecks.q: Evaluate limit x→0 of (√(x+4) − 2)/x.
steps: 2. Multiply numerator and denominator by (√(x+4) + 2).
3. Numerator becomes x + 4 − 4 = x. So the expression is x / [x(√(x+4) + 2)].

quickChecks.q: Evaluate limit x→1 of (√(x+8) − 3)/(x − 1).
steps: 2. Multiply numerator and denominator by (√(x+8) + 3).
3. Numerator becomes x + 8 − 9 = x − 1. So we get (x − 1) / [(x − 1)(√(x+8) + 3)].

quickChecks.q: Evaluate limit x→4 of (√(x+5) − 3)/(√x − 2).
steps: 2. Roots on top and bottom, so use both conjugates: multiply by (√(x+5) + 3) and by (√x + 2).
3. Numerator: x + 5 − 9 = x − 4. Denominator: x − 4.
4. Expression becomes (x − 4)(√x + 2) / [(x − 4)(√(x+5) + 3)].

concepts.title: Finding a and b When the Limit Value Is Given
concepts.oneLine: If the denominator goes to 0 and the limit is a finite number, the numerator must also go to 0 — that gives you one equation, and the cancelled limit gives you the second.
notes: Take limit x→3 of (x² + ax + b)/(x² − 9) = 5. Put x = 3 in the denominator: 9 − 9 = 0. No doubt about that, the bottom is approaching 0. The top is approaching 9 + 3a + b.

Now ask yourself what happens if that top number is not 0. Suppose 9 + 3a + b = 100. Then you have 100 upon something going to 0, and that blows up to infinity. Minus 100 gives minus infinity. And ½ upon 0 is not an indeterminate form either — ½/0 also runs off to infinity. A non-zero constant divided by something tending to 0 is never 5; it is always infinity.

So the only way this limit can settle at a finite 5 is if the numerator also approaches 0. That means 9 + 3a + b = 0. That single condition also tells you x = 3 is a root of the numerator, so (x − 3) is guaranteed to come out as a factor. Your first equation is free — you got it just by looking.

Now use the condition to kill b: b = −9 − 3a. The numerator becomes x² + ax − 9 − 3a = (x² − 9) + a(x − 3) = (x − 3)(x + 3 + a). The (x − 3) comes out exactly as promised. Cancel it with the (x − 3) in the denominator, put x = 3, set it equal to 5, and a drops out. Then b follows from the first equation. Two unknowns, two equations, done.

quickChecks.q: If limit x→2 of (x² + ax + b)/(x² − 4) = 3, find a and b.
steps: 1. Denominator at x = 2 is 0, and the limit is finite, so the numerator must be 0 at x = 2: 4 + 2a + b = 0.
2. So b = −4 − 2a, and the numerator becomes (x² − 4) + a(x − 2) = (x − 2)(x + 2 + a).
3. Cancel (x − 2) with the denominator's (x − 2)(x + 2) and put x = 2: (4 + a)/4 = 3.

quickChecks.q: If limit x→1 of (x² + ax + b)/(x² − 1) = 2, find a and b.
steps: 1. Numerator must vanish at x = 1: 1 + a + b = 0, so b = −1 − a.
2. Numerator = (x² − 1) + a(x − 1) = (x − 1)(x + 1 + a).
3. Cancel (x − 1) and put x = 1: (2 + a)/2 = 2.

quickChecks.q: If limit x→3 of (x² + ax + b)/(x − 3) = 4, find a and b.
steps: 1. Denominator → 0 and the limit is finite, so 9 + 3a + b = 0, giving b = −9 − 3a.
2. Numerator = x² + ax − 9 − 3a = (x − 3)(x + 3 + a).
3. Cancel (x − 3): limit = 3 + 3 + a = 6 + a = 4.
4. So a = −2 and b = −9 + 6 = −3. Check: x² − 2x − 3 = (x − 3)(x + 1), and at x = 3 that gives 4. ✓

concepts.title: Practice: Factorization and Rationalization Limits
concepts.oneLine: Two board-level 0/0 limits done by your own pen: one by rationalization, one where the given limit 5 fixes a = 24 — proof that 0/0 has no fixed value.
notes: Pick up your copy and solve these two yourself first. The full solution follows right after, but the solution is useless until your pen has already tried it. Understanding a worked solution and scoring marks are two different skills, and only the pen builds the second one.
Both are 0/0 at the point you are approaching. One clears by rationalizing, one clears by factorizing — the same two tools from the last two sections, nothing new.

Then look at the second answer: the limit is 5. The obvious question is how 0/0 became 5. It did not. 0/0 is an indeterminate form — it carries no value of its own, so the function around the point decides the answer. Here 0/0 comes out as 5 only when a = 24; change a and the same 0/0 gives you something else entirely.
That is the whole reason 0/0 is never written as 0 or as 1. Finish these two, check them against the worked steps, and then move on to the ∞/∞ form, which has its own fixed method.

quickChecks.q: Evaluate lim x→2 (x² − 4)/(x² − 3x + 2).
steps: 1. At x = 2: top = 0, bottom = 4 − 6 + 2 = 0, so it is 0/0.

quickChecks.q: Evaluate lim x→0 (√(4 + x) − 2)/x.
steps: 2. Multiply top and bottom by √(4 + x) + 2: top = (4 + x) − 4 = x.

quickChecks.q: Find a if lim x→2 (x² + ax − 2a − 4)/(x² − 4) = 3.
steps: 1. At x = 2 the top is 4 + 2a − 2a − 4 = 0 and the bottom is 0, so 0/0 for every a.
4. Put x = 2: (4 + a)/4. Set it equal to 3: 4 + a = 12 ⇒ a = 8.

concepts.title: The ∞/∞ Form: Divide by the Highest Power
concepts.quote: There is a reason I keep saying in class: we love an infinity in the denominator. Once you see why, the whole ∞/∞ form becomes a two-line job instead of a formula you have to remember.
concepts.oneLine: For the ∞/∞ form, divide the numerator and the denominator by the highest power of x — every leftover term with x underneath dies to 0, and what survives is your answer.
notes: Factorization and rationalization handled 0/0. The ∞/∞ form has its own method, and it rests on one single fact.

An infinity sitting in the denominator always pushes that term to 0. Look at 2/x, 3/x², 4/√x, 5/x^(4/3). As x → ∞, the bottom blows up in every one of them — infinity, infinity squared, root of infinity, infinity to the power 4/3 — and a fixed number divided by something that huge approaches 0. That is why you want infinities downstairs, not upstairs.

So when both the top and the bottom are heading to infinity, manufacture that situation. Divide the numerator and the denominator by the highest power of x in the question. Loosely it gets called the biggest infinity — but remember, in mathematics there is no big or small infinity. The phrase is only there to give you the feel of which term is in charge.
After dividing, every term that still has x underneath becomes 0, and the few bare numbers left give you the limit. No memorised shortcut, just the division done honestly.

quickChecks.q: Find limit x → ∞ of (5x − 2)/(3x + 4).
steps: 1. ∞/∞ form; the highest power is 1, so divide top and bottom by x.
3. 2/x → 0 and 4/x → 0, so it becomes 5/3.

quickChecks.q: Find limit x → ∞ of (4x³ + x)/(9 − 6x³).
steps: 1. Highest power is 3, so divide every term by x³.
3. 1/x² → 0 and 9/x³ → 0, so it becomes 4/(−6) = −2/3.

quickChecks.q: Find limit x → ∞ of (3x² + 7)/(2x³ − x).
steps: 1. The highest power in the question is 3, so divide every term by x³ — not by x².
4. Top becomes 0 and bottom becomes 2.

concepts.title: ∞/∞ with Exponential Terms
concepts.oneLine: In an ∞/∞ limit with exponentials, divide top and bottom by the largest base raised to x — every leftover proper fraction to the power x dies to 0.
notes: Look at limit x→∞ of (2·3ˣ + 5·2ˣ)/(7·3ˣ + 9·2ˣ). Put x = ∞ straight in: 3^∞ → ∞ and 2^∞ → ∞. So top is ∞, bottom is ∞. It is the ∞/∞ form, so the process is fixed.

Last time I divided by the highest power of x. Here I divide by the biggest infinity. Which grows faster, 2ˣ or 3ˣ? The bigger base wins, so 3ˣ is the dominant one. Divide every single term, top and bottom, by 3ˣ.
Now the expression is (2 + 5·(2/3)ˣ)/(7 + 9·(2/3)ˣ). And 2/3 is less than 1. A proper fraction raised to an infinite power always approaches 0. So both those pieces vanish and the limit is 2/7.

Why does (2/3)ˣ die? Take 0.66 and multiply it by 2/3 again — you have cut away a third of it. Cut away a third of what is left, and again. Keep cutting a number down by a third of itself and it heads to zero; nothing survives that, however big it started. The reverse picture is one grain of rice doubling day after day — multiply again and again and the number runs away completely. Here the multiplier is below 1, so it runs to 0.

quickChecks.q: Find limit x→∞ of (4·5ˣ + 3·4ˣ)/(9·5ˣ + 2·4ˣ).
steps: 1. Form is ∞/∞. Largest base is 5, so divide every term by 5ˣ.
4. Limit = 4/9.

quickChecks.q: Find limit x→∞ of (3ˣ⁺¹ + 2ˣ)/(3ˣ + 5·2ˣ).
steps: 1. First open 3ˣ⁺¹ = 3·3ˣ, so the top is 3·3ˣ + 2ˣ.
2. Largest base is 3. Divide every term by 3ˣ: (3 + (2/3)ˣ)/(1 + 5·(2/3)ˣ).

quickChecks.q: Find limit x→∞ of (7ˣ − 3ˣ)/(7ˣ + 3ˣ).
steps: 1. Largest base is 7. Divide every term by 7ˣ: (1 − (3/7)ˣ)/(1 + (3/7)ˣ).

concepts.title: When the Powers Are Unequal: Answer 0 or Infinity
concepts.oneLine: When the powers on top and bottom are unequal, still divide by the highest power of x you can see — the answer falls out as 0 or ±∞ on its own, and the sign of the leftover denominator decides which infinity.
notes: Look at the three limits we just did. The thought process was the same every single time: spot the highest power of x in the question, divide the top and the bottom by it, and let every 1/x, 1/x², 1/x³ go to 0. Nothing else.

Now a child gets confused the moment the powers are unequal. He starts hunting for a second rule — power up, power down, plus infinity, minus infinity. Put basic. There is no new concept here. The same division works whether the degrees match or not.

Take (−2x+3)/(x²+5). Highest power in sight is x², so divide above and below by x². On top, −2/x and 3/x² both die to 0. Below, x²/x² is 1 and 5/x² dies. You are left with 0/1, which is simply 0 — and notice this is not an indeterminate form at all, so there is nothing more to do.

Now flip it. Make the top a cube, (3x³−7)/(−2x²+5), and divide by x³. On top you keep 3 and lose 7/x³. Below, −2/x and 5/x³ both go to 0, but −2/x is approaching 0 from the negative side. So you have 3 divided by a tiny negative number, and that marches off to −∞. Apply logic, apply concept — that's all.

quickChecks.q: Evaluate lim x→∞ (5x + 2)/(x² − 3).
steps: 1. Highest power is x². Divide top and bottom by x².
3. Bottom: 1 − 3/x² → 1.
4. Limit is 0/1.

quickChecks.q: Evaluate lim x→∞ (4x³ + 1)/(x² + 7).
steps: 1. Highest power is x³. Divide top and bottom by x³.
3. Bottom: 1/x + 7/x³ → 0, and for large positive x both terms are positive, so it approaches 0 from above.
4. So we get 4 divided by a tiny positive number.

quickChecks.q: Evaluate lim x→∞ (2x² − 1)/(−5x + 3).
steps: 1. Highest power is x². Divide top and bottom by x².
3. Bottom: −5/x + 3/x² → 0, and the surviving term −5/x is negative, so it approaches 0 from below.
4. So we get 2 divided by a tiny negative number.

concepts.title: Practice: Three ∞/∞ Limits
concepts.oneLine: Three ∞/∞ limits in one minute: divide the whole fraction by the highest power on show, and the answer falls out as a ratio, as 0, or as infinity.
notes: You already know the idea. What matters now is speed. In an ∞/∞ limit, divide every term of the numerator and every term of the denominator by the highest power of x you can see in the whole fraction.
After that one division, read what survives. Anything of the form (number)/x^k dies to 0 as x → ∞. Whatever is left standing is your answer.

Three things can be left. Top and bottom both leave a number — the answer is that finite ratio. Top goes to 0 and bottom leaves a number — the answer is 0. Top leaves a number and bottom goes to 0 — the limit runs off to infinity.

One more thing about habits. Some people take x common from the top, then take x common from the bottom, then cancel. It works, but it is slower and a term goes missing somewhere. Divide once by the single highest power and you are done in one line.

steps: 1. Divide every term by x.

quickChecks.q: lim(x→∞) (5x² + x)/(x³ + 2x²)
steps: 1. Highest power is x³, so divide every term by x³.
2. Top: 5/x + 1/x² → 0. Bottom: 1 + 2/x → 1.
1. Highest power is x³, so divide every term by x³.
2. Top: 4 + 1/x³ → 4. Bottom: 9/x + 1/x² → 0.
3. Number over something going to 0.

concepts.title: ∞/∞ When the Polynomial Is Already Factored
concepts.oneLine: When the top and bottom are already factored, don't expand — count the degree, then split that power of n across the brackets: n(n+1)(2n+1)/((n²+2)(−3n+5)) → −2/3.
notes: Look at the question first, don't start writing. On top is n(n+1)(2n+1) — degree 1 plus degree 1 plus degree 1, so cubic. Below is (n²+2)(−3n+5) — degree 2 plus degree 1, again cubic.

That is all you need to know. Cubic over cubic means divide top and bottom by n³, exactly like every other ∞/∞ limit. The factored form is a gift, not extra work — count degrees and divide, never expand.

Now the nice part: the n³ does not have to go in one shot. It can be handed out bracket by bracket. On top: one n to the first factor, one n to (n+1), one n to (2n+1). Below: n² to (n²+2) and n to (−3n+5). Three n's up, three n's down — effectively both sides have been divided by n³.

Each bracket becomes something tiny. n/n = 1, (n+1)/n = 1 + 1/n → 1, (2n+1)/n = 2 + 1/n → 2. Below, (n²+2)/n² = 1 + 2/n² → 1 and (−3n+5)/n = −3 + 5/n → −3. So the whole thing goes to (1·1·2)/(1·(−3)) = −2/3.

quickChecks.q: Find limit as n → ∞ of n(n+2)(3n+1) / ((n²+1)(4n+7)).
steps: 1. Degrees: top 1 + 1 + 1 = 3, bottom 2 + 1 = 3. Cubic over cubic, divide by n³.
3. Bottom: (n²+1)/n² = 1 + 1/n² → 1, (4n+7)/n = 4 + 7/n → 4, so bottom → 4.

quickChecks.q: Find limit as n → ∞ of (2n+1)(3n−2) / ((n+4)(−n+5)).
steps: 1. Degrees: top 1 + 1 = 2, bottom 1 + 1 = 2. Divide by n², one n to each bracket.

quickChecks.q: Find limit as n → ∞ of n(n+1)(n+2) / ((2n+3)(n²+5)).
steps: 1. Degrees: top 3, bottom 1 + 2 = 3. Divide by n³.
3. Bottom: (2n+3)/n = 2 + 3/n → 2, (n²+5)/n² = 1 + 5/n² → 1, so bottom → 2.

concepts.title: The ∞−∞ Form: Rationalize First
concepts.oneLine: For ∞−∞ with square roots, multiply by the conjugate to turn it into ∞/∞, then divide by x — remembering that 1/x goes inside a root as 1/x².
notes: Look at limit x→∞ of √(x²−x+2) − √(x²+5x−7). Each quadratic is upward opening, so each one approaches infinity, and the square root of something going to infinity also goes to infinity. So this is ∞−∞.

Remember what the indeterminate forms were: 0/0, ∞/∞, ∞−∞. Two very large numbers subtracting — nobody can tell you the answer by looking. The value is not fixed, it depends on the problem. So you must do work on it first.

In ∞−∞ with roots, rationalize: multiply and divide by the conjugate, so the roots collapse through a² − b². Below there is nothing written, which means 1 is written — so multiply both top and bottom by √(x²−x+2) + √(x²+5x−7). Up above the x² terms cancel, and that is the question setter's whole design.

Now the care point. Inside the root the highest power is x², but after the root the overall highest power is only 1. So you divide top and bottom by x — and when 1/x goes inside a root, it goes in squared, as 1/x². Same way, if √5 is written and you push 2 inside, it becomes √(2²·5). Then every 1/x and 1/x² dies and only numbers are left.

quickChecks.q: Find limit x→∞ of √(x²+4x) − x.
steps: 1. Form is ∞−∞. Multiply and divide by √(x²+4x) + x.
2. Top: (x²+4x) − x² = 4x.
3. Limit = 4x / [√(x²+4x) + x].
4. Highest power is 1, so divide by x: 4 / [√(1 + 4/x) + 1].

quickChecks.q: Find limit x→∞ of √(x²+3x+1) − √(x²−x).
steps: 1. Form is ∞−∞. Multiply and divide by the conjugate √(x²+3x+1) + √(x²−x).
3. Divide top and bottom by x: (4 + 1/x) / [√(1 + 3/x + 1/x²) + √(1 − 1/x)].

quickChecks.q: Find limit x→∞ of √(x²+5x) − √(x²+2x).
steps: 1. Form is ∞−∞. Multiply and divide by √(x²+5x) + √(x²+2x).
2. Top: (x²+5x) − (x²+2x) = 3x.
3. Divide top and bottom by x: 3 / [√(1 + 5/x) + √(1 + 2/x)].

concepts.title: Limits as x → −∞: Substitute x = −t
concepts.quote: There is one place where good students lose a sure mark: the limit is at minus infinity and the answer comes out positive instead of negative. One substitution kills that mistake forever.
concepts.oneLine: Whenever x → −∞, put x = −t so that t → +∞, solve the whole question in t, and the sign can never go wrong.
notes: Everything so far about infinity limits is correct and never fails. But at x → −∞ there is one spot where it is easy to slip, and that is worth getting right the first time rather than unlearning later.
So do this with your eyes closed. If x → −∞ anywhere in the question, put x = −t. Then t → +∞, and the whole question is now a plus-infinity question you already know how to do.

Notice two things when you substitute. Since t = −x, x going to −∞ means t goes to +∞, so the limit written on your paper must change from x to t. And a term like 2x² becomes 2t² with no sign change, because the square eats the minus.

After that, nothing new. Divide top and bottom by the highest power of t, exactly as before, and read off the answer. Keep the number of decision-making steps in the exam as low as possible — you will be a much happier student.

quickChecks.q: Find the limit of x/√(9x² + 5) as x → −∞.
steps: 1. Put x = −t, so t → +∞.
2. The limit becomes t → +∞ of (−t)/√(9t² + 5).
3. Divide top and bottom by t: (−1)/√(9 + 5/t²).
4. 5/t² → 0, so the root becomes √9 = 3.

quickChecks.q: Find the limit of (3x − 1)/√(x² + 4) as x → −∞.
steps: 1. Put x = −t, so t → +∞.
3. Divide top and bottom by t: (−3 − 1/t)/√(1 + 4/t²).
4. Both 1/t and 4/t² → 0.

quickChecks.q: Find the limit of (2x + 7)/√(x² + 1) as x → −∞.
steps: 1. Put x = −t, so t → +∞.
2. The limit becomes t → +∞ of (−2t + 7)/√(t² + 1).
4. Both small terms → 0. Sign check: top is negative, bottom is positive, so the answer is negative.

concepts.title: Existence of a Limit: (x²+1)/(x+1) − (ax+b)
concepts.oneLine: Take the LCM, write the top in systematic powers of x, and kill the x² coefficient — that is the only way this limit can be finite.
notes: Look at limit x → ∞ of [(x²+1)/(x+1) − (ax − b)]. The first piece alone goes to infinity: divide top and bottom by x² and you get 1 above, 0 below. The second piece is linear, so it also goes to infinity. That is ∞ − ∞, and there is nothing yet to divide.

In the last question we rationalised; here we take the LCM. With x+1 below, the top becomes x²+1 − (ax − b)(x+1). Open it carefully and collect terms, and you get x²(1−a) + x(b−a) + (1+b), all over x+1. Watch the sign: the coefficient of x is b−a, not a−b, because of the minus sitting in front.

Now I convert the question. Say the whole limit equals L. Below, the highest power is x¹. Above, the highest power is x². An ∞/∞ form gives a finite constant only when the highest power above and below is the same. So the x² term must die: 1−a = 0, which forces a = 1.

Once x² is gone, divide top and bottom by x and the limit is simply b−a. If L = 5, then b−a = 5 with a = 1, so b = 6. If L = 0, the degree-1 term must also go, so b−a = 0 and a = b = 1 — then only the constant 1+b survives over x+1, which goes to 0.

quickChecks.q: If limit x → ∞ of [(x²+1)/(x+1) − (ax − b)] = 4, find a and b.
steps: 1. Same collected form: [x²(1−a) + x(b−a) + (1+b)] / (x+1).
2. Finite answer, so 1−a = 0 and a = 1.
3. Then the limit is b−a = 4, so b = 5.

quickChecks.q: Same expression, but the limit is 15. What are a and b?
steps: 1. The x² condition never changes: 1−a = 0, so a = 1.

quickChecks.q: Someone writes a = 3 and b = 0. What does limit x → ∞ of [(x²+1)/(x+1) − 3x] become?
steps: 1. Numerator = x² + 1 − 3x(x+1) = −2x² − 3x + 1.
2. So we need the limit of (−2x² − 3x + 1)/(x+1).
3. Power above is 2, power below is 1, and the leading coefficient above is negative.
4. So the value goes to −∞; the limit does not exist. This is exactly why a must be 1.
quickChecks.answer: It goes to −∞, so no finite limit exists.

concepts.title: Practice: Limit Existence Quiz and Bonus Problems
concepts.oneLine: Same existence question with the limit pinned at 4: kill the x² term to get a = 1, then read the x-coefficient b − a = 4 to get b = 5.
notes: The quiz was the same problem as before, with one extra piece of information: the limit is 4. So now a and b are both fixed, and you have to produce two numbers, not a condition.

Nothing new is needed here. Take the LCM, build the quadratic on top properly, and look at it. The bottom has power 1, so if an x² survives on top, the limit blows up. So the x² coefficient must be zero first — that single line gives you a.
Once a = 1, the top is linear and the bottom is linear. Divide top and bottom by x and the limit is just the coefficient of x on top. Set that equal to 4 and b falls out.
Three bonus problems follow for anyone who finishes early. Same logic, only the execution changes.

quickChecks.q: The limit as x → ∞ of [(x²+1)/(x+1) − ax + b] is 2. Find a and b.
steps: 1. Numerator after LCM: (1 − a)x² + (b − a)x + (1 + b).

quickChecks.q: The limit as x → ∞ of [(x²+x+1)/(x+1) − ax + b] is 3. Find a and b.
steps: 1. Numerator after LCM: (1 − a)x² + (1 − a + b)x + (1 + b).
2. 1 − a = 0 → a = 1, so the x-coefficient becomes b.

quickChecks.q: The limit as x → ∞ of [(2x²+3)/(x+1) − ax + b] is 1. Find a and b.
steps: 1. Numerator after LCM: (2 − a)x² + (b − a)x + (3 + b).

concepts.title: Limits of the Form (aⁿ + bⁿ)^(1/n): Take the Largest Term Common
concepts.oneLine: For a limit like (3ⁿ + 5ⁿ) to the power 1/n as n → ∞, take the largest base common — the answer is simply that largest base.
notes: Till now you met 0/0, ∞/∞, ∞ − ∞ and 0 × ∞. Add three more to your list: 1 to the power ∞, ∞ to the power 0, and 0 to the power 0. All three are indeterminate — you cannot write the answer by looking at them.

The logic for these is the same logic that runs through the whole topic: take the biggest thing out. Look at limit n → ∞ of (3ⁿ + 5ⁿ), whole power 1/n. Between 3 and 5, the bigger base is 5, so take 5ⁿ common from inside the bracket.

That gives 5ⁿ[(3/5)ⁿ + 1], whole power 1/n. Break the power: (AB) power 1/n is A power 1/n into B power 1/n. The first piece is 5ⁿ power 1/n, where n and 1/n cancel and only 5 survives. In the second piece (3/5)ⁿ → 0, because a proper fraction to the power infinity is 0, so the bracket becomes 1 and the power 1/n becomes 0. That is 1⁰, which is plain 1 — only 1^∞ is indeterminate, 1⁰ is not. Answer: 5.

Now the version with coefficients, like (3ⁿ⁺¹ + 2ⁿ⁺²) over (5·3ⁿ + 2ⁿ⁻¹). Students look at it and say sir this is something new. It is not. 3ⁿ⁺¹ is just 3·3ⁿ and 2ⁿ⁺² is just 4·2ⁿ, so it is the same question with numbers stuck in front. Write that one extra step on paper first, then divide top and bottom by the largest power — everything left over is a proper fraction and dies to 0.

quickChecks.q: Find limit n → ∞ of (2ⁿ + 7ⁿ), whole power 1/n.
steps: 1. Largest base is 7, so take 7ⁿ common: 7ⁿ[(2/7)ⁿ + 1], whole power 1/n.
2. 7ⁿ power 1/n = 7.
3. (2/7)ⁿ → 0, bracket → 1, power → 0, so that factor is 1⁰ = 1.

quickChecks.q: Find limit n → ∞ of (3ⁿ⁺¹ + 2ⁿ) / (3ⁿ + 2ⁿ⁺¹).
steps: 1. Rewrite: 3ⁿ⁺¹ = 3·3ⁿ and 2ⁿ⁺¹ = 2·2ⁿ, so the limit is (3·3ⁿ + 2ⁿ)/(3ⁿ + 2·2ⁿ).
2. Divide top and bottom by 3ⁿ: (3 + (2/3)ⁿ) / (1 + 2(2/3)ⁿ).
3. (2/3)ⁿ → 0, so it becomes 3/1.

quickChecks.q: Find limit n → ∞ of (4ⁿ + 5ⁿ + 6ⁿ), whole power 1/n.
steps: 1. Three terms, same rule: take the largest, 6ⁿ, common.
3. 6ⁿ power 1/n = 6; both fractions to the power n → 0, so the bracket → 1 and 1⁰ = 1.

concepts.title: Road Map: Standard Limits and the Algebraic Limit Formula
concepts.quote: The three basic techniques are behind us. From here, a whole set of limits stops needing tricks at all — you just know the answer, because there is a formula.
concepts.oneLine: After the three basic techniques come the standard limits — direct formulas for algebraic, trigonometric, exponential and logarithmic limits — and the algebraic one, (xⁿ − aⁿ)/(x − a) = n·aⁿ⁻¹, is the first of them.
notes: We have covered the three basic level techniques. Now step into the next room of the limit world, and you will find something different waiting: standard limits. These are the standard cases where you do not work the limit out — you recognise it and write the answer from a direct formula.

The order matters, so hold this map. Most students jump straight to trigonometric limits, but one family sits before them: the algebraic limit. After algebraic come trigonometric, then exponential, then logarithmic — each one in the same fashion, each one a direct formula.

The algebraic one is this: lim x→a of (xⁿ − aⁿ)/(x − a) = n·aⁿ⁻¹. Same base a on top and bottom, difference of powers above, plain difference below. Once this is in your hand, a question of this shape is finished in one line.

The usual sequence of this topic is deliberately changed here, because this is the order in which it actually becomes easy. And right after these standard formulas comes a technique called L'Hôpital's rule — that is where the next section goes.

quickChecks.q: Find lim x→2 of (x⁵ − 32)/(x − 2).
steps: 1. 32 = 2⁵, so this is (x⁵ − 2⁵)/(x − 2) with a = 2, n = 5.
2. Apply n·aⁿ⁻¹ = 5 × 2⁴.

quickChecks.q: Find lim x→3 of (x³ − 27)/(x − 3).
steps: 1. 27 = 3³, so a = 3 and n = 3.
2. Answer is n·aⁿ⁻¹ = 3 × 3² = 3 × 9.

quickChecks.q: Find lim x→1 of (x^(3/2) − 1)/(x − 1).
steps: 1. Here a = 1 and n = 3/2 — a fraction is allowed.
3. 1^(1/2) = 1, so the value is 3/2.

concepts.title: L'Hôpital's Rule
concepts.oneLine: If a limit sits in 0/0 or ∞/∞ form, differentiate the top alone and the bottom alone, put the value back in, and repeat until a finite number appears.
notes: Here is the rule. You have limit x→a of f(x)/g(x), and when you put x = a you get 0/0 or ∞/∞. Then you are allowed to replace it by limit x→a of f′(x)/g′(x) — the derivative of the numerator on top, the derivative of the denominator at the bottom.

This is not the quotient rule. You are not differentiating f(x)/g(x) as one function — there is no g(x)² at the bottom and no minus sign anywhere. Top differentiates on its own, bottom differentiates on its own.

Now substitute. If you get a finite number, the question is over, write the answer and move on. If you are still staring at 0/0 or ∞/∞, repeat the same step — differentiate top, differentiate bottom, substitute again. You can keep repeating as long as the form keeps coming back.

Why is this rule worth so much here? Because the one derivative everyone knows cold is the power rule: d/dx of xⁿ is nx^(n−1). Not every function is easy to differentiate, but in these limit questions the functions are powers of x, and that makes LH rule the fastest tool you own here.

quickChecks.q: Find limit x→2 of (x⁵ − 32)/(x − 2).
steps: 2. Top derivative: 5x⁴. Bottom derivative: 1.
3. Limit = 5x⁴ at x = 2 = 5 × 16.

quickChecks.q: Find limit x→4 of (x^(3/2) − 8)/(x² − 16).
steps: 2. Top derivative: (3/2)x^(1/2). Bottom derivative: 2x.
3. Put x = 4: top = (3/2) × 2 = 3, bottom = 8.
2. Top derivative: 2x. Bottom derivative: (1/3)x^(−2/3).
4. 6 ÷ (1/3) = 18, and dividing by 3^(−2/3) means multiplying by 3^(2/3).

concepts.title: Practice: Five L'Hôpital Questions
concepts.oneLine: Five algebraic 0/0 limits, each finished by differentiating top and bottom once — the whole point of L'Hôpital is that it is faster than factorising.
notes: The theory of the L'Hôpital rule is in place. Now watch what it does to real questions. Several of the five solved here are of a type that has actually come in JEE, and in every one of them L'Hôpital is the technique that saves you the most time.
Check the form first. All five are 0/0 — that is the only permission you need. Then differentiate the top and differentiate the bottom, separately, and put the value in.

Notice what the derivatives look like: every single one is just the x to the power n rule, the first derivative anybody learns. That is not an accident. In a L'Hôpital question the differentiation is never the hard part, so there is no excuse for a long calculation.
And when the limit is at x → 1, relax completely. One raised to any power is still one, so the substitution step is almost free.

quickChecks.q: Find lim x→2 of (x⁵ − 2⁵)/(x − 2).
steps: 1. At x = 2 it is 0/0.
2. Top derivative 5x⁴, bottom derivative 1.

quickChecks.q: Find lim x→1 of (x + x² + x³ − 3)/(x − 1).
steps: 1. At x = 1 the top is 1 + 1 + 1 − 3 = 0 and the bottom is 0.
2. Top derivative 1 + 2x + 3x², bottom derivative 1.
3. Put x = 1: 1 + 2 + 3 = 6. (Same as n(n + 1)/2 with n = 3.)
1. At x = a it is 0/0, and (a + 1)^(7/3) is a constant.
2. Top derivative (7/3)(x + 1)^(4/3), bottom derivative 1.
3. Put x = a.

concepts.title: The two trigonometric limit formulas
concepts.oneLine: sin(something)/same something and tan(something)/same something both tend to 1, as long as that 'something' itself is going to 0.
notes: Look at sin x / x and put x = 0. Top becomes 0, bottom becomes 0. It is a 0/0 form, and the limit of this particular 0/0 form is exactly 1.

Now generalise it. Suppose some function f(x) sits inside the sine, and the same f(x) sits in the denominator, and x is approaching a number a. If f(x) itself is approaching 0 as x approaches a, then you have sin of 0 divided by that same 0 — and that limit is 1.

So store it as a sentence, not as a formula: sin of something divided by the same something, when that something is tending to 0, is 1. Tan behaves identically — tan of something divided by the same something, with that something going to 0, is also 1.

Almost every student already knows these two lines. The marks are lost somewhere else — in checking that the 'something' really goes to 0, and in making the top and the bottom the same something. That is what we build next.

quickChecks.q: Find the limit of sin(3x)/(3x) as x → 0.
steps: 1. The something inside sine is 3x, and 3x also sits in the denominator — they match.
2. As x → 0, 3x → 0, so the condition is satisfied.

quickChecks.q: Find the limit of tan(x − 1)/(x − 1) as x → 1.
steps: 1. Here the something is x − 1, appearing inside tan and in the denominator.
2. As x → 1, x − 1 → 0, so the condition holds and the tan form applies.

quickChecks.q: Find the limit of sin(x²)/x² as x → 0.
steps: 1. The something is x², and the same x² is below.
2. As x → 0, x² → 0, so the sine form applies.

concepts.title: Forcing 'something' to approach zero
concepts.oneLine: If the angle inside sine does not go to zero on its own, rewrite it — sin θ as sin(90° − other angle) or sin(180° − x) — until the angle does go to zero, then match the denominator to it.
notes: The formula only fires on one shape: sine of something over the same something, with that something going to 0. So in every question, first ask two things. What is the something inside sine? Is that something approaching 0?

If the angle inside sine is already going to 0, your only job is to make the denominator carry that same angle. In sin(x−3)/(x²−9), the angle is x−3 and at x→3 it goes to 0. Factor the bottom as (x−3)(x+3), and the sin(x−3)/(x−3) part becomes 1. Whatever is left over, 1/(x+3), you just substitute: 1/6.

Now the harder case. The limit is 0/0 but the angle is wrong — cos x at x→π/2, or sin x at x→π where the angle goes to π, not 0. There is no formula for cos of something over the same something, so convert it into a sine whose angle does go to zero. cos x = sin(90° − x), and sin x = sin(180° − x). Both are free to write and both fix the angle.

After the conversion, shape the denominator. You were handed 2x − π but you need 90° − x on the bottom too, so pull out −2 and keep that −2 outside as a plain multiplier. The sine part goes to 1, the leftover number is the answer.

quickChecks.q: Find limit as x → 2 of sin(x−2)/(x²−4).
steps: 1. Angle inside sine is x−2; at x → 2 it goes to 0. Good.

quickChecks.q: Find limit as x → π/2 of cos x/(π−2x).
steps: 1. Put x = 90°: top 0, bottom 180° − 180° = 0, so 0/0 form.
2. cos x = sin(π/2 − x), and the angle π/2 − x → 0.

quickChecks.q: Find limit as x → π of tan x/(x−π).
steps: 1. Put x = π: tan π = 0 on top, 0 below, so 0/0 form, but the angle inside tan is going to π.
2. tan x = tan(x − π), since tan repeats every π. Now the angle x − π → 0.
3. So it is tan of something over the same something with that something → 0.

concepts.title: Shortcut: the coefficient of x is the answer
concepts.oneLine: For lim(x→0) sin(ax)/x the answer is just a — the coefficient of x inside the sine is the answer, and the same works for tan.
notes: Start from the one formula you already know: when something is approaching 0, sin(that something) divided by the same something approaches 1. That is the whole engine.

Now look at lim(x→0) sin(ax)/x. Put x = 0 inside the sine: a × 0 = 0, so the inside is approaching 0. Good. But below there is only x, not ax — so the sine and the denominator are not the same something.

So force it. Write a in the denominator to make it ax, and because an a went in below, an a must go in on top as well. Now it reads a × [sin(ax)/ax], the bracket goes to 1, and the answer is simply a — the coefficient of x inside the sine.

Keep this as a shortcut. It does not change for tan either: lim(x→0) tan(ax)/x is also a. In a long question where there is a lot of confusion, you will spot the coefficient of x and write the answer straight.

quickChecks.q: Find lim(x→0) sin(5x)/x.
steps: 1. The angle is 5x, the denominator is x.
2. Coefficient of x inside the sine is 5.

quickChecks.q: Find lim(x→0) tan(7x)/x.
steps: 1. Same shortcut works for tan.
2. Coefficient of x inside the tan is 7.

quickChecks.q: Find lim(x→0) sin(3x)/(3x).
steps: 1. Here the angle and the denominator are already the same something, 3x.
2. That something approaches 0, so this is directly the base formula.

concepts.title: Using the coefficient shortcut
concepts.quote: A limit that looks like a monster — sin minus tan on top, sin plus tan below — is a four-second question. One move: divide above and below by x.
concepts.oneLine: Divide top and bottom by x, read off the coefficient of x in each sin or tan, and the limit falls out — powers included.
notes: The last section fixed one fact: as x → 0, sin ax/x → a and tan ax/x → a. The coefficient of x is the answer. Now use it, don't just remember it.

Take the first one: the limit as x → 0 of sin³2x/x³. Do not touch the power yet. Look at sin 2x/x — coefficient of x inside sin is 2, so that piece is 2. The whole thing is that piece cubed, so the answer is 2³ = 8.

Now the one that causes the most hesitation: the limit as x → 0 of (sin ax − tan bx)/(sin cx + tan dx). Put x = 0 and you get 0/0, so something has to be done. Divide the numerator and the denominator by x — every single term then becomes a sin or tan over x, and each one is just its own coefficient.
Top becomes a − b. Bottom becomes c + d. So the limit is (a − b)/(c + d). With practice this one needs no writing at all — read the four coefficients off the question and say the answer out loud.

quickChecks.q: Find the limit as x → 0 of sin⁴3x/x⁴.
steps: 1. Write it as (sin 3x/x)⁴.
2. Limit of sin 3x/x = 3.
3. Apply the fourth power: 3⁴ = 81.

quickChecks.q: Find the limit as x → 0 of (sin 5x − tan 2x)/(sin 3x + tan 4x).
steps: 1. It is 0/0 form, so divide numerator and denominator by x.
3. Bottom: 3 + 4 = 7.
4. Limit = 3/7.

quickChecks.q: Find the limit as x → 0 of tan²7x/x².
steps: 1. Write it as (tan 7x/x)².
2. Limit of tan 7x/x = 7.
3. Square it: 7² = 49.

concepts.title: The only two trig identities a limit needs
concepts.oneLine: Almost every trigonometric limit runs on just two identities — 1 − cos2x = 2sin²x and cos C − cos D = −2 sin((C+D)/2) sin((C−D)/2).
notes: There is a fear in this chapter that limits demand heavy trigonometry. That is simply not true. In the entire limits chapter, only two trigonometric identities do almost all the work.

The first is 1 − cos2x = 2sin²x. Yes, cos2x has four standard forms — cos²x − sin²x, 1 − 2sin²x, 2cos²x − 1, and the tan form. But in limits you will reach for exactly one of them: the one that turns 1 − cos2x into 2sin²x. This one is ultra useful, because sine over angle is what we know how to send to 1.

The second is cos C − cos D = −2 sin((C+D)/2) sin((C−D)/2). Notice the minus sign sitting in front; it is part of the identity, not a typo. Any time you see a difference of two cosines on top of a limit, this converts it into a product of two sines — and a product of sines is something you can split and finish.

So the pattern is the same both times. A cosine shape is stuck; you cannot cancel anything. Convert it to sine, and the standard sinθ/θ machinery takes over. Cosine does not cancel; sine does. Beyond these two, a limit in this topic rarely needs another trigonometric formula.

quickChecks.q: Find lim x→0 (1 − cos2x)/x².
steps: 1. Use 1 − cos2x = 2sin²x.
2. Limit becomes 2sin²x/x² = 2(sinx/x)².
3. As x → 0, sinx/x → 1, so the value is 2 × 1.

quickChecks.q: Find lim x→0 (1 − cos x)/x².
steps: 1. Here the angle is x, so halve it: 1 − cos x = 2sin²(x/2).
2. Limit becomes 2sin²(x/2)/x².
3. Write it as 2 × [sin(x/2)/(x/2)]² × (x/2)²/x² = 2 × 1 × ¼.

quickChecks.q: Find lim x→0 (cos3x − cos5x)/x².
steps: 1. Take C = 3x, D = 5x in cos C − cos D = −2 sin((C+D)/2) sin((C−D)/2).
2. This gives −2 sin4x sin(−x) = 2 sin4x sin x.
3. Limit becomes 2 sin4x sin x/x² = 2 × (sin4x/x) × (sinx/x).
4. sin4x/x → 4 and sinx/x → 1, so the value is 2 × 4 × 1.

concepts.title: Why splitting a limit by x is legal
concepts.oneLine: Once every piece has a finite limit and no 0/0 is left, the limit splits across the pieces — that is the whole licence behind the divide-by-x shortcut.
notes: A limit is not some new creature with its own rules. The limit is just the value the function is heading to — so if each piece is heading to a finite number and no indeterminate form is left, the limit distributes over the pieces.

That is exactly what dividing by x achieves. Top was going to 0, bottom was going to 0, so it was 0/0 and stuck. The moment you divide and each bracket turns into a clean finite number, the 0/0 is gone and you are free to take limits piece by piece.
So the order matters. First kill the indeterminate form, then split. If you split while one piece is still 0/0 or still blowing up, you are not using a theorem, you are guessing.
And does this work for tan too? Yes. Whatever works for sin works exactly the same for tan. Same argument rule, same coefficient answer.

quickChecks.q: lim x→0 sin 5x / x
steps: 1. Inside sin the coefficient of x is 5, and 5x → 0.
2. So the limit is that coefficient.

quickChecks.q: lim x→0 (sin 3x + tan 4x)/x
steps: 1. It is 0/0, so split after dividing: (sin 3x)/x + (tan 4x)/x.
2. Each piece is finite: 3 and 4.

quickChecks.q: lim x→2 sin(x − 2)/(x² − 4)
steps: 1. 0/0 form. Factor: x² − 4 = (x − 2)(x + 2).
3. First bracket → 1 since x − 2 → 0 and matches.
4. Second bracket = 1/(2 + 2) = 1/4.

concepts.title: Standard 1 − cos questions
concepts.oneLine: Every 1 − cos limit becomes easy the moment you write 1 − cos θ = 2sin²(θ/2) and then read off the coefficient of x from each sine.
notes: The whole game is one identity: 1 − cos θ = 2sin²(θ/2). So 1 − cos mx becomes 2sin²(mx/2). That single step kills the 0/0 and leaves you with sines only.

Once everything is a sine, the limit of sin(ax)/x is just a — the coefficient of x inside the sine. So there is no need to multiply and divide by x any more. Divide top and bottom by x², look at each sine, and write its coefficient.

For cos mx − cos nx use the C − D formula instead: cos C − cos D = −2 sin((C+D)/2) sin((C−D)/2). Two sines appear, each gives its own coefficient, and the minus sign outside stays with you till the end.
The third type mixes sin and tan in the denominator. Same treatment — tan 7x/x goes to 7 exactly like a sine does. Count coefficients up, count coefficients down, divide.

quickChecks.q: Find lim x→0 (1 − cos4x)/x².
steps: 1. Standard form with m = 4, so the answer is m²/2.
2. Check it the long way: 1 − cos4x = 2sin²(2x), so limit = 2 · [sin2x/x]² = 2 · 2² = 8.

quickChecks.q: Find lim x→0 (cos3x − cos7x)/x².
steps: 1. Use −(m² − n²)/2 with m = 3, n = 7.
3. So the limit is −(−40)/2 = 20.

quickChecks.q: Find lim x→0 (1 − cos2x)/(sin4x · tan5x).
steps: 1. Top: 1 − cos2x = 2sin²x, so dividing by x² gives 2 · 1² = 2.
2. Bottom: (sin4x/x)(tan5x/x) → 4 · 5 = 20.

concepts.title: Oral practice: degrees, and 1 − cos in one line
concepts.oneLine: Oral trig limits: turn x degrees into radians first (so sin x° / x gives π/180), and finish any 1 − cos question in one line with a²/2.
notes: These are oral questions. You write only the answer behind your copy, not the method. That is exactly how these come in the paper — nobody checks your steps, only your number.

First trap: the question says x degree. Every limit formula in calculus is valid only when the angle is in radians. So convert first. 30° becomes 30 × π/180, so x° becomes x × π/180. The coefficient of x is π/180, and that is your answer.

Second pattern: the moment you see 1 − cos, replace it. 1 − cos of any angle is 2 sin² of half that angle. So 1 − cos 4x becomes 2 sin² 2x. Now the x² downstairs eats the sin², the 2 inside comes out squared, and the answer is 2 × 2² = 8.
For (1 − cos ax)/x² the answer is simply a²/2. Square the coefficient, divide by 2. 4 gives 8, 2 gives 2, 6 gives 18. It is ultra fast and it finishes your writing hassle completely.

quickChecks.q: lim x→0 (sin 3x°)/x
steps: 1. Convert: 3x° = 3x × π/180 = πx/60.
2. Coefficient of x inside sine is π/60.
3. So the limit is π/60.

quickChecks.q: lim x→0 (1 − cos 6x)/x²
steps: 1. 1 − cos 6x = 2 sin² 3x.
2. sin 3x / x gives 3, and it is squared, so 3² = 9.

quickChecks.q: lim x→0 (1 − cos x)/x²
steps: 1. Here a = 1, so use a²/2.

concepts.title: Oral practice: mixed sine and tan limits
concepts.oneLine: For a ratio of sines and tans at x → 0, divide every term by x and just read off the coefficients — 2/3 and 2 come out in seconds.
notes: These are oral questions. Not because they are easy, but because the whole method is one line: divide the numerator by x, divide the denominator by x, and read what each piece becomes.
Every sin(kx)/x goes to k. Every tan(kx)/x goes to k. So once you have divided by x, the question is just numbers. The coefficient is the answer — nothing else is left to do.
In the first one the top gives 2 and the bottom gives 3, so the answer is 2/3. In the second one the top gives 5 − 3 and the bottom gives 1, so the answer is 2.
It is tempting to start multiplying things out when the second one comes up. Don't. The moment you see sines and tans in a ratio with x → 0, your hand should go straight to dividing by x.

quickChecks.q: lim x→0 (sin 7x)/(tan 2x)
steps: 1. Divide top and bottom by x.
2. sin 7x / x → 7 and tan 2x / x → 2.
3. Limit = 7/2.

quickChecks.q: lim x→0 (tan 4x + sin 2x)/(sin 3x)
steps: 1. Divide every term by x.
2. tan 4x / x → 4, sin 2x / x → 2, sin 3x / x → 3.

quickChecks.q: lim x→0 (sin 9x − sin 4x)/(tan 5x)
steps: 1. Divide every term by x.
2. sin 9x / x → 9, sin 4x / x → 4, tan 5x / x → 5.

concepts.title: How the trigonometric-limit toolkit fits together
concepts.oneLine: Everything in this chapter so far is one line — sin of something over that same something goes to 1 — and the divide-by-x shortcut is just that line used faster.
notes: Look at where the chapter started. One single statement: sin of something upon that same something, as that something goes to 0, is 1. Nothing more.
The hardest question of the three is the one that hands you the shortcut — divide top and bottom by x, read off the number sitting with each angle.

Two trigonometry identities keep showing up in these limits. There is no rule that says which identity comes when — these two are simply the ones that turn up most often, so keep them on your fingertips. Once the shortcut is in your hands, questions of this type fall in seconds.
So the toolkit is: basic result, then shortcut, then the two identities for when the expression is not yet in sin-over-same-angle shape. Now attempt two on your own, and keep them quick.

quickChecks.q: lim x → 0 of (sin 7x − sin 2x) / sin x
steps: 1. Form is 0/0, so divide numerator and denominator by x.
2. sin 7x/x → 7, sin 2x/x → 2, sin x/x → 1.

quickChecks.q: lim x → 0 of (sin 4x + sin 6x) / sin 5x
steps: 1. Divide every term by x.
2. sin 4x/x → 4, sin 6x/x → 6, sin 5x/x → 5.

quickChecks.q: lim x → 0 of sin 3x / tan 5x
steps: 1. Divide top and bottom by x.
2. sin 3x/x → 3 and tan 5x/x → 5.
3. Limit = 3/5.

concepts.title: sin of infinity, and the 0 × ∞ form
concepts.oneLine: sin(∞) is just some unknown number between −1 and 1, so sin(2^x)/2^x → 0, while 2^x·sin(2^−x) is a 0 × ∞ form that you flip into sin(θ)/θ and get 1.
notes: Start with the format, always. In sin(2^x)/2^x, as x → ∞ the top is sin(∞) and the bottom is 2^∞ = ∞. So first settle what sin(∞) even means.

You could spend a long time trying to *feel* sin(∞), but feeling will not help you in the paper. Just remember this: sine of anything lives between −1 and 1, so sin(∞) is a finite oscillating number between −1 and +1 — which exact number, nobody knows.

Now the fraction is easy. Top is some finite thing between −1 and 1 — take ½, take −½, take 0, take 0·1 — and the bottom is a huge number. Any of them divided by ∞ gives 0, so the limit is 0. It was never an indeterminate form at all.

Change it slightly to 2^x · sin(2^−x) and the story flips. Here 2^x → ∞ and 2^−x = 1/2^∞ → 0, so sin(2^−x) → sin(0) type, and you get a genuine 0 × ∞ form. Push the 2^x down as 2^−x and it becomes sin(2^−x)/2^−x — sine of something upon the same something, with that something going to 0. Limit is 1. sin(something)/same something is 1 only when the something tends to 0 — that condition is the whole question.

quickChecks.q: Find lim x→∞ x · sin(1/x)
steps: 1. x → ∞ and 1/x → 0, so the form is ∞ × 0 — indeterminate.
2. Send x into the denominator: it becomes 1/x.
3. Limit = lim x→∞ sin(1/x)/(1/x), same something on top and bottom.
4. That something is 1/x and it tends to 0, so the result applies.

quickChecks.q: Find lim x→∞ (sin x)/x
steps: 1. Top is sin(∞) — a finite oscillating number between −1 and 1.
2. Bottom is x → ∞.
3. Finite bounded value divided by a very large number → 0.
4. The sin θ/θ result does not apply, because x → ∞, not 0.

quickChecks.q: Find lim x→∞ 3^x · sin(3^−x)
steps: 1. 3^x → ∞ and 3^−x = 1/3^x → 0, so the form is ∞ × 0.
2. Put 3^x in the denominator, where it becomes 3^−x.
3. Limit = lim x→∞ sin(3^−x)/3^−x, with the something equal to 3^−x → 0.

concepts.title: Limits at infinity containing a sine
concepts.oneLine: Check the format first: sin x/x as x → ∞ is a bounded number over infinity so it is 0, while x·sin(1/x) is a 0 × ∞ that rearranges into sin(something)/same something and gives 1.
notes: Before you touch anything, read the format. In these questions sin of infinity or cos of infinity will show up, and nobody can give you a value for those. All you are allowed to say is that it is a finite number oscillating between −1 and +1.

That is enough. Take sin x/x as x → ∞. On top sits a finite number trapped between −1 and +1, and below sits infinity. Any finite number divided by infinity is 0. So the answer is 0, and you never had to find sin ∞ at all.
Now x·sin(1/x) as x → ∞. Here x → ∞ and sin(1/x) → 0, so it is the 0 × ∞ form. We convert it into the 0/0 form: leave sin(1/x) as it is on top and write that x as 1 divided by (1/x) below.
Look at what you get — sin of something over the same something. That form gives 1 only when the something is approaching 0. And 1/x does approach 0 when x → ∞. So the limit is 1.

quickChecks.q: Evaluate limit of cos x / x² as x → ∞.
steps: 1. cos ∞ has no value; it is a finite number oscillating between −1 and +1.
2. Below, x² → ∞.
3. Finite over infinity gives 0.

quickChecks.q: Evaluate limit of x·sin(2/x) as x → ∞.
steps: 1. Format: ∞ × 0, so convert to 0/0.
2. Write it as sin(2/x) ÷ (1/x). To match the angle, multiply top and bottom by 2: 2 · [sin(2/x) ÷ (2/x)].
3. The box is 2/x, and 2/x → 0 as x → ∞, so sin(2/x)/(2/x) → 1.
4. Answer = 2 × 1.

quickChecks.q: Evaluate limit of (3 + sin x)/(x + 1) as x → ∞.
steps: 1. sin x stays between −1 and +1, so 3 + sin x stays between 2 and 4 — a finite number.
2. Below, x + 1 → ∞.
3. Finite over infinity gives 0.

concepts.title: sin x/x equals 1 only when x → 0
concepts.oneLine: sin x/x goes to 1 only when the angle itself goes to 0 — anywhere else you just substitute, so at x → π/2 the value is 2/π.
notes: The standard result is sin(something)/the same something → 1, and that something must be approaching 0. Three conditions, not one. Read them off the question before you write anything.
So in the first part, sin(1/x)/(1/x) looks new, but it is not. As x → ∞, 1/x → 0, and the angle upstairs and the quantity downstairs are both 1/x. Same something, going to 0 — the limit is 1.

The next one needs an identity, and if it does not click, nothing works. sin²x − sin²y is sin(x+y)·sin(x−y). Now with x → y, the piece sin(x−y)/(x−y) has its something going to 0, so that part is 1. The leftover sin(x+y) has nothing going to 0 — you simply put x = y in it and get sin 2y.

Now the standard mistake: claiming that sin x upon x is 1 when x is going to π/2. It is not. Check the format: here the angle is going to π/2, not 0, so just substitute. sin(π/2) = 1, divide by π/2, and the answer is 2/π — a perfectly finite number, not 1.

quickChecks.q: Find the limit of sin x/x as x → π/6.
steps: 1. The angle is going to π/6, not 0, so no standard result.
2. Substitute: sin(π/6)/(π/6) = (1/2) ÷ (π/6).

quickChecks.q: Find the limit of x·sin(2/x) as x → ∞.
steps: 1. Let t = 2/x, so as x → ∞, t → 0 and x = 2/t.
2. The expression becomes (2/t)·sin t = 2 × (sin t/t).
3. Same something and it is going to 0, so sin t/t → 1.

quickChecks.q: Evaluate the limit of (sin²x − sin²y)/(x² − y²) as x → y.
steps: 1. Top: sin²x − sin²y = sin(x+y)·sin(x−y). Bottom: x² − y² = (x−y)(x+y).
2. Write it as [sin(x−y)/(x−y)] × [sin(x+y)/(x+y)].
3. First bracket: same something going to 0, so it is 1.
4. Second bracket: nothing going to 0, so put x = y to get sin 2y/(2y).
5. Limit = sin 2y/(2y).

concepts.title: When a side identity is needed
concepts.oneLine: In limits only two identities come up again and again — 1 − cos2θ = 2sin²θ and cos C − cos D — but a side identity like sin C − sin D still shows up often enough that you must know it.
notes: We have just fixed sin x/x → 1 as x → 0. Now look at what a question can throw at you at most. The angle inside is never going to be friendly on its own — it comes as a difference of two sines or two cosines, and your job is only to turn that difference into a product.

In limits, two identities earn their place permanently: 1 − cos2θ = 2sin²θ, and cos C − cos D. The first one is the one you will use the most. The second one is slightly more important than it looks, because it appears in exactly the kind of question we did a moment ago, and once you convert it into a product, every factor becomes a sin x/x.

But do not stop at those two. Sometimes the numerator is sin C − sin D, and no amount of squeezing 1 − cos2θ will help you. Apply sin C − sin D = 2 cos((C+D)/2) sin((C−D)/2), send the sine part to sin x/x = 1, and the cosine part just takes the value at 0. That is how you land on a clean answer like 2 cos of something.
Such questions are fewer — but fewer does not mean zero. So keep the side identities in your pocket. You will not use them every day; the day you need one, there is no substitute for it.

quickChecks.q: Find the limit of (sin 3x − sin x)/x as x → 0.
steps: 1. Numerator is a difference of sines, so use sin C − sin D = 2 cos((C+D)/2) sin((C−D)/2) with C = 3x, D = x.
2. This gives 2 cos(2x) sin(x).
3. So the expression is 2 cos(2x) · (sin x/x).
4. As x → 0, sin x/x → 1 and cos 2x → 1.

quickChecks.q: Find the limit of (cos x − cos 3x)/x² as x → 0.
steps: 1. Use cos C − cos D = 2 sin((C+D)/2) sin((D−C)/2) with C = x, D = 3x.
2. This gives 2 sin(2x) sin(x).
3. So the expression is 2 · sin2x · sinx / x² = 2 · (sin2x/2x) · 2 · (sinx/x).
4. Each sine ratio → 1, leaving 2 · 2.

quickChecks.q: Find the limit of (1 − cos 2x)/x² as x → 0.
steps: 1. Use 1 − cos2θ = 2sin²θ with θ = x, so the numerator is 2 sin²x.
2. The expression becomes 2 · (sin x/x)².
3. As x → 0, sin x/x → 1.

concepts.title: The classic (tan x − sin x)/x³
concepts.oneLine: Turn tan into sin/cos, pull sin x out, replace 1 − cos x by 2sin²(x/2), and (tan x − sin x)/x³ gives ½.
notes: Look at (tan x − sin x)/x³ as x → 0. Top is 0, bottom is 0. And dividing by x once does not save you — you get 0/0 again. So direct work is dead here.

The moment tan, cot, sec or cosec sits inside a limit, convert it into sin and cos. Write tan x as sin x/cos x. Now the top is sin x/cos x − sin x, and sin x is common. Pull it out: sin x (1/cos x − 1). Take the LCM inside the bracket and the whole thing becomes sin x (1 − cos x) / (x³ cos x).
Now notice who the villain is. Cos is never the villain — at x → 0, cos x is simply 1, it never creates a 0/0. The problem is always 1 − cos x, and the cure is always 1 − cos x = 2sin²(x/2).
Put that in and split the x³ as x · x². sin x/x → 1, and sin²(x/2)/x² → (½)² = ¼. Multiply with the 2 in front: 2 × 1 × ¼ = ½.

quickChecks.q: Evaluate lim x→0 (1 − cos x)/x²
steps: 1. 0/0 form, and the villain is 1 − cos x.
2. Replace: 1 − cos x = 2sin²(x/2), so the limit is 2 sin²(x/2)/x².
3. sin(x/2)/x → ½, so sin²(x/2)/x² → ¼.

quickChecks.q: Evaluate lim x→0 (sin x − sin x cos x)/x³
steps: 1. Take sin x common on top: sin x (1 − cos x).
2. Replace 1 − cos x = 2sin²(x/2): limit is 2 · sin x · sin²(x/2)/x³.
3. Split x³ = x · x²: 2 · (sin x/x) · (sin²(x/2)/x²) = 2 × 1 × ¼.
4. Answer ½.

quickChecks.q: Evaluate lim x→0 (tan 2x − sin 2x)/x³
steps: 1. Convert tan 2x to sin 2x/cos 2x and take sin 2x common: sin 2x (1 − cos 2x)/(x³ cos 2x).
2. Here the angle is 2x, so 1 − cos 2x = 2sin²x.
3. Limit becomes 2 · (sin 2x/x) · (sin²x/x²) · (1/cos 2x).
4. sin 2x/x → 2, sin²x/x² → 1, 1/cos 2x → 1.

concepts.title: Subjective IIT question with tan 2θ
concepts.oneLine: For (x·tan2x − 2x·tanx)/(1 − cos2x)², turn tan2x into 2tanx/(1 − tan²x) so the top collapses to 2tan³x, write (1 − cos2x)² as 4sin⁴x, divide both sides by x⁴ and read off 1/2.
notes: Start by reading the question for what it is willing to give you. On top, every term carries an x, so pull it out: x(tan 2x − 2tan x). Below, you have a (1 − cos 2x)², and 1 − cos 2θ is always 2sin²θ, so that bracket becomes (2sin²x)² = 4sin⁴x.

Now the only ugly piece left is tan 2x − 2tan x. Don't drag the whole limit down the page while you fix one bracket — do that manipulation in a side box and bring back only the answer. Put tan 2x = 2tan x/(1 − tan²x), take 2tan x common, and you get 2tan³x/(1 − tan²x).

So the whole thing is x · 2tan³x divided by (1 − tan²x) · 4sin⁴x. Count powers: x times tan³x is x⁴ on top, sin⁴x is x⁴ below. Both sides are degree 4, so divide numerator and denominator by x⁴ and every x disappears.
Top becomes 2(tan x/x)³ → 2. Bottom becomes 4(sin x/x)⁴(1 − tan²x) → 4·1·1 = 4. Answer 1/2. The trigonometry is the whole battle here; the limit part is one line.

quickChecks.q: Find the limit as x → 0 of (tan 2x − 2tan x)/x³.
steps: 1. tan 2x − 2tan x = 2tan³x/(1 − tan²x).
2. Divide by x³: 2(tan x/x)³/(1 − tan²x).

quickChecks.q: Find the limit as x → 0 of (1 − cos 2x)²/x⁴.
steps: 1. 1 − cos 2x = 2sin²x, so (1 − cos 2x)² = 4sin⁴x.
2. Divide by x⁴: 4(sin x/x)⁴ → 4·1.

quickChecks.q: Find the limit as x → 0 of (x·tan 2x − 2x·tan x)/(1 − cos 4x)².
steps: 1. Numerator = x(tan 2x − 2tan x) = 2x·tan³x/(1 − tan²x).
2. Denominator: 1 − cos 4x = 2sin²2x, so (1 − cos 4x)² = 4sin⁴2x.
3. Divide top and bottom by x⁴: top → 2(tan x/x)³ → 2; bottom → 4(sin 2x/2x)⁴·2⁴ → 4·16 = 64.

concepts.title: Two harder manipulations at π/2 and π/6
concepts.oneLine: Both these limits are the same one trick dressed differently: force the question into sin(something)/(same something) with that something going to 0, and the constant left outside is your answer.
notes: First, always check the form. Put the value the limit is going to — π/2 in the first one, π/6 in the second — and you will see 0/0 both times. Only then do you start manipulating.

Now the two conditions for using sin θ/θ. One: there must be a sine on top. Two: the angle inside that sine must approach 0. Turning cos into sine is a joke — cos x = sin(π/2 − x) — and look what that does: as x → π/2, the angle (π/2 − x) → 0. Condition two clears itself.

The angle inside the sine and the thing below it must be exactly the same bracket — not similar, the same. So bend the denominator to show it: π − 2x is just 2(π/2 − x). Take the 2 out, square it, and the 4 comes outside.

In the second question the top is a sin x + b cos x. Pull out √(a² + b²) and the bracket becomes a single sine. Whatever constant is left standing outside after the sin θ/θ goes to 1 — that is your answer.

quickChecks.q: lim x→π/4 of (sin x − cos x)/(x − π/4)
steps: 1. Form check: sin π/4 − cos π/4 = 1/√2 − 1/√2 = 0, and the bottom is 0. So 0/0.
2. Here a = 1, b = −1, so √(a² + b²) = √2.
3. sin x − cos x = √2·[(1/√2) sin x − (1/√2) cos x] = √2·[sin x cos π/4 − cos x sin π/4] = √2 sin(x − π/4).
4. Limit = √2 · lim sin(x − π/4)/(x − π/4), and the angle → 0, so that part is 1.

quickChecks.q: lim x→π/3 of (sin x − √3 cos x)/(x − π/3)
steps: 1. Form check: sin π/3 − √3 cos π/3 = √3/2 − √3·(½) = √3/2 − √3/2 = 0, bottom is 0. So 0/0.
3. sin x − √3 cos x = 2·[(½) sin x − (√3/2) cos x] = 2·[sin x cos π/3 − cos x sin π/3] = 2 sin(x − π/3).
4. Limit = 2 · lim sin(x − π/3)/(x − π/3) = 2 · 1.

quickChecks.q: lim x→π of (1 + cos x)/(π − x)²
steps: 1. Form check: 1 + cos π = 1 − 1 = 0, and (π − π)² = 0. So 0/0.
2. Use 1 + cos θ = 2cos²(θ/2): the top is 2cos²(x/2).
3. Turn cos into sin: cos(x/2) = sin(π/2 − x/2) = sin((π − x)/2). So the top is 2·[sin((π − x)/2)]², and as x → π that angle → 0.
4. Match the bottom: (π − x)² = [2·(π − x)/2]² = 4·[(π − x)/2]².

concepts.title: Substituting x = a ± h to reach h → 0
concepts.oneLine: When nothing clicks at x → a, put x = a + h or x = a − h so that h → 0: plus h gives the right-hand limit, minus h gives the left-hand limit, and if the two agree the limit exists.
notes: Suppose the question says: find the limit of f(x) as x → a. You stare at it and nothing clicks. No factorisation, no neat conversion into a standard form. In that moment one thing always works: replace x by a + h, or by a − h, so that now h → 0.

Understand what you have actually done. Putting a + h means you are walking into a from the bigger side, so you are computing the right-hand limit. Putting a − h means you are walking in from the smaller side, so that is the left-hand limit.

And in most questions the limit does exist. When it exists, the right-hand limit and the left-hand limit are equal, and that common value is what we call the limit. So either substitution hands you the answer.

Why is this such a relief? Because h → 0 can never trouble you — every standard limit result in use here is built for something going to 0. x → π/2 can trouble you. x → π/6 can trouble you. h → 0 cannot. The only price is length: the calculation grows, so a clean manipulation is better when one is available. Keep this in your pocket as the fallback.

quickChecks.q: The limit is as x → π/2 and nothing is clicking. Write the substitution for the right-hand limit, and say what the new variable approaches.
steps: 1. Bigger side of π/2 means plus h.
2. Put x = π/2 + h at every place in the expression.
quickChecks.answer: x = π/2 + h, with h → 0. (For the left-hand limit it would be x = π/2 − h, again with h → 0.)

quickChecks.q: Evaluate the limit of (x² − 4)/(x − 2) as x → 2 by substitution, from both sides.
steps: 1. Right side: put x = 2 + h. Numerator = (2 + h)² − 4 = 4 + 4h + h² − 4 = 4h + h². Denominator = h.
2. (4h + h²)/h = 4 + h, and as h → 0 this gives 4.
3. Left side: put x = 2 − h. Numerator = (2 − h)² − 4 = 4 − 4h + h² − 4 = −4h + h². Denominator = −h.
4. (−4h + h²)/(−h) = 4 − h, and as h → 0 this gives 4.
5. Right-hand limit = left-hand limit = 4.

quickChecks.q: Check whether the limit of |x|/x as x → 0 exists, using 0 + h and 0 − h.
steps: 1. Right side: put x = 0 + h with h > 0, so |h|/h = h/h = 1. Right-hand limit = 1.
2. Left side: put x = 0 − h with h > 0, so |−h|/(−h) = h/(−h) = −1. Left-hand limit = −1.
quickChecks.answer: The limit does not exist — and this is exactly the kind of question where only doing both sides saves you.

concepts.title: The π/2 ± h substitution in action
concepts.oneLine: At x → π/2 put x = π/2 ± h, turn (1 + cos2x)/sin2x into 2sin²h/sin2h, divide top and bottom by h once, and both sides give 0.
notes: Here is the question: find the limit of (1 + cos2x)/sin2x as x → π/2. Put x straight in and you get 1 + cos π over sin π, which is 0/0. Nothing to read there.
So shift the point. For the left side write x = π/2 − h, for the right side x = π/2 + h. Now h → 0, and h → 0 is the only place where all these standard formulas actually live.

Convert the angle carefully. 2x becomes π − 2h on one side and π + 2h on the other. Cosine of both is −cos2h, so the top becomes 1 − cos2h = 2sin²h. The bottom is sin2h on the left side and −sin2h on the right side.

Now the finish. Many students see sin² on top and sin2h below and try to force the sinθ/θ = 1 formula in one shot. The powers do not match, so do it properly: divide the top and the bottom by h. Top gives 2 × (sinh/h) × sinh → 2 × 1 × sinh, bottom gives sin2h/h → 2. Top goes to 0, bottom sits at 2, so the value is 0. The right side is just −0, also 0. Both sides agree, so the limit is 0.

quickChecks.q: Find the limit of cos x/(π/2 − x) as x → π/2.
steps: 1. Put x = π/2 − h, so h → 0 and π/2 − x = h.
2. cos(π/2 − h) = sin h.
3. Limit = sinh/h as h → 0 = 1.

quickChecks.q: Find the limit of (1 + cos2x)/(π/2 − x)² as x → π/2.
steps: 1. Put x = π/2 − h. Then 2x = π − 2h and π/2 − x = h.
2. 1 + cos(π − 2h) = 1 − cos2h = 2sin²h.
3. Limit = 2sin²h/h² = 2 × (sinh/h)² → 2 × 1 = 2.
4. Check x = π/2 + h: top is again 2sin²h and the bottom is (−h)² = h², so the same value 2.

quickChecks.q: Find the limit of (1 − sin x)/(π/2 − x)² as x → π/2.
steps: 1. Put x = π/2 − h, so π/2 − x = h and h → 0.
2. sin(π/2 − h) = cos h, so the top is 1 − cos h = 2sin²(h/2).
4. The + h side gives the same, since (−h)² = h² and cos(−h) = cos h.

concepts.title: Greatest integer with trigonometric limits
concepts.oneLine: Near 0, sin x/x creeps up to 1 from below and tan x/x comes down to 1 from above — so a greatest integer sitting inside the limit gives 0 and 1, while one sitting outside the limit gives 1 and 1.
notes: Draw three graphs near x = 0: y = sin x, y = x, y = tan x. Close to the origin all three sit almost on top of each other, which is exactly why sin x/x and tan x/x both have limit 1.

But look at who is where. sin x is the smallest of the three, x is in the middle, tan x is the biggest. So sin x/x is small over big — it is just a shade below 1. And tan x/x is big over small — it is just a shade above 1.

Now the greatest integer is honest about that shade: [a number just below 1] is 0, and [a number just above 1] is 1. That is why the greatest integer inside the limit separates these two, even though the plain limits are identical.

Compare that with the greatest integer placed outside, on the final answer. A limit answer is never "4 plus" or "4 minus" — it is just 4. When the greatest integer is on the function, the limiting value goes into the bracket; when it is on the whole limit, you find the number first and then bracket it. In the second case there is nothing left to think about, which is why it is barely used in questions.

quickChecks.q: Find lim x→0 [tan x/x].
steps: 1. Near 0, tan x is above the line y = x, so tan x/x is just more than 1.
2. A value in (1, 2) has greatest integer 1.

quickChecks.q: Find [lim x→0 sin x/x].
steps: 1. The bracket is outside, so finish the limit first: lim x→0 sin x/x = 1.

quickChecks.q: Find lim x→0 [sin x/x] + [lim x→0 tan x/x].
steps: 1. First part: bracket inside, sin x/x is just below 1, so the bracket is 0.
2. Second part: bracket outside, lim tan x/x = 1, so [1] = 1.

concepts.title: Greatest integer questions solved
concepts.oneLine: For the greatest integer of a trig limit, never take the floor of the limit value — decide whether the expression sits just below or just above an integer, and floor that.
notes: Hold on to the two facts we built earlier. Near 0, sin x/x is slightly less than 1, and tan x/x is slightly greater than 1. That is the only ammunition you need here.

Now the greatest integer sits outside. If you first find the limit and then put the bracket on the answer, you are being careless — the limit is exactly 1, but the expression never actually reaches 1. Decide the side first, then floor it.
Reciprocals flip the side. If something is slightly greater than 1, its reciprocal is slightly less than 1, and vice versa. That one line separates [x/tan x] from [x/sin x].

When the angle does not match the denominator, fix the angle and let the number come outside. Write sin 2x/x as 2 · (sin 2x/2x), write tan 5x/x as 5 · (tan 5x/5x). Then multiply your "slightly below" or "slightly above" by that number and floor it.

quickChecks.q: lim(x→0) [tan 3x / x] = ?
steps: 1. tan 3x/x = 3 · (tan 3x/3x).
2. tan 3x/3x is slightly greater than 1.
3. Inside is slightly greater than 3, so the greatest integer is 3.

quickChecks.q: lim(x→0) [sin 4x / x] = ?
steps: 1. sin 4x/x = 4 · (sin 4x/4x).
2. sin 4x/4x is slightly less than 1.
3. Inside is slightly less than 4, so the greatest integer is 3.

quickChecks.q: lim(x→0) [3x / tan 3x] = ?
steps: 1. tan 3x/3x is slightly greater than 1.
2. 3x/tan 3x is its reciprocal, so it is slightly less than 1.
3. Greatest integer of a number just below 1 is 0.

concepts.title: Logarithmic limits: ln(1 + something)/same something
concepts.oneLine: ln(1 + something) divided by that same something tends to 1 as the something → 0, so in ln(1 + ax)/x the answer is just the coefficient a.
notes: Put x = 0 in ln(1 + x)/x. On top you get ln 1 = 0, and below you get 0. So it is a 0/0 form, and this one settles to 1.

Remember it in the same shape as the trigonometric limits: ln(1 + something) divided by that same something is 1, provided the something is approaching 0. The something does not have to be x. It can be ax, it can be −5x, it can be anything that is going to 0.
That is why the shortcut works. In ln(1 + ax)/x, the something is ax, and ax → 0 when x → 0. Below there is only x, so force an a below and an a above, and what survives is a.
So in the format ln(1 + ax)/x, the coefficient of x is the answer — exactly like in sine and cosine limits. If you see ln(1 + 3x)/x you write 3, and if you see ln(1 − 5x)/x you write −5.

quickChecks.q: Find lim x→0 ln(1 + 7x)/x
steps: 1. Standard format ln(1 + ax)/x.
2. Coefficient of x inside the bracket is 7.

quickChecks.q: Find lim x→0 ln(1 − 2x)/sin(3x)
steps: 1. Divide top and bottom by x.
3. Bottom: sin(3x)/x → 3.

quickChecks.q: Find lim x→0 [ln(1 + 4x) − ln(1 − 6x)]/x
steps: 1. Split into two fractions.
3. ln(1 − 6x)/x → −6, with a minus sign in front, so it contributes +6.

concepts.title: Base changing theorem for log limits
concepts.oneLine: The log limit formula only works in base e, so convert any other base first with log_b a = ln a / ln b — a base 3 log leaves you a clean 1/ln 3 outside.
notes: The formula lim(x→0) ln(1 + x)/x = 1 is valid only when the base is e. The moment you see log to the base 3, or base 2, or base 10, that formula has no permission to be applied.
So change the base first. Base changing theorem says log_b a = ln a / ln b. The log you have becomes a natural log divided by a plain constant.
That constant has nothing to do with x, so it simply walks out of the limit. What is left inside is the standard form you already know, worth 1, and the constant sits outside as your answer.
One more part of the same theorem, and it is a basic level thing you must know: if a log sits in the denominator, take its reciprocal and base and input interchange. That is, 1/log_b a = log_a b.

quickChecks.q: Find lim(x→0) log₅(1 + x)/x.
steps: 1. Base is 5, so convert: log₅(1 + x) = ln(1 + x)/ln 5.

quickChecks.q: Find lim(x→0) log₂(1 + 3x)/x.
steps: 1. Convert the base: log₂(1 + 3x) = ln(1 + 3x)/ln 2.
2. Limit = (1/ln 2) · lim(x→0) ln(1 + 3x)/x.
3. Make the inside and the denominator match: write it as (3/ln 2) · lim(x→0) ln(1 + 3x)/(3x), and that limit is 1.

quickChecks.q: Simplify 1/log₇2.
steps: 1. Reciprocal of a log interchanges base and input.
2. So 1/log₇2 = log₂7.

concepts.title: Log limits: forcing ln(1 + something) over the same something
concepts.oneLine: Every log limit must be forced into ln(1 + u)/u with the same u on top and bottom — divide and multiply by whatever that u is, and the limit becomes 1.
notes: Keep one picture in your head. If the numerator is ln(1 + u) and the denominator is the same u, and u → 0, the limit is 1. Nothing else is needed.

So when x is in the denominator and the log carries something else inside, you divide and multiply. Put the u you want in the denominator, and put the same u back on top as a separate factor. One part becomes 1, the other part you evaluate directly.
Two things must be true before you use it. Inside the log it has to be 1 plus something, and that something has to approach 0. If the log starts as ln(5 + x), 1 is not there yet — fix that first.

For ln(5 + x) − ln(5 − x) type numerators there are two routes, and both are correct. Take 5 common out of each log so the ln 5 terms cancel, or combine into a single log and then add 1 and subtract 1 inside. Taking the constant out is usually the quicker route, but learn the add-1-subtract-1 route too, because when the logs do not cancel it is the only one that still works.

quickChecks.q: lim x→0 ln(1 + 7x)/x
steps: 1. Inside the log it is 1 plus something, and 7x → 0.
2. Answer is the coefficient of x inside the log.

quickChecks.q: lim x→0 [ln(3 + x) − ln(3 − x)]/x
steps: 1. Take 3 common inside each log: ln 3 + ln(1 + x/3) − ln 3 − ln(1 − x/3).
2. The ln 3 terms cancel.
4. Add them.

quickChecks.q: lim x→0 ln(1 + 2x²)/sin²x
steps: 1. Divide the numerator and the denominator by x².
2. Numerator: ln(1 + 2x²)/x² → 2, since 2x² → 0.
3. Denominator: (sin x / x)² → 1.
4. Divide.

concepts.title: ln(cos 2x)/tan²3x: adding and subtracting 1 inside the log
concepts.oneLine: For ln(cos 2x)/tan²3x, write cos 2x as 1 + (cos 2x − 1) so that ln(1+u)/u becomes 1, and what is left is an old trigonometric limit that gives −2/9.
notes: First thing, always: put x = 0. cos 0 = 1, so the top is ln 1 = 0. Below, tan²0 = 0. It is 0/0, so the limit is alive and worth solving.

Inside a log the one shape worth having is 1 + something. Here it is ln(cos 2x), no 1 in sight. So write cos 2x as 1 + (cos 2x − 1). A 1 was added and a 1 taken back, so the question has not changed at all — only its shape has.

But the shape alone is not enough. The something, cos 2x − 1, must itself go to 0. Put x = 0: 1 − 1 = 0. Permission granted. Then force the same something below by multiplying and dividing by (cos 2x − 1), and that bracket becomes 1.

The log is gone. What is left is just (cos 2x − 1)/tan²3x, which is a trigonometric limit from the earlier section. Use 1 − cos 2x = 2sin²x, divide top and bottom by x², and the answer falls out as −2/9.

quickChecks.q: Find limit as x → 0 of ln(cos 3x)/x².
steps: 1. 0/0 form, so proceed. Write cos 3x = 1 + (cos 3x − 1), with cos 3x − 1 → 0.
2. Multiply and divide by (cos 3x − 1): limit = 1 × limit of (cos 3x − 1)/x².
3. cos 3x − 1 = −2sin²(3x/2), so the expression is −2sin²(3x/2)/x².
4. Divide top and bottom by x²: −2 × (3/2)² = −2 × 9/4 = −9/2.

quickChecks.q: Find limit as x → 0 of ln(cos 4x)/tan²2x.
steps: 1. 0/0 form. Write cos 4x = 1 + (cos 4x − 1), and cos 4x − 1 → 0.
2. The log bracket becomes 1, leaving limit of (cos 4x − 1)/tan²2x.
3. cos 4x − 1 = −2sin²2x, so it is −2sin²2x/tan²2x.
4. Divide top and bottom by x²: top → −2 × 2² = −8, bottom → 2² = 4.
5. So the value is −8/4 = −2.

quickChecks.q: Find limit as x → 0 of ln(cos x)/(1 − cos 3x).
steps: 1. 0/0 form. Write cos x = 1 + (cos x − 1), with cos x − 1 → 0, so the log bracket is 1.
2. Left with limit of (cos x − 1)/(1 − cos 3x) = −2sin²(x/2)/2sin²(3x/2).
3. Divide top and bottom by x²: top → −2 × (1/2)² = −1/2, bottom → 2 × (3/2)² = 9/2.

concepts.title: Quiz solutions: log limits mixed with 1 − cos x
concepts.oneLine: Turn the log into ln(1 + something) and 1 − cos θ into 2sin²(θ/2), then divide top and bottom by x² — every mixed log limit falls in two lines.
notes: These questions look scary because a log and a cosine are sitting in the same fraction. They are not. You already know the two tools: ln(1 + u)/u → 1 as u → 0, and 1 − cos θ = 2sin²(θ/2).

So the order of work never changes. First force the log into the 1 + something shape. Then kill the cosine with the half-angle identity. Now count the powers: both the top and the bottom behave like x², so divide top and bottom by x² and read off the two limits.

The first one in the set you could already do from the basics — divide top and bottom by x, the numerator gives 2, the denominator gives 1, answer 2. The next two are the same move, just one floor higher, at x² instead of x.

One small warning on the log step. When you write ln(1 + x²/3) over x², the answer is not 1. Whatever is added inside the log divided by that same thing gives 1, so what survives is the coefficient of x², which is 1/3.

quickChecks.q: Find the limit as x → 0 of ln(1 + x²/5) divided by (1 − cos x).
steps: 1. Denominator: 1 − cos x = 2sin²(x/2).
2. Divide top and bottom by x². Top: ln(1 + x²/5)/x² → 1/5.

quickChecks.q: Find the limit as x → 0 of x·ln(1 + 3x) divided by (1 − cos 2x).
steps: 1. Denominator: 1 − cos 2x = 2sin²x.
2. Divide top and bottom by x². Top: x·ln(1 + 3x)/x² = ln(1 + 3x)/x → 3.
