3. Bottom: 2 × (sin x/x)² = 2 × 1 = 2.

quickChecks.q: Find the limit as x → 0 of ln((4 + x²)/4) divided by (1 − cos(x/3)).
steps: 1. Take 4 out of the log: ln(1 + x²/4).
2. Denominator: 1 − cos(x/3) = 2sin²(x/6).
3. Divide top and bottom by x². Top → 1/4.

concepts.title: Why you cannot split a limit: the ∞ − ∞ trap
concepts.oneLine: Substitute h → 0 into the whole expression at once; splitting ln(1+2h)/h² − 2ln(1+h)/h² gives an ∞ − ∞ form and the false answer 0.
notes: Here is the wrong method, and it deserves a full page of respect, because once you see why it fails you will never make this mistake again. The tempting move is to write ln(1+2h)/h² as [ln(1+2h)/h] × (1/h), and 2ln(1+h)/h² as 2[ln(1+h)/h] × (1/h).
Then he put the limit in only the parts he liked. ln(1+2h)/h → 2, so the first piece becomes 2/h. ln(1+h)/h → 1, so the second piece becomes 2 × 1/h = 2/h. Then 2/h − 2/h = 0. Answer 0. Wrong.

When you put h → 0, you put it into the whole expression together, not into pieces you pick and choose. Look back at the worked examples: every time this came up, the substitution was done together. In that earlier question x² was divided by x² before the answer was written. Even though that one would also have worked split, the habit is what matters.

Now the conceptual reason. The first piece: ln(1+2h)/h → 2 and 1/h → ∞, so that term is going to ∞. The second piece: 2ln(1+h)/h → 2 and 1/h → ∞, so that term is also going to ∞. So the split form is ∞ − ∞ — an indeterminate form — and in an indeterminate form you cannot just cancel. If we were allowed to substitute wherever we felt like and postpone it elsewhere, every limit in the world would be easy. There is no shortcut left here except honest log manipulation.

quickChecks.q: A student writes lim(h → 0) [ln(1+3h)/h² − 3ln(1+h)/h²] = lim [3/h − 3/h] = 0. Is he right? Name the form he has created.
steps: 1. He used ln(1+3h)/h → 3, making the first term 3/h, which tends to ∞.
2. He used ln(1+h)/h → 1, making the second term 3/h, which also tends to ∞.
3. So his split expression is ∞ − ∞, an indeterminate form.
4. Cancelling inside an indeterminate form proves nothing, so 0 is not established.
quickChecks.answer: He is wrong. He has created an ∞ − ∞ form; the limit must be taken on the whole expression after combining the logs.

quickChecks.q: In lim(h → 0) [ln(1+2h)/h²], what does the single term tend to on its own, and why does that matter here?
steps: 1. Write it as [ln(1+2h)/h] × (1/h).
2. ln(1+2h)/h → 2 and 1/h → ∞, so the term tends to ∞.
3. The second term 2ln(1+h)/h² behaves the same way and also tends to ∞.
quickChecks.answer: It tends to ∞. That matters because both terms tend to ∞, so their difference is ∞ − ∞ and cannot be evaluated by cancelling.

quickChecks.q: State the one rule from this section in a single line, and say what it forces you to do before using the standard log limits.
steps: 1. The limiting value goes into the whole expression at once, never into selected pieces.
2. If substituting together gives an indeterminate form, you must rewrite the expression first.
3. Here that means combining ln(1+2h) and 2ln(1+h) into one log before any standard limit is used.
quickChecks.answer: Rule: substitute h → 0 into the whole expression together. It forces you to combine the two logs into one expression first, instead of applying standard limits term by term.

concepts.title: IIT subjective problem: [ln(1+2h) − 2ln(1+h)]/h²
concepts.quote: This one came in IIT as a subjective problem — full steps, no options to guess from. Watch how one log identity plus the add-1-subtract-1 habit finishes it in four lines.
concepts.oneLine: Merge the two logs into one, add and subtract 1 inside it, then force the denominator to become the same 'something' — the limit is −1.
notes: The wrong road is already clear to you: split the limit and you land on ∞ − ∞, and no amount of jugaad saves you after that. So there is only one road left — log manipulation. Combine the two logs into a single log first, and only then look at the limit.
Splitting h² is useless here. Notice this: if the denominator had been h instead of h², the answer would simply be 0 and we would be home. It is h² that makes the question worth asking.

There is no need to rewrite 'limit h→0' in every line. Take the numerator aside, clean it fully, and bring it back. Inside the log you must be able to see a 1 — so add 1 and subtract 1 and let the algebra do the rest.

Then the last discipline, the one most students skip. Seeing ln(1 + something) is not a reason to celebrate. First check that the something is going to 0, then force the denominator to be that exact same something, multiplying by it again to keep the balance. Whatever is left over gives you the answer.

quickChecks.q: Evaluate lim h→0 [ln(1+2h) − 2ln(1+h)]/h
steps: 1. Same numerator work: it becomes ln[1 − h²/(1+2h+h²)].
2. Force the matching denominator: the limit is 1 × lim h→0 [−h²/(1+2h+h²)]/h.
3. That is lim h→0 −h/(1+2h+h²) = 0/1.
quickChecks.answer: 0 — with only h below, the h² on top kills it. The h² denominator is what makes the original question interesting.

quickChecks.q: Evaluate lim h→0 [ln(1+3h) − 3ln(1+h)]/h²
steps: 1. Numerator = ln[(1+3h)/(1+h)³] and (1+h)³ = 1 + 3h + 3h² + h³.
2. Add 1, subtract 1: (1+3h)/(1+3h+3h²+h³) = 1 − (3h² + h³)/(1+3h+3h²+h³).
3. Force that same quantity below and multiply back; the log bracket → 1.
4. Left with lim h→0 −(3h² + h³)/[h²(1+3h+3h²+h³)] = lim h→0 −(3 + h)/(1+3h+3h²+h³) = −3/1.

quickChecks.q: Evaluate lim h→0 ln[1 + h²/(1+h)] / h²
steps: 1. The something is h²/(1+h); at h = 0 it is 0, so the standard limit is allowed.
2. Divide and multiply by h²/(1+h): the log bracket → 1.
3. Left with lim h→0 [h²/(1+h)]/h² = lim h→0 1/(1+h) = 1/1.

concepts.title: Exponential limits: (aˣ − 1)/x → ln a
concepts.oneLine: lim x→0 (aˣ − 1)/x = ln a, with base e it becomes 1, and in general (eᵘ − 1)/u → 1 whenever u → 0.
notes: Start with the basic form: limit as x → 0 of (aˣ − 1)/x. Put x = 0 and you get (1 − 1)/0, which is 0/0. The answer of this 0/0 form is ln a — that is the one formula of exponential limits.
Now the special case. Put a = e. Then limit as x → 0 of (eˣ − 1)/x = ln e = 1. Base e is the cleanest case because its log is 1.
Then generalise it. The letter x is not special. If eᵘ − 1 sits on top and the same u sits below, and u → 0, the limit is 1. Note that the −1 is not in the power; it is subtracted after.

That one line handles everything. In e³ˣ the "something" is 3x, so 3x must also appear below. If it does not, you force it there and balance it with the reciprocal outside. Same for e⁻⁵ˣ, where the something is −5x — minus sign included.

quickChecks.q: Find limit as x → 0 of (e⁷ˣ − 1)/x.
steps: 1. Power is 7x, so 7x must sit below.
3. Bracket → 1, answer is 1 ÷ (1/7).

quickChecks.q: Find limit as x → 0 of (5ˣ − 1)/x.
steps: 1. Basic form with a = 5, denominator is already x.
2. Apply (aˣ − 1)/x → ln a.

quickChecks.q: Find limit as x → 0 of (e⁻²ˣ − 1)/x.
steps: 1. The something is −2x, keep the sign.
3. Bracket → 1, answer is 1 ÷ (−1/2).

concepts.title: Exponential limit problems: common base, sin² and factorisation
concepts.oneLine: Force the standard form: take bˣ common to make (a/b)ˣ − 1, give every e^u − 1 and ln(1 + u) exactly the same u below it, and factorise aˣbˣ − aˣ − bˣ + 1 into (aˣ − 1)(bˣ − 1) so the answer is ln a · ln b.
notes: Every exponential limit wants one shape: (λˣ − 1)/x → ln λ. So with (aˣ − bˣ)/x there is no need to go hunting for some plus-1-minus-1 trick. Take bˣ common and force the 1 into place: bˣ · ((a/b)ˣ − 1)/x. As x → 0, bˣ → b⁰ = 1, and the new base can be anything you like — 50, 2/3, 10/7 — the answer is simply ln(a/b).

The same demand runs through e to the power u minus 1 and through ln(1 + u). Each one becomes 1 only when the exact same u is sitting below it. So in (e to the power sin²3x − 1)/x², write sin²3x below it, write sin²3x on top as well so the question stays the same, and the leftover sin²3x/x² gives 9.

In a product question, do this block by block. Ask each block what it needs below it, give it exactly that, then balance by writing the same thing back on top. One block becomes 1, the next block becomes 1, and all that survives is a ratio of sines you can finish in your head.

And one question on that slide is barely a limit question at all. aˣbˣ − aˣ − bˣ + 1 factorises into (aˣ − 1)(bˣ − 1). Split the x² as x · x, and each bracket gives its own log: ln a · ln b. Two logs in a product — stop right there, nothing further is possible.

quickChecks.q: Find the limit as x → 0 of (5ˣ − 3ˣ)/x.
steps: 1. Take 3ˣ common: 3ˣ · ((5/3)ˣ − 1)/x.

quickChecks.q: Find the limit as x → 0 of (e to the power sin²2x − 1)/x².
steps: 1. The something is sin²2x, so write sin²2x above and below.
2. [(e to the power sin²2x − 1)/sin²2x] → 1, since sin2x → 0.
3. sin²2x/x² → 2² = 4.

quickChecks.q: Find the limit as x → 0 of (2ˣ3ˣ − 2ˣ − 3ˣ + 1)/x².
steps: 2. Split x² as x · x: [(2ˣ − 1)/x] × [(3ˣ − 1)/x].
3. The limits are ln2 and ln3.

concepts.title: (e^{cos 2x} − e)/tan²3x: taking e common first
concepts.oneLine: If the numerator is not already e^something − 1, pull the constant e out first, then force the standard form and finish with trigonometric limits.
notes: In exponential limits nothing much can go wrong. Every single question wants the same shape on top: e^something − 1, with that something going to 0. That is the whole concept.

So when (e^αx − e^βx)/x shows up, there is nothing to think about. I take e^βx common, because I need a 1 sitting next to it. What is left is e^(α−β)x − 1 over x, and the answer is α − β. This one is an oral question. The same move works for (3^x − 2^x)/x: take 2^x common and you get ln(3/2).

Now the real question: when the second term is a plain constant like e, that constant is what you take common. In (e^cos 2x − e)/tan²3x, pull out e and the top becomes e^(cos 2x − 1) − 1. Check the power: at x = 0, cos 0 − 1 = 0. The power is approaching 0, so now you can use the standard limit.

After that it is the old trigonometry logic. Divide the power cos 2x − 1 out, write it as −2sin²x, divide top and bottom by x², and the sin and tan limits do the rest. The e you took out just waits outside and walks into the final answer.

quickChecks.q: Find the limit as x → 0 of (e^3x − e^5x)/x.
steps: 1. Take e^3x common: e^3x (1 − e^2x)/x, or take e^5x common — either way the form is α − β with α = 3, β = 5.
2. Using the result directly: 3 − 5.

quickChecks.q: Find the limit as x → 0 of (e^cos x − e)/x².
steps: 1. Take e common: e (e^(cos x − 1) − 1)/x².
2. The power cos x − 1 → 0, so multiply and divide by (cos x − 1); that bracket becomes 1.
3. Left with e (cos x − 1)/x². Write cos x − 1 = −2sin²(x/2), so it is e × (−2sin²(x/2))/x².

quickChecks.q: Find the limit as x → 0 of (5^x − 3^x)/x.
steps: 1. Take 3^x common: 3^x ((5/3)^x − 1)/x.
2. 3^x → 1 and (a^x − 1)/x → ln a with a = 5/3.

concepts.title: The 1^∞ form: λ = lim (base − 1) × power, answer e^λ
concepts.oneLine: For a 1^∞ limit, find λ = lim (base − 1) × power, and the answer is e^λ.
notes: You already know 0/0, ∞/∞, ∞ − ∞ and 0 × ∞. The one that gets left out is 1^∞. Its shape is easy to spot: variable in the base, variable in the power. Take the limit of the base on its own and it goes to 1; take the limit of the power on its own and it goes to ∞.
In that situation, find one number λ = lim (base − 1) × power, and the final answer is e^λ. That is the whole method. Nothing more.

Now look at what λ itself is. The base is approaching 1, so base − 1 is approaching 0, and the power is approaching ∞. So λ is always a 0 × ∞ form. And a 0 × ∞ you already know how to kill: bring the power down and it becomes 0/0.

So no new knowledge comes in here. Only the limits already covered — tan kx/x → k, sin kx/x → k, the 1 − cos identity. The one and only job in a 1^∞ question is to compute λ; the method for λ will always be some method you already have.

quickChecks.q: Find lim x→0 (1 + 2x²)^(cot²3x).
steps: 1. Base → 1, power → ∞, so 1^∞.
2. λ = lim 2x² · cot²3x = lim 2x² / tan²3x.
3. Divide top and bottom by x²: 2 / (tan3x/x)² = 2/3² = 2/9.

quickChecks.q: Find lim x→0 (cos 2x)^(1/x²).
steps: 1. Base → 1, power → ∞, so 1^∞.
2. λ = lim (cos 2x − 1)/x². Use cos2θ − 1 = −2sin²θ with θ = x: cos2x − 1 = −2sin²x.

quickChecks.q: Find lim x→∞ ((x² + 3)/(x² + 5x + 4))^x.
steps: 1. Base: divide top and bottom by x², it is ∞/∞ and goes to 1. Power: x → ∞. So 1^∞.
3. That is lim (−5x − 1)·x / (x² + 5x + 4) = lim (−5x² − x)/(x² + 5x + 4).
4. Divide top and bottom by x²: λ = −5.

concepts.title: Three 1^∞ problems solved
concepts.oneLine: For a 1^∞ limit with a rational base, take LCM in (base − 1), multiply by the power, solve that ∞/∞ by comparing coefficients of x — that value is λ, and the answer is e^λ.
notes: Look at the base and the power separately first. Here the base (x+3)/(x+1) goes to 1 as x → ∞, and the power x+2 goes to ∞. That is 1^∞, so the only thing I need is λ = lim (base − 1) × power, and the answer is e^λ.

While computing λ, do not carry the e along in every line — drop it, finish the limit, and raise e to the answer at the very end. Solutions that write the e in every step end up looking terrible for no gain. Keep the working clean.

Now (base − 1) with a rational base is just LCM work. (x+3)/(x+1) − 1 gives (x+3−x−1)/(x+1) = 2/(x+1). Multiply this by the power x+2 and you get (2x+4)/(x+1), which is an ∞/∞ form. There is no new method for this — it is the old ∞/∞: same degree on top and bottom, so take the coefficients of x. That gives λ = 2, so the answer is e².

The problem just before this one worked the same way, only bigger. There the x² on top cancelled with the x² below, one x survived, and multiplying by the power threw the whole thing into ∞/∞ once more. That leftover limit came out as −7, so the final answer was e^−7. Same two moves every time: (base − 1) × power, then the plain ∞/∞ limit.

steps: 1. Form is 1^∞, so find λ = lim ((x+5)/(x+2) − 1) × x.
3. Multiply by x: 3x/(x+2) → 3/1 = 3, so λ = 3.

concepts.title: Revision: the seven indeterminate forms and the technique for each
concepts.oneLine: Seven indeterminate forms, and for each one a fixed tool: factorise or rationalise for 0/0, divide by the biggest infinity for ∞/∞, LCM for ∞ − ∞, the λ formula for 1^∞, and convert 0 × ∞ into one of the first two.
notes: Count them up. 0/0, ∞/∞, 0 × ∞, ∞ − ∞ and 1^∞ are finished. That is five of the seven forms.

Naming the form is the whole game: the moment you write the form, the technique is fixed. For 0/0, factorise or rationalise. For ∞/∞, divide by the biggest infinity — there is no second technique there. For ∞ − ∞, take the LCM and the subtraction turns into a single fraction. For 1^∞ there is that extra formula with λ, and the answer comes out as e^λ.
0 × ∞ is the odd one. It has no technique of its own. Either the 0 comes down into the denominator or the ∞ comes down, and the form becomes 0/0 or ∞/∞ — then you use the tool you already know.

The remaining two are 0⁰ and ∞⁰. Both are negligible for your exam. The honest method for them is the L'Hôpital rule, which comes later anyway because continuity needs it, so these two are listed here only for completeness.

One more thing to notice before expansions. Every formula-based limit you learnt — the trig limits, the log limits, the exponential limits — is a 0/0 question underneath. The expansions we start next are also just another way of killing 0/0.

quickChecks.q: Name the form and the technique, then find lim x→∞ (3x² + 5x)/(2x² − 7).
steps: 1. Top → ∞ and bottom → ∞, so the form is ∞/∞.
2. Technique: divide by the biggest infinity, which is x².
4. As x → ∞, 5/x → 0 and 7/x² → 0, so the value is 3/2.

quickChecks.q: Name the form and the technique, then find lim x→0 (√(1 + x) − 1)/x.
steps: 1. Put x = 0: top = √1 − 1 = 0, bottom = 0, so the form is 0/0.
2. Technique: rationalise. Multiply top and bottom by (√(1 + x) + 1).
3. Top becomes (1 + x) − 1 = x, so the expression is x / [x(√(1 + x) + 1)].
4. Cancel x: 1/(√(1 + x) + 1). Put x = 0 to get 1/2.

quickChecks.q: Name the form and the technique, then find lim x→0 (1 + 3x)^(1/x).
steps: 1. Base → 1 and power → ∞, so the form is 1^∞.
2. Technique: the λ formula. λ = limit of power × (base − 1).
4. Answer = e^λ = e³.

concepts.title: Standard expansions you must memorise
concepts.oneLine: Six expansions — sin x, cos x, tan x, eˣ, ln(1+x) and (1+x)ⁿ — are the whole toolkit for expansion-based limits, and each one carries its own range of x where it is legal.
notes: The next weapon for a 0/0 limit is expansion. The idea behind it is the Taylor series: almost any function you meet can be rewritten as a polynomial in x, and once a function is a polynomial, a 0/0 limit becomes pure cancellation.

You do not need the derivation. For JEE, only six expansions matter: sin x, cos x, tan x, eˣ, ln(1+x), and the binomial expansion of (1+x)ⁿ. Everything else written around them on that page is decoration.

Keep the binomial one with the others. Do not treat it as a separate chapter. JEE does not care that you filed it under binomial theorem — it will hand you a (1+x)^(1/3) inside a limit and expect you to open it.

Each expansion comes with a range of x on which it is valid. sin x, cos x and eˣ hold for every real x. tan x needs x between −π/2 and π/2. ln(1+x) needs −1 < x ≤ 1, and the binomial expansion needs x between −1 and 1. Right now, note all six down in your copy, in your own hand. Give it a minute and a half — once it is written by you, it stays.

quickChecks.q: Write the first three non-zero terms of the expansion of sin x.
steps: 1. The series is x − x³/3! + x⁵/5! − …
3. So the first three terms are x − x³/6 + x⁵/120.

quickChecks.q: For which values of x is the expansion of ln(1+x) valid, and what is its third term?
steps: 1. The expansion is ln(1+x) = x − x²/2 + x³/3 − x⁴/4 + …
2. It holds only for −1 < x ≤ 1.
3. Counting terms: first x, second −x²/2, third +x³/3.
quickChecks.answer: Valid for −1 < x ≤ 1; the third term is x³/3.

quickChecks.q: Write the first three terms of (1+x)^(1/2) using the binomial expansion for any index.
steps: 1. Use (1+x)ⁿ = 1 + nx + n(n−1)x²/2! + … with n = ½.
2. Second term: nx = x/2.
3. Third term: n(n−1)/2! = (½)(½ − 1)/2 = (½)(−½)/2 = −1/8, so the term is −x²/8.
4. This is valid for −1 < x < 1.

concepts.title: Remembering the expansions, and rescaling them
concepts.oneLine: Rebuild each standard expansion from three facts — odd or even, its value at x = 0, and the alternating factorial pattern — then get sin 2x, e^(−x) or ln(1 − 2x) by substituting into the standard series instead of memorising a new one.
notes: Listen to this carefully, because it is a small thing that saves you a lot of memory. For every expansion I ask only three questions: is the function odd or even, what is its value at x = 0, and do the signs alternate? Those three answers write the series for me.

sin x is odd — put −x and the minus comes out — so only odd powers can appear. sin 0 = 0, so the right side must also be 0 at x = 0, which means it starts at x, not at 1. Signs alternate, factorials sit in the denominator, and sin x is done. cos x is even, so only even powers; cos 0 = 1, so it must begin with 1; then alternate with factorials. tan x is odd and tan 0 = 0, so it starts at x with odd powers only.

Now, tan has one honest catch. The powers follow that rule, but the coefficients — x, then x³/3, then 2x⁵/15 — have no pattern. Someone will ask you the coefficient of x⁷. The answer is simple: we neither know it nor do we need to know it. The day it is needed, we will know it.

e^x has no odd-even story at all, so every power turns up, all with plus signs, and e⁰ = 1 puts the 1 at the front. ln(1 + x) has ln 1 = 0, so it also starts at x, the denominators are plain 2, 3, 4 and the signs alternate. And here is the real saving: when the question says sin 2x, e^(−x) or ln(1 − 2x), you do not learn a new mantra. Put 2x, or −x, or −2x in place of x on both sides of the standard expansion. Every bracket must be raised to the full power — (2x)³, not 2x³.

quickChecks.q: Write the first three terms of cos 3x.
steps: 3. (3x)² = 9x² so the second term is 9x²/2; (3x)⁴ = 81x⁴ so the third is 81x⁴/24 = 27x⁴/8.

quickChecks.q: Write the first three terms of e^(2x).
steps: 2. Put 2x for x: 1 + 2x + (2x)²/2! + …
3. (2x)² = 4x², and 4x²/2 = 2x².

quickChecks.q: Write the first three terms of ln(1 − x).
steps: 2. The bracket is 1 + (−x), so put −x for x: (−x) − (−x)²/2 + (−x)³/3 − …
3. That is −x − x²/2 − x³/3 — all the terms are negative.

concepts.title: Expansion limits: match the minimum power, read off the coefficient
concepts.oneLine: Every expansion limit is a polynomial over a polynomial — if the limit is non-zero, the minimum power of x upstairs equals the one downstairs, and the answer is the ratio of those two coefficients.
notes: Look at what an expansion question actually is. You expand the numerator, you expand the denominator, and what you are left with is a polynomial upon polynomial, with x → 0. Nothing more.

So do what any student does: take the smallest power of x common from the top, take the smallest power of x common from the bottom, cancel. Now put x = 0. Every term that still carries an x dies. Only the coefficient of the minimum power survives, upstairs and downstairs — and their ratio is the limit.

That gives you the full picture in one line. If the minimum power on top is bigger than the one below, the answer is 0. If it is smaller, the answer is undefined — infinite. If the limit is a non-zero finite number, which is the usual case in questions, then the minimum power of x in the numerator must equal the minimum power of x in the denominator.

Now think about what that does for you. The b, the c, the beta, the gamma — the terms sitting above the minimum power — never touched the answer. Write 1 lakh in place of b, the answer does not move. So writing those higher-power terms is a waste of time, and in the exam I do not allow you that waste.

quickChecks.q: Find lim(x→0) of (3x² + 7x⁵) / (6x² + 11x⁴).
steps: 1. Minimum power on top is 2, minimum power below is 2 — they match, so expect a non-zero answer.
2. Coefficient of x² on top is 3. Coefficient of x² below is 6.
3. Answer is 3/6.

quickChecks.q: Find lim(x→0) of (5x⁶ + 2x⁷) / (4x³ + 9x⁸).
steps: 1. Minimum power on top is 6. Minimum power below is 3.
2. The power above is bigger than the power below, so the extra x's survive on top.
3. Check it: divide by x³ to get (5x³ + 2x⁴)/(4 + 9x⁵). Put x = 0 to get 0/4.

quickChecks.q: Find lim(x→0) of (8x³ + x⁹) / (2x⁵ + 5x⁶). Does a finite answer exist?
steps: 1. Minimum power on top is 3. Minimum power below is 5.
2. The minimum power below is bigger, so after cancelling x³ the denominator still carries an x.
3. Divide by x³: (8 + x⁶)/(2x² + 5x³). Put x = 0 to get 8/0.
quickChecks.answer: No finite limit — it is undefined, the value blows up to infinity.

concepts.title: Four expansion problems done by coefficient-picking
concepts.oneLine: When two functions cannot be combined, expand each one, pick only the coefficient of the single power that matches the lowest power in the denominator, and that coefficient is the limit.
notes: Look at x cos x − sin x. You cannot take x common, you cannot take cos common, you cannot force sin and cos together. Same with e^(x²) − cos x. In chemistry language these are two non-reactive functions — mixing them is like mixing stones into water. The stones never dissolve, no matter how hard you stir.

So stop trying to simplify and start expanding. But do not write the whole expansion. If you sit writing x, x², x³, x⁴, x⁵ up to the tenth term, that is pure waste of time, and in the exam I will not allow you that waste of time.

Here is the method. Look at the denominator and note its minimum power. Then in the numerator, write only the term carrying that same power and read off its coefficient. That one coefficient is your answer. I am assuming the limit comes out non-zero and finite, and that assumption is safe for previous-year questions — a limit that comes out zero makes a poor question, and nobody sets infinity over infinity here.
For e^(x²) do not learn a new series. In your copy eˣ is 1 + x + x²/2! + … Put x² wherever x sits: e^(x²) = 1 + x² + x⁴/2! + … Now the coefficient of x² is simply 1. Look at nothing else.

quickChecks.q: Limit as x → 0 of (e^(x²) − 1 − x²)/x⁴.
steps: 1. Need the coefficient of x⁴.
3. The −1 kills the constant, the −x² kills the x² term, leaving x⁴/2!.
4. Coefficient = 1/2.

quickChecks.q: Limit as x → 0 of (sin x − x cos x)/x³.
steps: 1. Need the coefficient of x³.
2. In sin x it is −1/3! = −1/6.
3. In −x cos x: x cos x = x − x³/2!, so with the minus it gives +1/2.

quickChecks.q: Limit as x → 0 of (e^(x²) + cos x − 2)/x².
steps: 1. Constants: 1 from e^(x²), 1 from cos x, minus 2 — they cancel, so the limit is finite.
2. Need the coefficient of x².
3. From e^(x²) it is 1; from cos x it is −1/2! = −1/2.

concepts.title: When the coefficient vanishes: zero and undefined limits
concepts.oneLine: Compare the lowest surviving power upstairs with the power downstairs: bigger gives 0, equal gives the ratio of those two coefficients, smaller means no finite limit — and the setter has already made sure it is one of the first two.
notes: In every expansion limit you end up with one power of x on top and one power of x at the bottom. Only the smallest surviving power on each side matters. Everything above it dies as x → 0.

So three things can happen. If the lowest power upstairs is bigger than the power downstairs, you are left with x or x² sitting on top, and the answer is 0. If the two powers are equal, the answer is just the minimum-power coefficient upstairs divided by the one downstairs. If the lowest power upstairs is smaller than the power downstairs, the thing blows up — and nobody sets a limit whose answer is infinity.

Watch the 0 case, because students get scared of it. Suppose the denominator is x³ and you work out the coefficient of x³ upstairs and it comes out 0. That is not a mistake. It means your numerator really begins at x⁴, and x⁴ over x³ is x, which goes to 0. Answer 0, full marks.

Now flip sides and think like the person setting the paper. If he puts x³ downstairs, he must arrange the numerator so that the x and x² terms cancel completely — their coefficients must be 0 — otherwise his own question has no answer. Your job is easy; the setter's job is the headache. Which is why the rule is: trust the question, expand only up to the power you need, and stop.

quickChecks.q: The denominator is x³. Upstairs the coefficients of x, x² and x³ are all 0, and the coefficient of x⁴ is 5. Find the limit as x → 0.
steps: 1. Lowest surviving power upstairs = 4, power downstairs = 3.
2. 4 > 3, so the expression behaves like 5x⁴/x³ = 5x.

quickChecks.q: The denominator is 2x⁴. Upstairs the coefficients of x, x² and x³ are 0 and the coefficient of x⁴ is 7. Find the limit as x → 0.
steps: 1. Lowest power upstairs = 4 = power downstairs, so they match.
2. x⁴ cancels from top and bottom.
3. Limit = 7 ÷ 2.

quickChecks.q: You expand and find the lowest surviving power upstairs is x² while the denominator is x³. What does that tell you?
steps: 1. 2 < 3, so the expression behaves like 1/x near 0.
2. That has no finite value as x → 0, so the limit does not exist.
3. No setter gives such a question, so the x² coefficient upstairs must really be 0.
quickChecks.answer: No finite limit — so go back and recheck the x² coefficient; it has to cancel.

concepts.title: Finding a, b, c from a given expansion limit
concepts.oneLine: If the limit is finite, expand every term only up to the power sitting in the denominator, force all the lower-power coefficients to zero, and set the matching coefficient equal to the given limit.
notes: Look at the denominator first. If it is x², then x² is the lowest power the whole question cares about, so expand eˣ, cos x and e^{−x} only up to x². Not one term more.

Now the numerator becomes (something) + (something)x + (something)x². The limit is given as a finite number, 2. So the constant term and the x term have no choice: both of their coefficients must be exactly 0, and the coefficient of x² must be the answer, 2.

That gives three equations in a, b, c. Nothing clever after that, just solving. Same story with x³ in the denominator: expand to x³, kill the x coefficient, and equate the x³ coefficient to the limit.
One more thing. If the given limit were 0, the top coefficient would be 0 too. And it can never be ∞ here, because these expansions only live near x = 0. Don't make that complicated.

quickChecks.q: Find a and b if limit as x → 0 of (a·sin x + b·tan x)/x³ = 1/2.
steps: 1. Expand to x³: sin x = x − x³/6, tan x = x + x³/3.
2. Numerator = (a + b)x + (−a/6 + b/3)x³.
3. Finite limit, so a + b = 0, which gives b = −a.
5. Then b = 1. Check: −sin x + tan x = −(x − x³/6) + (x + x³/3) = x³/2. ✓

quickChecks.q: Find a, b, c if limit as x → 0 of (a·eˣ + b·e^{−x} + c·cos x)/x² = 2.
steps: 1. Expand to x²: eˣ = 1 + x + x²/2, e^{−x} = 1 − x + x²/2, cos x = 1 − x²/2.
2. Constant: a + b + c = 0. Coefficient of x: a − b = 0. Coefficient of x²: a/2 + b/2 − c/2 = 2.
3. From a − b = 0, a = b. So 2a + c = 0 and 2a − c = 4.
4. Add them: 4a = 4, a = 1. So b = 1 and c = −2.
5. Check: numerator = (1 + x + x²/2) + (1 − x + x²/2) − 2(1 − x²/2) = 2x². ✓

quickChecks.q: Find a and b if limit as x → 0 of (a·tan x − sin bx)/x³ = 1/2.
steps: 1. Expand to x³: a·tan x = ax + a·x³/3, sin bx = bx − b³x³/6.
2. Coefficient of x must be 0: a − b = 0, so a = b.
3. Coefficient of x³ = 1/2: a/3 + b³/6 = 1/2.
4. With a = b: b/3 + b³/6 = 1/2. Multiply by 6: 2b + b³ = 3, so b³ + 2b − 3 = 0 and b = 1.
5. So a = 1, b = 1. Check: tan x − sin x = (x + x³/3) − (x − x³/6) = x³/2. ✓

concepts.title: Expansion limits that need the binomial expansion
concepts.oneLine: When the denominator is x², expand the bracket and read off one number: the x² coefficient n(n−1)/2! times the square of the whole bracket term.
notes: First, recognition. Nobody writes a limit like this by accident. The moment you see a hand-built mixture on top — a bracket with a fractional power, or an exponential stitched to a trigonometric function with a constant added — and x² sitting in the denominator, it is an expansion question. Nature does not produce such functions; a question setter does.
Now the machinery. For (1+2x)^(1/3) nothing is multiplied out. I use the general binomial expansion: 1 + ny + n(n−1)/2! · y², where here n = 1/3 and y is the whole 2x — not just x.
So the x² coefficient is (1/3)(1/3 − 1)/2! multiplied by 2², because squaring 2x gives 4x². That single number is the answer.

Why only that number? Because the denominator is x², and the question is set so that every power below x² cancels on top. If the setter fails to cancel them, the question is simply wrong and everyone gets a bonus — so your job is only to find the x² coefficient.

quickChecks.q: Find the limit as x → 0 of [(1+3x)^(1/2) − 1 − 3x/2] ÷ x².
steps: 2. Variable part: (3x)² = 9x². So the x² term is (−1/8)(9x²) = −9x²/8.
3. The 1 and (1/2)(3x) = 3x/2 are already cancelled on top, so divide −9x²/8 by x².

quickChecks.q: Find the limit as x → 0 of [(1−x)^(1/3) − 1 + x/3] ÷ x².
steps: 1. Here y = −x and n = 1/3. Linear term: (1/3)(−x) = −x/3, which is cancelled by the +x/3 in the question.
2. Coefficient: (1/3)(1/3 − 1)/2! = −1/9. Variable part: (−x)² = x².
3. So the x² term is −x²/9, and dividing by x² gives −1/9.

quickChecks.q: Find the limit as x → 0 of [(1+4x)^(3/2) − 1 − 6x] ÷ x².
steps: 1. n = 3/2, y = 4x. Linear term: (3/2)(4x) = 6x, cancelled by the −6x on top. Good, the setting is clean.
3. Variable part: (4x)² = 16x². So the x² term is (3/8)(16x²) = 6x².
4. Divide by x²: the limit is 6.

concepts.title: L'Hôpital's rule: two limits nothing else cracks
concepts.oneLine: When a limit is 0/0 or ∞/∞, differentiate the top and the bottom separately and put the value back in — LH rule cracks limits that factorising and expansions cannot touch.
notes: Recall the funda of LH rule. If a limit is in 0/0 form or ∞/∞ form, write the derivative of the numerator on top and the derivative of the denominator below, then put the value in again.
If the answer comes, you are done. If the form is still 0/0 or ∞/∞, repeat the same process. LH rule only gives a wrong answer if you apply it to a limit that was never 0/0 or ∞/∞ in the first place.

Now why does it matter so much? Because in the first question there is simply no other good technique. x − 1 is a factor of the top and of the bottom, so yes, you can cancel it — but that means two long divisions of fifth-degree polynomials. Tell me honestly, at what level is that a waste of time in an exam.

The second one is worse. ln(1 + x) has an expansion; ln x has no expansion. So expansions are out, factorising is out, and one differentiation finishes it in a single shot. LH rule is not an alternate method — it has its own questions that no other method can do.

quickChecks.q: Evaluate lim x→1 of (x³ − 3x² + 2)/(x³ + x² − 2).
steps: 1. Put x = 1: top is 1 − 3 + 2 = 0, bottom is 1 + 1 − 2 = 0. So 0/0 form.
2. Differentiate separately: top → 3x² − 6x, bottom → 3x² + 2x.

quickChecks.q: Evaluate lim x→∞ of (ln x)/x³.
steps: 1. As x → ∞ both parts go to ∞, so it is ∞/∞ form.
2. Differentiate: top → 1/x, bottom → 3x².
3. So the limit is lim x→∞ of 1/(3x³), which is 0.

quickChecks.q: Evaluate lim x→1 of (x⁵ − 1)/(x³ − 1) using LH rule.
steps: 1. Put x = 1: top 0, bottom 0. So 0/0 form.
2. Differentiate: top → 5x⁴, bottom → 3x².

concepts.title: Quiz: four limits to do by LH rule
concepts.oneLine: Four limits on the slide — three quiz and one bonus — all of which you could expand, but every one of them is to be done by L'Hôpital's rule.
notes: Three of these are quiz questions with options. The fourth one is a bonus, and the bonus has no options at all. You have to produce the number yourself.

Every one of these can be done by expansion. That is not the point here. Let the answer come out of L'Hôpital's rule, because the method only becomes yours when you use it on questions you could have solved another way.

Look at the second one carefully. It is sine of something divided by that same something — the kind of limit your hand solves on its own. Even there, check the form, then differentiate the top and the bottom separately.
Take two minutes. Don't rush, don't guess the option. Finish at least three, and if a doubt comes out of the differentiation step, that is the doubt worth chasing down.

quickChecks.q: Find the limit of sin3x / x as x → 0, by the LH rule.
steps: 1. Put x = 0: sin0 / 0 = 0/0, so the rule applies.
2. Differentiate top and bottom separately: 3cos3x / 1.
3. Put x = 0: 3cos0 = 3.

quickChecks.q: Find the limit of (eˣ − 1) / x as x → 0, by the LH rule.
steps: 1. Put x = 0: (1 − 1)/0 = 0/0, so the rule applies.
2. Differentiate top and bottom separately: eˣ / 1.
3. Put x = 0: e⁰ = 1.

quickChecks.q: Find the limit of (1 − cos x) / x² as x → 0, by the LH rule.
steps: 1. Put x = 0: (1 − 1)/0 = 0/0, so the rule applies.
2. Differentiate once: sin x / 2x. At x = 0 this is again 0/0, so apply the rule a second time.
3. Differentiate again: cos x / 2. Put x = 0: 1/2.

concepts.title: Quiz solutions, and differentiating w.r.t. the right variable
concepts.oneLine: Whatever the arrow starts from is the variable and whatever it points to is a constant — differentiate only with respect to that variable, and stop LH the moment a standard limit shows up.
notes: Start with the first one, limit x → 0 of (eˣ − 1 − x)/x². Put x = 0 and you get 0/0, so LH is allowed. Differentiate top and bottom: top becomes eˣ − 1, bottom becomes 2x.

Now stop and look at what you have written. (eˣ − 1)/x is a standard limit and it is 1, so the answer is ½. Once a standard limit appears, you stop differentiating — carrying on with LH is pure waste of time.

The next two are about one habit only: reading the arrow. In x → a, x is moving and a is a fixed number, so d/dx of a³ is 0 and d/dx of sin a is 0. In α → β it is exactly the same story with different letters — α is the variable, β is the constant, so sin²β differentiates to 0, not to something with a cos in it. That single confusion is what spoils the third answer.
And the bonus, (x − sin x)/x³ = 1/6, you can finish either way: LH twice, or LH once and then 1 − cos x = 2 sin²(x/2). Both reach the same place, so pick whichever is faster in your hand.

quickChecks.q: Find limit x → a of (x² − a²)/(cos x − cos a).
steps: 1. 0/0 form at x = a, so LH rule applies. x is the variable, a is a constant.
2. Top: derivative of x² − a² is 2x. Bottom: derivative of cos x − cos a is −sin x.
3. Put x = a: 2a/(−sin a).

quickChecks.q: Find limit x → 0 of (tan x − x)/x³.
steps: 1. 0/0 form. LH once: top sec²x − 1, bottom 3x².
2. sec²x − 1 = tan²x, so the limit is tan²x/(3x²).
3. (tan x)/x → 1, so this is (1/3) × 1 × 1.

quickChecks.q: Find limit x → 0 of (e²ˣ − 1 − 2x)/x².
steps: 1. 0/0 form. LH once: top 2e²ˣ − 2, bottom 2x.
2. That is (e²ˣ − 1)/x = 2 × (e²ˣ − 1)/(2x).
3. (e²ˣ − 1)/(2x) → 1, so the value is 2. Check with expansion: coefficient of x² in e²ˣ is 4/2 = 2.

concepts.title: Continuity at a point: LHL = RHL = f(a)
concepts.oneLine: A function is continuous at x = a only when the left hand limit, the right hand limit and f(a) are all equal and all finite — any one of them missing or different makes it discontinuous.
notes: Continuity is a direct application of limits. Nothing new to learn, only one condition to check. One test first: if a graph is continuous at a point, you did not have to pick up your pen to draw it through that point. Pen stays on the paper, graph is continuous there.

Now the written version. Look at x = a on a smooth graph. Go a little to the left of a, the graph approaches b. Go a little to the right of a, the graph again approaches b. And exactly at a, the value is also b. So left hand limit = right hand limit = value of the function. That is continuity at x = a.

For continuity at x = a, all three — LHL, RHL and f(a) — must be equal, and all three must be some finite number. If even one of them is different, or one of them is undefined, the graph is discontinuous at that point.
Finding the limits is work you already know. The value of the function needs no brain at all — if I ask for the value at exactly x = a, you simply put a into the function. That is it.

quickChecks.q: A graph approaches 5 from the left of x = 2, approaches 5 from the right of x = 2, and has a solid point at (2, 5). Continuous at x = 2?
steps: 2. All three equal and finite.

quickChecks.q: At x = 3 there is a hollow circle at height 7, and the graph on both sides runs into it. No other dot is drawn at x = 3. Continuous at x = 3?
steps: 1. LHL = 7 and RHL = 7, so the limit exists.
2. Hollow circle with no solid dot means f(3) is not defined.
3. Third box is empty, so the three are not equal.
quickChecks.answer: No — discontinuous at x = 3 because f(3) is not defined

quickChecks.q: At x = 1, LHL = 4, f(1) = 4, and RHL = 6. Continuous at x = 1?
steps: 1. LHL = f(1) = 4, so two boxes match.
2. RHL = 6 ≠ 4, so the third does not.
quickChecks.answer: No — discontinuous at x = 1, a jump at that point

concepts.title: Continuity of piecewise-defined functions
concepts.oneLine: At any point of a piecewise function, test three things — the rule just below, the rule just above and the rule exactly at the point — and call it continuous only if all three give the same number.
notes: At a point x = a you want three numbers: f(a⁻), f(a⁺) and f(a). Nothing else.

For f(a⁻), look at the definition that is valid for x slightly smaller than a, and take its limit. For f(a⁺), take the definition valid for x slightly bigger than a. For f(a), find the line of the definition that holds at exactly x = a and put x = a into it — no thinking needed there.
If these three are equal, the function is continuous at that point. If even one of them misbehaves, it is discontinuous at that point. That is the whole story.
In the two questions here, none of the limits were indeterminate forms. They were plain substitution. So the only real skill being tested was reading the function correctly.

quickChecks.q: Is f(x) = x² + 1 for x < 2, f(x) = 2x + 1 for x ≥ 2 continuous at x = 2?
steps: 1. Just below 2 the rule is x² + 1, so LHL = 2² + 1 = 5.
2. At 2 and just above, the rule is 2x + 1, so RHL = 2(2) + 1 = 5 and f(2) = 5.
3. All three equal 5.

quickChecks.q: Is f(x) = x + 5 for x ≤ 0, f(x) = x² + 2 for x > 0 continuous at x = 0?
steps: 1. Just below 0 the rule is x + 5, so LHL = 0 + 5 = 5.
2. At exactly 0 the same rule holds, so f(0) = 5.
3. Just above 0 the rule is x² + 2, so RHL = 0² + 2 = 2.
4. LHL = f(0) = 5 but RHL = 2.

quickChecks.q: For f(x) = x² for x < 1, f(x) = 1 for 1 ≤ x < 2, f(x) = x + 1 for x ≥ 2, check continuity at x = 1 and at x = 2.
steps: 1. At x = 1: LHL = 1² = 1, and since 1 ≤ x < 2 gives f(x) = 1, RHL = 1 and f(1) = 1. All three equal 1.
2. At x = 2: just below 2 the rule is 1, so LHL = 1.
3. At 2 and just above, the rule is x + 1, so RHL = 3 and f(2) = 3.
4. LHL = 1 but RHL = f(2) = 3.
quickChecks.answer: Continuous at x = 1, discontinuous at x = 2.

concepts.title: 1/x and e^(1/x) at x = 0: the LHL/RHL trap
concepts.oneLine: At x = 0, 1/x runs to +∞ from the right and −∞ from the left, so e^(1/x) blows up on one side and dies on the other — which is why (e^(1/x)−1)/(e^(1/x)+1) has RHL +1 and LHL −1.
notes: Start with the only fact you need. If x is a tiny positive number, 1/x is huge and positive, so as x → 0⁺, 1/x → +∞. If x is a tiny negative number like −0.00001, then 1/x = −100000, so as x → 0⁻, 1/x → −∞.

You can also just look at the graph of y = 1/x. Just to the right of 0 the curve shoots up to +∞, just to the left of 0 it dives down to −∞. The two sides of x = 0 behave completely differently, so at x = 0 you must always do LHL and RHL separately.

Now push this through the exponential. On the left, e^(1/x) becomes e^(−∞), and e^(−∞) = 1/e^(∞) = 1/∞ → 0. So the left side is harmless — numbers go in, a number comes out, no indeterminate form at all.

On the right, e^(1/x) becomes e^(+∞) → ∞, and (∞−1)/(∞+1) is the ∞/∞ form. The technique for ∞/∞ is always the same: divide the top and the bottom by the biggest thing, and here the biggest thing is e^(1/x) itself. After dividing, every leftover term is 1/e^(1/x) = 1/∞ → 0, and the answer falls out.

quickChecks.q: Find the LHL and RHL of f(x) = 1/(1 + e^(1/x)) at x = 0.
quickChecks.answer: LHL = 1, RHL = 0, so the limit does not exist at x = 0.

quickChecks.q: Evaluate the LHL and RHL of f(x) = (2e^(1/x) + 1)/(e^(1/x) + 3) at x = 0.
steps: 1. x → 0⁻: e^(1/x) → 0, so the value is (2·0 + 1)/(0 + 3) = 1/3. Determinate, no work needed.
2. x → 0⁺: e^(1/x) → ∞, so the form is ∞/∞. Divide top and bottom by e^(1/x): (2 + 1/e^(1/x))/(1 + 3/e^(1/x)).
3. Both 1/e^(1/x) terms → 0, so the value is (2 + 0)/(1 + 0) = 2.

quickChecks.q: If f(x) = (e^(1/x) − 1)/(e^(1/x) + 1) for x ≠ 0 and f(0) = −1, is f continuous at x = 0?
steps: 1. LHL = −1 and RHL = +1 for this function.
2. For continuity you need LHL = RHL = f(0).
3. Here LHL = f(0) = −1, but RHL = +1 ≠ −1, so the two-sided limit does not exist.
quickChecks.answer: No. f is discontinuous at x = 0; matching f(0) to the LHL alone cannot fix it.

concepts.title: Quiz: continuity with e^(1/x), greatest integer, and a bonus k
concepts.oneLine: Stop reading and attempt three continuity questions on your own: one more e^(1/x) function, one greatest-integer function, and a bonus where you must find the value of k.
notes: You have just seen what happens to 1/x and e^(1/x) at x = 0. Now put it in your own hand rather than reading it off a page. So here are two quiz questions plus one bonus — work them through before reading on.

The first quiz is one more function built on e^(1/x). The second one needs only a little knowledge of the greatest integer function — I will not even call it challenging. Then comes the bonus, and in the bonus there are no options at all: you have to produce the value of k that makes the function continuous.

For every one of these three, only three things matter: the left hand limit, the right hand limit, and the value of the function at that point. If all three are equal, the function is continuous there. If any one of them disagrees, or does not even exist, it is not. That is the whole quiz.

Do not leave the bonus blank because there is no option to pick. A wrong attempt shows where the thinking broke; a blank shows nothing. Give it three honest minutes, then come to the next part and we will solve all three together.

quickChecks.q: f(x) = e^(1/x) for x ≠ 0 and f(0) = 0. Is f continuous at x = 0?
steps: 2. RHL: as x → 0⁺, 1/x → +∞, so e^(1/x) → ∞, which is not a finite value.
3. f(0) = 0, so LHL = f(0) = 0, but the RHL does not exist finitely.
4. All three are not equal, so the test fails.
quickChecks.answer: Not continuous at x = 0, because the right hand limit is not finite.

quickChecks.q: f(x) = [x], the greatest integer function. Is f continuous at x = 2?
steps: 1. LHL: for x just below 2, say 1.9, [x] = 1, so LHL = 1.
2. RHL: for x just above 2, say 2.1, [x] = 2, so RHL = 2.
4. LHL = 1 ≠ 2 = RHL, so the two sides disagree.
quickChecks.answer: Not continuous at x = 2; there is a jump of 1 there.

quickChecks.q: f(x) = kx + 1 for x ≤ 2 and f(x) = 3x − 1 for x > 2. Find k so that f is continuous at x = 2.
steps: 1. LHL = value from the first piece at x = 2: 2k + 1. This is also f(2).
2. RHL = value from the second piece as x → 2⁺: 3(2) − 1 = 5.
3. For continuity, 2k + 1 = 5.

concepts.title: Quiz solutions: finding k, the 0/∞ form, and [x] + [−x]
concepts.oneLine: Every continuity question here is one of two things — a limit you set equal to f(a), or a function you build from both sides: k = 1 for (1 − cos4x)/8x², x/(1 + e^(1/x)) is continuous at 0, and [x] + [−x] breaks only at the integers.
notes: Start with the bonus. k is simply the value of the function at x = 0, and for continuity that value has to match the limit. So the whole question is just "find the limit" — k is whatever the limit turns out to be.

Here there is no left-hand, right-hand drama: the same expression sits on both sides of 0, so one limit settles it. Use 1 − cos θ = 2sin²(θ/2), split the square into sin2x × sin2x, and each sin2x/x goes to 2. Top 8, bottom 8, k = 1. L'Hôpital's rule gives the same 1, so take whichever is faster for you.

The second one is where the exam tries to trick you. On the right of 0, e^(1/x) blows up, so you get 0 divided by something huge. 0/∞ is not an indeterminate form — a very small number divided by a very large number is just 0. On the left, 1/x goes to −∞, so e^(1/x) dies to 0, the denominator settles at 1, and you get 0/1 = 0. Both sides 0, the function value is 0, continuous.

The last one is an old funda. Put any integer in [x] + [−x] and you get 0; put anything else and you get −1. So the limit near an integer is −1 while the value at the integer is 0 — that mismatch is the discontinuity, and it happens at integers only, nowhere else.

quickChecks.q: f(x) = (1 − cos4x)/(2x²) for x ≠ 0 and f(0) = k. Find k for continuity at x = 0.
steps: 1. k must equal the limit as x → 0.
2. 1 − cos4x = 2sin²2x, so f(x) = 2sin²2x/(2x²) = (sin2x/x)².
3. sin2x/x → 2, so the square → 4.

quickChecks.q: f(x) = x/(3 + e^(1/x)) for x ≠ 0. What must f(0) be for f to be continuous at 0?
steps: 1. As x → 0+, e^(1/x) → ∞, so the denominator → ∞ and the numerator → 0. That is 0/∞ = 0.
2. As x → 0−, e^(1/x) → 0, so the denominator → 3 and the numerator → 0, giving 0/3 = 0.
3. LHL = RHL = 0, so the value at 0 must be the same.

quickChecks.q: For f(x) = [x] + [−x], find f(−2.5) and f(−2), and say whether f is continuous at x = −2.
steps: 2. At x = −2: [−2] = −2 and [2] = 2, so the sum is 0.
3. Near −2 the function is −1 on both sides, but its value at −2 is 0, so limit ≠ value.
quickChecks.answer: f(−2.5) = −1, f(−2) = 0, and f is discontinuous at x = −2.

concepts.title: Fixing constants by continuity: cot4x/cot2x and f(π/4)
concepts.oneLine: A cot/cot ratio flips into tan and collapses to the ratio of angles, and when a function is continuous on an open interval its value at an inside point is forced to equal the limit there — found fastest by the LH rule.
notes: First the 1^∞ one. The piece on the right of 0 is e raised to cot 4x / cot 2x, and the piece on the left is a (1 + something)^(big power) shape. For continuity at 0 all three must agree: left hand limit = right hand limit = the value b at x = 0.

cot 4x / cot 2x is not 4x/2x — cot is 1/tan, so the ratio flips and becomes tan 2x / tan 4x, which tends to 2x/4x = ½. Divide top and bottom by x, use tan θ / θ → 1 on each, and only the angles survive. So the right hand limit is e^(1/2).

Now the second one. The function is given on 0 to 90 degrees, that is on (0, π/2), and it is continuous there. π/4 sits inside that interval, so f(π/4) has no freedom at all: it must equal the limit of the given expression as x → π/4.

You could put x = π/4 + h or x = π/4 − h and take h → 0 — that is the honest method, set out in detail earlier. But here the denominator differentiates to a finite number in one shot, so when the denominator's derivative is a clean finite number, go straight for the LH rule. Answer: −½.

quickChecks.q: Find the limit of cot 3x / cot 7x as x → 0.
steps: 1. Flip the cots: cot 3x / cot 7x = tan 7x / tan 3x.
2. Divide top and bottom by x: (tan 7x / 7x)·7x ÷ (tan 3x / 3x)·3x.
3. Each tan θ/θ → 1, leaving 7x/3x = 7/3.

quickChecks.q: f(x) = e^(cot 6x / cot 2x) for x > 0 and f(0) = k. If f is continuous from the right at x = 0, find k.
steps: 1. Power: cot 6x / cot 2x = tan 2x / tan 6x.
2. This tends to 2x/6x = 1/3.
3. So the right hand limit is e^(1/3), and continuity gives k = e^(1/3).
quickChecks.answer: k = e^(1/3), the cube root of e

quickChecks.q: f(x) = (1 − cot x)/(4x − π) for x ≠ π/4. If f is continuous on (0, π/2), find f(π/4).
steps: 1. At x = π/4: numerator 1 − cot(π/4) = 1 − 1 = 0, denominator 0. So 0/0.
2. LH rule: d/dx(1 − cot x) = cosec²x, d/dx(4x − π) = 4.
3. cosec(π/4) = √2, so cosec²(π/4) = 2.
4. Limit = 2/4 = ½, and continuity gives f(π/4) = ½.

concepts.title: Only the change points can break continuity
concepts.oneLine: A piecewise function can only break where its definition changes, so making the two values agree at each of those points — here π/4 and π/2 — makes it continuous on the whole interval.
notes: Look at the question we started with. The function lives on 0 to π, and its definition changes at π/4 and at π/2. Everywhere else it is one single standard formula, and a standard formula has no reason to break.

So the only places a piecewise function can be discontinuous are the points where its definition changes. At π/4 there is a chance of discontinuity. At π/2 there is a chance of discontinuity. Nowhere else.

Now the work is tiny. Equate the value from the left and the value from the right at π/4, and make both equal f(π/4) — the function is continuous at π/4. Do exactly the same at π/2 — it is continuous at π/2.

Both change points cleared means the function is continuous on all of 0 to π. That is the whole answer, in one line. Same move as the previous part, where we fixed the constant using cot4x/cot2x at π/4 — only now there are two joints instead of one.

quickChecks.q: A function on 0 to π is given by three formulas, with the definition changing at π/4 and π/2. How many points do you actually need to test for continuity?
steps: 1. Each piece is one standard formula, so it is continuous inside.
2. Discontinuity is possible only where the definition changes.
quickChecks.answer: Two — x = π/4 and x = π/2.

quickChecks.q: f(x) = 2x + k for x ≤ 2 and f(x) = x² for x > 2. Find k so that f is continuous.
steps: 1. The only change point is x = 2.
2. Left side and value at 2: 2(2) + k = 4 + k.
3. Right-hand limit: 2² = 4.
4. Equate: 4 + k = 4, so k = 0.

quickChecks.q: f(x) = sin x for 0 ≤ x < π/2 and f(x) = c for π/2 ≤ x ≤ π. Find c so that f is continuous on 0 to π.
steps: 1. The only change point is x = π/2.
2. Left-hand limit: sin(π/2) = 1.
3. Right-hand value and f(π/2) are both c.
4. Equate: c = 1.

concepts.title: Continuity of [x]·x²: define the function yourself
concepts.oneLine: For f(x) = [x]·x² on [−2, 1], write [x] as a constant on each unit interval, then test only the change points: the function breaks at x = −1 and x = 1 only.
notes: Do not get disturbed by [x]·x². Look at it as two separate things multiplied: x² is the variable part, and [x] is just a constant — provided you have fixed the interval of x first, [x] is a plain number, nothing more.
So split the domain [−2, 1] at every integer. From −2 up to −1, [x] is −2. From −1 up to 0, [x] is −1. From 0 up to 1, [x] is 0. And x = 1 sits alone at the end, where [x] is exactly 1.

From here on, f(x) = [x]·x² is not written any more. Write the actual function on each piece: −2x², then −x², then 0, and at x = 1 the value 1. Once the function is defined piece by piece, continuity is only a question of LHL, RHL and the value at the change points.

Check x = −1: from the left the piece is −2x², so LHL = −2; from the right it is −x², so RHL = −1, and f(−1) = −1. Left and right do not match, so it breaks. At x = 0 the left piece −x² gives 0, the right piece gives 0, and f(0) = 0 — perfectly continuous. At x = 1 the left piece gives 0 but f(1) = 1, so it breaks again. In JEE this defining step is the whole question; the rest is routine.

quickChecks.q: For f(x) = [x]·x on [1, 3), define f on each piece and check continuity at x = 2.
steps: 3. LHL at 2 = lim x→2⁻ (x) = 2. RHL at 2 = lim x→2⁺ (2x) = 4. f(2) = 4.
4. LHL ≠ RHL.

quickChecks.q: Is f(x) = [x]·x² continuous at x = −2 on the interval [−3, −1]?
For f(x) = [x]·x² on [−1, 1), check continuity at x = 0.
steps: 3. LHL at 0 = lim x→0⁻ (−x²) = 0. RHL at 0 = 0. f(0) = 0·0² = 0.
quickChecks.answer: Continuous at x = 0, because LHL = RHL = f(0) = 0.

concepts.title: End points: one-sided continuity
concepts.oneLine: At the left end of the domain you only check right-continuity, at the right end only left-continuity — so an end point can never confuse you.
notes: Take a graph that is defined from x = a to x = b, and nothing outside. Draw it without lifting the pen from a to b and it is continuous at every point in between, because at an interior point the left hand limit, the right hand limit and the value of the function all agree.

Now stand at x = a. There is nothing behind a, so a left hand limit at a has no meaning at all. So at the left end I only compare f(a) with the right hand limit: that is right-continuity. At x = b nothing exists in front of b, so I only compare f(b) with the left hand limit: left-continuity.

This is also why what happens outside the domain is irrelevant. If something wild is going on behind a or ahead of b, it does not matter — the drawing starts at a and finishes at b, and in between the pen never leaves the page.

Say I tell you to analyse a function from 10 to 100. You will not ask me what happened before 10 or after 100. At 10 you look at the value and at numbers slightly bigger than 10. At 100 you look at the value and at numbers slightly smaller than 100. One sided check at each end — that is the whole story.

quickChecks.q: A function is defined only on 2 ≤ x ≤ 7. Write down exactly what must be checked at x = 2 and at x = 7.
steps: 1. x = 2 is the left end: nothing exists behind 2, so no left hand limit is required.
2. Requirement at 2: right hand limit = f(2).
3. x = 7 is the right end: nothing exists ahead of 7, so no right hand limit is required.
4. Requirement at 7: left hand limit = f(7).
quickChecks.answer: Right-continuity at x = 2 and left-continuity at x = 7.

quickChecks.q: A function is defined only on 0 ≤ x ≤ 5. At x = 0, f(0) = 3 and the function approaches 3 from the right. Is it continuous at x = 0?
steps: 1. x = 0 is the left end point, so only right-continuity is tested.
2. Right hand limit at 0 = 3 and f(0) = 3, so they are equal.
3. The missing left hand limit is not a defect — those points are outside the domain.

quickChecks.q: A function is defined only on −1 ≤ x ≤ 1. The left hand limit at x = 1 is 4 but f(1) = 6. Is x = 1 a point of continuity?
steps: 1. x = 1 is the right end point, so only left-continuity is tested.
2. Left hand limit at 1 = 4 and f(1) = 6, and 4 ≠ 6.
3. The single required check fails.
quickChecks.answer: No — x = 1 is a point of discontinuity.

concepts.title: A limit doesn't need an indeterminate form
concepts.oneLine: Every continuity question is just a limit — either in a piecewise function or in one you define yourself — and a determinate form has a limit too: it is simply the value of the function.
notes: Hold on to the whole chapter so far in two lines. Either you are asked for the limit of a piecewise defined function — left hand limit, right hand limit — or you are the one who defines the function first and then takes the left hand limit and the right hand limit. There is nothing beyond these two shapes in continuity.
Now the small thing that trips people. A limit does not need an indeterminate form to exist. Everything just done was determinate form.

And in a determinate form the limit is just the value of the function. Put the value in and you are done. 0/0 and ∞/∞ are the only cases where you have to bring in a method; everywhere else substitution is the method.

Go back to the very first idea of a limit. Something like the limit of 5x + 6 as x → 1 has the answer 11. That is a limit too. Because the definition of a limit at a point is simply this: as you approach that point from a little below or a little above, what value is the function giving you? For 5x + 6 near x = 1 that value is 11, so the limit is 11. Simple thing — don't make it heavy.

quickChecks.q: Find the limit of 3x + 1 as x → 2.
steps: 1. Substitute x = 2: 3(2) + 1 = 7.
2. Finite value, so the form is determinate.
3. Limit = value of the function.

quickChecks.q: Find the limit of x² − 4 as x → 3.
steps: 1. Substitute x = 3: 3² − 4 = 9 − 4 = 5.
2. Determinate form, no method needed.
3. Limit = 5.

quickChecks.q: For f(x) = 2x + 1 for x < 1 and f(x) = 5 for x ≥ 1, find the left hand limit and the right hand limit at x = 1, and say whether f is continuous there.
steps: 1. LHL: use the x < 1 branch, 2x + 1 → 2(1) + 1 = 3.
2. RHL: use the x ≥ 1 branch, which is the constant 5, so RHL = 5.
3. f(1) = 5 from the second branch.
4. LHL = 3 ≠ RHL = 5, so the limit does not exist at x = 1 and f is discontinuous there.
5. Notice both one-sided limits were determinate — the problem is that they disagree, not that any limit was missing.
quickChecks.answer: LHL = 3, RHL = 5, f(1) = 5; not continuous at x = 1

concepts.title: Removable vs irremovable discontinuity — and why the names
concepts.oneLine: Removable means the limit at the point exists but is not equal to f(a), so one value can repair it; irremovable means the one-sided limits disagree, so no single value can.
notes: Here is the whole test in two lines. Removable discontinuity: the limit at the point exists, but it is not equal to the value of the function there. Irremovable discontinuity: the limit at the point does not exist. Nothing more.

Now the reason behind the name, because that is what makes it stick. Take f(x) = sin x / x for x ≠ 0, with f(0) = 2. Both the left-hand and the right-hand limit are 1, so the limit exists and is 1, while the value sitting at 0 is 2. One is not two, so f is discontinuous at 0.
But look how little it takes to fix. Write 1 in place of 2 at x = 0 and the function is continuous — the change is at one single point and nowhere else. That is why it is called removable.

Now the other one: f(x) = x + 3 for x < 0 and sin x / x for x ≥ 0. Left-hand limit 3, right-hand limit 1, so the limit does not exist. The tempting patch is to multiply the sin x / x piece by 3 — and at x = 0 that does close the gap. But then the value at π/6, at π/2, at 90°, everywhere has changed. You did not repair a point, you defined a brand new function. That gap cannot be removed.

quickChecks.q: f(x) = (x² − 9)/(x − 3) for x ≠ 3 and f(3) = 7. Which kind of discontinuity at x = 3, and what value repairs it?
steps: 2. So the limit as x → 3 is 3 + 3 = 6, the same from both sides, hence it exists.
3. f(3) = 7 and 7 ≠ 6, so f is discontinuous at x = 3.
4. Limit exists, so one value fixes it.

quickChecks.q: f(x) = |x| / x for x ≠ 0 and f(0) = 0. What kind of discontinuity at x = 0?
steps: 1. For x < 0, |x| = −x, so |x| / x = −1 and the left-hand limit is −1.
2. For x > 0, |x| = x, so |x| / x = 1 and the right-hand limit is 1.
3. −1 ≠ 1, so the limit at 0 does not exist.

quickChecks.q: f(x) = sin x / x for x ≠ 0 and f(0) = k. For which k is f continuous at 0, and what is the discontinuity called for every other k?
steps: 1. The limit at 0 is 1 from both sides, so it exists.
2. Continuity at 0 needs f(0) = limit, that is k = 1.
3. For any other k the limit still exists but is not equal to f(0).
quickChecks.answer: k = 1 gives continuity; for every other k it is a removable discontinuity.

concepts.title: Isolated-point and missing-point discontinuity
concepts.oneLine: Removable discontinuity splits into two: isolated point, where f(a) exists but is not the limit, and missing point, where f(a) is not defined at all.
notes: In removable discontinuity the limit at x = a always exists. That is settled. The only question left is what f(a) itself is doing.
Two things can go wrong: either f(a) is given but is not equal to the limit, or f(a) is not given at all. That is why removable has exactly two sub-types, and nothing more.

First case. The limit exists, say the curve is heading to a certain height, but f(a) has been defined separately at some other height. The function's value at a sits alone, away from the curve. This is called isolated point discontinuity — the value at a is isolated.

Now the graph, and draw it properly. At x = a put a hollow circle: that hollow circle is telling you the limit. Then put a dark circle at the height where f(a) actually is. Hollow circle = limit, dark circle = f(a). In the second case you draw only the hollow circle — there is no dark circle anywhere on x = a, because f(a) is simply missing. That one is missing point discontinuity.

quickChecks.q: At x = 2, the limit of f(x) is 5 and f(2) = 3. Name the discontinuity.
steps: 1. Limit exists at x = 2, so it is removable.
2. f(2) is given and f(2) = 3 ≠ 5.
3. f(a) given but different from the limit → isolated point.
quickChecks.answer: Isolated point discontinuity (a sub-type of removable).

quickChecks.q: At x = 1, the limit of f(x) is 4 but f(1) is not defined. Name the discontinuity.
steps: 1. Limit exists at x = 1, so it is removable.
2. f(1) is not given at all, so the value is missing.
3. Limit exists, f(a) missing → missing point.
quickChecks.answer: Missing point discontinuity (a sub-type of removable).

quickChecks.q: A graph has a hollow circle at x = a and no dark circle anywhere on x = a. Does the limit exist, and which type is it?
steps: 1. The hollow circle marks the limit, so the limit exists.
2. No dark circle on x = a means f(a) is not defined.
3. So it is removable, and the f(a)-missing case.
quickChecks.answer: The limit exists; it is missing point discontinuity.

concepts.title: Irremovable: jump and oscillating discontinuity
concepts.oneLine: If both one-sided limits exist but are unequal you have a jump discontinuity; if the one-sided limits do not exist at all, as in sin(1/x) near 0, the discontinuity is essential — and neither can be repaired by redefining one point.
notes: Take the second case. Here the limit does not exist, but not because the function is wild — because LHL and RHL both exist and are simply different numbers. Left side says one thing, right side says another.

To kill this discontinuity you would have to rewrite the value of the function at every point, not just at x = a — so you would end up with a brand new function. That is why we do not call it removable. This is a jump discontinuity.

Now the sharper case. The one-sided limits do not exist at all. Think of sin(1/x) as x approaches 0: nobody in the world can hand you a value, because the thing keeps oscillating between −1 and +1 forever, faster and faster.

So here LHL and RHL are both unknown — nothing to compare, nothing to patch. This one we call essential discontinuity. The name itself is barely worth marks; what matters is that you can look at a function and say which of the three boxes it falls into.

quickChecks.q: f(x) = |x|/x for x ≠ 0 and f(0) = 0. Classify the discontinuity at x = 0.
steps: 2. For x > 0, |x| = x, so f(x) = 1. RHL = 1.
3. Both exist, both finite, but −1 ≠ 1.

quickChecks.q: f(x) = cos(1/x) for x ≠ 0 and f(0) = 1. What type of discontinuity is at x = 0?
steps: 1. As x → 0, the angle 1/x → ∞.
2. cos of that keeps oscillating between −1 and +1 and never settles.
3. So neither LHL nor RHL exists.

quickChecks.q: For the greatest integer function f(x) = [x], classify the discontinuity at x = 2.
steps: 1. Just left of 2, the values are 1, so LHL = 1.
2. Just right of 2, the values are 2, so RHL = 2.
3. Both exist, but 1 ≠ 2, so no single value at x = 2 can join them.

concepts.title: Type 1: continuity questions that are two limits in disguise
concepts.oneLine: Continuity at x = 0 only means LHL = RHL = f(0), so a three-piece "continuity" question like this is really two limit questions wearing one coat.
notes: First, the one line to carry out of the last section. If the two-sided limit at the point exists, the discontinuity is removable; if the limit does not exist, it is irremovable. Remember nothing else, remember that.

Now the question pattern. In continuity and differentiability, Type 1 is the one where a function is given in pieces, you are told it is continuous at a point, and you are asked for the unknown constants. Continuity has no real role there. You write LHL = RHL = f(0) and you are suddenly doing two limits.

So do not stare at the definition. Go straight to the right-hand side piece, take its limit as x → 0⁺, go to the left-hand side piece, take its limit as x → 0⁻, and set both equal to the given value of f(0). Two equations, two unknowns, done.

One honest warning. If you do not know limits properly, you cannot learn them here — this is not the place to learn limits. But here is the good news for the exam: when a limit is asked through continuity, the limit is always kept easy. A limit asked directly can be brutal; a limit hiding inside a continuity question is standard.

quickChecks.q: f(x) = (1 − cos 4x)/x² for x > 0 and f(0) = k. For f to be continuous from the right at x = 0, find k.
steps: 1. 1 − cos 4x = 2sin²2x, so the expression is 2sin²2x/x².
3. Continuity needs f(0) = RHL.

quickChecks.q: f(x) = ln(1 − 3x)/x for x < 0 and f(0) = a. Find a so that f is continuous from the left at x = 0.
steps: 1. Coefficient of x inside the log is −3.
2. So the limit as x → 0⁻ is −3.
3. Set f(0) equal to that limit.

quickChecks.q: f(x) = (1 − cos mx)/sin²3x for x > 0, f(x) = ln(1 − bx)/x for x < 0, f(0) = 2. If f is continuous at x = 0, find m and b.
steps: 1. RHL: 1 − cos mx = 2sin²(mx/2); divide top and bottom by x².
2. Top → 2·(m/2)² = m²/2; bottom → (sin3x/x)² = 9. So RHL = m²/18.
3. LHL = −b.
5. −b = 2 gives b = −2; m²/18 = 2 gives m² = 36.

concepts.title: Type 2 set-up: sum of points where [x²−x+3] is discontinuous
concepts.oneLine: A hardcore-function continuity question gives you f(x) = [x² − x + 3] on a closed interval and asks for the sum of all x where f breaks — and the first move is always to graph the quadratic on that interval, never to touch the bracket.
notes: So far our continuity questions were two limits in disguise. Now I write the second type for you — the hardcore function type. Here the function itself is built to spoil your condition.

The shape is this. I give you f(x) = [x² − x + 3], and I write clearly that the bracket is the greatest integer function. Then restrict x, say x belongs to [−1, 2], so things don't run away. Then the question: find the sum of all values of x where f is discontinuous.

Read that last line properly. It is not asking how many breaks. If f breaks at three or four places, those x values have to be added up into one number. So the real work is to find every single break point, not just to prove a break exists.

And here is the plan of attack. Before you think about the bracket at all, draw the graph of the quadratic y = x² − x + 3 on [−1, 2]. The bracket only reacts to what the quadratic does. Once you can see how high and how low the quadratic goes on that interval, you know exactly which integer levels it crosses — and those crossings are the discontinuities. The next part does that graph: vertex first, then the two end values.

quickChecks.q: You are handed f(x) = [x² − x + 3], x ∈ [−1, 2], and asked for the sum of all discontinuity points. What is your very first move, and why?
steps: 1. Do not start with the greatest integer rules.
2. Graph the inside quadratic y = x² − x + 3 on [−1, 2]: find its lowest point and its values at x = −1 and x = 2.
3. That gives the complete set of values the quadratic takes, so it shows exactly which integer levels it crosses.
quickChecks.answer: Graph the quadratic on the given interval first — the integers that fall inside its range are the only places where f can jump.

quickChecks.q: For f(x) = [x² + 1] with x ∈ [0, 2], which integer levels must you chase?
steps: 1. The inside function is g(x) = x² + 1, increasing on [0, 2].
2. g(0) = 1 and g(2) = 5, so g takes every value from 1 to 5.
3. The integer levels strictly between the two end values are 2, 3 and 4.
4. Solve x² + 1 = 2, 3, 4 to get x = 1, √2, √3 — all inside [0, 2].
quickChecks.answer: The levels y = 2, 3, 4, giving the break points x = 1, √2 and √3.

quickChecks.q: For f(x) = [x² − 4x + 7] with x ∈ [1, 3], does the graph step give you any break point strictly inside the interval?
steps: 1. Inside function g(x) = x² − 4x + 7. Lowest point at x = 2, where g(2) = 4 − 8 + 7 = 3.
3. So on [1, 3] the quadratic only takes values from 3 up to 4.
4. There is no integer level strictly between 3 and 4 for the curve to cut inside the interval, so [g(x)] stays 3 throughout (1, 3).
quickChecks.answer: No — strictly inside the interval there is no jump at all. One graph killed the whole question.

concepts.title: Graphing the quadratic on [−1, 2]: vertex and end values
concepts.oneLine: For y = x² − x + 3 on [−1, 2], three numbers fix the whole graph: vertex (½, 11/4) from −b/2a and −D/4a, and the two end values f(−1) = 5, f(2) = 5.
notes: The target is [x² − x + 3] on [−1, 2]. But the bracket comes later. First comes the ordinary graph of y = x² − x + 3 on that interval, drawn correctly, because every step after this reads off that picture.

a = 1, so it opens upward. Vertex x = −b/2a, vertex y = −D/4a — those two give you the bottom of the parabola in one line. Here b = −1, so x = +½. And D = b² − 4ac = 1 − 12 = −11, so y = −(−11)/4 = 11/4. Vertex is (½, 11/4).

Now the two ends, because on a closed interval the ends decide the top. f(−1) = 1 + 1 + 3 = 5. f(2) = 4 − 2 + 3 = 5. Both 5 — and that is not luck, both −1 and 2 sit 3/2 away from x = ½, so the parabola is at the same height on both.

So on [−1, 2] the curve comes down from 5 at x = −1, bottoms out at 11/4 at x = ½, and climbs back to 5 at x = 2. Lowest value 11/4, highest value 5 — the whole graph lives between y = 11/4 and y = 5. That one fact is all the next step needs.

quickChecks.q: Find the vertex and the end values of y = x² + x + 3 on [−1, 2].
Find the range of f(x) = x² − 2x + 4 on [0, 3].
steps: 1. −b/2a = 2/2 = 1, and 1 lies inside [0, 3].
2. D = 4 − 16 = −12, so the minimum is −D/4a = 12/4 = 3.
3. f(0) = 4 and f(3) = 9 − 6 + 4 = 7, so the maximum is 7.

quickChecks.q: For f(x) = x² − 4x + 7 on [1, 4], give the lowest and highest values.
steps: 1. −b/2a = 4/2 = 2, which lies inside [1, 4].
2. D = 16 − 28 = −12, so the minimum is −D/4a = 3 at x = 2.

concepts.title: Greatest integer of the quadratic: building the step graph
concepts.oneLine: On [−1, 2] the curve x² − x + 3 falls 5 → 4 → 3 → 11/4 and climbs back 3 → 4 → 5, so its greatest integer is a staircase of flat steps 5, 4, 3, 2, 3, 4, 5 with breaks at α₁, 0, 1, α₄ and x = 2.
notes: The value of the function is one thing. Its greatest integer is another. So forget the formula for a minute and only track the levels: coming down to the vertex and going back up, which whole numbers does the curve actually pass?

It starts at f(−1) = 5. Falling, it gives 4 somewhere — call that x-value α₁. It gives 3 at x = 0, and that one is already marked, so α₂ = 0. Then it bottoms out at 11/4 = 2.75. That is 2 point something, so it never gives 2. Climbing back it gives 3 again at α₃ = 1, gives 4 again at α₄, and finishes on an exact 5 at x = 2.

Four crossings, four names. Between two neighbouring crossings the curve stays trapped between the same two integers, so the greatest integer there is one fixed number — you are only drawing a horizontal line. That is why the plain parabola was worth the effort: the step graph now costs nothing.

The only care needed is the circles. At each α the curve sits exactly on an integer, so one side gets the dark circle and the other gets the hollow one. And x = −1 and x = 2 both give exactly 5, which the steps never reach again — two isolated points, sitting alone at height 5.

quickChecks.q: For f(x) = x² − x + 3, what is [f(x)] for x strictly between 0 and 1?
steps: 1. f(0) = 3 and f(1) = 1 − 1 + 3 = 3, so the curve leaves 3 and returns to 3.
2. In between it dips to its lowest value 11/4 = 2.75 at x = ½.
3. So f(x) stays in [2.75, 3) there — at least 2, never 3.

quickChecks.q: Is the y = 2 step closed or open at x = 1? Give the reason.
steps: 1. Put x = 1 in the function: f(1) = 1 − 1 + 3 = 3.
2. [3] = 3, not 2, so x = 1 does not belong to the y = 2 step.
quickChecks.answer: Open — hollow circle at x = 1. The dark circle at x = 1 belongs to the y = 3 step that starts there.

quickChecks.q: Which integer heights does [f(x)] take on the whole of [−1, 2]?
steps: 1. Falling from 5 the steps are 5 (at the end point only), then 4, then 3, then 2 across the vertex.
2. Rising again the steps are 3, then 4, and 5 once more at x = 2.
3. So the heights used are 2, 3, 4 and 5, with 5 occurring only as the two isolated points.
quickChecks.answer: 2, 3, 4 and 5 — and 5 only at x = −1 and x = 2

concepts.title: The points of discontinuity and their sum
concepts.oneLine: Every jump of [x² − x + 3] on [−1, 2] sits at −1, α₁, 0, α₃, α₄ and 2, and sum of roots gives α₁ + α₄ = 1, α₂ = 0, α₃ = 1, so the total is 3.
notes: From the step graph we already built, the function jumps wherever x² − x + 3 crosses an integer, and it also behaves oddly at the two ends. At x = −1 and at x = 2 the quadratic is exactly 5, and 5 is an isolated value of the function — nothing near it takes the value 5. So both end points are points of discontinuity too.
That gives the full list: −1, α₁, 0, α₃, α₄ and 2. The question is designed to look hard: six points, and two of them are ugly irrational numbers. The sum needed is −1 + α₁ + 0 + α₃ + α₄ + 2.

Now ask what α₁ and α₄ actually are. Both are points where the quadratic equals 4. So they are the two roots of x² − x + 3 = 4, that is x² − x − 1 = 0. The roots themselves are not needed, only their sum, and sum of roots is 1 — done in one line.

The same idea finishes α₂ and α₃: put the quadratic equal to 3. x² − x + 3 = 3 gives x(x − 1) = 0, so x = 0 and x = 1. We already knew 0, so α₃ = 1. Add everything: −1 + 0 + 1 + 2 + (α₁ + α₄) = 2 + 1 = 3.

quickChecks.q: In the same problem, find the sum of all x in [−1, 2] where x² − x + 3 = 5.
steps: 1. x² − x + 3 = 5 gives x² − x − 2 = 0.
2. (x − 2)(x + 1) = 0, so x = −1 and x = 2 — both are the end points.
quickChecks.answer: 1 (the two points are x = −1 and x = 2)

quickChecks.q: Both points where x² − 5x + 9 equals 4 lie inside the given interval. What is their sum?
steps: 1. x² − 5x + 9 = 4 gives x² − 5x + 5 = 0.
2. Discriminant = 25 − 20 = 5 > 0, so two real roots exist.
3. Sum of roots = −(−5)/1 = 5.

quickChecks.q: Given α₁ + α₄ = 1, α₂ = 0, α₃ = 1, and that −1 and 2 are also points of discontinuity, what is the total sum?
steps: 1. Sum = −1 + α₁ + α₂ + α₃ + α₄ + 2.

concepts.title: Why greatest-integer questions are really about range
concepts.oneLine: A greatest-integer question is really a range question: find what the inside value ranges over, and each step of [x] reads off as 'integer included, next integer excluded'.
notes: Look at where the difficulty actually sat. It was never continuity — it was whether you are good with the greatest integer function. Once you can read the steps, the rest of the question falls out.

The whole step graph follows from one sentence: the integer is included, and you run up to the next integer without touching it. So from 3 included up to just before 4, y = 3. From 4 included up to just before 5, y = 4. At exactly 5, the value jumps and becomes 5.

Now use it on our interval. Between α2 and α3 the inside value stays below 3 but above 2, so there y = 2, with a hollow circle at both ends. At α2 itself and at α3 itself the value is 3 — leave those two points aside, they are separate.

This is why these points are easy to find: you do not solve anything, you read the step. Asked when a quadratic equals 50, you would have to put 50 in and solve for x. Here the integers themselves hand you the breakpoints.

quickChecks.q: x lies between 4 and 5 and is not equal to 5. What is [x]?
steps: 1. Here 4 ≤ x < 5.
2. By the rule, [x] = 4 on this whole portion.

quickChecks.q: An expression stays strictly between 3 and 4 on an interval. What is its greatest integer there?
steps: 1. The value is above 3 and below 4.
2. Everything from 3 up to just before 4 has greatest integer 3.
quickChecks.answer: 3, with hollow circles at both ends of that piece

quickChecks.q: What is [5], and which flat piece does that point belong to?
steps: 1. 5 is an exact integer, so [5] = 5.
2. The rule 5 ≤ x < 6 gives y = 5, so the point belongs to the next step up, not to y = 4.
quickChecks.answer: [5] = 5; it sits on the piece y = 5

concepts.title: Final answer 3, and why the graph was essential
concepts.oneLine: The last step is pure addition — α₁+α₄+α₂+α₃+2−1 = 3 — but every α in it came from the graph, which alone showed that the quadratic runs from 2.75 up to 5 and so touches only 3, 4 and 5.
notes: Let us close the loop. α₁ and α₄ together gave 1, α₂ came out 0 and α₃ came out 1. So the four α's add to 2, then +2 takes you to 4, and −1 brings you to 3.
That addition needs no graph at all. Everything that went into the addition needed nothing but the graph.

Think about what we actually had to know. The value is 5 at x = −1 and 5 again at x = 2, and the curve never drops below 2.75. From that the values of the function live between 2.75 and 5, so the only integers the curve ever touches on this interval are 3, 4 and 5. A greatest-integer question on a quadratic is a range question: find the range, list the integers inside it, and those are your break points.

Notice the setting too. Both ends were deliberately brought to the same level, 5 at the start and 5 at the end, which keeps the counting clean. And had the curve dipped lower — say below 2 — more integers would have entered and there would have been more values to take. The graph is what tells you that, nothing else does.
