4. As x → 0, π sin²x → 0, so the first factor → 1, and sin²x/x² → 1.
5. So the limit is 1 · π · 1 = π.

marking.step: Replace cos²x = 1 − sin²x so the argument becomes π − π sin²x
Use sin(π − θ) = sin θ to rewrite the numerator as sin(π sin²x)
For small x, sin(π sin²x) ≈ π sin²x, so the quotient ≈ π (sin²x)/x²
Use ((sin x)/x)² → 1 to get the limit π

ladder.tier: L4 JEE Advanced — multi-concept, a non-obvious first move
ladder.q: For a positive integer n let f(x) = x^n sin(1/x) for x ≠ 0 and f(0) = 0. Find the smallest n for which f is differentiable at x = 0 AND f ′ is continuous at x = 0.
steps: 1. n = 1: (f(x) − f(0))/x = sin(1/x), which oscillates and has no limit as x → 0, so f is not differentiable at 0.
2. n = 2: (f(x) − f(0))/x = x sin(1/x), and |x sin(1/x)| ≤ |x| → 0, so f ′(0) = 0 and f is differentiable at 0.
3. For n = 2 and x ≠ 0, f ′(x) = 2x sin(1/x) − cos(1/x). The first term → 0 but cos(1/x) has no limit as x → 0, so f ′ has no limit at 0 and is not continuous there.
5. For n = 3 and x ≠ 0, f ′(x) = 3x² sin(1/x) − x cos(1/x), and |f ′(x)| ≤ 3x² + |x| → 0 = f ′(0), so f ′ is continuous at 0.
6. Hence the smallest such n is 3.

marking.step: From the definition, f′(0) = lim x→0 x^(n−1) sin(1/x), which exists (and is 0) exactly when n ≥ 2
For x ≠ 0 differentiate: f′(x) = n x^(n−1) sin(1/x) − x^(n−2) cos(1/x)
Continuity of f′ at 0 needs x^(n−2) cos(1/x) → 0, which forces n > 2
Take the smallest integer meeting both conditions: n = 3

ladder.tier: L4 JEE Advanced — multi-concept, a non-obvious first move
ladder.q: Let a and b be real numbers such that lim x→0 (x(1 + a cos x) − b sin x)/x³ = 1. Find a and b.
steps: 1. Expand to order x³: x(1 + a cos x) = x + a x − a x³/2 + …, and b sin x = b x − b x³/6 + ….
2. Numerator = (1 + a − b)x + (−a/2 + b/6)x³ + ….
3. For the quotient by x³ to have a finite limit, the coefficient of x must vanish: 1 + a − b = 0, so b = 1 + a.
4. Then the limit equals the x³ coefficient: −a/2 + b/6 = 1.
5. Substitute b = 1 + a: −a/2 + (1 + a)/6 = 1. Multiply by 6: −3a + 1 + a = 6, so −2a = 5 and a = −5/2.

marking.step: Expand to order x³: x cos x = x − x³/2 + …, sin x = x − x³/6 + …
Collect the numerator as (1 + a − b)x + (−a/2 + b/6)x³ + O(x⁵)
For the x³ limit to be finite the x-coefficient must vanish: 1 + a − b = 0; matching the value gives −a/2 + b/6 = 1
Solve the two equations: a = −5/2 and b = −3/2

ladder.tier: L4 JEE Advanced — multi-concept, a non-obvious first move
ladder.q: Let [t] denote the greatest integer less than or equal to t. Define f(x) = [x] + √(x − [x]) for all x ∈ ℝ. Find the number of points in the interval (−2, 2) at which f is continuous but NOT differentiable.
steps: 1. On any interval [n, n + 1) with n an integer, f(x) = n + √(x − n), which is continuous there and differentiable for x > n.
2. So the only candidate points are the integers in (−2, 2), namely −1, 0, 1.
3. Continuity at an integer n: f(n) = n + √0 = n; the right limit is n; the left limit is lim x→n⁻ ((n − 1) + √(x − (n − 1))) = (n − 1) + √1 = n. All three agree, so f is continuous at every integer.
4. Differentiability at n: the right difference quotient is (f(n + h) − f(n))/h = √h/h = 1/√h → +∞ as h → 0⁺.
5. So the right derivative does not exist (finitely) at any integer, and f is not differentiable at n = −1, 0, 1.
6. Therefore the count is 3.

marking.step: On each interval [n, n+1) write f(x) = n + √(x − n), which is smooth in the interior
At an integer n the left limit is (n − 1) + 1 = n = f(n), so f is continuous at every integer
The right derivative of √(x − n) at x = n is infinite (vertical tangent), so f is not differentiable at any integer
List the integers in (−2, 2): x = −1, 0, 1, giving 3 such points

ladder.tier: L4 JEE Advanced — multi-concept, a non-obvious first move
ladder.q: Let f(x) = (x² − 1)|x² − 3x + 2| + cos|x| for all x ∈ ℝ. Find all points at which f is not differentiable.
steps: 1. cos|x| = cos x for every real x (cosine is even), which is differentiable everywhere, so it contributes no bad points.
2. |x² − 3x + 2| = |x − 1| |x − 2|, so the only candidates are x = 1 and x = 2.
3. At x = 1: put u = x − 1. Then (x² − 1)|x − 1||x − 2| = u(u + 2) · |u| · (1 − u) for x near 1 (where |x − 2| = 2 − x = 1 − u).

4. This equals (u|u|) · (u + 2)(1 − u). The function u|u| is differentiable with derivative 2|u| (so derivative 0 at u = 0), and (u + 2)(1 − u) is a polynomial, so the product is differentiable at u = 0, i.e. at x = 1.
5. At x = 2: near 2, |x − 1| = x − 1, so the term is (x² − 1)(x − 1)|x − 2| = S(x)|x − 2| with S(2) = 3 · 1 = 3 ≠ 0.
6. Left derivative there is −S(2) = −3 and right derivative is +S(2) = +3; they differ, so f is not differentiable at x = 2.
7. Hence x = 2 is the only such point.

marking.step: Note cos|x| = cos x is differentiable on all of ℝ, so only the modulus term matters
Factor |x² − 3x + 2| = |x − 1||x − 2|, so failures can occur only at x = 1 and x = 2
At x = 1 the prefactor x² − 1 contributes its own (x − 1), so the product behaves like (x − 1)|x − 1|·(smooth) and both one-sided derivatives are 0 — differentiable
At x = 2 the prefactor is non-zero, so the sign change of |x − 2| makes the derivative jump: exactly 1 point, x = 2

ladder.tier: L5 Advanced hardest — the toughest this chapter justifies
ladder.q: Let f(x) = x² |cos(π/x)| for x ≠ 0 and f(0) = 0. Determine whether f ′(0) exists (and its value), and find all points of the interval (0, 1) at which f is not differentiable.
steps: 1. Since |cos(π/x)| ≤ 1, we have |f(x)| ≤ x² for all x, so |(f(x) − f(0))/x| ≤ |x| → 0.
2. Hence f ′(0) exists and f ′(0) = 0, even though cos(π/x) oscillates infinitely often near 0.
3. Away from 0, f is a product of x² (smooth) and |cos(π/x)|, and the absolute value can only create trouble where cos(π/x) = 0.
5. Such x lies in (0, 1) exactly when 2/(2k + 1) < 1, i.e. 2k + 1 > 2, i.e. k ≥ 1: the points 2/3, 2/5, 2/7, 2/9, … — infinitely many.
6. At x₀ = 2/(2k + 1) the zero of cos(π/x) is simple, because d/dx cos(π/x) = (π/x²) sin(π/x) and |sin(π/x₀)| = 1, so the derivative there is ±π/x₀² ≠ 0.
7. A simple zero inside an absolute value produces unequal one-sided derivatives, and the smooth factor x₀² > 0 does not cancel it; so f is not differentiable at each such x₀.
8. At every other point of (0, 1) the function cos(π/x) is non-zero, so |cos(π/x)| is smooth there and f is differentiable.
ladder.answer: f ′(0) = 0; f is not differentiable exactly at the points x = 2/(2k + 1) for k = 1, 2, 3, … (that is, 2/3, 2/5, 2/7, …), so infinitely many points of (0, 1)

marking.step: Bound the difference quotient: |f(x) − f(0)|/|x| = |x||cos(π/x)| ≤ |x| → 0, so f′(0) = 0
Away from 0, f is a product of smooth functions wherever cos(π/x) ≠ 0, so it is differentiable there
Solve cos(π/x) = 0: π/x = (2k + 1)π/2, i.e. x = 2/(2k + 1); those lying in (0, 1) are k = 1, 2, 3, … giving 2/3, 2/5, 2/7, …
At each such point cos(π/x) changes sign with non-zero derivative while x² ≠ 0, so the modulus creates a corner — infinitely many non-differentiable points in (0, 1)

ladder.q: Let f ∶ ℝ → ℝ satisfy f(x + y) = f(x)·f(y) for all real x and y, with f(0) ≠ 0 and f ′(0) = 3. Prove that f is differentiable at every real point, and find f(x).
steps: 1. First pin down f(0). Putting x = y = 0 gives f(0) = f(0)², so f(0)(f(0) − 1) = 0. Since f(0) ≠ 0, we get f(0) = 1.
2. Next note f never vanishes: f(x) = f(x/2 + x/2) = f(x/2)², so f(x) ≥ 0 for every x; and if f(a) = 0 for some a then f(0) = f(a)f(−a) = 0, contradicting f(0) = 1. So f(x) > 0 everywhere.
3. Now form the difference quotient at an arbitrary point x and use the functional equation to factor out f(x): [f(x + h) − f(x)]/h = [f(x)f(h) − f(x)]/h = f(x)·[f(h) − 1]/h.
4. Since f(0) = 1, the quotient [f(h) − 1]/h = [f(0 + h) − f(0)]/h tends to f ′(0) = 3 as h → 0.
5. Hence the limit exists at every x, so f is differentiable everywhere, and f ′(x) = 3f(x). Differentiability at the single point 0 has propagated to the whole line.
6. Solve f ′ = 3f with f positive: (f ′/f) = 3, so logₑ f(x) = 3x + c; and f(0) = 1 forces c = 0.
7. Therefore f(x) = e^(3x). A check: e^(3(x + y)) = e^(3x)e^(3y), f(0) = 1 and f ′(0) = 3.

marking.step: Put x = y = 0 to get f(0)² = f(0), and use f(0) ≠ 0 to conclude f(0) = 1
Show f(x) > 0 for every x, via f(x) = f(x/2)² and f(0) = f(a)f(−a)
Factor the difference quotient as f(x)·[f(h) − 1]/h and identify the limit as f ′(0), giving f ′(x) = 3f(x) and differentiability everywhere
Integrate f ′/f = 3 and apply f(0) = 1 to obtain f(x) = e^(3x)

ladder.tier: L5 Advanced hardest — the toughest this chapter justifies
ladder.q: Let f(x) = min{|x|, |x − 1|, |x − 3|} for x ∈ ℝ. Find every point at which f fails to be differentiable, and state how many such points there are.
steps: 1. f is the lower envelope of three V-shaped graphs with vertices at x = 0, x = 1 and x = 3. Two kinds of point can break differentiability: the vertex of whichever branch is currently the minimum, and a point where the minimum switches from one branch to another.
2. Find the switching points by equating the branches in pairs. |x| = |x − 1| at x = 1/2; |x − 1| = |x − 3| at x = 2; |x| = |x − 3| at x = 3/2.
3. Now identify which branch is least on each stretch. For x ≤ 1/2 we have |x| ≤ |x − 1| and also |x| ≤ |x − 3|, so f(x) = |x|.

4. For 1/2 ≤ x ≤ 2 we have |x − 1| ≤ |x| and |x − 1| ≤ |x − 3|, so f(x) = |x − 1|. For x ≥ 2 the least is |x − 3|, so f(x) = |x − 3|. The crossing at x = 3/2 is never active, because |x − 1| is strictly smaller than both branches there.
5. Vertices lying inside their own stretch: x = 0 inside (−∞, 1/2], x = 1 inside [1/2, 2], and x = 3 inside [2, ∞). Each gives a corner, with one-sided derivatives −1 and +1.

6. Switching points: at x = 1/2 the active branch changes from |x| (slope +1 just to the left) to |x − 1| (slope −1 just to the right), so the derivative jumps. The same happens at x = 2, where the slope goes from +1 to −1.
7. Everywhere else f coincides locally with a single linear piece, so it is differentiable there.
8. The points of failure are therefore x = 0, 1/2, 1, 2 and 3 — five in all.
ladder.answer: f fails to be differentiable exactly at x = 0, 1/2, 1, 2 and 3, that is at five points

marking.step: Recognise f as the lower envelope of three modulus graphs and that only vertices of active branches and switch-over points can break differentiability
Locate the pairwise crossings x = 1/2, 3/2, 2 and determine which branch is the minimum on each stretch, discarding the inactive crossing x = 3/2
Collect the active vertices x = 0, 1 and 3, checking one-sided derivatives −1 and +1 at each
Check the switch-over points x = 1/2 and x = 2 give a jump from slope +1 to slope −1, and conclude there are five points in all

testBank.q: lim x -> 0 (1 - cos 5x)/(x sin 3x) equals
steps: 1. The form is 0/0, so put the only identity that matters: 1 - cos 5x = 2 sin^2(5x/2).
2. Divide the numerator and the denominator by x^2. The numerator becomes 2 [sin(5x/2)/x]^2, and the coefficient of x inside the sine is 5/2, so it approaches 2 x (5/2)^2 = 25/2.
3. The denominator becomes (sin 3x)/x, which approaches 3.
4. Hence the limit is (25/2)/3 = 25/6.

testBank.q: lim x -> infinity [sqrt(x^2 + 5x + 3) - x] equals
steps: 1. Both terms approach infinity, so this is infinity - infinity and nothing can be said until the root is removed.
2. Rationalise: multiply and divide by sqrt(x^2 + 5x + 3) + x. The numerator becomes (x^2 + 5x + 3) - x^2 = 5x + 3.
3. The overall highest power is 1, so divide the numerator and the denominator by x. Inside the root, dividing by x means dividing every term by x^2.
4. The expression becomes (5 + 3/x)/[sqrt(1 + 5/x + 3/x^2) + 1], and every term with x in the denominator approaches 0, giving 5/(1 + 1) = 5/2.

testBank.q: lim x -> minus infinity (3x + 5)/sqrt(4x^2 + 1) equals
steps: 1. Whenever x -> minus infinity, put x = -t so that t -> plus infinity and no sign decision is left to chance.
2. The expression becomes (-3t + 5)/sqrt(4t^2 + 1).
3. Divide the numerator and the denominator by t; inside the root that means dividing by t^2: (-3 + 5/t)/sqrt(4 + 1/t^2).
4. The limit is -3/2. Note the sanity check: for large negative x the numerator is negative and the root is positive, so the answer has to be negative.
1. Check the two halves separately: the base approaches 1 and the power approaches infinity, so this is 1^infinity.
2. lambda = lim (base - 1) x power = lim [(1 + x - 1 - 2x)/(1 + 2x)] x (1/x).
4. The answer is e^lambda = e^(-1), not lambda.

testBank.q: lim x -> 0 ln(cos 2x)/tan^2 3x equals
steps: 1. The log needs a 1 inside it, so write cos 2x = 1 + (cos 2x - 1).
2. Put u = cos 2x - 1, which approaches 0. Then ln(1 + u)/u approaches 1, so the limit equals lim (cos 2x - 1)/tan^2 3x.
3. cos 2x - 1 = -2 sin^2 x. Divide the numerator and the denominator by x^2: the numerator approaches -2 and (tan 3x/x)^2 approaches 9.
4. The limit is -2/9.

testBank.q: lim x -> 0 (e^x - e^(sin x))/(x - sin x) equals
steps: 1. The form is 0/0. Take e^(sin x) common in the numerator: e^(sin x) [e^(x - sin x) - 1].
2. Now the quotient is e^(sin x) x [e^(something) - 1]/same something, with something = x - sin x approaching 0.
3. The bracket approaches 1 and e^(sin x) approaches 1.
4. The limit is 1. No expansion of x - sin x is needed, because the same quantity sits upstairs and downstairs.

testBank.q: lim x -> 0 (x - sin x)/(x - tan x) equals
steps: 1. Use the expansions. x - sin x = x - (x - x^3/3! + ...) = x^3/6 - ...
3. The minimum power is 3 on both sides, so the limit is the ratio of the coefficients of x^3.

testBank.q: Let f(x) = (1 - cos 4x)/x^2 for x < 0, f(0) = a, and f(x) = sqrt(x)/(sqrt(16 + sqrt(x)) - 4) for x > 0. If f is continuous at x = 0, then a equals
steps: 1. Continuity at 0 needs LHL = RHL = f(0) = a, so this is two limit problems wearing one hat.
2. LHL: (1 - cos 4x)/x^2 = 2 sin^2 2x/x^2, which approaches 2 x 2^2 = 8.
3. RHL: rationalise by multiplying with sqrt(16 + sqrt(x)) + 4. The denominator becomes (16 + sqrt(x)) - 16 = sqrt(x), which cancels the numerator, leaving sqrt(16 + sqrt(x)) + 4.
4. As x -> 0+ that approaches 4 + 4 = 8. Both one-sided limits are 8, so a = 8.

testBank.q: If [ ] denotes the greatest integer function, the number of points in the interval (0, 3) at which f(x) = [x^2] is discontinuous is
steps: 1. A greatest integer function breaks exactly where its input crosses an integer, so this is a range question.
2. As x runs over (0, 3), x^2 runs over (0, 9), taking every value in between exactly once because x^2 is increasing there.
3. x^2 becomes the integers 1, 2, ..., 8 at x = 1, sqrt 2, sqrt 3, 2, sqrt 5, sqrt 6, sqrt 7, sqrt 8, all of which lie in (0, 3).
4. x^2 = 9 happens at x = 3, which is outside the open interval. So there are 8 points.

testBank.q: The number of points at which f(x) = (x - 2)|x^2 - 4| is not differentiable is
steps: 1. Only the points where the modulus opens, x = 2 and x = -2, are suspects; everywhere else f is a polynomial.
2. For |x| > 2, f(x) = (x - 2)^2 (x + 2); for |x| < 2, f(x) = -(x - 2)^2 (x + 2). The function is continuous everywhere.
3. Derivative of (x - 2)^2 (x + 2) is (x - 2)^2 + 2(x - 2)(x + 2). At x = 2 this is 0, and the other branch gives -0 = 0, so f is differentiable at x = 2: the squared factor flattens the corner.
4. At x = -2 the same derivative gives 16, while the inner branch gives -16. So f fails to be differentiable at exactly one point, x = -2.

testBank.q: lim x -> pi/2 (1 + cos 2x)/(pi - 2x)^2 equals
steps: 1. The form is 0/0, and the sine must be manufactured with its argument approaching 0.
3. So the expression is (2/4) [sin(pi/2 - x)/(pi/2 - x)]^2, and pi/2 - x approaches 0.
4. The bracket approaches 1, so the limit is 1/2. Putting x = pi/2 + h and letting h -> 0 gives the same answer.

testBank.q: Let f(x) = x sin(1/x) for x not equal to 0 with f(0) = 0, and let g(x) = x^2 sin(1/x) for x not equal to 0 with g(0) = 0. Which of the following are TRUE?
opts: g is differentiable at x = 0 and g'(0) = 0
steps: 1. sin(1/x) is only an oscillating number in [-1, 1], so |x sin(1/x)| is at most |x|, which approaches 0 = f(0). Hence (A) is true.
2. For f, first principles give f'(0) = lim h -> 0 [h sin(1/h) - 0]/h = lim sin(1/h), which oscillates and has no limit. (B) is false.
3. For g, g'(0) = lim h -> 0 [h^2 sin(1/h)]/h = lim h sin(1/h) = 0, so (C) is true. Note that direct differentiation fails here, which is exactly why the definition is used.
4. For x not 0, g'(x) = 2x sin(1/x) - cos(1/x). The first term approaches 0 but cos(1/x) oscillates, so lim x -> 0 g'(x) does not exist and (D) is false.

testBank.q: Let f(x) = (e^(1/x) - 1)/(e^(1/x) + 1) for x not equal to 0 and f(0) = 0. Which of the following are TRUE?
opts: The right hand limit of f at x = 0 is 1
The left hand limit of f at x = 0 is -1
f has a removable discontinuity at x = 0
f has an irremovable (jump) discontinuity at x = 0, the jump being 2
steps: 1. As x -> 0+, 1/x -> plus infinity, so e^(1/x) -> infinity and the form is infinity/infinity. Divide the numerator and the denominator by e^(1/x): (1 - e^(-1/x))/(1 + e^(-1/x)) -> (1 - 0)/(1 + 0) = 1. (A) is true.
2. As x -> 0-, 1/x -> minus infinity, so e^(1/x) -> 0 and there is no indeterminate form at all: the value is (0 - 1)/(0 + 1) = -1. (B) is true.
3. The two one-sided limits are finite and unequal, so the limit does not exist. A discontinuity is removable only when the limit exists, so (C) is false.
4. This is precisely a jump discontinuity, and the jump is RHL - LHL = 1 - (-1) = 2. (D) is true.

testBank.q: Let [ ] denote the greatest integer function and f(x) = x^2 [x] for all real x. Which of the following are TRUE?
opts: f is discontinuous at every non-zero integer
steps: 1. Replace [x] by the constant it equals on each side. Just above 0, [x] = 0, so f(x) = 0; just below 0, [x] = -1, so f(x) = -x^2.
2. Both branches approach 0 and f(0) = 0, so (A) is true; their derivatives are 0 and -2x, both 0 at x = 0, so (B) is true.

3. At x = 1: just above, f(x) = x^2 with value 1 at x = 1; just below, f(x) = 0. The left hand limit is 0 but f(1) = 1, so f is discontinuous and therefore non-differentiable at 1. (C) is false, even though the one-sided derivatives are 2 and 0.
4. At any integer n not 0: the left hand limit is (n - 1)n^2 while f(n) = n x n^2, and these differ by n^2, which is not 0. So (D) is true.

testBank.q: Let f be continuous at x = a and let g be discontinuous at x = a. Which of the following statements are ALWAYS true?
opts: f + g is discontinuous at x = a
f g is discontinuous at x = a
f - g is discontinuous at x = a
If f(a) is not 0, then f g is discontinuous at x = a
steps: 1. If f + g were continuous at a, then g = (f + g) - f would be a difference of two functions continuous at a, hence continuous at a. That contradicts the hypothesis, so (A) is true, and the same argument gives (C).
2. (B) is false: take f identically 0. Then f g is identically 0, which is continuous, however badly g behaves. More generally the product can survive whenever the limit of f at a is 0.

3. (D) is true: if f is continuous at a with f(a) not 0, then f is non-zero in a neighbourhood of a, so g = (f g)/f. If f g were continuous at a, g would be a quotient of functions continuous at a with non-vanishing denominator, hence continuous at a, a contradiction.
4. Remember also the case not listed: if f and g are both discontinuous at a, nothing at all can be said about the sum, difference or product.

testBank.q: Which of the following limits are equal to 1? ([ ] denotes the greatest integer function.)
steps: 1. (A) is the standard formula, and the something inside the sine does approach 0. True.
2. (B): sin(infinity) is only an oscillating number in [-1, 1], and a finite quantity divided by infinity approaches 0. The value is 0, not 1. False.
3. (C): the form is infinity x 0. Write it as sin(1/x)/(1/x), where 1/x approaches 0, so the limit is 1. True.
4. (D): sin x/x approaches 1 from below, because sin x is smaller than x for small positive x. The greatest integer of a number slightly smaller than 1 is 0, so the limit is 0, not 1. False.

testBank.q: Let [ ] denote the greatest integer function and { } the fractional part, and let f(x) = 2[x] + 3{x} - 7x^2. Which of the following are TRUE?
opts: At x = 1 the right hand derivative and the left hand derivative are both -11
steps: 1. Always replace {x} by x - [x] and then replace [x] by the constant it equals on the interval. Just above x = 1: [x] = 1 and {x} = x - 1, so f(x) = 2 + 3(x - 1) - 7x^2, whose limit at 1 is -5 and whose derivative 3 - 14x equals -11 at x = 1. Also f(1) = 2 + 0 - 7 = -5.
2. Just below x = 1: [x] = 0 and {x} = x, so f(x) = 3x - 7x^2, whose limit at 1 is -4 and whose derivative 3 - 14x again equals -11 at x = 1.

3. The left hand limit -4 is not equal to f(1) = -5, so f is discontinuous at 1: (A) is true and (B) is true, which is exactly the warning that equal one-sided derivatives cannot save a discontinuous function. Hence (C) is false.
4. At x = 0: just below, [x] = -1 and {x} = x + 1, so f(x) = -2 + 3(x + 1) - 7x^2 = 1 + 3x - 7x^2, whose limit is 1, while f(0) = 0. So f is discontinuous at 0 and (D) is false.

testBank.q: Evaluate lim h -> 0 [ln(1 + 2h) - 2 ln(1 + h)]/h^2.
steps: 1. Do not split this into two limits. Each piece behaves like a finite quantity divided by h, so splitting manufactures an infinity - infinity form and the apparent answer 0 is wrong.
2. Combine the logs: ln(1 + 2h) - ln[(1 + h)^2] = ln[(1 + 2h)/(1 + 2h + h^2)].
3. Force a 1 inside: (1 + 2h)/(1 + 2h + h^2) = 1 - h^2/(1 + h)^2. So the numerator is ln(1 + u) with u = -h^2/(1 + h)^2, which approaches 0.
4. Write it as [ln(1 + u)/u] x (u/h^2). The bracket approaches 1 and u/h^2 = -1/(1 + h)^2 approaches -1, so the limit is -1.

testBank.q: Let a and b be real numbers such that lim x -> 0 (a tan x + b sin x)/x^3 = 3/2. Find the value of a - b.
steps: 1. Expand: tan x = x + x^3/3 + ... and sin x = x - x^3/6 + ...
2. So the numerator is (a + b)x + (a/3 - b/6)x^3 + ...
3. The denominator has minimum power 3, so for a finite limit the coefficient of x must vanish: a + b = 0, giving b = -a.
4. Then the coefficient of x^3 is a/3 + a/6 = a/2, and matching coefficients gives a/2 = 3/2, so a = 3 and b = -3.
5. Hence a - b = 6.

testBank.q: Let [ ] denote the greatest integer function and f(x) = [x^2 - x + 3] for x in [-1, 2]. Find the sum of all the values of x in [-1, 2] at which f is discontinuous.
steps: 1. This is a range question, so graph the quadratic first. The vertex is at x = 1/2 with value 3 - 1/4 = 11/4, and the end values are f(-1) = 1 + 1 + 3 = 5 and f(2) = 4 - 2 + 3 = 5. So the quadratic runs over [11/4, 5] on this interval.
2. The greatest integer function breaks where the quadratic crosses the integers 3 and 4 (the value 5 is attained only at the two end points).
3. x^2 - x + 3 = 4 gives x^2 - x - 1 = 0, whose roots (1 - sqrt 5)/2 and (1 + sqrt 5)/2 both lie in [-1, 2] and add to 1.
4. x^2 - x + 3 = 3 gives x^2 - x = 0, that is x = 0 and x = 1, both in the interval.
5. The end points also fail: f(-1) = 5 while the right hand limit there is 4, and f(2) = 5 while the left hand limit is 4, so one-sided continuity fails at both.

testBank.q: Evaluate lim n -> infinity (2^n + 3^n + 7^n)^(1/n).
steps: 1. Take the largest term common: (2^n + 3^n + 7^n)^(1/n) = 7 x [(2/7)^n + (3/7)^n + 1]^(1/n).
2. A proper fraction raised to an infinite power approaches 0, so the bracket approaches 1 while the power 1/n approaches 0.
3. 1^0 is not an indeterminate form, so the bracket contributes 1.
4. The limit is 7, the largest base.

testBank.q: If [ ] denotes the greatest integer function, find the number of points in the interval (-2, 2) at which f(x) = [x] + |x - 1| is not differentiable.
steps: 1. [x] is discontinuous at every integer, and the integers inside (-2, 2) are -1, 0 and 1.
2. A function discontinuous at a point is non-differentiable there, irrespective of what the one-sided derivatives do, so x = -1, 0, 1 are all non-differentiable points.
3. |x - 1| contributes a corner only at x = 1, which is already on the list.
4. At every other point of the interval [x] is locally a constant and |x - 1| is smooth, so f is differentiable there. The count is 3.

testBank.q: Let f be differentiable with f'(5) = 7. Find the value of lim t -> 0 [f(5 + t) - f(5 - t)]/(2t).
steps: 1. Substituting t = 0 gives f(5) - f(5) = 0 over 0, so the form is 0/0 and L'Hopital applies, differentiating with respect to t.
2. The derivative of f(5 + t) with respect to t is f'(5 + t). The derivative of f(5 - t) is -f'(5 - t), because of the chain rule, and that minus sign is the whole question.
3. So the limit becomes lim t -> 0 [f'(5 + t) + f'(5 - t)]/2.
4. Putting t = 0 gives [f'(5) + f'(5)]/2 = f'(5) = 7. The tempting answer 0 comes from losing the chain-rule sign.

testBank.q: Evaluate lim x -> 0 (1 - cos 2x)(3 + cos x)/(x tan 4x).
steps: 1. The form is 0/0. Replace 1 - cos 2x by 2 sin^2 x; the factor 3 + cos x is harmless and approaches 4.
2. Divide the numerator and the denominator by x^2. The numerator becomes 2 (sin x/x)^2 (3 + cos x), which approaches 2 x 1 x 4 = 8.
3. The denominator becomes (tan 4x)/x, which approaches 4.
4. The limit is 8/4 = 2.

testBank.q: Let f(x) = 1/(x - 1) and g(x) = 1/(x - 2). Find the number of points at which f(g(x)) is discontinuous.
steps: 1. Compute f(g(x)) = 1/[1/(x - 2) - 1]. Taking the LCM gives (x - 2)/[1 - (x - 2)] = (x - 2)/(3 - x).
2. Wherever a denominator vanishes the function is undefined and therefore discontinuous, so x = 3 is one such point.
3. But the simplification is only valid where g itself is alive. At x = 2 the inner function blows up, so f(g(x)) is not defined there either; that is the inner-function trap.
4. The points are x = 2 and x = 3, so the count is 2.

testBank.q: Consider the function f : (-pi/2, pi/2) -> (-infinity, infinity) defined by f(x) = (|x| + |x - 1|) sin x + [x sin x], where [x sin x] is the greatest integer less than or equal to x sin x. Let alpha be the total number of points in the interval (-pi/2, pi/2) at which f is NOT continuous, and let beta be the total number of points in the interval (-pi/2, pi/2) at which f is NOT differentiable. Then the value of alpha + beta is
steps: 1. The first term (|x| + |x - 1|) sin x is continuous everywhere, so every discontinuity must come from the greatest integer term.
2. Put u(x) = x sin x. It is even, u(0) = 0, and it increases as |x| increases; on (-pi/2, pi/2) its values fill [0, pi/2), with pi/2 about 1.571. So [u] is 0 while u < 1 and 1 while 1 <= u < pi/2.
3. u(x) = 1 at exactly two points, x = c and x = -c with c about 1.114, both inside the interval, and [u] jumps by 1 at each. Hence alpha = 2.
4. Those two points are discontinuities, so they are non-differentiable as well.

5. At x = 0 the modulus |x| is multiplied by sin x, and |x| sin x has both one-sided derivatives equal to 0 (the vanishing sine kills the corner); |x - 1| = 1 - x is smooth near 0 and [u] = 0 there. So f is differentiable at 0.

6. At x = 1 the term |x - 1| sin x has right hand derivative sin 1 and left hand derivative -sin 1, and sin 1 is not 0, so f is not differentiable at x = 1. Here [u] = 0 locally, since u(1) = sin 1 is about 0.841.
7. Therefore beta = 2 + 1 = 3 and alpha + beta = 5.

testBank.q: For a real number alpha, let [alpha] denote the greatest integer less than or equal to alpha. For a finite set S, let |S| denote the number of elements in S. Consider the functions f : (-3, 3) -> (-infinity, infinity) and g : (-3, 3) -> (-infinity, infinity) defined by f(x) = [x^3] ln(1 + sin^2(pi(x - [x]))) and g(x) = x^3 sin^2(pi ln(1 + x - [x])). Let A = {x in (-3, 3) : f is discontinuous at x} and B = {x in (-3, 3) : g is discontinuous at x}. Then the value of |A| + 2|B| - |A intersect B| is
steps: 1. For f, note that sin(pi(x - [x])) differs from sin(pi x) only in sign, so the log factor is L(x) = ln(1 + sin^2(pi x)). It is continuous everywhere, and it vanishes exactly at the integers.
2. [x^3] jumps where x^3 crosses an integer. On (-3, 3) we have x^3 in (-27, 27), so x = k^(1/3) for k = -26, -25, ..., 26: that is 53 points.

3. At such a point, f = [x^3] L is discontinuous unless the finite jump of [x^3] is multiplied by a factor approaching 0, that is unless L vanishes there. Among the 53 points exactly five are integers, namely -2, -1, 0, 1, 2, and at those the one-sided limits and the value of f are all 0.

5. For g, the only suspects are the integers, where x - [x] jumps. As x -> n-, x - [x] -> 1, so sin^2(pi ln(1 + x - [x])) -> sin^2(pi ln 2), which is not 0; the left hand limit is n^3 sin^2(pi ln 2). But g(n) = n^3 sin^2(0) = 0.
6. So g is discontinuous at every integer except 0: B = {-2, -1, 1, 2} and |B| = 4.
7. A consists of cube roots of integers that are not themselves integers, so A intersect B is empty.
8. Therefore |A| + 2|B| - |A intersect B| = 48 + 8 - 0 = 56.

testBank.q: Let a, b, c be real numbers such that lim x -> 0 (a e^x - b cos x + c e^(-x))/(x sin x) = 2. Find a, b and c.
steps: 1. The denominator x sin x behaves like x^2, so its minimum power is 2 and the limit is finite and non-zero. Hence the numerator must have minimum power 2 as well, and its x^2 coefficient must be 2.
2. Expand to the x^2 term only: a e^x = a(1 + x + x^2/2), -b cos x = -b(1 - x^2/2), c e^(-x) = c(1 - x + x^2/2).
3. Constant term must vanish: a - b + c = 0. Coefficient of x must vanish: a - c = 0.
4. Coefficient of x^2 must equal 2: a/2 + b/2 + c/2 = 2.
5. From a = c and b = a + c = 2a, the last equation gives a/2 + a + a/2 = 2a = 2, so a = 1.
6. Hence a = 1, c = 1 and b = 2. Writing any power above x^2 would have been wasted work.

testBank.q: Let f(x) = x^3 - x^2 + x + 1 and define g(x) = max{f(t) : 0 <= t <= x} for 0 <= x <= 1, and g(x) = 3 - x for 1 < x <= 2. Find the number of points in (0, 2) at which g is not differentiable.
steps: 1. First settle what the maximum is. f'(x) = 3x^2 - 2x + 1 has discriminant 4 - 12 < 0 with a positive leading coefficient, so f' > 0 for all x and f is strictly increasing.
2. Therefore the maximum of f on [0, x] is attained at t = x, so g(x) = f(x) for 0 <= x <= 1.
3. Check continuity at x = 1: g(1) = f(1) = 1 - 1 + 1 + 1 = 2, and 3 - x approaches 2 as x -> 1+. So g is continuous at 1.
4. Left hand derivative at 1 is f'(1) = 3 - 2 + 1 = 2; right hand derivative is -1. They differ, so g has a corner at x = 1.
5. On (0, 1) and on (1, 2) both branches are polynomials, hence differentiable. So exactly one point, x = 1.

testBank.q: Let alpha and beta be real numbers such that lim x -> 0 (x^2 sin(beta x))/(alpha x - sin x) = 1. Find the value of 6(alpha + beta).
steps: 1. Expand the numerator: x^2 sin(beta x) = beta x^3 - beta^3 x^5/6 + ..., so its minimum power is 3 (assuming beta is not 0, which the value 1 of the limit forces).
2. Expand the denominator: alpha x - sin x = (alpha - 1)x + x^3/6 - ...
3. If alpha were not 1, the denominator would have minimum power 1, which is smaller than 3, and the limit would be 0, not 1. So alpha = 1 and the denominator becomes x^3/6 + ...
4. Now both minimum powers are 3, and the limit is the ratio of their coefficients: beta/(1/6) = 6 beta = 1, so beta = 1/6.
5. Hence 6(alpha + beta) = 6(1 + 1/6) = 7.

testBank.q: Let [ ] denote the greatest integer function and f(x) = |x| [x] on the interval (-2, 2). Find the number of points of (-2, 2) at which f is discontinuous, and the number of points at which f is not differentiable.
steps: 1. Define the function piecewise yourself. On (-2, -1): [x] = -2 and |x| = -x, so f(x) = 2x. On [-1, 0): [x] = -1 and |x| = -x, so f(x) = x. On [0, 1): [x] = 0, so f(x) = 0. On [1, 2): [x] = 1 and |x| = x, so f(x) = x.
2. At x = -1: the left hand limit is 2(-1) = -2 while f(-1) = -1, so f is discontinuous, hence non-differentiable.

3. At x = 0: the left hand limit is 0 and f(0) = 0, so f is continuous. But the left hand derivative is 1 (from f(x) = x) and the right hand derivative is 0 (from f(x) = 0), so f is not differentiable: a genuine corner.
4. At x = 1: the left hand limit is 0 while f(1) = 1, so f is discontinuous, hence non-differentiable.
5. Every other point lies inside one of the four open pieces, where f is linear. So 2 points of discontinuity and 3 points of non-differentiability.
testBank.answer: discontinuous at 2 points (x = -1 and x = 1); not differentiable at 3 points (x = -1, 0 and 1)

commonMistakes: 1. Treating 0/0 as a number, or substituting x = 9.9999 to guess the answer.
Fix: 0/0 is only a signal that work is pending — factorize, rationalize or divide; never plug in a nearby decimal.
▶ where this comes up in the lecture
2. Letting x → −∞ directly inside a square root, so the sign of the answer comes out wrong.
Fix: Always put x = −t so t → +∞, because √t² = t only for positive t; (x+5)/√(2x²+1) then gives −1/√2, not +1/√2.
▶ where this comes up in the lecture
3. Using sin x/x = 1 wherever a sine appears.
Fix: It is 1 only when the angle itself → 0; at x → π/2 the value of sin x/x is simply 2/π. Reshape the problem so the angle tends to 0 before using the formula.
▶ where this comes up in the lecture
4. Splitting a limit into two parts while a part is still indeterminate.
Fix: Substitute the limiting value into the whole expression at once; splitting ln(1+2h)/h² − 2ln(1+h)/h² makes a fake ∞ − ∞ and a fake answer of 0. Split only when each piece is already finite.
▶ where this comes up in the lecture
5. Applying ln(1+u)/u → 1 to a log that is not to base e.
Fix: Convert first with log_b a = ln a / ln b; a base-3 log leaves an extra 1/ln 3 in the answer.
▶ where this comes up in the lecture
6. Reading the angle in degrees as if it were radians.
Fix: Every trig limit formula is in radians, so x degrees = πx/180; that is why the answer becomes π/180 and not 1.
▶ where this comes up in the lecture
7. Computing LHD and RHD without checking continuity, then calling the function differentiable because they matched.
Fix: Check LHL = RHL = f(a) first; a discontinuous point is non-differentiable even when both derivatives come out equal.
▶ where this comes up in the lecture
8. For f(g(x)), reporting only the points where the simplified expression breaks.
Fix: Add every point where the inner function itself blows up — there the whole calculation is meaningless, so it is a point of discontinuity too.
▶ where this comes up in the lecture
9. Differentiating f(5 − t) with respect to t and forgetting the inner −1.
Fix: Chain rule gives −f'(5 − t), so [f(5+t) − f(5−t)]/2t → f'(5), not 0.
▶ where this comes up in the lecture
10. Guessing where a greatest-integer function breaks instead of drawing it.
Fix: Graph the inside function on the given interval first; only the integer levels it actually crosses, plus the interval ends, can be points of discontinuity.
▶ where this comes up in the lecture
shortcuts: Name the form before you touch the question First substitute and see which of the seven forms you have. 0/0 means factorize or rationalize, ∞/∞ means divide by the biggest term, ∞−∞ means take the LCM or rationalize, 1^∞ means the λ formula. Name the form before writing anything else — a right method applied to the wrong form is one of the commonest ways to lose a limit question. Lecture 3
▶ watch Ankit Sir explain it

For ∞/∞, divide by the biggest infinity — and never expand brackets Anything finite over infinity goes to 0, so divide the top and the bottom by the highest power (or by the dominant exponential, like 3ˣ). If the polynomial is already in factors, do not expand: count the degree, split the division across the factors. n(n+1)(2n+1)/((n²+2)(−3n+5)) is cubic over cubic, so the answer is just 2/(−3) = −2/3. Lecture 1
▶ watch Ankit Sir explain it

The coefficient of x is the answer Since sin(something)/same something → 1, you get lim sin(ax)/x = a and lim tan(ax)/x = a. So divide the numerator and the denominator by x and read the coefficients off: (sin ax − tan bx)/(sin cx + tan dx) → (a − b)/(c + d). No multiplying and dividing, no extra lines. Lecture 2
▶ watch Ankit Sir explain it

Two trig identities carry everything 1 − cos 2θ = 2sin²θ and cos C − cos D = −2 sin((C+D)/2) sin((C−D)/2). From the first you get the standard results on sight: (1 − cos mx)/x² = m²/2 and (cos mx − cos nx)/x² = −(m² − n²)/2. Learn these two and you can stop hunting for identities. Lecture 2
▶ watch Ankit Sir explain it

1^∞: λ = (base − 1) × power, answer e^λ Confirm the base → 1 and the power → ∞, then compute λ = lim (base − 1)·power and write e^λ. Bring any cot down as 1/tan so the leftover 0·∞ becomes a clean 0/0. ((x+3)/(x+1))^{x+2} gives λ = 2(x+2)/(x+1) → 2, so the answer is e². Lecture 3
▶ watch Ankit Sir explain it

Manufacture ln(1+u)/u and e^u − 1 over u Both of those go to 1 when u → 0, so force that shape. Inside a log, write the argument as 1 + (argument − 1): ln(cos 2x) = ln(1 + (cos 2x − 1)). If the numerator is not already e^u − 1, pull the constant out: e^{cos 2x} − e = e(e^{cos 2x − 1} − 1). What is left is always an easy trig limit. Lecture 3
▶ watch Ankit Sir explain it

Expansion limits: match the minimum power, read the ratio After expanding, every such limit is polynomial over polynomial. For a finite non-zero answer the lowest power of x on top must equal the power downstairs, and the answer is the ratio of those two coefficients. So write only the one term you need — higher powers are wasted ink, and to find unknowns you simply set the lower-power coefficients to zero. Lecture 3
▶ watch Ankit Sir explain it

Continuity first, derivatives second For a piecewise function at a joining point: check LHL = RHL = f(a) first. If it fails, write non-differentiable and move on — equal LHD and RHD cannot rescue a broken graph. If it passes, differentiate the x > a piece and put a in for the RHD, the x < a piece for the LHD. That pattern covers most of the questions in this chapter. Lecture 5
▶ watch Ankit Sir explain it
chapters.mindMap: Limits, Continuity and Differentiability The seven indeterminate forms 0/0 is the parent form Infinity over infinity and 0 times infinity reduce to it by a reciprocal Infinity minus infinity needs a conjugate or an LCM 1 to the power infinity has its own formula, e to the lambda Infinity to the power 0 and 0 to the power 0 are museum pieces: take the largest term common, or use L'Hôpital No indeterminate form means just substitute ● ● ● Algebraic limits Factorise and cancel for polynomials Multiply by the conjugate for surds Divide by the largest infinity at infinity Put x = minus t when x runs to minus infinity A finite limit with a vanishing denominator forces the numerator to vanish Largest term common for the nth root of a sum of nth powers ● ● ● Standard limits Sine or tangent of something, over that same something, goes to 1 The coefficient of x inside is the answer 1 minus cosine of a doubled angle is twice a sine squared Log of 1 plus something, over the same something, goes to 1 a to the x, minus 1, over x, goes to log a Every one of them is a 0/0 form in disguise ● ● ● Heavy artillery 1 to the power infinity: lambda is the limit of base minus 1, times the power Expansions: match the minimum power and read off one coefficient L'Hôpital: differentiate top and bottom, then repeat if the form returns Expand when two functions are added and nothing can be combined Reach for L'Hôpital when differentiating visibly simplifies the function ● ● ● Continuity Left limit, right limit and the value, all equal and all finite Only the change points and the zeros of a denominator can break it One-sided continuity at the end points of the domain 1 over x and e to the 1 over x are the standard traps at zero Composites: carry the three limiting values of chapters.title: Differentiation

concepts.title: Product and Quotient Rules for Several Functions
concepts.oneLine: For a product of any number of functions, differentiate one factor at a time and hold the rest — three functions give three terms — and for a quotient write (u′v − uv′)/v².
notes: Take u, v and w, all functions of x. To differentiate the product uvw, you move along the product one factor at a time: differentiate u and freeze v and w, then differentiate v and freeze u and w, then differentiate w and freeze u and v. Add the three pieces.

The number of terms you get is exactly the number of functions you are multiplying — three functions, three terms; fifty functions, fifty terms. That is why the two-function version needs no separate rule. Two is just this rule with one factor less.

The quotient rule follows the same freeze-one-move-one habit. For u/v, draw the long bar, put v² underneath, then on top freeze v and differentiate u, and after that freeze u and differentiate v, with a minus between them: (u′v − uv′)/v².
Order matters on top. The term with u′ comes first and carries the plus sign; the term with v′ comes second and carries the minus.

quickChecks.q: Differentiate x² · sin x · eˣ.
steps: 1. u = x², v = sin x, w = eˣ — three factors, so expect three terms.
2. Differentiate x², freeze the rest: 2x · sin x · eˣ.
3. Differentiate sin x, freeze the rest: x² · cos x · eˣ.
4. Differentiate eˣ, freeze the rest: x² · sin x · eˣ.
quickChecks.answer: 2x sin x eˣ + x² cos x eˣ + x² sin x eˣ

quickChecks.q: Differentiate (sin x)/x².
steps: 1. u = sin x, v = x², so the answer is (u′v − uv′)/v².
2. u′ = cos x and v′ = 2x, and v² = x⁴.
3. Top: cos x · x² − sin x · 2x = x(x cos x − 2 sin x).
4. Divide by x⁴ and cancel one x.

quickChecks.q: Differentiate x · ln x · tan x.
steps: 1. Three factors: u = x, v = ln x, w = tan x.
2. Differentiate x, freeze the rest: 1 · ln x · tan x = ln x tan x.
3. Differentiate ln x, freeze the rest: x · (1/x) · tan x = tan x.
4. Differentiate tan x, freeze the rest: x · ln x · sec²x.
quickChecks.answer: ln x tan x + tan x + x ln x sec²x

concepts.title: Practice: Products of Three and Four Functions
concepts.oneLine: For a product of three or four functions, write one term per function: differentiate that one, leave every other factor untouched.
notes: Close the notes and try these yourself. x²·2ˣ·sin x first, then 2ˣ·ln x·sin x·x. Pick up your copy and actually write them, because reading a worked solution is not the same as producing it.

Count the functions, and that is how many terms your answer has. Three functions, three terms. Four functions, four terms. In each term you differentiate exactly one factor and copy the rest down as they are.

For x²·2ˣ·sin x: derivative of x² is 2x, derivative of 2ˣ is 2ˣ ln 2, derivative of sin x is cos x. Three terms, done. For the four-function one you do the same march: 2ˣ, then ln x, then sin x, then x — and the derivative of x is just 1.

One more thing about how you practise this. Do not sit and grind the final simplification like a donkey. The moment the differentiation is written and the concept feels settled, leave the question and move to the next one.

quickChecks.q: Differentiate y = x³·eˣ·cos x
steps: 1. Three functions, three terms.
2. Differentiate x³: 3x²·eˣ·cos x
3. Differentiate eˣ: x³·eˣ·cos x
4. Differentiate cos x: −x³·eˣ·sin x
quickChecks.answer: dy/dx = 3x²eˣ cos x + x³eˣ cos x − x³eˣ sin x

quickChecks.q: Differentiate y = x·ln x·sin x
steps: 1. Differentiate x: 1·ln x·sin x
2. Differentiate ln x: x·(1/x)·sin x = sin x
3. Differentiate sin x: x·ln x·cos x
quickChecks.answer: dy/dx = ln x·sin x + sin x + x·ln x·cos x

quickChecks.q: Differentiate y = 3ˣ·x²·tan x
steps: 1. Differentiate 3ˣ: 3ˣ·ln 3·x²·tan x
2. Differentiate x²: 3ˣ·2x·tan x
3. Differentiate tan x: 3ˣ·x²·sec²x
quickChecks.answer: dy/dx = 3ˣ ln 3·x² tan x + 2x·3ˣ tan x + 3ˣ x² sec²x

concepts.title: Chain Rule for Composite Functions
concepts.oneLine: For a composite function, differentiate the outer function keeping the inside untouched, then multiply by the derivative of the inside — layer by layer until you reach plain x.
notes: Chain rule is for a composite function. If you have f(g(x)), the derivative is f′(g(x))·g′(x). Read it slowly: first differentiate the f function, and inside it you still write g(x), untouched. Then multiply by the derivative of the g function.

The inside never changes when you differentiate the outside. That one sentence saves most of the marks here. Students write the outer derivative and quietly simplify the inside — that is where the answer dies.
Try cos(ln x). Outer function is cos, so its derivative carries the negative sign: −sin, and inside sin the ln x stays as it is. Now differentiate ln x, which is 1/x. Multiply. Done.

The same process just repeats if there are three layers, like √(sin x²). Keep peeling until the layer you are differentiating is plain x — then you stop. Nothing new to learn, only one more multiplication.

quickChecks.q: Differentiate y = sin(ln x).
steps: 1. Outer is sin, so it becomes cos with the inside kept: cos(ln x).
2. Inner is ln x, derivative 1/x.
3. Multiply.

quickChecks.q: Differentiate y = ln(sin x).
steps: 1. Outer is ln, so it gives 1/sin x.
2. Inner is sin x, derivative cos x.
3. Multiply: cos x/sin x = cot x.

quickChecks.q: Differentiate y = √(tan x).
steps: 1. Outer is the power ½, so it gives 1/(2√(tan x)).
2. Inner is tan x, derivative sec²x.
3. Multiply.

concepts.title: Differentiating a Function of y with Respect to x
concepts.oneLine: When the variable inside is y and not x, every derivative carries one extra factor — dy/dx.
notes: Take sin y and differentiate it with respect to x. The outer function is sine, so the first step gives cos y. But that is not the end of it. Inside sits y, and I am differentiating with respect to x, so y must also be differentiated — and the derivative of y with respect to x is dy/dx. The answer is cos y · dy/dx.

Before you write a single thing, ask: the function is in one variable, but with respect to which variable are you differentiating? If the two are the same, nothing extra appears. If they are different, a factor comes out and you must write it.

Now the obvious question — why did none of this happen in the earlier set of questions? Because there the inside was always x. Differentiating x with respect to x gives 1, so that extra factor was sitting there all along; it was just 1, and multiplying by 1 changes nothing. That is the only reason you never saw it.
So the method does not change at all. Peel one layer at a time, outside first, and keep peeling until the thing inside is x. The moment the thing inside is y, the peeling ends in dy/dx instead of 1.

quickChecks.q: Differentiate cos y with respect to x.
steps: 1. Derivative of cosine gives −sin y.
2. Inside is y, so multiply by dy/dx.

quickChecks.q: Differentiate sin y² with respect to x.
steps: 1. Outer sine gives cos(y²).
2. Next layer y² gives 2y.
3. Innermost y gives dy/dx.
4. Multiply all three.

quickChecks.q: Differentiate y⁵ with respect to x.
steps: 1. Power of y gives 5y⁴.
2. Then y with respect to x gives dy/dx.

concepts.title: Watch the Variable You Differentiate With Respect To
concepts.oneLine: The same function gives three different derivatives depending on the respect variable: d/dx of ln x is 1/x, d/dt is (1/x)(dx/dt), and d/dy is (1/x)(dx/dy).
notes: Before you differentiate anything, ask two questions. Which variable is the function written in? And with respect to which variable are you differentiating? If those two letters are not the same, a chain-rule factor must appear.

Take ln x. Differentiate it with respect to x and both letters match, so the answer is just 1/x. Differentiate the same ln x with respect to t and you first get 1/x, then you must differentiate x with respect to t, so the answer is (1/x)(dx/dt). With respect to y it is the same story: (1/x)(dx/dy).

Same thing happens with sin y. d/dy of sin y is cos y and nothing more, because the function is in y and I am differentiating with respect to y. But d/dx of sin y is cos y · (dy/dx) — I differentiate the sine first, then the derivative of the inside variable y with respect to x.

This is also why y³ differentiated with respect to x gives 3y² (dy/dx), not 3y². The 3y² is the outside part. The dy/dx is the price you pay because the function was in y and the respect variable was x.

quickChecks.q: Differentiate cos x with respect to t.
steps: 1. Function is in x, respect variable is t. Letters differ.
2. Differentiate the outside: derivative of cos x is −sin x.
3. Attach the derivative of x with respect to t: dx/dt.

quickChecks.q: Differentiate y² with respect to y, and then y² with respect to x.
steps: 1. With respect to y: letters match, so the answer is 2y.
2. With respect to x: differentiate the outside to get 2y, then attach dy/dx.

quickChecks.q: Differentiate ln y with respect to x.
steps: 1. Function is in y, respect variable is x. Letters differ.
2. Differentiate the log first: 1/y.
3. Attach the derivative of y with respect to x: dy/dx.

concepts.title: Second Derivative of an Implicit Relation
concepts.oneLine: To get d²y/dx² from an implicit relation, differentiate your dy/dx expression again with respect to x, treat the bracket as a power instead of a fraction, and finally put the value of dy/dx back in.
notes: In a double derivative no new function shows up. Everything stays the same as the first round. You differentiate once, you get dy/dx in terms of y, and then you simply differentiate that same expression again with respect to x.
Keep saying it out loud while you work: differentiating with respect to x. So y³ does not give 3y², it gives 3y² × dy/dx. The y carries a dy/dx every single time, because y is a function of x.

Now comes the part where this differs from most solutions. When dy/dx comes out as 2/(3y² − 1), almost everybody reaches for the quotient rule. There is no need. The 2 is a constant, so treat the rest as 1/t, whose derivative is −1/t², and then chain rule the bracket. The algebra stays much shorter.
One last step people forget: your answer still has a dy/dx sitting in it. Put the value you already found back in, so the final d²y/dx² is purely in terms of y.

quickChecks.q: If y³ + y = x, find d²y/dx².
steps: 1. Differentiate with respect to x: 3y² (dy/dx) + dy/dx = 1.
2. So (3y² + 1) dy/dx = 1, giving dy/dx = 1/(3y² + 1).
3. Differentiate again as a power: −1/(3y² + 1)² × 6y (dy/dx) = −6y (dy/dx)/(3y² + 1)².
4. Put dy/dx = 1/(3y² + 1) back in.

quickChecks.q: If y² = 4x, find d²y/dx².
steps: 1. Differentiate with respect to x: 2y (dy/dx) = 4, so dy/dx = 2/y.
2. The 2 is a constant, so differentiate 1/y: −1/y² × dy/dx. That gives −2 (dy/dx)/y².
3. Put dy/dx = 2/y back in: −2 × 2/y³.

quickChecks.q: If y³ − y = 4x, find d²y/dx².
steps: 1. Differentiate with respect to x: (3y² − 1) dy/dx = 4, so dy/dx = 4/(3y² − 1).
2. Again as a power: 4 × (−1/(3y² − 1)²) × 6y (dy/dx) = −24y (dy/dx)/(3y² − 1)².
3. Substitute dy/dx = 4/(3y² − 1).

concepts.title: Board Proof: y = (x + √(x² + a²))ⁿ
concepts.oneLine: For y = (x + √(x² + a²))ⁿ, chain rule plus one LCM step rebuilds the bracket in the numerator and gives dy/dx = ny/√(x² + a²).
notes: Look at y = (x + √(x² + a²))ⁿ. There is no point writing that long bracket ten times over. Give it a name — call the bracket B — and write y = Bⁿ.

Now it is just the power rule with the chain rule: dy/dx = n·Bⁿ⁻¹ × (derivative of the bracket). Inside the bracket, x differentiates to 1, and √(x² + a²) differentiates to 2x/(2√(x² + a²)) — the 2 and the 2 cancel, so it is x/√(x² + a²).

So far dy/dx = n·Bⁿ⁻¹ (1 + x/√(x² + a²)). Here comes the step the whole question is built on. Take the LCM inside that bracket and the original bracket is born again in the numerator: 1 + x/√(x² + a²) = (x + √(x² + a²))/√(x² + a²).

Now the powers add. Bⁿ⁻¹ × B¹ = Bⁿ, and n − 1 + 1 = n. And Bⁿ was our y in the first place, so dy/dx = ny/√(x² + a²). The last step of this proof is always LCM — that is the only thing you need to remember here.

quickChecks.q: If y = (x + √(x² + 4))⁷, find dy/dx.
steps: 1. Here a² = 4 and n = 7, so the same proof applies.
3. LCM inside the bracket: (x + √(x² + 4))/√(x² + 4).
4. Powers add: 6 + 1 = 7.

quickChecks.q: Show that d/dx √(x² + a²) = x/√(x² + a²).
steps: 1. Outer function is the square root: derivative is 1/(2√(x² + a²)).
2. Inner function is x² + a²: derivative is 2x.
3. Multiply: 2x/(2√(x² + a²)).
4. The 2 and the 2 cancel.

quickChecks.q: Take n = 1, so y = x + √(x² + a²). Check that dy/dx = y/√(x² + a²).
steps: 1. dy/dx = 1 + x/√(x² + a²).
2. LCM: (√(x² + a²) + x)/√(x² + a²).
3. The numerator is exactly y.
quickChecks.answer: dy/dx = y/√(x² + a²), which matches ny/√(x² + a²) with n = 1.

concepts.title: When the Outer Function Is Unnamed: f(sin x) and f(g(x))
concepts.oneLine: For y = f(inner), dy/dx = f'(inner) × (derivative of inner) — and f'(inner) just means put the inner expression wherever x sat.
notes: Take y = f(sin x). People freeze here because they cannot see what f is. You do not need to see it. Differentiate the outer function as it is, then multiply by the derivative of whatever is sitting inside.
So dy/dx = f'(sin x) × cos x. Read f'(sin x) exactly as it is written: take the derivative function f', and in place of x put sin x. That is all the dash is telling you to do.

Now the same idea with an ugly inner. If y = f((2x − 1)/(x + 1)), then dy/dx = f'((2x − 1)/(x + 1)) × d/dx[(2x − 1)/(x + 1)]. The first piece needs no work from you — you just copy the inner expression inside f'. The second piece is honest labour: it is a quotient, so quotient rule.

And remember what dy/dx was asking in the first place: the function given is y, and you are differentiating it with respect to x. Everything inside that is not x has to pay its own derivative. That payment is the second factor.

quickChecks.q: If y = f(x²), find dy/dx.
steps: 1. First factor: f'(x²) — copy x² inside f'.
2. Second factor: d/dx(x²) = 2x.

quickChecks.q: If y = f(cos x), find dy/dx.
steps: 1. First factor: f'(cos x).
2. Second factor: d/dx(cos x) = −sin x.

quickChecks.q: If y = f((x − 1)/(x + 1)), find dy/dx.
steps: 1. First factor: f'((x − 1)/(x + 1)).
2. Second factor by quotient rule with u = x − 1, v = x + 1: [(x + 1)(1) − (x − 1)(1)]/(x + 1)².
3. Numerator = x + 1 − x + 1 = 2, so the derivative of the inside is 2/(x + 1)².

concepts.title: IIT 2006: Proving F(x) Is Constant
concepts.oneLine: When the data is f′ = g and f″ = −f, differentiate F(x) = f(x/2)² + g(x/2)² once and everything cancels: F′(x) = 0 for every x, so F is constant and F(10) = F(5) = 5.
notes: Read the data first. You are not given f or g themselves, only relations between their derivatives: f′ = g and f″ = −f. When the data is about derivatives, differentiate the function they are asking about — that is the whole hint.

So differentiate F. Square first, then the function, then the inside: F′(x) = 2·f(x/2)·f′(x/2)·½ + 2·g(x/2)·g′(x/2)·½. The 2 from the square and the ½ from x/2 cancel each other in both terms, which leaves F′(x) = f(x/2)·f′(x/2) + g(x/2)·g′(x/2).

Now use the data to remove f′ and g′. Since f′ = g holds at every input, f′(x/2) = g(x/2). For g′, differentiate f′ = g once more with respect to x: f″ = g′. And f″ = −f, so g′ = −f, which gives g′(x/2) = −f(x/2). Put both in: F′(x) = f(x/2)·g(x/2) − g(x/2)·f(x/2) = 0.

The last line is where students lose the question. Plenty of functions have zero derivative at some point — the derivative of x² is 2x, zero only at x = 0 — but that tells you nothing. Here F′(x) = 0 for all x, and only a constant function does that, because the derivative of a constant is 0. So F is constant: F(5) = 5 means F(10) = 5, and F(100) = 5 too.

quickChecks.q: f and g satisfy f′ = g and f″ = −f for all x. If G(x) = [f(2x)]² + [g(2x)]² and G(1) = 9, find G(7).
steps: 1. Differentiate: G′(x) = 2·f(2x)·f′(2x)·2 + 2·g(2x)·g′(2x)·2.
3. From f′ = g: f′(2x) = g(2x). From f″ = g′ and f″ = −f: g′ = −f, so g′(2x) = −f(2x).
4. G′(x) = 4[f(2x)g(2x) − g(2x)f(2x)] = 0 for all x, so G is constant.
5. G(1) = 9, so G(x) = 9 everywhere.

quickChecks.q: f is twice differentiable with f″(x) = −f(x) for all x. Let h(x) = [f(x)]² + [f′(x)]². If f(0) = 0 and f′(0) = 2, find h(3).
steps: 2. Put f″ = −f: h′(x) = 2f(x)f′(x) − 2f′(x)f(x) = 0 for all x.
3. So h is constant.

quickChecks.q: The derivative of y = x³ is 0 at x = 0. Can you conclude x³ is a constant function? Why does the IIT question's conclusion hold?
steps: 1. dy/dx = 3x², which is 0 only at x = 0, not for other values of x.
2. Constant needs the derivative to vanish at every x, not at one point.
3. In the IIT question F′(x) = 0 came out as an identity, true for all x, with nothing substituted — that is why F is constant.
quickChecks.answer: No. x³ is not constant; zero derivative at a single point proves nothing. F is constant only because F′(x) = 0 for all x.

concepts.title: Implicit Functions and How to Differentiate Them
concepts.oneLine: Implicit only means y is not written alone — differentiate both sides as they stand, remember every y carries dy/dx, then collect all the dy/dx terms on one side.
notes: Two words first: explicit and implicit. Explicit is the way your mother speaks when she is done being patient — "bring the potatoes, and bring them now." No doubt, no decoding. Implicit is when the same thing is said in a roundabout way and you are left to work it out.

Functions are the same. When y is written out plainly in terms of x, that is explicit. When x and y are tangled together in one relation and y is not sitting alone on one side, we call it implicit. There is no strict definition here and functions are not split into two camps — it is only a way of speaking.

So there is no new rule to learn. Differentiate both sides with respect to x exactly as they are written, and the only thing you must never forget is that y is itself a function of x, so every y you differentiate hands you a dy/dx. Product rule where there is a product, chain rule where there is a function of y.

After that it is pure bookkeeping. Push every dy/dx term to one side, take dy/dx common, and divide by whatever is left. And please do not go hunting for a fancier method here — I know the partial derivative shortcut, I am deliberately not giving it to you. You have a pressure cooker at home; there is no reason to boil potatoes in an open pot.

quickChecks.q: If x² + y² = 25, find dy/dx.
steps: 1. Differentiate both sides: 2x + 2y·dy/dx = 0.
2. 2y·dy/dx = −2x, so dy/dx = −x/y.

quickChecks.q: If xy + y = 1, find dy/dx.
steps: 1. Product rule on xy: y + x·dy/dx. Derivative of y: dy/dx. Derivative of 1: 0.
2. So y + x·dy/dx + dy/dx = 0.
3. Collect: (x + 1)·dy/dx = −y, so dy/dx = −y/(x + 1).

quickChecks.q: If y = x·sin y, find dy/dx.
steps: 1. Differentiate both sides: dy/dx = sin y + x·cos y·dy/dx.
2. Bring the dy/dx terms together: dy/dx − x·cos y·dy/dx = sin y.
3. Take dy/dx common: (1 − x·cos y)·dy/dx = sin y, so dy/dx = sin y/(1 − x·cos y).

concepts.title: Board Favourite: Make It Explicit First
concepts.oneLine: When a relation hides x and y under square roots, square it once, cancel the surds, pull y out explicitly — then differentiate the easy function instead of grinding the implicit one.
notes: Look at the relation x√(1+y) + y√(1+x) = 0. Your hand itches to differentiate straight away, surds and all. You can. The answer will come. But you will be dragging two square roots through every line.

Before you differentiate, ask one question: can y be written alone in terms of x? Here it can. Shift one term across, square both sides, and the roots vanish. What is left is a neat algebraic equation that factorises.
Once it factorises you get x + y + xy = 0, which gives y = −x/(1+x). That is an explicit function now. One quotient rule and you are done — dy/dx = −1/(1+x)².
So the moral is simple. Implicit differentiation is a tool, not a punishment. If squaring once turns the implicit form into an explicit one, do the squaring and let the calculus be short.

quickChecks.q: If x√(1−y²) + y√(1−x²) = 0, find dy/dx.
steps: 2. Square: x²(1−y²) = y²(1−x²).
3. x² − x²y² = y² − x²y², so x² = y².
4. The two terms must have opposite signs, so y = −x.
5. Differentiate the explicit form.

quickChecks.q: If y√(1+x) = x√(1+y), find dy/dx.
steps: 1. Square both sides: y²(1+x) = x²(1+y).
2. y² − x² + xy(y − x) = 0.
3. Factor: (y − x)(y + x + xy) = 0.
4. Test x + y + xy = 0 with x = 1: it gives y = −½, and then y√(1+x) = −0.707 while x√(1+y) = 0.707 — rejected.
5. So the curve is y = x, an explicit function.

concepts.title: Trigonometric Substitution for Inverse-Trig Relations
concepts.oneLine: When a relation is tied up in √(1 − x²) and √(1 − y²), put x = sin θ and y = sin φ, write the range −90° ≤ θ ≤ 90° at once, and the modulus disappears so the relation collapses to sin⁻¹x + sin⁻¹y = π/2.
notes: Look at the relation. x and y are locked together inside square roots. Nothing factors, nothing cancels, and implicit differentiation straight away will give you a mess. So do not attack it — translate it. Put x = sin θ and y = sin φ.

The moment you write x = sin θ, also write θ = sin⁻¹x, so θ lies between −90° and 90°. That second line is the whole section. Because now √(1 − x²) = √(1 − sin²θ) = √(cos²θ) = |cos θ|, and only the range lets you throw that modulus away.

Why does it go? sin⁻¹ always returns an angle in the first or the fourth quadrant, and cos is positive in both. So |cos θ| = cos θ, and |cos φ| = cos φ. This range is not a matter of choice — it comes free with the definition of sin⁻¹. Write the modulus first and then kill it with the range, because that is the step the checker is looking for.

Now the relation becomes sin θ cos φ + cos θ sin φ = 1, which is sin(θ + φ) = 1, so θ + φ = π/2. Your implicit relation just turned explicit: sin⁻¹x + sin⁻¹y = π/2. Differentiate both sides, remember the right side is a constant so it dies to 0, and that zero is exactly where the minus sign in your answer is born.

quickChecks.q: If x = sin θ with θ = sin⁻¹x, simplify √(1 − x²).
steps: 1. √(1 − x²) = √(1 − sin²θ) = √(cos²θ) = |cos θ|.
2. θ = sin⁻¹x lies between −90° and 90°, so cos θ ≥ 0.

quickChecks.q: Given sin⁻¹x³ + sin⁻¹y³ = π/2, find dy/dx.
steps: 1. Differentiate both sides with respect to x; the right side is a constant, so it gives 0.
3. Cancel 3 and move the first term across: (y²/√(1 − y⁶)) · dy/dx = −x²/√(1 − x⁶).

quickChecks.q: Take x = −½ and θ = sin⁻¹x. Is √(1 − x²) equal to cos θ or −cos θ?
steps: 1. θ = sin⁻¹(−½) = −30°, which is inside −90° to 90°, in the fourth quadrant.
2. cos(−30°) = √3/2, a positive number.
quickChecks.answer: cos θ — both sides are √3/2. A negative x does not flip the sign; the range still rules.

concepts.title: Parametric Differentiation and Its Second Derivative
concepts.oneLine: For a parametric curve, dy/dx = (dy/dt)/(dx/dt), and then d²y/dx² = d/dt(dy/dx) × dt/dx — never (d²y/dt²)/(d²x/dt²).
notes: Sometimes x and y are not tied to each other directly. Both are written through a third letter, t, the parameter. So you cannot differentiate y with respect to x in one shot.
What you do is differentiate y with respect to t, differentiate x with respect to t, and divide. That gives dy/dx = (dy/dt)/(dx/dt). This much you already do comfortably.

Now read d²y/dx² for what it literally says: the derivative of dy/dx with respect to x. Your dy/dx came out in terms of t, so differentiate it with respect to t and then convert that t into x by multiplying with dt/dx. And dt/dx is nothing but the reciprocal of dx/dt.
That is the process. There is no second process. Whatever you get as dy/dx, differentiate it with respect to t, multiply by 1/(dx/dt), and you are done.

quickChecks.q: If x = 2t and y = t², find d²y/dx².
steps: 1. dy/dt = 2t, dx/dt = 2, so dy/dx = 2t/2 = t.
2. Differentiate dy/dx with respect to t: d/dt(t) = 1.

quickChecks.q: If x = t³ and y = t², find d²y/dx².
steps: 1. dy/dt = 2t, dx/dt = 3t², so dy/dx = 2t/(3t²) = 2/(3t).
2. Differentiate with respect to t: d/dt(2/(3t)) = −2/(3t²).

quickChecks.q: If x = t² and y = t³, find d²y/dx².
steps: 1. dy/dt = 3t², dx/dt = 2t, so dy/dx = 3t²/(2t) = 3t/2.
2. Differentiate with respect to t: d/dt(3t/2) = 3/2.

concepts.title: Second derivative of a parametric function
concepts.oneLine: For x and y both in terms of t, d²y/dx² = d/dt(dy/dx) × 1/(dx/dt) — never the ratio of the two second derivatives.
notes: Take x = g(t) and y = f(t). You already know the first step: dy/dx = (dy/dt)/(dx/dt) = f′(t)/g′(t). Nice and clean.

Now look at what you are holding. f′(t)/g′(t) is a function of t, but you have been asked to differentiate with respect to x. So differentiate it with respect to t, and then multiply by dt/dx — that is the whole chain rule step, and that is the step children drop.
And dt/dx is nothing new. Since dx/dt = g′(t), its reciprocal gives dt/dx = 1/g′(t). Same logic as the previous slide, nothing extra to remember.
So d²y/dx² = d/dt( f′/g′ ) × 1/g′. Put the quotient rule on f′/g′ and you get (g′f″ − f′g″)/(g′)², and that one more 1/g′ pushes the bottom to (g′)³. That is the final shape.

quickChecks.q: If x = t² and y = t³, find d²y/dx².
steps: 1. dy/dt = 3t², dx/dt = 2t.
2. dy/dx = 3t²/2t = 3t/2.

quickChecks.q: If x = at² and y = 2at, find d²y/dx².
steps: 1. dy/dt = 2a, dx/dt = 2at.

quickChecks.q: For x = g(t), y = f(t), write d²y/dx² in terms of f′, f″, g′, g″ — and say where the cube in the denominator comes from.
steps: 1. dy/dx = f′/g′.
2. Quotient rule in t gives (g′f″ − f′g″)/(g′)².
3. Multiply by dt/dx = 1/g′, which adds one more g′ to the bottom.
quickChecks.answer: d²y/dx² = (g′f″ − f′g″)/(g′)³; the square comes from the quotient rule and the third g′ from dt/dx.

concepts.title: IIT question: d²x/dy² from dy/dx
concepts.oneLine: Start from dx/dy = 1/(dy/dx), differentiate both sides with respect to y, and you land on d²x/dy² = −(d²y/dx²)/(dy/dx)³ in two lines.
notes: First, the one fact everything rests on, the one we used earlier in today's class: dx/dy = 1/(dy/dx). Write that line down. That is the whole starting point.
Now differentiate both sides with respect to y. On the left, the derivative of dx/dy with respect to y is simply d²x/dy². That side is easy.

The right side is where students slip. 1/(dy/dx) is a function of x, not of y. So differentiate it with respect to x, and then multiply by dx/dy to convert it into a derivative with respect to y. If it helps, think of it as dx/dx cancelling and dy/dy surviving — you are doing d/dy on both sides, honestly.

Then it is just the chain rule. Derivative of 1/(something) is −1/(something)², so you get −1/(dy/dx)² times the derivative of dy/dx with respect to x, which is d²y/dx². Finally replace that leftover dx/dy by 1/(dy/dx), and the square becomes a cube. Proved.

quickChecks.q: If y = x², find d²x/dy² in terms of x.
steps: 1. dy/dx = 2x and d²y/dx² = 2.
3. Simplify: −1/(4x³).

quickChecks.q: If y = x³, find the value of d²x/dy² at x = 2.
steps: 1. dy/dx = 3x² and d²y/dx² = 6x.

quickChecks.q: If y = eˣ, show that d²x/dy² = −1/y².
steps: 1. dy/dx = eˣ and d²y/dx² = eˣ.
2. d²x/dy² = −eˣ/(eˣ)³ = −eˣ/e³ˣ = −e⁻²ˣ.
3. Since y = eˣ, this is −1/y².

concepts.title: Differentiating an expression in x with respect to y
concepts.oneLine: To differentiate any function of x with respect to y, differentiate it with respect to x as usual and then multiply by dx/dy.
notes: Look at what we just did in that IIT question. The thing we were differentiating was a function of x, but the variable we were differentiating against was y. So we used the chain rule: differentiate the function of x with respect to x, and then write dx/dy next to it.
Make this a habit: function of x, with respect to y → do it with respect to x first, then multiply by dx/dy. Nothing else changes. Your old differentiation skill stays exactly the same.
Take d/dy(1/x). The derivative of 1/x with respect to x is −1/x². Now tag on dx/dy, and you get −(1/x²)·dx/dy. And if you ever need dx/dy as a number, remember it is just 1 divided by dy/dx.

Now make the inside harder. d/dy(1/ln x): first differentiate 1/(something) → −1/(ln x)². Then the derivative of that something, ln x, which is 1/x. Then dx/dy. So you get −(1/(ln x)²)·(1/x)·dx/dy. Same chain rule, one more link.

quickChecks.q: Find d/dy(x³).
steps: 1. Differentiate with respect to x: 3x².
2. Multiply by dx/dy.

quickChecks.q: Find d/dy(√x).
steps: 1. Differentiate with respect to x: 1/(2√x).
2. Multiply by dx/dy.

quickChecks.q: Find d/dy(1/x²).
steps: 1. Write it as x⁻². Differentiate with respect to x: −2x⁻³ = −2/x³.
2. Multiply by dx/dy.

concepts.title: Kill the parameter before you differentiate
concepts.oneLine: If the parameter can be killed, kill it first — squaring and adding x²+y² = t+1/t with x⁴+y⁴ = t²+1/t² collapses everything to x²y² = 1, and then dy/dx is one line.
notes: Parameter questions of this family are common. And the first instinct is always wrong: you reach for dy/dt and dx/dt and start grinding.

Look at what you are given instead. Both equations are built from t + 1/t and t² + 1/t². Square the first one and the t part matches the second one exactly, so it cancels. If the parameter can be disappeared, disappear it before you differentiate.

What is left is x²y² = 1. No t. From here, differentiate and you are done in one line. And this is the real gain: if I ask you the double derivative, or the triple, it makes no difference now — the parametric form would have punished you for each one.
This is not to say the normal parametric method fails. It works. This is simply the much better method, so where t can go, let it go.

quickChecks.q: x = t + 1/t and y = t − 1/t. Find dy/dx by killing the parameter.
steps: 1. x² = t² + 2 + 1/t² and y² = t² − 2 + 1/t².
2. Subtract: x² − y² = 4. t is gone.
3. Differentiate with respect to x: 2x − 2y(dy/dx) = 0.

quickChecks.q: x = a cos t, y = a sin t. Find dy/dx without using dy/dt.
steps: 1. Square and add: x² + y² = a².
2. Differentiate with respect to x: 2x + 2y(dy/dx) = 0.

quickChecks.q: From x²y² = 1 with y = 1/x, find d²y/dx².
steps: 2. dy/dx = −x⁻² = −1/x².
3. Differentiate again: d²y/dx² = 2x⁻³.

concepts.title: Differentiating one function with respect to another
concepts.oneLine: To differentiate u with respect to v, divide their x-derivatives: du/dv = (du/dx)/(dv/dx).
notes: Look at what the question is really asking. Call the first function u and the second one v. The question wants du/dv — nothing more.

Now compare it with the parametric work we just finished. There, x was a function of t and y was a function of t, and we wrote dy/dx = (dy/dt)/(dx/dt). Here u is a function of x and v is a function of x. So x is playing exactly the role t was playing: x is the hidden parameter.

That gives you the whole chapter in one line: du/dv = (du/dx)/(dv/dx). Differentiate the first function, differentiate the second function, divide. Both derivatives are ordinary product-rule, chain-rule work — a joke by now.
So you need no new technique and no new rules for this topic. Spot u, spot v, differentiate each one with respect to x, and put the second one underneath.

quickChecks.q: Differentiate x³ with respect to x².
steps: 1. u = x³, v = x², so du/dv = (du/dx)/(dv/dx).
2. du/dx = 3x², dv/dx = 2x.
3. du/dv = 3x²/2x = 3x/2.

quickChecks.q: Differentiate sin x with respect to cos x.
steps: 1. u = sin x, v = cos x.
2. du/dx = cos x, dv/dx = −sin x.
3. du/dv = cos x/(−sin x) = −cot x.

quickChecks.q: Differentiate ln x with respect to x².
steps: 1. u = ln x, v = x².
2. du/dx = 1/x, dv/dx = 2x.

concepts.title: du/dv at a point: a JEE-style example
concepts.oneLine: To get the derivative of f(tan x) with respect to g(sec x), divide the two x-derivatives first and substitute x = π/4 only at the end.
notes: Here is the question. You are given f′(1) = 2 and g′(√2) = 4, and you have to find the derivative of f(tan x) with respect to g(sec x) at x = π/4.
Do not look for anything new. Call the top u = f(tan x), the bottom v = g(sec x), and use du/dv = (du/dx) ÷ (dv/dx). Both derivatives are plain chain rule.
Top: du/dx = f′(tan x) × sec²x. Bottom: dv/dx = g′(sec x) × sec x tan x. Notice the bottom has two factors after g′ — sec x differentiates to sec x tan x, not to sec x.

Now substitute. The argument inside f′ becomes tan(π/4) = 1, and inside g′ it becomes sec(π/4) = √2 — that is exactly why the question handed you f′(1) and g′(√2). Put the numbers in and the whole thing collapses to 1/√2.

quickChecks.q: If f′(1/√2) = 4 and g′(1/√2) = 2, find the derivative of f(sin x) with respect to g(cos x) at x = π/4.
steps: 1. du/dx = f′(sin x) · cos x and dv/dx = g′(cos x) · (−sin x).
2. At x = π/4, sin x = cos x = 1/√2.

quickChecks.q: If f′(√3) = 6 and g′(2) = 3, find the derivative of f(tan x) with respect to g(sec x) at x = π/3.
steps: 1. Ratio = [f′(tan x) · sec²x] / [g′(sec x) · sec x · tan x].
2. At x = π/3: tan x = √3, sec x = 2, sec²x = 4.

quickChecks.q: If f′(4) = 3 and g′(8) = 2, find the derivative of f(x²) with respect to g(x³) at x = 2.
steps: 1. du/dx = f′(x²) · 2x and dv/dx = g′(x³) · 3x².
2. At x = 2: x² = 4 and x³ = 8, so use f′(4) = 3 and g′(8) = 2.

concepts.title: Why variable^variable needs logarithmic differentiation
concepts.oneLine: From x and 2 you can build four functions — x², 2^x, 2² and x^x — and only the last one, variable to the power variable, has no standard derivative, so you take log on both sides to bring the power down.
notes: Look at x² first. Here the base is the variable and the power is a constant, so this is a polynomial function and the derivative is 2x. No thinking needed.

Now flip it: 2^x. Base constant, power variable — that is an exponential function, and its derivative is known too. Flip once more and take 2². Both base and power are constants, so this is just 4, a constant, and its derivative is 0. Three functions, three known answers.

Now the fourth one: x^x. Base is a variable and the power is also a variable. Variable to the power variable does not fall into any standard category, so there is no formula you can put on it. It is not polynomial, not exponential, not constant. Try to force any of those three formulas and you get a wrong answer.

So in such a question the power has to come down from upstairs to the front. The one tool that brings a power down is log, so we take log on both sides. That single step turns an impossible form into an ordinary differentiation, and that is why this is the most used type of question in this whole topic.

quickChecks.q: Out of x³, 3^x and x^x, which ones can you differentiate straight away with a standard formula?
steps: 1. x³ is variable to the power constant, so it is polynomial and the derivative is 3x².
2. 3^x is constant to the power variable, so it is exponential and the derivative is 3^x ln 3.
3. x^x is variable to the power variable, so it belongs to no standard category.
quickChecks.answer: x³ and 3^x are direct; x^x needs log on both sides first.

quickChecks.q: What is the derivative of 3⁴?
steps: 1. Base and power are both constants, so 3⁴ is just the number 81.
2. The derivative of a constant is 0.

quickChecks.q: For y = (sin x)^x, write only the first step.
steps: 1. The base sin x is a variable quantity and the power x is also a variable, so this is variable to the power variable.
2. No standard formula applies, so bring the power down by taking log on both sides.
3. ln y = x ln(sin x).
quickChecks.answer: Take log on both sides: ln y = x ln(sin x).

concepts.title: Logarithmic differentiation: x^x and x^y + y^x = a^b
concepts.oneLine: Take ln on both sides to pull the power down, differentiate, multiply back by y — and for x^y + y^x = a^b, log each term separately, then solve for dy/dx.
notes: The whole problem with x^x is that the power is not a number. So I bring the power down first. Take ln on both sides, and x^x becomes x·ln x — now it is just a product, and product rule finishes it.
One log pulls down one power. If the power itself carries a power, like a tower, you simply take the log a second time. The question gets longer, the concept does not change at all.
Now x^y + y^x = a^b. Here many students want to take ln of the whole left side. Don't. ln of a sum has no formula — ln(a + b) is not ln a + ln b. There is nothing to gain from a direct log here.

So split it. Call x^y as y₁ and y^x as y₂. Then y₁ + y₂ = a^b, and a^b is just a constant, so dy₁/dx + dy₂/dx = 0. Differentiate y₁ by taking log, differentiate y₂ by taking log, put both back, take dy/dx common and solve.

quickChecks.q: If y = x^x, find dy/dx at x = e.
steps: 1. dy/dx = x^x (1 + ln x).
2. Put x = e: dy/dx = e^e (1 + ln e) = e^e (1 + 1).

quickChecks.q: If y = x^(2x), find dy/dx.
steps: 1. Take ln: ln y = 2x·ln x.
2. Differentiate: (1/y)·dy/dx = 2·ln x + 2x·(1/x) = 2 ln x + 2.
3. Multiply by y = x^(2x): dy/dx = x^(2x)·2(1 + ln x).

quickChecks.q: If x^y = y^x, find dy/dx.
steps: 1. Both sides are products after a log, so take ln on both sides: y·ln x = x·ln y.
2. Differentiate: ln x·(dy/dx) + y/x = ln y + (x/y)·(dy/dx).
3. Collect dy/dx terms: (dy/dx)(ln x − x/y) = ln y − y/x.

concepts.title: Log differentiation as an optional shortcut for products and quotients
concepts.oneLine: Taking log before differentiating is a choice for long products and quotients, but for a variable raised to a variable power it is the only way.
notes: In the last part log was taken because there was no choice: x^x, and x^y + y^x = a^b. A variable sitting on a variable power cannot be touched by the product rule or the chain rule. Log was the only door.

Now comes the second use, and this one is softer. If you are handed a long product or a long quotient of ordinary functions, taking log breaks the whole thing into a sum of simple logs. Differentiating a sum is always lighter work than differentiating a product chain. So the second use of logarithmic differentiation is only a shortcut for products and quotients — not a rule you are forced to follow.

Take y²·x = x² + 1. You can differentiate it directly with the product rule, or take log first. Both are right, and both take roughly the same number of lines. Nobody can mark you wrong for either, so pick the one your hand is faster at.

Here is the line that matters in the exam. If there is no variable to the power of a variable anywhere, log is your decision; the moment a variable sits on a variable power, there is no decision left — log is the only way out. And if the power itself is another function piled on top, like y₁ raised to y₂, nothing moves until you bring that power down with log.

quickChecks.q: Find dy/dx if y²x³ = x + 1.
steps: 1. Take log: 2 log y + 3 log x = log(x + 1).
2. Differentiate: (2/y)(dy/dx) + 3/x = 1/(x + 1).

quickChecks.q: Differentiate y = (x + 1)(x + 2)(x + 3) using log.
steps: 1. Take log: log y = log(x + 1) + log(x + 2) + log(x + 3).
quickChecks.answer: dy/dx = (x + 1)(x + 2)(x + 3)[1/(x + 1) + 1/(x + 2) + 1/(x + 3)] — the product rule gives the same answer, so here log was only a choice.

quickChecks.q: In which of these is taking log compulsory, and why? (i) y = x³·sin x (ii) y = x^(sin x)
steps: 1. In (i) no variable sits on a variable power, so the product rule works directly — log is only a choice.
2. In (ii) the power sin x is itself a function of x, so no product or chain rule can touch it until the power comes down.
quickChecks.answer: Only (ii). A variable to the power of a variable leaves no decision — log is the only way out.

concepts.title: Worked example: y as a half power of x^x
concepts.oneLine: For y = √(xˣ), pull the root into the power first — ln y = (x/2)ln x — and you land on dy/dx = (y/2)(1 + ln x).
notes: Here y is √(xˣ). Before you touch log, clean the power. A square root is just a half power, and powers multiply — so xˣ raised to ½ is x to the power x/2.
Now take log: ln y = (x/2)ln x. One root gone, one product left, and that product is routine to differentiate.
