Differentiate both sides. On the left you get (1/y)(dy/dx) — never forget that 1/y, the chain rule puts it there. On the right the ½ stays outside and x ln x differentiates to 1 + ln x.
So (1/y)(dy/dx) = ½(1 + ln x), which gives dy/dx = (y/2)(1 + ln x). Leave the answer in terms of y if the options are written that way; otherwise put y = √(xˣ) back in.

quickChecks.q: Write √(xˣ) as a single power of x.
steps: 1. √ means a half power: (xˣ)^½.
2. Powers multiply: x^(x · ½).

quickChecks.q: If y = (xˣ)^(1/3), find dy/dx.
steps: 1. y = x to the power x/3, so ln y = (x/3)ln x.
3. Multiply by y.

quickChecks.q: If y = √(x³ˣ), find dy/dx.
steps: 1. y = x to the power 3x/2, so ln y = (3x/2)ln x.
3. Multiply by y.

concepts.title: Infinite power towers: spot the repetition
concepts.oneLine: In an infinite tower or an infinite radical, find the block that is the whole expression again, call it y (or y², or x + y), and you get a one-line equation you already know how to differentiate.
notes: One honest word first. This is not a new technique of differentiation — it is a problem type. Everything I use here, log differentiation and implicit differentiation, you already have.

The only new skill is recognition. Walk your eye down the expression and ask: from where does the whole thing start repeating? Replace that repeating block by y, and a monster of infinite length becomes a two-symbol equation.

When the outside has a root or a half power and the inside is messy, use the n trick. Write n for the whole ugly power, simplify the powers like a normal index question, and then look at what n actually was. Very often n turns out to be y² sitting right there.

One caution on where to start. The repetition begins after the first symbol, not before it. In √(x + √(x + …)) the thing under the first root is x and then the same radical again, so that block is x + y — not x, and not y alone.

quickChecks.q: Find the value of y if y = √(12 + √(12 + √(12 + …))).
steps: 1. Under the first root: 12 and then the same radical, which is y. So y = √(12 + y).
2. Square: y² = 12 + y, i.e. y² − y − 12 = 0.
3. Factorise: (y − 4)(y + 3) = 0, so y = 4 or y = −3.
4. A square root is non-negative, so reject −3.

quickChecks.q: If y = √(3x + √(3x + √(3x + …))), find dy/dx.
steps: 1. The block under the first root is 3x + y, so y = √(3x + y).
2. Square: y² = 3x + y.
3. Differentiate: 2y(dy/dx) = 3 + dy/dx.
4. Collect: (dy/dx)(2y − 1) = 3.

quickChecks.q: For y = x^(x^(x^…)), find dy/dx at the point where y = 2.
steps: 1. The tower gives y = x^y, so with y = 2 we get x² = 2, that is x = √2.
2. Derivative of the tower: dy/dx = y²/(x(1 − y ln x)).

concepts.title: Differentiating inverse trig functions: simplify first
concepts.oneLine: For y = sin⁻¹(2x√(1−x²)) type functions, put x = sin θ, simplify with the correct principal-range case, and only then differentiate — and the answer changes with the interval of x.
notes: Look at y = sin⁻¹(2x√(1−x²)). Do not attack it with the chain rule. Simplify first, differentiate last — that is the whole method here.

Put x = sin θ, which means θ = sin⁻¹x. In this question x is given between −1/√2 and 1/√2, so θ sits between −π/4 and π/4. Now √(1−sin²θ) is |cos θ|, and on −π/4 to π/4 cos θ is positive, so the mod goes away and the inside becomes 2 sin θ cos θ = sin 2θ.

So y = sin⁻¹(sin 2θ). We never cancel sin⁻¹ and sin blindly. But here θ is between −π/4 and π/4, so 2θ is between −π/2 and π/2 — exactly the principal range — and only because of that y = 2θ = 2 sin⁻¹x. Differentiate: dy/dx = 2/√(1−x²).

Change the interval and the answer changes. For x from 1/√2 to 1 the simplified form is π − 2 sin⁻¹x, and for x from −1 to −1/√2 it is −π − 2 sin⁻¹x. In both of those the derivative is −2/√(1−x²). The differentiation is never the hard part; the interval of x decides the sign.

quickChecks.q: Find dy/dx for y = sin⁻¹(2x√(1−x²)) at x = 0.6.
steps: 1. 0.6 is less than 1/√2 ≈ 0.707, so we are in the middle case: y = 2 sin⁻¹x.

quickChecks.q: Find dy/dx for y = sin⁻¹(2x√(1−x²)) at x = 0.8.
steps: 1. 0.8 is greater than 1/√2, so y = π − 2 sin⁻¹x.

quickChecks.q: Simplify and differentiate y = sin⁻¹(2x√(1−x²)) at x = −½.
steps: 1. −½ lies between −1/√2 and 1/√2, so y = 2 sin⁻¹x.

concepts.title: Derivative of an inverse function you cannot write down
concepts.oneLine: When the inverse g of f cannot be written down, differentiate f(g(x)) = x to get g′(a) = 1/f′(g(a)) — the only real work is spotting which input of f returns a.
notes: Take f(x) = x³ + x + 1. Try to find its inverse. You would have to solve a cubic for x, and you do not have that machinery. So the inverse exists, but you cannot write it.

Now the paper says: g(x) is the inverse of f. Find g′(3). This looks impossible because g itself is unknown. It is not. Use the one relation that is always true for an inverse pair: f(g(x)) = x. Or g(f(x)) = x. Both are correct, and both take the same amount of work — pick whichever comes to your mind first.

Differentiate f(g(x)) = x by the chain rule: f′(g(x)) · g′(x) = 1. Put x = 3, since 3 is the point you want. You get f′(g(3)) · g′(3) = 1. So the whole question has collapsed into one small question: what is g(3)?

And g means reverse mapping. Asking for g(3) is asking: which number goes into f so that f returns 3? Check x = 1: 1 + 1 + 1 = 3. So g(3) = 1. After that it is school arithmetic — f′(x) = 3x² + 1, so f′(1) = 4, and g′(3) = ¼.

quickChecks.q: f(x) = x³ + 2x + 3 and g is the inverse of f. Find g′(6).
steps: 3. Which input gives 6? f(1) = 1 + 2 + 3 = 6, so g(6) = 1.

quickChecks.q: f(x) = x⁵ + 2x + 1 and g is the inverse of f. Find g′(4).
steps: 1. f′(g(x)) · g′(x) = 1, and at x = 4 this is f′(g(4)) · g′(4) = 1.
2. Which input gives 4? f(1) = 1 + 2 + 1 = 4, so g(4) = 1.

quickChecks.q: f(x) = x³ + 3x + 2 and g is the inverse of f. Find g′(2).
steps: 2. Which input gives 2? f(0) = 0 + 0 + 2 = 2, so g(2) = 0. Do not forget to test 0.

concepts.title: The g(f(x)) = x route, and g′ at other points
concepts.oneLine: Differentiate g(f(x)) = x to get g′(f(x))·f′(x) = 1, then find g′(k) by asking which x makes f(x) = k.
notes: Second one, and I don't want to put any different logic. Start from g(f(x)) = x, because g undoes f. Differentiate both sides, chain rule on the left: g′(f(x))·f′(x) = 1.
That is the same relation we got the other way round. Nothing new to remember. The only real work in these questions is finding which x to put in.

Look at it like this. f is the forward mapping, g is the reverse mapping. The number sitting inside g′ is an output of f. So ask yourself one question: which x goes into f so that this number comes out? Here f is x³ + x + 1, and f(1) = 3, so for g′(3) put x = 1 and get g′(3) = 1/f′(1).

If you can make that mapping you will never get stuck; if you can't make it, you're finished. Here nobody gets stuck. Want −1? f(−1) = −1. Want 11? f(2) = 11. Cool and calm, read the mapping backwards, put that x in, done.

quickChecks.q: f(x) = x³ + x + 1, g is its inverse. Find g′(1).
steps: 1. Need f(x) = 1: x³ + x + 1 = 1 gives x³ + x = 0, so x = 0.

quickChecks.q: Same f and g. Find g′(−9).
Same f and g. Find g′(31).

concepts.title: Which points a questioner can actually ask g′ at
concepts.oneLine: An inverse-derivative question is always set at a value that comes from a small, friendly input — so don't solve the cubic, just scan x = 0, ±1, ±2, 3 and find the input that produces the given number.
notes: Take the function f(x) = x³ + x + 1 again, with g as its inverse. Someone could be clever and compute f(13) = 13³ + 13 + 1 = 2211, then ask you for g′(2211). Technically it is a valid question. Practically it is a dead question.

Think about why. To answer it you must guess that 2211 came from 13. Nobody sitting in an exam hall has 13 in their head. And if that setter had used 33 instead of 13, nobody would get anywhere — so it is not a test of skill, it is a test of luck.

A question setter picks the input first, and he picks it from 0, 1, 2, −1, −2, at most 3 — then he gives you the output. So the number printed in the paper is always f of something small. Your job is to run backwards through that short list.
Say x = 3. Then f(3) = 27 + 3 + 1 = 31. So the paper says "find g′(31)", and you spot 3 instantly. That is a fair, practical JEE question — and that is the only kind you will ever be given.

quickChecks.q: f(x) = x³ + x + 1 and g is its inverse. Find g′(3).
steps: 1. Hunt the input: f(1) = 1 + 1 + 1 = 3, so g(3) = 1.

quickChecks.q: Same f. Find g′(11).
Same f. Find g′(−9).
steps: 1. Try the negatives: f(−2) = −8 − 2 + 1 = −9, so g(−9) = −2.

concepts.title: Higher-order derivative proofs: substitute y back
concepts.oneLine: For y = (ax+b)eᵐˣ, don't differentiate twice blindly — spot that the bracketed part is y itself, substitute it, and the proof y″ − 2my′ + m²y = 0 falls out in two lines.
notes: This is the higher-order derivative problem type. It used to come in boards, and in objective papers its weight is small — but keep it known, because then its question becomes very easy instead of a panic.
Understand one thing honestly: there is no new technique here. Differentiation is already over. This is pure manipulation — the whole question is about where you choose to substitute.
The first instinct is "differentiate, then see". Fine. y′ = aeᵐˣ + m(ax+b)eᵐˣ. Now stop and look. That (ax+b)eᵐˣ is exactly y. So write y′ = aeᵐˣ + my instead of carrying the long bracket forward.

Why is that the right instinct? Because the answer you have to prove is written in y″, y′ and y. If a highlighted chunk equals y, put y there and then differentiate. Differentiate once more, and wherever a lonely aeᵐˣ is left, trap it from the first line as y′ − my. Done.

quickChecks.q: If y = (3x+2)e⁵ˣ, prove that y″ − 10y′ + 25y = 0.
steps: 1. y′ = 3e⁵ˣ + 5(3x+2)e⁵ˣ = 3e⁵ˣ + 5y.
2. So 3e⁵ˣ = y′ − 5y.
3. Differentiate: y″ = 15e⁵ˣ + 5y′ = 5(3e⁵ˣ) + 5y′.
4. Substitute: y″ = 5(y′ − 5y) + 5y′ = 10y′ − 25y.
quickChecks.answer: y″ − 10y′ + 25y = 0 (it is the standard result with m = 5).

quickChecks.q: If y = x e²ˣ, show that y″ − 4y′ + 4y = 0.
steps: 2. y′ = e²ˣ + 2x e²ˣ = e²ˣ + 2y, so e²ˣ = y′ − 2y.

quickChecks.q: If y = (2x+1)e⁻³ˣ, find the relation between y″, y′ and y.
steps: 1. y′ = 2e⁻³ˣ − 3(2x+1)e⁻³ˣ = 2e⁻³ˣ − 3y, so 2e⁻³ˣ = y′ + 3y.
3. Substitute: y″ = −3(y′ + 3y) − 3y′ = −6y′ − 9y.

concepts.title: Second higher-order proof: choosing the substitution
concepts.oneLine: On y = eⁿˣ·cos(bx + c), put eⁿˣ = y/cos(bx + c) — the sin/cos ratio turns into a tan, eⁿˣ disappears, and y₂ − 2n y₁ + (n² + b²) y = 0 falls out in two lines; going direct gets you there too.
notes: We are on the same manipulation as before, but now with the cos version: y = eⁿˣ·cos(bx + c). Differentiate once and you get two pieces — one of them is exactly y again.

Here is the small thing worth doing. Instead of carrying eⁿˣ around, write eⁿˣ = y / cos(bx + c) and push it in. The eⁿˣ cancels, the sin over cos collapses into a tan, and the whole second derivative is now in terms of y and y₁ only.

Both routes are correct — substituting is shorter, going direct is longer but it also reaches the answer. There is no definition that tells you which one to pick. You pick it by having done enough questions.

One warning though. Don't start by substituting, get stuck halfway, and then switch to direct — that half-and-half solution is where the mess happens. Choose a road and finish on it. On a brand-new question the choice takes a moment to make, and that is completely normal.

quickChecks.q: If y = eⁿˣ·sin(bx + c), show that y₂ − 2n y₁ + (n² + b²) y = 0.
steps: 1. θ = bx + c, so y = eⁿˣ sin θ.
2. y₁ = eⁿˣ(n sin θ + b cos θ), and the first piece is n y, so y₁ = n y + b eⁿˣ cos θ.
3. So b eⁿˣ cos θ = y₁ − n y.
4. Differentiate again: y₂ = n y₁ + b(n eⁿˣ cos θ − b eⁿˣ sin θ) = n y₁ + n(y₁ − n y) − b² y.
5. So y₂ = 2n y₁ − (n² + b²) y.
quickChecks.answer: y₂ − 2n y₁ + (n² + b²) y = 0 — exactly the same relation as the cos version.

quickChecks.q: y = e³ˣ·cos 2x. Write the relation between y₂, y₁ and y.
steps: 1. Compare with eⁿˣ cos(bx + c): n = 3, b = 2, c = 0.
3. Put these into y₂ − 2n y₁ + (n² + b²) y = 0.

quickChecks.q: y = e⁴ˣ·cos x. Find y₁/y using the substitution trick.
steps: 1. y₁ = e⁴ˣ(4 cos x − sin x).
2. Put e⁴ˣ = y / cos x: y₁ = y(4 − sin x / cos x).
3. Divide by y.

flashcards.q: State the product rule for a product of three functions.
flashcards.a: $$\frac{d}{dx}(uvw) = u'vw + uv'w + uvw'$$Differentiate one factor at a time and freeze the other two, then add the pieces. Three factors give three terms, and the same march works for four factors or fifty.

flashcards.q: State the quotient rule, and say what sits in the denominator.
flashcards.a: $$\frac{d}{dx}\left(\frac{u}{v}\right) = \frac{u'v - uv'}{v^{2}}$$The denominator is the square of the bottom function. On top, the term carrying the derivative of the numerator comes first and the term with the derivative of the denominator follows with a minus.

flashcards.q: A product has 2 to the power x inside it. What is its derivative, and what goes wrong most often?
flashcards.a: $$\frac{d}{dx}(a^{x}) = a^{x}\ln a$$It is 2 to the power x times log 2. Two habits spoil it: copying the e to the power x rule and dropping the log, or treating it as a power and writing x times 2 to the power x minus one.

flashcards.q: How many terms must the derivative of a product have?
flashcards.a: Exactly as many as there are factors — three functions give three terms, fifty functions give fifty terms. In each term one factor is differentiated and every other factor is copied down untouched, so if you wrote four factors and your answer has three terms you skipped one.

flashcards.q: Differentiate x squared times 2 to the power x times sin x.
flashcards.a: $$\frac{d}{dx}\left(x^{2}\,2^{x}\sin x\right) = 2x\,2^{x}\sin x + x^{2}\,2^{x}\ln 2\,\sin x + x^{2}\,2^{x}\cos x$$Three functions, so count on three terms. If your answer has fewer terms than the product had factors, you skipped one.

flashcards.q: What one check tells you at a glance that a product derivative is incomplete?
flashcards.a: $$(uvwz)' = u'vwz + uv'wz + uvw'z + uvwz'$$Count the functions before you start, because that number is how many terms the answer must have. Four factors mean four terms, and the derivative of plain x is simply one.

flashcards.q: State the chain rule for a composite function.
flashcards.a: $$\frac{d}{dx}\,f(g(x)) = f'(g(x))\cdot g'(x)$$Differentiate the outer function with the inside kept exactly as it is, then multiply by the derivative of the inside. Keep peeling until the layer you differentiate is plain x.

flashcards.q: Why is the derivative of cos of log x not minus sin x?
flashcards.a: $$\frac{d}{dx}\cos(\ln x) = -\frac{\sin(\ln x)}{x}$$The inside never changes when you differentiate the outside, so the first factor is minus sine of log x, and you still owe the derivative of the inside, one over x. Count the layers before you start, because three layers mean three factors.

flashcards.q: While you differentiate the outside of a composite function, what happens to the inside?
flashcards.a: Nothing at all — it is copied exactly as it stands. You then owe a multiplication by the derivative of that inside, and you keep peeling until the layer you are differentiating is plain x.

flashcards.q: y is a function of x. Differentiate y cubed with respect to x.
flashcards.a: $$\frac{d}{dx}\left(y^{3}\right) = 3y^{2}\,\frac{dy}{dx}$$Three y squared times dy by dx. The extra factor was always there, even when the inside was x, because the derivative of x with respect to x is simply one.

flashcards.q: Why did the extra factor never show up while the inside was x?
flashcards.a: $$\frac{dx}{dx} = 1$$It was there all along, but it was one. The derivative of x with respect to x is one, and multiplying by one changes nothing. The moment the inside is y the peeling ends in dy by dx instead.

flashcards.q: The same function, log x, is differentiated with respect to x, to t and to y. Give all three answers.
flashcards.a: $$\frac{d}{dt}(\ln x) = \frac{1}{x}\cdot\frac{dx}{dt}$$One over x; one over x times dx by dt; one over x times dx by dy. Same function, three different questions.

flashcards.q: Which two questions must you ask before you differentiate anything?
flashcards.a: $$\frac{d}{dx}\big(f(y)\big) = f'(y)\cdot\frac{dy}{dx}$$Which variable the function is written in, and with respect to which variable it is being differentiated. If the two letters are not the same, a factor is left behind, and the respect variable always goes in the denominator of it.

flashcards.q: Which letters decide whether a chain-rule factor appears at all?
flashcards.a: The letter inside the function and the letter under the d. Same letter means a plain derivative and you stop there; different letters mean the plain derivative times the derivative of the inside letter with respect to the respect letter.

flashcards.q: If y cubed minus y equals 2x, find dy by dx and then the second derivative.
flashcards.a: $$y^{3}-y=2x \;\Rightarrow\; \frac{dy}{dx}=\frac{2}{3y^{2}-1},\qquad \frac{d^{2}y}{dx^{2}}=-\frac{24y}{\left(3y^{2}-1\right)^{3}}$$Differentiating gives dy by dx in terms of y. Differentiate that again, then substitute the first derivative back so the answer is purely in y.

flashcards.q: Your dy by dx has come out as a constant over a bracket. What is the short route to the second derivative?
flashcards.a: $$\frac{d}{dx}\left(\frac{1}{t}\right) = -\frac{1}{t^{2}}\cdot\frac{dt}{dx}$$Do not open the quotient rule. Write it as the constant times the bracket to the power minus one and chain rule it. Two lines instead of six, and far fewer sign slips. Remember that the bracket differentiates with a dy by dx attached.

flashcards.q: Does a second derivative bring in any new function?
flashcards.a: $$\frac{d}{dx}\left(y^{n}\right) = n\,y^{\,n-1}\,\frac{dy}{dx}$$No. Everything stays as it was in the first round — you simply differentiate your dy by dx expression once more with respect to x. Say with respect to x before every line, and each y term then collects its dy by dx automatically.

flashcards.q: If y is x plus the root of x squared plus a squared, all raised to the power n, prove the standard result for dy by dx.
flashcards.a: $$\frac{dy}{dx} = \frac{n\left(x+\sqrt{x^2+a^2}\right)^{n}}{\sqrt{x^2+a^2}} = \frac{ny}{\sqrt{x^2+a^2}}$$Name the bracket, apply the power rule with the chain rule, then take the LCM inside the bracket. The bracket is reborn in the numerator, the powers add from n minus one back to n, and that power is the given y.

flashcards.q: Why name the long bracket before you differentiate it?
flashcards.a: Because most of the errors in this proof are copying errors. Write the bracket once, carry its name raised to the power n through the working, and restore the bracket only in the last line.

flashcards.q: y is f of sin x. What is dy by dx, and what does f dash of sin x mean?
flashcards.a: $$\frac{dy}{dx} = f'(\sin x)\cdot \cos x$$It means work out f dash and then put sin x wherever x stood. Multiply that by the derivative of the inside, cos x. Writing only the first factor leaves the answer incomplete.

flashcards.q: Reading f of sin x, why is the product rule the wrong tool?
flashcards.a: Because it is one function acting on another, not a product. Differentiate the outer function as it stands with the inner expression copied inside f dash, then multiply by the derivative of that inside.

flashcards.q: f dash equals g and f double dash equals minus f. F of x is the square of f of x over two plus the square of g of x over two, and F of 5 is 5. Find F of 10.
flashcards.a: $$f' = g,\quad f'' = -f \;\Rightarrow\; g' = -f$$Five. Differentiating F gives f times g minus g times f, which is zero, and that holds for every x, so F is constant and takes the value 5 everywhere.

flashcards.q: A function has zero derivative at one point. Is it constant?
flashcards.a: $$F'(x) = 0 \ \ \forall x \in \mathbb{R} \;\Rightarrow\; F(x) = \text{constant}$$No. The derivative of x cubed is zero at the origin and x cubed is certainly not constant. You may only call a function constant when its derivative vanishes for every real x, with nothing substituted.

flashcards.q: Differentiate the square of h of x over two with respect to x.
flashcards.a: $$\frac{d}{dx}\left[h\!\left(\tfrac{x}{2}\right)\right]^2 = 2\,h\!\left(\tfrac{x}{2}\right)h'\!\left(\tfrac{x}{2}\right)\cdot\tfrac{1}{2}$$Chain rule in strict order — the square first, then the function, then the inside. The 2 from the square and the half from the inside cancel each other, which is why they disappear from the next line. Skipping that inner half is the habit that costs marks in a question where it does not cancel.

flashcards.q: The data gives only relations between derivatives. What is your first pen stroke?
flashcards.a: Differentiate the function the question has built. There is nothing to substitute until you make something to substitute into, so derivative data means differentiate.

flashcards.q: What new rule does an implicit relation need?
flashcards.a: $$\frac{d}{dx}\big(f(y)\big) = f'(y)\cdot\frac{dy}{dx}$$None at all. Differentiate both sides as written, remembering that every y you differentiate hands you a dy by dx, and that a term like x times cos y is a product and so must give two pieces. Then push all the dy by dx terms to one side, take it common and divide.

flashcards.q: If y equals x times cos y plus y times cos x, find dy by dx.
flashcards.a: $$\frac{dy}{dx} = \frac{\cos y - y\sin x}{1 + x\sin y - \cos x}$$Both terms are products, so each gives two pieces. Collect the dy by dx terms on the left, take it common, and divide by the bracket.

flashcards.q: What does implicit actually mean here, and which new rule does it need?
flashcards.a: It only means y is not sitting alone on one side — a way of speaking, not a separate category of function. No new rule is needed: differentiate both sides as written, let every y hand you a dy by dx, then collect those terms on one side, take it common and divide.

flashcards.q: If x times the root of one plus y, plus y times the root of one plus x, equals zero, show that dy by dx is minus one over the square of one plus x.
flashcards.a: $$\frac{dy}{dx} = \frac{-1}{(1+x)^2}$$Shift one term and square, so the roots die. What is left factorises, and the factor x equals y only fits the origin, so the curve is the other one. That gives y alone in terms of x, and one quotient rule finishes it.

flashcards.q: After squaring, the relation factorises and two factors appear. How do you choose?
flashcards.a: $$x\sqrt{1+y} + y\sqrt{1+x} = 0 \;\Longrightarrow\; x + y + xy = 0$$Test each factor against the original relation. The factor x equals y fits only at the origin, so the curve is the other one, and that is the factor that gives y alone in terms of x.

flashcards.q: If x times the root of one minus y squared, plus y times the root of one minus x squared, equals one, prove the value of dy by dx.
flashcards.a: $$\sin^{-1}x+\sin^{-1}y=\frac{\pi}{2}\ \Rightarrow\ \frac{dy}{dx}=-\frac{\sqrt{1-y^2}}{\sqrt{1-x^2}}$$Substitute x equal to sin theta and y equal to sin phi, open the moduli using the principal range, and the left side becomes the sine of theta plus phi. That is one, so the sum of the two inverse sines is pi by two, and differentiating a constant is what puts the minus in the answer.

flashcards.q: Why must you write the modulus before you simplify the root of one minus sin squared theta?
flashcards.a: $$\sqrt{1-\sin^2\theta}=|\cos\theta|=\cos\theta,\quad \theta\in\left[-\frac{\pi}{2},\frac{\pi}{2}\right]$$Because the root of cos squared theta is the modulus of cos theta. It opens only after you quote the inverse sine range, minus ninety to ninety degrees, where cosine is positive. The range is not your choice and a negative x does not flip it.

flashcards.q: Where does the range minus ninety to ninety degrees come from?
flashcards.a: It comes free with the definition of inverse sine, which always returns an angle in the first or the fourth quadrant. It is not your choice and a negative x does not change it. Cosine is positive in both quadrants, so the modulus opens with no case split.

flashcards.q: If x is t squared and y is 2t, find dy by dx and the second derivative.
flashcards.a: $$x=t^{2},\; y=2t \;\Rightarrow\; \frac{dy}{dx}=\frac{1}{t},\qquad \frac{d^{2}y}{dx^{2}}=-\frac{1}{2t^{3}}$$Divide the two t-derivatives for the first one. Then differentiate that with respect to t and multiply by dt by dx, which is one over 2t.

flashcards.q: What is the standard blunder in the second derivative of a parametric function?
flashcards.a: $$\frac{d^2y}{dx^2} = \frac{d}{dt}\left(\frac{dy}{dx}\right)\cdot\frac{dt}{dx}$$Dividing the two second t-derivatives, copying what worked for the first derivative. Only the first derivatives divide. You must differentiate dy by dx with respect to t and then multiply by dt by dx, which is the reciprocal of dx by dt.

flashcards.q: Which parametric step are you allowed to do only once?
flashcards.a: $$\frac{dt}{dx} = \frac{1}{dx/dt}$$Dividing one t-derivative by the other. That gives the first derivative and nothing more. For the second one go back to the definition — differentiate dy by dx with respect to t, then multiply by the reciprocal of dx by dt.

flashcards.q: For x equal to g of t and y equal to f of t, write the second derivative in terms of f and g.
flashcards.a: $$\frac{d^2y}{dx^2} = \frac{g'(t)f''(t) - f'(t)g''(t)}{\left(g'(t)\right)^{3}}$$The square in the denominator comes from the quotient rule on f dash over g dash, and the third g dash comes from dt by dx.

flashcards.q: Why is the denominator of the parametric second derivative a cube and not a square?
flashcards.a: $$\frac{dt}{dx} = \frac{1}{dx/dt} = \frac{1}{g'(t)}$$The square comes from the quotient rule on the ratio of the two first derivatives, and the third factor comes from dt by dx. If your denominator is squared, you dropped the chain-rule step.

flashcards.q: Express the second derivative of x with respect to y in terms of dy by dx and the second derivative of y.
flashcards.a: $$\frac{d^{2}x}{dy^{2}}=-\frac{\frac{d^{2}y}{dx^{2}}}{\left(\frac{dy}{dx}\right)^{3}}$$Start from dx by dy equals one over dy by dx and differentiate both sides with respect to y. Only first derivatives invert, which is where the minus sign and the cube come from.

flashcards.q: Which derivatives invert, and which do not?
flashcards.a: $$\frac{dx}{dy}=\frac{1}{\frac{dy}{dx}}$$Only the first ones. dx by dy is one over dy by dx, but the second derivative does not flip — you must differentiate that flipped relation again, and that is where the minus sign and the cube are born.

flashcards.q: What is the derivative of one over x with respect to y?
flashcards.a: $$\frac{d}{dy}\left(\frac{1}{x}\right) = -\frac{1}{x^{2}}\cdot\frac{dx}{dy}$$Differentiate with respect to x first, which gives minus one over x squared, and then attach dx by dy. Read the denominator of the differentiation before you write, because with respect to y means the upside-down factor.

flashcards.q: How do you differentiate an expression in x when the question says with respect to y?
flashcards.a: $$\frac{d}{dy}\,f(x) \;=\; \frac{d}{dx}f(x)\cdot\frac{dx}{dy}$$Differentiate it with respect to x exactly as you always would, then write dx by dy beside it. Two steps, every single time, and nothing else about your differentiation changes.

flashcards.q: x squared plus y squared is t plus one over t, and x to the fourth plus y to the fourth is t squared plus one over t squared. Find dy by dx.
flashcards.a: $$\frac{dy}{dx}=-\frac{y}{x}$$Before touching dy by dt, check whether t can be removed. Squaring the first equation lets the fourth-power terms be swapped out using the second, so every t cancels and only x squared y squared equals one survives. Keep it squared rather than taking a root, or you lose a branch. Differentiating gives minus y over x, which also proves the form the question usually asks for.

flashcards.q: Before you write dy by dt, what is worth five seconds?
flashcards.a: $$x^{2}y^{2}=1$$Checking whether the two given equations combine — try squaring, adding, subtracting or multiplying them. If the parameter walks out, what is left is one line of work and the higher derivatives come free.

flashcards.q: How do you differentiate one function with respect to another?
flashcards.a: $$\frac{du}{dv} = \frac{\;du/dx\;}{\;dv/dx\;}$$Label the first function u and the one after the words with respect to as v, then divide their x-derivatives: the derivative of the function you differentiate against always goes underneath. It is parametric differentiation with x as the parameter, so there is no new rule to hunt for.

flashcards.q: Which of the two functions goes underneath, and why is there no new rule to learn?
flashcards.a: The derivative of the function you are differentiating with respect to always goes in the denominator. It is parametric differentiation with x playing the part of the parameter, so with respect to is simply a division bar.

flashcards.q: Given f dash of one is 2 and g dash of root two is 4, differentiate f of tan x with respect to g of sec x at x equal to pi by four.
flashcards.a: $$\frac{d\,[f(\tan x)]}{d\,[g(\sec x)]}=\frac{f'(\tan x)\,\sec^{2}x}{g'(\sec x)\,\sec x\,\tan x}$$Write the ratio of the two chain-rule derivatives first and substitute only afterwards. The argument of f dash is tan x, which at pi by four is one, and of g dash is sec x, which is root two, so the given values are exactly the ones you need. Note that sec x differentiates to sec x tan x. The top is 2 times 2 and the bottom is 4 times root two, so the answer is one over root two.

flashcards.q: Why substitute the value of x only at the end?
flashcards.a: Because a number has derivative zero, so substituting early destroys the differentiation. Write the full ratio with f dash and g dash still untouched, and the arguments inside them then tell you which of the given values the setter meant you to use.

flashcards.q: Using only x and the number 2 you can build four functions. Which one has no standard derivative, and why?
flashcards.a: $$y = x^{x} \;\Rightarrow\; \ln y = x\ln x$$x to the power x. Variable to the power constant is polynomial, constant to the power variable is exponential, and constant to the power constant is just a number. Variable to the power variable is none of the three, so no formula fits and the power must be brought down by a log.

flashcards.q: Base variable, power constant — which standard form is that, and what is its derivative?
flashcards.a: $$\frac{d}{dx}\left(x^{n}\right) = n\,x^{n-1}$$The polynomial form, so the power comes down in front and the index drops by one. Checking the base and the power before you write is what stops you forcing this formula onto a variable power.

flashcards.q: Differentiate y equal to x to the power x.
flashcards.a: $$\frac{dy}{dx} = x^{x}\,(1 + \ln x)$$Take log on both sides to get log y equal to x log x, differentiate, and multiply back by y.

flashcards.q: How do you handle x to the power y plus y to the power x equal to a constant?
flashcards.a: $$\frac{dy}{dx} = -\,\frac{y\,x^{\,y-1} + y^{x}\ln y}{x^{y}\ln x + x\,y^{\,x-1}}$$There is no log of a sum, so do not take a log of the whole left side. Name the two terms, take a log inside each one, differentiate both, add them to zero because the right side is a constant, then take dy by dx common and solve.

flashcards.q: A sum of two variable-to-the-variable terms sits on one side. Why not take a log of the whole side?
flashcards.a: Because a log breaks a product, not a sum, and the log of a sum has no expansion. Name the two terms separately, take a log inside each one, differentiate both, and only then collect dy by dx.

flashcards.q: Is taking a log compulsory for a long product or quotient?
flashcards.a: $$\frac{d}{dx}\big(\log y\big) = \frac{1}{y}\,\frac{dy}{dx}$$No. There it only breaks the work into a sum of logs, both routes are equally correct and about equally long, so use whichever your hand is faster at. It becomes compulsory the moment a variable sits on a variable power. And remember that differentiating log y leaves a dy by dx behind.

flashcards.q: Which log laws are the reason a log helps on a long product or quotient?
flashcards.a: $$\log(AB) = \log A + \log B,\qquad \log\left(\frac{A}{B}\right) = \log A - \log B$$A log turns a product into a sum of logs and a quotient into a difference. Differentiating a sum term by term is lighter work than dragging a whole product chain through the product rule, which is why the log is worth taking here even though it is not compulsory.

flashcards.q: When is taking a log a choice, and when is it compulsory?
flashcards.a: Scan the question for a variable sitting on a variable power. If there is none, the log is only a shortcut for a long product or quotient and both routes are equally correct. The moment a variable sits on a variable power, there is no decision left.

flashcards.q: If y is the square root of x to the power x, find dy by dx.
flashcards.a: $$\frac{dy}{dx} = \frac{y}{2}\,(1 + \ln x)$$Clean the power first: a root is a half power and powers multiply, so y is x to the power x over two. Then take the log and differentiate, and the one over y on the left is what puts the y into the answer.

flashcards.q: Why clean the power before you take the log?
flashcards.a: $$y = \sqrt{x^x} = x^{x/2}$$Because a root is only a half power and powers multiply, so the root vanishes into the index and one clean product is left. Taking a log while the root is still sitting there costs you a full line and one extra chain rule.

flashcards.q: Differentiate the infinite tower of x to the power x to the power x and so on.
flashcards.a: $$\frac{dy}{dx} = \frac{y^{2}}{x\,(1 - y\ln x)}$$The power is the whole expression again, so the tower collapses to y equal to x to the power y. Take the log and differentiate implicitly.

flashcards.q: Differentiate the infinite nested radical, the root of x plus the root of x plus and so on.
flashcards.a: $$\frac{dy}{dx} = \frac{1}{2y - 1}$$Under the first root sits x and then the same radical again, so the block is x plus y. Squaring gives a short relation, and ordinary implicit differentiation finishes it.

flashcards.q: Where does the repetition start in an infinite nested radical?
flashcards.a: $$y^{2} = x^{\,y^{2}}$$After the first symbol, not before it. Cover the first root with your thumb and check that what is left is letter for letter the original expression. Replacing only the x, or writing y as root x plus y, loses the question.

flashcards.q: What is actually new in an infinite tower question?
flashcards.a: $$y = \sqrt{x + \sqrt{x + \sqrt{x + \cdots}}} \;\Rightarrow\; y^{2} = x + y$$Only the recognition. Log differentiation and implicit differentiation are tools you already have, so this is a problem type rather than a technique. The skill is spotting the block from which the whole expression repeats and putting y there.

flashcards.q: Simplify and differentiate the inverse sine of 2x times the root of one minus x squared.
flashcards.a: $$\sin^{-1}\!\left(2x\sqrt{1-x^{2}}\right)=2\sin^{-1}x,\qquad -\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\le x\le \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}$$Put x equal to sin theta, open the modulus, and the inside becomes sin of 2 theta. Cancel the inverse sine only when 2 theta is inside the principal range, which is what fixes the branch.

flashcards.q: Does that function have one derivative or three?
flashcards.a: $$\sin^{-1}\!\left(2x\sqrt{1-x^{2}}\right)=\pi-2\sin^{-1}x,\qquad \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\le x\le 1$$Three bands. On the middle band the derivative is two over the root of one minus x squared, and on both outer bands it is minus two over that root. The differentiation is never the hard part; the interval of x decides the sign.

flashcards.q: Where do the marks sit in an inverse-trig differentiation question?
flashcards.a: In the simplification, not the differentiation. Substitute x equal to sine theta, turn the given interval of x into an interval for theta, double it and see where it lands. That one check gives you the right case, and the derivative then takes seconds.

flashcards.q: f of x is x cubed plus x plus one and g is its inverse, which cannot be written down. Find g dash of three.
flashcards.a: $$f(x)=x^{3}+x+1,\; f(1)=3 \;\Rightarrow\; g'(3)=\frac{1}{f'(1)}=\frac{1}{4}$$Differentiate f of g of x equal to x to get f dash of g of x times g dash of x equal to one, then ask which input of f returns three. One does, and f dash of one is four.

flashcards.q: The inverse cannot be written down, so what is the only unknown you ever need?
flashcards.a: $$f(g(x)) = x \quad\text{and}\quad g(f(x)) = x$$The value of g at the point asked, and that is just a reverse-mapping question: which number fed into f comes out as that point. Try small integers — zero, one, minus one, two — because the setter always keeps it a neat one.

flashcards.q: For the same function, find g dash of minus one and g dash of eleven.
flashcards.a: $$f(-1)=-1 \;\Rightarrow\; g'(-1)=\frac{1}{f'(-1)}=\frac{1}{4}$$The other route, g of f of x equal to x, gives exactly the same relation and the same work. Read the forward mapping backwards: f of minus one is minus one, and f of two is eleven.

flashcards.q: Why is g dash of three not one over f dash of three?
flashcards.a: $$g'(f(a)) = \frac{1}{f'(a)}$$Because three is an output of f, not an input. f dash is always evaluated at the input you located. Here the input is one, so the answer is a quarter, not one over f dash of three.

flashcards.q: Which of the two defining relations should you start from?
flashcards.a: $$g(f(x)) = x$$Whichever comes to mind first. Both give the same relation after the chain rule and the solution is exactly as long either way, so do not spend time deciding. The only real work is finding which x the function sends to the number inside g dash.

flashcards.q: For f of x equal to x cubed plus x plus one, why can a setter ask for g dash of thirty-one but not g dash of 2211?
flashcards.a: $$f(3)=31 \;\Rightarrow\; g'(31)=\frac{1}{f'(3)}=\frac{1}{28}$$Because you find the input by inspection. Thirty-one comes from three, which you spot at once, but 2211 comes from thirteen, and nobody has that in their head in an exam hall. A setter picks the input from zero, plus or minus one, plus or minus two, at most three, then prints the output.

flashcards.q: At which point is f dash evaluated when you want the derivative of the inverse?
flashcards.a: $$g'(y_0) = \frac{1}{f'(x_0)}, \quad \text{where } f(x_0) = y_0$$At the input, never at the printed output. Locate the input that f sends to the given value first, then differentiate f once and evaluate it there.

flashcards.q: If y is the bracket ax plus b times e to the power mx, prove the second-order relation it satisfies.
flashcards.a: $$y'' - 2my' + m^{2}y = 0$$After the first product rule, the bracket times the exponential is y itself, so substitute it. Differentiate again and trap the leftover exponential using the same first line. If an exponential is still in your last line, you owe one more substitution.

flashcards.q: A chunk of your first derivative turns out to be the whole of y again. What do you do?
flashcards.a: $$ae^{mx} = y' - my$$Write y in its place instead of carrying the long bracket forward, because the relation you must prove is written in the second derivative, the first and y. Then differentiate again and trap any leftover exponential using that same first line.

flashcards.q: If y is e to the power nx times the cosine of bx plus c, what relation holds between the second derivative, the first and y?
flashcards.a: $$y_2 - 2n\,y_1 + (n^2+b^2)\,y = 0$$Replace the exponential by y over the cosine, the sine over cosine collapses into a tangent, and the exponential disappears. The sine version satisfies exactly the same relation.

flashcards.q: You begin a higher-order proof by substituting y back and then get stuck. What should you not do?
flashcards.a: $$\frac{y_1}{y} = n - b\tan(bx+c)$$Do not switch to the direct route in the middle of the same solution. A half-substituted answer is where sign errors and lost terms live. Pick one road and finish on it; both routes reach the result.

flashcards.q: Why divide the first derivative by y when an exponential multiplies a sine or a cosine?
flashcards.a: $$\frac{y_1}{y} = n - b\tan(bx+c)$$The exponential cancels on its own and the sine over cosine collapses into a tangent, so after one division the relation already sits in terms of y and its first derivative.

ladder.tier: L1 Drill — one formula applied directly
ladder.q: Differentiate y = a^x sin x ln x with respect to x, where a > 0.
steps: 1. Three factors, so the product rule gives three terms: differentiate one factor at a time and leave the other two alone.
2. Differentiate a^x: a^x ln a sin x ln x.
3. Differentiate sin x: a^x cos x ln x.
4. Differentiate ln x: a^x sin x (1/x).
ladder.answer: dy/dx = a^x ln a sin x ln x + a^x cos x ln x + (a^x sin x)/x

ladder.tier: L1 Drill — one formula applied directly
ladder.q: Differentiate y = sqrt(sin(x^2)) with respect to x.
steps: 1. Three layers: square root outside, sine next, x^2 innermost. Work outside in.
2. Outer layer: d/dx of (something)^(1/2) is 1/(2 sqrt(something)), so you get 1/(2 sqrt(sin(x^2))).
3. Next layer: the derivative of sin(x^2) brings cos(x^2).
4. Innermost: the derivative of x^2 is 2x. Multiply the three factors and cancel the 2.

ladder.tier: L1 Drill — one formula applied directly
ladder.q: For x > 0, differentiate y = x^x with respect to x.
steps: 1. x^x is variable to the power variable. It is neither a power function nor an exponential, so no standard formula applies - take a log.
2. ln y = x ln x.
3. Differentiate both sides with respect to x, product rule on the right: (1/y) dy/dx = 1 + ln x.
4. Multiply back by y = x^x.

ladder.tier: L1 Drill — one formula applied directly
ladder.q: y is a differentiable function of x. Write down d/dx of each of y^3, cos(y^2) and x^3.
steps: 1. Whenever you differentiate a function of y with respect to x, the chain rule leaves a factor dy/dx behind.
2. d/dx (y^3) = 3y^2 dy/dx.
3. d/dx cos(y^2): the derivative of cosine gives -sin(y^2), then the derivative of y^2 gives 2y dy/dx.
4. d/dx (x^3) = 3x^2. The chain factor is there too, but it is dx/dx = 1, which is why you never write it.

ladder.tier: L2 JEE Main standard — two or three steps, one main idea
ladder.q: If x = t^2 and y = 2t, find dy/dx and d2y/dx2 in terms of t.
steps: 1. Neither x nor y is given in terms of the other, so differentiate each with respect to the parameter: dx/dt = 2t and dy/dt = 2.
2. dy/dx = (dy/dt)/(dx/dt) = 2/(2t) = 1/t.
3. For the second derivative you must differentiate 1/t with respect to x, not with respect to t. Use the chain rule: d2y/dx2 = d/dt (1/t) times dt/dx.
5. So d2y/dx2 = (-1/t^2)(1/(2t)) = -1/(2t^3). Never write (d2y/dt2)/(d2x/dt2) - that is 0/2 = 0 and it is wrong.

ladder.tier: L2 JEE Main standard — two or three steps, one main idea
ladder.q: If x^2 + y^2 = 4, find dy/dx and d2y/dx2 in terms of y.
steps: 1. Differentiate the relation with respect to x: 2x + 2y dy/dx = 0, so dy/dx = -x/y.
2. Differentiate again, quotient rule on -x/y, remembering that y is a function of x: d2y/dx2 = -[y - x (dy/dx)]/y^2.
3. Substitute the dy/dx you already have: d2y/dx2 = -[y + x^2/y]/y^2 = -(y^2 + x^2)/y^3.
4. Finally use the original relation x^2 + y^2 = 4 to tidy it up.

ladder.tier: L2 JEE Main standard — two or three steps, one main idea
ladder.q: Differentiate x^5 with respect to x^3.
steps: 1. Call u = x^5 and v = x^3. The question wants du/dv, and du/dv = (du/dx)/(dv/dx) with x acting as the parameter.
2. du/dx = 5x^4 and dv/dx = 3x^2.

ladder.tier: L2 JEE Main standard — two or three steps, one main idea
ladder.q: For x > 0, differentiate y = (x^x)^(1/2) with respect to x.
steps: 1. Simplify the index first: powers multiply, so y = x^(x/2).
2. Take a log: ln y = (x/2) ln x.
3. Differentiate, product rule on the right: (1/y) dy/dx = (1/2) ln x + (x/2)(1/x) = (1/2)(1 + ln x).
4. Multiply back by y.

ladder.tier: L2 JEE Main standard — two or three steps, one main idea
ladder.q: For x > 0 let y = sqrt(x) + 1/sqrt(x). Show that 2x dy/dx + y = 2 sqrt(x).
steps: 1. Write the function with fractional powers so that one rule does both terms: y = x^(1/2) + x^(-1/2).
3. Multiply by 2x: 2x dy/dx = x^(1/2) - x^(-1/2).
4. Now add y = x^(1/2) + x^(-1/2). The x^(-1/2) terms cancel.
5. 2x dy/dx + y = 2x^(1/2) = 2 sqrt(x), as required.
ladder.answer: Proved: with y = x^(1/2) + x^(-1/2), 2x dy/dx = x^(1/2) - x^(-1/2), and adding y cancels the x^(-1/2) terms to leave 2 sqrt(x)

ladder.tier: L3 Harder Main — two concepts combined, or a case split
ladder.q: If e^y = y^x with x > 1 and y > 1, find dy/dx.
steps: 1. Take logarithms of both sides to bring the exponents down: y = x ln y.
2. Differentiate with respect to x, using the product rule on the right and remembering y is a function of x: dy/dx = ln y + x(1/y)(dy/dx).
3. Collect the derivative: (dy/dx)(1 - x/y) = ln y, that is (dy/dx)(y - x)/y = ln y.
4. So dy/dx = y ln y/(y - x).
5. The relation y = x ln y also gives ln y = y/x, so the answer may be written dy/dx = y(y/x)/(y - x) = y^2/(x(y - x)).
ladder.answer: dy/dx = y ln y/(y - x), equivalently y^2/(x(y - x))

ladder.tier: L3 Harder Main — two concepts combined, or a case split
ladder.q: If sqrt(1 - x^2) + sqrt(1 - y^2) = a(x - y), where a is a constant, show that dy/dx = sqrt(1 - y^2)/sqrt(1 - x^2).
steps: 1. The roots 1 - x^2 and 1 - y^2 are the signal for a sine substitution. Put x = sin A and y = sin B with A = sin inverse x and B = sin inverse y, both in (-pi/2, pi/2).
2. Then sqrt(1 - x^2) = cos A and sqrt(1 - y^2) = cos B, since cosine is positive on that interval, and the relation becomes cos A + cos B = a(sin A - sin B).
3. Apply the sum formulae: 2 cos((A + B)/2) cos((A - B)/2) = 2a cos((A + B)/2) sin((A - B)/2).
4. Cancel the common factor: cot((A - B)/2) = a, so A - B = 2 cot inverse a, a constant.
5. So sin inverse x - sin inverse y is constant. Differentiating, 1/sqrt(1 - x^2) - (1/sqrt(1 - y^2)) dy/dx = 0.
6. Rearranging gives the result. The whole question is the substitution; the differentiation is one line.

ladder.tier: L3 Harder Main — two concepts combined, or a case split
ladder.q: Let y = sin inverse (2x sqrt(1 - x^2)) for x in [-1, 1]. Find dy/dx on each part of the domain.
steps: 1. Put x = sin theta with theta = sin inverse x in [-pi/2, pi/2]. Then 2x sqrt(1 - x^2) = 2 sin theta cos theta = sin 2theta, so y = sin inverse (sin 2theta).
2. You may only cancel sin inverse against sin when the angle lies in [-pi/2, pi/2]. So split by the value of 2theta.
3. If mod x is at most 1/sqrt 2 then 2theta lies in [-pi/2, pi/2] and y = 2theta = 2 sin inverse x, giving dy/dx = 2/sqrt(1 - x^2).
4. If x lies in (1/sqrt 2, 1) then 2theta lies in (pi/2, pi) and sin inverse (sin 2theta) = pi - 2theta, so y = pi - 2 sin inverse x and dy/dx = -2/sqrt(1 - x^2).
5. If x lies in (-1, -1/sqrt 2) then 2theta lies in (-pi, -pi/2) and sin inverse (sin 2theta) = -pi - 2theta, so y = -pi - 2 sin inverse x and dy/dx = -2/sqrt(1 - x^2).
6. At x = plus or minus 1/sqrt 2 the one-sided derivatives disagree, so y is not differentiable there.
ladder.answer: dy/dx = 2/sqrt(1 - x^2) for mod x < 1/sqrt 2, and -2/sqrt(1 - x^2) for 1/sqrt 2 < mod x < 1

ladder.tier: L3 Harder Main — two concepts combined, or a case split
ladder.q: Let y = f(x) be twice differentiable with dy/dx not zero. Prove that d2x/dy2 = -(d2y/dx2)/(dy/dx)^3.
steps: 1. First derivatives do invert: dx/dy = 1/(dy/dx).

2. Now differentiate both sides with respect to y. The right-hand side is built out of x, so differentiate it with respect to x and multiply by dx/dy - that is the chain rule and it is the only step students drop.
3. d2x/dy2 = d/dx [1/(dy/dx)] times dx/dy = [-1/(dy/dx)^2] (d2y/dx2) times dx/dy.
4. Replace dx/dy by 1/(dy/dx) to finish.
5. Note that d2x/dy2 is NOT the reciprocal of d2y/dx2 - the extra factor of (dy/dx) and the minus sign are the content of the question.

ladder.tier: L4 JEE Advanced — multi-concept, a non-obvious first move
ladder.q: For x in (0, pi/2) let y = (sin x)^(cos x) + (cos x)^(sin x). Find dy/dx.
steps: 1. Each term has a variable base and a variable exponent, so take logarithms of each separately. Never take the logarithm of the sum.
2. Let u = (sin x)^(cos x). Then ln u = cos x ln sin x, so (1/u)(du/dx) = -sin x ln sin x + cos x (cos x/sin x).
3. Hence du/dx = (sin x)^(cos x)[cos^2 x/sin x - sin x ln sin x].
4. Let v = (cos x)^(sin x). Then ln v = sin x ln cos x, so (1/v)(dv/dx) = cos x ln cos x + sin x(-sin x/cos x).
5. Hence dv/dx = (cos x)^(sin x)[cos x ln cos x - sin^2 x/cos x].
6. Finally dy/dx = du/dx + dv/dx.
ladder.answer: dy/dx = (sin x)^(cos x)[cos^2 x/sin x - sin x ln sin x] + (cos x)^(sin x)[cos x ln cos x - sin^2 x/cos x]

ladder.tier: L4 JEE Advanced — multi-concept, a non-obvious first move
ladder.q: Let f(x) = x + e^x for every real x. Show that f is invertible and, if g is its inverse, find g'(1) and g'(1 + e).
steps: 1. f'(x) = 1 + e^x, which is positive for every real x, so f is strictly increasing and therefore one-one. Its range is all of R, so f is invertible.
2. The inverse cannot be written in closed form, so use g'(f(x)) = 1/f'(x) instead of trying to differentiate g directly.
3. For g'(1), find the x with f(x) = 1. Trying x = 0 gives 0 + 1 = 1, so that x is 0. Then f'(0) = 1 + 1 = 2 and g'(1) = 1/2.
4. For g'(1 + e), find the x with f(x) = 1 + e. Trying x = 1 gives 1 + e, so that x is 1. Then f'(1) = 1 + e.
ladder.answer: g'(1) = 1/2 and g'(1 + e) = 1/(1 + e), approximately 0.269

ladder.tier: L4 JEE Advanced — multi-concept, a non-obvious first move
ladder.q: Let x = e^t cos t and y = e^t sin t. Find dy/dx, and show that at t = pi/4 the tangent to the curve is parallel to the y-axis.
steps: 1. Differentiate each coordinate with respect to t, using the product rule.
2. dx/dt = e^t cos t - e^t sin t = e^t(cos t - sin t).
3. dy/dt = e^t sin t + e^t cos t = e^t(sin t + cos t).
4. Dividing, the factor e^t cancels: dy/dx = (sin t + cos t)/(cos t - sin t).
5. At t = pi/4 the denominator cos t - sin t is zero while the numerator is sqrt 2, which is not zero, so dy/dx is undefined there.
6. An undefined slope with a non-zero numerator means a vertical tangent, that is a tangent parallel to the y-axis. Equivalently dx/dt = 0 while dy/dt is not zero at that value of t.
ladder.answer: dy/dx = (sin t + cos t)/(cos t - sin t); at t = pi/4 the denominator vanishes while the numerator is sqrt 2, so the tangent is vertical, that is parallel to the y-axis

ladder.tier: L4 JEE Advanced — multi-concept, a non-obvious first move
ladder.q: If sin y = x sin(a + y), where a is a constant with sin a not zero, find dy/dx.
steps: 1. Differentiate both sides with respect to x. On the right you need the product rule, and every y differentiated leaves a dy/dx: cos y dy/dx = sin(a + y) + x cos(a + y) dy/dx.
2. Collect the dy/dx terms: dy/dx [cos y - x cos(a + y)] = sin(a + y).
3. The answer is wanted in y alone, so eliminate x using the given relation: x = sin y/sin(a + y).
4. The bracket becomes [cos y sin(a + y) - sin y cos(a + y)]/sin(a + y) = sin((a + y) - y)/sin(a + y) = sin a/sin(a + y).
5. Hence dy/dx = sin(a + y) times sin(a + y)/sin a.

ladder.tier: L5 Advanced hardest — the toughest this chapter justifies
ladder.q: Let y = x^2 e^x. Use the Leibniz rule to prove that the n-th derivative of y is e^x (x^2 + 2nx + n(n - 1)) for every positive integer n, and hence find the value of the 10th derivative at x = 0.
steps: 1. The Leibniz rule for the n-th derivative of a product is sum over k from 0 to n of C(n, k) times the k-th derivative of the first factor times the (n - k)-th derivative of the second.
2. Take the first factor to be x^2. Its derivatives are x^2, 2x, 2, and then 0 for every k greater than 2, so the sum has only three surviving terms.
3. Every derivative of e^x is e^x, so that factor contributes e^x throughout.
4. The three terms are C(n, 0) x^2 e^x, C(n, 1)(2x) e^x and C(n, 2)(2) e^x.
5. That is e^x [x^2 + 2nx + 2 n(n - 1)/2] = e^x (x^2 + 2nx + n(n - 1)), as required.
6. Putting n = 10 and x = 0: e^0 (0 + 0 + 10 times 9) = 90.
ladder.answer: The n-th derivative is e^x (x^2 + 2nx + n(n - 1)); at n = 10 and x = 0 its value is 90

ladder.tier: L5 Advanced hardest — the toughest this chapter justifies
ladder.q: Let A, n, b and c be constants and y = A e^(nx) cos(bx + c). Prove that d2y/dx2 - 2n dy/dx + (n^2 + b^2) y = 0.
steps: 1. Differentiate once: dy/dx = A e^(nx)[n cos(bx + c) - b sin(bx + c)].
2. The first piece is n y, so dy/dx = n y - A b e^(nx) sin(bx + c). Keep the sine piece as A e^(nx) sin(bx + c) = (n y - dy/dx)/b rather than expanding - the substitution is the whole skill here.
3. Differentiate dy/dx again: d2y/dx2 = n dy/dx - b[A n e^(nx) sin(bx + c) + A b e^(nx) cos(bx + c)].
4. Replace A e^(nx) cos(bx + c) by y and A e^(nx) sin(bx + c) by (n y - dy/dx)/b.
5. d2y/dx2 = n dy/dx - n(n y - dy/dx) - b^2 y = 2n dy/dx - (n^2 + b^2) y, which rearranges to the required relation.
6. The phase c never appears in the relation - only n and b do. If your answer contains c you have expanded where you should have substituted.
ladder.answer: d2y/dx2 - 2n dy/dx + (n^2 + b^2) y = 0, as required

ladder.tier: L5 Advanced hardest — the toughest this chapter justifies
ladder.q: Let x, y > 0 satisfy x^y = y^x with y not equal to x, and let y be a differentiable function of x. Find dy/dx.
steps: 1. Take logarithms of both sides: y ln x = x ln y.
2. Differentiate both sides with respect to x, applying the product rule on each side.
3. Left side: (dy/dx) ln x + y/x. Right side: ln y + x(1/y)(dy/dx).
4. Collect the derivative on one side: (dy/dx)(ln x - x/y) = ln y - y/x.
5. Write each bracket over a common denominator: ln y - y/x = (x ln y - y)/x and ln x - x/y = (y ln x - x)/y.
6. Dividing gives dy/dx = [(x ln y - y)/x] times [y/(y ln x - x)] = y(x ln y - y)/(x(y ln x - x)).
7. The condition y not equal to x keeps the denominator away from the degenerate point of the curve, where x = y makes both brackets vanish together.
ladder.answer: dy/dx = y(x ln y - y)/(x(y ln x - x))

ladder.tier: L5 Advanced hardest — the toughest this chapter justifies
ladder.q: Let x = g(t) and y = f(t) be twice differentiable functions of a parameter t with g'(t) not zero. Prove that d2y/dx2 = (g'(t) f''(t) - f'(t) g''(t))/(g'(t))^3, and say why (d2y/dt2)/(d2x/dt2) is not the answer.
steps: 1. First derivative: dy/dx = (dy/dt)/(dx/dt) = f'(t)/g'(t).

2. Second derivative means the derivative of dy/dx with respect to x. What you have in hand is a function of t, so you must differentiate it with respect to t and then multiply by dt/dx - this is the step the whole question is testing.
3. d/dt [f'(t)/g'(t)] = (g'(t) f''(t) - f'(t) g''(t))/(g'(t))^2 by the quotient rule.
4. dt/dx = 1/(dx/dt) = 1/g'(t), because first derivatives do invert.
5. Multiplying gives d2y/dx2 = (g' f'' - f' g'')/(g')^3.

6. Why the shortcut fails: d2y/dt2 and d2x/dt2 are perfectly good objects, but their ratio is not d2y/dx2 - the cancellation that works for dy/dt over dx/dt has no analogue for second derivatives. Test it on x = t^2, y = 2t: the ratio gives 0, while the correct answer is -1/(2t^3).

testBank.q: If y = (x + sqrt(x^2 + a^2))^n, where n and a are constants, then dy/dx equals
steps: 1. Write y = B^n with B = x + sqrt(x^2 + a^2), so dy/dx = n B^(n-1) dB/dx.
3. Take the LCM: dB/dx = (sqrt(x^2 + a^2) + x)/sqrt(x^2 + a^2) = B/sqrt(x^2 + a^2). The bracket has rebuilt itself in the numerator.
4. Hence dy/dx = n B^(n-1) B/sqrt(x^2 + a^2) = n B^n/sqrt(x^2 + a^2) = n y/sqrt(x^2 + a^2).

testBank.q: If x = t^2 and y = 2t, then the value of d2y/dx2 at t = 2 is
steps: 1. dy/dt = 2 and dx/dt = 2t, so dy/dx = 2/(2t) = 1/t.
2. Now dy/dx is a function of t while you must differentiate with respect to x, so use the chain rule: d2y/dx2 = d/dt (1/t) times dt/dx.
4. At t = 2 this is -1/(2 times 8) = -1/16.
5. Note what you must not do: (d2y/dt2)/(d2x/dt2) = 0/2 = 0, which is not the answer. Second derivatives do not divide.

testBank.q: Let y = x^5 + x for x > 0, and regard x as a function of y. Then d2x/dy2 at x = 1 equals
steps: 1. dy/dx = 5x^4 + 1, so at x = 1 the value is 6.
2. d2y/dx2 = 20x^3, so at x = 1 the value is 20.

testBank.q: For x > 0, let y = x^(x^x). Then dy/dx equals
steps: 1. Variable to the power variable, twice over, so take a log: ln y = x^x ln x.
2. Differentiate with respect to x, product rule on the right: (1/y) dy/dx = (d/dx (x^x)) ln x + x^x (1/x).
3. You already know d/dx (x^x) = x^x (1 + ln x).
4. So (1/y) dy/dx = x^x (1 + ln x) ln x + x^x/x = x^x (ln x + (ln x)^2 + 1/x).
5. Multiply back by y = x^(x^x).

testBank.q: If y = sin inverse (2x sqrt(1 - x^2)) and x lies in (1/sqrt 2, 1), then dy/dx equals
steps: 1. Simplify before differentiating. Put x = sin theta with theta = sin inverse x, so theta lies in (pi/4, pi/2) for this range of x.
2. Then 2x sqrt(1 - x^2) = 2 sin theta cos theta = sin 2theta, so y = sin inverse (sin 2theta).
3. But 2theta lies in (pi/2, pi), outside the range of sin inverse. There sin inverse (sin 2theta) = pi - 2theta.
4. So y = pi - 2 sin inverse x and dy/dx = -2/sqrt(1 - x^2).
5. Had you cancelled sin inverse against sin without checking the range you would have written +2/sqrt(1 - x^2), which is the trap.

testBank.q: Let f(x) = x^3 + x + 1 for every real x, and let g be the inverse function of f. Then g'(11) equals
steps: 1. f'(x) = 3x^2 + 1 > 0, so f is strictly increasing and the inverse g exists.
2. From f(g(x)) = x, differentiating gives f'(g(x)) g'(x) = 1, so g'(11) = 1/f'(g(11)).
3. You cannot write g down, so find the a with f(a) = 11 by inspection: a^3 + a + 1 = 11 gives a^3 + a - 10 = 0, and a = 2 works (8 + 2 = 10).

testBank.q: If sqrt(1 - x^6) + sqrt(1 - y^6) = a(x^3 - y^3), where a is a constant, then dy/dx equals
steps: 1. The sixth powers under the roots are the signal for a trigonometric substitution. Put x^3 = sin A and y^3 = sin B, with A and B in (-pi/2, pi/2).
2. The relation becomes cos A + cos B = a(sin A - sin B).
3. Use the sum formulae: 2 cos((A + B)/2) cos((A - B)/2) = 2a cos((A + B)/2) sin((A - B)/2), so cot((A - B)/2) = a.
4. Hence A - B is a constant, that is, sin inverse (x^3) - sin inverse (y^3) is constant.
5. Differentiate: 3x^2/sqrt(1 - x^6) = (3y^2/sqrt(1 - y^6)) dy/dx.

testBank.q: Let f and g be differentiable with f'(1) = 2 and g'(sqrt 2) = 4. The derivative of f(tan x) with respect to g(sec x) at x = pi/4 is
steps: 1. Write u = f(tan x) and v = g(sec x). Then du/dv = (du/dx)/(dv/dx) - treat x as a parameter, exactly as in a parametric problem.
2. du/dx = f'(tan x) sec^2 x and dv/dx = g'(sec x) sec x tan x.
3. At x = pi/4: tan x = 1, sec x = sqrt 2, sec^2 x = 2.
4. du/dx = f'(1) times 2 = 4; dv/dx = g'(sqrt 2) times sqrt 2 times 1 = 4 sqrt 2.
5. So du/dv = 4/(4 sqrt 2) = 1/sqrt 2. Differentiate first, substitute the point afterwards.

testBank.q: For x > 0, let y = x^(x^(x^ ... )) continued to infinity, and suppose y ln x is not equal to 1. Then dy/dx equals
steps: 1. Spot the repetition: the whole tower sits in the exponent as well, so y = x^y.
2. Take a log: ln y = y ln x.
3. Differentiate with respect to x: (1/y) dy/dx = (dy/dx) ln x + y/x.
4. Collect: (dy/dx)(1/y - ln x) = y/x, that is (dy/dx)(1 - y ln x)/y = y/x.
5. So dy/dx = y^2/(x(1 - y ln x)).

testBank.q: If x^y = e^(x - y) with x > 0, then dy/dx equals
steps: 1. Take a log on both sides: y ln x = x - y.
2. This already gives y explicitly: y(1 + ln x) = x, so y = x/(1 + ln x). Making it explicit is quicker than carrying the implicit form.
3. Differentiate by the quotient rule: dy/dx = [(1 + ln x) - x(1/x)]/(1 + ln x)^2.
4. The numerator is 1 + ln x - 1 = ln x, so dy/dx = ln x/(1 + ln x)^2.

testBank.q: Let f(x) = x^3 + x + 1 for every real x and let g be the inverse of f. Then which of the following statements is (are) TRUE?
steps: 1. f'(x) = 3x^2 + 1 is always positive, so f is strictly increasing and g exists. From g(f(a)) = a, differentiating gives g'(f(a)) f'(a) = 1, that is g'(f(a)) = 1/f'(a).
2. f(1) = 3 and f'(1) = 4, so g'(3) = 1/4. Statement (A) is true.
3. f(0) = 1 and f'(0) = 1, so g'(1) = 1. Statement (B) is true.
5. f(2) = 11 and f'(2) = 13, so g'(11) = 1/13, not 1/4. Statement (D) is false.

testBank.q: For y = x^x on (0, infinity), which of the following statements is (are) TRUE?
opts: the least value of y on (0, infinity) is e^(-1/e)
steps: 1. x^x is variable to the power variable, so no power or exponential formula applies: take a log. ln y = x ln x.
2. Differentiating, (1/y) dy/dx = ln x + 1, so dy/dx = x^x (1 + ln x). Statement (A) is true and (B) is false - the power rule needs a constant index.
3. x^x is never zero on (0, infinity), so dy/dx = 0 exactly when 1 + ln x = 0, that is x = 1/e. Statement (C) is true.
4. dy/dx is negative for x < 1/e and positive for x > 1/e, so x = 1/e gives the least value, namely (1/e)^(1/e) = e^(-1/e). Statement (D) is true.

testBank.q: For x > 0 let y = sqrt(x + sqrt(x + sqrt(x + ... ))) continued to infinity, with y > 0. Then which of the following statements is (are) TRUE?
steps: 1. Everything under the first root is x plus the whole expression again, so y = sqrt(x + y), that is y^2 = x + y. Statement (B) is true.

2. Differentiate the relation with respect to x: 2y dy/dx = 1 + dy/dx, so dy/dx (2y - 1) = 1 and dy/dx = 1/(2y - 1). Statement (D) is true, and (A) is the slip you make if you forget that the inner y also depends on x.
3. Solving y^2 - y - x = 0 with y > 0 gives y = (1 + sqrt(1 + 4x))/2, so 2y - 1 = sqrt(1 + 4x).
4. Hence dy/dx = 1/sqrt(1 + 4x) as well, so statement (C) is true.

testBank.q: Let a > 0 and let x = a(cos t + t sin t), y = a(sin t - t cos t) for t in (0, pi/2). Then which of the following statements is (are) TRUE?
steps: 1. dx/dt = a(-sin t + sin t + t cos t) = a t cos t.
2. dy/dt = a(cos t - cos t + t sin t) = a t sin t.
3. So dy/dx = (a t sin t)/(a t cos t) = tan t: statement (A) is true and (B) is false.
4. For the second derivative, differentiate tan t with respect to t and multiply by dt/dx: d2y/dx2 = sec^2 t times 1/(a t cos t).
5. That is sec^3 t/(a t), so statement (D) is true and (C) is false - (C) is what you get if you drop the factor dt/dx.

testBank.q: Let f be twice differentiable on the real line with f'(x) = g(x) and f''(x) = -f(x) for every x. Define F(x) = (f(x/2))^2 + (g(x/2))^2 and suppose F(5) = 5. Then which of the following statements is (are) TRUE?
steps: 1. Differentiate F with the chain rule, keeping the inner derivative of x/2: F'(x) = 2 f(x/2) f'(x/2) (1/2) + 2 g(x/2) g'(x/2) (1/2) = f(x/2) f'(x/2) + g(x/2) g'(x/2).
3. Hence F'(x) = f(x/2) g(x/2) - g(x/2) f(x/2) = 0 for every x, so statement (A) is true.

4. A derivative that vanishes at one point proves nothing - cos x has zero derivative at x = 0 and is not constant. A derivative that vanishes for every x does force the function to be constant, and that is what you have here.
5. F(5) = 5 therefore fixes the constant at 5, so F takes the value 5 at every point: (C) and (D) are true and (B) is false.
6. This is the shape of the 2006 IIT problem Ankit Sir works through in the lecture.

testBank.q: Let a be a constant with sin a not equal to zero, and let y be the differentiable function of x defined near x = 0 by sin y = x sin(a + y), with y = 0 when x = 0. Then which of the following statements is (are) TRUE?
opts: if a = pi/2 then dy/dx = cos^2 y
steps: 1. Differentiate sin y = x sin(a + y) with respect to x, writing a factor dy/dx each time a y is differentiated: cos y dy/dx = sin(a + y) + x cos(a + y) dy/dx.
2. Collect: dy/dx [cos y - x cos(a + y)] = sin(a + y).
3. The relation gives x = sin y/sin(a + y), so the bracket is [cos y sin(a + y) - sin y cos(a + y)]/sin(a + y) = sin(a + y - y)/sin(a + y) = sin a/sin(a + y).
4. Hence dy/dx = sin^2(a + y)/sin a: statement (A) is true and (B) is false.
5. At x = 0 the given branch has y = 0, so dy/dx = sin^2 a/sin a = sin a. Statement (C) is true.
6. If a = pi/2 then sin(a + y) = cos y and sin a = 1, so dy/dx = cos^2 y. Statement (D) is true.

testBank.q: Let f(x) = x^3 + x + 1 for every real x and let g be the inverse of f. The value of 1/g'(31) is ______.
steps: 1. g'(b) = 1/f'(a) where f(a) = b, so 1/g'(31) = f'(a) for the a with f(a) = 31.
2. Find a by inspection: a^3 + a + 1 = 31 gives a^3 + a - 30 = 0, and a = 3 works (27 + 3 = 30).

testBank.q: For x > 0 let y = (x^x)^(1/2). The value of (2/y)(dy/dx) at x = e is ______.
steps: 1. Powers multiply, so y = x^(x/2). Write it this way before you touch the log.
2. ln y = (x/2) ln x. Differentiate, product rule on the right: (1/y) dy/dx = (1/2) ln x + (x/2)(1/x) = (1/2)(1 + ln x).
3. So (2/y)(dy/dx) = 1 + ln x.
4. At x = e this is 1 + 1 = 2.

testBank.q: If x = t^2 and y = 2t, the value of d2y/dx2 at t = -1 is ______.
steps: 1. dy/dx = (dy/dt)/(dx/dt) = 2/(2t) = 1/t.
4. The value is 0.5.

testBank.q: Let y = (ax + b) e^(3x), where a and b are arbitrary constants. If d2y/dx2 + p dy/dx + q y = 0 holds for every choice of a and b, then p + q is ______.
steps: 1. With m = 3, dy/dx = a e^(mx) + m(ax + b) e^(mx) = a e^(mx) + m y.
2. So a e^(mx) = dy/dx - m y - substitute this back rather than expanding everything, which is the whole skill in these questions.
3. Differentiating again, d2y/dx2 = a m e^(mx) + m dy/dx = m(dy/dx - m y) + m dy/dx = 2m dy/dx - m^2 y.
4. Hence d2y/dx2 - 2m dy/dx + m^2 y = 0, so p = -2m = -6 and q = m^2 = 9.

testBank.q: The derivative of (1 + x^2)^3 with respect to x^2, evaluated at x = 1, is ______.
steps: 1. Let u = (1 + x^2)^3 and v = x^2. You need du/dv = (du/dx)/(dv/dx).
2. du/dx = 3(1 + x^2)^2 (2x) and dv/dx = 2x.
3. So du/dv = 3(1 + x^2)^2. Equivalently, put v = x^2 at the start: u = (1 + v)^3 and du/dv = 3(1 + v)^2.
4. At x = 1, du/dv = 3 times 4 = 12.

testBank.q: For x > 0 let y = sqrt(x + sqrt(x + sqrt(x + ... ))) continued to infinity, with y > 0. The value of 1/(dy/dx) at x = 6 is ______.
steps: 1. The expression repeats inside itself, so y^2 = x + y.
2. At x = 6: y^2 - y - 6 = 0 gives y = 3, taking y > 0.
3. Differentiating the relation, 2y dy/dx = 1 + dy/dx, so dy/dx = 1/(2y - 1) and 1/(dy/dx) = 2y - 1.
4. At x = 6 this is 2(3) - 1 = 5.

testBank.q: Let R denote the set of all real numbers. Consider the polynomial function f: R -> R defined by f(x) = (d10/dx10)((x^2 - 1)^10), for all x in R. Here (d10/dx10)((x^2 - 1)^10) is the 10th order derivative of the function (x^2 - 1)^10. Then which of the following statements is (are) TRUE?
opts: The coefficient of x^8 in the polynomial f(x) is (-10)(18!/8!)
The value of f(1) + f(-1) is equal to 10! times 2^11
The degree of the polynomial f(x) is 10
The constant term of the polynomial f(x) is -(10!/5!)
steps: 1. Expand first: (x^2 - 1)^10 = sum over k from 0 to 10 of C(10, k) (-1)^(10 - k) x^(2k), a polynomial of degree 20.

2. Differentiating ten times kills every term with 2k < 10 and sends x^(2k) to [(2k)!/(2k - 10)!] x^(2k - 10). So f(x) = sum over k from 5 to 10 of C(10, k) (-1)^(10 - k) [(2k)!/(2k - 10)!] x^(2k - 10).
3. Degree: the surviving top term is k = 10, giving (20!/10!) x^10. A degree 20 polynomial differentiated ten times has degree 10, so (C) is TRUE.
5. Constant term: set k = 5, giving C(10, 5) (-1)^5 (10!/0!) = -252 times 10!. Since 10!/5! = 30240 while 252 times 10! = 914457600, these are not equal and (D) is FALSE.

6. f(1) + f(-1): every exponent 2k - 10 is even, so f is an even function and f(1) + f(-1) = 2 f(1). To get f(1), factorise (x^2 - 1)^10 = (x - 1)^10 (x + 1)^10 and use the Leibniz rule for the 10th derivative of a product. At x = 1 every term in which (x - 1)^10 has been differentiated fewer than ten times still carries a factor (x - 1) and so vanishes; only the term 10! times (x + 1)^10 survives, giving f(1) = 10! times 2^10.
7. Hence f(1) + f(-1) = 10! times 2^11 and (B) is TRUE. The correct options are (A), (B) and (C), which is the official key for this question.

testBank.q: Let A, n, b and c be constants and let y = A e^(nx) cos(bx + c). If d2y/dx2 - 2n dy/dx + k y = 0 holds for every real x, then k equals
steps: 1. dy/dx = A e^(nx)[n cos(bx + c) - b sin(bx + c)] = n y - A b e^(nx) sin(bx + c).
2. So A e^(nx) sin(bx + c) = (n y - dy/dx)/b. Keep this to substitute later rather than expanding everything - that is the whole trick in these proofs.
3. Differentiate dy/dx again: d2y/dx2 = n dy/dx - b[A n e^(nx) sin(bx + c) + A b e^(nx) cos(bx + c)].
4. Now A e^(nx) cos(bx + c) = y and A e^(nx) sin(bx + c) = (n y - dy/dx)/b, so d2y/dx2 = n dy/dx - n(n y - dy/dx) - b^2 y = 2n dy/dx - (n^2 + b^2) y.
5. Hence d2y/dx2 - 2n dy/dx + (n^2 + b^2) y = 0 and k = n^2 + b^2. Note that c never appears - it only shifts the phase.

testBank.q: Let a > 1 and let x = sqrt(a^(sin inverse t)), y = sqrt(a^(cos inverse t)) for t in (-1, 1). Then dy/dx equals
steps: 1. Differentiating each of x and y in t is possible but ugly. Look instead for a way to kill the parameter.
2. x y = sqrt(a^(sin inverse t) times a^(cos inverse t)) = sqrt(a^(sin inverse t + cos inverse t)).
3. But sin inverse t + cos inverse t = pi/2 for every t in (-1, 1), so x y = a^(pi/4), a constant.
4. Differentiate x y = constant with respect to x: y + x dy/dx = 0.
5. So dy/dx = -y/x. With the parameter gone, any higher derivative is just as easy.

testBank.q: For x not equal to zero, let y = tan inverse ((sqrt(1 + x^2) - 1)/x). Then dy/dx equals
steps: 1. Do not differentiate this as it stands. The 1 + x^2 under a root asks for x = tan theta, with theta = tan inverse x in (-pi/2, pi/2) and theta not zero.
2. Then sqrt(1 + x^2) = sec theta, so the argument becomes (sec theta - 1)/tan theta = (1 - cos theta)/sin theta.
3. Use 1 - cos theta = 2 sin^2(theta/2) and sin theta = 2 sin(theta/2) cos(theta/2): the argument is tan(theta/2).
4. theta/2 lies in (-pi/4, pi/4), inside the range of tan inverse, so the cancellation is legal and y = theta/2 = (1/2) tan inverse x.
5. Hence dy/dx = 1/(2(1 + x^2)). The simplification was the question; the differentiation was one line.

testBank.q: For the curve x = t^2, y = t^3 with t > 0, d2y/dx2 at t = 2 equals
steps: 2. d2y/dx2 = d/dt(dy/dx) divided by dx/dt = (3/2)/(2t) = 3/(4t).
3. At t = 2 this is 3/8.

testBank.q: Let c be a constant and let x, y > 0 satisfy x^y + y^x = c, with y a differentiable function of x. Find dy/dx.
steps: 1. There is no formula for the log of a sum, so do not take a log of the whole relation. Split it: let y1 = x^y and y2 = y^x, with y1 + y2 = c.
2. Differentiating, dy1/dx + dy2/dx = 0.
3. For y1 = x^y: ln y1 = y ln x, so (1/y1) dy1/dx = (dy/dx) ln x + y/x, giving dy1/dx = x^y ln x dy/dx + y x^(y - 1).
4. For y2 = y^x: ln y2 = x ln y, so (1/y2) dy2/dx = ln y + (x/y) dy/dx, giving dy2/dx = y^x ln y + x y^(x - 1) dy/dx.
5. Add and set the sum to zero: dy/dx (x^y ln x + x y^(x - 1)) = -(y x^(y - 1) + y^x ln y).
6. Hence dy/dx = -(y x^(y - 1) + y^x ln y)/(x^y ln x + x y^(x - 1)).
testBank.answer: dy/dx = -(y x^(y - 1) + y^x ln y)/(x^y ln x + x y^(x - 1))

commonMistakes: 1. Using the two-function product rule on three or four factors, so one term goes missing.
Fix: Count the factors first and write that many terms before filling any of them in.
▶ where this comes up in the lecture
2. Writing the quotient rule numerator backwards as (uv′ − u′v).
Fix: It is (u′v − uv′)/v² — the derivative of the top comes first; say it out loud once before you write it.
▶ where this comes up in the lecture
3. Differentiating sin y or y³ with respect to x and stopping at cos y or 3y².
Fix: If the inner variable is y, the chain is not finished: every such term ends in ·dy/dx.
▶ where this comes up in the lecture
4. Ignoring the respect variable, so d/dt or d/dy of a function of x is answered as if it were d/dx.
Fix: Differentiate with respect to x first, then multiply by dx/dt (or dx/dy) — d/dt(ln x) = (1/x)(dx/dt).
▶ where this comes up in the lecture
5. Writing d²y/dx² = (d²y/dt²)/(d²x/dt²) for a parametric curve.
Fix: Differentiate dy/dx with respect to t and then multiply by dt/dx = 1/(dx/dt). The ratio of second derivatives is simply not a rule.
▶ where this comes up in the lecture
6. Replacing √(1 − x²) by cos θ without a word about the modulus.
Fix: It is |cos θ|; state that θ = sin⁻¹x lies in −90° to 90°, where cos θ ≥ 0, and then drop the modulus. That sentence carries a mark.
▶ where this comes up in the lecture
7. Attacking sin⁻¹(2x√(1 − x²)) with the chain rule directly, or quoting 2/√(1 − x²) for every x.
Fix: Substitute x = sin θ, simplify to 2θ, then fix the principal-range case — the answer changes sign outside |x| < 1/√2.
▶ where this comes up in the lecture
8. Differentiating x^x as x·x^(x−1) or as x^x·ln x.
Fix: Neither the power rule nor the exponential rule applies when base and power both move. Take log on both sides: dy/dx = x^x(1 + ln x).
▶ where this comes up in the lecture
9. Taking log of a whole sum, e.g. writing ln(x^y + y^x) = y ln x + x ln y.
Fix: Log breaks products, not sums. Name each term separately (u = x^y, v = y^x), log each one, then add u′ + v′ = 0.
▶ where this comes up in the lecture
10. Answering g′(3) as 1/f′(3) when g is the inverse of f.
Fix: First find the input x₀ with f(x₀) = 3, then g′(3) = 1/f′(x₀). Hunt the friendly input — it is always a small number like 0, ±1, ±2 or 3.
▶ where this comes up in the lecture
shortcuts: n factors give n terms For a product of several functions, do not look for a special formula. Differentiate one factor at a time and hold the rest frozen. Three factors give three terms, four factors give four terms. Then pull out whatever is common — that is usually the whole marked answer. Lecture 7
▶ watch Ankit Sir explain it

Peel the layers, outside first Read a composite function from the outside in, and write the derivative in the same order. For √(sin x²): derivative of the root, times derivative of sin, times derivative of x². You never have to think about the whole thing at once — one layer per factor. Lecture 7
▶ watch Ankit Sir explain it

Chain rule, not quotient rule, for the second derivative Once dy/dx comes out as a fraction, write it as a product with a negative power before differentiating again. For dy/dx = −x/y, treat it as −x·y⁻¹. Far less algebra than the quotient rule, and the a² or the constant usually collapses out at the end. Lecture 7
▶ watch Ankit Sir explain it

Make it explicit before you differentiate If a surd or a root is the only thing stopping you from writing y in terms of x, square it away first and differentiate the clean form. Grinding the implicit form works, but it takes three times the space and that is where the sign errors hide. Lecture 7
▶ watch Ankit Sir explain it

Kill the parameter if it dies easily Before you compute dy/dt and dx/dt, check whether squaring, adding, multiplying or dividing the two parametric equations removes t altogether. Once the pair collapses to something like x²y² = 1, dy/dx and every higher derivative are almost free. Lecture 8
▶ watch Ankit Sir explain it

du/dv is parametric differentiation in disguise To differentiate u with respect to v, do not invent anything: du/dv = (du/dx)/(dv/dx). Here x is just playing the role of the parameter t. The same single line handles 'differentiate sin x with respect to cos x' and the hardest f(tan x) vs g(sec x) question. Lecture 8
▶ watch Ankit Sir explain it

In a tower, hunt for the repetition In an infinite power tower or nested radical, find the block that is identical to the whole expression and replace it by y. x^x^x^… becomes y = x^y; √(x + √(x + …)) becomes y² = x + y. One short equation, then differentiate. Never try to differentiate the tower as written. Lecture 8
▶ watch Ankit Sir explain it

Log is compulsory only for variable^variable Taking log is the only way out when a variable sits on a variable power (x^x, x^sin x, x^y). For a long product or quotient of ordinary functions it is just a convenience — log turns it into a sum of logs, so use it if you like, but you are allowed to use the plain product rule. Lecture 8
▶ watch Ankit Sir explain it
chapters.mindMap: Differentiation Three rules, every question Standard derivative table has to be automatic Product rule: one term per factor, freeze the rest Quotient rule: the denominator squared underneath Chain rule: outside in, one layer at a time Count the layers before you start writing ● ● ● With respect to what? Differentiating against x, t or y are three different questions Every y differentiated with respect to x leaves a dy by dx With an x inside, the hidden factor is just one An unnamed outer function stays named, with the inside copied in A function of x against y picks up dx by dy, the upside-down factor ● ● ● When y is not a formula in x Implicit needs no new rule, only careful bookkeeping Collect every dy by dx on one side, take it common, divide Square away the surds and make y explicit when you can Substitute sines to untangle an inverse-trig relation Write the modulus first, then open it with the principal range Second derivative: differentiate again, then substitute dy by dx back ● ● ● Parametric work First derivative is the ratio of the two t-derivatives Second derivative: differentiate in t, then multiply by dt by dx Dividing the two second derivatives is the classic blunder General shape carries the cube of dx by dt underneath Kill the parameter whenever the two equations combine ● ● ● Swapping the roles of x and y Only first derivatives invert Second derivative of x against y carries a minus and a cube One function against another is parametric with x as parameter Differentiate both separately, then divide Substitute the point at the very end, never at the start ● ● ● Variable to the power variable No standard formula fits, so a log is compulsory One log pulls down one power; a tower needs a second A sum of two such terms needs one log per term, never a log of the sum For ordinary products and quotients a log is only your choice Clean the powers before you take the log ● ● ● Towers and nested radicals A problem type, not a new technique Find the block that is the whole expression again The repeat starts after the first symbol A root outside means square first, then spot the repeat Then it is ordinary implicit or log work ● ● ● Inverse functions, trig and otherwise Simplify an inverse-trig expression before you differentiate The interval of x decides which branch and which sign The double-angle form has three branches Cancel inverse sine and sine only inside the principal range For an inverse function, g dash at an output is one over f dash at the input Never invert the function; hunt the friendly input instead ● ● ● Higher-order derivative proofs No new technique, only a choice of where to substitute If a chunk of the first derivative equals y, write y there Trap the leftover exponential from that same line No exponential may survive in the final relation Pick substituting or going direct, and finish on that road ● ● ●

chapters.title: Applications of Derivatives

concepts.title: Why rates matter: the growing circle and the balloon
concepts.quote: Blow air into a balloon at a steady speed. When it is small the balloon swells fast; when it is big it barely grows — same air every second. Once you feel why, this entire chapter needs almost no new formula.
concepts.oneLine: Equal increases in radius do not give equal increases in area or volume — that unequal response is the whole idea behind rate measure.
