notes: Look at the full chapter honestly: there is no new formula waiting for you here. The whole concept of rate measure is the one line you already know — dy/dx is the rate of change of y with respect to x. Everything else is just reading a situation correctly.

So build the feel first. Take a circle of radius 2 cm and push the radius to 3.5 cm. Now from 3.5 cm push it again by the same 1.5 cm, up to 5 cm. Both times you added exactly 1.5 cm of radius, but the second ring you added covers much more area than the first one. Equal increases in radius do not produce equal increases in area — the bigger the circle already is, the more area one extra centimetre brings.

Now the balloon seller. Assume each blow puts in the same amount of air, say 2 cubic centimetres every second, so the change in volume per second is constant. When the balloon is tiny, that same air makes the radius shoot up fast. When the balloon is already big, the same air changes the radius by a very small amount.

Same change in volume, completely different change in radius — because the radius you already have decides how much a little extra volume can do. Reading that sentence as dV/dt and dr/dt is what the rest of this chapter does.

quickChecks.q: A circle's radius goes from 1 cm to 2 cm, and then from 2 cm to 3 cm. Which step adds more area, and by how much?
steps: 1. Areas: π(1)² = π, π(2)² = 4π, π(3)² = 9π
2. First step: 4π − π = 3π cm²
3. Second step: 9π − 4π = 5π cm²
4. Difference: 5π − 3π = 2π cm²
quickChecks.answer: The second step adds more — 5π cm² against 3π cm², that is 2π cm² extra, even though both added 1 cm of radius.

quickChecks.q: A spherical balloon's radius goes from 1 cm to 2 cm, then from 2 cm to 3 cm. How much volume does each step need?
steps: 3. First step: (32/3)π − (4/3)π = (28/3)π cm³
quickChecks.answer: First step needs (28/3)π cm³, the second needs (76/3)π cm³ — nearly three times the air for the same 1 cm of radius.

quickChecks.q: Air is blown into a balloon at a steady 2 cm³ per second. Is the radius increasing faster when the radius is 1 cm or when it is 5 cm?
steps: 1. dV/dt = 2 cm³/s is the same in both cases
2. Volume depends on r³, so a bigger balloon needs far more volume for the same 1 cm of radius
3. So the same 2 cm³ moves the radius much more at r = 1 than at r = 5
quickChecks.answer: Faster at r = 1 cm. The bigger the balloon, the slower the radius grows for the same air per second.

concepts.title: Relating two rates: differentiating A = πr² and V = (4/3)πr³
concepts.oneLine: Differentiate the relation with respect to time: A = πr² gives dA/dt = 2πr·dr/dt, V = (4/3)πr³ gives dV/dt = 4πr²·dr/dt, and the r sitting in those formulas is always the instantaneous radius.
notes: Start with the simplest relation you know. Area of a circle is A = πr². Now differentiate both sides with respect to time t, because both A and r are changing as time passes. You get dA/dt = 2πr·dr/dt.

Read that carefully. Suppose the radius grows by 1.5 cm every second, so dr/dt = 1.5 and it stays constant. Even then dA/dt is not constant, because it carries an r with it. Even when dr/dt is constant, dA/dt is proportional to the radius. Add 1.5 cm to a tiny circle and the area barely moves; add the same 1.5 cm to a circle of radius 1 km and the area jumps enormously.

That r in the formula is the radius at that particular moment, and the word we use for it is instantaneous. If at some instant r = 50 and from there the radius is growing at 1.5 cm/s, then the instantaneous radius is 50 and dr/dt = 1.5. You put 50 in, not any other value.

Volume works the same way. V = (4/3)πr³, so dV/dt = (4/3)π·3r²·dr/dt = 4πr²·dr/dt. Now turn it around: if the man blowing the balloon keeps dV/dt constant, then dr/dt = (dV/dt)/(4πr²), so dr/dt is proportional to 1/r². As the balloon gets bigger, its radius slows down like 1/r², and that is exactly why a big balloon looks like it has stopped growing even though the same air is going in.

So this whole topic is just that: two quantities are changing together, you write the relation between them, and you differentiate it with respect to time. There is no separate formula to remember here.

quickChecks.q: A circle's radius is increasing at 1.5 cm/s. How fast is the area increasing at the instant r = 20 cm?
steps: 1. dA/dt = 2πr·dr/dt.
2. Put r = 20 and dr/dt = 1.5: dA/dt = 2π(20)(1.5).

quickChecks.q: A balloon's radius is growing at 1.5 cm/s. How fast is its volume growing when r = 10 cm?
steps: 1. dV/dt = 4πr²·dr/dt.

quickChecks.q: Air is blown into a spherical balloon at a constant 100π cm³/s. Find dr/dt when r = 5 cm, and say what happens to dr/dt when r doubles to 10 cm.
steps: 1. dV/dt = 4πr²·dr/dt, so dr/dt = (dV/dt)/(4πr²).
4. Doubling r divides dr/dt by 4, because dr/dt is proportional to 1/r².
quickChecks.answer: dr/dt = 1 cm/s at r = 5 cm; it drops to ¼ cm/s at r = 10 cm, i.e. four times slower.

concepts.title: Rate of increase of the area of a circle
concepts.oneLine: With A = πr², dA/dt = 2πr·dr/dt, so r = 20 cm and dr/dt = 2 cm/s give dA/dt = 80π cm²/s.
notes: Read the question once more. The radius of a circle is increasing at a uniform rate of 2 cm/s — that sentence is just dr/dt = 2. And "at the instant when the radius is 20 cm" is telling you where to stand when you read the speedometer.

Come back to the balloon. Blow the same amount of air into a small balloon whose radius is 6 cm and the radius jumps; blow that same air into a big balloon of radius 25 cm and the radius barely moves. The rate depends on the radius at that instant, which is exactly why the question hands you r = 20.
Now the work. Area A = πr². Differentiate both sides with respect to t: dA/dt = π·2r·dr/dt. Only after that do you put the numbers in — r = 20 and dr/dt = 2.
That gives π × 2 × 20 × 2 = 80π. Area is in cm², time in seconds, so the unit is cm²/s. The circle's area is growing at 80π cm²/s at that moment.

quickChecks.q: The radius of a circle increases at 3 cm/s. How fast is the area increasing when r = 5 cm?
steps: 1. A = πr², so dA/dt = 2πr·(dr/dt).
2. Substitute r = 5, dr/dt = 3: dA/dt = 2π × 5 × 3.

quickChecks.q: Same circle, radius increasing at 2 cm/s. Find the rate of increase of the circumference when r = 20 cm.
steps: 1. C = 2πr, so dC/dt = 2π·(dr/dt).
2. Substitute dr/dt = 2: dC/dt = 2π × 2.
3. Notice r does not appear — the circumference grows at the same rate for every radius.

quickChecks.q: The area of a circle is increasing at 20π cm²/s. How fast is the radius increasing when r = 10 cm?
steps: 1. dA/dt = 2πr·(dr/dt).
2. Substitute: 20π = 2π × 10 × (dr/dt) = 20π·(dr/dt).
3. So dr/dt = 1.

concepts.title: Signs and language: 'rate of change' vs 'rate of decrease'
concepts.oneLine: A decreasing quantity has a negative derivative, so 'rate of change' is reported with the minus sign, while 'rate of decrease' is reported as a positive magnitude.
notes: Take the question we just did, but turn it around. The radius of the circle is now decreasing at a uniform rate of 2 cm/s. Decreasing means dr/dt is negative, so dr/dt = −2 cm/s. Nothing else changes.

Run the same calculation at r = 20 cm and you get dA/dt = −80π cm²/s. The minus sign is not an error — it is information. It is telling you the area is shrinking, and that it is shrinking at 80π cm² every second.

So now read the question's language. If you are asked the rate of change of area, you must write −80π cm²/s, minus included, because whoever reads your answer learns the direction from that sign. If you are asked the rate of decrease of area, the question has already told you it is going down — it only wants the amount. You write +80π cm²/s.

Think of your own pocket. In the morning you had ₹20, by afternoon ₹5. If I ask how much your money changed, you say −15. If I ask how much it decreased, you do not say −15, you say 15. Saying 'decreased by −15' would actually mean it went up by 15. Same logic, exactly.

quickChecks.q: The radius of a circle is decreasing at 3 cm/s. Find the rate of change of its area when r = 10 cm.
steps: 1. dr/dt = −3 cm/s (decreasing).
3. dA/dt = −60π cm²/s; keep the minus, since 'rate of change' was asked.

quickChecks.q: For the same circle, radius decreasing at 3 cm/s, find the rate of decrease of the area when r = 10 cm.
steps: 1. Same working: dA/dt = 2π(10)(−3) = −60π cm²/s.
2. 'Rate of decrease' wants only the amount.
3. So the answer is the magnitude, 60π cm²/s.

quickChecks.q: You had ₹50 in the morning and ₹18 in the evening. Write (a) the change in your money, (b) the decrease in your money.
steps: 1. Change = 18 − 50 = −32, so change = −₹32.
2. Decrease asks for the amount only: ₹32.
3. Check: 50 − 32 = 18. Correct.

concepts.title: Rate of change of one area with respect to another
concepts.quote: The question says "rate of change of the area of the second square with respect to the first square" — and suddenly it looks scary. It is not. Once you see that dA₂/dA₁ is just one derivative divided by another, the whole question is over in two lines.
concepts.oneLine: To get the rate of change of one area with respect to another, write both areas in terms of the same variable x and divide dA₂/dx by dA₁/dx.
notes: Picture two squares. Square 1 has side x, square 2 has side y. So A₁ = x² and A₂ = y². Nothing new yet — this is just area of a square, twice.
In this question a relation between y and x is given: y = x − x². So A₂ = (x − x²)². Now both areas are functions of the same single variable x, and that is the whole game.
When you are asked dA₂/dA₁, treat x as the parameter: dA₂/dA₁ = (dA₂/dx) ÷ (dA₁/dx). The dx cancels, so you are allowed to do this, and it turns an impossible-looking derivative into two easy ones.

So differentiate the top with the chain rule, differentiate the bottom, and divide. Read the language of every question carefully — "with respect to" tells you exactly which one goes in the denominator.

quickChecks.q: The sides of two squares are x and y with y = 2x. Find dA₂/dA₁.
steps: 1. A₁ = x², A₂ = y² = 4x².
2. dA₂/dx = 8x and dA₁/dx = 2x.
3. dA₂/dA₁ = 8x / 2x = 4.

quickChecks.q: The sides of two squares are x and y with y = x + 3. Find dA₂/dA₁.
steps: 1. A₁ = x², A₂ = (x + 3)².
2. dA₂/dx = 2(x + 3) and dA₁/dx = 2x.

quickChecks.q: In the problem above (y = x − x²), find the value of dA₂/dA₁ at x = ¼.
steps: 1. From the worked example, dA₂/dA₁ = (1 − x)(1 − 2x).
3. Multiply: 3/8.

concepts.title: Point on a curve where y changes 8 times as fast as x
concepts.quote: One line of English — "the y coordinate is changing 8 times as fast as the x coordinate" — and most students freeze. Convert it into dy/dx = 8 and the whole question is two lines of work.
concepts.oneLine: "y changes 8 times as fast as x" means dy/dt = 8·dx/dt, so dt cancels and you just solve dy/dx = 8 on the curve, then put each α back into the curve to get β.
notes: Take any point P(α, β) on the curve. Walk a little along the curve from one place to another: there is some horizontal change and some vertical change, and their ratio is not the same everywhere. Near a flat part x changes a lot and y barely moves; near a steep part y shoots up while x hardly moves.

That ratio is exactly what the question is controlling. The y coordinate changes at rate dy/dt, the x coordinate at rate dx/dt, and "y is changing 8 times as fast as x" says dy/dt = 8 · dx/dt. Divide both sides by dx/dt, the dt cancels, and the question becomes: find the point on the curve where dy/dx = 8.

Now it is routine. Differentiate the curve 6y = x³ + 2 to get 6 dy/dx = 3x². Put dy/dx = 8 at the point x = α, so 48 = 3α², giving α² = 16 and α = ±4. Two values of α, so two points — never stop at one.
α alone is not the answer. The point lies on the curve, so it must satisfy 6β = α³ + 2. Put α = 4 and then α = −4 separately, and you get both β values.

quickChecks.q: On the curve 6y = x³ + 2, find the points where the y coordinate changes 2 times as fast as the x coordinate.
steps: 1. Condition: dy/dx = 2.
2. Differentiate: 6 dy/dx = 3x², so 6(2) = 3α², giving α² = 4 and α = ±2.

quickChecks.q: On the curve y = x², at which point is the y coordinate changing 6 times as fast as the x coordinate?
steps: 1. Condition: dy/dx = 6.
2. Differentiate: dy/dx = 2x, so 2α = 6 and α = 3.
3. On the curve: β = α² = 9.
quickChecks.answer: (3, 9) — only one point, because the slope equation here is linear in α.

quickChecks.q: On the curve y = x³ − 3x, find the points where the y coordinate changes 9 times as fast as the x coordinate.
steps: 1. Condition: dy/dx = 9.
2. Differentiate: dy/dx = 3x² − 3, so 3α² − 3 = 9, giving 3α² = 12 and α = ±2.

concepts.title: Water leaking from a conical funnel: setting up the problem
concepts.oneLine: In a leaking cone, a steady dV/dt does not mean a steady level drop — read the question, halve the vertical angle, and mark down what is given (dV/dt) and what is asked (dL/dt).
notes: Application of derivatives brings no brand new formula. It asks you to put common sense on paper. So read through the question first.

Water is dripping out of a conical funnel at a uniform rate of 4 cm³ per second, through a tiny hole at the vertex at the bottom. When the slant height of the water is 3 cm, find the rate of decrease of the slant height. The vertical angle of the cone is 120°.

Now feel it before you solve it. Fill the cone with blue water up to the top. Every second the same 4 cm³ is removed. When the cone is full, that 4 cm³ is a wide, thin slice, so the level barely moves. When only a little water is left near the vertex, the same 4 cm³ is a narrow slice, so the level drops fast.

That is exactly why the question hands you a particular moment: slant height = 3 cm. dV/dt is constant at −4 cm³/s, but dL/dt is not constant — it depends on how much water is left, so it must be found at the given instant. And one more thing on the figure: the full vertical angle is 120°, so the half angle at the vertex is 60°. Slant height is the slanted side of the water cone; the depth of water is the vertical one. Do not mix the two.

quickChecks.q: A conical funnel has vertical angle 60° and water leaks out at 2 cm³/s. Write the semi-vertical angle and dV/dt with its sign.
steps: 1. Semi-vertical angle = 60°/2 = 30°.
2. Leaking out means the volume is decreasing, so the rate is negative.

quickChecks.q: In our cone (vertical angle 120°), the water has slant height L. Write its radius r and its depth h in terms of L.
steps: 1. Half angle at the vertex = 60°.

quickChecks.q: The question asks for "the rate of decrease of the slant height when the slant height is 3 cm". Which derivative are you solving for, and at which value do you evaluate it?
steps: 1. Rate of change of slant height with time is dL/dt.
2. "Decrease" means dL/dt is negative, so you report −dL/dt.
3. The instant is fixed by the given slant height.

concepts.title: Volume of the water cone in terms of slant height, and finding dL/dt
concepts.oneLine: Use the semi-vertical angle to write r = L sin60 and h = L cos60, so V = (π/8)L³, and one differentiation gives the slant height falling at 32/(27π) cm/s.
notes: The water inside the funnel is itself a cone. Call it the water cone — that is the only cone that matters now. Its volume is V = (π/3)r²h, where r and h belong to the water, not to the funnel.

But the question talks about slant height. It says: at the moment the slant height of the water is 3 cm, find how fast the slant height is dropping. So every letter in the volume formula must become L before the derivative is touched.

This is where the semi-vertical angle earns its keep. In that right triangle, L is the hypotenuse, the angle at the top is 60°, r sits opposite 60° and h sits beside it. So r = L sin60 = √3L/2 and h = L cos60 = L/2.
Put both in: V = (π/3) × (3L²/4) × (L/2) = (π/8)L³. One variable, one derivative, done. Shape the formula first, differentiate second — that order saves you every time.

quickChecks.q: Same funnel, semi-vertical angle 60°, but water leaks at 2 cm³/s. How fast is the slant height decreasing when L = 4 cm?
steps: 1. V = (π/8)L³, so dV/dt = (3π/8)L² dL/dt.
2. Put dV/dt = −2 and L = 4, so L² = 16.
4. dL/dt = −1/(3π) cm/s.

quickChecks.q: A conical vessel has semi-vertical angle 30°. Water drains at 3 cm³/s. Find the rate of decrease of the slant height when L = 2 cm.
steps: 1. r = L sin30 = L/2 and h = L cos30 = √3L/2.
3. dV/dt = √3π(3L²)/24 × dL/dt = (√3π/8)L² dL/dt.
4. Put dV/dt = −3 and L² = 4: −3 = (√3π/8)(4) dL/dt = (√3π/2) dL/dt.

quickChecks.q: For a water cone of semi-vertical angle 45°, write V in terms of the slant height L.
steps: 1. r = L sin45 = L/√2 and h = L cos45 = L/√2.
3. Rationalise: V = √2πL³/12.

concepts.title: Same cone: rate of decrease of height and of radius
concepts.oneLine: Because h = L/2 and r = (√3/2)L, you just differentiate those two relations and carry dL/dt straight through: |dh/dt| = 16/(27π) cm/s and |dr/dt| = 16√3/(27π) cm/s.
notes: Look at what the question gives you. Slant height data and a volume rate — so you write the volume in terms of L, exactly as we did a minute ago, and you get dL/dt = −32/(27π) cm/s. That number is already ours. We are not earning it twice.

Now the question changes its target: rate of decrease of height, rate of decrease of radius. And you already have both relations from the geometry. Vertical angle is 120°, so the semi-vertical angle is 60°, which gives h = L cos 60° = L/2 and r = L sin 60° = (√3/2)L.

Both h and r are just constant multiples of L, so differentiating with respect to t only drags that same constant along: dh/dt = ½ · dL/dt and dr/dt = (√3/2) · dL/dt. Put the number in and you are finished.

One habit worth building. Write the answer as |dh/dt| and |dr/dt| with the modulus sign from the start. The question itself says "decrease", so the minus is already spoken in the words — your final answer must be a clean positive number.

quickChecks.q: For the same cone of vertical angle 120°, at an instant dL/dt = −4 cm/s. Find the rate of decrease of the height and of the radius.
steps: 1. h = L/2, so dh/dt = ½ × (−4) = −2 cm/s.
3. Rates of decrease are the moduli.

quickChecks.q: In the same cone, the height is decreasing at 5 cm/s. Find the rate of decrease of the slant height and of the radius.
steps: 1. dh/dt = ½ · dL/dt, so −5 = ½ · dL/dt, giving dL/dt = −10 cm/s.

quickChecks.q: In the same cone, at the instant when the slant height of the water is 6 cm, what are h and r?
steps: 1. Semi-vertical angle is 60°, so h = L cos 60° = 6 × ½ = 3 cm.

concepts.title: Same cone: rate of decrease of total surface area
concepts.oneLine: For the water cone with r = (√3/2)L, write TSA = πr² + πrL in slant height alone to get TSA = ((3+2√3)π/4)L², so d(TSA)/dt = ((3+2√3)π/2)·L·dL/dt — then put L = 3 cm and the dL/dt from part 1.
notes: First, be very clear about what surface we are measuring. I am not talking about the container. I am talking about the water sitting inside it, and that water is itself a cone.
So the water has a curved side and an open circle on top. That gives total surface area TSA = πr² + πrL, where πr² is the flat circle at the top and πrL is the curved part.

Now look at the data. You are given the slant height, and you are given how fast the slant height is changing. So before you touch d/dt, make r disappear. For this cone r = (√3/2)L, so TSA = π·(3L²/4) + π·(√3/2)L² = ((3+2√3)π/4)·L².

That ugly bracket is just a constant — leave it alone. Differentiating with respect to time, d(TSA)/dt = ((3+2√3)π/4)·2L·dL/dt = ((3+2√3)π/2)·L·dL/dt. Put L = 3 cm and the dL/dt you already found in part 1, and you are done.

quickChecks.q: For this same cone of water, the slant height is 2 cm and dL/dt = −1 cm/s. How fast is the total surface area of the water decreasing?
Same cone. Find the rate of decrease of only the curved surface area of the water when L = 4 cm and dL/dt = −½ cm/s.
steps: 2. d(CSA)/dt = √3π·L·dL/dt.
3. Put L = 4, dL/dt = −½: d(CSA)/dt = √3π·4·(−½) = −2√3π.

quickChecks.q: Same cone. Water leaves at 6π cm³/s. When L = 4 cm, find dL/dt and then the rate of decrease of the total surface area.
steps: 2. dV/dt = (3πL²/8)·dL/dt. With L = 4: dV/dt = 6π·dL/dt.
3. dV/dt = −6π, so 6π·dL/dt = −6π, giving dL/dt = −1 cm/s.
quickChecks.answer: dL/dt = −1 cm/s, and the total surface area is decreasing at (6+4√3)π cm²/s.

concepts.title: When the cone is given by its height and radius instead of its angle
concepts.oneLine: Height and radius are just the semi-vertical angle in disguise — tanθ = r/h — and the volume must be written in whichever variable the question gives you data for.
notes: In everything we did till now, the semi-vertical angle was the hero. We wrote r = l sinθ, h = l cosθ, and the whole solution followed. So a question that gives you height and radius instead feels like a different species. It is not.

In a right cone, r/h is the tangent of the semi-vertical angle — so tanθ = r/h, and from that one ratio you get sinθ and cosθ by drawing the small right triangle. Here 45/60 = 3/4. Opposite 3, adjacent 4, hypotenuse 5. So sinθ = 3/5 and cosθ = 4/5, and you are back in familiar territory.

Now the second half of the idea, and this is where marks are won. A cone has three measurements you can be asked about — volume, curved surface, total surface — and three lengths to write them in: l, h, r. Write the expression in the same variable the question gives or asks the rate of. Rate of decrease of slant height given? Volume in l. Rate of radius? Volume in r. Rate of height? Volume in h.

And if you have already written it in the wrong variable, don't rub out the page. In a cone everything is interrelated — r = l sinθ, h = l cosθ, r = h tanθ. One substitution shifts your expression into the variable you need. Total surface area is the ugliest of the lot, so for that one especially, pick the variable first and write once.

quickChecks.q: A cone has height 8 cm and radius 6 cm. Find tanθ, sinθ and cosθ for its semi-vertical angle.
steps: 2. Right triangle for 3/4: opposite 3, adjacent 4, hypotenuse 5.
3. So sinθ = 3/5 and cosθ = 4/5.

quickChecks.q: For a cone with tanθ = 3/4, the rate of decrease of the height is given. Write the volume in terms of h and find dV/dt.
steps: 1. Data is about h, so write V in h alone: r = h tanθ = 3h/4.
2. V = ⅓πr²h = ⅓π(9h²/16)h = 3πh³/16.
3. Differentiate: dV/dt = (9πh²/16) · dh/dt.

quickChecks.q: A cone has height 12 cm and radius 5 cm, and the question gives the rate of decrease of the slant height. Which variable do you choose, and what is the volume in that variable?
steps: 1. Data is dl/dt, so write everything in l.
2. tanθ = 5/12, so hypotenuse = 13, giving sinθ = 5/13 and cosθ = 12/13.
3. V = ⅓π l³ sin²θ cosθ = ⅓π l³ × (25/169) × (12/13) = ⅓π l³ × 300/2197.
quickChecks.answer: Choose l; V = 100πl³/2197, so dV/dt = (300πl²/2197) · dl/dt.

concepts.title: Man walking away from a lamppost: how fast his shadow grows
concepts.oneLine: Call the man's distance from the pole x and his shadow y, read tanθ from the big and the small right triangle, get 3y = 2x, then differentiate once to get dy/dt = (2/3)·dx/dt.
notes: First, understand the shadow itself, because most people never do. Light leaves the top of the lamppost in every direction. Wherever it reaches the ground, the ground is bright. Some of those rays hit the man — his head, his back, his legs, his shoes — and they cannot get through him.

So behind the man there is a patch of ground that no light reaches. That dark patch is his shadow. The shadow ends exactly where the ray that just grazes the top of his head lands on the ground. That one ray decides everything.

Now set up the picture. Let x be the man's distance from the foot of the lamppost, and let y be the length of his shadow. Then dx/dt is how fast he walks and dy/dt is how fast his shadow lengthens — that is what we want. Remember, speed is the rate of change of distance from a fixed point, and here the fixed point is the foot of the pole.

That grazing ray makes an angle θ with the ground. It sits in two right triangles at once. Write tanθ from the big triangle and tanθ from the small triangle, equate them, and the relation between x and y falls out. After that, differentiate with respect to t and you are done. No similarity language is needed anywhere here.

quickChecks.q: Same 5 m lamppost, same 2 m man, but now he walks away at 1.5 m/s. How fast does his shadow lengthen?
steps: 1. The relation does not change: 3y = 2x.
3. dy/dt = 1.

quickChecks.q: A 2 m tall man walks away from a 6 m high lamppost at 5 m/s. Find the rate at which his shadow grows.
steps: 1. tanθ = 6/(x + y) from the big triangle and tanθ = 2/y from the small one.
3. Differentiate: 2·dy/dt = dx/dt, so dy/dt = 5/2.

quickChecks.q: In the problem above (5 m pole, 2 m man, 6 m/s), how fast is the tip of the shadow moving away from the pole?
steps: 1. The tip's distance from the pole is x + y, not y.
2. From 3y = 2x, y = 2x/3, so x + y = x + 2x/3 = 5x/3.

concepts.title: Aeroplane flying horizontally: drawing the picture and the 2-minute distance
concepts.oneLine: An aeroplane flying horizontally recedes from a point on the ground more slowly as it goes, and at 15 km/h it has covered only 1/2 km horizontally in 2 minutes.
notes: Picture yourself on the roof, eyes at ground level, and the plane directly overhead. In the next 30 seconds it covers some horizontal distance and looks far away. In the 30 seconds after that it covers exactly the same horizontal distance, but now it hardly seems to have moved.

Your eye does not measure the horizontal distance in the air — it measures the slant distance from you to the plane. Early on, almost all of the horizontal motion gets added to that slant line. Later the line is already long and nearly flat, so the same horizontal step adds very little to it.

It is exactly the kite feeling. At the start the kite seems to run away from you fast. At the end you keep letting out thread and it looks like nothing is growing. Same thread going out, slower growth in what you feel.

Now the question. The bird — call the plane a lazy bird, 15 km/h is nothing for a plane — flies horizontally at a constant height of 2/3 km. It passes over a fixed point on the ground; take that instant as t = 0. We want the rate at which it is receding from that point when t = 2 minutes. First job: find where it is at t = 2. Speed is in km per hour and time is in minutes, so convert before you touch anything else: 15 km in 60 minutes is 15/60 km per minute, and in 2 minutes that is 1/2 km. Height stays 2/3 km, horizontal distance is 1/2 km, and the red slant line joining you to the bird is the distance whose rate we chase in the next section.

quickChecks.q: The same plane flies at 15 km/h. How far has it gone horizontally 4 minutes after passing over you?
steps: 1. Speed = 15/60 km per minute.

quickChecks.q: A plane flies horizontally at 18 km/h. What horizontal distance does it cover in 2 minutes?
steps: 1. Speed = 18/60 km per minute.

quickChecks.q: In the problem above, at t = 2 minutes the height is 2/3 km and the horizontal distance is 1/2 km. How far is the plane from you at that instant?
steps: 1. The distance z is the slant side: z² = x² + y².
3. Take 36 as the common denominator: 9/36 + 16/36 = 25/36.

concepts.title: Differentiating z² = x² + y² to find the rate of receding
concepts.oneLine: Differentiate z² = x² + y² with the height y fixed, then put in x = 1/2 km and z = 5/6 km at t = 2 minutes to get dz/dt = 9 km/h.
notes: Look at the triangle again. The height of the plane is fixed at 2/3 km, the horizontal distance from the point on the ground is x, and the straight line from that point to the plane is z. Pythagoras gives z² = x² + y², and the height is the constant one, so z² = x² + 4/9.

This relation is true at every instant of the flight, not just at t = 2 minutes — that is exactly why I am allowed to differentiate it. Differentiate both sides with respect to time: the 4/9 is a constant, so it dies and gives 0, and I am left with 2z·dz/dt = 2x·dx/dt. The 2s cancel, so z·dz/dt = x·dx/dt.

Only now bring in the moment t = 2 minutes. The plane flies at 15 km/h, so in 2 minutes, which is 1/30 of an hour, it has covered x = 1/2 km. Then z = √(1/4 + 4/9) = √(9/36 + 16/36) = √(25/36) = 5/6 km.
Differentiate first, substitute the instant second. Put the numbers in: (5/6)·dz/dt = (1/2)(15), so dz/dt = 9 km/h. That is the rate at which the plane is receding from the point it flew over.

quickChecks.q: An aeroplane flies horizontally at a constant height of 4 km with a speed of 10 km/h and passes over a point P on the ground. How fast is its distance from P increasing when it is 3 km horizontally away from P?
steps: 1. z² = x² + 16, true at every instant.
2. Differentiate: 2z·dz/dt = 2x·dx/dt, so z·dz/dt = x·dx/dt.

quickChecks.q: An aeroplane flies horizontally at a constant height of 5 km with a speed of 13 km/h. At what rate is it receding from the point it flew over when its distance from that point is 13 km?
steps: 2. z·dz/dt = x·dx/dt gives 13·dz/dt = 12 × 13 = 156.

quickChecks.q: In the problem above, suppose the height were 0, so the plane flew along the ground straight through the point at 15 km/h. What would dz/dt be?
steps: 1. With y = 0, z² = x², so z = x.
2. Then dz/dt = dx/dt = 15.
quickChecks.answer: dz/dt = 15 km/h, the same as the plane's speed — the receding rate can never beat the speed, it only equals it when the height is 0.

concepts.title: Sliding ladder: distance of the midpoint from the corner
concepts.oneLine: For the midpoint P of a slipping ladder, write its distance from the corner as 4s² = x² + y², differentiate, and you see at once that both dx/dt and dy/dt are needed.
notes: Put the corner at O, the foot of the ladder at (x, 0) and the top at (0, y). The ladder's length is fixed, so as the foot slips out, x grows and y shrinks. The foot slipping horizontally at 20 cm/s is exactly dx/dt = 20 cm/s — rate of change of distance from a fixed point.

Now focus on P, the midpoint of the ladder. Its coordinates are (x/2, y/2), so if s = OP, then s² = x²/4 + y²/4. Clear the fraction and write it as 4s² = x² + y² — that one clean line is the whole setup.

Differentiate both sides with respect to t: 8s·ds/dt = 2x·dx/dt + 2y·dy/dt, and after cancelling the 2's, 4s·ds/dt = x·dx/dt + y·dy/dt. Look at the right side. Two terms, two different rates — you cannot finish with dx/dt alone, you must also know dy/dt.

And dy/dt is not free to choose. The ladder's own length gives x² + y² = (length)², so x·dx/dt + y·dy/dt = 0 at every instant. That is where dy/dt comes from, and that is why the values of x and y go in only at the moment θ = π/4 — differentiate first, substitute the instant afterwards.

quickChecks.q: A 10 m ladder slips with its foot at x = 6 m and its top at y = 8 m. The foot moves out at 20 cm/s. Find dy/dt.
steps: 1. Convert: dx/dt = 20 cm/s = 0.2 m/s.
2. Length fixed: x² + y² = 100, so x·dx/dt + y·dy/dt = 0.
quickChecks.answer: dy/dt = −0.15 m/s, i.e. the top is coming down at 15 cm/s.

quickChecks.q: For that same instant (10 m ladder, x = 6, y = 8), find s and ds/dt for the midpoint.
steps: 1. 4s² = x² + y² = 36 + 64 = 100, so s² = 25 and s = 5 m.
3. So 20·ds/dt = 0.
quickChecks.answer: s = 5 m (half the ladder) and ds/dt = 0 — the midpoint's distance from the corner never changes.

quickChecks.q: A ladder slips so that at one instant θ = π/4 and the foot is moving out at 12 cm/s. What is dy/dt there, and what is the midpoint's ds/dt?
steps: 1. At θ = π/4 the legs are equal, so x = y.
2. x·dx/dt + y·dy/dt = 0 with x = y gives dy/dt = −dx/dt = −12 cm/s.
3. 4s·ds/dt = x·dx/dt + y·dy/dt = 0, so ds/dt = 0.
quickChecks.answer: dy/dt = −12 cm/s (top falling at 12 cm/s), and ds/dt = 0 for the midpoint.

concepts.title: Velocity of the ladder's midpoint at a given angle
concepts.oneLine: For a sliding ladder, x = L cos θ and y = L sin θ, differentiating x² + y² = L² gives dy/dt = −(x/y)·dx/dt, and the midpoint's speed is ½√((dx/dt)² + (dy/dt)²) — which comes out b/√3 at θ = 60°.
notes: Put the corner at the origin. The foot of the ladder sits at (x, 0), the top at (0, y), and θ is the angle the ladder makes with the floor. Since the length L never changes, x = L cos θ and y = L sin θ.

There is no need to redraw the triangle every time. Only one relation is needed: x² + y² = L². Differentiate both sides with respect to t. L is a fixed number, so its derivative is 0, which gives 2x·dx/dt + 2y·dy/dt = 0.

That one line hands me dy/dt = −(x/y)·dx/dt, and this is true at every moment of the slide, not just at the angle in the question. The minus sign is the ladder's top coming down while the foot runs out. dx/dt is given as a constant b; θ only decides the ratio x/y.

Now the midpoint. It sits at (x/2, y/2), so both of its rates are exactly half of the ones just found. Its speed is the resultant of those two halves — that is the step where you must use all the data, and that is what makes this version of the question worth doing.

quickChecks.q: Same ladder, same constant dx/dt = b. Find dy/dt and the speed of the midpoint at θ = π/4.
steps: 1. x = L cos 45° = L/√2 and y = L sin 45° = L/√2, so x = y.
2. dy/dt = −(x/y)·dx/dt = −1 × b = −b.
3. Midpoint rates: b/2 and −b/2.
quickChecks.answer: dy/dt = −b, and the midpoint's speed is b/√2 (= b√2/2).

quickChecks.q: Now take the other easy angle: θ = π/6, with dx/dt = b again. Find dy/dt and the midpoint's speed.
steps: 1. x = L cos 30° = L√3/2 and y = L sin 30° = L/2.
3. Midpoint rates: b/2 and −√3b/2.
4. Speed = √(b²/4 + 3b²/4) = √(b²) = b.
5. Check with the circle shortcut: b/(2 sin 30°) = b/(2 × ½) = b. ✓
quickChecks.answer: dy/dt = −√3 b, and the midpoint's speed is exactly b.

quickChecks.q: A 10 m ladder's foot is pulled away from the wall at 3 m/s. How fast is its midpoint moving when the ladder makes 60° with the floor?
steps: 3. Midpoint rates: 3/2 m/s and −√3/2 m/s.
4. Speed = √(9/4 + 3/4) = √3 m/s ≈ 1.73 m/s. The length 10 never mattered.

concepts.title: Approximation Formula from the First-Principle Derivative
concepts.oneLine: For a very small h, the first-principle derivative rearranges into f(a+h) ≈ f(a) + h·f'(a) — the working formula for every approximation question.
notes: Errors and approximation is a very small topic, but it is built on something you have had with you for a year. The derivative from first principle: f'(a) = lim h→0 [f(a+h) − f(a)]/h. Recall it once and we are almost done.

Now read the limit carefully. h → 0 means h is a very small quantity. So drop the limit sign and keep the honest statement: for very small h, f'(a) is approximately [f(a+h) − f(a)]/h. Equality becomes ≈, and that ≈ is the whole topic.

From there it is just shifting. Cross multiply with h to get h·f'(a) ≈ f(a+h) − f(a). Send f(a) across. f(a+h) ≈ f(a) + h·f'(a) — this one line is the formula for every approximation question you will ever see.

Read the formula in words and you will never misuse it. The value at a slightly shifted point is the old value plus the small shift times the rate of change at the old point. You pick a as a point where f(a) is exact and easy, and h as the small leftover.

quickChecks.q: For f(x) = x², use the approximation formula to find f(5.02).
steps: 1. Take a = 5 and h = 0.02, since 5² is exact and h is small.

quickChecks.q: Approximate √25.3 using f(a+h) ≈ f(a) + h·f'(a).
If you have to approximate 217^(1/3), what should you choose as a and as h, and why?
steps: 1. Take f(x) = x^(1/3) and look for the nearest perfect cube below 217.
2. 216 = 6³, so f(216) = 6 is exact. Choose a = 216.
3. Then h = 217 − 216 = 1, which is small compared to 216.
quickChecks.answer: a = 216 and h = 1, because 216 is a perfect cube so f(a) = 6 is exact and the leftover h is tiny

concepts.title: Approximating 217^(1/3) Using the Derivative
concepts.oneLine: To approximate 217^(1/3), take f(x) = x^(1/3), a = 216, h = 1 in f(a+h) ≈ f(a) + h·f′(a), giving 6 + 1/108 ≈ 6.0093 — close, but only approximate because h = 1 is not small.
notes: We built the formula f(a+h) ≈ f(a) + h·f′(a) in the last part. Now for the one place it actually earns its keep: approximating awkward values.
The whole game is choosing f, a and h. You want an 'a' whose value you know in your sleep. Here 217 is one more than 216, and 216 = 6³, so take f(x) = x^(1/3), a = 216, h = 1.
Pick 'a' as the nearest number whose value you already know, and let h be the small leftover. After that it is mechanical: f(216) = 6, f′(x) = (1/3)x^(−2/3), so f′(216) = 1/(3·36) = 1/108.

Now about the word 'approximate'. The formula was derived assuming h is very small. Is 1 a very small number? No. So if you work out 217^(1/3) by this formula and then by a calculator, the two values will differ. Make h smaller and the gap shrinks.

quickChecks.q: Find the approximate value of 28^(1/3).
Find the approximate value of √26.
Find the approximate value of 1003^(1/3), given 1000^(1/3) = 10.

concepts.title: Approximating tan 46° — and Where the Error Comes From
concepts.oneLine: Split 46° as π/4 + π/180 and use f(a+h) ≈ f(a) + h·f'(a): tan 46° ≈ 1 + π/90 ≈ 1.035, and the error stays small only because h is small.
notes: A fair question at this point: can't all of this be done with the binomial theorem? For powers, yes. But ask for tan 46° and binomial has nothing to say. This one formula, f(a+h) ≈ f(a) + h·f'(a), works for every function — you only need an angle where you already know the value and the derivative.

So read the formula properly. a is the number where the function value is known to you, and where the derivative is also known. Here that is 45°: tan 45° = 1, and sec² 45° = 2. The new angle, 46°, is a + h with h = 1°.

Now the one thing that trips people. Derivative formulas of calculus are valid only when the angle is in radian. You cannot feed 1 degree into h. Convert it: 1° = π/180 radian. Then tan 46° ≈ tan(π/4) + (π/180)·sec²(π/4) = 1 + 2π/180 = 1 + π/90.

Put π ≈ 22/7 and you get 1 + 22/630 ≈ 1.0349. Search tan 46° anywhere and you will get 1.0355. It does not match exactly, it matches for about two decimal places. The formula was born from the derivative, where h is infinitesimally small; our h = 1° is small but not that small, and that gap is the error. Make h smaller and the approximate value sits closer to the true one.

quickChecks.q: Approximate tan 44° using the same method.
steps: 1. f(x) = tan x, a = π/4, and this time h = −1° = −π/180 radian.
quickChecks.answer: tan 44° ≈ 0.9651 (true value 0.9657, so two decimals agree)

quickChecks.q: Approximate sin 31°.
You approximate tan 46° with h = 1° and a friend approximates tan 50° with h = 5°, both from a = 45°. Whose answer is closer to the true value, and why?
steps: 1. Both use f(a + h) ≈ f(a) + h·f'(a), which is exact only as h tends to 0.
2. The error grows as h grows, so compare the two h values: 1° against 5°.
quickChecks.answer: Mine, for tan 46°, because h = 1° is the smaller angle — the smaller the h, the smaller the error.

concepts.title: Tangent and Normal: The Three Fundamentals
concepts.quote: Three lines in your copy, and the whole of tangent-normal opens up. Write them down once properly and you will never be clueless in front of such a question again.
concepts.oneLine: Every tangent-normal question runs on three facts: the point-slope form y − y₁ = m(x − x₁), dy/dx at a point is the slope of the tangent there, and (slope of tangent)(slope of normal) = −1.
notes: Listen carefully, because this is the basic level funda that gets used everywhere in Advanced. You have not done coordinate geometry yet, so it may feel slightly heavy the first time. Learn it anyway — the tangent sits in the JEE Advanced syllabus and in every other competitive syllabus.

Fundamental one. Take a line passing through the point (x₁, y₁), and suppose its slope is m. Then the equation of that line is y − y₁ = m(x − x₁). So if you know one point on a line and its slope, the line's equation is finished. This is called the point-slope form.

Fundamental two. Now take a curve y = f(x), and a point P(x₁, y₁) given to you on it. To write the tangent at P you need the slope of the tangent, and the very first definition already gave it: the derivative at a point gives the slope of the tangent at that point. So dy/dx evaluated at (x₁, y₁) is your m, and then fundamental one takes over.

Fundamental three. The normal is the line perpendicular to the tangent at that same point. From straight lines, for two perpendicular lines m₁m₂ = −1. So (slope of tangent)(slope of normal) = −1, always. These three things are all that go into writing a tangent or a normal.

quickChecks.q: A line passes through (2, 3) and its slope is 4. Write its equation.
steps: 1. Point-slope form: y − y₁ = m(x − x₁), with x₁ = 2, y₁ = 3, m = 4.

quickChecks.q: For the curve y = x², find the slope of the tangent and the slope of the normal at the point (3, 9).
steps: 1. dy/dx = 2x.
2. At x = 3: dy/dx = 6, so the slope of the tangent is 6.
3. Use (slope of tangent)(slope of normal) = −1: 6 × m = −1.
quickChecks.answer: Slope of tangent = 6, slope of normal = −1/6

quickChecks.q: At a point on a curve the slope of the tangent is −2/5. What is the slope of the normal there?
steps: 1. m₁m₂ = −1, so m₂ = −1/m₁.

concepts.title: Tangent and Normal to 2x² − 3y² = −10 at (1, 2)
concepts.oneLine: Differentiate the curve as it stands, put the point in to get the tangent slope 1/3, flip-and-negate it to −3 for the normal, and write both lines through (1, 2).
notes: Here is the question: find the equation of the tangent and the normal to the curve 2x² − 3y² = −10 at the point (1, 2). First check the point actually lies on the curve — 2(1) − 3(4) = 2 − 12 = −10. It does.

Now, this curve is a hyperbola. You will meet it properly later in coordinate geometry, and there you may feel you must remember a special tangent formula. Forget the formula — differentiate the equation as it is, and the derivative at the point is the slope of the tangent.

Differentiate both sides with respect to x. The 2x² gives 4x. The −3y² gives −6y·dy/dx, because y is a function of x and the chain rule asks for that dy/dx. The −10 on the right is a constant, so it gives 0.

So 4x − 6y·dy/dx = 0. Put x = 1 and y = 2: 4 − 12·dy/dx = 0, which gives dy/dx = 4/12 = 1/3. That is the slope of the tangent at (1, 2), so the slope of the normal is −3. Both lines pass through (1, 2), so y − y₁ = m(x − x₁) finishes the job twice.

quickChecks.q: Find the tangent and the normal to 3x² − 2y² = 10 at (2, 1).
steps: 1. Check: 3(4) − 2(1) = 12 − 2 = 10. The point is on the curve.
2. Differentiate: 6x − 4y·dy/dx = 0.
3. At (2, 1): 12 − 4·dy/dx = 0, so dy/dx = 3. Tangent slope m = 3.
4. Normal slope = −1/3.

quickChecks.q: Find the tangent and the normal to x² + 2y² = 9 at (1, 2).
steps: 1. Check: 1 + 2(4) = 1 + 8 = 9. The point is on the curve.
2. Differentiate: 2x + 4y·dy/dx = 0.
3. At (1, 2): 2 + 8·dy/dx = 0, so dy/dx = −1/4. Tangent slope m = −1/4.
4. Normal slope = 4.

quickChecks.q: Find the tangent and the normal to x² + y² = 25 at (3, 4).
steps: 1. Check: 9 + 16 = 25. The point is on the curve.
2. Differentiate: 2x + 2y·dy/dx = 0, so dy/dx = −x/y.
3. At (3, 4): dy/dx = −3/4. Tangent slope m = −3/4.
4. Normal slope = 4/3.
quickChecks.answer: Tangent: 3x + 4y − 25 = 0. Normal: 4x − 3y = 0 (it passes through the centre, as a circle's normal always does).

concepts.title: Tangent and Normal on a Parametric Curve
concepts.oneLine: For a parametric curve, dy/dx = (dy/dt)/(dx/dt); find the t that matches both coordinates of the given point, then write the tangent and normal as usual.
notes: Look at the point first, not the curve. At (1, 2) the tangent is y − 2 = (slope of tangent)(x − 1) and the normal is y − 2 = (slope of normal)(x − 1). That part never changes, whatever form the curve comes in.
So the only question left is the slope. In parametric form you never differentiate y with respect to x directly — you divide: dy/dx = (dy/dt)/(dx/dt). Here dy/dt = 2 and dx/dt = 2t, so dy/dx = 1/t.
Now the one new step: which t gives the point (1, 2)? Put y = 2 in y = 2t and you get t = 1. Put x = 1 in x = t² and you get t = ±1. The value must work for both, so t = 1.

With t = 1, slope of tangent = 1/t = 1 and slope of normal = −1. Drop them into the two lines and you are finished. And notice what the curve actually was: x = t², y = 2t is the standard parabola y² = 4x in disguise.

quickChecks.q: For x = t², y = 2t, find the tangent and the normal at (4, 4).
steps: 1. y = 2t gives t = 2; x = t² gives t = ±2; both match at t = 2.
2. dy/dx = 1/t = 1/2, so slope of normal = −2.
3. Tangent: y − 4 = ½(x − 4) → x − 2y + 4 = 0.

quickChecks.q: For x = t², y = 2t, find the tangent and the normal at (9, −6).
steps: 1. y = 2t gives t = −3; x = t² gives t = ±3; both match at t = −3.
2. dy/dx = 1/t = −1/3, so slope of normal = 3.

quickChecks.q: For x = t², y = 2t, what is the parameter value at (1, −2), and what is the slope of the tangent there?
steps: 1. y = −2 in y = 2t gives t = −1.
2. x = 1 in x = t² gives t = ±1, and only t = −1 fits both.
3. Slope of tangent = 1/t = −1.
quickChecks.answer: t = −1, slope of tangent = −1 (so the normal there has slope 1).

concepts.title: Tangent to a Modulus Curve at x = −2: the Vicinity Trick
concepts.oneLine: A tangent only feels the graph in a tiny neighbourhood, so near x = −2 you replace |x| by −x and differentiate an ordinary curve.
notes: Think about what a tangent actually is. Take the tangent at one point P, then bend the graph far away from P — send it up into the sky or down into the ground — does your tangent at P change? It does not. A tangent at a point only knows what the graph is doing in the vicinity of that point — vicinity means neighbourhood. Far ahead and far behind do not exist for it. The graph can be discontinuous somewhere else, non-differentiable somewhere else, it makes no difference to you.

Now put that thought into our question: find the tangent and normal to y = |x|² − |x| at x = −2. Only the numbers sitting just to the left and just to the right of −2 matter. Every one of them is negative.

And for a negative number, |x| = −x. That is confirmed, no cases, no doubt. So in the vicinity of x = −2 the curve is simply y = x² + x — an ordinary parabola, no mod anywhere, and it differentiates like anything else.

The rest is routine. Slope from dy/dx at x = −2, the point from y at x = −2, then y − y₁ = m(x − x₁) for the tangent and the negative reciprocal for the normal. The whole mod drama is over in one line.

quickChecks.q: Find the tangent to y = |x|² + 3|x| at x = −1.
steps: 1. Around x = −1, x is negative, so |x| = −x.
2. Curve becomes y = x² − 3x near x = −1.
3. y at x = −1 is 1 + 3 = 4, so the point is (−1, 4).
4. dy/dx = 2x − 3, so slope at x = −1 is −2 − 3 = −5.
5. Tangent: y − 4 = −5(x + 1).

quickChecks.q: Find the normal to y = x·|x| at x = −2.
steps: 1. Around x = −2, |x| = −x, so y = x·(−x) = −x².
2. y at x = −2 is −4, so the point is (−2, −4).
3. dy/dx = −2x, so the tangent slope is 4.
4. Normal slope = −1/4, so y + 4 = −(1/4)(x + 2).

quickChecks.q: Find the tangent to y = x² − |x| at x = 3.
steps: 1. Around x = 3 every number is positive, so |x| = x.
2. Curve becomes y = x² − x near x = 3.
3. y at x = 3 is 9 − 3 = 6, so the point is (3, 6).
4. dy/dx = 2x − 1, so slope at x = 3 is 5.
5. Tangent: y − 6 = 5(x − 3).

concepts.title: Variety 2 Setup: When the Slope Is Given
concepts.oneLine: Variety 2 hands you the slope and hides the point, so use slope = −a/b on the given line to convert a 'normal parallel to this line' condition into a known tangent slope, and then hunt the point.
notes: Write these two headings in your copy. Variety 1: tangent and normal at a given point — that is everything we did till now. Variety 2: the slope of the tangent or the normal is given, find the equation.

In Variety 2 your whole job is to use the given slope to find the point. Once the point is in your hand, the question becomes a joke, because it is now Variety 1. Slope → point → equation. That is the full thought process.

For this you must be fast with one fact. If a line is written as ax + by + c = 0, its slope is −a/b. There are many ways to prove it; the easiest is to differentiate the line itself with respect to x. You get a + b·dy/dx = 0, so dy/dx = −a/b.

And why is dy/dx giving the slope of a line, when dy/dx is supposed to be the slope of the tangent? Think about it. If I draw a tangent to a straight line at any point on it, I get the same line back. The tangent to a line is the line itself, so differentiating a line always hands you its slope.

quickChecks.q: Find the slope of the line 3x − 4y + 7 = 0.
steps: 1. Here a = 3 and b = −4.

quickChecks.q: The normal to a curve at a point P is parallel to x + 2y = 5. What is dy/dx at P?
steps: 1. Parallel, so slope of normal = slope of x + 2y − 5 = 0 = −1/2.
2. Tangent ⟂ normal, so slope of tangent = −1/(−1/2) = 2.
3. dy/dx at P is the slope of the tangent.

quickChecks.q: The tangent to a curve at a point Q is parallel to 4x + y = 1. Write the slope of the tangent and of the normal at Q.
steps: 1. Slope of 4x + y − 1 = 0 is −a/b = −4/1 = −4.
2. Parallel, so slope of tangent at Q = −4.
3. Slope of normal = −1/(−4) = 1/4.

concepts.title: Finding the Point Where the Tangent Slope Is 9 on y = x³ − 3x
concepts.oneLine: When the slope is given instead of the point, write two relations for (α, β) — it lies on the curve, and dy/dx at it equals the given slope — then solve for both points.
notes: Here the normal at some point is parallel to 2x + 18y = 9. The slope of a line is minus the x coefficient over the y coefficient, so that line has slope −2/18 = −1/9. The normal has slope −1/9, so the tangent has slope 9. Whether the question hands you 9 for the tangent or −1/9 for the normal, it is the same question.
Now call the unknown point (α, β). You have two unknowns, so you need two relations. The first relation is the one everyone forgets: (α, β) lies on the curve, so it must satisfy it — β = α³ − 3α.
The second relation comes from the slope. Differentiate: dy/dx = 3x² − 3. At (α, β) this must equal 9, so 3α² − 3 = 9, giving α² = 4 and α = ±2. Put each α back into relation one to get its β.

That is the whole of this second variety. In the first variety you were given the point and you found the slope; here you are given the slope and you hunt down the point. Once both points are in your hand, writing the tangent or normal equation is just point-slope work.

quickChecks.q: Find the points on y = x³ − 3x where the tangent is parallel to the x-axis.
steps: 1. Parallel to the x-axis means tangent slope = 0.
2. dy/dx = 3x² − 3 = 0, so x² = 1 and x = ±1.

quickChecks.q: Find the points on y = x³ − 3x at which the normal is parallel to 2x + 48y = 5.
steps: 1. Slope of the line = −2/48 = −1/24, so slope of normal = −1/24 and slope of tangent = 24.
2. Relation 1: β = α³ − 3α.
3. Relation 2: 3α² − 3 = 24, so 3α² = 27, α² = 9, α = ±3.

quickChecks.q: Find the point on y = x² − 4x where the tangent has slope 2.
steps: 1. Relation 1: β = α² − 4α.
2. Relation 2: dy/dx = 2x − 4, so 2α − 4 = 2, giving α = 3.

concepts.title: Practice: Normal Parallel to a Given Line
concepts.oneLine: When the slope is given and the point is unknown, you always need two equations: one from the point lying on the curve, one from the derivative matched to the required tangent slope.
notes: Read the question slowly. It asks for the normal to be parallel to a given line. The derivative never gives you the slope of the normal — the derivative is always the slope of the tangent, so convert first: m of normal × m of tangent = −1.
Now the routine. The unknown point is (h, k), so you need two equations in two unknowns. One comes from the derivative: dy/dx at that point equals the tangent slope you just worked out.

The second one is the one students forget. The point sits on the curve, so it must satisfy the curve's equation. In every one of these, the first equation is the one you get from the point satisfying the curve — write it down before you touch the derivative.
That is the second type of question in this topic. Type one: point is given, find the tangent or normal. Type two: slope is given, find the point. Both are two equations, nothing more.

quickChecks.q: Find the point on y = x² where the normal is parallel to the line x + 4y = 5.
steps: 1. Line slope: 4y = 5 − x, y = (5 − x)/4, slope = −1/4.
2. Normal slope = −1/4, so tangent slope = −1/(−1/4) = 4.
3. Point (h, k) on curve: k = h².
4. dy/dx = 2x, so 2h = 4 and h = 2.
5. Then k = 2² = 4.

quickChecks.q: Find the point on y = x² − 3x + 2 where the normal is parallel to the line x − y = 3.
steps: 1. Line slope: y = x − 3, slope = 1.
2. Normal slope = 1, so tangent slope = −1/1 = −1.
3. Point (h, k) on curve: k = h² − 3h + 2.
4. dy/dx = 2x − 3, so 2h − 3 = −1 and h = 1.

quickChecks.q: Find the points on y = x³ where the normal is parallel to the line x + 12y = 0.
steps: 1. Line slope: 12y = −x, y = −x/12, slope = −1/12.
2. Normal slope = −1/12, so tangent slope = 12.
3. Point (h, k) on curve: k = h³.
4. dy/dx = 3x², so 3h² = 12, h² = 4, h = ±2.
5. h = 2 gives k = 8; h = −2 gives k = −8.

concepts.title: Shortest Distance from a Curve to a Line Lies Along the Common Normal
concepts.oneLine: The nearest point on a curve to a line lies along their common normal, so you just find the point where the tangent is parallel to that line.
notes: Picture it. Here is the parabola, and here is the straight line. Pick different points on the curve and the distance to the line keeps changing — and remember, distance from a point to a line always means perpendicular distance.

Between any two curves, the shortest distance (and the longest too) is measured along their common normal. Common normal means one single line that is normal to both of them. In our picture, the segment OP is normal to the line and normal to the curve at P. That is why it carries the shortest distance.

Now use the slopes. If the given line has slope m, then the common normal at P has slope −1/m. And the tangent at P is perpendicular to that normal, so the tangent has slope m — the same slope as the line itself.

So "the point on the curve closest to the line" is nothing but "the point where the tangent is parallel to the line". That is the exact question from the last section, only dressed differently. Solve dy/dx = m for x, get the point, and if the distance is asked, finish with the perpendicular distance formula.

quickChecks.q: Find the point on y = x² + 4 that is closest to the line y = 2x + 5.
steps: 1. Slope of the line = 2, so at the closest point the tangent slope must be 2.
2. dy/dx = 2x, so 2x = 2 gives x = 1.

quickChecks.q: Find the shortest distance between the parabola y = x² + 4 and the line y = 4x − 1.
steps: 1. Slope of the line = 4, so tangent slope at the nearest point P is 4.
3. Write the line as 4x − y − 1 = 0 and use the perpendicular distance formula: |4(2) − 8 − 1| / √(4² + 1²) = 1/√17.

quickChecks.q: On the curve y = x², which point is nearest to the line y = 4x − 9, and what is the slope of the common normal there?
steps: 1. Slope of the line = 4, so the tangent at the nearest point has slope 4.
2. dy/dx = 2x, so 2x = 4 gives x = 2 and y = 4.
3. The common normal is perpendicular to the line, so its slope is −1/4.
quickChecks.answer: Nearest point (2, 4); common normal has slope −1/4

concepts.title: Variety 3: Tangent from an External Point
concepts.oneLine: From an outside point (λ, μ), name the point of contact (α, β) and solve two equations: (α, β) lies on the curve, and (β − μ)/(α − λ) = dy/dx at (α, β).
notes: Close the loop before starting. In variety 1 the point P was on the curve and you were asked for the tangent — differentiate, put the point in dy/dx, slope in hand, story over. In variety 2 the point was on the curve but the slope was given instead — tangent slope or normal slope, it makes no difference — and you had to hunt the point P.

Variety 3 is the last one in this series: the point given to you is outside the curve. From that outside point you have to write the tangent (and the normal the same way). Here too the whole fight is one thing: find the point where the line actually touches the curve.

So call the point of contact (α, β) and call the given outside point (λ, μ). Two unknowns, so exactly two equations are needed. First: (α, β) lies on the curve, so it satisfies the curve's equation. Second: the line from (λ, μ) to (α, β) is the tangent itself, so its slope (β − μ)/(α − λ) must equal dy/dx at (α, β).

Look at what changed from variety 2. There the slope was handed to you in the question; here you build it yourself from the two points using y₂ − y₁ over x₂ − x₁, that old coordinate geometry slope of the line joining two points. Then you solve the two equations together. α usually comes out of a quadratic — that is the curve telling you there are two tangents from an outside point, not one.
In the next part I take a shifted parabola and do exactly this from a point outside it, for the pair of tangents.

quickChecks.q: Find the point of contact of the tangent drawn from (0, 0) to y = x² + 2.
steps: 1. Let the point of contact be (α, β). Equation 1 (on the curve): β = α² + 2.
2. dy/dx = 2x, so derivative at (α, β) is 2α.
3. Equation 2 (slope from the outside point): (β − 0)/(α − 0) = 2α, so β = 2α².
4. Compare: α² + 2 = 2α² ⇒ α² = 2 ⇒ α = ±√2, and β = 2(2) = 4.
5. Check: for α = √2 the slope is 2√2, so the tangent is y = 2√2 x; putting it in the curve gives x² − 2√2x + 2 = 0 with discriminant 8 − 8 = 0, one touch point.
quickChecks.answer: Points of contact (√2, 4) and (−√2, 4); the two tangents are y = 2√2 x and y = −2√2 x.

quickChecks.q: A tangent to y = x² is drawn from the point (2, 0). Find both points of contact.
steps: 1. Point of contact (α, β) with β = α² (equation 1).
2. Derivative at (α, β) is 2α.
3. Slope condition: (α² − 0)/(α − 2) = 2α ⇒ α² = 2α(α − 2) = 2α² − 4α.
5. β = 0 and β = 16, with slopes 0 and 8.
quickChecks.answer: (0, 0) with tangent y = 0, and (4, 16) with tangent y = 8x − 16.

quickChecks.q: Find the tangent drawn from the origin to y = x² − 3x + 3.
steps: 1. Point of contact (α, β): β = α² − 3α + 3 (equation 1).
2. dy/dx = 2x − 3, so derivative at (α, β) is 2α − 3.
3. Slope from (0, 0): β/α = 2α − 3 ⇒ β = 2α² − 3α.
4. Compare: α² − 3α + 3 = 2α² − 3α ⇒ α² = 3 ⇒ α = ±√3.
5. For α = √3: slope = 2√3 − 3, tangent y = (2√3 − 3)x; substituting gives x² − 2√3x + 3 = 0, discriminant 12 − 12 = 0, so it really touches.
quickChecks.answer: Two tangents, y = (2√3 − 3)x and y = (−2√3 − 3)x, touching at α = √3 and α = −√3.

concepts.title: Pair of Tangents from (1, 1) to y = x² − 5x + 6
concepts.quote: In coordinate geometry, a pair of tangents from an outside point to a shifted parabola is a heavy question. Follow it through and you will see calculus finish it in four lines, with no formula to remember.
concepts.oneLine: From the outside point (1, 1) let the tangent touch y = x² − 5x + 6 at (α, β), write the two relations, kill β, and α = 0 or 2 hands you both tangents: 5x + y = 6 and x + y = 2.
notes: Here the curve is y = x² − 5x + 6 and the point is (1, 1). Notice this is a shifted parabola, and somebody is asking for a pair of tangents from an external point. In coordinate geometry that is a decent, very good question.

Do not worry yet about how many tangents come out — one, two, twenty, it does not matter at this stage. Say only this: the tangent from (1, 1) touches the curve somewhere, call that contact point (α, β). Once you name the contact point (α, β), every external-point question becomes just two relations.

Relation one: (α, β) is on the curve, so β = α² − 5α + 6. Relation two: differentiate, dy/dx = 2x − 5, so the slope at the contact point is 2α − 5. That same line also joins (α, β) and (1, 1), so its slope is (β − 1)/(α − 1). Set the two equal.

Now eliminate β, because that makes the work easier. Cross multiply, substitute β from relation one, and everything collapses to α² − 2α = 0, so α = 0 or α = 2. Put these back in relation one to get β, and the question has turned into the plain old "write the tangent at this point" question from the start of the chapter.

quickChecks.q: Find the pair of tangents from the origin (0, 0) to the curve y = x² − 3x + 4.
steps: 1. Let the contact point be (α, β): β = α² − 3α + 4.
2. dy/dx = 2x − 3, so the slope at the contact point is 2α − 3.
3. Slope of the line joining (α, β) and (0, 0) is β/α, so 2α − 3 = β/α, giving 2α² − 3α = β.
4. Substitute β: 2α² − 3α = α² − 3α + 4, so α² = 4 and α = 2 or α = −2.
5. α = 2 gives β = 4 − 6 + 4 = 2, slope = 1, tangent y − 2 = 1(x − 2), that is y = x.
6. α = −2 gives β = 4 + 6 + 4 = 14, slope = −7, tangent y − 14 = −7(x + 2), that is y = −7x.
quickChecks.answer: Contact points (2, 2) and (−2, 14); tangents y = x and y = −7x.

quickChecks.q: The tangents from (1, −4) to y = x² − 4x + 3 touch it at two points. Find those contact points and both tangent equations.
steps: 1. Contact point (α, β): β = α² − 4α + 3.
2. dy/dx = 2x − 4, so the slope at the contact point is 2α − 4.
4. Left side: 2α² − 6α + 4. Right side after substituting β: α² − 4α + 7.
5. So α² − 2α − 3 = 0, that is (α − 3)(α + 1) = 0, giving α = 3 or α = −1.
6. α = 3 gives β = 9 − 12 + 3 = 0, slope = 2, tangent y − 0 = 2(x − 3), that is y = 2x − 6.
7. α = −1 gives β = 1 + 4 + 3 = 8, slope = −6, tangent y − 8 = −6(x + 1), that is y = −6x + 2.
quickChecks.answer: Contact points (3, 0) and (−1, 8); tangents y = 2x − 6 and y = −6x + 2.

quickChecks.q: Find the pair of tangents from (0, −4) to y = x².
steps: 1. Contact point (α, β): β = α².
2. dy/dx = 2x, so the slope at the contact point is 2α.
4. Substitute β = α²: 2α² = α² + 4, so α² = 4 and α = ±2.
5. α = 2 gives β = 4, slope = 4, tangent y − 4 = 4(x − 2), that is y = 4x − 4.
6. α = −2 gives β = 4, slope = −4, tangent y − 4 = −4(x + 2), that is y = −4x − 4.
quickChecks.answer: Contact points (2, 4) and (−2, 4); tangents y = 4x − 4 and y = −4x − 4.

concepts.title: Angle of Intersection of Two Curves and Orthogonality
concepts.oneLine: The angle between two curves is the angle between their tangents at the common point, tan θ = |(m₂ − m₁)/(1 + m₁m₂)|, and when m₁m₂ = −1 the curves cut orthogonally.
notes: Here is the whole idea. The angle of intersection of two curves is the angle between their tangents at the point where they meet. A curve has no single direction, but its tangent does. So we stop looking at the curves and look at the two straight lines touching them at that point.

Once you are down to two lines, you already know the formula from straight lines: tan θ = |(m₂ − m₁)/(1 + m₁m₂)|, where m₁ and m₂ are the two slopes. So the work is just this — find the common point, differentiate both curves, put x of that point in, get m₁ and m₂, plug in.

Orthogonality is the special case. If the angle of intersection is 90°, then m₁m₂ = −1 — and that one line is usually the entire solution. When a question says "show that the curves cut orthogonally", you are not expected to compute any angle. Find the two slopes at the common point and show their product is −1.
Notice that both slopes must be taken at the same point — the point of intersection. That is the only place the two tangents actually meet, so that is the only place an angle between them exists.

quickChecks.q: Find the angle of intersection of y = x² and y = x³ at the point (1, 1).
steps: 1. For y = x²: dy/dx = 2x, so m₁ = 2 at x = 1.
2. For y = x³: dy/dx = 3x², so m₂ = 3 at x = 1.

quickChecks.q: Two curves meet at a point where the tangent slopes are 2 and −1/2. What is the angle between the curves?
steps: 1. Multiply the slopes: m₁m₂ = 2 × (−1/2) = −1.
2. Product is −1, so 1 + m₁m₂ = 0 and the tangents are perpendicular.

quickChecks.q: Find the angle of intersection of y = x² and x = y² at (1, 1).
steps: 1. Both curves pass through (1, 1): 1 = 1² and 1 = 1².
2. For y = x²: dy/dx = 2x, so m₁ = 2 at (1, 1).
3. For x = y²: differentiate to get 1 = 2y dy/dx, so dy/dx = 1/(2y) = 1/2 at (1, 1). So m₂ = 1/2.

concepts.title: Practice: Angle Between y² = 4x and a Circle
concepts.oneLine: For y² = 4x and x² + y² = 5 at (1, 2), implicit differentiation gives m₁ = 1 and m₂ = −½, so tan θ = 3 and θ = tan⁻¹3.
notes: The two curves are y² = 4x and x² + y² = 5, and they cross at (1, 2). Check it in your head first: 2² = 4 × 1, and 1 + 4 = 5. Both satisfied, so the point is genuinely common.

Now differentiate each curve implicitly and put the point in. For the parabola, 2y(dy/dx) = 4, so dy/dx = 2/y, which is 1 at (1, 2). For the circle, 2x + 2y(dy/dx) = 0, so dy/dx = −x/y, which is −½ at (1, 2).
Two slopes in hand, you are done: just feed m₁ and m₂ into tan θ = |(m₁ − m₂)/(1 + m₁m₂)|. Write m₁ − m₂ or m₂ − m₁ on top, it makes no difference, the modulus kills the sign.

Here that gives tan θ = |(1 + ½)/(1 − ½)| = (3/2)/(1/2) = 3, so θ = tan⁻¹3. There is no concept hiding anywhere in this problem. If it went wrong for you, it was arithmetic, and one look at these steps at home will clear it in fifteen seconds.

quickChecks.q: The same curves y² = 4x and x² + y² = 5 also meet at (1, −2). Find the angle of intersection there.
steps: 2. Circle: m₂ = −x/y = −1/(−2) = ½.
quickChecks.answer: tan θ = 3, so θ = tan⁻¹3 — the same angle as at (1, 2)

quickChecks.q: Two curves cross at a point where the slopes are m₁ = 2 and m₂ = −3. Find the angle between them.
Find the angle of intersection of y² = 4x and x² = 4y at (4, 4).
steps: 1. y² = 4x gives dy/dx = 2/y, so m₁ = 2/4 = ½.
2. x² = 4y gives dy/dx = x/2, so m₂ = 4/2 = 2.

concepts.title: Angle at Which y = sin x and y = cos x Cross
concepts.oneLine: sin x and cos x cross where tan x = 1, the two slopes there are always +1/√2 and −1/√2, so the angle between them is tan⁻¹(2√2).
notes: First find where they meet. Put sin x = cos x and divide both sides by cos x. You get tan x = 1, so x = π/4.

You may object that π/4 is not the only one. Correct. If the question restricts x from 0 to 90°, π/4 is your only crossing. If no range is given, 5π/4 is also a crossing point, because tan x = 1 again there.

But look carefully at 5π/4. There sin x = −1/√2 and cos x = −1/√2. The slope of y = sin x is cos x, so it becomes −1/√2. The slope of y = cos x is −sin x, so it becomes +1/√2. The two slopes have just swapped places — one is +1/√2 and the other is −1/√2, exactly as at π/4. So the angle comes out the same.

That is why the story ends here. Whether the examiner gives you 0 to 90° or gives you nothing, you are putting the same pair of slopes into the angle formula. The restriction only saves you writing time, it does not change the answer. And keep the derivatives straight: sin differentiates to plus cos, cos differentiates to minus sin.

quickChecks.q: Solve sin x = cos x for x in [0, 2π].
steps: 1. Divide both sides by cos x: tan x = 1.
2. tan is 1 at π/4, and repeats every π, so the next one is π/4 + π = 5π/4.
3. Both lie inside [0, 2π].

quickChecks.q: At x = π/4, write the slopes of y = sin x and y = cos x.
steps: 1. y = sin x gives dy/dx = cos x, so slope = cos(π/4) = 1/√2.
2. y = cos x gives dy/dx = −sin x, so slope = −sin(π/4) = −1/√2.

quickChecks.q: Find the angle at which y = sin x and y = −cos x cross, taking the crossing at x = 3π/4.
steps: 1. Check the point: sin x = −cos x gives tan x = −1, so x = 3π/4 is a crossing.
2. For y = sin x: m₁ = cos(3π/4) = −1/√2.
3. For y = −cos x: dy/dx = sin x, so m₂ = sin(3π/4) = 1/√2.

concepts.title: Length of Tangent, Normal, Subtangent and Subnormal — Definitions
concepts.oneLine: At the point P, PT is the length of the tangent and PN is the length of the normal; their shadows on the x-axis are the subtangent and the subnormal.
notes: Take a curve and mark a point P on it. Through P draw the tangent line, and through P draw the normal line. The tangent meets the x-axis at a point we call T, and the normal meets the x-axis at a point we call N.

Now read the names off the figure. The segment from P down to T is PT, and PT is called the length of the tangent — the distance from the point of contact to where the tangent cuts the x-axis. In exactly the same way, the segment from P to N is PN, and PN is called the length of the normal.

Next come the two "sub" words. Subtangent and subnormal are nothing but the projections of PT and PN on the x-axis — their shadows lying flat on the axis. So drop the shadow of PT on the x-axis and that piece is the subtangent; drop the shadow of PN on the x-axis and that piece is the subnormal.

That is all four things. How to actually get their lengths is no work at all — you just write the relations in the right-angled triangle that the figure already gives you. We do that next, starting with the triangle that contains the tangent.

quickChecks.q: At a point P on a curve, the tangent meets the x-axis at T. What is the segment PT called?
steps: 1. P is the point of contact and T is where the tangent cuts the x-axis.
2. The distance between these two points is the required name.
quickChecks.answer: PT is the length of the tangent.

quickChecks.q: The normal at P meets the x-axis at N. Name PN, and name the projection of PN on the x-axis.
steps: 1. PN joins the point P to the point N on the x-axis, so PN is the length of the normal.
2. Its shadow lying on the x-axis is the "sub" version of the normal.
quickChecks.answer: PN is the length of the normal, and its projection on the x-axis is the subnormal.

quickChecks.q: Someone writes: "Subtangent is the projection of the normal on the x-axis." Correct the statement.
steps: 1. Subtangent must come from the tangent, not the normal.
2. Swap the words to match the pairs.
quickChecks.answer: Subtangent is the projection of the length of the tangent PT on the x-axis; the projection of the normal PN is the subnormal.

concepts.title: Deriving the Four Lengths from the Right Triangle
concepts.oneLine: Drop the perpendicular, read the right triangle: subtangent = |y₁/m| and length of tangent = |y₁√(1 + 1/m²)| — then swap m for 1/m and the normal pair falls out.
notes: Look at the triangle made by the tangent. The vertical side is y₁, the angle at the x-axis is θ, and the slope is tan θ = m. Everything you need is already in the picture.
The subtangent is the base of that triangle. Base with y₁ and θ known means tan θ = y₁/(subtangent), so subtangent = y₁/m. We write mod because a length cannot be negative and y₁ can be.

The length of the tangent is the hypotenuse, PT. For the hypotenuse you use sin θ, not tan θ: sin θ = y₁/PT, so PT = y₁ cosec θ. From tan θ = m the triangle has sides m, 1 and √(1 + m²), so cosec θ = √(1 + m²)/m. Pull the m inside the root and you get PT = y₁√(1 + 1/m²).

For the normal pair there is nothing new to derive. In the tangent formulas, replace m by 1/m — take the reciprocal — and you land on subnormal = |y₁m| and length of normal = |y₁√(1 + m²)|. Keep the derivation as insurance: if the formula slips in the exam, draw this small triangle and recover it in seconds.

quickChecks.q: For y = x², find the subtangent and the subnormal at the point (2, 4).
steps: 2. Subtangent = |y₁/m| = |4/4| = 1.
3. Subnormal = |y₁m| = |4 × 4| = 16.

quickChecks.q: For the same curve y = x² at (2, 4), find the length of the tangent and the length of the normal.
steps: 3. Length of normal = |y₁√(1 + m²)| = 4√(1 + 16) = 4√17.
quickChecks.answer: Length of tangent = √17, Length of normal = 4√17

quickChecks.q: For y = x³ at (1, 1), find the length of the normal and the subnormal.
steps: 1. m = dy/dx = 3x² = 3(1)² = 3, and y₁ = 1.
2. Length of normal = |y₁√(1 + m²)| = √(1 + 9) = √10.
3. Subnormal = |y₁m| = |1 × 3| = 3.

concepts.title: Practice: Length of Tangent
concepts.oneLine: A length-of-tangent question is a one-formula job: find m = dy/dx at the point, then put |y/m|·√(1+m²) — and if the formula slips, redraw the right triangle and read it off.
notes: This is a practice stop, not new theory. You already have the four lengths from the right triangle in the previous part, so here you only do what the exam asks: read the point, differentiate, put m in, and finish.
Order matters. Find dy/dx first, then put the point in to get the number m, then the length. If you put the point in before differentiating, you have differentiated a constant and lost the question.

And keep the fallback alive. The formula is just the hypotenuse of the little triangle you drew — point on top, foot on the x-axis, tangent cutting the axis. If the formula slips in the hall, redraw that triangle and rebuild it in two lines.
These four lengths sit only in the Advanced syllabus. That is exactly why they are not worth skipping — skipping them is how an easy four marks goes missing.

quickChecks.q: Find the length of the tangent to y = x² at the point (1, 1).
steps: 1. dy/dx = 2x, so at (1, 1), m = 2.
2. Length of tangent = |y/m|·√(1+m²) = |1/2|·√(1+4).

quickChecks.q: Find the length of the tangent to y² = 4x at the point (1, 2).
steps: 1. Differentiate: 2y·(dy/dx) = 4, so dy/dx = 2/y.

quickChecks.q: For y = x³ at (1, 1), find the subtangent and the length of the tangent.
steps: 1. dy/dx = 3x², so at (1, 1), m = 3.
2. Subtangent = |y/m| = 1/3.

concepts.title: Mean Value Theorem: what it covers and where it fits
concepts.oneLine: The mean value theorem has two parts — Rolle's theorem and Lagrange's mean value theorem — and it is an Advanced-only, small-weight topic, so write against it "not in mains", not "only for Advanced".
notes: We start applications of derivatives with a small one: the mean value theorem. I am being honest with you from the first line — this is in the JEE Advanced syllabus only. It is not in your Mains syllabus.

Then why take it up now, before the big topics? Because increasing-decreasing and maxima-minima are tied to each other. Once that chain starts, it runs long and there is no clean place to slip a small topic in. A small topic placed in the middle of a big chain is a topic that gets forgotten.

There are two parts inside the mean value theorem. One is Rolle's theorem, and the second is Lagrange's mean value theorem. Both come at introductory level — the full theory here, the same way tangent and normal were built up, and practice questions on your own after that.

Now hear the weight correctly. Increasing-decreasing and maxima-minima are the most important topics of applications of derivatives — Mains, Advanced, state-level, everywhere. The mean value theorem is the opposite: even back when it was in the Mains syllabus it was never a primary topic, and in Advanced too it plays a very small role. So we learn it properly, we just don't spend our hours here.

quickChecks.q: The mean value theorem splits into how many parts? Name them.
steps: 1. Recall the two results we are going to do in this topic.
2. First: Rolle's theorem.
3. Second: Lagrange's mean value theorem.
quickChecks.answer: Two parts — Rolle's theorem and Lagrange's mean value theorem.

quickChecks.q: Is the mean value theorem in the JEE Main syllabus? What should you write in your notes against it?
steps: 1. It is in the JEE Advanced syllabus only.
2. So a Mains question will not be asked from it.
3. Note it as the fact, not as a guess about Advanced.
quickChecks.answer: No, it is not in Mains. Write "not in mains" — not "only for Advanced".

quickChecks.q: Which topics of applications of derivatives carry the most weight, and in which exams?
steps: 1. Compare the small topic with the big chain.
2. Mean value theorem: very small role, and Advanced only.
3. Increasing-decreasing and maxima-minima: asked in Mains, Advanced and state-level exams alike.
quickChecks.answer: Increasing-decreasing and maxima-minima — they are the most important topics of applications of derivatives in Mains, Advanced and state-level competition.

concepts.title: Rolle's theorem: the three conditions and what they force
concepts.oneLine: If f is continuous and differentiable from a to b and f(a) = f(b), then f'(c) = 0 for at least one c between a and b — somewhere the tangent goes flat, parallel to the x-axis.
notes: Take any function f(x) on an interval from a to b. First it has to be continuous there: no break anywhere between a and b, the pen never leaves the page. Second it has to be differentiable there: no sharp corner anywhere between a and b, the curve turns smoothly.

Now the third condition, and it is the most important one: f(a) = f(b). The value of the function at the two end points must be the same. Students check the first two out of habit and forget this one.

If all three hold, Rolle's theorem says the derivative of the function must be zero at at least one point between a and b. And what is the derivative? It is the slope of the tangent. So slope of tangent = 0 at some c between a and b, and slope zero means that tangent is parallel to the x-axis — because every line parallel to the x-axis has slope 0.

Take two graphs. The first is continuous and smooth from a to b with equal end values, and there is exactly one point where the tangent is flat; call it x = c₁. The second graph has the same equal end values, but there you can mark three such points — c₁, c₂ and c₃ — each one with a tangent parallel to the x-axis. Rolle promises you at least one such point; it never says only one.

quickChecks.q: For f(x) = x² − 4x + 3 on the interval 1 to 3, does Rolle's theorem apply, and if yes find c.
steps: 1. It is a polynomial, so it is continuous and differentiable everywhere — no break, no sharp corner.
2. f(1) = 1 − 4 + 3 = 0 and f(3) = 9 − 12 + 3 = 0, so f(1) = f(3). All three conditions hold.
3. f'(x) = 2x − 4. Put f'(c) = 0, so 2c − 4 = 0, giving c = 2.
4. c = 2 lies between 1 and 3, so it is a valid point.

quickChecks.q: For f(x) = |x| on the interval −1 to 1, can you use Rolle's theorem?
steps: 1. f(−1) = 1 and f(1) = 1, so the end values are equal — the third condition is fine.
2. The graph is continuous, no break anywhere.
3. But at x = 0 there is a sharp corner, so f is not differentiable at x = 0, which lies inside the interval.
quickChecks.answer: No. The second condition fails because of the sharp corner at x = 0, so Rolle's theorem cannot be applied.

quickChecks.q: A graph is continuous and smooth from a to b with f(a) = f(b), and the tangent is parallel to the x-axis at three different points inside. Does this contradict Rolle's theorem?
steps: 1. Rolle guarantees f'(c) = 0 for at least one c between a and b.
2. Three such points means the guarantee is satisfied three times over, not broken.
3. This is exactly the second graph above, with c₁, c₂ and c₃.
quickChecks.answer: No contradiction. 'At least one' allows one, three or more such points.

concepts.title: Verifying Rolle's theorem on a cubic
concepts.oneLine: To verify Rolle's theorem, tick continuity, tick differentiability, show f(a) = f(b), then solve f′(c) = 0 and keep only the roots lying inside (a, b).
notes: The statement in one line: if a continuous and differentiable function takes the same value at the two end points, then somewhere in between its derivative must be zero. Now look at what the question actually looks like.

You are asked to verify Rolle's theorem for f(x) = x(x − 1)(x − 2) on [0, 2]. Start with the easy part. It is a cubic polynomial, so continuity on [0, 2] and differentiability on (0, 2) are automatic — no work needed there.
That leaves only one condition to actually check: the values at the end points must be equal. Here f(0) = 0 and f(2) = 0, so f(0) = f(2). All three conditions are satisfied.

Now the conclusion is guaranteed: f′(c) = 0 for some c inside. So differentiate, set f′(c) = 0, solve, and then do the one step students forget — keep only those roots of f′(c) = 0 that lie strictly between 0 and 2. Here both roots lie inside, so both are valid answers.
