quickChecks.q: Verify Rolle's theorem for f(x) = x² − 4x + 3 on [1, 3].
steps: 1. Polynomial, so continuous on [1, 3] and differentiable on (1, 3).
4. c = 2 lies in (1, 3), so it is accepted.

quickChecks.q: Verify Rolle's theorem for f(x) = x³ − 4x on [−2, 2].
steps: 1. Polynomial, so continuity and differentiability are automatic.
4. Both values lie strictly between −2 and 2, so both are accepted.

quickChecks.q: Verify Rolle's theorem for f(x) = x(x − 3)² on [0, 3] and state the value of c.
steps: 1. Polynomial, so continuous on [0, 3] and differentiable on (0, 3).
4. Set f′(c) = 0: c = 3 or c = 1. Now filter — c = 3 is an end point, not inside (0, 3), so reject it.
5. Only c = 1 survives.
quickChecks.answer: Verified, with c = 1 (c = 3 is rejected as it is an end point).

concepts.title: Rolle's theorem questions: finding (a, b) and choosing a valid function
concepts.oneLine: Rolle's theorem gives you two equations for free — f(1) = f(2) and f′(c) = 0 — and that is enough to pin down (a, b) = (5, 8); and any function built on [x] is rejected on sight, because it is not continuous.
notes: Both questions here are from the old Mains papers. They look like theory, but they are pure calculation — you only have to read the three conditions of Rolle's theorem as three pieces of data.

In the first one the function is a cubic polynomial, so continuity on [1, 2] and differentiability on (1, 2) are free. Don't waste a line proving them. The only usable conditions left are f(1) = f(2) and the given f′(4/3) = 0 — one equation each, two unknowns, done.

The second question is the other face of the same theorem: given four functions, which one is Rolle's theorem not applicable to? Here you check the conditions instead of using them. The greatest integer function jumps at every integer, so it is discontinuous — Rolle's theorem cannot even start.

The remaining options were all continuous and differentiable, with equal values at the two end points. So the one with [x] inside it is the answer. Spot the discontinuity and you have the answer without a single calculation.

quickChecks.q: Rolle's theorem holds for f(x) = x³ − ax² + bx + 1 on [1, 3], with f′(5/3) = 0. Find a and b.
steps: 1. f(1) = 2 − a + b and f(3) = 28 − 9a + 3b. Equating: 8a − 2b = 26, so 4a − b = 13.
4. Check: f′(x) = 3x² − 14x + 15 = (3x − 5)(x − 3), zero at x = 5/3, which lies inside (1, 3).

quickChecks.q: Is Rolle's theorem applicable to f(x) = x − [x] on [0, 1]?
steps: 1. End values: f(0) = 0 − 0 = 0 and f(1) = 1 − 1 = 0, so f(0) = f(1). This condition is satisfied.
2. But as x approaches 1 from the left, x − [x] approaches 1, while f(1) = 0. So the function is not continuous on [0, 1].
3. Continuity fails, so the theorem does not apply.
quickChecks.answer: No — it is discontinuous at x = 1, even though the end values are equal.

quickChecks.q: Is Rolle's theorem applicable to f(x) = |x − 1| on [0, 2]?
steps: 1. f(0) = 1 and f(2) = 1, so the end values are equal, and the function is continuous everywhere.
2. But at x = 1 the graph has a sharp corner: the left slope is −1 and the right slope is +1, so f is not differentiable at x = 1, which lies inside (0, 2).
3. Differentiability fails, so Rolle's theorem does not apply — and indeed f′(x) is −1 or +1 everywhere else, never 0.

concepts.title: Lagrange's Mean Value Theorem: tangent parallel to the chord
concepts.quote: Rolle's theorem needed the two end values to be equal. Drop that one condition and you get its big brother — Lagrange's Mean Value Theorem, which works on almost every curve you will meet in JEE.
concepts.oneLine: For a function continuous on [a, b] and differentiable on (a, b), there is some interior point c where the tangent slope f'(c) equals the chord slope (f(b) − f(a))/(b − a).
notes: Keep the first two conditions exactly as they were: f must be continuous on the closed interval [a, b] and differentiable on the open interval (a, b). The third condition of Rolle's theorem — that f(a) = f(b) — is thrown away here. That is the only change.

Now look at the two end points on the graph. Call the left one P, so its coordinates are (a, f(a)). Call the right one Q, so its coordinates are (b, f(b)). Join P to Q and you get a chord. Its slope is the difference of the y's over the difference of the x's, that is (f(b) − f(a))/(b − a).

LMVT says this chord slope is equal to the slope of the tangent at some point c inside the interval: f'(c) = (f(b) − f(a))/(b − a). In the picture, that simply means the tangent at that point comes out parallel to the chord. On the curve above there were three such points, and all three tangents were parallel to PQ — the theorem only promises you at least one.

Why is this the general version of Rolle's theorem? Put f(a) = f(b) back in. The numerator f(b) − f(a) becomes zero, so the whole chord slope is zero, and f'(c) = 0. Make the end values equal and LMVT collapses straight into Rolle's theorem.

quickChecks.q: For f(x) = x² on [1, 3], what value must f'(c) be equal to by LMVT?
steps: 3. LMVT says f'(c) equals this chord slope.

quickChecks.q: A function is continuous on [a, b], differentiable on (a, b), and f(a) = f(b) = 5. What does LMVT give you?
steps: 1. Chord slope = (f(b) − f(a))/(b − a) = (5 − 5)/(b − a) = 0.
2. So f'(c) = 0 for some c in (a, b).
3. This is exactly Rolle's theorem.
quickChecks.answer: f'(c) = 0 — LMVT reduces to Rolle's theorem

quickChecks.q: For f(x) = 2x + 1 on [1, 5], find the chord slope and say which points c satisfy LMVT.
steps: 3. f'(x) = 2 for every x, so f'(c) = 2 is true at every interior point.
quickChecks.answer: Chord slope = 2, and every c in (1, 5) works

concepts.title: Finding c from LMVT: f(x) = √x on [4, 9]
notes: Read the question once. f(x) = √x, a = 4, b = 9, and you have to find c. That is all. When the question hands you a, b and f(x) and asks for c, it is a pure plug-in: write (f(b) − f(a))/(b − a) = f'(c) and fill the slots.
So fill them. f(b) = f(9) = √9 = 3. f(a) = f(4) = √4 = 2. And b − a = 9 − 4 = 5. The right side of the equation is just 1/5 — a clean number, done before you have touched calculus.
Now the left side. The derivative of √x is 1/(2√x), so f'(c) = 1/(2√c). Set the two equal and solve: 1/(2√c) = 1/5 gives 2√c = 5, so √c = 5/2 and c = 25/4.

Last step, and it is the step people skip. Check that c sits inside the open interval. 25/4 = 6.25, which lies between 4 and 9. The theorem only promises a c in (a, b), so a c outside that interval is a signal you have made a slip, not an answer.

quickChecks.q: f(x) = √x on [1, 4]. Find c using LMVT.
f(x) = x² on [2, 4]. Find c using LMVT.
f(x) = 1/x on [1, 2]. Find c using LMVT.
steps: 2. f'(c) = −1/c², so −1/c² = −1/2 gives c² = 2.
3. c = √2 ≈ 1.41 (take the positive root, since c must lie in (1, 2)).

concepts.title: Using LMVT to bound a function value from derivative data
concepts.oneLine: If you know f at one point and bounds on f′, LMVT gives f(b) = f(a) + (b − a)·f′(c), so the smallest and largest allowed f′ hand you the smallest and largest possible f(b).
notes: Here is the real job of LMVT in a paper. If you know the value of the function at one point and you know something about the derivative, you can comment on the value of the function at another point.
We know f(1) = 3 and we are asked about f(5). So apply LMVT on [1, 5]. It gives (f(5) − f(1))/(5 − 1) = f′(c) for some c in (1, 5). Cross multiply: f(5) − f(1) = 4·f′(c), so f(5) = 3 + 4·f′(c).

Now the question becomes a good question. Suppose we are told 1 < f′(x) < 2. The whole of f(5) now depends on one unknown, f′(c), and we know the window it lives in. When the derivative is smallest, f(5) is smallest; when the derivative is largest, f(5) is largest.
Put 1 in place of the derivative: 3 + 4(1) = 7, the minimum. Put 2: 3 + 4(2) = 11, the maximum. That is the whole solution — no graph, no cases.

quickChecks.q: f is differentiable, f(2) = 5 and 2 ≤ f′(x) ≤ 3. Find the minimum and maximum possible value of f(6).
f(1) = 3 and 1 < f′(x) < 2. What is the maximum possible value of f(4)?
steps: 2. Maximum asked, so take the largest derivative, 2: 3 + 3(2) = 3 + 6 = 9.

quickChecks.q: f(0) = 1 and f′(x) ≤ 4 for every x. Show that f(3) cannot exceed 13.
steps: 2. Since f′(c) ≤ 4, we get 3·f′(c) ≤ 12.

concepts.title: Increasing functions: strictly increasing vs non-decreasing
concepts.oneLine: Both kinds of increasing graphs have f′ ≥ 0 — the difference is only whether f′ = 0 at isolated points (strictly increasing) or over a whole interval (non-decreasing).
notes: Picture a graph that keeps climbing from start to finish, never flat anywhere. That one is called monotonically increasing, or strictly increasing. Same thing, two names.
Now picture a second graph. It climbs, then between a and b it goes flat, then it climbs again. This one is just increasing, also called non-decreasing — because at least it never came down.

Here is the part students get wrong. For both graphs the derivative is greater than or equal to zero. The derivative data is identical. The only difference is where the zeros sit: in the strictly increasing graph f′ = 0 only at separate isolated points, never over a stretch, while in the non-decreasing graph f′ = 0 all the way across an interval.

Practically, the flat-in-the-middle graph almost never shows up in questions. So when a question says a function is increasing, or strictly increasing, or monotonically increasing, you write f′ ≥ 0 on that interval and move on.

quickChecks.q: Is f(x) = x⁵ strictly increasing?
steps: 2. f′(x) = 0 only at x = 0, a single isolated point.
3. For every other x, 5x⁴ > 0.
quickChecks.answer: Yes — f′ ≥ 0 with a zero only at the isolated point x = 0, so it is strictly (monotonically) increasing.

quickChecks.q: A question says f is increasing monotonically between 10 and 20. What is the condition on f′?
steps: 1. Monotonically increasing means f′ cannot be negative anywhere on that stretch.
2. So for every x between 10 and 20, f′(x) is either 0 or positive.

quickChecks.q: A graph rises, stays flat for the whole interval (1, 4), then rises again. What is it called, and why not strictly increasing?
steps: 1. On (1, 4) the graph is constant, so f′ = 0 there.
2. That zero covers a whole interval, not isolated points.
3. Everywhere else f′ > 0, so f′ ≥ 0 still holds.
quickChecks.answer: Increasing (non-decreasing), not strictly increasing — because f′ = 0 over an entire interval instead of at isolated points.

concepts.title: The derivative sign scheme: the working rule for monotonicity
concepts.oneLine: For any monotonicity question: differentiate, build the sign scheme of f′, then call the function increasing wherever f′ > 0 and decreasing wherever f′ < 0.
notes: Look at what the definition finally hands you. If f′(x) > 0 on an interval, f is increasing there. If f′(x) < 0 on an interval, f is decreasing there. That is the whole conclusion, nothing more.

So the working rule is: any function is given, you differentiate it, you make the sign scheme of f′, and wherever f′ is positive the function is increasing, wherever f′ is negative it is decreasing. Get that rule down and the rest of the chapter is just practice.

One more line that saves marks. If f′(x) ≥ 0 on an interval and f′ becomes 0 only at separate points, the function is still strictly increasing there. A single point where the derivative is 0 does not make an interval, so it cannot break the increase. Same thing on the other side with f′(x) ≤ 0 and strictly decreasing.

Notice that increasing and decreasing are always claimed on an interval, never at one isolated point. The sign scheme is exactly the tool that gives you those intervals. Differentiate, sign scheme, declare — in that order, every time.

quickChecks.q: Where is f(x) = 5 − 2x increasing and where is it decreasing?
steps: 1. Differentiate: f′(x) = −2.
2. Sign scheme: f′ is negative for every x, no roots to mark.
3. f′ < 0 everywhere, so the function is decreasing everywhere.
quickChecks.answer: Strictly decreasing on all of ℝ; increasing nowhere.

quickChecks.q: Use the rule on f(x) = x³. Is it strictly increasing on ℝ?
steps: 1. Differentiate: f′(x) = 3x².
2. f′(x) ≥ 0 for every x, and f′(x) = 0 only at the single point x = 0.
3. That lone zero does not make an interval, so the increase is not broken.
quickChecks.answer: Yes, f is strictly increasing on all of ℝ.

quickChecks.q: Find the intervals where f(x) = x³ − 3x is increasing and where it is decreasing.
steps: 1. Differentiate: f′(x) = 3x² − 3 = 3(x − 1)(x + 1).
2. Roots of f′: x = −1 and x = 1. Mark them on the number line.
3. Sign scheme: for x < −1 take x = −2, f′ = 3(−3)(−1) = +9, so plus. For −1 < x < 1 take x = 0, f′ = 3(−1)(1) = −3, so minus. For x > 1 take x = 2, f′ = 3(1)(3) = +9, so plus.
4. Plus means increasing, minus means decreasing.

concepts.title: Intervals of monotonicity for polynomials
concepts.oneLine: Differentiate, factorise f′, plot its zeros on the number line, read the wave curve: f′ > 0 means strictly increasing, f′ < 0 means strictly decreasing — and the boundary points sit in both intervals.
notes: The last part built the rule. Now work through three functions and you will see that the rule never changes. Differentiate, find where the derivative is zero, put those points on a number line, and check the sign in each piece.

Wherever f′ is positive the function is strictly increasing, wherever f′ is negative it is strictly decreasing — that is the whole question. The factorised form of f′ is what makes the signs readable, so always take the common number out and factorise before you do anything else.

Sometimes the derivative has no sign change at all. In part C the derivative came out as x²(5x² + 3). The bracket can never be zero, x² is never negative, so f′ ≥ 0 everywhere and the function just keeps climbing on the whole real line.

One doubt always comes up here: why is −1 included in the increasing interval and also in the decreasing interval? Because increasing and decreasing are statements about an interval, not about a single point. The graph rises up to −1 and falls after −1, so writing the endpoint on both sides changes nothing. In the next class you will see that these boundary points are exactly the local maxima and minima.

quickChecks.q: Find the intervals of increase and decrease for f(x) = x³ − 12x.
steps: 2. Zeros of f′ at x = −2 and x = 2; wave curve gives + − +.
quickChecks.answer: Strictly increasing on (−∞, −2] ∪ [2, ∞); strictly decreasing on [−2, 2].

quickChecks.q: Find the intervals of monotonicity of f(x) = x³ + 3x² − 24x.
steps: 3. Zeros at x = −4 and x = 2; signs + − +.
quickChecks.answer: Strictly increasing on (−∞, −4] ∪ [2, ∞); strictly decreasing on [−4, 2].

quickChecks.q: Show that f(x) = x⁷ + x⁵ is increasing for every real x.
steps: 2. x⁴ ≥ 0 and 7x² + 5 ≥ 5 > 0, so f′ ≥ 0 for all x, zero only at x = 0.

concepts.title: Where is a trigonometric function increasing? Analysing cos x − ½
concepts.oneLine: For a trigonometric function, increasing still means f′(x) > 0 — differentiate first, then settle the sign of that derivative with a sign scheme or a test value.
notes: The rule never changes. Increasing means f′(x) > 0, decreasing means f′(x) < 0. The only new thing in a trigonometric question is that the derivative is not a product of neat brackets, so you cannot just read the sign off a factorisation.
When factorisation does not settle it, you check the value of the derivative at a point inside the interval. That one habit saves you on every question of this type.

And please write the sign scheme of the derivative. How you write it is your business — there is no fixed rule, no one format being imposed. Write it in your own way, but write it. Mistakes in this chapter come mostly from doing the sign work in the head.

So here the function was sin x − x/2. Differentiate: the derivative of sin x is cos x, and the derivative of x/2 is ½. That gives f′(x) = cos x − ½, and now the whole question has become one small inequality — cos x > ½. We solve that one with a graph next.

quickChecks.q: For f(x) = 2 sin x − x, write the condition for f to be increasing.
steps: 2. Increasing needs f′(x) > 0, so 2 cos x − 1 > 0.
3. That is cos x > ½.
quickChecks.answer: f is increasing where cos x > ½.

quickChecks.q: For f(x) = sin x + x/2, write the condition for f to be increasing.
steps: 1. f′(x) = cos x + ½.
2. Increasing needs cos x + ½ > 0.
3. That is cos x > −½.
quickChecks.answer: f is increasing where cos x > −½.

quickChecks.q: Is f(x) = sin x − x/2 increasing at x = π/3? Use a test value.
steps: 1. f′(x) = cos x − ½.
2. At x = π/3, cos x = ½.
3. So f′(π/3) = ½ − ½ = 0, which is not greater than 0.
quickChecks.answer: No — f′ = 0 there, so x = π/3 is a boundary point, not a point of increase.

concepts.title: Solution: solving cos x − ½ > 0 with a graph
concepts.oneLine: To find where cos x − ½ is positive, draw y = cos x and the line y = ½ on the same axes: the function increases wherever the curve sits above the line, which is (−π/3, π/3) and then the same window repeated at every 2nπ.
notes: Differentiate first. The derivative here is cos x − ½. The function increases exactly where cos x − ½ > 0, so the whole question has shrunk to one sign question.
The derivative is zero where cos x = ½. One such point you know by heart: cos π/3 = ½. But there are many such points, so don't stop at one.

Take 0 to π/2 first, just to feel it. At x = 0, cos x is 1. It drops to ½ at π/3, and keeps falling to 0 at π/2. So from 0 to π/3 the cosine is above ½, the derivative is positive, and the graph is rising. After π/3 it goes negative.

Now do it in general: plot y = cos x, then plot the straight line y = ½ across it, and just look for the stretches where the curve is above the line. Cosine is ½ at +60° in the first quadrant and at −60° in the fourth quadrant, so the curve sits above the line between −π/3 and π/3. Cosine repeats after 2π, so the same window comes back at 2π − π/3 to 2π + π/3, then at 4π − π/3 to 4π + π/3, and so on.

quickChecks.q: Solve cos x − ½ > 0 for x in [0, 2π].
steps: 1. Need cos x > ½, so draw y = cos x on [0, 2π] and the line y = ½.
2. In [0, 2π] the cosine equals ½ at x = π/3 and at x = 2π − π/3 = 5π/3.
3. The curve is above the line just after 0 (cos 0 = 1) and again just before 2π (cos 2π = 1).

quickChecks.q: Where is cos x − ½ negative for x in (0, 2π)?
steps: 1. This is the part where the cosine curve is below the line y = ½.
2. The boundary points are the same: π/3 and 5π/3.
3. Between them the cosine dips down to −1 at π, which is well below ½.

quickChecks.q: The next increasing interval after (2π − π/3, 2π + π/3) — write it down.
steps: 1. The pattern is (2nπ − π/3, 2nπ + π/3).
2. Here n = 1 gave (2π − π/3, 2π + π/3), so take n = 2.

concepts.title: Checking options by quadrant: where sin 2x increases or decreases
concepts.oneLine: For f(x) = sin 2x, differentiate to 2cos 2x, scale the interval to 2x, and let the quadrant of 2x decide the sign: positive on (0, π/4) so f increases, negative on (π/4, π/2) so f decreases.
notes: Increasing-decreasing means one thing first: differentiate. For f(x) = sin 2x, f′(x) = 2cos 2x. Don't put extra wisdom into it, son — that is the whole setup.
The 2 in front is positive always, so the sign of f′ is just the sign of cos 2x. So never study the interval of x — scale it and study the interval of 2x.
Option says (0, π/4). Double it: 2x goes from 0 to π/2, the first quadrant, where cos is positive. So f′ > 0 and sin 2x is increasing there.

Next option says (π/4, π/2). Double it: 2x goes from π/2 to π, the second quadrant, where cos is negative. So f′ < 0 and sin 2x is decreasing there. Positive cos 2x on the interval means increasing, negative means decreasing — that one line checks every option.

quickChecks.q: Is f(x) = sin 2x increasing or decreasing on (π/2, 3π/4)?
steps: 1. f′(x) = 2cos 2x.
2. x from π/2 to 3π/4 gives 2x from π to 3π/2, the third quadrant.
3. cos is negative in the third quadrant, so f′ < 0.

quickChecks.q: Is f(x) = sin 2x increasing or decreasing on (3π/4, π)?
steps: 1. f′(x) = 2cos 2x.
2. x from 3π/4 to π gives 2x from 3π/2 to 2π, the fourth quadrant.
3. cos is positive in the fourth quadrant, so f′ > 0.

quickChecks.q: Is f(x) = sin 3x increasing on (0, π/6)?
steps: 1. f′(x) = 3cos 3x.
2. x from 0 to π/6 gives 3x from 0 to π/2, the first quadrant.
3. cos is positive there, so f′ > 0.
quickChecks.answer: Yes, it is increasing on (0, π/6).

concepts.title: Least value of k for which a function increases on an interval
concepts.quote: This question comes back again and again: find the least k for which the function is strictly increasing on (1, 2). Most students start solving two inequalities. Here is why one is enough.
concepts.oneLine: For f′ = 2x + k on (1, 2) the derivative runs from k + 2 to k + 4, so making the smallest value k + 2 ≥ 0 is enough — the least k is −2.
notes: The function is to be strictly increasing for x in (1, 2), so the whole question is about the sign of the derivative on that interval. Here f′(x) = 2x + k.

Now put the two ends in. At x = 1 the derivative is k + 2. At x = 2 the derivative is k + 4. Tell me a simple thing — which of these is small and which is big? One has 2 added to k, the other has 4 added to k, so k + 2 is the minimum and k + 4 is the maximum.

So as x moves from 1 to 2, the derivative moves from k + 2 up to k + 4. For strictly increasing, this derivative must stay positive throughout. If the smallest value is already positive, every bigger value is automatically positive — so I only need to control the minimum.
That gives one condition: k + 2 ≥ 0, so k ≥ −2. The smallest k allowed is −2, and at k = −2 the derivative starts from 0 and climbs to 2. No second inequality, no case work.

quickChecks.q: Find the least value of k for which f′(x) = 2x + k is strictly increasing on (2, 5).
steps: 2. Smaller one is k + 4, so that is the minimum of f′.
3. Set k + 4 ≥ 0, giving k ≥ −4.

quickChecks.q: For f(x) = x² + kx, find the least k so that f is strictly increasing on (−3, −1).
steps: 3. k − 6 is the smaller, so it is the minimum.
4. Set k − 6 ≥ 0, giving k ≥ 6.

quickChecks.q: Find the least value of k for which f′(x) = 4x + k is strictly increasing on (1, 3).
steps: 2. Minimum of f′ is k + 4.
3. Set k + 4 ≥ 0, giving k ≥ −4.

concepts.title: Maximum k for kx + 4 sin x + 3 cos x to be strictly decreasing
concepts.oneLine: If f(x) = kx + 4 sin x + 3 cos x must be strictly decreasing for all real x, then f′(x) lies between k − 5 and k + 5, and forcing the maximum k + 5 ≤ 0 gives k ≤ −5, so k_max = −5.
notes: Start the way we always do. Strictly decreasing for all x ∈ R means f′(x) must be negative for every single x, not just somewhere. So differentiate first: f′(x) = k + 4 cos x − 3 sin x.

Now look at the tail of that derivative. 4 cos x − 3 sin x is our old friend, the a sin x + b cos x format, and its value always stays between −5 and +5 because √(4² + 3²) = 5. Both ends are written out fully so there is no confusion later: f′(x) sits between k − 5 and k + 5.

So k − 5 is the smallest the derivative can ever be and k + 5 is the largest, whatever x you throw in. The condition is that it should always be ≤ 0. Make the maximum negative and the minimum dies automatically — so all you need is k + 5 ≤ 0.

That gives k ≤ −5, and the largest such k is −5. If you are still unsure about the other end, check it in one step: k + 5 is negative, and k − 5 is just k + 5 with a further −10 added, so it is even more negative. Both ends are safely below zero.

quickChecks.q: Find the maximum k for which f(x) = kx + 5 sin x + 12 cos x is strictly decreasing for all x ∈ R.
steps: 1. f′(x) = k + 5 cos x − 12 sin x.
2. √(5² + 12²) = √169 = 13, so 5 cos x − 12 sin x lies between −13 and 13.
4. Need the maximum ≤ 0: k + 13 ≤ 0, so k ≤ −13.

quickChecks.q: Find the minimum k for which f(x) = kx − 3 sin x + 4 cos x is strictly increasing for all x ∈ R.
steps: 1. f′(x) = k − 3 cos x − 4 sin x.
2. √(3² + 4²) = 5, so −3 cos x − 4 sin x lies between −5 and 5.
3. Hence k − 5 ≤ f′(x) ≤ k + 5.
4. Increasing needs f′ ≥ 0 everywhere, so push the minimum up: k − 5 ≥ 0, i.e. k ≥ 5.

quickChecks.q: Find the maximum k for which f(x) = kx + sin x + cos x is strictly decreasing for all x ∈ R.
steps: 1. f′(x) = k + cos x − sin x.
2. √(1² + 1²) = √2, so cos x − sin x lies between −√2 and √2.
4. Need the maximum ≤ 0: k + √2 ≤ 0, so k ≤ −√2.

concepts.title: One more k-question: increasing on (3, 5)
concepts.oneLine: On (3, 5) the derivative is smallest at x = 3, so 3k + 12 ≥ 0 is the only condition you need — that gives k ≥ -4 and the function is increasing on the whole interval.
notes: Increasing on (3, 5) means one thing only: f′(x) ≥ 0 for every x between 3 and 5. You cannot test every point, so find where f′ is smallest and make that smallest value non-negative.
Differentiate and put in the two ends. At x = 3 the derivative comes out 3k + 12, and at x = 5 it comes out bigger. So on this interval f′ is climbing — the left end carries the smallest value.

So force only the left end to be non-negative: 3k + 12 ≥ 0, which gives k ≥ -4. Once f′(3) ≥ 0, the value at 5 is already bigger, and every point in between sits between the two. Positive at 3 ⇒ positive right across (3, 5).
Notice what was not needed. No second inequality for x = 5, and no hunting for an intersection. One end, one inequality, done.

quickChecks.q: On (2, 6) a function has f′(2) = 2k + 10 and f′ increasing across the interval. For what k is the function increasing on (2, 6)?
steps: 1. f′ is increasing, so its least value on (2, 6) is at the left end, x = 2.
3. k ≥ -5. The value at x = 6 is bigger, so it is already positive.

quickChecks.q: On (1, 4) a function has f′(1) = k + 7 and f′ rises as x rises. Find the least value of k for which the function is increasing on (1, 4).
steps: 1. Smallest derivative value is at x = 1: f′(1) = k + 7.
2. Need k + 7 ≥ 0, so k ≥ -7.
3. The least such k is -7.
quickChecks.answer: k = -7 is the least value; the condition is k ≥ -7

quickChecks.q: On (3, 5) a function has f′ increasing, with f′(5) = 5k + 20. For what k is the function decreasing on (3, 5)?
steps: 1. Decreasing needs f′(x) ≤ 0 all through (3, 5).
2. Since f′ is increasing, the largest value on the interval is at the right end, x = 5.
3. So force the largest value down: 5k + 20 ≤ 0, giving 5k ≤ -20, k ≤ -4.
4. Then f′(3) < f′(5) ≤ 0, so f′ stays negative on the whole interval.

concepts.title: Recap: increasing, decreasing and monotonic functions
concepts.oneLine: Differentiate, find where the derivative is zero, mark those points on the number line, and read the sign: f′ > 0 means increasing, f′ < 0 means decreasing.
notes: Here is the full method. Differentiate the function. Find the points where f′(x) = 0. Put those points on the number line. Now check the sign of f′ in each interval.
Wherever f′(x) > 0 the function is increasing, and wherever f′(x) < 0 the function is decreasing. That is it. No new idea is coming after this.

Two names you must get right. If f′(x) ≥ 0 for every x in the domain, we call f monotonically increasing. If f′(x) ≤ 0 for every x in the domain, we call f monotonically decreasing. Notice the ≥ and the ≤ — the derivative is allowed to touch zero, it just must not change sign.
Theory is total this much. From here on we only change the shape of the question: find k, find a, make it increase on an interval, make it increase on all of R. Same sign test every single time.

quickChecks.q: f′(x) = 2x + 6k. For which k is the function increasing on [1, 2]?
steps: 1. f′ is linear with positive slope, so its smallest value on [1, 2] is at x = 1.

quickChecks.q: f′(x) = 4x + k. For which k is the function increasing on [2, 7]?
steps: 1. Smallest value of f′ on [2, 7] is at x = 2.
3. Need k + 8 ≥ 0.

quickChecks.q: f(x) = -x³. Is it monotonically increasing or monotonically decreasing on R?
steps: 2. x² ≥ 0 for every real x, so -3x² ≤ 0 for every real x.
3. f′ ≤ 0 on the whole domain, and it is zero only at x = 0.

concepts.title: Making a cubic increasing on all of R
concepts.oneLine: "Increasing on all of R" means f′(x) ≥ 0 for every x, and since f′ of a cubic is a quadratic, you only need positive leading coefficient and D ≤ 0.
notes: Read the words and translate them straight away. "Increasing on R" means f′(x) ≥ 0 for every x in the domain, and the domain of a cubic is all of R. So there is no hunting for intervals here; the inequality has to hold everywhere.
Now look at what f′ actually is. Differentiate a cubic and you get a quadratic. So the whole question becomes: when is a quadratic greater than or equal to 0 for all real x?

You already know the answer from quadratics. It must open upward (coefficient of x² positive) and its discriminant must be less than or equal to 0. Then the graph sits on or above the x-axis the whole way.

Watch the ≤ carefully. If D = 0 the parabola just touches the axis at one point, so f′ = 0 at a single x and nothing else. The function still keeps rising, so that case is allowed and the end values of a stay in your answer.

quickChecks.q: For which values of a is f(x) = x³ + ax² + 12x + 1 increasing on all of R?
steps: 1. f′(x) = 3x² + 2ax + 12, and f′(x) ≥ 0 is needed for all x.
2. Coefficient of x² is 3 > 0, so only D ≤ 0 is left.

quickChecks.q: A cubic has f′(x) = x² + 2ax + 9. Find a so that the cubic is increasing on all of R.
steps: 1. Need x² + 2ax + 9 ≥ 0 for all x; leading coefficient is 1 > 0, fine.

quickChecks.q: Can a cubic with f′(x) = −2x² + ax − 3 be increasing on all of R for some a?
steps: 1. The x² coefficient of f′ is −2, so the parabola opens downward.
2. A downward parabola goes to −∞ on both sides, so f′ must become negative somewhere, whatever a is.
quickChecks.answer: No value of a works — the first condition (positive leading coefficient) already fails.

concepts.title: Monotonicity of a product f·g from the signs of f, f′, g, g′
concepts.oneLine: For u = f·g, differentiate first and read the sign of u′ = f′g + f g′ off the given signs — and remember that "increasing" tells you nothing about "positive".
notes: There is almost no theory to learn here. The whole chapter is variety of problems, and most of them crack open the moment you take a derivative.

Here you are given two continuous functions f and g, and asked to comment on f·g. So put u = f·g and differentiate: u′ = f′g + f g′. Now the question will always hand you some data about f, f′, g, g′ — and you just put the signs in.

You are not thinking cleverly here, you are only multiplying signs: a positive times a positive is positive, a negative times a negative is positive. If every term of u′ comes out positive, u′ > 0, and that means u is monotonic increasing. Done.

One more thing, because this is where students get stuck. The sign of a function and the sign of its derivative are completely unrelated pieces of data. A graph can rise forever and still sit below the x-axis. A graph can fall forever and still stay above it. So do not get confused by "always negative but increasing" — it is a perfectly normal function.

quickChecks.q: f is always negative and monotonic decreasing; g is always positive and monotonic increasing. What can you say about f·g?
steps: 1. u = f·g, so u′ = f′g + f g′.
2. f < 0, f decreasing ⟹ f′ < 0. g > 0, g increasing ⟹ g′ > 0.
3. f′g = (−)(+) = negative.
4. f g′ = (−)(+) = negative.
5. Negative + negative = negative, so u′ < 0 everywhere.

quickChecks.q: f is always positive and monotonic decreasing; g is always negative and monotonic increasing. Comment on the monotonicity of f·g.
steps: 2. f > 0, f decreasing ⟹ f′ < 0. g < 0, g increasing ⟹ g′ > 0.
3. f′g = (−)(−) = positive.
4. f g′ = (+)(+) = positive.
5. So u′ > 0 for every x.

quickChecks.q: True or false: if a function is decreasing on R then it must become negative somewhere. Justify with an example.
steps: 1. Take y = e^(−x) on R.
2. Its derivative is −e^(−x) < 0 for all x, so it is decreasing everywhere.
3. But e^(−x) > 0 for all x, so it never touches or crosses the x-axis.
quickChecks.answer: False. e^(−x) decreases on all of R yet stays positive throughout — the sign of a function is independent of the sign of its derivative.

concepts.title: Objective question: which of these functions is monotonic?
concepts.oneLine: "Which of these is monotonic" is really one question: does the derivative keep a single sign over the whole domain?
notes: Here is the question. Which of the following functions are monotonic: sin(tan x) and 2^sin x? Put it in objective form, because that is how you will meet it in the paper. Option A: only the first one. Option B: only the second one. Option C: both are monotonic. Option D: none — meaning neither of them is monotonic.

Now switch your brain off for a second. Nothing new is coming here: differentiate, and look at the sign of the derivative. That is the whole chapter, and honestly it stays that way even when we reach maxima and minima.

And fix the word monotonic properly. Increasing is monotonic. Decreasing is also monotonic. So if f′(x) ≥ 0 for every x in the domain, f is monotonically increasing; if f′(x) ≤ 0 for every x in the domain, f is monotonically decreasing. Either one qualifies.

The key word is *throughout*. The sign must hold on the whole domain, not on a piece of it you happen to like. The moment the derivative is positive somewhere and negative somewhere else, that function is out — and then option D starts looking very interesting.

quickChecks.q: Is f(x) = 2^x monotonic on ℝ?
steps: 2. 2^x > 0 for every real x, and ln 2 > 0, so f′(x) > 0 for all x.
3. One sign throughout the domain.

quickChecks.q: Is g(x) = sin x monotonic on ℝ?
steps: 1. g′(x) = cos x.
2. cos 0 = 1 > 0, but cos π = −1 < 0.
3. The derivative changes sign inside the domain.
quickChecks.answer: No — sin x is not monotonic on ℝ.

quickChecks.q: Is h(x) = −x³ monotonic on ℝ?
steps: 2. x² ≥ 0 always, so h′(x) ≤ 0 for every real x, and it is 0 only at x = 0.
3. The derivative never becomes positive, so the sign never flips.
quickChecks.answer: Yes — monotonically decreasing on ℝ (decreasing is monotonic too).

concepts.title: Solution: sin(tan x) and 2^sin x are both non-monotonic
concepts.oneLine: Differentiate, throw away every factor that is always positive, and look only at what is left: if that part changes sign, the function is not monotonic.
notes: Start with f(x) = sin(tan x) on (0, π/2). Differentiate: f′(x) = cos(tan x) · sec²x. On this interval sec²x is always positive, so it cannot decide anything.

So everything depends on cos(tan x). Now watch the input of cos. As x runs from 0 to π/2, tan x runs from 0 to ∞. So the input of cos is sweeping 0 to ∞, which means cos becomes zero again and again and flips sign thousands of times. The derivative is positive sometimes and negative sometimes, so f is non-monotonic.
Now the second one, f(x) = 2^(sin x). Differentiate: f′(x) = 2^(sin x) · ln 2 · cos x. Here 2^(sin x) is a positive number and ln 2 is a positive number, so again they get no vote.

That leaves cos x. Over 0 to 2π, cos x becomes 0 and changes sign, so this derivative is also positive in one place and negative in another. Non-monotonic again. So in that question, none of the given functions was monotonic — the answer is "none of these".

quickChecks.q: Is f(x) = 2^(tan x) monotonic on (0, π/2)?
steps: 1. f′(x) = 2^(tan x) · ln 2 · sec²x.
2. 2^(tan x) > 0, ln 2 > 0, and sec²x > 0 on (0, π/2).
3. Every factor is always positive, so nothing can change sign.

quickChecks.q: Is f(x) = cos(tan x) monotonic on (0, π/2)?
steps: 1. f′(x) = −sin(tan x) · sec²x.
2. sec²x > 0, so the sign comes from −sin(tan x).
3. tan x sweeps 0 to ∞, so sin(tan x) crosses zero again and again and changes sign.

quickChecks.q: Is f(x) = 3^(cos x) monotonic on (0, 2π)?
steps: 1. f′(x) = 3^(cos x) · ln 3 · (−sin x).
2. 3^(cos x) > 0 and ln 3 > 0, so the sign is the sign of −sin x.
3. On (0, 2π), sin x is positive before π and negative after π, so −sin x changes sign at π.

concepts.title: Composite functions: proving monotonicity straight from the definition
concepts.oneLine: Push x₁ > x₂ through the functions one at a time: an increasing function keeps the inequality, a decreasing function reverses it — so f∘g with f decreasing and g increasing comes out decreasing.
notes: Start with the only thing you actually need: what increasing and decreasing mean. Increasing is a statement about input and output moving together — bigger input, bigger output. Decreasing is the opposite — bigger input, smaller output.

Now turn that into a move you can do on paper. Write x₁ > x₂. Apply an increasing function to both sides and the inequality stays as it is; apply a decreasing function to both sides and the inequality reverses. That single line is the whole chapter of composite results.
For f∘g you apply the functions in the order they touch the input. In f(g(x)) the inner function g goes first, then f. So push x₁ > x₂ through g, see what you get, then push that through f.

At the end, compare the input relation with the output relation. If x₁ was the bigger input but f(g(x₁)) is the smaller output, then input and output are moving opposite ways — and that is exactly the definition of a decreasing function. No formula was remembered anywhere in this proof; it was only analysis.

quickChecks.q: f and g are both increasing. Prove that f∘g is increasing.
steps: 1. Assume x₁ > x₂.
2. g is increasing, so applying g keeps the sign: g(x₁) > g(x₂).
3. f is increasing, so applying f keeps the sign again: f(g(x₁)) > f(g(x₂)).
4. Bigger input gave the bigger output, so input and output agree.

quickChecks.q: f is increasing and g is decreasing. Is f∘g increasing or decreasing?
steps: 1. Assume x₁ > x₂.
2. g is decreasing, so applying g reverses the sign: g(x₁) < g(x₂).
3. f is increasing, so applying f keeps this sign: f(g(x₁)) < f(g(x₂)).
4. Bigger input gave the smaller output.

quickChecks.q: f and g are both decreasing. What can you say about f∘g?
steps: 1. Assume x₁ > x₂.
2. g is decreasing, so the sign reverses: g(x₁) < g(x₂).
3. f is decreasing, so the sign reverses once more: f(g(x₁)) > f(g(x₂)).
4. Bigger input gave the bigger output.

concepts.title: Ordering g(f(x+1)) and g(f(x−1))
concepts.oneLine: Start from x + 1 > x − 1 and push it through f then g: each decreasing function flips the inequality, each increasing function leaves it alone.
notes: Begin with the one thing that is true for every real x: x + 1 > x − 1. You added 1 on one side and subtracted 1 on the other, so the left is always ahead. This is your starting inequality, and nothing in the question can change it.

Now push it through the functions, one at a time, in the order they act. Here g′ > 0, so g is increasing, and f′ < 0, so f is decreasing. In g(f(x+1)) the inner function f acts first, so apply f first.

An increasing function keeps the relation between input and output the same; a decreasing function reverses it. So applying f to x + 1 > x − 1 flips the sign: f(x+1) < f(x−1). Then applying g to that flips nothing, because g is increasing: g(f(x+1)) < g(f(x−1)).

That is the whole method. Write the base inequality, apply the functions from inside out, and flip the sign once for every decreasing function you pass through. The remaining options in such a question are the same two steps with the signs of f′ and g′ changed — do them yourself for practice.

quickChecks.q: If f′(x) < 0 and g′(x) < 0 for all x, compare g(f(x+1)) and g(f(x−1)).
steps: 1. Start with x + 1 > x − 1.
2. f is decreasing, so applying f reverses it: f(x+1) < f(x−1).
3. g is decreasing too, so applying g reverses it again: g(f(x+1)) > g(f(x−1)).
4. Two decreasing functions, two flips, so the original direction returns.

quickChecks.q: If f′(x) > 0 and g′(x) < 0 for all x, compare g(f(x+1)) and g(f(x−1)).
steps: 1. Start with x + 1 > x − 1.
2. f is increasing, so the inequality stays: f(x+1) > f(x−1).
3. g is decreasing, so applying g reverses it: g(f(x+1)) < g(f(x−1)).

quickChecks.q: If f′(x) < 0 and g′(x) > 0 for all x, compare g(f(x+3)) and g(f(x)).
steps: 1. Start with x + 3 > x.
2. f is decreasing, so applying f reverses it: f(x+3) < f(x).
3. g is increasing, so applying g changes nothing: g(f(x+3)) < g(f(x)).

concepts.title: Monotonicity when the function is discontinuous
concepts.oneLine: The sign-of-derivative test only works where the function is differentiable — at a jump point, go back to the basic definition, and that jump can even be a local minimum.
notes: Till now every function we tested was continuous and differentiable throughout. So a natural question: if the function is discontinuous somewhere, does increasing and decreasing mean something new? No. Nothing new at all.

Go back to the basic definition. Increasing means: as x increases, the value of the function increases. Decreasing means: as x increases, the value of the function decreases. The derivative is only the mathematical form that definition is written in.

Now here is the catch. If the function is discontinuous at a point, it is non-differentiable there, so at that point the derivative does not exist and you cannot talk about its sign at all. The rule "f ′(x) > 0 throughout, so increasing" is valid only when the function is differentiable at every point of the interval.

And a discontinuous function can still have a local maximum or a local minimum, which is not what most people expect. Local minimum simply means the value is smaller than the values at the neighbouring points; local maximum means it is bigger. That is exactly how a jump point can turn out to be a local minimum while the derivative stays positive on both sides.

quickChecks.q: f ′(x) > 0 for all x ≠ 2, and at x = 2 the graph jumps down: the value at 2 lies below the values just to the left of 2. Is f monotonically increasing on the real line?
steps: 1. f is discontinuous at x = 2, so f ′(2) does not exist and the derivative test cannot cover the whole line.
2. Take x₁ just less than 2 and x₂ = 2. Then x₁ < x₂ but f(x₁) > f(x₂).
3. The basic definition is violated at x = 2.
quickChecks.answer: No. It is increasing on (−∞, 2) and on (2, ∞) separately, but not monotonically increasing on the whole line.

quickChecks.q: In the same graph, what do you call the point x = 2, and why can't you find it by solving f ′(x) = 0?
steps: 1. Compare f(2) with the values at points just on either side of 2: f(2) is smaller than both.
2. Smaller than the neighbouring values means a local minimum.
3. f ′(2) does not exist at all, so the equation f ′(x) = 0 never looks at this point.
quickChecks.answer: x = 2 is a local minimum. It is caught by comparing values with the neighbours, not by setting the derivative to zero.

quickChecks.q: State the exact condition under which "f ′(x) > 0 on an interval" lets you declare f increasing on that interval.
steps: 1. The derivative form is only a translation of the definition "output rises as x rises".
2. That translation holds only where the derivative exists.
quickChecks.answer: f must be continuous on the closed interval and differentiable at every point inside it. One point of discontinuity and you must go back to the definition x₁ < x₂ ⇒ f(x₁) < f(x₂).

concepts.title: Jump graphs: local maxima, and when a jump is still monotonic
concepts.oneLine: At a jump, forget the derivative and just compare f(a) with the values immediately on both sides: biggest means local maximum, smallest means local minimum, in between means the function is still monotonically increasing.
notes: The rule f′(x) > 0 for increasing and f′(x) < 0 for decreasing is only a tool. It works when the function is differentiable at every point of the interval. At a jump there is no derivative, so there is nothing to call positive or negative — and that is exactly where students lose the question.

So go back to the basic definition. Monotonically increasing means that as x grows, the value of the function never comes down — and local maximum at x = a means f(a) is bigger than or equal to the values at the points just next to it on both sides. Nothing more is needed.

Now three graphs, all with a break at x = a. First graph: it increases, jumps up, and increases again. The value at a is included at the bottom of the jump, the values just after are higher, so nothing ever comes down — monotonically increasing. Second graph: it increases right up to the top dot at x = a, and then after the jump the graph restarts from a lower value and increases again. A dip appears. f(a) is bigger than the values before and after, so x = a is a local maximum and the function is non-monotonic.

Third graph: at x = a the function takes its value, and the part after the jump starts from a higher value and keeps increasing. No dip anywhere, no local maximum, no local minimum — monotonically increasing again. Notice the trap: in all three graphs the derivative was positive wherever it existed, yet only two of them are monotonic. The same logic read upside down gives local minima: if the dot at x = a sits lower than the values on both sides, that point is a local minimum.

quickChecks.q: f has a break at x = 2. On the left the graph rises up to f(2) = 7, and for x > 2 the graph starts at 5 and increases. Is f monotonically increasing on its domain? Any local extremum at x = 2?
steps: 1. Values just before 2 are less than 7, since the graph rises up to f(2) = 7.
2. Values just after 2 start from 5, which is less than 7.
3. So f(2) = 7 is greater than the neighbouring values on both sides.
4. Going from x = 2 to a point just after, the value drops from 7 to about 5.
quickChecks.answer: Not monotonically increasing. x = 2 is a point of local maxima.

quickChecks.q: g rises towards 4 as x → 1 from the left, g(1) = 6, and for x > 1 the graph starts from 6 and keeps increasing. Classify g.
steps: 1. Values just before 1 are near 4, which is less than g(1) = 6.
2. Values just after 1 are greater than 6.
3. So g(1) is neither largest nor smallest in its neighbourhood — no local maximum, no local minimum.
4. The value never comes down as x grows.
quickChecks.answer: Monotonically increasing, with no local extremum at x = 1.

quickChecks.q: h increases up to values near 5 as x → 3 from the left, h(3) = 1, and for x > 3 the graph starts from 4 and increases. What is x = 3?
steps: 1. Values just before 3 are near 5, which is greater than h(3) = 1.
2. Values just after 3 are near 4, again greater than 1.
3. So h(3) ≤ h(x) for every x just next to 3 on both sides.
4. That matches the definition of a local minimum, and the fall from 5 to 1 also breaks monotonicity.
quickChecks.answer: x = 3 is a point of local minima, and h is non-monotonic.

concepts.title: Piecewise function: the range of b for monotonic decrease
concepts.oneLine: A piecewise function is monotonically decreasing only if every branch falls AND the value at the joint does not jump up: for x²−4x+5 (x ≤ 0) with 2x+b (x > 0) the answer is φ, and with −2x+b it is b ≤ 5.
notes: Take f(x) = x² − 4x + 5 for x ≤ 0 and 2x + b for x > 0. Draw the first branch. It is an upward parabola with vertex at x = 2, so to the left of 2 it is falling — and we only need x ≤ 0, which sits fully on the falling side. Its derivative 2x − 4 is negative for every negative x, and at x = 0 the branch gives the value 5.

Now the second branch, 2x + b. Its y-intercept is b, and its slope is +2. Shift b up, shift b down, it does not matter — a line with a positive slope is increasing, and no value of b can turn an increasing line into a decreasing one. So for monotonic decrease, b belongs to φ.

Change one sign and the question comes alive: let the second branch be −2x + b. Now both pieces fall. But falling pieces are not enough — the joint at x = 0 has to behave. The left branch has already reached 5 at x = 0, and just after 0 the line starts from b. For the drop to continue we need b ≤ 5.

If b goes above 5, look at what you have: the graph drops to 5 at x = 0, then jumps up to b, then drops again. The value at x = 0 is now smaller than the values on both sides of it, so x = 0 becomes a local minimum — and the function is no longer monotonic. At a discontinuity the derivative tells you nothing; only the basic definition, comparing values, settles it.

quickChecks.q: f(x) = x² − 6x + 10 for x ≤ 0 and 3x + b for x > 0. Find all b for which f is monotonically decreasing.
steps: 1. First branch: f′(x) = 2x − 6, which is negative for every x ≤ 0, so it falls (vertex at x = 3).
2. Second branch: slope is +3, so it rises for every x > 0 whatever b is.
3. A rising branch cannot be repaired by moving b.

quickChecks.q: f(x) = x² − 2x + 3 for x ≤ 0 and −5x + b for x > 0. Find the range of b for monotonic decrease.
steps: 1. First branch: f′(x) = 2x − 2 < 0 for all x ≤ 0, so it falls. Its value at x = 0 is 0 − 0 + 3 = 3.
2. Second branch has slope −5, so it falls too.
3. Joint condition: f(0) = 3 must not be below the start of the next branch, which is b. So 3 ≥ b.

quickChecks.q: For f(x) = x² − 4x + 5 for x ≤ 0 and −2x + b for x > 0, find all b for which x = 0 is a local minimum.
steps: 1. f(0) = 5, coming from the falling parabola arm, so just to the left of 0 the values are above 5.
2. For x = 0 to be a local minimum, the values just to the right must also be above 5.
3. Just to the right the function starts from b and then decreases, so we need b > 5.

concepts.title: Increasing does not mean positive — pinning the sign with one value
concepts.oneLine: Increasing says nothing about sign on its own — but f(a) = 0 together with f′ > 0 for x ≥ a forces f(x) ≥ 0 for every x ≥ a.
notes: One myth has to go first. "If f is increasing, then f is positive" — wrong. Picture a curve climbing steadily but sitting entirely below the x-axis. It is increasing at every point and still negative at every point.

The reverse myth dies the same way. "If f is decreasing, then f is negative" — also wrong. A curve can fall all the way and still stay above the axis. So from increasing or decreasing alone, you can never comment on positive or negative.

There is exactly one situation where you can. Suppose you are given f(a) = 0 and f′(x) > 0 for all x ≥ a. Fix the curve to the axis at x = a, then let it only climb. It can never come back below the axis, so f(x) ≥ 0 for all x ≥ a.

Now see why the value at a is doing all the work. Hide f(a) and keep only f′ > 0, and the same shape can sit anywhere — the lowest copy is negative throughout, the highest copy is positive throughout, and a middle copy cuts the axis at some α, negative before α and positive after. The derivative decides the shape; the one known value decides where that shape sits.

quickChecks.q: f(a) = 0 and f′(x) < 0 for all x ≥ a. What is the sign of f(x) for x ≥ a?
steps: 1. f′ < 0 after a means f is decreasing on [a, ∞).
2. So for x > a, f(x) < f(a) = 0.
3. Including the endpoint, f(a) = 0.

quickChecks.q: f(a) = 0 and f′(x) > 0 for all x ≤ a. What is the sign of f(x) for x ≤ a?
steps: 1. f is increasing on (−∞, a], so going backwards from a the values get smaller.
2. For x < a, f(x) < f(a) = 0.
3. At x = a, f(a) = 0.

quickChecks.q: f′(x) > 0 for all real x and f(2) = 5. What can you say about the sign of f for x ≥ 2, and for x < 2?
steps: 1. For x > 2: f is increasing, so f(x) > f(2) = 5 > 0, and f(2) = 5 itself is positive.
2. For x < 2: f(x) < 5, which allows positive, zero or negative values.
3. So the anchor only controls the side on which the curve climbs away from it.
quickChecks.answer: f(x) > 0 for all x ≥ 2; for x < 2 nothing can be said.

concepts.title: Comparing two expressions with calculus: x vs tan⁻¹x
concepts.oneLine: To compare two expressions, make their difference one function u, fix the sign of u′, and then read u at the starting point of the interval — that is how x ≥ tan⁻¹x on [0, ∞) falls out.
notes: Think back to the comparison questions of childhood. Two ugly fractions, and the instruction was: which one is bigger? You never converted them to decimals. You made one number out of them — the difference — and looked only at its sign.

If the difference is positive the first one is bigger, if it is negative the second one is bigger. That is the whole idea, and it works just as well when the two things are functions. Now compare x with tan⁻¹x on 0 to ∞. Take u(x) = x − tan⁻¹x and ask only one thing: is u positive or negative?

For that, differentiate. u′(x) = 1 − 1/(1 + x²) = x²/(1 + x²). The numerator is a square and the denominator is 1 plus a square, so u′ is never negative — it is positive for every x ≠ 0. So u is increasing on 0 to ∞.

But increasing alone tells you nothing about positive or negative. So pin it with one value: u(0) = 0 − tan⁻¹0 = 0. The function starts at 0 and only climbs after that. So u(x) ≥ 0 for x in [0, ∞), which means x ≥ tan⁻¹x on that whole interval.

quickChecks.q: Compare 17/13 and 22/17.
steps: 3. So x = 3/221, which is positive.

quickChecks.q: Prove that x ≥ sin x for all x in [0, ∞).
steps: 1. Let u(x) = x − sin x.
2. u′(x) = 1 − cos x, and cos x ≤ 1 always, so u′(x) ≥ 0 — u is increasing.
4. Increasing from 0 gives u(x) ≥ 0 on [0, ∞).
quickChecks.answer: x ≥ sin x on [0, ∞), equality at x = 0.

quickChecks.q: For x ≤ 0, which is bigger: x or tan⁻¹x?
steps: 1. Same u(x) = x − tan⁻¹x, and u′(x) = x²/(1 + x²) ≥ 0, so u is increasing on the whole real line.
2. u(0) = 0, and to the left of 0 an increasing function must be below its value at 0.
3. So u(x) ≤ 0 for x ≤ 0.
quickChecks.answer: tan⁻¹x ≥ x for x ≤ 0 — the inequality flips, with equality at x = 0.

concepts.title: Fixing the sign of a numerator: is sin x / x monotonic?
concepts.oneLine: For f(x) = sin x / x the quotient rule gives f′(x) = (x cos x − sin x)/x², and since x² is always positive the entire monotonicity question collapses to the sign of x cos x − sin x.
notes: First the mirror of what we just did. Take a function that is decreasing, and whose value at the starting point is 0. Then as you move right it can only come down from 0. So a decreasing function that starts at 0 stays negative for the whole interval. Same logic as before, flipped.
Now a very common question: discuss the monotonicity of f(x) = sin x / x. The final answer is not the point right now. Watch the machinery, because that is what gets asked.
Apply the quotient rule. Denominator becomes x². In the numerator, hold x and differentiate sin x to get cos x, then minus, hold sin x and differentiate x to get 1. So f′(x) = (x cos x − sin x)/x².

Look at the denominator. x² is always positive, so it can never flip the sign. The sign of f′(x) is exactly the sign of x cos x − sin x. If that numerator is always negative, f is strictly decreasing; if it is always positive, f is strictly increasing. That is why the very next thing I ask you to prove is sin x − x cos x > 0 for x in (0, 1).

quickChecks.q: Given f(x) = sin x / x and that x cos x − sin x < 0 for all x in (0, π/2), what is the monotonic nature of f on (0, π/2)?
steps: 1. f′(x) = (x cos x − sin x)/x².
2. Denominator x² > 0 on (0, π/2).
3. Numerator is negative on (0, π/2), so f′(x) < 0 there.
quickChecks.answer: f is strictly decreasing on (0, π/2).

quickChecks.q: For f(x) = cos x / x, find f′(x) and write the expression whose sign decides the monotonicity.
steps: 1. Quotient rule: numerator = x · (−sin x) − cos x · 1 = −x sin x − cos x.
2. Denominator = x².
3. So f′(x) = (−x sin x − cos x)/x² = −(x sin x + cos x)/x².
4. x² > 0, so the sign of f′(x) is the sign of −(x sin x + cos x).
quickChecks.answer: f′(x) = (−x sin x − cos x)/x²; the deciding expression is −(x sin x + cos x), i.e. the sign of x sin x + cos x with a minus in front.

quickChecks.q: Let g(x) = sin x − x cos x with g(0) = 0. If g is increasing on (0, 1), what is the sign of g there, and what does that say about f(x) = sin x / x?
steps: 1. g is increasing and g(0) = 0, so g(x) > g(0) = 0 for x in (0, 1).
2. So sin x − x cos x > 0, which means x cos x − sin x < 0 on (0, 1).
3. That numerator is exactly the numerator of f′(x), and x² > 0.
quickChecks.answer: g > 0 on (0, 1), so f′(x) < 0 there — f(x) = sin x / x is strictly decreasing on (0, 1).

concepts.title: Proving sin x − x cos x > 0, and the monotonicity of sin x / x
concepts.oneLine: On (0, 1), f(x) = sin x − x cos x has f(0) = 0 and f′(x) = x sin x > 0, so f > 0; hence sin x / x is decreasing and x / sin x is increasing.
notes: Take f(x) = sin x − x cos x and differentiate. The cos x terms cancel and you are left with f′(x) = x sin x.
Now look at the interval (0, 1). Here x is positive. And remember x is in radians, so the input to sine runs from 0 to about 57°, where sine is positive. So f′(x) > 0 on the whole interval.
A function that starts at 0 and only climbs can never be negative. Since f(0) = 0 and f is increasing on (0, 1), f(x) > 0 there. That is the proof: sin x − x cos x > 0 on (0, 1).

This is exactly the piece that was stuck in the last question. The derivative of sin x / x has numerator x cos x − sin x, which is the negative of what we just proved, so the numerator is negative and the denominator x² is positive. Decreasing. And since sin x / x is decreasing and stays positive on (0, 1), its reciprocal x / sin x is increasing — no further work needed.

quickChecks.q: Prove that tan x − x > 0 for all x in (0, 1).
steps: 1. Let f(x) = tan x − x.
2. f′(x) = sec²x − 1 = tan²x.
3. On (0, 1), tan x ≠ 0, so f′(x) = tan²x > 0 and f is increasing.
5. Starts at 0 and only climbs, so f(x) > 0.

quickChecks.q: Prove that x − sin x > 0 on (0, 1), and say what that tells you about sin x / x.
steps: 1. Let f(x) = x − sin x, so f′(x) = 1 − cos x.
2. On (0, 1), cos x < 1, so f′(x) > 0 and f is increasing.
4. Divide by x > 0: sin x / x < 1.
quickChecks.answer: x − sin x > 0 on (0, 1), so sin x / x < 1 there.

quickChecks.q: If g(x) = sin x / x is decreasing on (0, 1), what can you say about 1 / g(x), and what must you check first?
steps: 1. First check the sign: on (0, 1) both sin x and x are positive, so g(x) > 0 and never 0.
2. A positive decreasing function has an increasing reciprocal.
3. So 1 / g(x) = x / sin x is increasing on (0, 1).
quickChecks.answer: x / sin x is increasing on (0, 1); you must first check that sin x / x stays positive (never zero) on the interval.

concepts.title: x / tan x is decreasing on (0, 1)
concepts.oneLine: Differentiate x / tan x, call the doubtful numerator h(x) = tan x − x sec²x, show h′ < 0 with h(0) = 0, so the numerator stays negative and x / tan x decreases on (0, 1).

concepts.title: Comparing e^(1/e) with π^(1/π), and e^π with π^e
concepts.oneLine: To compare e^(1/e) with π^(1/π), read both as f(x) = x^(1/x), log-differentiate to get f′(x) = x^(1/x)(1 − ln x)/x², and the sign of 1 − ln x settles everything — then raise both sides to the power eπ to compare e^π with π^e.
notes: Look at e^(1/e) and π^(1/π). Both are the same shape: a number raised to one over itself. So define f(x) = x^(1/x), and the question becomes nothing more than comparing f(e) with f(π).

Once you have to compare the value of one function at two points, you do not need the exact values — you only need to know where that function is increasing and where it is decreasing. Think of a rough graph: if f is falling in some stretch, then the smaller point there has the bigger value. If f is rising, the bigger point has the bigger value. That is all.

To get that information, take log on both sides: ln f(x) = (ln x)/x. Differentiating gives f′(x)/f(x) = (1 − ln x)/x². And in AOD the whole job is to differentiate — all this log work is only so that the differentiation becomes easy.

Now the sign. The domain is x > 0 (a negative base in an exponential like this is not defined), f(x) = x^(1/x) is always positive there, and x² is positive. So the sign of f′ rides entirely on 1 − ln x, which is zero at x = e. Positive before e, negative after e — so f rises on (0, e) and falls on (e, ∞).

quickChecks.q: Which is bigger: 3^(1/3) or 4^(1/4)? Hence compare 3⁴ and 4³.
steps: 1. Use f(x) = x^(1/x). Both 3 and 4 are greater than e, so both lie where f is decreasing.
2. 3 < 4, and on a decreasing stretch the smaller input gives the bigger value, so f(3) > f(4), i.e. 3^(1/3) > 4^(1/4).
3. Raise both sides to the power 12 (positive, so the sign stays): 3^(12/3) > 4^(12/4), i.e. 3⁴ > 4³.

quickChecks.q: Compare e^(1/e) with 3^(1/3). Hence compare e³ and 3^e.
steps: 1. f(x) = x^(1/x) has its peak at x = e, so f(e) is the largest value of all.
3. Raise both sides to the power 3e: (e^(1/e))^(3e) = e³ and (3^(1/3))^(3e) = 3^e.
4. So e³ > 3^e. Rough check: e³ ≈ 20.1 and 3^e ≈ 19.8. ✓

quickChecks.q: Compare π^(1/π) with 4^(1/4). Hence compare π⁴ and 4^π.
steps: 1. Both π and 4 are greater than e, so both sit on the decreasing side of f(x) = x^(1/x).
3. Raise both sides to the power 4π: (π^(1/π))^(4π) = π⁴ and (4^(1/4))^(4π) = 4^π.
4. So π⁴ > 4^π. Rough check: π⁴ ≈ 97.4 and 4^π ≈ 77.9. ✓

concepts.title: Local and global maxima and minima — the four terms
concepts.quote: Four terms, and two of them you already know by a different name. Global maximum is nothing but the maximum value of the function — the same thing you have been finding since class 11.
concepts.oneLine: Local maxima/minima compare a value only with its immediate neighbours; global maxima/minima are just the maximum and minimum value of the whole function.
notes: Before we start, remember how we did increasing and decreasing. The moment a function stopped being monotonic, we had no language for it until we brought in maxima and minima. Maxima-minima and increasing-decreasing always travel together, exactly the way limits travelled with continuity.

So we take four terms: local maxima, local minima, global maxima, global minima. Local maxima has only one logic — the value is bigger than its immediate neighbours on both sides. Local minima is the mirror image — the value is smaller than its immediate neighbours.
That neighbour logic is also why it survives a discontinuous function. You are not asking anything about the curve far away, only about the points just to the left and just to the right.

Now global. Ask me the maximum value of sin x and you say 1 without thinking. That 1 is the global maximum. Global maximum means the overall maximum value the function can give anywhere, and global minimum means the overall minimum. Global is not new maths, it is a new name — given only so that you can separate "overall best" from "best among neighbours".

quickChecks.q: Find the global maximum and global minimum of 5 sin x + 12 cos x.
steps: 2. The expression lies between −13 and 13.

quickChecks.q: What is the global maximum of cos x, and what is its global minimum?
steps: 1. cos x takes all values from −1 to 1, and touches both.
2. So the overall largest value is 1 and the overall smallest is −1.

quickChecks.q: A continuous function has f(2) = 7, f(1.9) = 6.5 and f(2.1) = 6.8. Is x = 2 a local maxima or a local minima?
steps: 1. Compare f(2) with its immediate neighbours: 7 > 6.5 and 7 > 6.8.
2. It is bigger than both neighbours, so the local maxima logic holds.
quickChecks.answer: Local maxima at x = 2 (and this says nothing about the global maximum)

concepts.title: Reading maxima, minima and range off a graph, end points included
concepts.oneLine: The overall maximum and minimum of a function are simply its highest and lowest values — they may sit at a local extremum or at an end point, and the range runs from the lowest to the highest.
notes: Start with the first graph. It rises to a hump, comes down to a dip, and goes up again. Call the value at the hump capital M and the value at the dip small m.

Here capital M is a local maximum, and it also happens to be the global maximum. Small m is a local minimum, and it is also the global minimum. So the smallest value of the function is m, the largest is M, and the range is from m to M.

Now the second graph. Same kind of shape, but the curve starts low at the left end and climbs high at the right end. Ask where the smallest value is and your eye lands on the left end point; ask where the largest value is and it lands on the right end point. The end point values are not local maxima or minima at all, yet they are the overall minimum and overall maximum of the function. The range is still from small m to capital M — only now m and M are sitting at the ends.

The definitions of local max and local min have not changed: a local maximum only has to beat the values just next to it, and a local minimum only has to be below the values just next to it. What is happening far away does not matter. And "global" needs no new definition — when I ask for the maximum value of the function, maximum means maximum: the highest value it reaches, whether that happens at a local maximum or at an end point.

quickChecks.q: On a closed interval a function starts at 2 at the left end, rises to a local maximum of 7, falls to a local minimum of 1, then rises to 9 at the right end. Write the greatest value, the least value and the range.
steps: 1. Candidate values: end points 2 and 9, local maximum 7, local minimum 1.
2. Greatest of {2, 9, 7, 1} is 9, at the right end point.
3. Least of {2, 9, 7, 1} is 1, at the local minimum.
quickChecks.answer: Greatest value 9 (right end point), least value 1 (local minimum), range [1, 9].

quickChecks.q: A function on a closed interval starts at 6 at the left end, dips to a local minimum of −2, rises to a local maximum of 3, and ends at −5 at the right end. Find the range.
steps: 1. Candidate values: 6 and −5 at the ends, −2 at the local minimum, 3 at the local maximum.
2. Greatest is 6, at the left end point.
3. Least is −5, at the right end point.
4. So here neither global value is a local extreme.
quickChecks.answer: Range is [−5, 6]; both extremes sit at the end points.

quickChecks.q: A function has a local maximum of value 4 inside the interval, and at both end points its value is 4 as well; its only local minimum is 0. Is the local maximum the global maximum?
steps: 1. Compare all candidates: 4 (local maximum), 4 and 4 (end points), 0 (local minimum).
2. The highest value is 4 and it is reached at the local maximum as well as at both ends.
3. Global maximum is about the value, not about one special point.
quickChecks.answer: Yes — the global maximum value is 4, and it is attained at the local maximum and at both end points. Range [0, 4].

concepts.title: Critical points: f′ = 0 or f′ undefined
concepts.quote: Most students carry one wrong line in their head: "critical point means derivative zero." That half-definition is exactly where marks leak in maxima-minima questions.
concepts.oneLine: A critical point of f is a point c where f′(c) = 0 or f′(c) does not exist — these are the only contenders for local maxima and minima.
notes: We have already played with f′ = 0 in increasing-decreasing. Now I want one small concept in place before we apply everything: the critical point.
A point c is a critical point of f if either f′(c) = 0, or f′(c) does not exist. Both halves matter. The second half is the one everybody drops.

Why should "derivative fails to exist" matter? Think of a graph like that: at x = a the curve breaks, there is a discontinuity, so no derivative exists there. And yet a peak or a valley can sit exactly at that point. So it counts.

And why the name critical? Because at such a point there is a chance of a local maximum or a local minimum. Remember the slide just before this — out of four points, two gave a local max or min and two gave nothing. So critical points are contenders for maxima and minima, not winners; you still have to analyse each one further. One more thing: a critical point of an interval is always an interior point of that interval.

quickChecks.q: For a function f, f′(x) = 0 at x = 2 and x = 3, and f′ does not exist at x = 5. How many critical points does f have?
steps: 1. From f′ = 0: x = 2 and x = 3 → 2 points.
2. From f′ not existing: x = 5 → 1 point.
3. Both conditions count towards the same list.
quickChecks.answer: 3 critical points: x = 2, x = 3 and x = 5.

quickChecks.q: f′(c) = 0. Can you now say f has a local maximum or a local minimum at c?
steps: 1. f′(c) = 0 makes c a critical point.
2. A critical point is only a contender for a local max or min.
3. Further analysis is needed before deciding.
quickChecks.answer: No — not necessarily. c is a candidate only.

quickChecks.q: Is an end point of an interval a critical point of that interval?
steps: 1. A critical point of an interval is its interior point.
2. An end point is not interior to the interval.
quickChecks.answer: No — critical points of an interval lie inside it.

concepts.title: Finding critical points in a given interval
concepts.oneLine: A critical point is an interior point of the interval where f′ is either 0 or undefined — so find both kinds, then throw away anything sitting on the boundary.
notes: We already know the definition. Critical points are the contenders for local maxima and local minima — nothing more. So our whole job in these questions is to collect the contenders inside the given interval.

Two kinds of points qualify. The ones where f′ = 0, and the ones where f′ does not exist — including the point where the derivative shoots off to infinity. Many students only hunt for the first kind and lose the second one completely.

And one more filter on top: a critical point of an interval is always an interior point of that interval. If a candidate lands exactly on an endpoint, it is a boundary point, and a boundary point can never be a critical point.

Work through the three problems. First one: both roots fall inside, so both survive. Second one: one root plus one blow-up point, so two survive. Third one: one root is an endpoint, so only one survives.

quickChecks.q: f′(x) = (x − 1)(x − 5). Find the critical points in the interval (0, 3).
steps: 1. f′(x) = 0 gives x = 1 and x = 5.
2. x = 1 lies inside (0, 3), so it is an interior point. Accepted.
3. x = 5 is outside (0, 3) altogether, so it is not a candidate here.
4. f′ is a polynomial, so it is defined everywhere — no second kind of critical point.
quickChecks.answer: x = 1 is the only critical point.

quickChecks.q: For f(x) = (x − 3)^(2/3), f′(x) = 2 / (3 (x − 3)^(1/3)). Find the critical points in (1, 5).
steps: 1. Try f′(x) = 0: the numerator is 2, which is never 0. So no critical point of the first kind.
2. Now look for where f′ is undefined. At x = 3 the denominator becomes 0, so f′ approaches infinity and f′(3) does not exist.
3. x = 3 lies inside (1, 5), so it is an interior point.
quickChecks.answer: x = 3 is the only critical point, and it comes from f′ being undefined, not from f′ = 0.

quickChecks.q: f′ is zero at x = 2 and x = 5, and defined everywhere. Find the critical points in the interval 2 to 6.
steps: 1. Candidates: x = 2 and x = 5.
2. x = 2 is an endpoint of the interval, so it is a boundary point — rejected.
3. x = 5 lies strictly between 2 and 6, so it is an interior point — accepted.
quickChecks.answer: x = 5 is the only critical point.

concepts.title: Existence of a critical point as a range condition
concepts.oneLine: A critical point exists only if f′(x) = 0 is solvable, so once it reduces to cos x = 2(a − 1) the whole question becomes −1 ≤ 2(a − 1) ≤ 1.
notes: Differentiate, set the derivative to zero. That much is routine, and here the derivative is easy. You land on cos x = 2(a − 1).
Now pause. The question is not to find x. It is only whether some x can exist. The moment an equation only has to be *solvable*, it becomes a range question, not a solving question.

Look at the two sides separately. The left side is cos x, and cos x can never step outside [−1, 1]. The right side, 2(a − 1), is just a fixed number sitting there. Two sides can only be equal if they live in the same range — if the right side is parked far away from [−1, 1], no x on earth will match it.
So force the right side into the left side's range: −1 ≤ 2(a − 1) ≤ 1. Divide by 2, add 1, and the answer walks out. That is the full question.

quickChecks.q: For f(x) = sin x − 3(a + 1)x, find all a for which f has a critical point.
steps: 1. f′(x) = cos x − 3(a + 1), set it to 0, so cos x = 3(a + 1).

quickChecks.q: For f(x) = cos x + (2a − 5)x, find all a for which f′(x) = 0 has a solution.
steps: 1. f′(x) = −sin x + (2a − 5), set it to 0, so sin x = 2a − 5.
2. sin x also lives in [−1, 1], so −1 ≤ 2a − 5 ≤ 1.
4. Divide by 2: 2 ≤ a ≤ 3.

quickChecks.q: Flip the question above: for which a does f(x) = sin x − 2(a − 1)x have no critical point at all?
steps: 1. A critical point exists exactly when a ∈ [½, 3/2].
2. No critical point means a is outside that block.
3. So a < ½ or a > 3/2.

concepts.title: First Derivative Test for Local Maxima and Minima
concepts.quote: Every maximum and minimum sits at a critical point — but not every critical point is a maximum or a minimum. One sign check tells you which one you are looking at.
concepts.oneLine: At a critical point, f′ going − to + gives a local minimum, + to − gives a local maximum, and no sign change gives a point of inflection.
notes: Recall the critical point: a point where the derivative is zero or undefined. At a critical point there is only a chance of a maximum or a minimum — it is not guaranteed. Sometimes there is nothing there at all.
The test for deciding is the first derivative test, and the good news is that you already know it. It is exactly the increasing–decreasing work from earlier, just read around one point.

Take a critical point x = c₁. If the derivative is negative before c₁ and positive after it, the function was falling and then starts rising — so a valley is formed at c₁. That is a local minimum. Flip it: derivative positive before c₁ and negative after it means the function rose and then fell, so c₁ is a local maximum.

Now the third case. If the sign of the derivative does not change at c₁ — positive before and positive after, or negative before and negative after — then it is neither a local maximum nor a local minimum. Such a point is called a point of inflection, and we will take it up separately.

quickChecks.q: x = 3 is a critical point of f. f′ is positive for x slightly less than 3 and negative for x slightly more than 3. What is at x = 3?
steps: 1. Derivative positive before 3, so the function is increasing there.
2. Derivative negative after 3, so the function is decreasing there.
3. Rising then falling means a peak, and the sign change is + to −.

quickChecks.q: x = −2 is a critical point of f, with f′ negative on both sides of −2. What is at x = −2?
steps: 1. The sign of f′ does not change across −2.
2. So the function is decreasing before and decreasing after, with no turn.
3. No sign change means neither local maximum nor local minimum.
quickChecks.answer: Neither — x = −2 is a point of inflection.

quickChecks.q: At a critical point x = c₁, f′ < 0 for x < c₁ and f′ > 0 for x > c₁. Maximum, minimum or neither?
steps: 1. Negative derivative before c₁ means the function is decreasing.
2. Positive derivative after c₁ means the function is increasing.
3. Falling then rising forms a valley; the sign change is − to +.

concepts.title: First Derivative Test on an Integral Function (Newton–Leibniz)
concepts.oneLine: Differentiate an integral with x² on top by Newton–Leibniz, throw away the factors that can never be zero, and read every maximum and minimum off one sign line.
notes: Take f(x) = ∫₀^{x²} e^t(t−9)(t−4)(t+2)dt. Nobody can integrate that cleanly, and nobody wants you to. The question only asks where f has local maxima and minima, and for that you need f′(x), not f(x).

Newton–Leibniz hands it to you. Put the upper limit in place of t everywhere in the integrand, then multiply by the derivative of that upper limit. The lower limit is 0, a constant, so its term has derivative 0 and simply disappears.

So f′(x) = 2x·e^(x²)(x²−9)(x²−4)(x²+2), and now the whole question is a sign scheme question. Two of those factors can never be zero: e^(x²) is always positive, and x²+2 is positive plus positive. Strike them out and only 2x(x−3)(x+3)(x−2)(x+2) decides the sign.

Five simple roots: −3, −2, 0, 2, 3. On the far right of 3 every factor is positive, so f′ is positive, and from there the sign flips at each root. Then read it with one sentence in your head: derivative going negative to positive means the function was falling and started rising, so that is a local minimum; positive to negative is a local maximum.

quickChecks.q: If g(x) = ∫₀^{x²} e^t(t−1)(t+3)dt, find the points of local maximum and local minimum of g.
steps: 1. Newton–Leibniz: g′(x) = e^(x²)(x²−1)(x²+3)·2x.
2. e^(x²) and x²+3 are always positive, so strike them out.
3. Sign is decided by 2x(x²−1) = 2x(x−1)(x+1), so critical points are x = −1, 0, 1.
4. For x > 1 all factors are positive, so g′ > 0, and the sign flips at each root: + on x > 1, − on (0, 1), + on (−1, 0), − on x < −1.
5. x = −1 is − to +, x = 0 is + to −, x = 1 is − to +.
quickChecks.answer: Local minima at x = −1 and x = 1; local maximum at x = 0.

quickChecks.q: If h(x) = ∫₀^{x}(t−2)(t−5)dt, where does h have a local maximum and where a local minimum?
steps: 1. Upper limit is just x, whose derivative is 1, so h′(x) = (x−2)(x−5).
2. Critical points x = 2 and x = 5.
3. For x > 5 both factors are positive, so h′ > 0; then − on (2, 5) and + on x < 2.
4. x = 2 is + to −, x = 5 is − to +.
quickChecks.answer: Local maximum at x = 2, local minimum at x = 5.

quickChecks.q: In the main example the integrand has the factor (t+2). Why does it not give a critical point, and which factor does x = 0 come from?
steps: 1. After substituting t = x², the factor (t+2) becomes x²+2, which is at least 2 and so never zero.
2. x = 0 is not from the integrand at all; it comes from the 2x, the derivative of the upper limit x².
quickChecks.answer: x²+2 is always positive so it gives no critical point; x = 0 comes from the 2x produced by Newton–Leibniz, and it is a local minimum.

concepts.title: Sign Scheme Traps and a Point of Inflection in a Degree-5 Polynomial
concepts.oneLine: Sign scheme: a minus sitting in front flips every sign, and a squared factor does not flip anything — so f′ = 0 there is a point of inflection, not a maximum or minimum.
notes: In the first one you had f′(x) = −(x − 2)(x + 2). Almost everyone wrote + − + across −2 and 2. That is the sign scheme of (x − 2)(x + 2), not of ours.

There is a negative sitting in front, so the scheme starts from negative: − + − . Read it and the answers flip too — x = −2 becomes a local minimum and x = 2 becomes a local maximum. This was the only mistake possible in that question, and it was enough.

Then the degree-5 one. f′(x) = x²(x − 1)(x − 3), so f′ = 0 at x = 0, 1 and 3 — all three are critical points. But walk the signs: +, +, −, +. At x = 0 the derivative is zero and the sign does not change, so it is neither a local maximum nor a local minimum — it is a point of inflection. The squared factor is the reason: an even power never changes sign.
And notice what we actually did in both: took f′, made its sign scheme, read where f rises and where it falls. Maximum–minimum and increasing–decreasing are the same piece of work wearing two names.

quickChecks.q: f′(x) = −(x − 1)(x − 5). Classify x = 1 and x = 5.
steps: 1. Minus in front, so test a far-left value: x = 0 gives −(−1)(−5) = −5, negative.
3. − to + at x = 1; + to − at x = 5.
quickChecks.answer: Local minimum at x = 1, local maximum at x = 5.

quickChecks.q: f′(x) = (x − 2)²(x − 5). Classify x = 2 and x = 5.
steps: 1. x = 0: (4)(−5), negative. x = 3: (1)(−2), negative. x = 6: (16)(1), positive.
2. Scheme: −, −, + across 2 and 5.
3. The factor (x − 2) has an even power, so no flip at x = 2.
