quickChecks.answer: x = 2 is a point of inflection (f′ = 0, no sign change); x = 5 is a local minimum.

quickChecks.q: f′(x) = x³(x − 4). Classify x = 0 and x = 4.
steps: 2. Scheme: +, −, + across 0 and 4.
3. The power on x is 3, which is odd, so the sign does flip at x = 0 — do not confuse it with the x² case.
quickChecks.answer: Local maximum at x = 0, local minimum at x = 4.

concepts.title: Practice: Classifying Critical Points from the Derivative
concepts.oneLine: Find the critical points, put the sign of f′ on a number line, and read each point off: negative to positive is a local minimum, positive to negative is a local maximum.
notes: Both of these start the same way. Differentiate, set f′(x) = 0, and collect the critical points. That is all the question is really asking you to do first.

Now the only skill left is reading the sign of f′ around each point. Negative to positive means the function was falling and is now rising, so that point is a local minimum; positive to negative is a local maximum. Say it as a picture in your head: a valley, then a peak.
In the first one only one critical point came, x = −1. Behind it f′ was negative, in front of it f′ was positive. Negative to positive, so x = −1 is a local minimum. Done in one line.

The second one needed a little more differentiation, nothing more. After the derivative the factors gave three critical points: x = −2, x = 0 and x = 1. The signs across them run − + − +, so you get minimum, maximum, minimum. Only x = 0 is a local maximum; the other two are local minima.

quickChecks.q: f′(x) = (x + 2)(x − 4). Classify the critical points.
steps: 1. f′(x) = 0 gives x = −2 and x = 4.
2. Test x = −3: (−1)(−7) = 7, positive. So f′ > 0 for x < −2.
3. Signs alternate: + − +.
4. At x = −2: + to − → maximum. At x = 4: − to + → minimum.
quickChecks.answer: Local maximum at x = −2, local minimum at x = 4.

quickChecks.q: f′(x) = 3x² − 6x. Classify the critical points.
steps: 1. Factorise: 3x(x − 2) = 0, so x = 0 and x = 2.
2. Test x = −1: 3(−1)(−3) = 9, positive. So f′ > 0 for x < 0.
3. Signs alternate: + − +.
4. At x = 0: + to − → maximum. At x = 2: − to + → minimum.
quickChecks.answer: Local maximum at x = 0, local minimum at x = 2.

quickChecks.q: f′(x) = x(x + 3)(x − 2). Classify the critical points.
steps: 3. Simple roots, so signs alternate: − + − +.
4. At x = −3: − to + → minimum. At x = 0: + to − → maximum. At x = 2: − to + → minimum.
quickChecks.answer: Local minima at x = −3 and x = 2, local maximum at x = 0.

concepts.title: Finding an Unknown Constant from a Given Critical Point
concepts.oneLine: A given critical point is an equation: set f′ there equal to 0 to find the unknown constant, then put it back and run the sign scheme to say which point is the maximum and which is the minimum.
notes: The question hands you one fact: x = 1 is a critical point. A critical point means the derivative is 0 there, so f′(1) = 0 — that single line is the equation that gives you a. One unknown, one equation.
The function is a fraction, so the derivative comes from the quotient rule. Differentiate, put x = 1, set it to 0, and you get a = −7. That much is comfortable.

Now, knowing a = −7 is only half the question. The maximum and the minimum are still to be found, so put a = −7 back into f′ and look at it again. The numerator now breaks into two clean brackets, (x − 1) and (3x + 2), so the critical points are x = 1 and x = −2/3.

Finish with the sign line. The denominator of f′ is squared, so it can never change sign — only the two brackets decide. Reading left to right the pattern is + − +, so f′ turns + to − at x = −2/3 (local maximum) and − to + at x = 1 (local minimum). If your basics are strong, there is nothing here to get stuck on.

quickChecks.q: x = 2 is a critical point of f(x) = (x² + a)/(x + 1). Find a, then classify both critical points.
steps: 1. Quotient rule: f′(x) = [2x(x + 1) − (x² + a)]/(x + 1)² = (x² + 2x − a)/(x + 1)².
3. Numerator becomes x² + 2x − 8 = (x + 4)(x − 2), so the critical points are x = −4 and x = 2.
4. Signs are + − +: + to − at x = −4, − to + at x = 2.
quickChecks.answer: a = 8; x = −4 is a local maximum and x = 2 is a local minimum.

quickChecks.q: x = 1 is a critical point of f(x) = (x² + a)/(x + 2). Find a and say what x = 1 is.
steps: 3. x² + 4x − 5 = (x + 5)(x − 1), so the critical points are x = −5 and x = 1.
4. Signs + − +, so f′ goes − to + at x = 1.
quickChecks.answer: a = 5; x = 1 is a local minimum, and x = −5 is a local maximum.

quickChecks.q: x = 2 is a critical point of f(x) = (ax² + 1)/x. Find a, then classify x = 2 and x = −2.
steps: 1. Split it: f(x) = ax + 1/x, so f′(x) = a − 1/x².
4. 4x² > 0 always, so the signs come from (x − 2)(x + 2): + − +.
quickChecks.answer: a = 1/4; x = −2 is a local maximum and x = 2 is a local minimum.

concepts.title: Number of Solutions by Graphing: Cubic versus Logarithm
concepts.oneLine: When one side is a cubic and the other a log, don't solve — sketch both: 3x² − 2x³ tops out at 1 and log₂((x²+1)/x) bottoms out at 1, so they meet at exactly one point, (1,1).
notes: Look at what you have been given. On the left, a cubic; on the right, a logarithm. There is no algebra that cracks that. When you cannot solve an equation, you count its solutions by drawing both sides and looking at where they cross.

Start with f(x) = 3x² − 2x³. Then f'(x) = 6x − 6x² = 6x(1 − x). So the critical points are x = 0 and x = 1. The sign of f' tells the whole story: negative before 0, positive between 0 and 1, negative after 1. And the values are clean — f(0) = 0, f(1) = 3 − 2 = 1. So the curve falls, turns at (0, 0), rises to the peak (1, 1), and falls again.

Now the log. g(x) = log₂((x² + 1)/x), so the domain is x > 0 — the whole fight is only on the positive side. Split the fraction: (x² + 1)/x = x + 1/x, so g(x) = log₂(x + 1/x). And you already know x + 1/x ≥ 2 for x > 0, with equality only at x = 1.

Put the two together. The input of the log is never less than 2, so g(x) ≥ log₂2 = 1, and g touches 1 only at x = 1. The cubic, on x > 0, never goes above its peak value 1, and it reaches 1 only at x = 1. One curve stays at or below 1, the other stays at or above 1, and both hit 1 at the same x — so there is exactly one solution, the point (1, 1).

quickChecks.q: What is the greatest value of 3x² − 2x³ for x > 0?
steps: 2. On x > 0, f' is positive for 0 < x < 1 and negative for x > 1, so x = 1 is the maximum.

quickChecks.q: How many solutions does 3x² − 2x³ = 2 have for x > 0?
steps: 1. On x > 0 the largest value of 3x² − 2x³ is 1, at x = 1.
2. Since 2 > 1, the curve never reaches the line y = 2.

quickChecks.q: How many solutions does log₂((x² + 1)/x) = 2 have?
steps: 1. Domain: x > 0. Split the log: log₂(x + 1/x) = 2.
4. Both 2 + √3 and 2 − √3 are positive, so both are allowed.

concepts.title: Second Derivative Test
concepts.oneLine: At a critical point where f′ = 0, a positive f″ means local minimum and a negative f″ means local maximum.
notes: The single derivative test is absolutely correct in its place. It is not being replaced. I only want your knowledge to be complete, because there will be a question in JEE where seeing the sign scheme is hard.

Maybe you are short of time, maybe the factors confuse you, maybe you just blank out. But you have already differentiated the function once, so differentiating that derivative again is easy. That is when the second derivative test comes in handy.

The line is very simple. First, f′(a) = 0, so x = a is a contender for maxima or minima. That is a point where either one could come. Now check f″ at that point: if f″(a) is positive it is a local minimum, and if f″(a) is negative it is a local maximum.

Learn the way of remembering it, because it feels strange. At the critical point the single derivative was zero — leave that alone. Then the double derivative gives you the opposite feeling: negative sounds like it should mean minimum, but negative means maxima, and positive means minima.

quickChecks.q: For f(x) = x² − 6x + 5, find the critical point and classify it using f″.
steps: 2. f″(x) = 2, which is positive at x = 3.
3. Positive f″ means local minimum. Value: f(3) = 9 − 18 + 5 = −4.
quickChecks.answer: Local minimum at x = 3, with minimum value −4.

quickChecks.q: For f(x) = 4 − x², find the critical point and classify it using f″.
steps: 1. f′(x) = −2x = 0 gives x = 0.
2. f″(x) = −2, which is negative at x = 0.
3. Negative f″ means local maximum. Value: f(0) = 4.
quickChecks.answer: Local maximum at x = 0, with maximum value 4.

quickChecks.q: For f(x) = x³ − 3x, classify both critical points using f″.
steps: 1. f′(x) = 3x² − 3 = 0 gives x² = 1, so x = 1 and x = −1.
3. At x = 1, f″ = 6 > 0, so local minimum; f(1) = 1 − 3 = −2.
4. At x = −1, f″ = −6 < 0, so local maximum; f(−1) = −1 + 3 = 2.
quickChecks.answer: Local minimum at x = 1 with value −2, local maximum at x = −1 with value 2.

concepts.title: Using the Second Derivative Test, and When It Fails
concepts.oneLine: Find the critical point, put it into f″: positive means local minimum, negative means local maximum, and zero means the test tells you nothing.
notes: Take f(x) = x² + x + 1. This is an upward opening parabola, so you already know it has a local minimum. Let us see the test agree with you.
f′(x) = 2x + 1, so the critical point is x = −½. Now f″(x) = 2, and that is 2 everywhere, whatever x you put. Positive double derivative means that critical point is a local minimum.

Second one: f(x) = x·eˣ. By product rule f′(x) = eˣ(x + 1), so f′ = 0 at x = −1. Differentiate again and you get f″(x) = eˣ(x + 2), and at x = −1 that is e⁻¹ × 1 = 1/e, a positive number. Local minimum again, exactly what the first derivative test would have told you from the sign change negative to positive.

Now the honest part. If at your critical point the double derivative also comes out 0, the second derivative test concludes nothing — it does not say maximum, it does not say minimum, it does not even say there is no extremum. Go back to the first derivative and check the sign change on the two sides. There is an nth derivative test for such cases, but you will never need it in your paper, so do not load your head with it.

quickChecks.q: Classify the critical point of f(x) = x² − 6x + 5 by the second derivative test.
steps: 1. f′(x) = 2x − 6, so f′ = 0 gives x = 3.

quickChecks.q: Classify the critical point of f(x) = x·e²ˣ.
steps: 1. f′(x) = e²ˣ + x·2e²ˣ = e²ˣ(1 + 2x), so f′ = 0 gives x = −½.

quickChecks.q: What does the second derivative test say about f(x) = x⁴ at its critical point?
steps: 1. f′(x) = 4x³, so f′ = 0 gives x = 0.
3. f″ = 0 at the critical point, so the test concludes nothing. Use f′: it is negative for x < 0 and positive for x > 0.
quickChecks.answer: The second derivative test fails; the sign change of f′ shows x = 0 is a local minimum.

concepts.title: Practice: Three Questions by the Second Derivative Test
concepts.oneLine: Three questions, one rule: solve f′(x) = 0, drop each critical point into f″, and let the sign of f″ name the maximum or the minimum.
notes: The first question needed nothing clever. Critical points came out as x = ±2, and f″ = −6x. Negative at x = 2, so local maximum. Positive at x = −2, so local minimum. Done.

A sign scheme would have been just as fast here, and that is a fair point. But you still have to carry the second derivative test in your head, because the day it is the only quick route, there is no time to invent it.

The second question is the one to be careful with. After differentiating, the derivative is undefined at x = −2. That is not a maximum or a minimum — there the graph runs away to infinity. Only x = 0 and x = −4 are the real candidates, and f″ sorts them out in one line each.

The third one is where this test actually earns its place. Trigonometry is where you get confused with signs, so stop guessing and just compute. f″ = −2 sin x, put π/3 and 5π/3 into it, read the sign, write the answer.

quickChecks.q: Classify the extrema of f(x) = x³ − 3x.
steps: 1. f′(x) = 3x² − 3 = 0 gives x² = 1, so x = 1 and x = −1.
3. f″(1) = 6, positive, so local minimum.
4. f″(−1) = −6, negative, so local maximum.
quickChecks.answer: Local minimum at x = 1, local maximum at x = −1.

quickChecks.q: Find and classify the extrema of f(x) = x²/(x + 1).
steps: 2. f′(x) = 1 − 1/(x + 1)² = x(x + 2)/(x + 1)², which is 0 at x = 0 and x = −2.
3. x = −1 is outside the domain, so it is not a candidate at all.
5. f″(0) = 2, positive, so local minimum, value f(0) = 0.
6. f″(−2) = 2/(−1)³ = −2, negative, so local maximum, value f(−2) = 4/(−1) = −4.
quickChecks.answer: Local minimum at x = 0 with value 0, local maximum at x = −2 with value −4.

quickChecks.q: Classify the extrema of f(x) = 2 cos x + x in [0, 2π].
steps: 1. f′(x) = −2 sin x + 1 = 0 gives sin x = ½.
2. sin is positive in the first and second quadrants, so x = π/6 and x = π − π/6 = 5π/6.
3. f″(x) = −2 cos x.
4. At x = π/6: cos x = √3/2, so f″ = −√3, negative, local maximum.
5. At x = 5π/6: cos x = −√3/2, so f″ = √3, positive, local minimum.
quickChecks.answer: Local maximum at x = π/6, local minimum at x = 5π/6.

concepts.title: Why the Second Derivative Test Works
concepts.oneLine: If f′ turns from negative to positive at x = a, then f′ itself is increasing there, so f″(a) > 0 — that is the whole second derivative test.
notes: Start with the first derivative test, the one you already know. Draw the sign scheme of f′(x) and mark the critical point x = a on it. Suppose f′ is negative just before a and positive just after a. Negative to positive at a critical point means x = a is a point of local minimum. That much is old news.
Now the real question: if anything in this world goes from negative to positive, is it increasing or decreasing? Increasing, obviously. It was below zero, then it climbed above zero.

So apply that to f′ itself. Here f′ is going from negative to positive across x = a, which means f′ is an increasing function near a. And if any function is increasing, its own derivative is positive. The derivative of f′ is f″. So f″(a) > 0 — exactly the condition the second derivative test gives for a local minimum.

The same logic runs the other way for a maximum. There f′ goes from positive to negative, so f′ is decreasing, so the derivative of f′ is negative, so f″(a) < 0. Nothing new was ever added to the theory — the second derivative test is just the first derivative test said in another language.

quickChecks.q: At a critical point x = c, f′ is positive just before c and negative just after. What is the sign of f″(c), and what kind of point is c?
steps: 1. f′ goes from positive to negative, so f′ is decreasing near c.
2. A decreasing function has a negative derivative, and the derivative of f′ is f″.
quickChecks.answer: f″(c) < 0, and x = c is a point of local maximum.

quickChecks.q: You are told f′(2) = 0 and f″(2) > 0. Without drawing anything, what is happening at x = 2?
steps: 1. f″(2) > 0 means f′ is an increasing function at x = 2.
2. f′ is increasing and passes through zero at x = 2, so f′ is negative just before 2 and positive just after.
3. Negative to positive at a critical point is a minimum.
quickChecks.answer: x = 2 is a point of local minimum.

quickChecks.q: A student says: "f″(a) > 0, so f is increasing at x = a." Is this correct?
steps: 1. f″ > 0 tells you about f′, not about f — it says f′ is increasing.
2. Here f′(a) = 0 and f′ is rising through zero, so f is actually decreasing before a and increasing after a.
quickChecks.answer: Wrong. f″(a) > 0 means f′ is increasing; f has a local minimum at a, so f is not increasing at a.

concepts.title: The Two Meanings of the Sign of f″: Monotonic f′ and Concavity
concepts.oneLine: f″ > 0 means f′ is increasing (the reading that actually solves questions) and the graph is concave upward — lying above its tangents; f″ < 0 flips both.
notes: Suppose a question says f″(x) > 0 on some interval. Two things are true there. First, f′ is an increasing function. Second, the graph is concave upward.

In almost every question you will ever solve, the meaning you need is the first one: f″ > 0 means f′ is increasing. Keep that at the front of your mind. Concavity is the picture; the increasing f′ is the tool.
Flip the sign and everything flips. If f″(x) < 0 on an interval, then f′ is a decreasing function there, and the graph is concave downward. Again, the useful one is f′ decreasing.

Now the picture, so you know what the words mean. Take a curve and draw the tangent at any point on it. If the graph always sits above its tangent, the curve is concave upward; if the graph always sits below its tangent, it is concave downward. And notice: this is not decided by the first derivative at all. It is decided by the second.

quickChecks.q: For y = x², say whether y′ is increasing or decreasing, and whether the graph is concave upward or downward.
steps: 2. y″ = 2, which is positive for every x.
3. y″ > 0 ⇒ y′ is increasing, and the graph is concave upward.
quickChecks.answer: y′ is increasing and the graph is concave upward for all x.

quickChecks.q: A question tells you f″(x) < 0 on an interval. What are the two meanings, and which one do you use?
steps: 1. Meaning 1: f′ is a decreasing function on that interval.
2. Meaning 2: the graph is concave downward there, lying below its tangents.
3. Meaning 1 is the one that carries the solution forward.
quickChecks.answer: f′ is decreasing (the useful reading) and the graph is concave downward.

quickChecks.q: Check y = e⁻ˣ. Is it increasing or decreasing, and is it concave upward or downward?
steps: 1. y′ = −e⁻ˣ. Since e⁻ˣ > 0 always, y′ < 0, so the function is decreasing.
2. y″ = e⁻ˣ, which is positive for every x.
3. y″ > 0 ⇒ concave upward.
quickChecks.answer: Decreasing everywhere, but concave upward everywhere — proof that the two questions are answered by two different derivatives.

concepts.title: Point of Inflection
concepts.oneLine: A point of inflection is the point where the concavity of the graph changes, and it is always decided by the second derivative test.
notes: Here is the clean definition. A point of inflection is the point where the concavity of the graph changes. Nothing more complicated than that.

Concavity change means the graph is concave downward on one side of the point and concave upward on the other side (or the other way round). So look at the dot on the graph: just before it the curve bends one way, just after it the curve bends the opposite way. That dot is your point of inflection.

Now the part you must never mix up. A point of inflection is always decided by the second derivative test, never by the first. The first derivative tells you about increase, decrease, maxima and minima. Concavity is the second derivative's job, so the point where concavity flips is the second derivative's job too.
So in any question, the moment you read the words point of inflection, your hand should go straight to f″(x). Find where f″ changes its sign — that is the point you have to report.

quickChecks.q: A graph is concave downward just before x = 2 and concave upward just after x = 2. Is x = 2 a point of inflection?
steps: 1. Check the concavity on the left of x = 2: concave downward, so f″ < 0 there.
2. Check the concavity on the right of x = 2: concave upward, so f″ > 0 there.
3. The concavity has changed across x = 2, so by definition the point qualifies.
quickChecks.answer: Yes, x = 2 is a point of inflection.

quickChecks.q: Which derivative decides a point of inflection — the first or the second?
steps: 1. A point of inflection is about a change of concavity.
2. Concavity is read off the sign of f″, not f′.
3. So the decision is made by the second derivative test.

quickChecks.q: For a curve, f″ < 0 for every x on both sides of x = 1 and on the whole domain. Can x = 1 be a point of inflection?
steps: 1. f″ < 0 on the left of x = 1, so the graph is concave downward there.
2. f″ < 0 on the right of x = 1 as well, so the graph is still concave downward.
3. The concavity never changes, so the required flip does not happen.
quickChecks.answer: No, x = 1 is not a point of inflection.

concepts.title: y = x³: The Standard Point of Inflection
concepts.oneLine: For y = x³ the double derivative y″ = 6x changes sign at x = 0, so the origin is a point of inflection — not a maximum, not a minimum.
notes: A point of inflection is the point where the concavity changes. Take the most common example of all: y = x³. To the right of 0 the curve rises in a concave upward shape, and to the left of 0 it is concave downward.

Test it with a tangent. Pick any point to the right of 0, draw the tangent there, and the curve sits above the tangent — concave upward. Pick any point to the left of 0, draw the tangent, and the curve sits below the tangent — concave downward.

Now bring in derivatives. Here y′ = 3x², which is 0 at x = 0, and that critical point gives neither a maximum nor a minimum. The real story is in y″ = 6x: it is 0 at x = 0, positive to the right of 0 and negative to the left of 0.

That sign change in y″ is exactly why x = 0 is a point of inflection: concave up on one side, concave down on the other. For inflection, the sign scheme of the double derivative decides everything; the single derivative has nothing to say here.

quickChecks.q: For y = x³, is x = 0 a maximum, a minimum, or a point of inflection?
steps: 1. y′ = 3x², so y′ = 0 at x = 0 — a critical point.
2. y″ = 6x, which is negative for x < 0 and positive for x > 0.
3. The concavity changes from downward to upward at x = 0.
quickChecks.answer: A point of inflection — neither a maximum nor a minimum.

quickChecks.q: Find the point of inflection of y = x³ + 2.
steps: 2. y″ = 0 gives x = 0.
3. Sign of y″: negative for x < 0, positive for x > 0 — the sign flips.
4. Value: y = 0³ + 2 = 2.

quickChecks.q: Find the point of inflection of y = (x − 1)³.
steps: 2. y″ = 0 gives x = 1.
3. Sign of y″: negative for x < 1, positive for x > 1 — concavity changes.

concepts.title: Practice: Locating Points of Inflection
concepts.quote: This second question was pure hard work — the calculation is long and f″ turns out to be zero at three different points. But once you see that all you need is the sign scheme of f″, the fear goes away.
concepts.oneLine: Inflection points come from the sign scheme of f″, not f′ — and since the second derivative of a cubic is linear, every cubic has exactly one.
notes: Look at what the question is actually asking. Points of inflection have nothing to do with f′ = 0. You need the points where the concavity flips, and that is read off the sign scheme of f″.

So the method is fixed, every single time. Differentiate once, differentiate again, set f″ = 0, mark those points on a number line, and check the sign of f″ on each side. A point is an inflection point only where f″ actually changes sign.

In this question f″ became zero at three points, and the sign of f″ flipped at all three. So you report three points of inflection. Be warned — the calculation here is heavy. There is nothing clever hiding in it, it is just hard work, and you should be able to do this much hard work.

Now the part worth remembering forever. Every cubic in the world has exactly one point of inflection, because the second derivative of a cubic is linear, and a linear function changes its sign at exactly one point. A quadratic has none at all — its f″ is a constant, so it never changes sign. Its concavity never flips.

quickChecks.q: Find the point of inflection of f(x) = x³ − 6x² + 9x + 2.
steps: 3. f″(x) = 0 gives x = 2.
4. For x < 2, f″ < 0 (concave down); for x > 2, f″ > 0 (concave up). Sign changes.
quickChecks.answer: x = 2 — and you could have written it straight away as −b/3a = 6/3 = 2.

quickChecks.q: Does f(x) = 2x² + 5x + 7 have a point of inflection?
steps: 2. f″(x) = 4, a constant.
3. A non-zero constant never changes sign.
quickChecks.answer: No. Its concavity never flips — no quadratic has a point of inflection.

quickChecks.q: f″(x) = 0 at x = 1 for f(x) = (x − 1)⁴. Is x = 1 a point of inflection?
steps: 3. f″(1) = 0, but (x − 1)² ≥ 0, so f″ > 0 on both sides of 1.
quickChecks.answer: No. f″ = 0 there but there is no sign change, so no inflection point.

concepts.title: JEE Main: Monotonicity of φ(x) = f(x) + f(2−x) when f″ > 0
concepts.oneLine: For φ(x) = f(x) + f(2−x) with f″ > 0, f′ is strictly increasing, so f′(x) = f′(2−x) forces x = 1, and one test value in each part shows φ decreases on (0,1) and increases on (1,2).
notes: Start the way you always start when the question says "comment on φ". Differentiate. φ′(x) = f′(x) − f′(2−x), and remember the −1 from the chain rule on 2−x, which is why the second term comes with a minus sign.

For critical points put φ′(x) = 0, so f′(x) = f′(2−x). Now the whole class writes x = 2−x, so x = 1. The answer is right, the logic is half done. Equal outputs do not mean equal inputs in general — sin x = sin y does not force x = y, because x = π − y also works, and x² + 5 = y² + 5 is happy with x = −1, y = 1.

Equal outputs force equal inputs only when the function is one-one, and that is exactly what f″ > 0 gives you: f′ is strictly increasing. So f′(x) = f′(2−x) really does give x = 2−x, that is x = 1. This is the line the examiner is looking for.

Now the sign scheme on (0,2) with the single critical point x = 1. Take any number between 1 and 2, say 1.5: φ′(1.5) = f′(1.5) − f′(0.5), and since f′ is increasing, the bigger input wins, so this is positive. Take 0.4 from (0,1): φ′(0.4) = f′(0.4) − f′(1.6) < 0. So φ is decreasing on (0,1) and increasing on (1,2).

quickChecks.q: f″(x) > 0 on (0,4) and φ(x) = f(x) + f(4−x). Find the critical point and the intervals of increase and decrease.
steps: 2. φ′ = 0 gives f′(x) = f′(4−x); f″ > 0 makes f′ one-one, so x = 4−x, that is x = 2.
3. Test x = 3: f′(3) − f′(1) > 0 since f′ is increasing.
quickChecks.answer: Critical point x = 2; φ decreasing on (0,2) and increasing on (2,4).

quickChecks.q: f″(x) > 0 on (0,6) and φ(x) = f(x) + f(6−x). Is φ increasing or decreasing at x = 4?
steps: 2. 4 > 2 and f′ is strictly increasing, so f′(4) > f′(2).
3. Hence φ′(4) > 0.
quickChecks.answer: Increasing at x = 4 (the critical point sits at x = 3, and 4 lies to its right).

quickChecks.q: f″(x) < 0 on (0,2) and φ(x) = f(x) + f(2−x). Is x = 1 a maximum or a minimum of φ?
steps: 1. Critical point is still x = 1, because f′ is strictly decreasing and so still one-one.
3. At x = 1.5: f′(1.5) − f′(0.5) < 0, so φ′ < 0 just right of 1.
4. Sign goes + to −.
quickChecks.answer: x = 1 is a point of maximum.

concepts.title: JEE Advanced: Degree-4 Polynomial from Extrema and a Limit
concepts.oneLine: If lim(x→0) [1 + f(x)/x²] = 3 for a degree-4 polynomial, the x and constant terms must vanish and the x² coefficient must be 2 — then f′(1) = f′(2) = 0 finishes it.
notes: Start with what "extremum at 1 and 2" gives you. It does not tell you which one is a maximum and which is a minimum — anything can happen between them. All it tells you is f′(1) = 0 and f′(2) = 0. That is your given data, nothing more.

Now the limit. First, that bracket is not the greatest integer function and not the fractional part. In the exam, if a bracket means greatest integer, the paper will say "[·] denotes the greatest integer". If it means fractional part, it will say so. No guessing nonsense. So lim(x→0) [1 + f(x)/x²] = 3 simply becomes lim(x→0) f(x)/x² = 3 − 1 = 2.

Here is the move: write the general degree-4 polynomial f(x) = ax⁴ + bx³ + cx² + dx + e, divide every term by x², and ask which terms can survive at x → 0. You get ax² + bx + c + d/x + e/x². The first three are fine: at x = 0 they give 0 + 0 + c. But d/x and e/x² blow up. The limit exists only if those two die, so d = 0 and e = 0, and then the limit is exactly c, so c = 2.

So f(x) = ax⁴ + bx³ + 2x². From here the story is simple: f′(x) = 4ax³ + 3bx² + 4x, put f′(1) = 0 and f′(2) = 0, get a and b, and compute f(2). The calculation is a bit dirty but mechanical — the interpretation of the limit was the real question.

quickChecks.q: f is a polynomial of degree 4 with lim(x→0) f(x)/x² = 5. What can you say about its coefficients?
steps: 1. Write f(x) = ax⁴ + bx³ + cx² + dx + e.
2. f(x)/x² = ax² + bx + c + d/x + e/x².
3. For the limit at 0 to exist, d = 0 and e = 0.
4. Then the limit is c, so c = 5.
quickChecks.answer: d = 0, e = 0 and c = 5, i.e. f(x) = ax⁴ + bx³ + 5x².

quickChecks.q: For f(x) = ½x⁴ − 2x³ + 2x², verify that x = 1 and x = 2 really are the extremum points, and find f(1).
steps: 2. So f′(x) = 0 at x = 0, 1, 2 — both 1 and 2 are there, as required.
quickChecks.answer: f′(x) = 2x(x − 1)(x − 2), so x = 1 and x = 2 are extremum points, and f(1) = ½.

quickChecks.q: A degree-4 polynomial f has extremum at x = 1 and x = 2, and lim(x→0) [2 + f(x)/x²] = 3. Find a and b in f(x) = ax⁴ + bx³ + cx².
steps: 1. lim(x→0) f(x)/x² = 3 − 2 = 1, so d = 0, e = 0 and c = 1.
2. f(x) = ax⁴ + bx³ + x², so f′(x) = 4ax³ + 3bx² + 2x.
5. Subtract: 4a − 1 = 0, so a = ¼. Then 3b = −2 − 1 = −3, so b = −1.
quickChecks.answer: a = ¼ and b = −1, i.e. f(x) = ¼x⁴ − x³ + x².

concepts.title: Global maxima and minima: check critical points AND end points
concepts.quote: You have known since childhood what "the biggest value" means. The only thing JEE adds is one honest question: does the biggest value have to come at a critical point?
concepts.oneLine: On an interval, the biggest and smallest values of a function need not sit at a critical point, so always compare f at every critical point and at both end points.
notes: Global maximum and global minimum are not new ideas. Overall, across the whole interval, which value is the largest and which is the smallest — that is all we are asking.
So here is the real question. Is it necessary that the largest value comes at a critical point? Not at all. It can come at an end point of the interval.

That is why in every global maxima or global minima question you find the value of the function at the critical points and at the end points, and then compare. The derivative only hands you the candidates inside; the two ends are candidates too, and nobody tells you about them.
Keep it mechanical. List the critical points in the interval, add both end points to that list, compute f at each one, and pick the largest and smallest from your list. No guessing from the shape.

quickChecks.q: Find the global maximum and global minimum of f(x) = 2x + 1 on [0, 3].
steps: 1. f′(x) = 2, which is never 0, so there is no critical point inside the interval.
2. Only the end points are candidates: f(0) = 1 and f(3) = 7.
quickChecks.answer: Global maximum 7 at x = 3, global minimum 1 at x = 0 — both at end points.

quickChecks.q: Find the global maximum and global minimum of f(x) = x² on [-1, 3].
steps: 1. f′(x) = 2x = 0 gives the critical point x = 0, which lies in the interval.
3. Compare 0, 1 and 9.
quickChecks.answer: Global maximum 9 at x = 3 (an end point), global minimum 0 at x = 0 (the critical point).

quickChecks.q: Find the global maximum and global minimum of f(x) = x³ - 3x on [0, 3].
steps: 1. f′(x) = 3x² - 3 = 0 gives x = 1 and x = -1; only x = 1 lies in (0, 3).
3. Compare -2, 0 and 18.
quickChecks.answer: Global maximum 18 at x = 3 (end point), global minimum -2 at x = 1 (critical point).

concepts.title: Range of a cubic on an interval, and what changes when an end point is excluded
concepts.oneLine: On a closed interval the range comes from the values at the critical points and at the end points — biggest is the maximum, smallest the minimum — but if an end point is excluded, that value is only approached, so the minimum (or maximum) does not exist.
notes: Take f(x) = 2x³ − 9x² + 12x + 6. Differentiate: f′(x) = 6x² − 18x + 12 = 6(x − 1)(x − 2). So the critical points are x = 1 and x = 2.

Sign of f′ goes plus, minus, plus. So f increases up to 1, falls from 1 to 2, then increases again. That makes x = 1 a point of local maximum and x = 2 a point of local minimum. Now I only need the heights: f(0) = 6, f(1) = 11, f(2) = 10, f(3) = 15. With these four numbers you can sketch the curve between 0 and 3 and answer every version of the question in one shot.

For the range on a closed interval, collect the values at the critical points and at the end points — the largest is the maximum and the smallest is the minimum. Nothing more is needed. On [0, 2] my candidates are 6, 11, 10, so the range is [6, 11].

Now the real point of this section. If an end point is excluded, check whether that value is reached anywhere else on the curve. On (0, 2] the value 6 comes only from x = 0, which is gone, so f only approaches 6 — the minimum does not exist, and the range becomes (6, 11]. But on [0, 2) the value 10 at x = 2 is lost and nothing changes, because the rising part from 6 to 11 already passes through 10. Range is still [6, 11].

quickChecks.q: For f(x) = 2x³ − 9x² + 12x + 6, find the range on [1, 3].
steps: 1. Critical points inside or at the ends: x = 1 and x = 2. End points: 1 and 3.
3. Largest 15, smallest 10.

quickChecks.q: Same f. Find the range on [1, 2).
steps: 1. f falls from f(1) = 11 to f(2) = 10 on this stretch, and x = 2 is excluded.
2. 11 is attained at x = 1, but 10 is never reached — f only approaches 10.
3. No other x in [1, 2) gives 10, since f is strictly decreasing there.
quickChecks.answer: (10, 11]. Maximum = 11; the minimum value does not exist.

quickChecks.q: Same f. Find the range on (0, 3].
steps: 2. Maximum 15 is at x = 3, which is included.
3. The smallest value 6 came only from x = 0, which is excluded, so f approaches 6.
quickChecks.answer: (6, 15]. Maximum = 15; the minimum value does not exist.

concepts.title: Quiz set: maximum and minimum on a given interval
concepts.oneLine: Two quiz problems on global maximum and minimum over a given interval, to be solved by the critical-point-plus-end-point method, in about four minutes.
notes: You will look at these two and say, sir, this is easy, there is nothing new here. You are right. There is nothing new. But easy and settled are two different things.
If you move ahead and the concept has not settled, the problem will show up later, in a question where you cannot afford it. So pause here. Pen down, both questions solved on paper, not in the head.

The method is the same one we have been using. Differentiate, set f′(x) = 0, keep only the critical points that actually lie inside the given interval, then put those points and both end points into f(x) and compare the values. The biggest value is the global maximum, the smallest is the global minimum.
Both questions are set out here, and the third one after them is a bonus. Do them like a test, then come back and check against the worked solution.

quickChecks.q: Find the maximum and minimum values of f(x) = x² − 4x + 1 on [0, 3].
steps: 1. f′(x) = 2x − 4, so f′(x) = 0 gives x = 2, which lies in [0, 3].
2. End points and critical point: f(0) = 1, f(2) = 4 − 8 + 1 = −3, f(3) = 9 − 12 + 1 = −2.
3. Compare the three values: largest is 1, smallest is −3.
quickChecks.answer: Maximum value 1 at x = 0; minimum value −3 at x = 2.

quickChecks.q: Find the maximum and minimum values of f(x) = x³ − 3x on [0, 2].
steps: 1. f′(x) = 3x² − 3 = 0 gives x = 1 and x = −1. Only x = 1 lies in [0, 2], so drop x = −1.
3. Largest value is 2, smallest is −2.
quickChecks.answer: Maximum value 2 at x = 2; minimum value −2 at x = 1.

quickChecks.q: Find the maximum and minimum values of f(x) = 12x − x³ on [−1, 3].
steps: 1. f′(x) = 12 − 3x² = 0 gives x² = 4, so x = 2 or x = −2. Only x = 2 lies in [−1, 3].
3. Compare: largest is 16, smallest is −11 — and the minimum sits at an end point, exactly as warned.
quickChecks.answer: Maximum value 16 at x = 2; minimum value −11 at x = −1.

concepts.title: Bonus problem: minimum and maximum of 2x³ − 9x² + 12x + 5 on [0,3]
concepts.oneLine: On [0,3] the maximum of 2x³ − 9x² + 12x + 5 is 14 at x = 3 and the minimum is 5 at x = 0 — both at the endpoints, not at the turning points.
notes: Here is the bonus question: f(x) = 2x³ − 9x² + 12x + 5, and you have to find the minimum and maximum for x from 0 to 3.

Closed interval, continuous function. So there are only four numbers to look at: the two endpoints x = 0 and x = 3, and the points inside where f′(x) = 0. Nothing else can win — the largest and smallest values live only at the endpoints or at the stationary points.
Differentiate and the cubic becomes easy. f′(x) = 6x² − 18x + 12 = 6(x − 1)(x − 2), so x = 1 and x = 2, and both lie inside [0,3]. Good, both stay as candidates.

Now just put all four values in and compare: 5, 10, 9, 14. The biggest is 14 at x = 3, the smallest is 5 at x = 0. The turning points x = 1 and x = 2 gave 10 and 9 — only local winners, they lost to the ends.

quickChecks.q: Same function f(x) = 2x³ − 9x² + 12x + 5, but now for 0 ≤ x ≤ 2. Find the maximum and minimum.
steps: 1. f′(x) = 6(x − 1)(x − 2), so x = 1 and x = 2; here x = 2 is itself the endpoint.
2. Candidates: x = 0, 1, 2.
4. Compare 5, 10, 9.
quickChecks.answer: Maximum = 10 at x = 1, minimum = 5 at x = 0. Shrink the interval and the answer changes — that is why the endpoints must always be checked.

quickChecks.q: Find the maximum and minimum of f(x) = x³ − 3x on [0,2].
steps: 1. f′(x) = 3x² − 3 = 3(x − 1)(x + 1), so x = 1 and x = −1; only x = 1 lies in [0,2].
2. Candidates: x = 0, 1, 2.
quickChecks.answer: Maximum = 2 at x = 2, minimum = −2 at x = 1. (x = −1 is discarded — it is outside the interval.)

quickChecks.q: Find the maximum and minimum of f(x) = x³ − 6x² + 9x + 1 on [0,5].
steps: 1. f′(x) = 3x² − 12x + 9 = 3(x − 1)(x − 3), so x = 1 and x = 3, both inside (0,5).
2. Candidates: x = 0, 1, 3, 5.
quickChecks.answer: Maximum = 21 at x = 5, minimum = 1, reached at both x = 0 and x = 3. The smallest value can occur at more than one point — write both.

concepts.title: Quiz answers and what the options were testing
concepts.oneLine: The quiz answers: question 1 is 'none of these' because not one option is the actual maximum value, question 2 is option A, and the two JEE Main problems coming up answer to 122 and 9.
notes: Question 2 is option A. Question 1 is 'none of these'.

Why 'none of these'? Because when the four options are checked against the value actually computed, not a single one of them is the maximum value. If your number is right and no option matches it, 'none of these' is the answer — it is not a trap, it is the answer.
Then two more short ones, both old JEE Main questions. The answer to the first is 122. The answer to the second is 9. If you worked them out, you already know where you stand.
That second one comes next, starting from f′(x) on [0, 1]. Try to supply the steps yourself as they come.

quickChecks.q: You compute the maximum value of a function on a closed interval as 14. The options are 9, 10, 11 and 'none of these'. What do you mark?
steps: 1. Your computed value is 14.
2. Compare with the options: 9 ≠ 14, 10 ≠ 14, 11 ≠ 14.
3. No option represents the maximum value.

quickChecks.q: A question asks for the maximum value of f on [0, 3]. You find the maximum occurs at x = 2 and f(2) = 25. Which number is the answer?
steps: 1. x = 2 is the point of maximum, not the maximum value.
2. The maximum value is f(2) = 25.

concepts.title: JEE Main: extremes of x^(3/5)/(1 + x^(3/5)) type function on [0,1]
concepts.oneLine: Differentiate x^(3/5)/(1+x)^(3/5) on [0,1], watch the numerator collapse to 1, and since there is no critical point inside, the minimum and maximum are simply f(0) and f(1).
notes: You are told to study f(x) = x^(3/5)/(1+x)^(3/5) only between 0 and 1. So do not waste a second on what happens outside that interval. Whatever turns up, turns up inside [0,1].

Quotient rule, slowly. Keep the bottom, differentiate the top; keep the top, differentiate the bottom, with the minus sign. Then pull out the common 3/5 and the common (1+x)^(6/5), and what is left is just two fractional-power terms inside a bracket.

Now the one step everybody skips: take the LCM inside that bracket. The denominators are x^(2/5) and (1+x)^(2/5), so each term gets pushed to a full power 1, because 3/5 + 2/5 = 1. The bracket becomes (1+x) − x, the x cancels, and the numerator is plain 1.

A numerator of 1 can never be zero, so there is no critical point inside (0,1) — the minimum and maximum have to sit at the end points. The only places the derivative misbehaves are x = 0, which is an end point I am checking anyway, and x = −1, which is not even in my interval. So just put in 0 and 1 and compare.

quickChecks.q: Find the minimum and maximum of f(x) = x^(2/5)/(1+x)^(2/5) on [0,1].
steps: 2. Numerator is 1, so no critical point in (0,1); f′ > 0, so f is increasing.
quickChecks.answer: Minimum 0 at x = 0, maximum (½)^(2/5) ≈ 0.76 at x = 1.

quickChecks.q: Find the minimum and maximum of f(x) = x/(1+x) on [0,2].
steps: 1. f′(x) = [(1+x) − x]/(1+x)² = 1/(1+x)², which is never zero.
2. No critical point inside, and f′ > 0, so f increases.
quickChecks.answer: Minimum 0 at x = 0, maximum 2/3 at x = 2.

quickChecks.q: For the same f(x) = x^(3/5)/(1+x)^(3/5), what are the extreme values on [1,2]?
steps: 1. f′(x) = (3/5)/[x^(2/5)(1+x)^(8/5)] > 0 on [1,2], and again no critical point.
2. So both answers are at the ends: f(1) = (½)^(3/5) ≈ 0.66 and f(2) = (2/3)^(3/5) ≈ 0.78.

concepts.title: Two critical points inside, but the maximum still at an end point
concepts.oneLine: On [0, 2] the function x(1 − x)² has two critical points, 1/3 and 1, but the largest of the four values is f(2) = 2, so the maximum sits at the end point.
notes: Take f(x) = x(1 − x)² on the closed interval [0, 2]. Differentiate: f′(x) = (1 − x)² − 2x(1 − x) = (1 − x)(1 − 3x). So f′(x) = 0 at x = 1/3 and x = 1, and both of them sit inside [0, 2].

Now do not get excited about those critical points. On a closed interval the maximum is simply the biggest number in the list f(a), f(b) and f at every critical point — nothing more. So the list has four entries, not two.
At the critical points: f(1/3) = (1/3)(2/3)² = 4/27, and f(1) = 1 × 0 = 0. At the end points: f(0) = 0, and f(2) = 2 × (−1)² = 2.

Compare: 4/27, 0, 0, 2. The winner is 2, and it came from the end point x = 2. The smallest is 0, and that happens twice — at x = 0 and at x = 1. Two critical points inside, and still neither of them is the maximum.

quickChecks.q: Find the maximum value of f(x) = x(x − 2)² on [0, 3].
steps: 2. Critical points: x = 2/3 and x = 2, both inside [0, 3].
5. List: 0, 32/27 (≈ 1.19), 0, 3. The biggest is 3.
quickChecks.answer: Maximum value = 3, at the end point x = 3.

quickChecks.q: Find the maximum and the minimum value of f(x) = x³ − 3x on [−2, 3].
steps: 1. f′(x) = 3x² − 3 = 3(x − 1)(x + 1), so the critical points are x = −1 and x = 1, both inside [−2, 3].
4. List: −2, 2, −2, 18. Biggest is 18, smallest is −2.
quickChecks.answer: Maximum = 18 at x = 3 (end point); minimum = −2, attained at x = 1 and at x = −2.

quickChecks.q: Same function f(x) = x(1 − x)², but now on [0, 1]. What is the maximum value?
steps: 1. f′(x) = (1 − x)(1 − 3x), so the critical points are x = 1/3 and x = 1; here x = 1 is an end point.
3. List: 0, 4/27, 0. Now the biggest is 4/27.
quickChecks.answer: Maximum value = 4/27, at x = 1/3. Shrinking the interval moved the maximum from an end point back to a critical point — which is exactly why you must list all of them every time.

concepts.title: Maximum over a set defined by an inequality: x² − 11x + 30 ≤ 0
concepts.oneLine: When the domain is hidden inside an inequality, solve the inequality first — then any critical point outside that interval is simply thrown away and only the end points compete.
notes: Look at the set carefully. x² − 11x + 30 ≤ 0 factorises as (x − 5)(x − 6) ≤ 0, so x lies between 5 and 6, both included. That is your interval: [5, 6]. Nothing else about the question has changed.
Now do the usual work. f′(x) = 9x² − 36x + 27, take 9 common, x² − 4x + 3 = 0, so the critical points are x = 1 and x = 3.

And here is the point of the whole question. 1 and 3 are nowhere near [5, 6], so they are not critical points of this problem at all — a point outside the domain does not exist for you. The function has no turning point inside [5, 6], so it just climbs or falls across it, and the winner has to be an end point.

So only x = 5 and x = 6 need checking. One of them is the maximum, and it comes out as 122 at x = 6. A natural doubt here: why not also put in 1 and 3? Because the question asks for the maximum on [5, 6], and 1 and 3 are not in [5, 6]. That is the full answer.

quickChecks.q: Find the maximum value of f(x) = x³ − 6x² + 9x + 5 on the set S = {x ∈ ℝ : x² − 9x + 20 ≤ 0}.
steps: 2. f′(x) = 3x² − 12x + 9 = 3(x − 1)(x − 3); critical points x = 1, 3, both outside [4, 5], so both rejected.

quickChecks.q: For f(x) = 2x³ − 3x² − 12x + 1 on S = {x ∈ ℝ : x² − 7x + 12 ≤ 0}, find both the maximum and the minimum value.
steps: 2. f′(x) = 6x² − 6x − 12 = 6(x − 2)(x + 1); critical points x = 2 and x = −1, neither lies in [3, 4], so both are discarded.
quickChecks.answer: Maximum = 33 at x = 4, minimum = −8 at x = 3.

quickChecks.q: Same cubic as above, f(x) = 3x³ − 18x² + 27x − 40, but now on S = {x ∈ ℝ : x² − 13x + 40 ≤ 0}. What is the maximum?
steps: 2. f′(x) = 9(x − 1)(x − 3); critical points 1 and 3 are still outside [5, 8], so again only the end points matter.

concepts.title: Both critical points inside the interval: 2x³ − 9x² + 12x + 5 on [0,3]
concepts.oneLine: For 2x³ − 9x² + 12x + 5 on [0,3] both critical points x = 1 and x = 2 are inside the interval, so compare all four values f(0), f(1), f(2), f(3) — the maximum is 14 at x = 3.
notes: Read the question first. It says: on 0 to 3, find the maximum. So the interval is closed, and that single word decides the whole method.
Differentiate. f′(x) = 6x² − 18x + 12 = 6(x − 1)(x − 2), so the critical points are x = 1 and x = 2. Now check the gate: are they inside [0,3]? Yes, both of them are.
The moment both critical points lie inside the interval, you must find the value of the function at all four points — the two critical points and the two end points. Nothing more, nothing less.

Put the four numbers in a column: f(0) = 5, f(1) = 10, f(2) = 9, f(3) = 14. The biggest is 14 and the smallest is 5. So the maximum is 14 at x = 3 and the minimum is 5 at x = 0. Notice the answer came from an end point, not from a critical point — that is exactly why you cannot skip them.

quickChecks.q: Find the maximum and minimum of f(x) = 2x³ − 3x² − 12x + 1 on [−2,3].
steps: 2. Both lie in [−2,3], so compare x = −2, −1, 2, 3.
quickChecks.answer: Maximum = 8 at x = −1; minimum = −19 at x = 2.

quickChecks.q: Find the maximum and minimum of f(x) = x³ − 3x + 2 on [0,2].
steps: 2. x = −1 is outside [0,2], so drop it. Candidates: x = 0, 1, 2.
quickChecks.answer: Maximum = 4 at x = 2; minimum = 0 at x = 1.

quickChecks.q: Find the maximum and minimum of f(x) = x³ − 6x² + 9x + 1 on [0,5].
steps: 2. Both lie in [0,5], so compare x = 0, 1, 3, 5.
quickChecks.answer: Maximum = 21 at x = 5; minimum = 1, reached at both x = 0 and x = 3.

concepts.title: Analysis of a cubic: the graph, the constant, and the number of real roots
concepts.oneLine: For a cubic, the number of real roots is decided by the signs of the local maximum and local minimum values, not by the critical points — shift only the constant and the root count changes.
notes: Take the cubic we already worked with: f(x) = 2x³ − 9x² + 12x + 5. Differentiate it and you get 6(x − 1)(x − 2), so the critical points are x = 1 and x = 2. From the sign change, x = 1 is a local maximum and x = 2 is a local minimum.

Now put the heights in. f(1) = 10, f(2) = 9, and f(0) = 5. The curve rises to 10, dips to 9, and climbs away. Both turning points sit above the x-axis, so the graph can cut the axis only once on its way up from the far left. One real root.

Now define h(x) = 2x³ − 9x² + 12x + 5 − 9.5, that is h(x) = 2x³ − 9x² + 12x − 4.5. The derivative is untouched, so the critical points are still x = 1 and x = 2 — the shape is identical. Only every height drops by 9.5: the local maximum becomes 10 − 9.5 = 0.5 and the local minimum becomes 9 − 9.5 = −0.5.

Now the peak is above the axis and the valley is below it, so the curve must cross the axis three times. Same critical points, same shape, different constant — the root count changed because the local maximum and local minimum values changed sign. A real root just means an intersection with the x-axis, and what decides those crossings is where the two turning heights lie, not where the turning points lie.

quickChecks.q: How many real roots does 2x³ − 9x² + 12x − 8 have?
steps: 1. Derivative is unchanged: critical points x = 1 (local max) and x = 2 (local min).
3. Both turning values are below the x-axis, so the curve meets the axis only on its final rising branch.

quickChecks.q: How many real roots does 2x³ − 9x² + 12x − 4.75 have?
steps: 1. Critical points are again x = 1 and x = 2.
2. Value at x = 1: 2 − 9 + 12 − 4.75 = 0.25 (positive local maximum).
3. Value at x = 2: 16 − 36 + 24 − 4.75 = −0.75 (negative local minimum).
4. Peak above the axis, valley below it — three crossings.

quickChecks.q: How many distinct real roots does 2x³ − 9x² + 12x − 4 have?
steps: 1. Critical points x = 1 and x = 2 as always.
2. Value at x = 1: 2 − 9 + 12 − 4 = 1 (above the axis).
3. Value at x = 2: 16 − 36 + 24 − 4 = 0 — the local minimum sits exactly on the x-axis.
4. So the curve cuts the axis once on the left and then just touches it at x = 2 instead of crossing twice.
quickChecks.answer: Two distinct real roots (x = 2 is a repeated root).

concepts.title: Condition for a cubic to have three distinct real roots
concepts.oneLine: A cubic has three real and distinct roots exactly when its local maximum value M and its local minimum value m have opposite signs, that is M·m < 0.
notes: Take any cubic and find its two turning points. Call the local maximum point (α, M) and the local minimum point (β, m). Here α and β are the x-values where f′(x) = 0, and M and m are the function values there.

Now picture the curve. It comes up from below, touches the top at height M, turns down to height m, then rises again forever. For the curve to cut the x-axis three times, the top must be above the axis and the bottom must be below it: M > 0 and m < 0.
Those two signs together mean just one thing: the product M·m must be negative. So the full condition for three real and distinct roots is M·m < 0, nothing more.
Notice what is being multiplied. Not α and β, not the constant term — the two values M and m. That is the whole trick, and the next part uses it to find the range of a parameter.

quickChecks.q: Does f(x) = x³ − 3x have three real and distinct roots?
steps: 2. Local maximum at x = −1: M = (−1)³ − 3(−1) = −1 + 3 = 2.
3. Local minimum at x = 1: m = 1³ − 3(1) = 1 − 3 = −2.
quickChecks.answer: Yes — three real and distinct roots.

quickChecks.q: Check f(x) = x³ − 3x + 2.
steps: 4. M·m = 4 × 0 = 0, which is not negative.
quickChecks.answer: No — the minimum sits on the x-axis, so one root is repeated (x = 1 twice). Not three distinct roots.

quickChecks.q: Check f(x) = x³ − 3x + 5.
quickChecks.answer: No — both turning points are above the x-axis, so the cubic has only one real root.

concepts.title: Using M·m < 0 to find the range of a parameter
concepts.oneLine: A cubic with a parameter has three distinct real roots exactly when the product of its local maximum value and local minimum value is negative — so differentiate, get the two critical points, plug them into f, and force M·m < 0.
notes: Look at the recipe first. Differentiate the cubic, set f′(x) = 0, and two critical points come out. One of them gives the local maximum value, call it M, the other gives the local minimum value, call it m. Two critical points, the function value at each, product negative — that is the whole question.

Why does that work? The shape of the graph does not change when the parameter changes — it is the same hump-and-valley cubic, only sliding up and down. All that moves is where the x-axis sits. If the axis passes between the hump and the valley, the curve cuts it three times. If it passes above the hump or below the valley, you get only one cut.
So M·m < 0 is just a short way of saying the x-axis sits in between: the local maximum is above it (positive) and the local minimum is below it (negative). Nothing more is hidden in it.

Here the two critical points come out as 3 and −3. So all you need is the value of the function at 3 and at −3, and then force their product to be less than 0. Notice how the cubic is written so that the parameter sits alone as the loose constant — then f(3) and f(−3) are that constant plus or minus a number, and there is no substituting twice. Take any other cubic with a parameter and the logic is letter for letter the same.

quickChecks.q: For what values of k does x³ − 12x + k = 0 have three distinct real roots?
steps: 1. f′(x) = 3x² − 12 = 0 gives x = 2 and x = −2.

quickChecks.q: For what values of c does x³ − 3x + c = 0 have three distinct real roots?
steps: 1. f′(x) = 3x² − 3 = 0 gives x = 1 and x = −1.
3. Product < 0: (c − 2)(c + 2) < 0, so c² < 4.

quickChecks.q: Does x³ − 27x + 54 = 0 have three distinct real roots?
steps: 1. Critical points are still x = 3 and x = −3.
3. Product = 0, not less than 0, so the condition fails — the valley is sitting on the x-axis.
4. Indeed x³ − 27x + 54 = (x − 3)²(x + 6).
quickChecks.answer: No — x = 3 is a repeated root, so there are only two distinct real roots (3 and −6)

concepts.title: Word problems: the one genuine critical point
concepts.oneLine: Eliminate one variable, differentiate, and trust the single genuine critical point — x + y = 60 with x·y³ maximum gives x = 15, y = 45.
notes: The question says x + y = 60, and x·y³ must be maximum. Call the thing you have to maximise P, so P = x·y³. Right now you cannot differentiate P, because two variables are sitting inside it.

So use the constraint to throw one of them out. From x + y = 60 we get y = 60 − x, and P becomes a pure function of x: P = x(60 − x)³. Now differentiate, set dP/dx = 0, and read off your critical points.

Here dP/dx = (60 − x)²(60 − 4x), so the critical points are x = 60 and x = 15. Put x = 60 and y becomes 0, so the product x·y³ becomes 0 — that is the smallest possible value, not the largest. In a maximisation word problem there is always exactly one genuine critical point; the others are fake, and they are fake because they make the quantity zero.
So the answer is x = 15, y = 45. Check it in your head: just left of 15 the derivative is positive, just right of 15 it is negative, so P is rising then falling — a maximum.

quickChecks.q: x + y = 12. Find x and y so that x·y² is maximum.
steps: 1. P = x·y² and y = 12 − x, so P = x(12 − x)².
3. Critical points: x = 12 and x = 4.
4. x = 12 gives y = 0 and P = 0, so it is the fake one.
5. x = 4 gives y = 8 and P = 4 × 64 = 256.

quickChecks.q: x + y = 40. Find x and y so that x³·y is maximum.
steps: 1. P = x³·y and y = 40 − x, so P = x³(40 − x) = 40x³ − x⁴.
3. Critical points: x = 0 and x = 30.
4. x = 0 gives P = 0, so it is the fake one.

quickChecks.q: x + y = 15. Find x and y so that x·y² is maximum.
steps: 3. Critical points: x = 15 (gives y = 0, P = 0 — fake) and x = 5.

concepts.title: Word-problem practice: largest rectangle, open box, cone of maximum volume
concepts.quote: Put the pen in your hand now. I am setting you three problems, and every one of them has exactly one genuine critical point waiting for you.
concepts.oneLine: Three fixed-constraint word problems to attempt yourself: the largest rectangle of given perimeter, the open box cut from a square sheet, and the cone of given slant height with maximum volume.
notes: The theory is done. Now to feel it, here are three questions — work them like a test before reading on.
First: of all the rectangles with a given perimeter, which one has the largest area? That is the short one. Do this first, no matter what — it is the one step never to skip.

Then two bonus ones, both of which have come in competitive exams and in the board paper too. One: from a square sheet of tin, cut equal squares from the four corners, fold up the flaps, and make an open box of the largest volume. Two: of all the cones with a given slant height, which one has the maximum volume?

Each one follows the same road. Write the quantity you want to maximise, use the given condition to throw out one variable, differentiate, and set it to zero. In a word problem the condition is not decoration — it is the thing that turns two variables into one.

quickChecks.q: A rectangle has perimeter 40 cm. Find the largest possible area.
steps: 1. Let the sides be x and y, so 2(x + y) = 40, giving y = 20 − x.
3. dA/dx = 20 − 2x = 0 gives x = 10.
4. d²A/dx² = −2 < 0, so this is a maximum. Then y = 10.
quickChecks.answer: The square of side 10 cm, with area 100 cm².

quickChecks.q: From a square sheet of tin of side 12 cm, equal squares of side x are cut from the four corners and the flaps are folded up to make an open box. Find x for the largest volume, and that volume.
steps: 1. Base is (12 − 2x) by (12 − 2x) and the height is x, so V = x(12 − 2x)², with 0 < x < 6.
3. Setting it to zero gives x = 6 or x = 2. Reject x = 6, as it is outside the domain.
quickChecks.answer: x = 2 cm, and the maximum volume is 128 cm³.

quickChecks.q: Show that the cone of given slant height l with maximum volume has height l/√3, and find that volume.
steps: 1. With radius r and height h, r² + h² = l², so r² = l² − h².
2. V = (1/3)πr²h = (1/3)π(l² − h²)h = (1/3)π(l²h − h³), with 0 < h < l.
3. dV/dh = (1/3)π(l² − 3h²) = 0 gives h = l/√3.
4. d²V/dh² = (1/3)π(−6h) < 0 there, so it is a maximum.

concepts.title: Largest rectangle with a given perimeter is a square
concepts.oneLine: With the perimeter fixed, write the area as x(c − x), set the derivative to zero, and you get x = y = c/2 — the biggest rectangle of a given perimeter is always a square.
notes: Take any rectangle. Call one side x and the next side y. The perimeter is fixed, so write it as 2c = 2(x + y), which means x + y = c.
Read that carefully. x and y are both free to change, but c is a constant. That is the whole structure of a maximisation word problem: one constraint, two variables.

Two variables cannot be differentiated, so use the constraint to kill one: y = c − x, and area A = xy becomes A = x(c − x) = cx − x². Now there is only x in the expression, so it can finally be differentiated.

dA/dx = c − 2x. Put it zero and x = c/2. That is the only critical point we get, so that is the answer. Put it back: y = c − c/2 = c/2. x = y, both sides equal — the rectangle of largest area is a square.

quickChecks.q: A rectangle has perimeter 36 cm. Find the sides giving the greatest area, and that area.
steps: 3. dA/dx = 18 − 2x = 0, so x = 9, and then y = 18 − 9 = 9.
quickChecks.answer: A 9 cm × 9 cm square, area 81 cm².

quickChecks.q: A wire 40 cm long is bent to form a rectangle. What is the largest area it can enclose?
steps: 1. The wire is the perimeter: 2(x + y) = 40, so x + y = 20.
3. dA/dx = 20 − 2x = 0, so x = 10 and y = 10.
quickChecks.answer: 100 cm², with the wire bent into a 10 cm × 10 cm square.

quickChecks.q: If the perimeter of a rectangle is P, show that its greatest area is P²/16.
steps: 3. dA/dx = P/2 − 2x = 0, so x = P/4, and y = P/2 − P/4 = P/4.
quickChecks.answer: Greatest area = P²/16, reached when both sides are P/4 (a square).

concepts.title: Open box from a square sheet: maximising the volume
concepts.oneLine: Cut x-by-x squares from the corners of a 6-unit square sheet and fold: V = (6 − 2x)²·x, dV/dx = 0 gives x = 1 or x = 3, and only x = 1 is genuine — so the largest volume is 16 cubic units.
notes: Take a square sheet of side 6. From each of the four corners cut out a small square of side x, then fold the four flaps up along the dotted lines. What stands up is an open box — open, because there is no lid.

Look at the base carefully. From each side of the sheet, x has been removed at one end and x at the other end, so the base is a square of side 6 − 2x. The flap folded up has height x. So the volume is V = (6 − 2x)²·x.

Now differentiate. Use the product rule and do not expand anything — keep (6 − 2x) as a block. dV/dx = (6 − 2x)² + x·2(6 − 2x)(−2), and taking (6 − 2x) common gives dV/dx = (6 − 2x)(6 − 6x). Setting this to zero gives x = 3 and x = 1, but x = 3 makes the base side 6 − 2(3) = 0 — there is no box at all.

So x must lie strictly between 0 and 3 for a box to exist, and the only critical point inside that range is x = 1. Put x = 1 back: V = (6 − 2)²·1 = 16. The genuine value is the one that still leaves you a real box.

quickChecks.q: A square sheet of side 12 cm has x-by-x squares cut from the corners and the flaps folded up. Find x for maximum volume and the maximum volume.
steps: 1. Base side = 12 − 2x, height = x, so V = (12 − 2x)²·x with 0 < x < 6.
3. Roots: x = 6 and x = 2. Reject x = 6 (base becomes 0).

quickChecks.q: Same construction on a square sheet of side 18 units. Find x for maximum volume and the maximum volume.
steps: 3. Roots: x = 9 and x = 3. Reject x = 9, it gives no box.
quickChecks.answer: x = 3 units, maximum volume = 432 cubic units.

quickChecks.q: In the 6-unit sheet problem, what is the volume at the rejected root x = 3, and why is that root useless?
steps: 1. Base side at x = 3 is 6 − 2(3) = 0.
3. dV/dx is indeed 0 there, but it is the smallest possible volume, not the largest, and the sheet has been cut away completely.
quickChecks.answer: V = 0; the whole base is cut away, so no box exists and the root is rejected.

concepts.title: Cone of given slant height with maximum volume
concepts.oneLine: For a cone of fixed slant height L, write r = L sinθ and h = L cosθ so V = (πL³/3)·sin²θ·cosθ, and dV/dθ = 0 gives tan²θ = 2, so the semi-vertical angle of maximum volume is tan⁻¹√2.
notes: Look at the cone. The slant height L is given, so L is a constant. The radius r and the height h both change, but they are not free — they are tied to the semi-vertical angle θ.

The axis, the radius and the slant side make a right triangle, with the right angle at the centre of the base. L is the hypotenuse, because it sits opposite the 90°. The side in front of θ is L sinθ, the side holding θ is L cosθ — so r = L sinθ and h = L cosθ.
Put that into V = ⅓πr²h. You get V = (πL³/3)·sin²θ·cosθ. Now there is only one variable left, θ, and everything in front of it is constant.

Differentiate with respect to θ and set it to zero. The sinθ factor comes out, and sinθ = 0 is nonsense here — a cone with zero angle has no volume. What is left is tan²θ = 2, so tanθ = √2 and θ = tan⁻¹√2.

quickChecks.q: For the cone of maximum volume with slant height L, find h and r.
steps: 1. At the maximum, tanθ = √2, so sinθ = √2/√3 and cosθ = 1/√3.
2. h = L cosθ = L/√3.

quickChecks.q: Using θ = tan⁻¹√2, show that the maximum volume is 2√3πL³/27.
steps: 1. V = (πL³/3)·sin²θ·cosθ with sin²θ = 2/3 and cosθ = 1/√3.
3. Rationalise: 2πL³/(9√3) = 2√3πL³/27.

quickChecks.q: A cone has slant height 3 cm. Find its maximum possible volume.
steps: 1. Maximum occurs at θ = tan⁻¹√2, where V = 2√3πL³/27.

flashcards.q: Rate measure adds almost no new formula to the chapter. What is the one idea it runs on, and what else do you need?
flashcards.a: $$\frac{dy}{dx}$$The derivative, read as the rate of change of y with respect to x. Beyond dy/dx you only need the mensuration formula of whatever shape the question describes — the area of a circle, the volume of a sphere, and so on.

flashcards.q: A balloon is blown up with the same amount of air every second. Why does it swell fast when it is small and barely grow when it is big?
flashcards.a: Equal increases in volume do not give equal increases in radius. The radius it already has decides how much a little extra volume can do, so the rate of change of the radius keeps dropping as the balloon gets bigger.

flashcards.q: A balloon is blown up so that air goes in at a constant rate. Write the two relations that connect the rates for a circle and for a sphere.
flashcards.a: $$V = \frac{4}{3}\pi r^3 \;\Rightarrow\; \frac{dV}{dt} = 4\pi r^2\,\frac{dr}{dt}$$Differentiate the area and the volume with respect to time. For a circle the rate of change of area is 2 pi r times the rate of change of radius; for a sphere the rate of change of volume is 4 pi r squared times the rate of change of radius. Put the instantaneous radius in only after differentiating.

flashcards.q: After you differentiate the area of a circle with respect to time, which value of the radius goes into the result?
flashcards.a: The instantaneous radius — its value at the exact moment the question asks about, never the starting one and never one you pick for convenience.

flashcards.q: The radius of a circle grows at 2 centimetres per second. How fast is the area growing at the instant the radius is 20 centimetres?
flashcards.a: $$\frac{dA}{dt} = 2\pi r \frac{dr}{dt}$$Differentiate the area while the radius is still a letter, then substitute: 2 pi times 20 times 2 gives 80 pi square centimetres per second. The unit is square centimetres per second, because area is measured in square centimetres.

flashcards.q: Why does substituting the radius into the area formula before differentiating give zero?
flashcards.a: Because it turns the area into a constant, and 400 pi has no derivative. Differentiate while the radius is still a variable and substitute the instant's values only at the final step.

flashcards.q: A question asks for the rate of decrease of the area and your working gives a rate of change of minus eighty pi. What do you write as the answer?
flashcards.a: $$\text{rate of decrease} = -\frac{dA}{dt}$$Eighty pi square centimetres per second, positive. The word decrease already carries the sign, so you report only the magnitude. You would write the minus sign only if the rate of change were asked.

flashcards.q: The question says the radius is decreasing. What do you write down before touching any formula?
flashcards.a: $$\frac{dr}{dt} < 0$$Translate the word into a sign first: decreasing means the rate of change of the radius is negative. Write that minus sign in at the start and let the formula carry it through.

flashcards.q: A working for a shrinking circle comes out as minus 80 pi. When do you keep the minus sign and when do you drop it?
flashcards.a: Rate of change keeps the sign exactly as the derivative came out. Rate of decrease already carries the direction in the question, so you report only the positive magnitude.

flashcards.q: How do you find the rate of change of one area with respect to another?
flashcards.a: $$\frac{dA_2}{dA_1}=\frac{dA_2/dx}{dA_1/dx}$$Push both areas down to one common variable x, differentiate each with respect to x, then divide. Whatever follows the words with respect to goes in the denominator. You never need a direct relation between the two areas.

flashcards.q: Two squares have sides x and y. Why is the ratio of their areas not the rate of change of one with respect to the other?
flashcards.a: A ratio of areas is not a rate. Differentiate each area with respect to the common variable first, and only then divide the two derivatives.

flashcards.q: Find the points on the curve 6y = x cubed + 2 at which the y-coordinate changes eight times as fast as the x-coordinate.
flashcards.a: $$\frac{dy}{dt} = 8\,\frac{dx}{dt} \;\Longrightarrow\; \frac{dy}{dx} = 8$$The condition is just a slope condition, dy/dx = 8. Differentiating the curve gives 6 dy/dx = 3x squared, so x squared = 16 and x is 4 or minus 4. The points are (4, 11) and (minus 4, minus 31/3).

flashcards.q: Before you put the slope value in, what do you do to the given curve 6y = x cubed + 2?
flashcards.a: $$6y = x^3 + 2 \;\Longrightarrow\; 6\,\frac{dy}{dx} = 3x^2$$Differentiate both sides with respect to x. That gives the slope as an expression in x, and only then do you set it equal to the value the question forces.

flashcards.q: What does the sentence y changes 8 times as fast as x actually say?
flashcards.a: It is about rates, not coordinates, so it is not y = 8x. The rate for y is 8 times the rate for x, the dt cancels, and it becomes the slope condition dy/dx = 8.

flashcards.q: A conical funnel has vertical angle 120 degrees. Which angle belongs inside the right triangle?
flashcards.a: $$\text{semi-vertical angle} = \frac{120^\circ}{2} = 60^\circ$$Half of it. Write 60 degrees on the figure the moment you read 120 degrees — every right triangle inside the cone uses the semi-vertical angle, never the full one.

flashcards.q: Water leaks out of a cone at a steady rate. Does the level fall at a steady rate?
flashcards.a: No. A steady rate for the volume does not give a steady rate for the level: full cone, slow drop; nearly empty, fast drop. That is why the question has to hand you one particular instant.

flashcards.q: Water drips from a conical funnel of vertical angle 120 degrees at 4 cubic centimetres per second. Find the rate of decrease of the slant height of the water when it is 3 centimetres.
flashcards.a: $$V = \frac{\pi}{8} L^3$$Halve the angle to 60 degrees, so the radius is L times root three over two and the depth is L over two. The volume becomes pi L cubed over 8, and differentiating gives three pi L squared over 8 times the rate for L equal to minus 4. At L = 3 the slant height is falling at 32 over 27 pi centimetres per second.

flashcards.q: The volume of the water cone has been written in slant height alone. What does one differentiation give, and when do you substitute?
flashcards.a: $$\frac{dV}{dt} = \frac{3\pi}{8} L^2 \frac{dL}{dt}$$Differentiate with respect to time, and put the instantaneous value of the slant height in afterwards. Substituting the number first is useless, because a number has no derivative.

flashcards.q: The data in a cone question is the slant height. Which variable should the volume be written in?
flashcards.a: The slant height alone. Force the whole formula into the single variable the data is about before differentiating — leaving both the radius and the depth alive makes you hunt for an extra relation later.

flashcards.q: The depth of the water is half its slant height. How do the two rates compare?
flashcards.a: $$\frac{dh}{dt} = \frac{1}{2}\,\frac{dL}{dt}$$The rates carry the identical constant — the one half simply rides along. No chain rule drama and no volume formula: multiply the rate for the slant height by one half.

flashcards.q: The rate for the slant height is already known and now the rate for the radius is asked. What is the shortest route?
flashcards.a: Differentiate the relation between the two lengths, not the volume all over again. When one variable is a fixed multiple of another, the rates carry that same multiple — one line, not one page.

flashcards.q: Which surfaces make up the total surface area of the water sitting in a cone?
flashcards.a: $$TSA = \pi r^2 + \pi r L$$The curved side plus the free water surface on top, a circle of radius r. The cone's own base circle never comes in, because the water tapers to a tip at the bottom.

flashcards.q: The constant in front of the surface area is an ugly surd. What do you do with it in the exam?
flashcards.a: Leave it ugly. Call it a single constant, write the area as that constant times the square of the slant height, differentiate, and substitute at the very end — the marks are in the derivative, not in the arithmetic.

flashcards.q: A cone question gives the height and the radius but never names an angle. Where is the semi-vertical angle hiding?
flashcards.a: $$\tan\theta = \frac{r}{h}$$In the ratio. The radius over the height is the tangent of the angle, and the sine and cosine then come straight off the little right triangle you draw.

flashcards.q: Why is it wrong to read the radius over the height as the sine of the semi-vertical angle?
flashcards.a: The radius is opposite the angle and the height is adjacent, so that ratio is the tangent. Sine needs the slant height — it is the radius over the slant height.

flashcards.q: A man walks away from a lamppost. How do you get a single relation between his distance from the pole and the length of his shadow?
flashcards.a: $$\tan\theta = \frac{5}{x+y} = \frac{2}{y}$$The grazing ray makes the same angle in both right triangles, so write the tangent once from the big triangle and once from the small one and put the two equal. One line gives the relation.

flashcards.q: In the lamppost picture, what is the base of the big right triangle?
flashcards.a: The man's distance from the pole plus the length of his shadow. His distance only reaches his feet, while the ray lands at the tip of the shadow, which is a further shadow-length on.

flashcards.q: The plane's speed is per hour and the question is set in minutes. What comes first?
flashcards.a: $$15\ \frac{\text{km}}{\text{hr}} = \frac{15}{60}\ \frac{\text{km}}{\text{min}}$$The conversion. Write the speed as a fraction carrying its units and multiply by the time in minutes, so the minutes cancel and only kilometres survive. If anything else survives, the conversion was wrong.

flashcards.q: An aeroplane flies horizontally. Which length in the picture is a constant, and which two change?
flashcards.a: The height is constant — flying horizontally makes it one fixed side of the triangle at every instant. The horizontal distance and the slant distance are the two that change, and they change at different rates.

flashcards.q: An aeroplane flies horizontally at a fixed height. How fast is it receding from a point on the ground directly below its earlier position?
flashcards.a: $$\frac{dz}{dt} = \frac{x}{z}\cdot\frac{dx}{dt}$$Differentiate the Pythagoras relation with the height held constant. The rate of receding is the plane's own speed multiplied by the horizontal distance over the slant distance, so it starts near zero and climbs towards the full speed.

flashcards.q: Why is the rate at which the plane recedes always less than its own speed?
flashcards.a: Because that rate is the speed multiplied by the horizontal distance over the slant distance, and the horizontal distance is always the smaller of the two. It is a free sanity check on the answer.

flashcards.q: A ladder has its foot on the x-axis and its top on the y-axis. Write the distance of its midpoint from the corner.
flashcards.a: $$4s^2 = x^2 + y^2,\quad s = OP$$The midpoint sits at half of each coordinate, so four times the square of that distance equals the square of the foot's distance plus the square of the top's height. Drop the four and every number after it is wrong.

flashcards.q: What do you learn by comparing the midpoint relation with the ladder's fixed-length relation?
flashcards.a: That the midpoint stays half a ladder away from the corner, a constant. Its rate is zero and it rides a circle about the corner — a check that kills a good many wrong answers.

flashcards.q: A ladder of fixed length leans on a wall and its foot slides away at a constant rate b. How fast is the midpoint of the ladder moving when the ladder makes 60 degrees with the floor?
flashcards.a: $$\frac{dy}{dt} = -\frac{x}{y}\cdot\frac{dx}{dt}$$The fixed length gives the rate for y as minus x over y times the rate for x, and the midpoint has half of each rate. Putting the 60 degree values in, the speed of the midpoint is b over root three, and it does not depend on the length of the ladder.

flashcards.q: Both coordinate rates for a sliding ladder are known. How do you get the speed of its midpoint?
flashcards.a: $$v_{\text{mid}} = \frac{1}{2}\sqrt{\left(\frac{dx}{dt}\right)^2 + \left(\frac{dy}{dt}\right)^2}$$Halve each rate, because the midpoint carries half of each, and then take the resultant — the square root of the sum of the squares of those halves. Forgetting the one half doubles the answer.

flashcards.q: Why does differentiating the ladder's length relation leave a zero on the right-hand side?
flashcards.a: Because the length of the ladder is fixed forever, so it has no rate of its own. That zero is exactly what forces the vertical rate to be minus the ratio of the two sides times the horizontal rate.

flashcards.q: State the approximation formula and say where it comes from.
flashcards.a: $$f(a+h) \approx f(a) + h\,f'(a)$$For a small h, the value at a plus h is the value at a plus h times the derivative at a. It is the first-principle definition of the derivative with the limit dropped and the h cross-multiplied.

flashcards.q: Why must the approximation formula be written with an approximately-equal sign and not an equals sign?
flashcards.a: Because the limit was dropped the moment the step stopped being zero. What is left is an approximation, and it stays close only while the step is very small.

flashcards.q: To approximate the cube root of 217, which function do you set up and what is its derivative?
flashcards.a: $$f(x) = x^{1/3} \;\Rightarrow\; f'(x) = \frac{1}{3}x^{-2/3}$$Take the cube root as the function; its derivative is one third of x to the power minus two thirds. Then split 217 as 216 plus 1, because 216 is the nearest perfect cube and the leftover is the small step.

flashcards.q: The approximate cube root of 217 does not agree with a calculator. What went wrong?
flashcards.a: Nothing. The formula assumes a very small step and here the step is 1, which is not small, so a visible gap is expected — that is why the question only asks for an approximation.

flashcards.q: Approximate tan 46 degrees, and say where the error comes from.
flashcards.a: $$\tan 46^{\circ} \approx 1 + \frac{\pi}{90}$$Take a as a quarter of pi and h as one degree, which is pi over 180 radians. The derivative of tan is the square of sec, which is 2 at a quarter of pi, so the answer is one plus pi over 90, about 1.035. The error exists because the formula wants h to be very small; one degree is small enough to agree to about two decimal places.

flashcards.q: The extra bit of angle in an approximation is 1 degree. What has to happen before it goes into the formula?
flashcards.a: $$1^{\circ} = \frac{\pi}{180}\ \text{radian}$$It has to become radian, because calculus derivatives assume radian. One degree is pi over 180, so the correction is pi over 180 times the derivative, not 1 times the derivative.

flashcards.q: In approximating the tangent of 46 degrees, why are the value and the derivative at the known angle two different numbers?
flashcards.a: The tangent of the known angle is 1, while the derivative there is the square of the secant, which is 2. Treating one as the other wrecks the correction term.

flashcards.q: What are the three fundamentals you need for every tangent and normal question?
flashcards.a: $$m_{\text{tangent}} \cdot m_{\text{normal}} = -1$$The point-slope form of a straight line; the derivative at the point is the slope of the tangent there; and the slope of the tangent times the slope of the normal is minus one.

flashcards.q: You have the slope of the tangent. How do you get the slope of the normal?
flashcards.a: $$m_{\text{tangent}} \cdot m_{\text{normal}} = -1$$Turn it upside down and then attach a minus sign, because the product of the two slopes is minus one. It is not simply the negative of the tangent slope.

flashcards.q: You differentiate an implicit curve that contains a y squared term. What is the part students drop?
flashcards.a: $$\frac{d}{dx}\left(y^{2}\right) = 2y\,\frac{dy}{dx}$$The dy/dx. Here y is a function of x, so every y term you differentiate must carry that factor along with it.

flashcards.q: The curve is a hyperbola and you cannot recall a standard tangent formula for it. What do you do?
