ladder.q: A right circular cone of semi-vertical angle 30 degrees is held with its vertex downwards and water is poured in at a uniform rate of 9 cm^3/s. Find the rate at which the curved surface area of the water cone is increasing at the instant when the depth of the water is 3 cm.
steps: 1. Put everything in terms of the depth h. With semi-vertical angle 30 degrees, r = h tan 30 = h/sqrt 3 and the slant height is l = h/cos 30 = 2h/sqrt 3.
3. Differentiate: dV/dt = (pi h^2/3)(dh/dt) = 9, so dh/dt = 27/(pi h^2). At h = 3 this gives dh/dt = 27/(9 pi) = 3/pi.
4. Curved surface: S = pi r l = pi (h/sqrt 3)(2h/sqrt 3) = 2 pi h^2/3.
5. Differentiate: dS/dt = (4 pi h/3)(dh/dt). At h = 3 that is (4 pi)(3/pi) = 12.
6. The pi cancels, which is why the answer comes out as a whole number.

ladder.tier: L5 Advanced hardest — the toughest this chapter justifies
ladder.q: Let f(x) = x^2 ln x for x > 0. Show that f has exactly one critical point in (0, infinity), classify it, find the least value of f, and show that f has exactly one point of inflection.
steps: 1. f'(x) = 2x ln x + x^2 (1/x) = 2x ln x + x = x(2 ln x + 1).
2. On (0, infinity) the factor x is never zero, so f'(x) = 0 forces 2 ln x + 1 = 0, that is ln x = -1/2 and x = e^(-1/2). That is the only critical point.
3. f''(x) = 2 ln x + 2 + 1 = 2 ln x + 3. At x = e^(-1/2) this is 2(-1/2) + 3 = 2 > 0, so the critical point is a local minimum.
4. It is in fact the global minimum: f' = x(2 ln x + 1) is negative for x < e^(-1/2) and positive for x > e^(-1/2), so f decreases then increases on the whole of (0, infinity).

6. For inflection, f''(x) = 2 ln x + 3 = 0 gives x = e^(-3/2), and f'' changes sign from negative to positive there, so that single point is a genuine point of inflection. Its height is f(e^(-3/2)) = e^(-3)(-3/2) = -3/(2e^3).
7. There is no local maximum: f(x) tends to 0 from below as x tends to 0 from the right, and to infinity as x tends to infinity.
ladder.answer: The only critical point is x = e^(-1/2); it is a local and global minimum with least value -1/(2e), approximately -0.184. There is no local maximum. The only point of inflection is x = e^(-3/2), where f = -3/(2 e^3)

ladder.tier: L5 Advanced hardest — the toughest this chapter justifies
ladder.q: Let f(x) = integral from 0 to x of (t - 1)(t - 2)^2 (t - 3)^3 dt, for x in R. Find all points of local maximum and all points of local minimum of f, and state how many there are of each.
steps: 1. By the fundamental theorem of calculus f'(x) = (x - 1)(x - 2)^2 (x - 3)^3, so the critical points are x = 1, 2, 3.
2. A zero of f' gives an extremum only if f' actually changes sign there, and that depends on whether the exponent is odd or even.
3. The factor (x - 2)^2 has an even exponent, so it is non-negative everywhere and never changes the sign of the product. The factors (x - 1) and (x - 3)^3 have odd exponents and do change sign.
4. So the sign of f' is the sign of (x - 1)(x - 3). For x < 1 that is positive; for 1 < x < 3 it is negative; for x > 3 it is positive.
5. At x = 1 the sign goes from + to -, a local maximum. At x = 3 it goes from - to +, a local minimum.
6. At x = 2 we have f'(2) = 0 but no sign change, so x = 2 is neither a maximum nor a minimum - the graph flattens and carries on downwards.
ladder.answer: One point of local maximum, at x = 1, and one point of local minimum, at x = 3. The critical point x = 2 is neither

testBank.q: The radius of a circle is decreasing at a uniform rate of 2 cm/s. Find the rate of decrease of its area at the instant when the radius is 20 cm.
steps: 1. A = pi r^2, so dA/dt = 2 pi r dr/dt.
2. Decreasing radius means dr/dt = -2 cm/s, and the instantaneous radius is r = 20.
4. The question asks for the rate of DECREASE, which is the magnitude. The minus sign has already been used up by the word 'decrease', so the answer is +80 pi cm^2/s.
5. Had the question said 'rate of change of area', the correct reply would have been -80 pi cm^2/s.

testBank.q: Water drips out of a conical funnel of vertical angle 120 degrees at a uniform rate of 4 cm^3/s through a tiny hole at the vertex. When the slant height of the water is 3 cm, the rate of decrease of the slant height is
steps: 1. The data is about the slant height, so write the volume of the water cone in terms of L alone.
2. The semi-vertical angle is 60 degrees, so r = L sin 60 = L root3/2 and h = L cos 60 = L/2.
4. Differentiate: dV/dt = (3 pi/8) L^2 dL/dt. Here dV/dt = -4 and L = 3.
6. The rate of decrease is the magnitude, 32/(27 pi) cm/s.

testBank.q: Using the approximation f(a + h) = f(a) + h f'(a), the value of tan 46 degrees is approximately
steps: 1. Take f(x) = tan x, a = pi/4 (where you know both the value and the derivative) and h = 1 degree.
2. Convert the increment to radians: h = pi/180. A calculus derivative is only valid for radian measure.
3. f(pi/4) = tan(pi/4) = 1 and f'(x) = sec^2 x, so f'(pi/4) = (root2)^2 = 2.
4. tan 46 degrees = 1 + (pi/180)(2) = 1 + pi/90, which is about 1.0349.
5. The true value is 1.03553, so the approximation is good to two decimal places - the small discrepancy is exactly the error caused by h not being infinitesimal.

testBank.q: The equation of the normal to the curve 2x^2 - 3y^2 = -10 at the point (1, 2) is
steps: 1. Check the point: 2(1) - 3(4) = -10, so (1, 2) lies on the curve.
2. Differentiate: 4x - 6y dy/dx = 0, so dy/dx = 2x/(3y).
3. At (1, 2): dy/dx = 2/6 = 1/3, which is the slope of the tangent.
4. Slope of the normal = -1/(1/3) = -3.
5. Normal through (1, 2): y - 2 = -3(x - 1), i.e. 3x + y - 5 = 0.
6. (The tangent there is x - 3y + 5 = 0, which is the distractor.)

testBank.q: The equation of the tangent to the curve y = x^2 - |x| at x = -2 is
steps: 1. A tangent only cares about the vicinity of the point, so open the modulus near x = -2 and ignore everything else.
2. All numbers near -2 are negative, so there |x| = -x and the curve is y = x^2 + x.
3. y(-2) = 4 - 2 = 2, so the point of contact is (-2, 2).
4. dy/dx = 2x + 1, which at x = -2 is -3.
6. You never needed to discuss the branch x > 0 at all.

testBank.q: The point on the parabola y = x^2 + 4 that is closest to the line y = 4x - 1, and that shortest distance, are
steps: 1. Between two curves the shortest (and the longest) distance lies along their common normal.
2. So at the required point the normal to the parabola is perpendicular to the line, which means the tangent to the parabola is PARALLEL to the line.
3. The line y = 4x - 1 has slope 4, so set dy/dx = 2x = 4, giving x = 2 and y = 4 + 4 = 8.
4. The point is (2, 8). Writing the line as 4x - y - 1 = 0, the distance is |4(2) - 8 - 1|/root(16 + 1) = 1/root17.
5. The whole question has collapsed into 'find the point where the tangent has slope 4', which is the standard slope-given variety.

testBank.q: The angle of intersection of the curves y^2 = 4x and x^2 + y^2 = 5 is
steps: 1. Find the common point: substitute y^2 = 4x into x^2 + y^2 = 5 to get x^2 + 4x - 5 = 0, i.e. (x + 5)(x - 1) = 0.
2. x = -5 is rejected because y^2 = 4x needs x >= 0, so x = 1 and y = +2 or -2. Take (1, 2).
3. Parabola: 2y dy/dx = 4, so m1 = 2/y = 1.
4. Circle: 2x + 2y dy/dx = 0, so m2 = -x/y = -1/2.
6. So theta = tan inverse 3. By symmetry the angle at (1, -2) is the same, and since m1 m2 = -1/2 the curves are not orthogonal.

testBank.q: For the parabola y^2 = 4ax, the length of the subnormal at a point on the curve is
opts: proportional to the ordinate of the point
proportional to the abscissa of the point
steps: 1. Subnormal = |y1 m|, where m = dy/dx at the point (x1, y1).
2. Differentiate y^2 = 4ax: 2y dy/dx = 4a, so m = 2a/y1.
3. Subnormal = |y1 (2a/y1)| = 2a.
4. The y1 cancels, so the subnormal is the constant 2a everywhere on the parabola.
5. (For comparison, the subtangent |y1/m| = y1^2/(2a) = 2x1 does depend on the point.)

testBank.q: If Rolle's theorem holds for f(x) = x^3 + b x^2 + a x on the interval [1, 2] with f'(4/3) = 0, then the ordered pair (a, b) is
steps: 1. A cubic is continuous and differentiable everywhere, so the first two conditions of Rolle's theorem are automatic.
2. The third condition is f(1) = f(2): 1 + b + a = 8 + 4b + 2a, which gives a + 3b = -7.
3. The conclusion of the theorem is used as data: f'(x) = 3x^2 + 2bx + a and f'(4/3) = 0.

testBank.q: The greatest value of k for which f(x) = k x + 4 sin x + 3 cos x is strictly decreasing for all real x is
steps: 1. f'(x) = k + 4 cos x - 3 sin x.
2. The expression a sin x + b cos x has range [-root(a^2 + b^2), root(a^2 + b^2)], and here root(16 + 9) = 5.
3. So f'(x) ranges over [k - 5, k + 5] as x varies.
4. Strictly decreasing everywhere needs f'(x) <= 0 for all x. Kill the largest value and the rest dies with it: k + 5 <= 0.
5. Hence k <= -5, and the greatest such k is -5.
6. (Sanity check: if k + 5 is negative then k - 5, which is 10 less, is more negative still.)

testBank.q: If x = 1 is a critical point of f(x) = (3x^2 + a x - 2 - a) e^x, then
opts: a = -7 and f has a local maximum at x = 1
a = 7 and f has a local minimum at x = 1
a = -7 and x = 1 is a point of inflection of f
a = -7 and f has a local minimum at x = 1
steps: 2. x = 1 is a critical point and e^x is never zero, so 3 + (a + 6) - 2 = 0, giving a + 7 = 0 and a = -7.
4. Critical points are x = -2/3 and x = 1; the sign scheme of (3x + 2)(x - 1) is + - +.
5. At x = -2/3 the derivative goes positive to negative: local maximum. At x = 1 it goes negative to positive: local minimum.
6. So the correct option is a = -7 with a local minimum at x = 1.
testBank.answer: a = -7 and f has a local minimum at x = 1

testBank.q: The number of real solutions of 3x^2 - 2x^3 = log base 2 of (x + 1/x) is
steps: 1. The right side needs x > 0, so work on (0, infinity). Neither side can be solved algebraically, so compare their graphs.
2. Left side f(x) = 3x^2 - 2x^3 has f'(x) = 6x - 6x^2 = 6x(1 - x), positive on (0, 1) and negative on (1, infinity).
3. So f increases to a maximum at x = 1 and f(1) = 3 - 2 = 1. Hence f(x) <= 1 on (0, infinity), with equality only at x = 1.
4. Right side: x + 1/x >= 2 for x > 0 (AM-GM), with equality only at x = 1, so g(x) = log base 2 of (x + 1/x) >= log base 2 of 2 = 1, with equality only at x = 1.
5. Therefore f(x) <= 1 <= g(x) throughout, and the two can be equal only where both equal 1, i.e. at x = 1.
6. Exactly one real solution.

testBank.q: For the curve y = x^3 - 3x, consider the points at which the tangent has slope 9. Which of the following is (are) TRUE?
opts: There are exactly two such points
The tangent at (2, 2) passes through the origin
steps: 1. dy/dx = 3x^2 - 3. Setting it equal to 9 gives 3x^2 = 12, so x = 2 or x = -2 - exactly two points, so (A) is true.
2. y(2) = 8 - 6 = 2 and y(-2) = -8 + 6 = -2, so the points are (2, 2) and (-2, -2). (B) is true.
3. At (-2, -2) the tangent slope is 9, so the normal slope is -1/9: y + 2 = -(1/9)(x + 2), i.e. 9y + 18 = -x - 2, i.e. x + 9y + 20 = 0. (C) is true.
4. Tangent at (2, 2): y - 2 = 9(x - 2), i.e. y = 9x - 16. At x = 0 this gives y = -16, not 0, so (D) is false.
5. Answer: A, B, C.
testBank.answer: There are exactly two such points; (2, 2) is one of them; The normal at (-2, -2) is x + 9y + 20 = 0

testBank.q: Tangents are drawn from the point (1, 1) to the curve y = x^2 - 5x + 6. Which of the following is (are) TRUE?
opts: The points of contact are (0, 6) and (2, 0)
One of the tangents has slope -5
The angle between the two tangents is tan inverse (2/3)
steps: 1. Let the point of contact be (p, q). First relation: it lies on the curve, so q = p^2 - 5p + 6.
2. Second relation: the chord from (1, 1) to (p, q) IS the tangent, so (q - 1)/(p - 1) = dy/dx at p = 2p - 5.
3. Substituting q: p^2 - 5p + 5 = (2p - 5)(p - 1) = 2p^2 - 7p + 5, so p^2 - 2p = 0 and p = 0 or p = 2.
4. p = 0 gives q = 6; p = 2 gives q = 4 - 10 + 6 = 0. The contacts are (0, 6) and (2, 0), so (A) is true.
5. Slopes 2p - 5: at p = 0 it is -5, at p = 2 it is -1. So (B) is true.
6. Product of slopes = 5, not -1, so (C) is false. tan theta = |(-5 + 1)/(1 + 5)| = 4/6 = 2/3, so (D) is true.
7. Answer: A, B, D.
testBank.answer: The points of contact are (0, 6) and (2, 0); One of the tangents has slope -5; The angle between the two tangents is tan inverse (2/3)

testBank.q: On the interval (0, 1), which of the following is (are) TRUE?
opts: sin x / x is strictly decreasing
x / tan x is strictly decreasing
x / sin x is strictly increasing
tan x / x is strictly decreasing
steps: 1. For sin x / x the derivative is (x cos x - sin x)/x^2, so the sign hangs on the numerator.
2. Put h(x) = sin x - x cos x. Then h'(x) = cos x - cos x + x sin x = x sin x > 0 on (0, 1), and h(0) = 0, so h > 0 there.
3. Hence x cos x - sin x < 0 and sin x / x is strictly decreasing: (A) is true. Its reciprocal x / sin x is a positive decreasing function inverted, so it is strictly increasing: (C) is true.
4. For x / tan x = x cot x the derivative is (sin x cos x - x)/sin^2 x. Put k(x) = sin x cos x - x; then k'(x) = cos 2x - 1 <= 0 and k(0) = 0, so k < 0 on (0, 1).
5. Hence x / tan x is strictly decreasing: (B) is true. Its reciprocal tan x / x is therefore strictly INCREASING, so (D) is false.
6. Answer: A, B, C.
testBank.answer: sin x / x is strictly decreasing; x / tan x is strictly decreasing; x / sin x is strictly increasing

testBank.q: Let f be twice differentiable with f''(x) < 0 for all x in (0, 6), and let psi(x) = f(x) + f(6 - x) on (0, 6). Which of the following are true?
steps: 1. f''(x) < 0 means f' is strictly decreasing on (0, 6).
3. For x < 3 we have 6 - x > x, so f'(6 - x) < f'(x) and psi'(x) > 0: psi increases on (0, 3).
4. For x > 3 the inequality reverses, so psi'(x) < 0: psi decreases on (3, 6).
5. At x = 3 the two arguments coincide, so psi'(3) = 0.
6. Answer: B, C, D.
testBank.answer: psi is increasing on (0, 3); psi'(3) = 0; psi is decreasing on (3, 6)

testBank.q: Let f(x) = 2x^3 - 9x^2 + 12x + 6. Which of the following is (are) TRUE?
opts: f has a local maximum value of 11 at x = 1
The range of f on [0, 2] is [6, 11]
The range of f on [0, 3] is [6, 15]
f(x) = 0 has three distinct real roots
steps: 1. f'(x) = 6x^2 - 18x + 12 = 6(x - 1)(x - 2), with sign scheme + - + across x = 1 and x = 2.
2. So x = 1 is a local maximum and x = 2 a local minimum. f(1) = 2 - 9 + 12 + 6 = 11, so (A) is true.
4. On [0, 2] compare the critical point and both end points: 6, 11, 10. Smallest 6, largest 11, and f is continuous, so the range is [6, 11]. (B) is true.
5. On [0, 3] compare 6, 11, 10, 15. Smallest 6, largest 15, so the range is [6, 15] - here both extremes sit at end points and the local extrema do no work at all. (C) is true.
6. Local maximum 11 and local minimum 10 are both positive, so the graph crosses the x-axis once only: just one real root. (D) is false.
7. Answer: A, B, C.
testBank.answer: f has a local maximum value of 11 at x = 1; The range of f on [0, 2] is [6, 11]; The range of f on [0, 3] is [6, 15]

testBank.q: Consider f(x) = x^(1/x) on (0, infinity). Which of the following is (are) TRUE?
opts: f attains its greatest value at x = e
steps: 1. Take logarithms: ln f(x) = (ln x)/x. Differentiating, f'(x)/f(x) = (1 - ln x)/x^2, so f'(x) = x^(1/x)(1 - ln x)/x^2.
2. x^(1/x) > 0 and x^2 > 0 on the domain, so the sign of f' is the sign of 1 - ln x: positive for x < e, negative for x > e.
3. So f increases on (0, e) and decreases on (e, infinity), with its greatest value at x = e. (C) is true, and (D) is false since (ln x)/x has the same sign scheme and so decreases on (e, infinity).
4. Now locate e and pi: e is about 2.72 and pi about 3.14, so both lie in the decreasing part from x = e onwards, with e the turning point. Hence f(e) > f(pi), i.e. e^(1/e) > pi^(1/pi). (A) is true.
5. Raise both sides to the positive power e pi (which preserves the inequality): (e^(1/e))^(e pi) = e^pi and (pi^(1/pi))^(e pi) = pi^e.
6. Hence e^pi > pi^e, so (B) is true. Answer: A, B, C.
testBank.answer: e^(1/e) > pi^(1/pi); e^pi > pi^e; f attains its greatest value at x = e

testBank.q: A bird flies horizontally at a constant height of 2/3 km with a constant speed of 15 km/h. Find the rate, in km/h, at which it is receding from a fixed point on the ground over which it passed 2 minutes earlier.
steps: 1. Let y be the horizontal distance travelled since it passed over the point and z the straight-line distance from that point. The height 2/3 km is constant.
2. Pythagoras: z^2 = y^2 + (2/3)^2, valid at every instant.
3. Differentiate with respect to t: 2z dz/dt = 2y dy/dt, so dz/dt = (y/z)(dy/dt), with dy/dt = 15 always.
4. Now feed in the instant t = 2 minutes. Speed in km per minute is 15/60, so y = (15/60)(2) = 1/2 km.

testBank.q: A man 2 m tall walks away from the foot of a lamp post 5 m high at 6 m/min. Find the rate, in m/min, at which the length of his shadow is increasing.
steps: 1. Let x be the man's distance from the foot of the post and y the length of his shadow, so dx/dt = 6.
2. The ray through the top of the man's head makes one angle theta with the ground, giving two right triangles.
3. Big triangle (post): tan theta = 5/(x + y). Small triangle (man): tan theta = 2/y.
4. Equate: 5y = 2(x + y), so 3y = 2x.
5. Differentiate: 3 dy/dt = 2 dx/dt, so dy/dt = (2/3)(6) = 4 m/min.
6. Note the answer does not depend on where the man currently is.

testBank.q: Let f(x) = root x on [4, 9] and let c be the number given by Lagrange's mean value theorem on this interval. Find the value of 4c.
steps: 1. f is continuous on [4, 9] and differentiable on (4, 9), so LMVT applies.
3. f'(x) = 1/(2 root x), so 1/(2 root c) = 1/5, giving root c = 5/2.
4. c = 25/4, which indeed lies in (4, 9).
5. Hence 4c = 25.

testBank.q: A function f is differentiable on R with f(1) = 3 and 1 <= f'(x) <= 2 for all x. Find the greatest possible value of f(5).
steps: 1. Apply LMVT on [1, 5]: (f(5) - f(1))/(5 - 1) = f'(c) for some c in (1, 5).
3. f(5) is largest when f'(c) is largest, i.e. f'(c) = 2.
4. Maximum f(5) = 3 + 8 = 11. (The minimum, with f'(c) = 1, would be 7.)
5. So f(5) lies in [7, 11] and the greatest possible value is 11.

testBank.q: Let f(x) = a x^4 + b x^3 + c x^2 + d x + e be a polynomial of degree 4 with extreme values at x = 1 and x = 2, and suppose lim x -> 0 of (1 + f(x)/x^2) = 3. Find f(2).
steps: 1. The limit condition says lim x -> 0 of f(x)/x^2 = 2.
2. f(x)/x^2 = a x^2 + b x + c + d/x + e/x^2. As x -> 0 the last two terms blow up unless they vanish identically, so d = 0 and e = 0, and then the limit is c.
3. Hence c = 2, so f(x) = a x^4 + b x^3 + 2x^2 and f'(x) = 4a x^3 + 3b x^2 + 4x.
4. Extreme values at x = 1 and x = 2 give f'(1) = 0 and f'(2) = 0: 4a + 3b + 4 = 0 and 32a + 12b + 8 = 0, i.e. 8a + 3b + 2 = 0.
5. Subtracting, 4a - 2 = 0, so a = 1/2, and then 3b = -4(1/2) - 4 = -6, so b = -2.

testBank.q: Let S be the set of real x with x^2 - 11x + 30 <= 0, and let f(x) = 3x^3 - 18x^2 + 27x - 40. Find the maximum value of f on S.
steps: 1. Solve the inequality first: x^2 - 11x + 30 = (x - 5)(x - 6) <= 0 gives S = [5, 6].
3. The critical points are x = 1 and x = 3, and NEITHER lies in [5, 6], so they are irrelevant to this question.
4. With no critical point inside, only the end points compete: f(5) = 375 - 450 + 135 - 40 = 20 and f(6) = 648 - 648 + 162 - 40 = 122.
5. f' > 0 on [5, 6] (both factors positive), so f increases there and the maximum is at x = 6.
6. Maximum value = 122.

testBank.q: Two positive numbers x and y satisfy x + y = 60, and x y^3 is as large as possible. Find x.
steps: 1. Write the quantity in one variable: P = x y^3 = x(60 - x)^3.
3. Setting dP/dx = 0 gives x = 60 or x = 15.
4. x = 60 is the fake critical point: it makes y = 0 and P = 0, which is the minimum, not the maximum. Reject it on sight.
5. The genuine critical point is x = 15, giving y = 45. (dP/dx > 0 for x < 15 and < 0 for 15 < x < 60, confirming a maximum.)

testBank.q: Equal squares are cut from the four corners of a square sheet of side 6 cm and the flaps are folded up to make an open box. Find the greatest possible volume of the box, in cm^3.
steps: 1. If the corner square has side x, the base of the box is a square of side 6 - 2x and the height is x.
4. Setting dV/dx = 0 gives x = 3 or x = 1. x = 3 leaves no base at all, so it is the fake root.
5. x = 1 is the genuine critical point, and dV/dx > 0 before it and < 0 after it, so it gives the maximum.

testBank.q: Consider the function f: (0, infinity) -> (-infinity, infinity) given by f(x) = root x log base e of x - x + 1. Then which one of the following statements is TRUE? (A) The derivative of the function f is decreasing in the interval (0, 1) (B) The function f has a local maximum at some point a in (0, infinity) (C) The function f has a local minimum at some point b in (0, infinity) (D) The function f has NEITHER a point of local maximum NOR a point of local minimum in the interval (0, infinity)
opts: (A) The derivative of the function f is decreasing in the interval (0, 1)
(B) The function f has a local maximum at some point a in (0, infinity)
(C) The function f has a local minimum at some point b in (0, infinity)
(D) The function f has NEITHER a point of local maximum NOR a point of local minimum in the interval (0, infinity)
steps: 1. f'(x) = (ln x)/(2 root x) + root x (1/x) - 1 = (ln x)/(2 root x) + 1/root x - 1.
2. Substitute t = root x, so t > 0 and ln x = 2 ln t. Multiplying f'(x) by the positive number root x gives root x f'(x) = (ln x)/2 + 1 - root x = ln t + 1 - t.
3. The standard inequality ln t <= t - 1 holds for all t > 0, with equality only at t = 1. So ln t + 1 - t <= 0, with equality only at t = 1, i.e. at x = 1.

4. Hence f'(x) <= 0 on the whole of (0, infinity) and f'(x) = 0 only at the single point x = 1. So f is strictly decreasing throughout, and the lone stationary point x = 1 shows no sign change in f': it is neither a local maximum nor a local minimum. Statements (B) and (C) are false and (D) is true.
5. Check (A): write f'(x) = g(t) = (ln t)/t + 1/t - 1 with t = root x. Then g'(t) = (1 - ln t)/t^2 - 1/t^2 = -(ln t)/t^2, which is POSITIVE for t in (0, 1) because ln t < 0 there.
6. Since t = root x increases with x, f' is increasing on (0, 1), not decreasing - indeed f' rises from -infinity up to 0. So (A) is false.
7. The answer is (D).
testBank.answer: (D) The function f has NEITHER a point of local maximum NOR a point of local minimum in the interval (0, infinity)

testBank.q: Let f(x) = integral from 0 to x^2 of e^t (t - 9)(t - 4)(t + 2) dt, for x in R. The numbers of points of local minimum and of local maximum of f are respectively
steps: 1. By Newton-Leibniz, differentiating an integral whose upper limit is g(x) = x^2 gives f'(x) = [integrand with t replaced by x^2] times g'(x).
3. e^(x^2) > 0 always and x^2 + 2 > 0 always, so neither can change the sign. Strip them out.
4. The sign of f' is the sign of x(x - 3)(x + 3)(x - 2)(x + 2), whose zeros are x = -3, -2, 0, 2, 3 - five critical points, all simple factors, so f' changes sign at each.
5. For x > 3 every factor is positive, so f' > 0. Walking leftwards the sign alternates: + on (3, infinity), - on (2, 3), + on (0, 2), - on (-2, 0), + on (-3, -2), - on (-infinity, -3).
6. Negative to positive gives a local minimum: x = -3, x = 0, x = 3 - three of them. Positive to negative gives a local maximum: x = -2, x = 2 - two of them.
7. So the answer is 3 and 2.

testBank.q: The equation 2x^3 - 9x^2 + 12x + k = 0 has three distinct real roots if and only if k lies in
steps: 1. Let f(x) = 2x^3 - 9x^2 + 12x + k. Then f'(x) = 6x^2 - 18x + 12 = 6(x - 1)(x - 2), independent of k.
2. Sign scheme + - + gives a local maximum at x = 1 and a local minimum at x = 2, whatever k is - the constant only slides the graph vertically.
3. Local maximum value M = f(1) = 2 - 9 + 12 + k = 5 + k. Local minimum value m = f(2) = 16 - 36 + 24 + k = 4 + k.
4. A cubic meets the x-axis three times exactly when the local maximum is above the axis and the local minimum below it, i.e. M m < 0.
6. Check with k = -4.5: M = 0.5 > 0 and m = -0.5 < 0, so three roots, as expected.

testBank.q: Among all right circular cones of a given slant height L, the one of greatest volume has semi-vertical angle theta and volume V. Then
opts: theta = tan inverse root2 and V = 2 pi L^3/(9 root3)
theta = pi/4 and V = pi L^3 root2/12
theta = tan inverse (1/root2) and V = 2 pi L^3/(9 root3)
theta = tan inverse root2 and V = pi L^3/(9 root3)
steps: 1. With slant height L fixed and semi-vertical angle theta, the radius is r = L sin theta and the height is h = L cos theta.
2. V = (1/3) pi r^2 h = (pi/3) L^3 sin^2 theta cos theta - now a function of theta alone.
3. dV/d theta = (pi L^3/3)[sin^2 theta (-sin theta) + cos theta (2 sin theta cos theta)] = (pi L^3/3) sin theta (2 cos^2 theta - sin^2 theta).
4. Set it to zero. sin theta = 0 gives a degenerate cone, so it is the fake root; the genuine one is 2 cos^2 theta = sin^2 theta, i.e. tan^2 theta = 2 and theta = tan inverse root2.
5. Then sin^2 theta = 2/3 and cos theta = 1/root3, so V = (pi/3) L^3 (2/3)(1/root3) = 2 pi L^3/(9 root3).
6. dV/d theta is positive before this theta and negative after it, so it is indeed a maximum.
testBank.answer: theta = tan inverse root2 and V = 2 pi L^3/(9 root3)

testBank.q: A ladder of fixed length L rests with its foot on the x-axis and its top against the y-axis. The foot slips away from the corner with constant speed b. When the ladder makes an angle pi/4 with the ground, the speed of its midpoint is
steps: 1. Let the foot be at (x, 0) and the top at (0, y), with x^2 + y^2 = L^2 and dx/dt = b. With theta the angle at the foot, x = L cos theta and y = L sin theta.

2. The midpoint is P = (x/2, y/2), so its distance from the corner is root(x^2 + y^2)/2 = L/2 - constant. So the RATE OF CHANGE OF THAT DISTANCE is zero, but the midpoint still moves: it travels on a circle of radius L/2.
3. Differentiate x^2 + y^2 = L^2: x dx/dt + y dy/dt = 0, so dy/dt = -(x/y) dx/dt = -b cot theta.
4. Velocity of P has components (1/2)dx/dt = b/2 and (1/2)dy/dt = -(b/2)cot theta.
5. Speed = (b/2) root(1 + cot^2 theta) = (b/2) cosec theta = b/(2 sin theta).
6. At theta = pi/4, sin theta = 1/root2, so the speed is b/(2/root2) = b/root2.
7. Note the trap: zero rate of change of the distance from the corner is not zero speed.

commonMistakes: 1. Substituting the instant's values into the formula before differentiating — putting r = 20 into A = πr² and then differentiating.
Fix: Differentiate the general relation first; substitute r = 20 and dr/dt = 2 only in the final line.
▶ where this comes up in the lecture
2. Mixing up the sign language: answering −42π for "rate of decrease", or answering 42π for "rate of change" when the quantity is shrinking.
Fix: Rate of change carries the sign; rate of decrease is reported as a positive magnitude. Read the last word of the question before writing the answer.
▶ where this comes up in the lecture
3. Using h in degrees in the approximation formula, so tan 46° comes out as 1 + 2 instead of 1 + 2(π/180).
Fix: Convert h to radians (1° = π/180 ≈ 0.01745) before multiplying by f'(a).
▶ where this comes up in the lecture
4. Writing the tangent's equation with the normal's slope, or forgetting that (slope of tangent)(slope of normal) = −1.
Fix: Write both numbers down as soon as you get dy/dx: m = dy/dx for the tangent, −1/m for the normal. Then write the equations.
▶ where this comes up in the lecture
5. Reporting only one point when the derivative condition is a quadratic with two roots.
Fix: Solve fully for α, then substitute every α back into the curve. Two roots means two points, and the exam wants both.
▶ where this comes up in the lecture
6. In Rolle's or Lagrange's theorem, keeping a c that lies outside (a, b), or applying the theorem without checking continuity and differentiability.
Fix: First check the three conditions — a greatest-integer or modulus piece usually kills one — then solve, then discard any root not strictly inside the interval.
▶ where this comes up in the lecture
7. Using the derivative sign test on a function that has a jump, and declaring it monotonically increasing because f' > 0 everywhere it exists.

Fix: The test is valid only where the function is continuous and differentiable. At a jump, go back to the definition and compare values across the break — the jump point may even be a local maximum or minimum.
▶ where this comes up in the lecture
8. Sign-scheme slips: starting the wave from + when the leading coefficient of f' is negative, and calling a repeated factor of f' a maximum or minimum.
Fix: Fix the sign of the rightmost interval from the leading coefficient first. If f' does not change sign across a root, that point is a point of inflection, not an extremum.
▶ where this comes up in the lecture
9. For a greatest or least value on an interval, comparing only the critical points — and keeping critical points that lie outside the interval.

Fix: Compare f at every critical point inside the interval and at both end points. Drop any critical point outside. If an end point is excluded, say the value is approached and the extreme does not exist.
▶ where this comes up in the lecture
10. Assuming an increasing function must be positive, or deciding a point of inflection from f' instead of f''.
Fix: Monotonicity alone says nothing about sign — pin it with one known value, e.g. f(a) = 0 with f' > 0 gives f ≥ 0 for x ≥ a. Inflection is always decided by the change of sign of f''.
▶ where this comes up in the lecture
shortcuts: Differentiate the relation, substitute at the very end In every rate question, first write the pure geometry relation (A = πr², V = (4/3)πr³, z² = x² + y²), then differentiate it with respect to t, and only then put in the values given "at that instant". The instant's numbers are data, not part of the formula. If you substitute r = 20 first, you are differentiating a constant and you will get 0. Lecture 9
▶ watch Ankit Sir explain it

In a cone, push everything into one variable The semi-vertical angle θ gives r = L sinθ and h = L cosθ. So V, h, r and the surface area all become constants times powers of L, and one differentiation answers every part of the question. If the question gives height and radius instead of the angle, that is the same thing in disguise: tanθ = r/h. Always write the volume in the variable the question gives you a rate for. Lecture 9
▶ watch Ankit Sir explain it

The one approximation formula f(a + h) ≈ f(a) + h·f'(a). Choose a as the nearest value you can compute exactly (216 for 217, 45° for 46°) and keep h small, because the smaller h is the closer you land. In trigonometry h must be in radians: 1° = π/180. Lecture 10
▶ watch Ankit Sir explain it

Slope of a line without differentiating, then convert the condition For ax + by + c = 0 the slope is −a/b. "Tangent parallel to that line" means dy/dx = −a/b. "Normal parallel to that line" means the normal has slope −a/b, so the tangent slope is b/a. Convert the words into one number for dy/dx before you touch the curve. Lecture 10
▶ watch Ankit Sir explain it

Unknown point? Write two equations about it Call the point (α, β). Equation one: it lies on the curve. Equation two: the derivative condition — either dy/dx at (α, β) equals the given slope, or, for a tangent drawn from an outside point (λ, μ), (β − μ)/(α − λ) equals that derivative. Two equations, two unknowns, and you are done. The same two lines solve the shortest-distance question too, because the nearest point lies along the common normal, so there the tangent is parallel to the line. Lecture 10
▶ watch Ankit Sir explain it

k-questions: only one end of the derivative's range matters For increasing on an interval you only have to force the minimum value of f' to be ≥ 0; for decreasing, only the maximum value of f' to be ≤ 0. On a short interval f' is usually monotonic, so that minimum or maximum sits at an end. And for a sin x + b cos x use the range ±√(a² + b²) straight away — that is how k + 4cos x − 3sin x becomes k − 5 to k + 5. Lecture 11
▶ watch Ankit Sir explain it

To compare two expressions, make their difference a function Put g(x) = LHS − RHS, differentiate, show g' keeps one sign, then read g at the start of the interval. Increasing with g(0) = 0 forces g ≥ 0; decreasing with g(0) = 0 forces g ≤ 0. That single routine proves x ≥ tan⁻¹x, proves sin x − x cos x > 0, and settles whether sin x / x is rising or falling. Lecture 12
▶ watch Ankit Sir explain it

A cubic has three distinct real roots exactly when M·m < 0 Find the two critical points, let M be the local maximum value and m the local minimum value. Three distinct real roots ⟺ M·m < 0, i.e. the local maximum is above the x-axis and the local minimum below it. One real root when M·m > 0. This is the standard way a parameter question on cubics is set. Lecture 14

chapters.title: Indefinite Integration

concepts.title: Integration as the reverse of differentiation, and the constant of integration
concepts.oneLine: Integration is just differentiation run backwards — you are handed the derivative and asked for the function — and since a constant dies on differentiating, every answer carries a + c.
notes: Think about how inverse functions were born. Someone said tan 60° = √3, so someone else reversed it and wrote tan⁻¹√3 = 60°. If f(3) = 10, then f⁻¹(10) = 3. The same reversing happened to d/dx.

Till now the question handed you a function and asked for its derivative. Asked for d/dx of x² + ln x, you fire back 2x + 1/x without thinking. Integration flips the question: you are handed the derivative 2x + 1/x and you must say which function it came from. So ∫(2x + 1/x)dx = x² + ln x.

Now one small thing. Suppose a constant c was sitting there — x² + ln x + c. Differentiate it and you still get 2x + 1/x, because the constant simply vanishes. So x² + ln x + 50, + 100, + 200, + 500 are all correct answers. One function has infinitely many integrals, and they differ only by a constant, which is why we always write + c.

This gives you the plan for the chapter. d/dx shifted to the other side becomes ∫, so every derivative formula you have learnt — and there are about twenty of them — turns into an integration formula for free. From d/dx(sin x) = cos x you instantly get ∫cos x dx = sin x + c. That is where this chapter starts.

quickChecks.q: Given d/dx(x³ + sin x) = 3x² + cos x, find ∫(3x² + cos x)dx.
steps: 1. The derivative is given, so the function is the answer to the integral.
2. Flip the given result: ∫(3x² + cos x)dx = x³ + sin x.
3. Attach the arbitrary constant.

quickChecks.q: You know d/dx(ln x) = 1/x. Write ∫(1/x)dx.
steps: 1. Read the derivative backwards: the function whose derivative is 1/x is ln x.
2. So ∫(1/x)dx = ln x, and a constant could have been attached.

quickChecks.q: Using the same reversing idea, find ∫2ˣ dx.
steps: 2. Reverse: ∫2ˣ ln 2 dx = 2ˣ + c.
3. Divide both sides by the number ln 2 and rename the constant.

concepts.title: The 17 standard integration formulas you must know by heart
concepts.quote: Here is the biggest tragedy of this chapter: students treat integration as a differentiation puzzle to solve every single time. Fix that today and the whole chapter opens up.
concepts.oneLine: Every derivative formula flips into an integration formula, and the 17 on today's list must be recalled instantly, not re-derived.
notes: Integration is the reverse process of differentiation. So the chapter starts in the simplest possible way: we take every derivative formula you already know and flip it into an integration formula.

Look at how the list is built. Four formulas come straight from the basic derivatives, six more from the next set of derivatives, four more that are not exactly derivative results but can still be proved using differentiation, and three more on top of that. 4 + 6 = 10, 10 + 4 = 14, 14 + 3 = 17. Seventeen formulas. That is the whole target of today's class: remember these 17.

Now the warning. If, asked for the integral of cos x, you first think "what is the derivative of sin x" and only then answer, your integration will stay weak forever. In the first few days a little differentiation is fine as a memory support. But ultimately these have to sit in your head as they are — hear tan x and sec²x should come to you with no detour.

The obvious question is how many more are coming. My honest answer: after these 17, hardly 3 or 4 more. I am giving you the complete formula set in two shifts — today is shift 1 with these 17, and in the next class I will give you the remaining four. After that, no new integration formula exists; everything else is a variation on these. So note all of them in your copy today.

quickChecks.q: ∫ sec²x dx = ?
steps: 1. Whose derivative is sec²x? d/dx (tan x) = sec²x.
2. Flip it and add the constant.

quickChecks.q: ∫ cosec²x dx = ?
steps: 1. d/dx (cot x) = −cosec²x.
2. So the function whose derivative is +cosec²x is −cot x.

quickChecks.q: ∫ 2ˣ dx = ?
steps: 1. Use the aˣ formula with a = 2: ∫ aˣ dx = aˣ/ln a + c.
2. Substitute a = 2.

concepts.title: The standard integration formulas you must know by heart
concepts.oneLine: The basic integration list — powers, 1/x, exponentials, sin and cos — plus the two log forms for sec x and cosec x, each of which can be written with a plus or a minus sign.
notes: One straight word. In 11th and 12th someone keeps telling you stories about integration. Forget the stories. If your target is JEE, these standard formulas have to sit in your head the way your own phone number sits in your head.
And this bears repeating: even if a formula slips out of your memory for a second, you must still know how to apply it. Knowing the line is half the job. Knowing where it fits is the other half.

Now the part students actually get confused by. ∫sec x dx and ∫cosec x dx each have two faces. The real formula for the first one is ln|sec x + tan x|. But sec x − tan x is just 1/(sec x + tan x), so the same answer becomes −ln|sec x − tan x| — the minus simply comes out in front.

Same story with cosec. cosec x − cot x and cosec x + cot x are reciprocals of each other, so the minus jumps out again. And if you push the trigonometry one step further — cosec as 1/sin, cot as cos/sin — you land on tan(x/2). Do this manipulation yourself with your own hand once; then you will never panic when the answer key prints a different-looking form.

quickChecks.q: Integrate x⁵ + 3/x.
steps: 1. Power rule on x⁵ with n = 5: x⁶/6.
2. The 3/x term is the n = −1 case: 3 ln|x|.
3. Add the constant.

quickChecks.q: Write ∫cosec x dx in the form that carries a minus sign in front of the log.
steps: 1. Standard form is ln|cosec x − cot x| + C.
2. cosec x − cot x = 1/(cosec x + cot x), so the reciprocal brings the minus out.

quickChecks.q: Integrate 2cos x − 5sin x + 2ˣ.
steps: 1. ∫cos x dx = sin x, so the first term gives 2 sin x.
2. ∫sin x dx = −cos x, so −5sin x gives +5 cos x.
3. ∫2ˣ dx = 2ˣ/ln 2.

concepts.title: Why tan, cot, sec, cosec sit apart — and the inverse-trig formulas
concepts.quote: Trigonometry has six functions. Look at the standard list and only sin and cos are sitting there. Where did tan, cot, sec and cosec go, and why do they get their own box?
concepts.oneLine: sin and cos integrals fall straight out of differentiation, the other four trigonometric functions need a separate technique, and the two inverse-trig forms 1/√(a²−x²) → sin⁻¹(x/a) and 1/(a²+x²) → (1/a)tan⁻¹(x/a) must be by heart.
notes: Go slowly here, so that nothing gets confused. Every formula in that standard list came out of differentiation. You knew the derivative, you read it backwards, and the integral was yours.

That is exactly why only sin and cos appear in the main list: their integrals come free from differentiation knowledge, and the other four do not. tan, cot, sec and cosec are not obtained by reading a derivative backwards. They need a different technique, which comes a little later. So those four stay together in their own group.

Learn them as a set of four: ∫tan x dx = ln|sec x| + C, ∫cot x dx = ln|sin x| + C, ∫sec x dx = ln|sec x + tan x| + C, ∫cosec x dx = ln|cosec x − cot x| + C. Each one has a second form too, but remember any one of the two and you are safe.

Then the two inverse-trig forms. 1/√(a²−x²) integrates to sin⁻¹(x/a) + C, and 1/(a²+x²) integrates to (1/a)tan⁻¹(x/a) + C. Notice the difference: in the sin⁻¹ form no 1/a comes out, in the tan⁻¹ form the 1/a does come out in front. The derivation of each one will come to you later; right now your whole focus is remembering them correctly.

quickChecks.q: Integrate 1/√(9 − x²) with respect to x.
steps: 1. Root in the denominator with a² − x², so the answer is sin⁻¹.
2. Here a² = 9, so a = 3.
3. No 1/a comes outside in this form.

quickChecks.q: Integrate 1/(16 + x²) with respect to x.
steps: 1. No root, and the form is a² + x², so the answer is tan⁻¹.
3. This form carries 1/a outside, so 1/4 sits in front.

quickChecks.q: Write ∫cosec x dx and ∫cot x dx from memory.
steps: 1. Both belong to the group of four that do not come from differentiation, so both answers are logs with a modulus.
2. cosec goes with the minus sign inside: cosec x − cot x.
3. cot gives sin inside the log.
quickChecks.answer: ∫cosec x dx = ln|cosec x − cot x| + C and ∫cot x dx = ln|sin x| + C

concepts.title: The linear change rule: replacing x by ax + b
concepts.oneLine: Every standard integration formula still works when x is replaced by the linear expression ax + b — just multiply the whole answer by 1/a.
notes: Look at the list of standard formulas just built. Write ax + b everywhere x used to sit and the formula does not break. It stays valid, with exactly the same shape.

Only one adjustment is needed: multiply the result by the reciprocal of the coefficient of x. The coefficient of x is a, so the extra factor is 1/a. Nothing else changes — the function, the power, the log, the inverse trig, all of it stays as it is.
So if the integral of f(x) is F(x) + C, then the integral of f(ax + b) is (1/a)·F(ax + b) + C. You already saw this pattern a minute ago with 1/a times tan⁻¹(x/a) — same 1/a, same reason.

The obvious question is where this 1/a comes from. The proof comes later, and it is not worth getting stuck here for. This chapter is long; if you stall on this one step you will keep circling the same place and never finish it. Hold the rule, use it, and the proof will make sense on its own later.

quickChecks.q: Integrate (2x + 3)⁵ with respect to x.
steps: 1. Standard formula: ∫xⁿ dx = x^(n+1)/(n+1) + C, with n = 5.
2. Put 2x + 3 in place of x: (2x + 3)⁶/6.
3. Coefficient of x is 2, so multiply by 1/2.

quickChecks.q: Integrate sin(3x + 1) with respect to x.
steps: 1. Standard formula: ∫sin x dx = −cos x + C.
2. Put 3x + 1 in place of x: −cos(3x + 1).
3. Coefficient of x is 3, so multiply by 1/3.

quickChecks.q: Integrate 1/(5x + 4) with respect to x.
steps: 1. Standard formula: ∫(1/x) dx = ln|x| + C.
2. Put 5x + 4 in place of x: ln|5x + 4|.
3. Coefficient of x is 5, so multiply by 1/5.

concepts.title: First examples of the 1/a rule
concepts.oneLine: For (ax + b) in place of x, integrate as usual and then multiply by 1/a — the reciprocal of the coefficient of x.
notes: Take the first one: ∫(5x/7 + 2/3)⁴ dx. The bracket is sitting exactly where x used to sit, so the power rule runs first — power up by one, divide by the new power. That gives (5x/7 + 2/3)⁵/5.
Now the correction. The coefficient of x inside the bracket is 5/7, so multiply by the reciprocal of the coefficient of x — here 7/5 — and only then write + C. Final answer: (7/25)(5x/7 + 2/3)⁵ + C.

Second one: ∫dx/(7 − 3x). This time the base formula is the log one, so the answer carries ln|7 − 3x|. The coefficient of x is −3, so multiply by 1/(−3): the answer is −⅓ ln|7 − 3x| + C. Divide by the coefficient of x, or multiply by 1/a — keep whichever language you remember.
One small thing that confuses people here. ∫dx is just ∫x⁰ dx, so the power rule gives x¹/1 = x. That is the whole reason the integral of a constant brings an x with it.

quickChecks.q: Find ∫(2x/3 + 1/5)³ dx.
steps: 1. Power rule on the bracket: (2x/3 + 1/5)⁴/4.
2. Coefficient of x is 2/3, so multiply by 3/2.

quickChecks.q: Find ∫dx/(5 − 2x).
steps: 1. Log formula: ln|5 − 2x|.
2. Coefficient of x is −2, so multiply by −½.

quickChecks.q: Find ∫(4x + 9)⁶ dx.
steps: 1. Power rule: (4x + 9)⁷/7.
2. Coefficient of x is 4, so multiply by ¼.

concepts.title: Integrating sin²x, cos²x, sin³x and cos³x by reducing to linear form
concepts.oneLine: sin²x, cos²x, sin³x and cos³x can never be integrated as they are — use the double-angle and triple-angle identities to turn them into a linear combination of 1, cos2x, sinx and sin3x, and then the standard formulas finish the job.
notes: Someone asks for ∫sin²x dx. You have no formula for a square, so you do not even try. You replace sin²x by (1 − cos2x)/2 and the square is gone.

Now everything inside is linear in x — a constant and a cos2x. The constant integrates to x, because a constant is really x⁰ and x⁰ integrates to x¹/1. And cos2x integrates to sin2x, divided by the coefficient of x, which is 2.

Cubes work the same way, only the identity changes. sin3x = 3sinx − 4sin³x, so 4sin³x = 3sinx − sin3x. Rearranging the triple-angle identity is the whole trick. For cosine, cos3x = 4cos³x − 3cosx, so 4cos³x = 3cosx + cos3x.

So the method is one line long: convert to linear form, integrate term by term, and divide by the coefficient of x every single time. These four integrals are not worth remembering as results. Rebuild them from the identity in a couple of seconds instead.

quickChecks.q: Find ∫cos²2x dx
steps: 1. cos²2x = (1 + cos4x)/2, so the integral is ½∫(1 + cos4x) dx.
2. ∫dx = x, and ∫cos4x dx = sin4x/4.
3. So we get ½(x + sin4x/4) + c.

quickChecks.q: Find ∫sin²(x/2) dx
steps: 1. Here the angle is x/2, so double it: sin²(x/2) = (1 − cosx)/2.
2. The integral is ½∫(1 − cosx) dx = ½(x − sinx) + c.

quickChecks.q: Find ∫sin³2x dx
steps: 1. Use 4sin³θ = 3sinθ − sin3θ with θ = 2x: 4sin³2x = 3sin2x − sin6x.
2. So the integral is ¼∫(3sin2x − sin6x) dx.
3. ∫sin2x dx = −cos2x/2 and ∫sin6x dx = −cos6x/6.
4. That gives ¼(−3cos2x/2 + cos6x/6) + c.

concepts.title: Integrating tan²x and cot²x
concepts.oneLine: tan²x and cot²x are never integrated directly — swap them for sec²x − 1 and cosec²x − 1, and both halves become standard forms.
notes: This one is worth repeating until it is automatic: if a squared trig function appears, your first job is to convert it into something whose integral you already know. tan²x and cot²x are the easiest cases of that rule.
Use the Pythagorean identities. tan²x = sec²x − 1, so ∫tan²x dx = ∫(sec²x − 1)dx = tan x − x + c. Same treatment for the other one: cot²x = cosec²x − 1, so ∫cot²x dx = −cot x − x + c.

Notice what happens. The sec²x part gives tan x straight away, and the −1 part gives −x. That lonely −x is the piece students forget, and it is the whole difference between a correct answer and a zero.

One more standard integral belongs right next to these: ∫cosec x dx = ln|tan(x/2)| + c. Keep it in the same memory slot, because the next topic sends every a sin x + b cos x denominator straight into this form.

quickChecks.q: Find ∫(tan²x + cot²x) dx
steps: 1. Convert both: tan²x = sec²x − 1 and cot²x = cosec²x − 1.
2. Integral becomes ∫(sec²x + cosec²x − 2)dx.
3. ∫sec²x dx = tan x, ∫cosec²x dx = −cot x, ∫2 dx = 2x.

quickChecks.q: Find ∫tan²(3x) dx
steps: 1. tan²(3x) = sec²(3x) − 1.
2. ∫sec²(3x)dx = (1/3)tan 3x, because of the 3 inside.

quickChecks.q: Find ∫(1 + cot²x) dx
steps: 1. 1 + cot²x is just cosec²x — no splitting needed.
2. ∫cosec²x dx = −cot x.

concepts.title: a sin x + b cos x in the denominator: converting to a single cosec
concepts.oneLine: Any a sin θ + b cos θ in the denominator squeezes into one sine: pull out √(a²+b²), write the rest as sin(θ − φ), and finish with the cosec formula plus the 1/a of the linear change.
notes: Look at the denominator first, not the integral. sin 2x − √3 cos 2x is the a sin θ + b cos θ shape with θ = 2x, a = 1, b = −√3. The moment you see that shape, your only job is trigonometry: turn two terms into one.

The way to do it is to take out √(a²+b²). Here that is √(1 + 3) = 2. Take 2 out and inside you are left with ½ sin 2x − (√3/2) cos 2x. Those two numbers are not random: ½ = cos π/3 and √3/2 = sin π/3.
So the bracket is sin 2x cos π/3 − cos 2x sin π/3, which is exactly sin(2x − π/3). The denominator is 2 sin(2x − π/3). Now flip it: the ½ comes outside and you are integrating cosec(2x − π/3).

And ∫cosec x dx = ln|tan(x/2)|. Here x has been replaced by 2x − π/3, which is a linear change — x → ax + b. So the half-angle becomes (2x − π/3)/2 = x − π/6, and because the coefficient of x is 2, you must multiply by its reciprocal, ½. That extra half is the mark people lose.

quickChecks.q: Evaluate ∫dx/(sin x + √3 cos x).
steps: 1. √(a²+b²) = √(1 + 3) = 2, so sin x + √3 cos x = 2[½ sin x + (√3/2) cos x].
2. ½ = cos π/3, √3/2 = sin π/3, so bracket = sin x cos π/3 + cos x sin π/3 = sin(x + π/3).
3. Integral = ½ ∫cosec(x + π/3) dx = ½ ln|tan((x + π/3)/2)| + c.
4. Coefficient of x is 1, so there is no extra factor this time.

quickChecks.q: Evaluate ∫dx/(√3 sin 2x − cos 2x).
steps: 2. √3/2 = cos π/6 and ½ = sin π/6, so bracket = sin(2x − π/6).
3. Integral = ½ ∫cosec(2x − π/6) dx.
4. Half-angle: (2x − π/6)/2 = x − π/12. Coefficient of x is 2, so one more ½.

quickChecks.q: Evaluate ∫dx/(sin 3x − cos 3x).
steps: 2. 1/√2 = cos π/4 = sin π/4, so bracket = sin(3x − π/4).
3. Integral = (1/√2) ∫cosec(3x − π/4) dx.
4. Half-angle: (3x − π/4)/2 = 3x/2 − π/8. Coefficient of x is 3, so multiply by 1/3.

concepts.title: sin⁻¹ and tan⁻¹ formulas with a linear change inside
concepts.oneLine: When the bracket inside is linear, use the same sin⁻¹ or tan⁻¹ formula with that bracket in place of x, then multiply the whole answer by the reciprocal of the coefficient of x.
notes: Look at dx/√(16 − (5x − 2)²). This is exactly the a² − x² shape. The a² is 16, so a = 4, and the thing sitting in the x slot is the bracket 5x − 2.

The formula does not change when x is replaced by a linear expression — you only have to multiply by the reciprocal of the coefficient of x. Here the coefficient of x inside is 5, so the answer carries a 1/5 in front.
So the first one is (1/5) sin⁻¹((5x − 2)/4) + c. Nothing else is different from the plain sin⁻¹ formula.

Now change the minus to plus and drop the root: dx/(16 + (5x − 2)²). That is the a² + x² shape, whose answer is (1/a) tan⁻¹(x/a). With a = 4 that is (1/4) tan⁻¹((5x − 2)/4), and the linear change adds another 1/5. Together they give 1/20.

quickChecks.q: Integrate dx/√(9 − (2x + 1)²).
steps: 1. a² = 9, so a = 3, and the x slot is 2x + 1.
2. Formula gives sin⁻¹((2x + 1)/3).
3. Coefficient of x inside is 2, so multiply by 1/2.

quickChecks.q: Integrate dx/(25 + (3x − 1)²).
steps: 1. a² = 25, so a = 5, and the x slot is 3x − 1.
2. Formula gives (1/5) tan⁻¹((3x − 1)/5).
3. Coefficient of x inside is 3, so multiply by 1/3.

quickChecks.q: Integrate dx/√(49 − (4x + 3)²).
steps: 1. a² = 49, so a = 7, and the x slot is 4x + 3.
2. Formula gives sin⁻¹((4x + 3)/7).
3. Coefficient of x inside is 4, so multiply by 1/4.

concepts.title: Slide practice: splitting an integrand
concepts.oneLine: Nothing on this slide is a standard integral as it stands — split the integrand into standard pieces first, then integrate term by term.
notes: Look at cot²x. There is no formula for it. But there is a formula for cosec²x, and cot²x = cosec²x − 1. One line of identity and the question is over.

Now look at cosec x(cot x − cosec x). A product again — and we have no product rule for integration. So open the bracket: cosec x cot x − cosec²x. Both pieces are standard. Whenever you see a product or a power of a trigonometric ratio, your first move is to split it, never to integrate it.
The same eye works on the algebraic-looking ones. 3/(5cos²x) is just (3/5)sec²x. And 4 sin x/cos²x is 4 · (sin x/cos x) · (1/cos x) = 4 sec x tan x. Rewrite until a formula stares back at you.

Do the whole slide yourself, in your head or in a rough copy, before you look at the worked solution. Don't even copy the question. Read it, split it in your mind, write only the answer at the back of your copy and check.

quickChecks.q: Integrate tan²x with respect to x.
steps: 1. tan²x = sec²x − 1.
2. ∫(sec²x − 1) dx = ∫sec²x dx − ∫1 dx = tan x − x.

quickChecks.q: Integrate sec x (sec x + tan x) with respect to x.
steps: 1. Open the bracket: sec²x + sec x tan x.
2. ∫sec²x dx = tan x and ∫sec x tan x dx = sec x.
3. Add them.

quickChecks.q: Integrate 2/(3 sin²x) with respect to x.
steps: 1. Take the constant out: (2/3) ∫ 1/sin²x dx.
2. 1/sin²x = cosec²x, and ∫cosec²x dx = −cot x.
3. So you get −(2/3) cot x.

concepts.title: The splitting technique on four problems
concepts.oneLine: Before you integrate anything, split the integrand by algebra — expand the square, divide by the common power, or factorise the numerator — until every piece is a standard integral.
notes: Four questions run back to back here, and all four run on the same idea. Do the algebra first, the integration last. Expand, divide or factorise until what is left is something you already know.
For (tan x + cot x)² I just used (a + b)². You get tan²x + cot²x + 2 tan x cot x. Now tan x × cot x is always 1, so the middle term is a plain 2.
Then tan²x becomes sec²x − 1 and cot²x becomes cosec²x − 1. The two −1s eat up that +2 and you are left with sec²x + cosec²x. That is why splitting is worth the effort — the ugly part cancels itself.
The last two are pure algebra on the numerator. One is divide and finish, one is a³ + b³. When the denominator is x² + 1, ask yourself what factor of the numerator can produce x² + 1.

quickChecks.q: Integrate (3ˣ + 4ˣ)/6ˣ with respect to x.
steps: 1. Divide each term by 6ˣ: (3/6)ˣ + (4/6)ˣ = (1/2)ˣ + (2/3)ˣ.
2. Apply ∫aˣ dx = aˣ/ln a to each base.

quickChecks.q: Integrate (x⁴ + 1)/(x² + 1) with respect to x.
steps: 1. Write the numerator as (x⁴ − 1) + 2.
2. (x⁴ − 1)/(x² + 1) = x² − 1 after cancelling, so the integrand is x² − 1 + 2/(x² + 1).
3. Integrate: x³/3 − x + 2 tan⁻¹x.

quickChecks.q: Integrate (tan x − cot x)² with respect to x.
steps: 1. Expand: tan²x + cot²x − 2 tan x cot x = tan²x + cot²x − 2.
2. Replace: (sec²x − 1) + (cosec²x − 1) − 2 = sec²x + cosec²x − 4.
3. Integrate: tan x − cot x − 4x.

concepts.title: A second route to (tan x + cot x)² using sin²x + cos²x = 1
concepts.oneLine: (tan x + cot x)² becomes 1/(sin²x cos²x); put sin²x + cos²x in place of that 1 — a single power, not the whole square — split, and you get sec²x + cosec²x again.
notes: Start the other way this time. Write tan x as sin x/cos x and cot x as cos x/sin x, add them, and the top becomes sin²x + cos²x while the bottom is sin x cos x. So tan x + cot x is just 1/(sin x cos x).
Now square it. The bottom is sin²x cos²x, and the top is (sin²x + cos²x)². Here is where most students start expanding. Don't.
That top is 1 whole squared, and 1² is still 1 — so instead of the whole square, write a single power: sin²x + cos²x. Same value, and now it splits beautifully.

Split term by term over sin²x cos²x. The first piece leaves 1/cos²x, the second leaves 1/sin²x, so you are back at sec²x + cosec²x. Integrate and the answer is tan x − cot x + c — exactly what the first method gave you.

quickChecks.q: Write tan x + cot x as a single fraction in the simplest form.
steps: 1. tan x + cot x = sin x/cos x + cos x/sin x.
2. Common denominator sin x cos x gives (sin²x + cos²x)/(sin x cos x).
3. The numerator is 1.
quickChecks.answer: 1/(sin x cos x), that is sec x cosec x

quickChecks.q: Evaluate ∫ dx/(sin²x cos²x).
steps: 1. Replace the 1 on top by sin²x + cos²x.
2. Split: sin²x/(sin²x cos²x) + cos²x/(sin²x cos²x) = sec²x + cosec²x.
3. Integrate: tan x − cot x.

quickChecks.q: In the step above, a student writes the numerator as (sin²x + cos²x)² because the original expression was squared. What should it be, and why?
steps: 1. sin²x + cos²x = 1, so (sin²x + cos²x)² = 1² = 1.
2. A single power sin²x + cos²x is also equal to 1.
3. Both are correct in value, but only the single power splits into two terms straight away.
quickChecks.answer: Write sin²x + cos²x with power one; the whole square is unnecessary work

concepts.title: Splitting with 1 − sin²x: the add-and-subtract trick
concepts.oneLine: When cos²x sits on top of (1 + x²)sin²x, write cos²x = 1 − sin²x — the fraction splits into cosec²x − 1/(1 + x²) and integrates to −cot x − tan⁻¹x + C.
notes: Look at the integral ∫ (x² + cos²x) / ((1 + x²)sin²x) dx. The denominator carries two pieces: (1 + x²) and sin²x. For this fraction to break into easy terms, each of those two pieces has to appear in the numerator so it can cancel.
Right now the numerator is x² + cos²x. The x² is halfway to (1 + x²) — it only needs a 1. And that 1 is hiding inside cos²x. So replace cos²x by 1 − sin²x.

The numerator becomes x² + 1 − sin²x. Now split it in two. Take (1 + x²) with the denominator: (1 + x²) cancels and you are left with 1/sin²x, which is cosec²x. Take the −sin²x: sin²x cancels and you are left with −1/(1 + x²).

So the whole thing is just ∫cosec²x dx − ∫dx/(1 + x²) = −cot x − tan⁻¹x + C. This is the plus-one-minus-one trick in its short form — instead of adding and subtracting 1 in the numerator, write cos²x = 1 − sin²x and the 1 arrives on its own.

quickChecks.q: Integrate ∫ (x² + sin²x) / ((1 + x²)cos²x) dx
steps: 1. Denominator is (1 + x²)·cos²x, so the numerator must produce 1 + x² and cos²x.
2. Write sin²x = 1 − cos²x, so the numerator becomes x² + 1 − cos²x.
3. Split: (1 + x²)/((1 + x²)cos²x) − cos²x/((1 + x²)cos²x) = sec²x − 1/(1 + x²).
4. Integrate each: ∫sec²x dx = tan x and ∫dx/(1 + x²) = tan⁻¹x.

quickChecks.q: Integrate ∫ cos²x / sin²x dx using the same trick
steps: 1. Replace cos²x by 1 − sin²x: the integrand becomes (1 − sin²x)/sin²x.
2. Split: 1/sin²x − sin²x/sin²x = cosec²x − 1.
3. Integrate: ∫cosec²x dx = −cot x and ∫1 dx = x.

quickChecks.q: Integrate ∫ sin²x / cos²x dx
steps: 1. Replace sin²x by 1 − cos²x: the integrand becomes (1 − cos²x)/cos²x.
2. Split: 1/cos²x − cos²x/cos²x = sec²x − 1.
3. Integrate: ∫sec²x dx = tan x and ∫1 dx = x.

concepts.title: Bonus set A–D: powers of (ax + b), degrees to radians, (aˣ + bˣ)²
concepts.oneLine: Power rule or ln for (ax + b), divide by the coefficient of x once, convert degrees to radians before touching any calculus formula, and expand (aˣ + bˣ)² before integrating.
notes: Everything here is the same linear substitution, dressed up six different ways. You integrate as if the bracket were a single x, then pay the price for the bracket: divide once by the coefficient of x.

So (2x + 3)⁵ gives (2x + 3)⁶/6, and because the coefficient of x is 2, you divide by 2 more. For a negative power like (7x − 5)⁻³ the rule does not change: the power goes to −3 + 1 = −2, you divide by −2, and then by 7. When the power is exactly −1, the power rule dies and ln takes over — that is why 1/(5 − 6x) becomes ln of the mod, divided by −6.

Now the one students lose marks on. Every calculus formula — limit, derivative, integral — is true only when the angle is in radians. cos(x°) is not cos x. You convert the way you always have: multiply the number by π/180. So x° is πx/180, and after integrating sin(πx/180) you divide by the new coefficient π/180, which is the same as multiplying by 180/π.

The last one is not an integration problem at all until you expand it. (aˣ + bˣ)² = a²ˣ + 2(ab)ˣ + b²ˣ. Three clean exponential terms: the first two have 2x inside, so they carry an extra 2 in the denominator, and the middle term has plain x, so it carries nothing extra.

quickChecks.q: Integrate (3x − 4)⁷ with respect to x.
steps: 1. Power 7 becomes 8, divide by 8: (3x − 4)⁸/8.
2. Coefficient of x is 3, so divide by 3: denominator 24.

quickChecks.q: Integrate 1/(4 − 9x) with respect to x.
steps: 1. Power −1, so the answer is ln|4 − 9x|.
2. Coefficient of x is −9, so divide by −9.

quickChecks.q: Integrate sin(x°) with respect to x.
steps: 1. Convert: x° = πx/180.
2. Integral of sin is −cos, so you get −cos(πx/180).
3. Divide by the coefficient π/180, that is multiply by 180/π.

concepts.title: ∫dx/(cos(x − a)cos(x − b)): the sin(α − β) trick
concepts.oneLine: For ∫dx/(cos(x − a)cos(x − b)), manufacture sin(b − a) in the numerator: the fraction splits into tan(x − a) − tan(x − b), and the answer is (1/sin(b − a))·ln|cos(x − b)/cos(x − a)| + C.
notes: Look at what sits in the denominator: a product of two cos terms. You cannot integrate that as it stands. So we do not touch the integral yet — we fix the fraction first.

When the denominator is a product, you manufacture the matching expansion in the numerator so that the fraction splits. Call the two angles α and β. Below you have cos α · cos β. Put sin(α − β) on top: that is sin α cos β − cos α sin β. Divide term by term by cos α cos β and the cos β cancels in the first piece, the cos α in the second. You are left with tan α − tan β.

Now the beautiful part. Here α = x − a and β = x − b, so α − β = (x − a) − (x − b) = b − a. The x has gone. sin(b − a) is just a number, so you are allowed to multiply and divide by it freely. That is why we write 1/sin(b − a) outside and sin(b − a) inside.

The same thinking handles the mixed case. If the denominator is sin α · cos β, put cos(α − β) = cos α cos β + sin α sin β on top; dividing gives cot α + tan β. The product below tells you what to build above: cos·cos asks for sin, sin·cos asks for cos. Practise this step until it is automatic, because after the split you only need ∫tan x dx = ln|sec x| and ∫cot x dx = ln|sin x|.

quickChecks.q: Evaluate ∫ dx/(cos(x − π/6)cos(x − π/3)).
steps: 1. Here a = π/6 and b = π/3, so α − β = b − a = π/3 − π/6 = π/6.
2. sin(π/6) = ½, so the constant outside is 1/sin(π/6) = 2.
3. Split: 2 ∫ [tan(x − π/6) − tan(x − π/3)] dx.
4. Integrate: 2[ln|sec(x − π/6)| − ln|sec(x − π/3)|] + C.

quickChecks.q: Evaluate ∫ dx/(cos(x − 2)cos(x − 5)).
steps: 1. a = 2, b = 5, so α − β = b − a = 3 and the constant outside is 1/sin 3.
2. Split: (1/sin 3) ∫ [tan(x − 2) − tan(x − 5)] dx.
3. Integrate and combine the logs.

quickChecks.q: Now the mixed case: evaluate ∫ dx/(sin(x − a)cos(x − b)).
steps: 1. Denominator is sin α · cos β with α = x − a, β = x − b, so put cos(α − β) on top.
2. α − β = b − a, so the constant outside is 1/cos(b − a).
3. The fraction splits as cot(x − a) + tan(x − b).
4. Integrate: (1/cos(b − a))[ln|sin(x − a)| + ln|sec(x − b)|] + C.

concepts.title: Quick quiz: remembering the 1/a factor
concepts.oneLine: For any integral in a linear 2 − 3x form, integrate as usual and then divide by the coefficient of x — and the minus sign comes along with it.
notes: These are the fifteen-second questions. You see 1/(2 − 3x), you already know ∫dx/x = ln|x|, so you write ln|2 − 3x| and you are nearly done.
Nearly done is not done: you must divide by the coefficient of x. Here the coefficient of x is −3, so the answer gets a 1/(−3) in front, which is the same as −(1/3).
That is exactly why option A was wrong and C was right. A had the log correct but no division, so it quietly dropped both the 1/3 and the minus.
Same rule, different function. In the next one the division is again by −3, and that is why a minus appears in front of the exponential. The function changes, the division does not.

quickChecks.q: Find ∫dx/(5 − 2x).
steps: 1. Integrate the 1/x form: ln|5 − 2x|.
2. Coefficient of x is −2, so divide by −2.
3. Value is −(1/2)ln|5 − 2x| + C.

quickChecks.q: Find ∫e^(4 − x) dx.
steps: 1. Integrate the exponential: e^(4 − x).
2. Coefficient of x is −1, so divide by −1.
3. Value is −e^(4 − x) + C.

quickChecks.q: Find ∫dx/(3x + 7).
steps: 1. Integrate the 1/x form: ln|3x + 7|.
2. Coefficient of x is +3, so divide by 3 — no minus this time.
3. Value is (1/3)ln|3x + 7| + C.

concepts.title: Proof of the linear-change rule by substitution
concepts.oneLine: If ∫f(x)dx = g(x) + c, then putting t = ax + b and dx = dt/a proves ∫f(ax + b)dx = g(ax + b)/a + c.
notes: A fair question: why does that 1/a appear at all? So let us prove it, and the proof is nothing but integration by substitution.
Start with what we already know from the previous class: ∫f(x)dx = g(x) + c. That is given. We want to show that ∫f(ax + b)dx = g(ax + b)/a + c, where a is the coefficient of x.

Put t = ax + b. Differentiate both sides with respect to x: the derivative of ax is a, the derivative of b is 0, and on the left you get dt/dx. So dt/dx = a. Cross multiply and you get dx = dt/a — that single step is where the 1/a is born.

Now the whole integral is in t: ∫f(t)·dt/a. The a is a constant, so pull it out: (1/a)∫f(t)dt = (1/a)·g(t) + c. Put t = ax + b back and you have g(ax + b)/a + c. This was the starting point of today's class, and we keep using it everywhere.

quickChecks.q: If t = 7 − 2x, write dx in terms of dt.
steps: 1. Differentiate both sides with respect to x: dt/dx = −2.
2. Cross multiply: dx = dt/(−2) = −dt/2.

quickChecks.q: Given ∫cos x dx = sin x + c, use t = 3x + 4 to find ∫cos(3x + 4)dx.
steps: 1. Let t = 3x + 4, so dt/dx = 3 and dx = dt/3.
2. The integral becomes ∫cos t · dt/3 = (1/3)∫cos t dt.
4. Put t = 3x + 4 back.

quickChecks.q: Given ∫x³dx = x⁴/4 + c, find ∫(5x + 1)³dx by substitution.
steps: 1. Let t = 5x + 1, so dt/dx = 5 and dx = dt/5.
2. The integral becomes ∫t³ · dt/5 = (1/5)∫t³dt.
4. Put t = 5x + 1 back.

concepts.title: General substitution: spot the inner function and its derivative
concepts.oneLine: If the question has an inner function and that function's derivative sitting outside, put the inner function equal to t and the whole thing collapses into a basic integral.
notes: Start from something you already know. ∫sin x dx = −cos x. Now the question maker does one small thing: he replaces x by tan⁻¹x. But then he is forced to also write the derivative of tan⁻¹x outside, which is 1/(1+x²). That is how sin(tan⁻¹x)/(1+x²) was born.

Same game again. ∫dx/(1+x²) = tan⁻¹x. He writes x⁶ in place of x², which is really (x³)², so now he must paste the derivative of x³ outside — 3x², or just x² if he wants to be kind. And ∫sec²x dx = tan x becomes sec²(x⁴) with x³ outside. Every such question is a known integral with x replaced by some function, and that function's derivative sitting outside.

So the solving method is just reading it backwards. Whatever function is sitting inside, call it t, differentiate it, and swap the outside part along with dx for dt. Every x must vanish; what is left is a formula you learnt in the basics.
This looks too easy, but keep it close. It is used in almost every question you will ever solve, because x will not sit there plainly every time — something new will keep coming in its place.

quickChecks.q: Integrate x²cos(x³) with respect to x.
steps: 1. Put t = x³, so 3x² dx = dt and x² dx = dt/3.
2. The integral becomes (1/3)∫cos t dt = (1/3)sin t + C.

quickChecks.q: Integrate 2x/(1+x⁴) with respect to x.
steps: 1. Read x⁴ as (x²)². Put t = x², so 2x dx = dt.
2. The integral becomes ∫dt/(1+t²) = tan⁻¹t + C.

quickChecks.q: Integrate x sec²(x² + 1) with respect to x.
steps: 1. Put t = x² + 1, so 2x dx = dt and x dx = dt/2.
2. The integral becomes (1/2)∫sec²t dt = ½ tan t + C.

concepts.title: Where substitution fits: basics plus substitution is the foundation
concepts.oneLine: Substitution does not give you a new way to integrate — it only converts a question into the basic forms, and basics plus substitution together are the foundation of this whole chapter.
notes: Look carefully at every substitution question so far. Was there ever a new way of integrating in any of them? No. Substitution adds no new integral to your list — it only converts the question into the basic forms you already know.

That is the entire job of a good substitution: pick the right t, and a frightening question becomes a basic one. Basic means exactly what we learnt before this topic — the standard list. Nothing more.

Now understand the flow of the chapter, because that matters more than any single question. First comes basics. Then comes substitution. And substitution never ends — it keeps coming back inside everything that follows.

In fact it was already there in basics. Writing the integral of sin(2x−3) as −cos(2x−3)/2 was substitution working quietly. So basics plus substitution is the foundation of the building — everything after this is just floors on top. That is why I want this foundation strong right now.

quickChecks.q: Integrate cos(5x + 2) with respect to x.
steps: 1. Put t = 5x + 2, so dt = 5 dx and dx = dt/5.
2. Integral becomes (1/5) × (integral of cos t dt) = (1/5) sin t.
3. Put t back.

quickChecks.q: Integrate sin(3 − 4x) with respect to x.
steps: 1. Put t = 3 − 4x, so dt = −4 dx and dx = −dt/4.
2. Integral becomes −(1/4) × (integral of sin t dt) = −(1/4)(−cos t) = (cos t)/4.
3. Put t back and check by differentiating: the two minus signs cancel and you get sin(3 − 4x).

quickChecks.q: After a correct substitution, what should the question always turn into?
steps: 1. Substitution does not create any new integral.
2. So the only possible landing place is the basic list.
quickChecks.answer: A basic standard integral. If it is not basic, the substitution needs changing.

concepts.title: Substitution practice: √x, ln x, tanⁿx sec²x, tan⁻¹(cos²x), 10ˣ
concepts.quote: Five questions, one skill. Nothing new to learn here — only the eye to see which function already has its derivative written next to it.
concepts.oneLine: In every one of these, t is the function whose own derivative is already sitting in the question — spot it and the integral finishes itself.
notes: Look at the whole slide once before you touch a pen. In each question some function is sitting there with its own derivative written beside it — that function is your t. Once the right t clicks, there is nothing left in the question.

Take √x. Its derivative is 1/(2√x), and 1/√x is exactly what is sitting in the denominator. Put t = √x and the 1/√x goes away with the dx. Same story for ln x: its derivative is 1/x, so t = ln x turns the whole thing into ∫dt/t, which is ln|t| — giving ln|ln x|.

In tanⁿx sec²x dx, sec²x is the derivative of tan x. So t = tan x makes it ∫tⁿ dt, and the power rule gives t^(n+1)/(n+1). In the next one 2 sin x cos x is written on top: that is the derivative of cos²x except for a minus sign. So t = cos²x, dt = −2 sin x cos x dx, and that extra minus is what puts the negative in front of tan⁻¹(cos²x).

The last one is the real trap. The derivative of 10ˣ is 10ˣ ln 10, the derivative of x¹⁰ is 10x⁹ — two different animals, and both of them are printed on top. So t = x¹⁰ + 10ˣ and the answer is a log. Substitution is not a clever technique; in the world of integration it is walking, sitting, eating — the basic thing you will use in almost every integral you ever solve.

quickChecks.q: Evaluate ∫ dx/(x (ln x)²)
steps: 1. 1/x is present, so t = ln x and dt = dx/x.
2. Integral becomes ∫ dt/t² = ∫ t^(−2) dt.
4. Put t back.

quickChecks.q: Evaluate ∫ tan³x sec²x dx
steps: 1. sec²x is the derivative of tan x, so t = tan x, dt = sec²x dx.
2. Integral becomes ∫ t³ dt = t⁴/4.
3. Put t back.

quickChecks.q: Evaluate ∫ (2 sin x cos x)/(1 + sin⁴x) dx
steps: 1. Bottom is 1 + (sin²x)², so watch sin²x.
2. d(sin²x) = 2 sin x cos x dx, and that is exactly the numerator — this time with no minus sign.
3. Put t = sin²x: integral becomes ∫ dt/(1 + t²) = tan⁻¹t.
4. Put t back.

concepts.title: Recap: substitution in ∫x²cos²(x³+2)dx
concepts.oneLine: Put t = x³+2 because its derivative x² is already sitting in the integrand, then kill the square on cos t with cos²t = (1+cos2t)/2.
notes: Look at ∫x²cos²(x³+2)dx before you touch anything. Inside the cos you have x³+2, and its derivative is 3x² — and an x² is already standing right there in the integrand. That is the whole signal.
So put t = x³+2. Then 3x²dx = dt, which means x²dx = dt/3. The integral becomes (1/3)∫cos²t dt. Nothing is left in x, which is exactly what a substitution must achieve.
Now cos²t. The earlier rule applies: never integrate a square of cos directly, bring it down with cos²t = (1+cos2t)/2. The 1/3 and the 1/2 join hands and give you 1/6 outside.

Pick as t the function whose derivative is already present in the question, and which makes the rest integrable. That one line is the whole substitution routine. Integrate 1 to get t, integrate cos2t to get sin2t divided by 2, then put x³+2 back in place of t.

quickChecks.q: Evaluate ∫x cos²(x²+5)dx
steps: 1. Derivative of x²+5 is 2x, and x is present. Put t = x²+5, so x dx = dt/2.
2. Integral = (1/2)∫cos²t dt = (1/4)∫(1+cos2t)dt.
4. Put t back: (x²+5)/4 + sin(2x²+10)/8 + C.

quickChecks.q: Evaluate ∫x²sin²(x³)dx
steps: 1. Put t = x³, so 3x²dx = dt and x²dx = dt/3.
2. Integral = (1/3)∫sin²t dt, and sin²t = (1−cos2t)/2.
4. Put t back: x³/6 − sin(2x³)/12 + C.

quickChecks.q: Evaluate ∫cos²(ln x)/x dx
steps: 1. Derivative of ln x is 1/x, and 1/x is present. Put t = ln x, so dx/x = dt.
2. Integral = ∫cos²t dt = (1/2)∫(1+cos2t)dt.
4. Put t back: (ln x)/2 + sin(2 ln x)/4 + C.

concepts.title: Choosing the substitution: three solved problems
concepts.oneLine: In substitution you are not applying a rule — you are hunting for the function whose derivative is already sitting in the question: t = tan x³, t = the whole denominator when sin 2x appears, t = sin⁻¹x².
notes: The same idea continues here. The only skill is this: look at the question and find the function whose derivative is already present, somewhere in the question. That function becomes t.

In the first one, put t = tan x³, because 3x² sec²x³ is sitting right there. In the second, sin 2x appears — and sin 2x is the derivative of cos²x as well as of sin²x — so take the whole denominator as t. In the third, put t = sin⁻¹x², because 2x/√(1−x⁴) is already written in the question.

There is no single rule here. Every question is different, so this is your own observation, your own thinking. If I just tell you "put t = tan x³", I have taught you nothing — you would not know what to do in the next question.
So read the question before you write anything. Ask only one thing: whose derivative is already here? That one question is the whole method.

quickChecks.q: Evaluate ∫ tan⁴x sec²x dx
steps: 1. sec²x is the derivative of tan x, so put t = tan x.
2. dt = sec²x dx.
3. ∫ t⁴ dt = t⁵/5.
4. Put t back.

quickChecks.q: Evaluate ∫ sin 2x / (3cos²x + 5sin²x) dx
steps: 1. sin 2x in the numerator — take t = 3cos²x + 5sin²x.
2. dt = (−3 sin 2x + 5 sin 2x) dx = 2 sin 2x dx, so sin 2x dx = dt/2.
4. Put t back.

quickChecks.q: Evaluate ∫ x / (√(1 − x⁴) · sin⁻¹x²) dx
steps: 1. Put t = sin⁻¹x², so dt = 2x/√(1 − x⁴) dx, giving x dx/√(1 − x⁴) = dt/2.
2. The integral becomes (1/2) ∫ dt/t.
4. Put t back.

concepts.title: Writing the answer directly: the f′/f and fⁿ·f′ patterns
concepts.oneLine: Three forms — f′/f, fⁿ·f′ and f′/√f — you can integrate by sight, and you write them directly only as far as you can do it without a mistake.
notes: By now you have seen enough questions to feel how substitution thinking works. There is no rule to hand over here. The feel comes from observing many problems, and observation does not turn into a law.

But there are three shapes where the answer is worth writing directly, every time. In each one the function is sitting there and its derivative is sitting beside it. Put t for f(x) and the integral becomes a baby integral in t — so why do the writing?

If 1/t comes, the answer is ln of f(x). If tⁿ comes, the answer is f(x)^(n+1)/(n+1). If t^(−½) comes, the answer is f(x)^(½) divided by ½, which is 2√f(x). Wherever you can see it, write the direct answer there.

If you are a little slower with this and still cannot see it directly, that is fine. Everyone works according to their own capability. But never do anything wrong just for the sake of going direct. Do as much as you can see cleanly, and write the rest with substitution.

quickChecks.q: ∫ 2x/(x² + 1) dx
steps: 1. Derivative of x² + 1 is 2x, which is exactly the numerator.
2. So this is the f′/f shape.

quickChecks.q: ∫ 3x²(x³ + 5)⁴ dx
steps: 1. Here f = x³ + 5 and f′ = 3x², which is sitting outside.
2. So this is the fⁿ·f′ shape with n = 4.
3. Raise the power to 5 and divide by 5.
1. f = x² + 4, f′ = 2x, which is on top.
2. So this is the f′/√f shape.
3. Answer is twice the root of f.

concepts.title: Thought process 2: substituting to remove a radical
concepts.quote: Everything in this part follows from one line you can write in your notebook: remove the radical sign. No new formula, no new theory — just common sense and one clean substitution.
concepts.oneLine: If a radical is sitting in the question, substitute the inside as a matching power — x−5 = t² for a square root, 2+x = t³ for a cube root — and what is left is a plain polynomial.
notes: Look at what is under the radical. If it is a square root of x−5, put x−5 = t². If it is a cube root of 2+x, put 2+x = t³. The power you choose is exactly the power that kills the root, nothing else.

Once you do that, differentiate both sides to get dx. For x−5 = t² you get dx = 2t dt. For 2+x = t³ you get dx = 3t² dt. Then also write x itself in terms of t, because the rest of the question still has x in it: x = 5 + t², or x = t³ − 2.
After the substitution the radical is gone. √(x−5) is simply t, and ∛(2+x) is simply t. Now expand the bracket, multiply, and you are integrating plain powers of t — the easiest thing in the chapter.
One small thing about √t². In indefinite integration do not drag a mod sign of t around; write it directly as t. Mod matters when you come to definite integration, and we will look at it there.

quickChecks.q: Integrate x√(x−1).
steps: 1. Square root with x−1 inside, so put x−1 = t², dx = 2t dt, x = 1 + t².
3. Put t = √(x−1) back.

quickChecks.q: Integrate x/√(x+4).
steps: 1. Put x+4 = t², so dx = 2t dt, x = t² − 4, and √(x+4) = t.
3. Put t = √(x+4) back.

quickChecks.q: Integrate x·∛(x−1).
steps: 1. Cube root, so put x−1 = t³, dx = 3t² dt, x = 1 + t³, and ∛(x−1) = t.
2. ∫ (1 + t³)·t·3t² dt = 3∫ (t³ + t⁶) dt = 3t⁴/4 + 3t⁷/7.
3. Put t = (x−1)^1/3 back.

concepts.title: Two different roots at once: put x+1 = t⁶, then split
concepts.oneLine: When two different roots of the same bracket appear, put the bracket equal to t raised to the LCM of the root orders — here x+1 = t⁶ — and finish the leftover t³/(t−1) by splitting or by shifting y = t−1.
notes: Look at the powers, not the question. One term has power 1/2, the other has power 1/3. Put x+1 = t² and the cube root survives; put x+1 = t³ and the square root survives.
So take the LCM of 2 and 3, which is 6, and put x+1 = t⁶. Now both powers become whole numbers and both radicals vanish together. That gives dx = 6t⁵ dt, √(x+1) = t³ and ∛(x+1) = t².

After cancelling, what is left is 6∫ t³/(t−1) dt. There is no technique and no formula here — this is only splitting, which came earlier. Write t³ as (t³ − 1) + 1 and the whole thing opens up into t² + t + 1 plus 1/(t−1).

There is a second route, if you prefer it: put y = t − 1, so t = y + 1 and dt = dy. Then the top becomes (y+1)³ over y, and you divide term by term. Both routes are correct — just remember to come all the way back to x at the end. Recall the two thought processes so far: first, spot that the derivative of some function is sitting in the question; second, substitute only to remove a radical sign, even when no derivative is visible. This question is thought process number 2.

quickChecks.q: Evaluate ∫ dx / (√x + ∛x).
steps: 1. LCM of 2 and 3 is 6, so put x = t⁶, dx = 6t⁵ dt, √x = t³, ∛x = t².
2. Integral = ∫ 6t⁵ dt/(t³ + t²) = 6 ∫ t³/(t + 1) dt.
5. Put t = ⁶√x back.

quickChecks.q: Evaluate ∫ dx / (x^(1/2) + x^(1/4)).
steps: 1. LCM of 2 and 4 is 4, so put x = t⁴, dx = 4t³ dt, x^(1/2) = t², x^(1/4) = t.
2. Integral = ∫ 4t³ dt/(t² + t) = 4 ∫ t²/(t + 1) dt.
