5. Put t = ⁴√x back.

quickChecks.q: In ∫ dx / ((x − 2)^(1/3) + (x − 2)^(1/4)), what substitution clears both radicals, and what does the denominator become?
steps: 1. The root orders are 3 and 4, and LCM of 3 and 4 is 12.
2. Put x − 2 = t¹², so dx = 12t¹¹ dt.
3. Then (x − 2)^(1/3) = t⁴ and (x − 2)^(1/4) = t³, so the denominator becomes t⁴ + t³ = t³(t + 1).
quickChecks.answer: x − 2 = t¹²; the integral becomes 12 ∫ t⁸/(t + 1) dt, a pure splitting question

concepts.title: Thought process 3: take the highest power of x common
concepts.oneLine: When no derivative is visible, pull the highest power of x out of the bracket — a negative power of x appears whose derivative is already sitting in the integrand.
notes: Thought process 1 was: the derivative of one part is written somewhere. Thought process 2 was: remove the radical sign. Now the third one, and this is a very common variety.

Take the power of x common — normally the highest power — so that a derivative gets created. Inside the bracket, taking x⁵ common does not mean only one term changes. Every single term of the bracket gets divided by x⁵. So x⁵ + 1 becomes x⁵(1 + x⁻⁵).

Why do this? Because 1 + x⁻⁵ differentiates to −5x⁻⁶, and the x⁵ you pulled out combines with the x already outside to give exactly x⁻⁶ dx in the numerator. The derivative was never in the question; you manufactured it.

One more thing about taking common. If the bracket is sitting under a power like 6/7, then whatever you pull out also carries that power. Pull x⁷ out of (x⁷ + 1)^(6/7) and outside you get (x⁷)^(6/7) = x⁶, not x⁷. Common can be taken from anywhere — just divide every term by it and respect the power.

quickChecks.q: Integrate ∫ dx / (x(x³ + 1))
steps: 1. Take x³ common: x³ + 1 = x³(1 + x⁻³).
2. Denominator = x · x³(1 + x⁻³) = x⁴(1 + x⁻³), so the integral is ∫ x⁻⁴ dx / (1 + x⁻³).
3. Put 1 + x⁻³ = t, so −3x⁻⁴ dx = dt, that is x⁻⁴ dx = −dt/3.
4. Integral = −(1/3) ∫ dt/t = −(1/3) ln|t| + C, and t = (x³ + 1)/x³.

quickChecks.q: Integrate ∫ dx / (x²(x⁵ + 1)^(4/5))
steps: 1. Take x⁵ common from the bracket. The power 4/5 travels with it: (x⁵)^(4/5) = x⁴, so (x⁵ + 1)^(4/5) = x⁴(1 + x⁻⁵)^(4/5).
2. Denominator = x² · x⁴ = x⁶ times (1 + x⁻⁵)^(4/5). Integral = ∫ x⁻⁶ dx / (1 + x⁻⁵)^(4/5).
3. Put 1 + x⁻⁵ = t, so −5x⁻⁶ dx = dt, that is x⁻⁶ dx = −dt/5.

quickChecks.q: Integrate ∫ dx / (x(x⁷ + 1))
steps: 1. Take x⁷ common: x⁷ + 1 = x⁷(1 + x⁻⁷).
2. Denominator = x · x⁷(1 + x⁻⁷) = x⁸(1 + x⁻⁷), so the integral is ∫ x⁻⁸ dx / (1 + x⁻⁷).
3. Put 1 + x⁻⁷ = t, so −7x⁻⁸ dx = dt, that is x⁻⁸ dx = −dt/7.
4. Integral = −(1/7) ln|t| + C, and t = (x⁷ + 1)/x⁷.

concepts.title: Linear upon linear: adjusting powers to substitute (x+2)/(x−1)
concepts.oneLine: When a fourth root hides (x−1)³(x+2)⁵, balance the two powers so that a linear upon linear becomes t — and it does not matter which of the two you call t, both roads land on the same answer.
notes: Look at the powers first: 3 and 5. They add up to 8, and 8 is a multiple of 4, the index of the root. That is the whole signal. It tells me I can force a linear upon linear inside the root and take the rest out cleanly.

The trick is balancing. To take (x+2)/(x−1) as t, note that (x+2) is already sitting with power 5, so (x−1) must be given the power 5 as well — and whatever goes below has to go above too. If you write power 5 below, you have to write power 5 above too; that is the one rule in this whole question. So (x−1)³ quietly becomes (x−1)³⁺⁵ = (x−1)⁸, and the fourth root of that walks out as (x−1)².

Why is that (x−1)² outside no trouble at all? Because of one fact: differentiate any linear upon linear and you get a constant on top and the square of the denominator at the bottom. Nothing else. So the exact piece needed for dx is already waiting, and a constant never troubles an integration.

Now do the same question upside down, taking (x−1)/(x+2) as t. Now (x−1) has power 3, so (x+2) gets power 3 too, (x+2)⁵ becomes (x+2)⁸, and this time (x+2)² comes out. Same length, same answer. So when the printed answer looks different from yours, don't panic — ((x+2)/(x−1))^(−1/4) and ((x−1)/(x+2))^(1/4) are the same thing written two ways.

quickChecks.q: Differentiate (2x+3)/(x−4) and say what shape the answer has.
steps: 2. Numerator: 2x − 8 − 2x − 3 = −11.
3. So the derivative is −11/(x−4)².
quickChecks.answer: −11/(x−4)² — a constant on top, the square of the denominator below, exactly as promised for every linear upon linear.

quickChecks.q: Evaluate ∫ dx / ⁴√((x+1)³(x+3)⁵).
steps: 1. Powers add: 3 + 5 = 8, a multiple of 4. Go ahead.
3. Fourth root: (x+1)² outside, power 5/4 inside. I = ∫ dx / [(x+1)² · t^(5/4)].

quickChecks.q: Evaluate ∫ dx / √((x+1)(x+2)³).
steps: 1. Powers add: 1 + 3 = 4, a multiple of 2, the index of the square root. Same game.
3. Square root: (x+2)² outside, power 1/2 inside. I = ∫ dx / [(x+2)² · t^(1/2)].

concepts.title: Quiz solutions: taking x² and x³ common
concepts.oneLine: In these quiz problems you take out of the bracket exactly the same power of x that sits inside it — x² in the first, x³ in the second — because the leftover power in the denominator, x³ or x⁴, is precisely the derivative you need for 1/x² or 1/x³.
notes: The first one was ∫ dx / (x²√(1 + x²)). Inside the root sits x², so x² is what comes out common: √(1 + x²) = √(x²(1/x² + 1)) = x√(1 + 1/x²). That x comes out of the root and joins the x² already there, so the denominator becomes x³.
Now look at what x³ is: d/dx (1/x²) = −2/x³, so dx/x³ is exactly the piece that matches t = 1 + 1/x². Nothing is left over, nothing is forced. That is why option (b) was correct.

The second one was the same story one step up: ∫ dx / (x³(1 + x³)^(1/3)). Here the bracket carries x³, so take x³ common: (1 + x³)^(1/3) = x(1 + 1/x³)^(1/3). One x comes out, the denominator becomes x⁴ — and 1/x⁴ is the derivative of 1/x³, since d/dx (1/x³) = −3/x⁴.

So the power inside the bracket decides everything. Take x^n common, and the denominator gives you x^(n+1), which is always the derivative of 1/x^n. Substitute t = 1 + 1/x^n and the integral becomes a one-line power rule.

quickChecks.q: Evaluate ∫ dx / (x²√(x² + 4)).
steps: 1. Take x² common inside the root: √(x² + 4) = x√(1 + 4/x²).
2. Integral = ∫ dx / (x³√(1 + 4/x²)).
3. t = 1 + 4/x² gives dt = −8/x³ dx, so dx/x³ = −dt/8.
5. Back in x: −√(x² + 4)/(4x) + C.

quickChecks.q: Evaluate ∫ dx / (x³(x³ + 8)^(1/3)).
steps: 1. Bracket has x³, so take x³ common: (x³ + 8)^(1/3) = x(1 + 8/x³)^(1/3).
2. Integral = ∫ dx / (x⁴(1 + 8/x³)^(1/3)).
3. t = 1 + 8/x³ gives dt = −24/x⁴ dx, so dx/x⁴ = −dt/24.

quickChecks.q: You take x³ common out of a bracket. Which power of x turns up in the denominator, and whose derivative is it?
steps: 1. One x leaves the bracket and multiplies the x³ already in the denominator, giving x⁴.
2. d/dx (1/x³) = −3/x⁴, so 1/x⁴ is the derivative of 1/x³ up to the constant −3.
quickChecks.answer: x⁴, and it is the derivative of 1/x³ — so substitute t = 1 + 1/x³.

concepts.title: The last set of formulas: the six quadratic formats
concepts.oneLine: The last set of integration formulas is just three quadratic forms — 1/QR, 1/√QR, √QR — each one also allowed a linear factor on top, giving six formats in all.
notes: Before starting, clear one doubt. These substitutions — x = a tan θ for a² + x², and writing things through 1 − cos 2θ over 1 + cos 2θ — are not new and they are not special to integration. They are general substitutions you have been using in maths all along. Integration did not invent them; integration only uses them to derive formulas.
And that is exactly what happens next. On the back of those substitutions comes one more set of formulas, and this one is the last set. After this there is nothing more to add.
Here is the whole set. Three basic forms: 1/QR, 1/√QR, and √QR. Then take those same three forms and multiply each by a linear: LR/QR, LR/√QR, and LR·√QR. That is six formats.

Fix the shorthand now. LR means a linear function, ax + b. QR means a quadratic, px² + qx + r. These six formats cover every integral of this family — I write "etc." only because a few look different on the surface but reduce straight back to one of the six. And one more thing before we open the formulas: in the world of integration, only three types of quadratic are actually possible. That is where we go next.

quickChecks.q: Which of the six formats is ∫ (2x + 5)/√(x² + 4x + 9) dx?
steps: 1. The numerator 2x + 5 is of the form ax + b, so it is an LR.
2. Under the root, x² + 4x + 9 is of the form px² + qx + r, so it is a QR.
3. LR on top, √QR below.

quickChecks.q: Classify ∫ √(3x² − x + 1) dx.
steps: 1. There is no linear multiplying it, so no LR.
2. 3x² − x + 1 is a QR, and it is sitting under a root.
3. Root quadratic standing alone.

quickChecks.q: In ∫ (x − 7)/(2x² + 3x + 5) dx, name the LR and the QR, and give the format.
steps: 1. LR = x − 7, that is a = 1, b = −7.
2. QR = 2x² + 3x + 5, that is p = 2, q = 3, r = 5.
3. Linear on top, plain quadratic below.

concepts.title: Only three kinds of quadratic matter in integration
concepts.oneLine: Complete the square and every quadratic in integration becomes one of only three things: x²+a², x²−a² or a²−x².
notes: Take any quadratic and make a perfect square out of it. After that step, only a constant is left over. That leftover is the whole story.

If the square opens upward and a positive constant is left, you have x²+a². If the square opens upward and a negative constant is left, you have x²−a². If the square opens downward and a positive constant is left, you have a²−x². In the world of integration, these three are the only quadratics that exist.

Now the two cases deliberately left out. First: if the quadratic is a perfect square with nothing left over, there is nothing new to teach. Ask me ∫1/(2x+3)² dx and you already know it — it is just a power.

Second: downward opening with a negative constant, like −(2x+3)²−16. That is negative everywhere, so its square root is never defined. A format whose √ is never defined cannot appear in a question, so we never talk about it. Three formats survive, and the nine formulas we are about to write sit on top of them.

quickChecks.q: Complete the square in x² + 6x + 13 and name its format.
steps: 3. Upward opening square with a positive constant left.

quickChecks.q: Complete the square in x² − 4x − 5 and name its format.
steps: 3. Upward opening square with a negative constant left.

quickChecks.q: Which format is 3 − 2x − x²?
steps: 1. Pull out the minus from the x terms: 3 − (x² + 2x).
2. x² + 2x = (x + 1)² − 1, so the expression is 3 − (x + 1)² + 1.
4. Downward opening square with a positive constant in front.

concepts.title: The nine standard formulas: 1/QR and 1/√QR
concepts.oneLine: Three quadratic formats × three shapes (1/Q, 1/√Q, √Q) give exactly nine standard integrals, and the first six are two you already know plus four log results.
notes: Last time we fixed that only three kinds of quadratic matter: a²+x², x²−a² and a²−x². Now pair each of those three with three shapes — the quadratic in the denominator, its square root in the denominator, and the square root sitting on top. Three formats times three shapes is nine, so there must be exactly nine standard formulas here, and there is no tenth.

Write the first set: dx/(a²+x²), dx/(x²−a²), dx/(a²−x²). Then the second set with a root below: dx/√(a²+x²), dx/√(x²−a²), dx/√(a²−x²). The third set is √(a²+x²), √(x²−a²) and √(a²−x²) themselves — that is the next part of class.

Two of these you did in the basics. dx/(a²+x²) gives (1/a)tan⁻¹(x/a) + c, and dx/√(a²−x²) gives sin⁻¹(x/a) + c. Nothing new, but leave their slots open in the list anyway so that when you revise in a month you don't sit and wonder where those two vanished.

That leaves the ones to actually learn. dx/(x²−a²) gives (1/2a)ln|(x−a)/(x+a)| + c, and dx/(a²−x²) gives (1/2a)ln|(a+x)/(a−x)| + c. Their honest derivation is partial fractions, which comes later — but holding them back now would break the chain of nine, so take the results as they stand. The root-below pair, dx/√(a²+x²) and dx/√(x²−a²), both come out as ln|x + √(that quadratic)| + c.

quickChecks.q: Integrate dx/(9+x²).
steps: 1. Format is a²+x² with no root, so a² = 9 and a = 3.
2. Use (1/a)tan⁻¹(x/a).

quickChecks.q: Integrate dx/(x²−25).
steps: 1. Format is x²−a² with a = 5, so 1/2a = 1/10.
2. x² is written first, so x goes first on top: |(x−5)/(x+5)|.

quickChecks.q: Integrate dx/√(x²−4).
steps: 1. Root of x²−a² in the denominator, with a = 2.
2. Use ln|x+√(x²−a²)|.

concepts.title: The √(quadratic) formulas and their shortcut
concepts.oneLine: For ∫√(quadratic) dx the whole answer is x/2 times the same root, plus or minus a²/2 times the integral of its reciprocal — the sign copied from the sign in front of a² inside the root.
notes: Before this, you already know the reciprocal family. ∫dx/√(same quadratic) is simply ln|x + √(same quadratic)| for a² + x² and for x² − a², and sin⁻¹(x/a) for a² − x². Keep those three in your hand, because the new formulas are built on top of them.

Now the three square-root ones. x/2 into the same thing, plus or minus a²/2 into the integral of its reciprocal. That is the entire shortcut. "Same thing" means exactly the expression you were asked to integrate, root and all.

The only decision left is the sign of the second piece. Look at the sign standing in front of a² inside the root: if it is + a², the second term is + a²/2; if it is − a², the second term is − a²/2. The sign of the a² term is copied straight from the sign of a² inside the root.

And the reciprocal part you do not invent — you already wrote it in the previous formulas. Root types with x² give you the ln form, and a² − x² gives you sin⁻¹(x/a). That is the last set of formulas in the whole of integration; after this, no new formula is coming.

quickChecks.q: ∫√(9 + x²) dx
steps: 1. Here a² = 9, so a = 3, and the root is of the a² + x² type.
2. x/2 into the same thing: x/2 · √(9 + x²).
3. a² is positive inside, so add (9/2) times the reciprocal integral ln|x + √(9 + x²)|.
1. a² = 16, so a²/2 = 8, and this is the x² − a² type.
2. x/2 into the same thing: x/2 · √(x² − 16).
3. a² is negative inside, so subtract: − 8 ln|x + √(x² − 16)|.
1. a² = 25, so a = 5, and this is the a² − x² type.
2. x/2 into the same thing: x/2 · √(25 − x²).
3. a² is positive inside, so + 25/2, and the reciprocal integral here is sin⁻¹(x/5).

concepts.title: Deriving 1/(a²−x²) and pairing the formulas to remember them
concepts.oneLine: Write the 1 on top as (a+x)+(a−x) over 2a and ∫dx/(a²−x²) falls out in four lines; its partner ∫dx/(x²−a²) then comes free by taking −1 common.
notes: 1/(a²−x²) and 1/(x²−a²) are the two formulas that get swapped in the exam. The answers differ only in what sits on top inside the log, and that is exactly the part your memory loses first.

Remember only one of a pair, and derive the other in one line. For the first one, the denominator factors as (a−x)(a+x). The only problem is the top: to split the fraction you need an x up there. So write the numerator as (a+x)+(a−x). That sum is 2a, not 1, so pull out 1/2a to keep it honest.

Now it splits into 1/(a−x) + 1/(a+x). Integrate: the first gives ln|a−x| divided by the coefficient of x, which is −1, so it comes with a minus. The second gives ln|a+x|. Subtract the logs and you have (1/2a)ln|(a+x)/(a−x)| + C.

For the partner, take −1 common. x²−a² = −(a²−x²), so the whole answer just picks up a minus sign. And a minus sitting outside a log goes inside as a reciprocal of the input — so (a+x)/(a−x) flips to (a−x)/(a+x), and since the mod is there, |a−x| = |x−a|. Done. The same economy works on the root pair: in ln|x+√(x²+a²)|, put −a² in place of a² and you have the other one.

quickChecks.q: ∫dx/(9 − x²)
steps: 1. This is 1/(a² − x²) with a² = 9, so a = 3.
1. This is 1/(x² − a²) with a = 5, so 1/2a = 1/10.
2. Here x comes first inside the log: (1/2a) ln|(x−a)/(x+a)|.

quickChecks.q: You remember ∫dx/√(x²+a²) = ln|x+√(x²+a²)| + C. Write ∫dx/√(x² − 16) from it.
steps: 1. In the remembered formula, put −a² in place of a².
2. So the answer becomes ln|x + √(x² − a²)| + C, with a² = 16.

concepts.title: Applying the formulas after a linear change: three examples
concepts.oneLine: Any standard formula still works when x is replaced by 5x+4 — write the formula unchanged, then divide by 5, the coefficient of x.
notes: First, you must be able to complete the square on your own. You have already done the quadratic chapter, so I will not teach it again here. Once the quadratic is sitting as a² − x² or a² + x², the question is finished.

Now the one rule for this whole section: if any formula has px+q sitting in place of x, the formula stays exactly as it is, and you divide the answer by p. So for 5x+4, you multiply by 1/5. Nothing else moves.

It is worth doing three times — once with 1/(a²−x²), once with 1/√(a²+x²), once with 1/√(a²−x²). Same three steps every time: spot the format, put a and the new x into the formula, then divide by the coefficient of x.
Mark that 1/5 out clearly as you write it. It is the only part that is new here, and the part most often forgotten.

quickChecks.q: Evaluate ∫ dx / √(16 − (3x+1)²)
steps: 1. Format 1/√(a²−x²) with a = 4, and x → 3x+1.
2. Formula: sin⁻¹(x/a) → sin⁻¹((3x+1)/4).
3. Coefficient of x is 3, so multiply by 1/3.

quickChecks.q: Evaluate ∫ dx / (25 − (2x+3)²)
steps: 1. Format 1/(a²−x²) with a = 5, and x → 2x+3.
3. Coefficient of x is 2, so multiply by 1/2, giving 1/20 outside.

quickChecks.q: Evaluate ∫ dx / √(4 + (5x+4)²)
steps: 1. Format 1/√(a²+x²) with a = 2, and x → 5x+4.
3. Coefficient of x is 5, so multiply by 1/5.

concepts.title: ∫√(4+(5x+3)²)dx, and the safe t-substitution
concepts.oneLine: For ∫√(4+(5x+3)²)dx use the (x/2)·√(same quadratic) + (a²/2)·(log form) pattern with the whole bracket 5x+3 as x, then multiply by 1/5 — and if that feels slippery, put t = 5x+3 first and spend one extra line.
notes: Look at ∫√(4+(5x+3)²)dx and ask only one question: which formula is this? It is √(x² + a²), where the "x" is the whole bracket 5x+3 and a² = 4, so a = 2.

The formula says: (x/2) × the same quadratic under the root, plus (a²/2) × the integral of the reciprocal of that same root. "Same thing" means exactly the same quadratic — whatever is written inside, copy it as it is, 4+(5x+3)². And the integral of that reciprocal is ln of x plus the same root.

So the answer carries (5x+3)/2 × √(4+(5x+3)²), plus (4/2) × ln|5x+3 + √(4+(5x+3)²)|. One last care: since the coefficient of x inside the bracket is 5, the whole thing gets multiplied by 1/5 — the reciprocal of 5.

Now, if somebody feels tangled in this, don't fight it. Put t = 5x+3 everywhere, so dx = dt/5, apply the plain formula in t slowly, and substitute back at the end. One extra line is never the problem; losing the whole question to save that line is.

quickChecks.q: Integrate ∫√(9 + (2x+1)²) dx
steps: 1. Form √(x²+a²) with "x" = 2x+1 and a² = 9.
4. Coefficient of x is 2, so multiply everything by 1/2.

quickChecks.q: Integrate ∫√(25 + (3x−2)²) dx, using t = 3x−2 first
steps: 1. Put t = 3x−2, so dt = 3 dx and dx = dt/3. The integral becomes (1/3)∫√(25+t²)dt.
2. Apply the plain formula with a² = 25: (1/3)[ (t/2)√(25+t²) + (25/2) ln|t + √(25+t²)| ] + C.
3. Substitute t = 3x−2 back.

quickChecks.q: Integrate ∫dx/√(16 + (4x+5)²)
steps: 1. This is the reciprocal form with "x" = 4x+5 and a² = 16.
2. Plain result: ln|4x+5 + √(16+(4x+5)²)|.
3. Coefficient of x is 4, so multiply by 1/4.

concepts.title: Linear over quadratic: split the linear as a·(quadratic)′ + b
concepts.oneLine: For any linear over quadratic — plain, under a root, or one over the root — write the linear as a·(derivative of the quadratic) + b, and the question splits into an ln piece and a standard-formula piece.
notes: We already have the three starting formats for 1/quadratic. The only thing spoiling a new question is a linear sitting with the quadratic — 5x+3 on top, or 5x+3 under a root. So the whole job is to get rid of that linear.
Write the linear as a·(derivative of the quadratic) + b. That is it. Compare the coefficient of x, compare the constant term, and a and b fall out in two seconds.

Now split. The piece carrying a has the exact derivative of the quadratic sitting on top of it, so it integrates to a·ln|quadratic| — a joke, no work. The piece carrying b is a pure constant over the quadratic, so you make the perfect square and use the starting format.

And notice what did not matter: whether the quadratic was plain, under a root, or in the denominator of a root. In every one of the three shapes, the first piece is derivative-over-function (put the quadratic as t) and the second piece is constant over quadratic. Same two steps, always.

quickChecks.q: Evaluate ∫ (3x+1)/(x²+2x+10) dx
steps: 1. Derivative of x²+2x+10 is 2x+2, so write 3x+1 = a(2x+2) + b.
2. Coefficient of x: 2a = 3, so a = 3/2.
3. Constant: 2a + b = 1, and 2a = 3, so b = −2.
5. First piece = (3/2)ln|x²+2x+10|.
6. Perfect square: x²+2x+10 = (x+1)² + 9, so a = 3 and the second integral is (1/3)tan⁻¹((x+1)/3).
7. Multiply that by −2.

quickChecks.q: For the quadratic x²+6x+13, write 7x−4 in the format a(derivative) + b and find a and b.
steps: 1. Derivative of x²+6x+13 is 2x+6, so 7x−4 = a(2x+6) + b.
2. Coefficient of x: 2a = 7, so a = 7/2.
3. Constant: 6a + b = −4, and 6a = 21, so b = −25.

quickChecks.q: Evaluate ∫ (4x−1)/(x²+8x+20) dx
steps: 1. Derivative of x²+8x+20 is 2x+8, so write 4x−1 = a(2x+8) + b.
2. Coefficient of x: 2a = 4, so a = 2.
3. Constant: 8a + b = −1, and 8a = 16, so b = −17.
5. First piece = 2ln|x²+8x+20|.
6. Perfect square: x²+8x+20 = (x+4)² + 4, so a = 2 and the second integral is (1/2)tan⁻¹((x+4)/2).
7. Multiply that by −17.

concepts.title: How to revise this class
concepts.oneLine: Revise this class in one fixed order — common substitutions, then the formula sheet, then its applications, then t for anything that won't go directly, and finally the linear-over-quadratic split.
notes: Is it all clear? Good. But clear is not enough here — this chapter only becomes yours with practice. That is why the questions come written out by hand, with the full logic, so that you never feel a gap anywhere.

When you open the notes, start with the first slide: the common substitutions. Then come to the handwritten slide, where every formula sits together in one place. Right after it come the applications of that sheet, including a few already covered earlier. Read it in that order and the logic clicks on its own.
After the applications, remember the fallback. If you cannot see your way through an expression, do not force a direct integration. Put t in place of the linear part and move forward.

Last comes the linear case. If a linear term shows up on top of a quadratic, there is only one way to handle it: write the linear as a constant times the derivative of the quadratic, plus a leftover constant. Once you split it like that, the integration becomes very easy. One example of it is written right there in the notes.

quickChecks.q: In ∫ (2x+3)/(x²+4x+5) dx, write the numerator as a·(derivative of the denominator) + b.
steps: 1. Derivative of x²+4x+5 is 2x+4.
2. Compare 2x+3 with a(2x+4)+b: 2a = 2, so a = 1.
3. Constants: 4a + b = 3 → 4 + b = 3 → b = −1.

quickChecks.q: You cannot see any direct formula for an expression that has a linear term inside. What is your next move?
steps: 1. Do not push for a direct integration.
2. Put t equal to that linear part and write dx in terms of dt.
quickChecks.answer: Substitute t for the linear part — never force the direct route.

quickChecks.q: In ∫ (3x+1)/(x²−2x+7) dx, find the constants in the linear split.
steps: 1. Derivative of x²−2x+7 is 2x−2.
3. Constants: −2a + b = 1 → −3 + b = 1 → b = 4.

concepts.title: Homework set: which technique each problem needs
concepts.oneLine: Before you solve a homework integral, label it: derivative sitting on top (substitution), a straight formula, or a linear format inside the function.
notes: Look at homework problems 1 and 2 first. In both of them the derivative is sitting right there with the function — the derivative of sin in one, the derivative of cos in the other. When the derivative of the inner part is already present in the question, that is your signal to substitute, and after the substitution you simply integrate.

This is not a new concept. It is the same substitution idea from this class, only dressed up in homework clothes. Put the inner function as t, the derivative takes care of dt, and what is left is a basic integral you already know.

Problems 3, 4, 5 and 6 are different. Nothing has to be substituted in these — they are direct. You recognise the standard form and you write the answer from the formula. They are here from the practice point of view, so do not complicate them.

Problem 7 is the linear format. The function has something like ax + b inside it instead of a plain x. Integrate it as if the inside were x, then divide by the coefficient of x. One scan of the question first, label the method, then solve — that habit saves you more time in the paper than any speed trick.

quickChecks.q: Which method does ∫ 2x cos(x²) dx need, and what is the answer?
steps: 1. The inner function is x², and its derivative 2x is already sitting in the question — so this is the derivative-present type.
2. Put x² = t, then 2x dx = dt.
3. The integral becomes ∫ cos t dt = sin t + c.
4. Put t back as x².

quickChecks.q: Which method does ∫ sec²x dx need, and what is the answer?
steps: 1. There is no inner function and no derivative hanging around — this is a standard form.
2. Write the answer directly from the formula.

quickChecks.q: Which method does ∫ cos(5x + 3) dx need, and what is the answer?
steps: 1. Inside the cos we have 5x + 3, a linear expression — so this is the linear format.
2. Integrate as if the inside were x: that gives sin(5x + 3).
3. Divide by the coefficient of x, which is 5.

concepts.title: What you can already integrate: the quadratic formats
concepts.oneLine: Right now you can already integrate any quadratic, and any quadratic multiplied by a linear — make the perfect square, then pick one of the nine standard formulas.
notes: Before we move ahead, fix in your head what you can already do. Any quadratic, and a quadratic multiplied by a linear — both of these you can now handle completely.
The method is the same both times. You make a perfect square out of the quadratic, and then you apply whichever of our nine standard formulas fits the shape you are left with.
That is it. No new thinking is needed in those two formats — just the perfect square, then the right formula off the list of nine.
That is what the homework set was for. If you are clear here, the rest moves forward with a lot of planning. It will take time. Let it take time.

quickChecks.q: You are given an integral whose denominator is a quadratic in x. What is your first step?
steps: 1. Do not look for a formula yet.
2. Write the quadratic as a perfect square plus or minus a constant.
3. Now the shape matches one of the nine standard formulas.
quickChecks.answer: Make the perfect square first, then apply the matching standard formula.

quickChecks.q: The integrand has a linear expression multiplied with a quadratic. Is this a new technique?
steps: 1. Check which of our settled formats it belongs to.
2. Quadratic, and quadratic multiplied by linear, are both already covered.
3. So the same perfect square route applies.
quickChecks.answer: No. It is already covered — perfect square, then one of the nine formulas.

quickChecks.q: After making the perfect square, how many standard formulas do you choose from?
steps: 1. Recall the list we built for these formats.
2. It is a fixed list, not an endless one.

concepts.title: Linear upon quadratic, and the sin inverse homework question
concepts.oneLine: Linear upon quadratic = (derivative of the quadratic) + constant, and the same eye for "what is the top the derivative of?" turns ∫ sin x dx/√(sin²x − sin²α) into a plain sin⁻¹ form with cos x = t.
notes: Start with the family we were on: linear upon quadratic. The whole concept is one line — write the linear numerator as λ(derivative of the quadratic) + μ, split the fraction, and you are left with constant upon quadratic. The first piece is a straight log, and the second piece is the standard quadratic format we did just now.
Now the homework question that everyone got stuck on. Here sin²α, tan²α, cos²α — anything with α in it is a constant, not a variable. Only x moves.

Look at the top: sin x dx. That is the derivative of cos x, so the substitution has to be cos x = t. But the bottom is written in sin²x, so first make the bottom speak the same language: sin²x − sin²α = (1 − cos²x) − (1 − cos²α) = cos²α − cos²x. Now top and bottom are both in cos x.
Put cos x = t, so −sin x dx = dt, which means sin x dx = −dt. The integral becomes −∫ dt/√(cos²α − t²), and that is our a² − x² format with a = cos α. Answer: −sin⁻¹(cos x/cos α) + C.

quickChecks.q: Evaluate ∫ sin x dx / √(4 − cos²x).
steps: 1. Top is sin x dx, so put cos x = t, giving sin x dx = −dt.
2. Integral = ∫ (−dt)/√(2² − t²) = −sin⁻¹(t/2) + C.
3. Put t = cos x back.

quickChecks.q: Evaluate ∫ cos x dx / √(9 − sin²x).
steps: 1. Top is cos x dx, so put sin x = t, giving cos x dx = dt (no minus this time).
2. Integral = ∫ dt/√(3² − t²) = sin⁻¹(t/3) + C.
3. Put t = sin x back.

quickChecks.q: Write the numerator of (2x + 3)/(x² + 4x + 5) as (derivative of the denominator) plus a constant.
steps: 1. Derivative of x² + 4x + 5 is 2x + 4.
3. The fraction splits as (2x + 4)/(x² + 4x + 5) − 1/(x² + 4x + 5).
quickChecks.answer: 2x + 3 = (2x + 4) − 1, so the integral is log|x² + 4x + 5| − ∫ dx/(x² + 4x + 5)

concepts.title: Root of (1+x)/(1−x) by trigonometric substitution
concepts.oneLine: The same root, ∫√((1+x)/(1−x)) dx, done by putting x = cos 2θ: the root collapses to cot θ, the integral becomes −4∫cos²θ dθ, and the answer comes back as −cos⁻¹x − √(1−x²) + C.
notes: Rationalising solves this one cleanly, and nothing here replaces that. In an exam, rationalising stays the first choice for this question.

There is a second road worth seeing. Whenever a root carries the pair (1+x) and (1−x) together, you can put x = cos 2θ. Then 1+x = 2cos²θ and 1−x = 2sin²θ, both perfect squares, and the root just opens up.

Divide those two and you get cot²θ, not tan²θ — the cos sits on top, so the root is cot θ. Then dx = −2 sin 2θ dθ, and you are integrating cot θ · (−2 sin 2θ) dθ. Break both into sin and cos, the sin θ cancels, and what survives inside is only cos²θ.

From there it is the half-angle form you know: cos²θ = (1+cos 2θ)/2. You get −2θ − sin 2θ + C, and since x = cos 2θ, that is −cos⁻¹x − √(1−x²) + C. Looks different from the rationalisation answer only until you use sin⁻¹x + cos⁻¹x = π/2 — the π/2 is swallowed by C and the two answers are the same.

quickChecks.q: In ∫√((1+x)/(1−x)) dx you put x = cos 2θ. What does the root become, and what is dx?
steps: 1. 1 + x = 1 + cos 2θ = 2cos²θ; 1 − x = 1 − cos 2θ = 2sin²θ.
2. Ratio = cos²θ/sin²θ = cot²θ, so the root is cot θ.
3. x = cos 2θ gives dx = −2 sin 2θ dθ.
quickChecks.answer: Root = cot θ and dx = −2 sin 2θ dθ.

quickChecks.q: Do the same integral ∫√((1+x)/(1−x)) dx by rationalising, and check it agrees with −cos⁻¹x − √(1−x²) + C.
steps: 1. Multiply top and bottom inside the root by (1+x): √((1+x)²/(1−x²)) = (1+x)/√(1−x²).
2. Split: ∫ dx/√(1−x²) + ∫ x dx/√(1−x²).
3. First part = sin⁻¹x. Second part: put 1 − x² = t, so x dx = −dt/2, giving −√(1−x²).
4. So the integral is sin⁻¹x − √(1−x²) + C.
5. Compare: −cos⁻¹x − √(1−x²) = sin⁻¹x − π/2 − √(1−x²). The two differ by the constant π/2.
quickChecks.answer: sin⁻¹x − √(1−x²) + C — same as the substitution answer, differing only by the constant π/2.

quickChecks.q: Now flip it: evaluate ∫√((1−x)/(1+x)) dx with x = cos 2θ.
steps: 1. The root is √(2sin²θ / 2cos²θ) = tan θ this time, and dx = −2 sin 2θ dθ.
2. Integral = −2 ∫ (sin θ/cos θ)(2 sin θ cos θ) dθ = −4 ∫ sin²θ dθ.
3. Use sin²θ = (1 − cos 2θ)/2: −2 ∫ (1 − cos 2θ) dθ = −2θ + sin 2θ + C.
4. Put back 2θ = cos⁻¹x and sin 2θ = √(1−x²).

concepts.title: Quadratic upon quadratic: reduce it by long division
concepts.quote: Linear upon quadratic you can already do with your eyes closed. So when an x² turns up on top as well, you don't learn anything new — you just make the top smaller.
concepts.oneLine: If the top's degree is not smaller than the bottom's, divide first — long division turns quadratic/quadratic into a constant plus linear/quadratic, and cubic/quadratic into a polynomial plus linear/quadratic.
notes: Look at the degrees first. If the top is linear and the bottom is quadratic, you know the move: write the top as a multiple of the derivative of the bottom, plus a constant. The moment an x² sits upstairs, that move cannot even start — the derivative of a quadratic is linear, so it can never give you an x².

So divide first: long division of the top by the bottom turns quadratic upon quadratic into a constant plus linear upon quadratic. And if the top is a cubic, the quotient is not a constant any more, it is a function of x — but the leftover piece is still linear upon quadratic.

After that there is nothing left to teach. Integrate the quotient term by term, and send the remainder part to the method you already have. The three questions here are set up and left unfinished on purpose, because finishing them is old work.
The same thinking survives a substitution. Put t for sin x in that last one and what you are staring at is a cubic in t over a quadratic in t — long division again.

quickChecks.q: Integrate (x² + 3)/(x² + 1) with respect to x.
steps: 1. Same degree on top and bottom, so divide: quotient is 1.
2. (x² + 3) − (x² + 1) = 2, so the fraction is 1 + 2/(x² + 1).
3. Integrate each piece: x + 2 tan⁻¹x.

quickChecks.q: Write (x² + 5x + 1)/(x² + x + 1) as a constant plus linear upon quadratic.
steps: 1. Quotient is 1 since both are degree 2 with leading coefficient 1.
2. (x² + 5x + 1) − (x² + x + 1) = 4x, so the remainder is 4x.

quickChecks.q: Reduce (x³ + 2x² + 3x + 4)/(x² + 1) by long division.
steps: 1. First term x: x(x² + 1) = x³ + x. Subtract: 2x² + 2x + 4.
2. Next term 2: 2(x² + 1) = 2x² + 2. Subtract: 2x + 2.
3. Quotient x + 2, remainder 2x + 2. Check: (x + 2)(x² + 1) + 2x + 2 = x³ + 2x² + 3x + 4.

concepts.title: The flow of the chapter so far
concepts.oneLine: Before the next trick, fix the order of the chapter in your head: ax+b in a standard formula → a hidden derivative → highest power of x common → trigonometric substitution → the nine quadratic forms → quadratic multiplied by a linear, a quadratic or a cubic.
notes: Look back at what we have built, in order. We started with substitution. If any standard formula has ax+b sitting inside it, the formula still works — you only divide by a, the coefficient of x. That was step one.

Then came the hunt for a derivative that is hiding. Sometimes it is not obvious: you put t = x·eˣ, or t = tan⁻¹x, and the derivative is already written right there in the question. Nothing fancy — once you have seen a few, your eye catches it.

After that came the first proper algebraic shape: the dirty polynomial. Take the highest power of x common, and the derivative gets created for you. From there it is plain substitution again. Then came a fresh thought process — trigonometric substitution — and on top of it, the nine quadratic forms: 1/quadratic, 1/√quadratic and √quadratic.

And the chapter does not stop there. Once the quadratic is handled, the same machinery survives when that quadratic is multiplied by a linear, by another quadratic, or by a cubic. That is where we are standing right now. If this flow is not in your mind, the chapter will eat your months; if it is, every new question is just "which stage is this?"

quickChecks.q: Which stage of the flow does ∫ dx/(x² + 6x + 13) belong to, and what is the answer?
steps: 1. Shape is 1/quadratic → stage 4, the nine quadratic forms.
2. Complete the square: x² + 6x + 13 = (x + 3)² + 4.
3. Standard form ∫ dt/(t² + a²) with t = x + 3, a = 2.

quickChecks.q: Which stage does ∫ dx/((x + 1)√(x² + 2x + 5)) belong to?
steps: 1. There is a √quadratic in the denominator, and a linear factor multiplying it.
2. So it is not the plain quadratic form — it is one layer above.
quickChecks.answer: Stage 5 — quadratic multiplied by a linear; clear the linear factor first, then it becomes a stage-4 quadratic form.

quickChecks.q: Solve ∫ dx/(x(1 + x⁵)) using the stage you would pick for it.
steps: 1. Dirty polynomial → stage 3: take the highest power of x common.
2. 1 + x⁵ = x⁵(x⁻⁵ + 1), so the denominator becomes x·x⁵(1 + x⁻⁵) = x⁶(1 + x⁻⁵).
3. Integral = ∫ x⁻⁶ dx/(1 + x⁻⁵).
4. Put t = 1 + x⁻⁵, so dt = −5x⁻⁶ dx, i.e. x⁻⁶ dx = −dt/5.
5. Integral = −(1/5)∫ dt/t = −(1/5) ln|t| + C.

concepts.title: Even powers only: divide by x² and hunt for a derivative
concepts.oneLine: When every power of x is even, divide top and bottom by x², then substitute t = x − a²/x or t = x + a²/x, whichever derivative the numerator matches.
notes: Look at the powers of x first. If every power you can see is even — x², x⁴, a constant — that is your signal. Divide the numerator and the denominator by x² and the whole question changes shape.

Say the denominator is x⁴ + kx² + a⁴. Divide each piece by x²: x⁴/x² gives x², kx²/x² gives k, and a⁴/x² gives a⁴/x². So the bottom becomes x² + a⁴/x² + k. Nothing is lost, the question is just dressed differently.

Now the reverse question. Look at the new numerator and ask: whose derivative is this? If the numerator is 1 + a²/x², integrate it in your head — 1 gives x, and a²·x⁻² gives −a²/x. So that numerator is the derivative of x − a²/x. So put t = x − a²/x. If instead the numerator is 1 − a²/x², the same check gives t = x + a²/x.

One piece is still missing: the denominator has x² + a⁴/x², and t only has x and a²/x. So square the substitution. Squaring t = x − a²/x gives t² = x² − 2a² + a⁴/x², so x² + a⁴/x² = t² + 2a². Put that in, and the denominator becomes a plain quadratic in t that you already know how to integrate.

quickChecks.q: In ∫ (x² + 1)/(x⁴ + 1) dx, what is the right substitution?
steps: 1. Divide numerator and denominator by x²: numerator becomes 1 + 1/x², denominator becomes x² + 1/x².
2. Whose derivative is 1 + 1/x²? It is x − 1/x.
3. So t = x − 1/x, and t² = x² − 2 + 1/x², giving x² + 1/x² = t² + 2.
quickChecks.answer: t = x − 1/x; the integral becomes ∫ dt/(t² + 2).

quickChecks.q: In ∫ (x² − 1)/(x⁴ + 3x² + 1) dx, what is the substitution and the denominator in t?
steps: 1. All powers are even, so divide top and bottom by x²: numerator 1 − 1/x², denominator x² + 1/x² + 3.
2. The numerator 1 − 1/x² is the derivative of x + 1/x, so t = x + 1/x.
3. Square: t² = x² + 2 + 1/x², so x² + 1/x² = t² − 2.
4. Denominator becomes t² − 2 + 3 = t² + 1.
quickChecks.answer: t = x + 1/x, and the integral becomes ∫ dt/(t² + 1).

quickChecks.q: Here a² = 2. If the numerator after dividing is 1 + 2/x² and the denominator is x² + 4/x² + 5, write the integral in t.
steps: 1. 1 + 2/x² is the derivative of x − 2/x, so t = x − 2/x.
2. Square: t² = x² − 4 + 4/x², so x² + 4/x² = t² + 4.
3. Denominator becomes t² + 4 + 5 = t² + 9.
quickChecks.answer: t = x − 2/x; the integral becomes ∫ dt/(t² + 9).

concepts.title: The board classics: x + 1/x and x − 1/x
concepts.quote: Most students see (x² − 1)/(x⁴ + x² + 1) and shut the book. Give me five minutes and you will finish four of the most asked integration questions with the same one line of work.
concepts.oneLine: Divide by x², let t = x + 1/x when the top is (1 − 1/x²) and t = x − 1/x when the top is (1 + 1/x²); the first lands on a log, the second on a tan inverse, and the 1/(1+x⁴) and x²/(1+x⁴) questions are just their difference and sum.
notes: These four questions travel together — label them A, B, C and D. In the board exam they are among the most-asked of this chapter. A and B look impossible and are actually the easiest once you divide by x².

The whole decision is made by the numerator. If after dividing you get (1 − 1/x²) on top, that is the derivative of x + 1/x, so t = x + 1/x. If you get (1 + 1/x²), that is the derivative of x − 1/x, so t = x − 1/x. Pick t from the top, never from the bottom — the numerator tells you which substitution the question wants.

Then square your t and the bottom collapses. With t = x + 1/x you get x² + 1/x² = t² − 2, and the denominator becomes t² minus a constant, which is a log. With t = x − 1/x you get x² + 1/x² = t² + 2, and the denominator becomes t² plus a constant, which is a tan inverse.

C and D are the free marks. ∫dx/(1+x⁴) is half of (B − B′) and ∫x²dx/(1+x⁴) is half of (B + B′), where B′ is the (x² − 1)/(x⁴ + 1) version. So you never solve C or D from scratch; you solve two easy even-power integrals and add or subtract them.

quickChecks.q: ∫ (x² + 1)/(x⁴ + 5x² + 1) dx
steps: 1. Divide by x²: top 1 + 1/x², bottom x² + 5 + 1/x².
2. Top is d(x − 1/x), so t = x − 1/x and x² + 1/x² = t² + 2.
3. Bottom = t² + 2 + 5 = t² + 7, so the integral is ∫ dt/(t² + 7) with a = √7.

quickChecks.q: ∫ (x² − 1)/(x⁴ − 3x² + 1) dx
steps: 1. Divide by x²: top 1 − 1/x², bottom x² − 3 + 1/x².
2. Top is d(x + 1/x), so t = x + 1/x and x² + 1/x² = t² − 2.
3. Bottom = t² − 2 − 3 = t² − 5, so the integral is ∫ dt/(t² − 5) = 1/(2√5) ln|(t − √5)/(t + √5)| + C.
4. Put t = x + 1/x back and multiply top and bottom inside the log by x.

quickChecks.q: ∫ (x² + 1)/(x⁴ − x² + 1) dx
steps: 1. Divide by x²: top 1 + 1/x², bottom x² − 1 + 1/x².
2. Top is d(x − 1/x), so t = x − 1/x and x² + 1/x² = t² + 2.
3. Bottom = t² + 2 − 1 = t² + 1, so the integral is ∫ dt/(t² + 1) = tan⁻¹ t + C.

concepts.title: The thought process behind the even-power slide
concepts.oneLine: Every one of these integrals is the same three questions: divide top and bottom by x², ask whose derivative is sitting on top, then force the denominator into that same variable — and if the numerator is a bare number, split it as (1+x²) + (1−x²).
notes: Look again at what happened in the last two questions. First move: divide the numerator and the denominator by x². Second move: look at the top and ask whose derivative that is. Third move: can the denominator be written in that same variable?

Those three questions are the whole chapter, not just these two sums. If the top becomes 1 − 1/x², that is the derivative of x + 1/x, so t = x + 1/x. If the top becomes 1 + 1/x², that is the derivative of x − 1/x, so t = x − 1/x. The denominator then has to be bent into t² − 2 or t² + 2.

Now the question that confuses everyone: what if the numerator is just a number, say 2? Then nothing is anybody's derivative yet. So manufacture it. Write 2 as (1 + x²) + (1 − x²) — one piece gives the x − 1/x case, the other piece gives the x + 1/x case, and you solve both separately.

That is why the focus belongs here and not on the final formula. The exam will dress the same question in sixth and eighth powers. If you remember only the answer you are finished; if you remember the three questions you will crack it.

quickChecks.q: Integrate (x² − 1)/(x⁴ + 3x² + 1) with respect to x.
steps: 1. Divide top and bottom by x²: ∫ (1 − 1/x²)/(x² + 3 + 1/x²) dx.
2. Top is the derivative of x + 1/x, so t = x + 1/x.
3. x² + 1/x² = t² − 2, so the denominator is t² − 2 + 3 = t² + 1.
4. ∫ dt/(t² + 1) = tan⁻¹ t + C.

quickChecks.q: Integrate (x² + 1)/(x⁴ + 1) with respect to x.
steps: 1. Divide top and bottom by x²: ∫ (1 + 1/x²)/(x² + 1/x²) dx.
2. Top is the derivative of x − 1/x, so t = x − 1/x.
3. x² + 1/x² = t² + 2, so the integral is ∫ dt/(t² + 2).
4. That gives (1/√2) tan⁻¹(t/√2) + C.

quickChecks.q: Integrate 2/(x⁴ + 1) with respect to x.
steps: 1. Bare numerator, so split: 2 = (1 + x²) + (1 − x²).
2. First piece, ∫ (x² + 1)/(x⁴ + 1) dx, is the question above: (1/√2) tan⁻¹((x² − 1)/(√2 x)).
3. Second piece, ∫ (x² − 1)/(x⁴ + 1) dx: divide by x², put t = x + 1/x, denominator becomes t² − 2.
5. Subtract the second from the first.

concepts.title: Practice: (x²−5) type integral with x + 5/x
concepts.oneLine: For ∫(x²−5)/(x⁴+x²+25) dx, divide top and bottom by x²: the top becomes 1 − 5/x², the bottom becomes t² − 9 with t = x + 5/x, and the answer is (1/6) ln|(t−3)/(t+3)|.
notes: This one is worth attempting on your own first — no hints, and time yourself while you do it.

The numerator was x² − 5. An even power on top with a constant, and a fourth-degree denominator below. The instant you see that shape, divide the top and the bottom by x² — that is the only move you need to look for.
Up above, (x² − 5)/x² becomes 1 − 5/x². That is exactly the derivative of x + 5/x. So t = x + 5/x, and dt is sitting right there in the numerator, waiting.

Down below, divide and you get x² + 1 + 25/x². Now t² = x² + 10 + 25/x², so x² + 1 + 25/x² is just t² − 9. The whole integral is ∫dt/(t² − 9), and that is a standard log: (1/6) ln|(t−3)/(t+3)|. Put t back and you are done.

quickChecks.q: Evaluate ∫ (x² − 1)/(x⁴ + x² + 1) dx.
steps: 1. Divide by x²: numerator 1 − 1/x², denominator x² + 1 + 1/x².
2. Take t = x + 1/x, so dt = (1 − 1/x²) dx.
3. t² = x² + 2 + 1/x², so the denominator is t² − 1, with a = 1.
5. Put t back and multiply inside the log by x/x.

quickChecks.q: Evaluate ∫ (x² − 2)/(x⁴ + 3x² + 4) dx.
steps: 1. Divide by x²: numerator 1 − 2/x², denominator x² + 3 + 4/x².
2. Numerator says t = x + 2/x, so dt = (1 − 2/x²) dx.
3. t² = x² + 4 + 4/x², so x² + 3 + 4/x² = t² − 1, with a = 1.
5. Substitute t = x + 2/x and clear the fractions.

quickChecks.q: Evaluate ∫ (x² − 3)/(x⁴ − 3x² + 9) dx.
steps: 1. Divide by x²: numerator 1 − 3/x², denominator x² − 3 + 9/x².
2. Take t = x + 3/x, so dt = (1 − 3/x²) dx.
3. t² = x² + 6 + 9/x², so x² − 3 + 9/x² = t² − 9, with a = 3.
5. Substitute t = x + 3/x and multiply top and bottom inside the log by x.

concepts.title: How the examiner hides it: division by x to the power n
concepts.oneLine: When an integrand is full of mixed powers of x with a constant or a negative power hiding inside, divide numerator and denominator by xⁿ (n found by trial) and the whole thing collapses to f′/f = ln|f|.
notes: The setter does not start from the question. He starts from the answer. He writes down any function he feels like — say ln|5x⁴ + 3/x³ + x + 5| — and then differentiates it.

Differentiating gives him 20x³ − 9/x⁴ + 1 on top and 5x⁴ + 3/x³ + x + 5 below. If he printed it in that form you would laugh, because the numerator is sitting there as the exact derivative of the denominator. So he hides it: he multiplies the top and the bottom by x⁴.

Now the paper reads ∫ (20x⁷ + x⁴ − 9)/(5x⁸ + x⁵ + 5x⁴ + 3x) dx. Ground and sky difference from what he started with — and nothing in it tells you to divide by x⁴. Whenever you see mixed, reversed powers like this, dividing numerator and denominator by xⁿ is the first move to try.

And what is n? n is nothing but the setter's mood. Here it is 4; in another question it may be 5. So do a little hit and trial — but with eyes open. After each division check one thing only: is the numerator now exactly the derivative of the denominator? The moment that happens, you stop and write ln|denominator| + C.

quickChecks.q: Evaluate ∫ (6x⁵ + x³ − 2)/(2x⁶ + x⁴ + x) dx.
steps: 1. Reversed powers, so try dividing numerator and denominator by xⁿ. Lowest power below is x, highest is x⁶, so try n = 3.
2. Numerator ÷ x³: 6x² + 1 − 2/x³.
3. Denominator ÷ x³: 2x³ + x + 1/x².
4. Check: derivative of 2x³ + 1/x² + x = 6x² − 2/x³ + 1 — exactly the new numerator.
5. So it is ∫ f′/f dx with f = 2x³ + 1/x² + x.

quickChecks.q: Evaluate ∫ (2x³ − 4)/(x⁴ + 3x² + 4x) dx.
steps: 1. Try dividing numerator and denominator by x².
2. Numerator ÷ x²: 2x − 4/x².
3. Denominator ÷ x²: x² + 3 + 4/x.
4. Check: derivative of x² + 4/x + 3 = 2x − 4/x² — matches the new numerator.
5. So it is ∫ f′/f dx with f = x² + 4/x + 3.

quickChecks.q: Evaluate ∫ (3x⁵ − 2)/(x⁶ + x) dx.
steps: 1. Try n = 3: divide top and bottom by x³.
2. Numerator ÷ x³: 3x² − 2/x³.
3. Denominator ÷ x³: x³ + 1/x².
4. Check: derivative of x³ + 1/x² = 3x² − 2/x³ — matches.
5. So it is ∫ f′/f dx with f = x³ + 1/x².

concepts.title: Roots in the denominator: choosing the substitution
concepts.oneLine: Root of a linear → put ax+b = t²; root of a quadratic → that trick dies, so put the linear part (or x itself) equal to 1/t.
notes: Keep the thread from the last section. We were killing the root. If the thing under the root is linear, say ax+b, you put ax+b = t². Clean, and you can walk back: x = (t²−b)/a.

Now shift the root to a quadratic — say x²+1 sits under it instead of x+1. Try t² here and you are stuck: getting x out of t is very hard, and every substitution question demands that you get x back. If that quadratic term were not there, x = t²−1 and we would be done. It is there. So that logic is finished.

So the rule changes. When the root is quadratic and the rest of the expression has a linear piece, put that linear part = 1/t. Both outside brackets linear? Same thing — put the linear one as 1/t and the work is done.

The hardest face is when the outside is also quadratic. Then ask: what is the linear feeling inside it? It is x itself. So put x = 1/t. That is the whole decision tree: root linear → t², root quadratic → 1/t on the linear part, nothing linear left → 1/t on x.

quickChecks.q: For ∫ dx / ((x+2)√(x+2)), which substitution do you pick and what does x become?
steps: 1. Under the root is x+2 — linear.
2. So put x+2 = t².
3. Recover x: x = t²−2, and dx = 2t dt. Recovery works, so the choice is valid.

quickChecks.q: For ∫ dx / ((x+1)√(x²+1)), what do you substitute?
steps: 1. Under the root is x²+1 — quadratic, so t² is out: you cannot get x back from x²+1 = t².
2. Look outside: the factor x+1 is linear.
3. So put the linear part equal to 1/t: x+1 = 1/t.

quickChecks.q: For ∫ dx / ((x²+4)√(x²+1)), what is the linear piece and what do you put?
steps: 1. Root is quadratic → the t² route is dead.
2. Outside is x²+4, also quadratic, so there is no linear bracket to use.
3. The only linear feeling left in the question is x itself.
4. So put x = 1/t.

concepts.title: x + 1 = t²: why patience after substitution pays
concepts.oneLine: Put x + 1 = t² and carry it all the way through: the root-in-the-denominator question turns into 2∫(t²+1)dt/(t⁴+t²+1), a format you already know how to finish.
notes: In part A we decided the substitution: x + 1 = t². Nothing clever after that, just honest work. x = t² − 1, √(x+1) = t, and dx = 2t dt.

Now convert every single piece. The numerator x + 2 becomes t² + 1. The quadratic x² + 3x + 3 becomes t⁴ + t² + 1. And the t sitting in the denominator from the root gets cancelled by the t that came out of dx.

So the whole thing is 2∫(t²+1)dt/(t⁴+t²+1). Look at it. Only even powers, a t²+1 on top, t⁴+t²+1 below — that is exactly the format we practised. The degree four did not make the question harder; it made the question standard.

This one is here for the process, not for the final answer. After a substitution, don't judge the question until you have finished converting it. Convert first, panic later — and you will find there is nothing left to panic about.

quickChecks.q: Using x + 1 = t², evaluate ∫ dx / [(x + 2)·√(x+1)].
steps: 1. x + 1 = t², so dx = 2t dt and √(x+1) = t.
3. Integral becomes ∫ 2t dt / [(t² + 1)·t] = 2∫ dt/(t² + 1).
4. = 2 tan⁻¹t + C.

quickChecks.q: Under the substitution x + 1 = t², what does x² + 3x + 3 become?
steps: 1. From x + 1 = t², x = t² − 1.
2. x² = (t² − 1)² = t⁴ − 2t² + 1.
4. Add: t⁴ − 2t² + 1 + 3t² − 3 + 3 = t⁴ + t² + 1.

quickChecks.q: Using x + 1 = t², evaluate ∫ (x + 2) dx / √(x+1).
steps: 1. x + 1 = t², so dx = 2t dt, √(x+1) = t, and x + 2 = t² + 1.
2. Integral becomes ∫ (t² + 1)·2t dt / t = 2∫ (t² + 1) dt.
4. Put t = √(x+1) back.

concepts.title: When to put x = 1/t
concepts.oneLine: When a linear or a quadratic sits outside the root of a quadratic, the only substitution that works is x = 1/t (or linear = 1/t) — nothing else will crack it.
notes: Look at the shape of the question, not at the numbers. You have something sitting outside the root — a linear like (x + 1), or a quadratic like (x² + 1) — and under the root there is another quadratic.

For this shape, the substitution is not something you derive; it is something you recognise. If the outside piece is linear, put that whole linear equal to 1/t. If the outside piece is a quadratic, put x = 1/t directly.
Why it works: the 1/t turns the outside factor into a t that comes up to the numerator, and the root collapses into √(something in t) divided by t. Everything simplifies in one stroke.

Linear under root quadratic → linear = 1/t. Quadratic under root quadratic → x = 1/t. Write that line in your formula book. The question coming next is built exactly on the second one, so keep it in front of you.

quickChecks.q: Which substitution will you use for ∫ dx / ((x + 1)√(x² + 1))?
steps: 1. Outside the root sits (x + 1) — a linear.
2. Under the root is a quadratic, x² + 1.
3. Linear outside, quadratic inside → put the whole linear equal to 1/t.

quickChecks.q: Which substitution will you use for ∫ dx / ((x² + 1)√(x² + 4))?
steps: 1. Outside the root sits (x² + 1) — a quadratic.
2. Under the root is a quadratic, x² + 4.
3. Quadratic outside, quadratic inside → put x = 1/t directly.

quickChecks.q: If x = 1/t, write dx and simplify √(x² + 4).
steps: 1. x = 1/t, so differentiating, dx = −dt/t².
3. Take the root: √(x² + 4) = √(1 + 4t²) / |t|.

concepts.title: Practice: quadratic under root quadratic with x = 1/t
concepts.oneLine: A quadratic outside and a quadratic under the root: put x = 1/t, take the LCM, and then t² = u turns it into linear under root linear.
notes: Do the degree check before anything else. Outside the root you have a quadratic, 1 + x². Under the root you also have a quadratic, 1 − x². The moment both are quadratic, x = 1/t is the move.

After you substitute, don't panic at the pile of fractions. Take the LCM everywhere — outside the root and under it as well. The ugly thing collapses into −∫ t dt / ((t² + 1)√(t² − 1)), and suddenly the question looks friendly.

Now read the top line carefully. t dt is the derivative of t², and every t downstairs sits as t², nothing else. So put t² = u and the integral becomes linear under root linear — a form you already know how to finish.

Linear under root linear is closed by putting the linear under the root equal to a square: u − 1 = v². That is it. Two substitutions or three, it does not matter, as long as you reach a form you can actually integrate.

quickChecks.q: Evaluate ∫ dx / (x²√(1 + x²)).
steps: 1. Put x = 1/t: dx = −(1/t²) dt, x² = 1/t², and √(1 + 1/t²) = √(t² + 1)/t for t > 0.
2. Integral = ∫ t² · [t/√(t² + 1)] · (−1/t²) dt = −∫ t dt / √(t² + 1).
3. t dt on top, so t² = u, 2t dt = du: −½ ∫ du/√(u + 1) = −√(u + 1).
4. Back: −√(t² + 1), and t = 1/x gives −√(1 + x²)/x.

quickChecks.q: Evaluate ∫ dx / (x²√(x² − 1)).
steps: 1. Put x = 1/t: dx = −(1/t²) dt, x² = 1/t², and √(1/t² − 1) = √(1 − t²)/t.
2. Integral = ∫ t² · [t/√(1 − t²)] · (−1/t²) dt = −∫ t dt / √(1 − t²).

quickChecks.q: Evaluate ∫ dx / ((1 + x²)√(x² − 1)).
steps: 1. Quadratic outside, quadratic under the root, so x = 1/t with dx = −(1/t²) dt.
2. LCM: 1 + 1/t² = (t² + 1)/t² and √(1/t² − 1) = √(1 − t²)/t, so the integral = −∫ t dt / ((t² + 1)√(1 − t²)).
3. Derivative of t² is on top: t² = u gives −½ ∫ du / ((u + 1)√(1 − u)) — linear under root linear.
4. Put 1 − u = v²: du = −2v dv, √(1 − u) = v, u + 1 = 2 − v². Integral = −½ ∫ (−2v dv)/((2 − v²) v) = ∫ dv/(2 − v²).

concepts.title: Partial fractions: splitting a fraction into smaller ones
concepts.quote: Look at x²/((x−1)(x−2)(x−3)) and you feel it is a monster. Split it into three small fractions and the integration becomes a joke — three logs, done.
concepts.oneLine: A proper fraction with distinct linear factors splits as A/(x−a₁) + B/(x−a₂) + C/(x−a₃); cross-multiply, put each root one by one to get A, B, C, and the integral is just logs.
notes: You already know the splitting trick from basics. It has a name: the partial fraction method. It is not an integration technique at all, it is pure algebra, and it is what turns an ugly fraction into small fractions you can integrate on sight.

One condition first. The fraction must be proper — the power of the numerator must be less than the power of the denominator. So if a quadratic sits below and a linear or constant p(x) sits above, you write it as A/(x−a₁) + B/(x−a₂). If three distinct linear factors sit below, the same logic gives A/(x−a₁) + B/(x−a₂) + C/(x−a₃).

Now see why it is worth the trouble. Once A, B and C are known, the integral is just A ln|x−a₁| + B ln|x−a₂| + C ln|x−a₃| + c — that part was available from day one. So in almost every such question, the real work is not integration at all. The real work is finding A, B, C.

And that is done by common sense. Cross-multiply by the whole denominator, and you get an identity in x — true for every value of x. So put the values that are smartest: x = a₁, then a₂, then a₃, because each one kills two terms and hands you one constant directly.

quickChecks.q: Evaluate ∫ 1/((x−1)(x−2)) dx
steps: 4. Integrate: −ln|x−1| + ln|x−2| + c.

quickChecks.q: Evaluate ∫ x/((x−1)(x+2)) dx
steps: 1. Numerator power 1, denominator power 2, so it is proper. Write x/((x−1)(x+2)) = A/(x−1) + B/(x+2), so x = A(x+2) + B(x−1).
4. Integrate: (1/3)ln|x−1| + (2/3)ln|x+2| + c.

quickChecks.q: Evaluate ∫ 1/(x(x−1)(x+1)) dx
steps: 5. Integrate: −ln|x| + (1/2)ln|x−1| + (1/2)ln|x+1| + c.

concepts.title: Rules for repeated linear and quadratic factors
concepts.oneLine: On top of a factor you always write one power less than the factor itself: a constant over a linear, px+q over a quadratic, and a repeated linear gets one term for every power.
notes: Look at the denominator first. Whatever is sitting below decides what you are allowed to write above it. The numerator is always one power less than the factor under it.

A linear factor like x − a₂ carries only a constant, so you write A/(x − a₂). A quadratic factor carries a full linear numerator, so you write (px + q)/(ax² + bx + c). Linear below means constant on top, quadratic below means linear on top.

Now the repeated one. If x − a₁ comes twice, that is (x − a₁)², and you need two terms: B/(x − a₁) and C/(x − a₁)². Take the LCM of those two and the numerator becomes B(x − a₁) + C, which is a linear — exactly one power less than the square below. That is the proof that both terms are needed.
The same logic scales. If (x − 7)⁵ is below, powers 4, 3, 2 and 1 are all allowed on top, so you write a term for every power from 1 up to 5. Nothing more than that.

quickChecks.q: Write the partial fraction form of x/((x − 3)²(x + 1)).
steps: 1. (x − 3)² is a repeated linear, so it gives two terms: A/(x − 3) and B/(x − 3)².
2. x + 1 is linear, so it gives a constant on top: C/(x + 1).
3. Degree check: the denominator is degree 3 and the numerator x is degree 1, so the fraction is already proper.

quickChecks.q: Write the partial fraction form of (2x + 5)/((x − 1)(x² + 4)).
steps: 1. x − 1 is linear, so only a constant on top: A/(x − 1).
2. x² + 4 is a quadratic, so a full linear on top: (px + q)/(x² + 4).
3. Add the two pieces.

quickChecks.q: Write the partial fraction form of 1/(x − 7)³.
steps: 1. The power below is 3, so the allowed powers on top are 1 and 2 — that means three terms in all, for (x − 7)¹, (x − 7)² and (x − 7)³.
2. Each numerator is a constant.
3. Check with the LCM (x − 7)³: the top becomes A(x − 7)² + B(x − 7) + C, which is a quadratic — one power less than 3.

concepts.title: Getting A, B and C out
concepts.oneLine: Put x = 1 and x = −3 to kill terms and read off B and C straight away; A needs one extra value of x or one coefficient comparison.
notes: Take ∫ (x² + 1)/((x − 1)²(x + 3)) dx. Degree 2 on top, degree 3 below, so it is a proper fraction and it splits as A/(x − 1) + B/(x − 1)² + C/(x + 3). That line should come out of your pen before anything else — repeated linear, so every power from 1 up to 2.
Once it is split, look at what is left to integrate. A/(x − 1) gives a ln, C/(x + 3) gives a ln, and B(x − 1)⁻² gives (x − 1)⁻¹ divided by −1. That part is finished in ten seconds.

So the real question is: how do you get A, B and C? Clear the denominators and you get an identity: x² + 1 = A(x − 1)(x + 3) + B(x + 3) + C(x − 1)². An identity is true for every value of x, so you are free to put in any number you like — and the numbers worth picking are the ones that kill terms.

Put x = 1: the A term and the C term both die, and B comes out direct. Put x = −3: the A and B terms die, and C comes out direct. Now only A is left, and for that you either put one more value like x = 2, or compare one coefficient — the constant term is the easiest. Both routes are legal, because it is an identity; pick whichever is less work on that day.

quickChecks.q: Write (x + 5)/((x − 2)²(x + 1)) as A/(x − 2) + B/(x − 2)² + C/(x + 1) and find A, B and C.
steps: 1. Identity: x + 5 = A(x − 2)(x + 1) + B(x + 1) + C(x − 2)².
4. Compare the x² coefficient: 0 = A + C, so A = −4/9.
5. Check with the constant term: −2A + B + 4C = 8/9 + 7/3 + 16/9 = 5 ✓.

quickChecks.q: Find A, B, C in 1/((x − 1)²(x + 1)) = A/(x − 1) + B/(x − 1)² + C/(x + 1), then integrate.
steps: 1. Identity: 1 = A(x − 1)(x + 1) + B(x + 1) + C(x − 1)².
4. Constant term (put x = 0): 1 = −A + B + C = −A + 3/4, so A = −1/4.
1. Identity: 2x = A(x + 2)(x − 1) + B(x − 1) + C(x + 2)².
4. Compare the x² coefficient: 0 = A + C, so A = −2/9.
5. Check the constant term: −2A − B + 4C = 4/9 − 4/3 + 8/9 = 0 ✓, which matches the 0 constant on the left.

concepts.title: Throughout x²: do the partial fraction in t, then come back
concepts.oneLine: When every term is in x², rename x² as t only inside the algebra, split it as linear-upon-linear, put x² back, and then integrate — two unknowns instead of four.
notes: Integrate (x² − 2)/((x² + 2)(2x² + 1)). The lazy eye sees two quadratic factors in the denominator and says: quadratic below, linear above. So (Ax + B)/(x² + 2) plus (Cx + D)/(2x² + 1). That gives you four unknowns. You will get the answer, yes. But who wants to sit with four unknowns in an exam?

Notice this. The whole expression is in terms of x² throughout — no lone x term anywhere. So call x² as t, and the whole thing becomes (t − 2)/((t + 2)(2t + 1)) — linear upon linear times linear, which splits with just two constants.

I am not doing integration by substitution here. The integral has not been touched, nor has dx. I stepped out of calculus into pure algebra, did the partial fraction there in t, re-substituted t = x², and walked back into calculus. Only then was the integration done.

And you cannot object to putting t = −2 or t = −1/2. It is an identity — LHS equals RHS for every value of t. I could put iota in there if I wanted and you still could not refuse me. That is the licence an identity gives you.

quickChecks.q: Integrate (x² + 1)/((x² + 2)(x² + 3)).
steps: 1. Pure x² throughout, so put x² = t in the algebra: (t + 1)/((t + 2)(t + 3)) = A/(t + 2) + B/(t + 3).
3. Back to x²: the expression is −1/(x² + 2) + 2/(x² + 3).

quickChecks.q: Integrate (x² − 4)/((x² + 1)(x² + 3)).
steps: 3. Sanity check at x = 0: −5/2 + 7/6 = −4/3, and the original gives −4/(1 × 3) = −4/3. Matches.
4. So the expression is −(5/2)·1/(x² + 1) + (7/2)·1/(x² + 3).

quickChecks.q: Integrate 1/((x² + 1)(x² + 4)).
steps: 4. Integrate: (1/3)·tan⁻¹x − (1/3)·(1/2)·tan⁻¹(x/2) + C.

concepts.title: Where indefinite integration stands, and what comes next
concepts.quote: Before we open a brand new technique, stop for two minutes and see the map. Knowing where you are in integration is half the battle in the exam hall.
concepts.oneLine: Three lectures in, we have done basics, substitution, the algebraic formats and partial fractions — integration by parts and the trigonometric formats are what remain.
notes: We started with the basics — the standard results you must be able to write without thinking. Then came substitution, and that was the big one. Almost every question after it quietly leans on it.

After substitution we did the algebraic formats, and that is a large family: the quadratic format, a linear expression under a root with a quadratic, the even-power questions I did with you in today's class, a quadratic under a root with a linear, and a quadratic under a root with a quadratic. Many of these are still substitution underneath, just dressed up in a particular shape.

Then partial fractions. Partial fractions is the easiest technique in all of integration — once you have pulled out the A, B, C, D, the integration that is left is barely integration at all. The whole difficulty sits in the splitting, and even that is mechanical.

Next comes integration by parts, and this one is genuinely new. Substitution and partial fractions were old ideas worked harder; integration by parts is the first place where you will feel a completely fresh technique. After that come the trigonometric formats, and with those this topic is finished.

quickChecks.q: Which family does ∫ dx/(x² + 4x + 13) belong to, and what is the integral?
steps: 1. The denominator is a quadratic with no root available, so this is the quadratic format.
2. Complete the square: x² + 4x + 13 = (x + 2)² + 3².
3. Now it is the standard shape with a = 3 and the variable x + 2.
quickChecks.answer: Quadratic format; the integral is (1/3)tan⁻¹((x + 2)/3) + C.

quickChecks.q: Which family does ∫ (2x + 3)/((x + 1)(x + 2)) dx belong to, and what is the integral?
steps: 1. Two distinct linear factors in the denominator, so this is partial fractions.
4. The integral becomes ∫ [1/(x + 1) + 1/(x + 2)] dx.
quickChecks.answer: Partial fractions; the integral is ln|x + 1| + ln|x + 2| + C.

quickChecks.q: Which family does ∫ 2x/(x² + 1) dx belong to, and what is the integral?
steps: 1. The numerator is the derivative of the denominator, so this is plain substitution.
2. Put t = x² + 1, then dt = 2x dx.
3. The integral is ∫ dt/t = ln|t| + C.
quickChecks.answer: Substitution; the integral is ln(x² + 1) + C.

concepts.title: Splitting a numerator that differs by a constant
concepts.oneLine: When the two factors in the denominator differ by a constant, write that constant as the difference of the factors itself — then the fraction splits into two easy logs with no substitution at all.
notes: Take ∫ dx/((x+1)(x+2)). The usual route is a substitution or the full partial-fraction setup. But notice this: the difference between the two brackets is 1, and the numerator is also 1.

So write the numerator as that difference. 1 = (x+2) − (x+1). Put that on top and split the fraction. One term cancels (x+2), the other cancels (x+1), and you are left with 1/(x+1) − 1/(x+2). Two logs, done — no substitution, no solving for A and B.
If the gap is some other constant, the idea does not change. For (x+1)(x+3) the gap is 2, so write 2 = (x+3) − (x+1), split, and pull a ½ outside. Same trick, one extra constant.

Now the honest part. This splitting always exists, but in complicated questions it is genuinely hard to spot — so keep the standard method as your fallback and use this only when the gap jumps out at you. Here the question was easy, so it came instantly.

quickChecks.q: Evaluate ∫ dx/((x+3)(x+4)).
steps: 1. Gap: (x+4) − (x+3) = 1, same as the numerator.
3. Integrate: ln|x+3| − ln|x+4| + C.

quickChecks.q: Evaluate ∫ dx/(x(x+1)).
steps: 3. Integrate: ln|x| − ln|x+1| + C.

quickChecks.q: Evaluate ∫ dx/((x+1)(x+3)).
steps: 3. Integrate: ½[ln|x+1| − ln|x+3|] + C.

concepts.title: Integration by Parts: the Product Rule of Integration
concepts.oneLine: To integrate a product, stop one function, integrate the other, then subtract the integral of (that integration × the derivative of the function you stopped).
notes: You already know the product rule for differentiation. To differentiate f × g, you stop g and write the derivative of f, then stop f and write the derivative of g. Integration has its own product rule, and that is what integration by parts is.

Here is the whole move. You have to integrate f × g. Stop f, and write the integration of g beside it — so the first piece is f × (∫g dx). Now put a minus sign, open one big integration sign and one big bracket.

Inside that bracket, copy the integration you just did, and multiply it by the derivative of the function you stopped. That is it. Stop one, integrate the other, minus, big integral, big bracket, the integration you did × the derivative of the stopped one.

You will be told to memorise an order of preference — ILATE, do this first, do that next. I don't work with that, and I don't need it. Common sense decides it, and the very first step for success is to pick the function whose integration you already know and integrate that one; the other one is the one you stop. Why the memorised order is unnecessary, I'll show you right after this.

quickChecks.q: Apply the rule to ∫ x cos x dx. Which function do you stop, and what do you get?
steps: 1. Both integrals are known — cos x and x alike — but stopping x is smarter, because its derivative is just 1.
2. Stop x, integrate cos x: first piece is x sin x.
3. Minus, big integral, big bracket: − ∫ (sin x)(derivative of x) dx = − ∫ sin x · 1 dx.
4. So we have x sin x − ∫ sin x dx = x sin x − (− cos x).
quickChecks.answer: x sin x + cos x + C

quickChecks.q: Do ∫ x eˣ dx the same way.
steps: 1. Stop x, integrate eˣ: first piece is x eˣ.
2. Minus, big integral, big bracket: − ∫ (eˣ)(derivative of x) dx = − ∫ eˣ dx.
3. x eˣ − eˣ.
quickChecks.answer: x eˣ − eˣ + C, that is eˣ(x − 1) + C

quickChecks.q: ∫ ln x dx. You only have one function here — how does the rule still work?
steps: 1. Write it as a product: ln x × 1.
2. The integration of ln x is not known; the integration of 1 is. So integrate 1 and stop ln x.
3. First piece: (ln x)(x) = x ln x.
4. Minus, big integral, big bracket: − ∫ x · (derivative of ln x) dx = − ∫ x · (1/x) dx = − ∫ 1 dx = − x.

concepts.title: Choosing What to Stop and What to Integrate (Common Sense Over ILATE)
concepts.oneLine: Decide by common sense, not ILATE: first integrate the function whose integral you know, and if you know both, stop the one whose derivative is easier.
notes: By parts needs you to pick one function to stop and one to integrate. Step one: look for the function whose integral you actually know, and integrate that one. The other one gets stopped — there is no choice left to make.
Take ∫xⁿ ln x dx. There is no formula for the integral of ln x, so ln x cannot be the one you integrate. Step one has already decided it: stop ln x, integrate xⁿ. No rule needed.

Now take ∫x sin x dx. Here step one gives you no hint — you know the integral of x and the integral of sin x. So move to step two. When both are integrable, stop the function whose derivative is easier. Between x and sin x, the derivative of x is 1. Simplest thing in the world. So stop x and integrate sin x.

That is the whole method. Two functions, check if only one is integrable; if both are, compare derivatives. This is better than any list you were told to memorise, and it also makes the formula itself easier to hold in your head.

quickChecks.q: Integrate x · ln x.
steps: 1. Integral of ln x does not exist as a formula, so step one decides: stop ln x, integrate x.
2. ∫x dx = x²/2, so first term is x² ln x/2.
3. Second term: ∫(1/x)(x²/2) dx = (1/2)∫x dx = x²/4.

quickChecks.q: Integrate x · cos x.
steps: 1. Both are integrable, so step two: derivative of x is 1, easier than −sin x. Stop x.
2. ∫cos x dx = sin x, so first term is x sin x.
3. Second term: subtract ∫(1)(sin x) dx = −cos x, so it contributes + cos x.
quickChecks.answer: x sin x + cos x + C

quickChecks.q: Integrate x³ · ln x.
steps: 1. Same family as the first example with n = 3. Stop ln x, integrate x³.
2. ∫x³ dx = x⁴/4, so first term is x⁴ ln x/4.
3. Second term: ∫(1/x)(x⁴/4) dx = (1/4)∫x³ dx = x⁴/16.

concepts.title: First Set of By-Parts Examples: x·e^3x, x²·tan⁻¹x, ln x, sin⁻¹x
concepts.oneLine: In every by-parts question, stop the function you cannot integrate — and if you see only one function, read it as 1 times that function.
notes: Look at the first one, x·e³ˣ. Here both parts can be integrated, so you get to choose. Common sense says stop x, because its derivative is 1 and the x dies immediately; integrate e³ˣ, which gives e³ˣ/3.
Now x²·tan⁻¹x. You do not know the integral of tan⁻¹x, so there is no choice at all — stop tan⁻¹x and integrate x². That is the whole decision. No rule, no ILATE chanting.

Then come ln x and sin⁻¹x, where the student protests: sir, there is only one function. Son, there are two — multiply by 1, integrate the 1, and stop the function you cannot integrate. If I knew the integral of ln x, I would have simply told you the answer and the question would not exist.

One more thing, and it is where marks leak. Writing the by-parts line is not the answer. The integral left inside the bracket is solved with the earlier tools — division, splitting, substitution. In the tan⁻¹x question, divide x³ by 1+x²; in the sin⁻¹x question, put t = 1−x². Nothing new.

quickChecks.q: Integrate x·e²ˣ.
steps: 1. Stop x, integrate e²ˣ to get e²ˣ/2.
2. First term: x·e²ˣ/2.
3. Minus ∫ 1 × e²ˣ/2 dx = e²ˣ/4.

quickChecks.q: Integrate tan⁻¹x.
steps: 1. Write it as 1 × tan⁻¹x. Stop tan⁻¹x, integrate 1 to get x.
2. First term: x·tan⁻¹x.
3. Minus ∫ x/(1+x²) dx. Derivative of 1+x² is 2x, so this is ½·ln(1+x²).

quickChecks.q: Integrate x·ln x.
steps: 1. You cannot integrate ln x, so stop it and integrate x, giving x²/2.
2. First term: (x²/2)·ln x.
3. Minus ∫ (1/x)·(x²/2) dx = ∫ x/2 dx = x²/4.

concepts.title: x·sin⁻¹x/√(1−x²) and the Integral of (sin⁻¹x)²
concepts.oneLine: On ∫ x·sin⁻¹x/√(1−x²) dx the substitution t = sin⁻¹x finishes it in one line, but the deliberately clumsy by-parts route forces you to find ∫(sin⁻¹x)² dx — and that is the real prize of the question.
notes: Look at x·sin⁻¹x/√(1−x²) and two roads open up. Put t = sin⁻¹x and the whole thing collapses into ∫ t·sin t dt — one by-parts and you are done. That is the honest road, and in the exam that is the road you take.

Now take the other road. Keep x as it is and stare at the rest: sin⁻¹x/√(1−x²) is exactly sin⁻¹x times the derivative of sin⁻¹x. So it is f·f′, and its integral is (sin⁻¹x)²/2. Apply by parts with x as the first function and that piece as the second.

The first term comes out clean, but the leftover is −½∫(sin⁻¹x)² dx. Most students stop here and call the method bad. The method is not bad — it just handed you a new question, and that question is far more important than the one you started with.

For ∫(sin⁻¹x)² dx, don't fight it directly. Put x = sin t, so dx = cos t dt, and the integral becomes ∫ t² cos t dt. Integration by parts twice, convert t back to x, and you have it. Then push it back into the first line — and watch the big ugly term cancel completely, leaving the same answer the honest road gave you.

quickChecks.q: Find ∫ tan⁻¹x/(1+x²) dx.
steps: 1. 1/(1+x²) is the derivative of tan⁻¹x, so this is f·f′ with f = tan⁻¹x.
2. Hence the integral is f²/2.

quickChecks.q: Find ∫ θ² sin θ dθ.
steps: 1. By parts with θ² first: = θ²(−cos θ) + ∫ 2θ cos θ dθ.
2. Second by-parts: ∫ θ cos θ dθ = θ sin θ − ∫ sin θ dθ = θ sin θ + cos θ.
3. So the answer is −θ² cos θ + 2[θ sin θ + cos θ].
quickChecks.answer: −θ² cos θ + 2θ sin θ + 2 cos θ + C

quickChecks.q: Find ∫ x·cos⁻¹x/√(1−x²) dx.
steps: 1. Put t = cos⁻¹x, so x = cos t and dx/√(1−x²) = −dt.
2. The integral becomes ∫ cos t · t · (−dt) = −∫ t cos t dt.
3. ∫ t cos t dt = t sin t + cos t, so the integral is −t sin t − cos t + C.
4. Back to x: t = cos⁻¹x, sin t = √(1−x²), cos t = x.

concepts.title: Never Miss the Substitution: cos√x and tan⁻¹(tan 3θ)-Type Integrals
concepts.oneLine: Before you reach for by parts, ask what substitution kills the awkward part — √x = t turns ∫cos√x into ∫t·cos t, and x = tan θ turns an inverse-tan monster into ∫θ·sec²θ.
notes: In the whole of integration, substitution is the step you must never forget — the most basic one is ax + b, and from there you build up. When a question looks ugly, the first question is not "by parts or not". The first question is "what should be substituted?"

Look at ∫cos√x dx. What is making it ugly? Only the radical sign. So make the radical disappear: put √x = t, which means x = t² and dx = 2t dt. Now the integral is 2∫t·cos t dt — a plain by-parts question you have already solved.

Second one is bigger but the same idea. ∫tan⁻¹((3x − x³)/(1 − 3x²)) dx is honestly not an integration question at all; it is a trigonometry question wearing an integral sign. Put x = tan θ and that whole fraction is tan 3θ, so you are left with ∫tan⁻¹(tan 3θ)·sec²θ dθ.

Here one student always objects: tan⁻¹(tan 3θ) is not always 3θ. Correct. But this is an indefinite integral, there is no interval given, and the two differ only by a constant — the slope is 3θ's slope either way, and a constant gets swallowed by the + C. So write 3θ and move on. And at the very end, make θ disappear: tan θ = x gives θ = tan⁻¹x and sec θ = √(1 + x²).

quickChecks.q: Evaluate ∫sin√x dx.
steps: 1. Put √x = t, so x = t² and dx = 2t dt.
2. Integral = 2∫t·sin t dt.
3. By parts: 2[−t·cos t + ∫cos t dt] = 2[−t·cos t + sin t].
4. Put t = √x back.

quickChecks.q: Evaluate ∫e^√x dx.
steps: 1. Put √x = t, so dx = 2t dt.
2. Integral = 2∫t·e^t dt.
3. By parts: 2[t·e^t − ∫e^t dt] = 2[t·e^t − e^t].
4. Put t = √x back.

quickChecks.q: Evaluate ∫tan⁻¹(2x/(1 − x²)) dx.
steps: 1. Put x = tan θ, so dx = sec²θ dθ and 2x/(1 − x²) = tan 2θ.
2. Integral = ∫tan⁻¹(tan 2θ)·sec²θ dθ = 2∫θ·sec²θ dθ (constant goes into C).
3. By parts: 2[θ·tan θ − ln|sec θ|].
4. Back-substitute θ = tan⁻¹x, tan θ = x, sec θ = √(1 + x²).

concepts.title: (2x+5)·√(3x−8): By Parts Beats Substitution
concepts.oneLine: For a linear function times a root-linear, stop the linear factor and integrate the radical — by parts finishes it in two lines, faster than putting 3x−8 = t².
notes: Look at the shape first: a linear function multiplied by the square root of another linear function. The old instinct is to put 3x−8 = t², and yes, that works. But there is a quicker road.

Ask one question only: which factor has the easy derivative? Here the derivative of 2x+5 is just 2 — so stop 2x+5 and integrate √(3x−8). The integral of the root is (3x−8)^(3/2) divided by 3/2, and then divided by 3, because the coefficient of x inside is 3. That gives (2/9)(3x−8)^(3/2).

Now the fun step. Open a big integral sign, a big bracket, and close with dx. Inside the bracket goes the derivative of the part you stopped (that is 2) times the thing you just integrated, copied exactly as it stands — no mental simplification, no re-thinking. So you get 2 × (2/9)(3x−8)^(3/2), which is (4/9)(3x−8)^(3/2).

That last integral is a pure power. Power becomes 5/2, divide by 5/2, and divide by 3 once more for the coefficient inside. Done. ILATE does not help you here because both factors are algebraic — the deciding rule is simply "whose derivative is simple".

quickChecks.q: Evaluate ∫(x+1)√(2x−3) dx
Evaluate ∫(3x−1)√(x+4) dx
steps: 1. Stop 3x−1 (derivative 3), integrate √(x+4): (x+4)^(3/2) ÷ (3/2) = (2/3)(x+4)^(3/2). Coefficient inside is 1, so no extra division.

quickChecks.q: Evaluate ∫(2x+1)√(x−1) dx
steps: 1. Stop 2x+1 (derivative 2), integrate √(x−1): (2/3)(x−1)^(3/2).

concepts.title: ∫e^(ax)·cos(bx) dx — the Returning (Cyclic) Integral
concepts.oneLine: When neither piece gets simpler, call the integral I, apply by parts twice keeping the same choice, and when I comes back solve for it: ∫e^(ax)·cos(bx) dx = e^(ax)(b·sin bx + a·cos bx)/(a² + b²) + C.
