notes: Look at ∫e^(ax)·cos(bx) dx honestly. Which one do you integrate? Integrating e^(ax) gives you e^(ax)/a, integrating cos(bx) gives you sin(bx)/b. Nothing improved. Differentiate either one and it is equally bad. The usual common sense is useless here.

This is the moment the panic sets in: if ILATE is not followed, is the question lost? No. Here it is done the other way round on purpose — e^(ax) kept as the first function and cos(bx) integrated. ILATE is a helper, not a law — if your choice makes the next line cleaner, take it.

Do by parts once and you get e^(ax)·sin(bx)/b minus a/b times ∫e^(ax)·sin(bx) dx. Do by parts a second time, with the same choice, and the original integral walks back into your answer. That is the cyclicity. The moment the integral returns, you stop integrating and start solving: name it I, move all the I terms to one side, divide.
Six lines and it is finished. And the answer has a neat cross-over worth remembering: b rides with sin bx, a rides with cos bx, and a² + b² sits underneath.

quickChecks.q: Find ∫e^(2x)·cos(3x) dx.
steps: 1. Compare with e^(ax)·cos(bx): a = 2, b = 3.
2. Denominator a² + b² = 4 + 9 = 13.
3. Numerator e^(ax)(b·sin bx + a·cos bx) = e^(2x)(3·sin 3x + 2·cos 3x).

quickChecks.q: Find ∫e^x·cos x dx.
steps: 1. Here a = 1 and b = 1.
3. Numerator becomes e^x(1·sin x + 1·cos x) = e^x(sin x + cos x).

quickChecks.q: Find ∫e^(3x)·cos(2x) dx.
steps: 3. b goes with sin, a goes with cos: e^(3x)(2·sin 2x + 3·cos 2x).

concepts.title: Practice Set: Five By-Parts Problems with Hints
concepts.oneLine: Five by-parts questions to attempt yourself — at least three, with only the first move given: multiply x/(1+sin x) by 1 − sin x, split sec³x as sec x·sec²x, and substitute t = 1/x before you part cos(1/x)/x³.
notes: By now the by-parts formula should not be something you look up. It should sit in your head like a reflex, so that the only thinking left in a question is *which factor to differentiate*. These five are not repeats of the solved ones; they are fresh, and that is the point.

Before you reach for by parts, always check whether a substitution clears the question first. That is where most students lose these. They see a product, jump straight to u and v, and then sit in the jungle with something uglier than what they started with.

So I am giving you only a light direction on three of them. In the x/(1+sin x) one, multiply top and bottom by 1 − sin x — the denominator becomes beautiful, it turns into cos²x. In the sec³x one, write it as sec x into sec²x, and then it is an ordinary by-parts. In the cos(1/x)/x³ one, put t in place of 1/x first; after that the question becomes very clean and common.

That is all the help you get. Target is five, attempt any three of your own choice — but I want at least three successful attempts, not three half-attempts. Which three you pick is your decision; finishing them is not optional.

quickChecks.q: What is your first move on ∫ x/(1 − sin x) dx?
steps: 1. Same idea, opposite sign: multiply numerator and denominator by 1 + sin x.
2. Denominator becomes 1 − sin²x = cos²x, so you get x(1 + sin x)/cos²x.
3. Split: x sec²x + x sec x tan x.
4. Now by parts on each piece.
quickChecks.answer: Rationalise with 1 + sin x, giving ∫x sec²x dx + ∫x sec x tan x dx, then by parts.

quickChecks.q: In ∫ sec³x dx, which factor do you integrate and which do you differentiate?
steps: 1. Split sec³x = sec x · sec²x.
2. ∫sec²x dx = tan x, so sec²x is the part to integrate.
3. d(sec x)/dx = sec x tan x, so sec x is the part to differentiate.
quickChecks.answer: Integrate sec²x (it gives tan x), differentiate sec x.

quickChecks.q: What substitution opens up ∫ sin(1/x)·(1/x³) dx, and what does the integral become?
steps: 1. Put t = 1/x, so x = 1/t and dx = −dt/t².
2. 1/x³ = t³, so the integral is ∫ sin t · t³ · (−1/t²) dt.
3. Cancel: −∫ t sin t dt.
quickChecks.answer: t = 1/x turns it into −∫ t sin t dt, which is a single by-parts.

concepts.title: x/(1+sin x): Rationalise, Then By Parts Twice
concepts.oneLine: Multiply x/(1+sin x) by (1−sin x) on top and bottom, and the question splits into x·sec²x and x·sec x·tan x — two by-parts problems where you stop x and integrate the trig.
notes: The problem here is the plus sign. 1 + sin x in the denominator is a sum, and you cannot integrate past a sum sitting downstairs. So kill it the way you kill √ problems — multiply top and bottom by the conjugate, 1 − sin x.
Now the denominator is 1 − sin²x, which is cos²x. The numerator is x(1 − sin x). Split it: x/cos²x minus x·sin x/cos²x. That is x·sec²x − x·sec x·tan x, two separate integrals, and both are by parts.
In both of them x is the part you stop. Stop x, differentiate it to 1, and integrate the trig piece. For the first, ∫sec²x dx = tan x. For the second, ∫sec x·tan x dx = sec x. That is the whole game.

Put the two answers together and the two log terms merge into one clean ln|1 + sin x|. Keep this method in your hand — the very next question, ∫sec³x dx, runs on exactly the same idea of stopping one factor.

quickChecks.q: Evaluate ∫ x/(1 − sin x) dx.
steps: 1. Multiply top and bottom by (1 + sin x): ∫ x(1 + sin x)/cos²x dx = ∫ x·sec²x dx + ∫ x·sec x·tan x dx.
2. First: x·tan x + ln|cos x|. Second: x·sec x − ln|sec x + tan x|.
3. Add them: x·tan x + x·sec x + ln|cos x| − ln|sec x + tan x|.
4. The logs merge: ln|cos x/(sec x + tan x)| = ln|cos²x/(1 + sin x)| = ln|1 − sin x|.
quickChecks.answer: x(tan x + sec x) + ln|1 − sin x| + C

quickChecks.q: Evaluate ∫ x·sec²x dx.
steps: 1. By parts, stop x: x·∫sec²x dx − ∫(1·∫sec²x dx) dx.
2. = x·tan x − ∫tan x dx.
3. ∫tan x dx = −ln|cos x|, so the answer is x·tan x + ln|cos x|.

quickChecks.q: Evaluate ∫ x·sec x·tan x dx.
steps: 1. ∫sec x·tan x dx = sec x, so stop x and integrate the rest.
2. = x·sec x − ∫1·sec x dx.
3. ∫sec x dx = ln|sec x + tan x|.
quickChecks.answer: x·sec x − ln|sec x + tan x| + C

concepts.title: ∫sec³x dx — the Classic Board Question
concepts.oneLine: Write sec³x as sec x·sec²x, do by parts once, turn tan²x into sec²x − 1, and the same integral comes back — shift it to the left to get I = (sec x·tan x + ln|sec x + tan x|)/2 + C.
notes: We had just finished x·sec²x and x·sec x·tan x in today's class, so every piece you need is already in your hand. Now look at sec³x. There is no single formula for it, so split it: sec³x = sec x·sec²x.
Take sec x as the first function and sec²x as the second, because sec²x integrates cleanly to tan x. By parts gives I = sec x·tan x − ∫tan x·(sec x·tan x) dx, which is sec x·tan x − ∫sec x·tan²x dx.
Now the one move that finishes the problem. Replace tan²x by sec²x − 1. The integral breaks into ∫sec³x dx − ∫sec x dx, and ∫sec³x dx is I again.
So I = sec x·tan x − I + ln|sec x + tan x|. Bring the I across: 2I = sec x·tan x + ln|sec x + tan x|. Divide by 2 and you are done — I = (sec x·tan x + ln|sec x + tan x|)/2 + C.

quickChecks.q: Evaluate ∫cosec³x dx.
steps: 1. Let J = ∫cosec x·cosec²x dx; by parts with cosec x first, since ∫cosec²x dx = −cot x.
2. J = −cosec x·cot x − ∫(−cot x)(−cosec x·cot x) dx = −cosec x·cot x − ∫cosec x·cot²x dx.
3. Use cot²x = cosec²x − 1: J = −cosec x·cot x − J + ∫cosec x dx.
4. 2J = −cosec x·cot x + ln|cosec x − cot x|.
quickChecks.answer: ½(−cosec x·cot x + ln|cosec x − cot x|) + C

quickChecks.q: Evaluate ∫sec x·tan²x dx.
steps: 1. Write tan²x = sec²x − 1, so the integral is ∫sec³x dx − ∫sec x dx.
2. Put in the result just proved: ½(sec x·tan x + ln|sec x + tan x|) − ln|sec x + tan x|.
3. Combine the two ln terms: ½ sec x·tan x − ½ ln|sec x + tan x|.
quickChecks.answer: ½(sec x·tan x − ln|sec x + tan x|) + C

quickChecks.q: Evaluate ∫sec³x dx from 0 to π/4.
steps: 1. Use ½(sec x·tan x + ln|sec x + tan x|).
2. At x = π/4: sec x = √2, tan x = 1, so the value is ½(√2 + ln(√2 + 1)).
3. At x = 0: sec x = 1, tan x = 0, so the value is ½(0 + ln 1) = 0.

concepts.title: cos⁻¹x/x³: By Parts, Then Take the Highest Power Common
concepts.oneLine: For ∫cos⁻¹x/x³ dx, integrate x⁻³ by parts first, then finish the leftover ∫dx/(x²√(1−x²)) by taking the highest power of x common out of the root.
notes: Two things multiplied, one of them inverse trigonometric. That is a by parts question. cos⁻¹x is the first function, x⁻³ is the one to integrate, and ∫x⁻³ dx = x⁻²/(−2), which is −1/(2x²).

Now write the signs honestly. The derivative of cos⁻¹x carries its own minus, and by parts puts another minus in front of the second integral. Those two minuses multiply into a plus, so what is left over is ½∫dx/(x²√(1−x²)), with the by parts minus still in front of it.

Here comes the real step. Whenever a root is stuck in the denominator with powers of x around it, take the highest power of x common from inside the root. Here 1 − x² = x²(1/x² − 1), so √(1−x²) = x√(x⁻²−1), and the full denominator becomes x³√(x⁻²−1).

Look at what that did. The derivative of x⁻² − 1 is −2/x³, and dx/x³ is exactly what is sitting outside the root. So t = x⁻² − 1 goes through in one line: ∫dt/√t is 2√t, and the whole thing closes as −cos⁻¹x/(2x²) + √(1−x²)/(2x) + C. Different route from the usual x = sin θ, but just as clean.

quickChecks.q: Evaluate ∫ sin⁻¹x / x³ dx.
steps: 1. By parts with sin⁻¹x as the first function and ∫x⁻³ dx = −1/(2x²).
3. From class, ∫ dx/(x²√(1−x²)) = −√(1−x²)/x.

quickChecks.q: Evaluate ∫ dx / (x²√(1−x²)) by taking the highest power common.
steps: 1. 1 − x² = x²(1/x² − 1), so √(1−x²) = x√(x⁻²−1) and the denominator becomes x³√(x⁻²−1).
2. Put t = x⁻² − 1, so dt = −2 dx/x³, which gives dx/x³ = −dt/2.
3. Integral = −½ ∫ dt/√t = −√t = −√(x⁻²−1) = −√(1−x²)/x + C.

quickChecks.q: Evaluate ∫ dx / (x²√(4−x²)).
steps: 1. 4 − x² = x²(4/x² − 1), so √(4−x²) = x√(4x⁻²−1) and the denominator becomes x³√(4x⁻²−1).
2. Put t = 4x⁻² − 1, so dt = −8 dx/x³, which gives dx/x³ = −dt/8.
3. Integral = −⅛ ∫ dt/√t = −⅛ · 2√t = −¼√(4x⁻²−1).
4. And √(4x⁻²−1) = √(4−x²)/x, so the answer is −√(4−x²)/(4x) + C.

concepts.title: Comparing Routes on the Same Integral: x = sin θ, x = 1/t, or Highest Power Common
concepts.oneLine: The same integral can be cracked by x = sin θ, by x = 1/t, or by taking the highest power common — all three give the same answer, and taking the highest power common finishes in one shot.
notes: Look at the integral again: √(1 − x²)/x. One route is to put x = sin θ. Perfectly correct, you will reach the answer. Another reads it as a quadratic under a root and puts x = 1/t. Also correct, also reaches the answer.

But the way I did it was to take the highest power common from under the root. That turns the expression into something that integrates immediately, in a single shot. That is why it is the route to prefer — not because the others are wrong, but because this one is the fastest.

Then comes the real doubt. The substitution route gives an answer that is not in the same shape as the by-parts one: it carries cos⁻¹x × (1/x² − 2) type terms, while by parts carries cos⁻¹x/(−2x²). Different faces, same person.

When two answers look different, take the common factor out of one of them and compare. Here you pull cos⁻¹x/2 out as the common factor, and what is left inside is 1/x² − 1 type terms. Do that honestly and the two answers sit on top of each other. Nothing else to prove.

quickChecks.q: Write √(1 − x²) with the highest power taken common from under the root.
steps: 1. Under the root, the highest power of x is x².
2. Write 1 − x² = x²(1/x² − 1).
3. Pull x² out of the root: √(x²(1/x² − 1)) = x√(1/x² − 1) for x > 0.

quickChecks.q: For ∫ √(1 − x²)/x dx you put x = 1/t. What does dx become, and what does the x in the denominator turn into?
steps: 1. x = 1/t, so differentiate: dx = −(1/t²) dt.
2. The 1/x in the integrand becomes t.
3. So the x in the denominator stops being a denominator — it comes up as a factor t.

quickChecks.q: Two answers are written as (cos⁻¹x)(1/x² − 1)/2 and (cos⁻¹x)/(2x²) − (cos⁻¹x)/2. Are they the same?
steps: 1. Take cos⁻¹x/2 common from the second form.
2. Second form becomes (cos⁻¹x/2)(1/x² − 1).
3. That is exactly the first form.
quickChecks.answer: Yes, they are the same — taking the common factor out shows it immediately.

concepts.title: ∫ln(x+√(x²+1)) dx by the Substitution t = x+√(x²+1)
concepts.oneLine: Put t = x+√(x²+1); then 1/t = √(x²+1) − x, dx = ½(1 + 1/t²) dt, and one by-parts on ln t gives x ln(x+√(x²+1)) − √(x²+1) + C.
notes: Put t = x+√(x²+1). Now take the reciprocal of both sides and watch what happens: multiply top and bottom by √(x²+1) − x, the denominator becomes (x²+1) − x² = 1, and you are left with 1/t = √(x²+1) − x. Multiplying up and down by the same thing is always allowed, and here it pays you back beautifully.

Once you have t = x+√(x²+1) and 1/t = √(x²+1) − x, subtract and add them: t − 1/t = 2x and t + 1/t = 2√(x²+1). I am not saying you will need both in every problem. I am saying this is the total knowledge of this substitution, so keep both on the side of your page.

Now for dx. Differentiate: dt/dx = 1 + x/√(x²+1) = (x+√(x²+1))/√(x²+1) = t/√(x²+1). Don't cancel differentials carelessly here — cross multiply properly: dx = √(x²+1) dt / t. And √(x²+1) is just half of (t + 1/t), so dx = ½(t + 1/t)(1/t) dt = ½(1 + 1/t²) dt.

The integral is now ∫ln t · ½(1 + 1/t²) dt. Stop the log, integrate the rest: ∫(1 + t⁻²) dt = t − 1/t. By parts gives ½[(t − 1/t)ln t − ∫(t − 1/t)(1/t) dt], and that last integral is ∫(1 − 1/t²) dt = t + 1/t. Then your side note turns it straight back into x: ½[2x ln t − 2√(x²+1)] = x ln(x+√(x²+1)) − √(x²+1) + C.

quickChecks.q: If t = x+√(x²+1), find 1/t and then t − 1/t.
steps: 1. 1/t = 1/(x+√(x²+1)); multiply top and bottom by √(x²+1) − x.
2. Bottom = (x²+1) − x² = 1, so 1/t = √(x²+1) − x.

quickChecks.q: With the same t, write dx completely in terms of t and dt.
steps: 2. Cross multiply: dx = √(x²+1) dt / t.
3. Replace √(x²+1) by ½(t + 1/t): dx = ½(t + 1/t)(1/t) dt.

quickChecks.q: Check the answer: differentiate x ln(x+√(x²+1)) − √(x²+1) and see if you get back ln(x+√(x²+1)).
steps: 2. Product rule on the first term: ln(x+√(x²+1)) + x/√(x²+1).
3. d/dx of √(x²+1) = x/√(x²+1), and it carries a minus sign.
4. The two x/√(x²+1) terms cancel.
quickChecks.answer: You get ln(x+√(x²+1)), so the answer is correct

concepts.title: The Same Log Integral Done Directly: Stop the Log, Integrate 1
concepts.oneLine: For ∫ln(x+√(1+x²)) dx, pair the log with 1, integrate the 1 to get x, and the derivative of the log collapses to 1/√(1+x²) — giving x·ln(x+√(1+x²)) − √(1+x²) + C in one line.
notes: There is only one function sitting in front of you, so supply the second one yourself: 1. In by parts the log stays as the first function and 1 is the second. Integrating 1 gives x, so the first term is x·ln(x+√(1+x²)).

Now the minus part: minus the integral of x times the derivative of the log. Differentiate ln(x+√(1+x²)) and you get 1/(x+√(1+x²)) multiplied by (1 + x/√(1+x²)). Take √(1+x²) common inside the bracket: it becomes (x+√(1+x²))/√(1+x²). The bracket (x+√(1+x²)) cancels top and bottom and only 1/√(1+x²) survives — that cancellation is the whole reason this integral is a one-liner.

So the leftover job is just ∫ x/√(1+x²) dx. The derivative of 1+x² is 2x, so x dx is half of d(1+x²). A power of −½ integrates to a power of +½ divided by ½, that is twice, and half of twice is one. Clean answer: √(1+x²).

Put it together and the whole thing is x·ln(x+√(1+x²)) − √(1+x²) + C. Exactly what substitution gave us, with a third of the writing. When a log or an inverse function stands alone, don't hunt for a substitution — give it a 1 and go by parts.

quickChecks.q: Find ∫ln x dx by the same trick.
steps: 1. Write it as ∫ln x · 1 dx, with log as the first function.
2. By parts: x·ln x − ∫ x · (1/x) dx.
3. The x cancels: x·ln x − ∫1 dx.

quickChecks.q: Differentiate ln(x+√(x²+4)).
steps: 2. Take √(x²+4) common inside: (√(x²+4)+x)/√(x²+4).
3. The bracket (x+√(x²+4)) cancels.

quickChecks.q: Evaluate ∫ln(x+√(x²+4)) dx.
steps: 1. Pair it with 1: by parts gives x·ln(x+√(x²+4)) − ∫ x · 1/√(x²+4) dx.
2. For the second integral, x dx = ½ d(x²+4).
4. Keep the minus sign in front of it.

concepts.title: Forcing the Derivative of the Denominator Before Integration by Parts
concepts.oneLine: When nothing works, multiply and divide the integrand so the derivative of the denominator appears on top — then by parts collapses in one step.
notes: Normal integration by parts came earlier. Here the logic is slightly different, and it is one of those JEE-style formats where the question looks impossible at first glance.

The whole idea is one sentence: look at the denominator, find its derivative, and then forcefully create that derivative in the numerator by multiplying and dividing by the same thing. Once the derivative of the denominator is sitting on top, that whole piece becomes integrable on its own, and the leftover factor becomes your first function for by parts.

Why does it collapse? Because after by parts you have to differentiate that leftover first function — and its derivative brings back exactly the bracket you had in the denominator. Everything cancels, and what is left is a basic integral like ∫sec²x dx.

One honest warning. This is difficult to click even after reading it once — but if the idea stays in your head, it can click at the right time in a question where nothing else is working. The same trick works with powers too: with an x⁴ expression, you multiply and divide by x³, because the derivative of x⁴ is 4x³.

quickChecks.q: Integrate (x cos x) / (x sin x + cos x)² with respect to x.
steps: 1. The numerator is already the derivative of the base — no forcing needed here.
2. Put t = x sin x + cos x, so dt = x cos x dx.
3. The integral becomes ∫ t⁻² dt = −1/t.

quickChecks.q: Integrate x² / (sin x − x cos x)² with respect to x.
steps: 1. Derivative of the denominator's base: d/dx (sin x − x cos x) = cos x − (cos x − x sin x) = x sin x.
2. So x sin x is what is needed on top. Split x² = x · x, multiply one x by sin x and divide the other by sin x: the integrand is (x / sin x) × [ x sin x / (sin x − x cos x)² ].
3. The second part integrates to −1 / (sin x − x cos x).
4. By parts with first function x / sin x: answer = −x / (sin x (sin x − x cos x)) + ∫ [1/(sin x − x cos x)] × (sin x − x cos x)/sin²x dx.
5. The bracket cancels and ∫ cosec²x dx = −cot x.
quickChecks.answer: −cot x − x / (sin x (sin x − x cos x)) + C, which tidies to −(x sin x + cos x) / (sin x − x cos x) + C

quickChecks.q: Integrate x⁷ / (1 + x⁴)² with respect to x.
steps: 1. The derivative of x⁴ is 4x³, so x³ is the factor you want. Split x⁷ = x⁴ · x³.
2. Put t = x⁴, so dt = 4x³ dx. The integral becomes (1/4) ∫ t / (1 + t)² dt.
4. That is (1/4) [ ln|1 + t| + 1/(1 + t) ]. Put t = x⁴ back.

concepts.title: The ∫eˣ(f + f′) and ∫(f + x f′) Formulas
concepts.oneLine: If you see eˣ(f + f′), the integral is just eˣf(x) + c; if you see (f + x f′), it is just x f(x) + c.
notes: Look at the first one. Inside the integral there is eˣ, and next to it a function plus its own derivative. Then the whole integral is just eˣ times that function, plus c. Nothing else to do.

Say the bracket is x³ + x⁵ + ln x + 3x² + 5x⁴ + 1/x. Half of it is f, half of it is f′. The derivative of x³ + x⁵ + ln x is exactly 3x² + 5x⁴ + 1/x, so the answer is eˣ(x³ + x⁵ + ln x) + c. A thousand questions can be built like this, and every one of them dies in one line.

The real work is the selection — deciding which piece is f. Take eˣ(tan x + ln sec x). If you call tan x the function, its derivative is sec²x, and sec²x is nowhere in the bracket, so the setting is not happening. Flip it: the derivative of ln sec x is (1/sec x)·sec x·tan x = tan x. So f = ln sec x, f′ = tan x, and the answer is eˣ·ln sec x + c.

The second formula is the same idea with x in place of eˣ, and it is less important. If the bracket is f(x) plus x·f′(x), the integral is x·f(x) + c. Both of these come straight out of integration by parts, which I prove for you next.

quickChecks.q: Find ∫eˣ(x + 1) dx
steps: 1. Take f(x) = x, so f′(x) = 1.
2. Bracket = f + f′, so answer is eˣ f(x) + c.

quickChecks.q: Find ∫eˣ(ln x + 1/x) dx
steps: 1. Take f(x) = ln x, so f′(x) = 1/x.
2. Bracket = f + f′, so answer is eˣ f(x) + c.

quickChecks.q: Find ∫(tan x + x sec²x) dx
steps: 1. Take f(x) = tan x, so f′(x) = sec²x.
2. Bracket = f + x f′, so the second formula applies and the answer is x f(x) + c.

concepts.title: Proving Both Formulas from Integration by Parts
concepts.oneLine: Both formulas are just integration by parts done once: split the integral, apply by parts to one piece, and the other piece cancels — leaving eˣf(x) + c and x f(x) + c.
notes: Take the first one: ∫eˣ(f(x) + f′(x))dx. Split it into two integrals, ∫eˣf(x)dx + ∫eˣf′(x)dx. Now notice something — you can apply by parts on either of the two pieces and you will reach the same answer. Take the first piece.

In ∫eˣf(x)dx, f is the one to differentiate, because f′ is already sitting there in the other term. So f(x) is the first function and eˣ is the second: it becomes f(x)·eˣ − ∫f′(x)·eˣ dx. Add this to the second term ∫eˣf′(x)dx and that whole integral cancels, leaving eˣf(x) + c. That is the proof — one line.

The second formula goes exactly the same way. ∫(f(x) + x f′(x))dx splits into ∫f(x)dx + ∫x f′(x)dx. Put by parts on ∫x f′(x)dx: differentiate x, integrate f′. You get x f(x) − ∫f(x)dx, and that leftover integral kills the ∫f(x)dx in front. Answer: x f(x) + c.

If you prefer, apply by parts on the other piece instead — write ∫f(x)dx as ∫1·f(x)dx, differentiate f and integrate 1. You will land on the same place. Keep both derivations at this basic level in your head; then even when the question hides the form, you can rebuild the formula instead of guessing it.

quickChecks.q: Use the first formula to evaluate ∫eˣ(sin x + cos x)dx.
steps: 1. Match the bracket to f(x) + f′(x). Take f(x) = sin x, then f′(x) = cos x.
2. The bracket is exactly f(x) + f′(x), so the answer is eˣf(x) + c.
3. Check by differentiating: d/dx(eˣ sin x) = eˣ sin x + eˣ cos x = eˣ(sin x + cos x). ✓

quickChecks.q: Evaluate ∫(ln x + 1)dx using the second formula.
steps: 1. Try f(x) = ln x, so f′(x) = 1/x and x f′(x) = x·(1/x) = 1.
2. So ln x + 1 = f(x) + x f′(x), which fits the form exactly.
3. Hence the integral is x f(x) + c = x ln x + c.
4. Check: d/dx(x ln x) = ln x + x·(1/x) = ln x + 1. ✓

quickChecks.q: In proving ∫eˣ(f + f′)dx = eˣf, you apply by parts to ∫eˣf(x)dx. Which factor do you differentiate, and which integral cancels?
steps: 1. Differentiate f(x) and integrate eˣ, because the term f′ is already present in the original bracket.
2. By parts gives eˣf(x) − ∫eˣf′(x)dx.
3. That −∫eˣf′(x)dx cancels with the +∫eˣf′(x)dx coming from the split.
quickChecks.answer: Differentiate f(x) (integrate eˣ); the ∫eˣf′(x)dx terms cancel, leaving eˣf(x) + c.

concepts.title: General Version with eᵍ⁽ˣ⁾
concepts.oneLine: If the power of e is g(x) instead of x, then ∫e^{g(x)}(f(x)·g′(x) + f′(x))dx = e^{g(x)}·f(x) + c.
notes: You already know the basic one: ∫eˣ(f(x) + f′(x))dx = eˣ·f(x) + c. Now put g(x) in the power instead of x.

The moment the power becomes g(x), g(x) also comes in the answer. And one more thing changes inside the bracket: the function f(x) no longer sits alone — it must be multiplied by g′(x), the derivative of the power. So the bracket reads f(x)·g′(x) + f′(x), and the answer is e^{g(x)}·f(x) + c.
That is the only change. Nothing else moves. The f′(x) term stays exactly as it was.

See how such a question is built, because that is how you learn to read it backwards. Pick the power: x³. Pick the function: tan x. Then write its derivative, sec²x, as the second term. And alongside tan x write the derivative of x³, which is 3x². The question is ready — and so is the answer.

quickChecks.q: Evaluate ∫e^{x²}(2x tan x + sec²x)dx
steps: 1. Power is x², so g(x) = x² and g′(x) = 2x.
2. 2x is sitting with tan x, so f(x) = tan x.
3. Leftover term sec²x = f′(x). Pattern fits.

quickChecks.q: Evaluate ∫e^{x³}(3x² ln x + 1/x)dx
steps: 1. g(x) = x³, so g′(x) = 3x².
2. 3x² comes with ln x, so f(x) = ln x.
3. Leftover 1/x is the derivative of ln x. Pattern fits.

quickChecks.q: Evaluate ∫e^{sin x}(x cos x + 1)dx
steps: 1. Power is sin x, so g(x) = sin x and g′(x) = cos x.
2. cos x is sitting with x, so f(x) = x.
3. Leftover term is 1, which is the derivative of x. Pattern fits.

concepts.title: Trigonometric Examples on the eˣ Formula
concepts.oneLine: Open sin 4x and 1 − cos 4x with the double angle formulas, split the fraction, and the integrand turns into f + f′ (or f g′ + f′) so the eˣ formula finishes it in one line.
notes: We have been doing these two expansions since school. sin 4x = 2 sin 2x cos 2x, and 1 − cos 4x = 2 sin² 2x. The same 1 − cos θ = 2 sin² (θ/2) that you used all through limits.

So whenever you see sin 4x over 1 − cos 4x, open both and cancel: you are left with cot 2x. And the leftover −4/(1 − cos 4x) becomes −2 cosec² 2x, which is exactly the derivative of cot 2x. One is f, the other is f′, and ∫ eˣ (f + f′) dx = eˣ f + C closes it.

The second question is on the general form, so read the format very carefully. With e^g(x) outside, the function must come multiplied by g′(x), and the other term must be f′(x). If the g′ is not visible, create it: write 1/(2x) as 2 × 1/(4x) and the 2 becomes your g′.
After that, only one question remains: is the leftover term really f′ of the function you picked? For f = 1/(4x) it is −1/(4x²), and that is what sits there. Then just write e^g(x) f(x) + C.

quickChecks.q: Simplify sin 4x / (1 − cos 4x) to a single trigonometric ratio.
steps: 1. sin 4x = 2 sin 2x cos 2x.
2. 1 − cos 4x = 2 sin² 2x.
3. Divide: (2 sin 2x cos 2x)/(2 sin² 2x) = cos 2x / sin 2x.

quickChecks.q: Evaluate ∫ eˣ (sin 2x − 2)/(1 − cos 2x) dx
steps: 1. Split: ∫ eˣ [ sin 2x/(1 − cos 2x) − 2/(1 − cos 2x) ] dx.
2. sin 2x = 2 sin x cos x and 1 − cos 2x = 2 sin² x.
3. First piece becomes cot x; second piece becomes −2/(2 sin² x) = −cosec² x.
4. So f = cot x and f′ = −cosec² x, which is eˣ (f + f′).

quickChecks.q: Evaluate ∫ e³ˣ (3x − 1)/x² dx
steps: 1. Split: 3x/x² − 1/x² = 3/x − 1/x².
2. Here g(x) = 3x, so g′(x) = 3. Write 3/x as 3 × 1/x, giving f(x) = 1/x.
3. Check: f′(x) = derivative of 1/x = −1/x², which is the leftover term.
4. So the integrand is e³ˣ [ f g′ + f′ ] and the answer is e^g(x) f(x) + C.

concepts.title: Splitting the Numerator to Create f and f′
concepts.oneLine: When eˣ sits with a linear numerator over a power of a different bracket, force the numerator to become the bracket below minus a constant — the integral then falls straight into f + f′.
notes: Look at the first one: ∫eˣ(1+x)/(2+x)² dx. The bracket below is 2+x, but above sits 1+x. So add 1 and subtract 1 by force and write 1+x = (2+x) − 1. Whatever bracket is sitting in the denominator, force the numerator to become that same bracket minus a number.

Now split the fraction. One piece gives (2+x)/(2+x)² = 1/(2+x), and the other gives −1/(2+x)². Check the side piece: the derivative of 1/(2+x) is exactly −1/(2+x)². So f and f′ are both on the page, and the answer is eˣ·1/(2+x) + C.
The same pen stroke clears B and C. In ∫eˣ(x+3)/(x+5)³ dx write x+3 = (x+5) − 2, and in ∫eˣ(x−1)/(x+1)³ dx write x−1 = (x+1) − 2. Nothing else is needed — no substitution, no by-parts.

After the split, with a cube below, the first piece is 1/(bracket)² — that is the f. Its derivative is −2/(bracket)³, and that −2 is exactly the constant the split handed you. So the answer is just eˣ times that f.

quickChecks.q: Evaluate ∫eˣ(x+2)/(x+3)² dx.
Evaluate ∫eˣ·x/(x+2)³ dx.
Evaluate ∫eˣ(x+2)/(x+4)³ dx.

concepts.title: A Two-Step Split: ∫eˣ(x²+1)/(x+1)²dx
concepts.oneLine: Force the denominator into the numerator twice — first ±2x, then ±1 — and ∫eˣ(x²+1)/(x+1)²dx collapses to the eˣ(f + f′) form.
notes: The target is always the same shape: eˣ(f + f′). If the bracket can be written as some f plus its own derivative, the integral is eˣf and the question is finished.

So look at what is downstairs — (x+1)² — and manufacture it upstairs. x²+1 is not (x+1)², but it is only 2x away: add 2x and subtract 2x. Divide, and one piece becomes plain eˣ, the other becomes −2eˣ·x/(x+1)².

Now the second piece is a smaller copy of the same problem, so the same move repeats one layer down. Upstairs is x, downstairs carries (x+1), so write x = (x+1) − 1. That gives 1/(x+1) − 1/(x+1)², and since the derivative of 1/(x+1) is −1/(x+1)², that bracket is exactly f + f′.
There is no trick to hunt for. Force the denominator to appear in the numerator — once, and then again. That is why this feels easy: it is common sense repeated, not something you had to spot.

quickChecks.q: Evaluate ∫eˣ·x/(x+1)² dx.
steps: 2. Take f = 1/(x+1); then f′ = −1/(x+1)², so the bracket is f + f′.
3. ∫eˣ(f + f′)dx = eˣf.

quickChecks.q: Evaluate ∫eˣ(x²+4x+1)/(x+1)² dx.
steps: 1. Make (x+1)² upstairs: x²+4x+1 = (x²+2x+1) + 2x = (x+1)² + 2x.
2. Divide: the integrand is eˣ + 2eˣ·x/(x+1)².
3. First piece gives eˣ; the second is 2 times the previous question, so it gives 2eˣ/(x+1).
4. Add and take eˣ common: eˣ[1 + 2/(x+1)] = eˣ(x+3)/(x+1).

quickChecks.q: Check the answer: differentiate eˣ(x−1)/(x+1) and show you get back eˣ(x²+1)/(x+1)².
steps: 2. Product rule: d/dx(eˣu) = eˣ(u + u′) = eˣ[1 − 2/(x+1) + 2/(x+1)²].
quickChecks.answer: eˣ(x²+1)/(x+1)², the original integrand — so the answer is right.

concepts.title: Using the x f′ Form: ∫(ln(ln x) + 1/ln x)dx
concepts.oneLine: If the question gives you f(x) but not its partner x·f′(x), write the partner in yourself and subtract it the same line — then check whether the leftover is itself an f + x f′ pair.
notes: Nothing new is needed here. The whole question runs on one form: if the integrand is f(x) + x·f′(x), the answer is x·f(x) + C. Your only job is to spot f and build its partner.

The first piece written is ln(ln x), so take that as f. Its derivative is (1/ln x)·(1/x), that is 1/(x ln x), and the form wants x·f′, which is 1/ln x. Now look at the question: 1/ln x is not there, so write it in by hand — and subtract it in the same line, because nothing comes free.

The bracket just built gives x·ln(ln x) straight away. What is left over is −1/ln x + 1/(ln x)². Observe it instead of panicking. Take g = 1/ln x; then x·g′ is exactly −1/(ln x)², so the leftover is itself a g + x·g′ pair. Same trick, second time, no new idea.
You can also put ln x = t, so x = eᵗ and dx = eᵗ dt. It works and gives the same answer, only it is longer — in the paper that costs you minutes. That route is left for you to finish on your own.

quickChecks.q: Evaluate ∫(ln(ln x) + 1/ln x)dx
steps: 1. Take f(x) = ln(ln x). Then f′(x) = 1/(x ln x), so x·f′(x) = 1/ln x.
2. The integrand is already f + x·f′, so nothing has to be added or subtracted.
3. Answer is x·f(x) + C.

quickChecks.q: Evaluate ∫(1/ln x − 1/(ln x)²)dx
steps: 1. Take f(x) = 1/ln x. Then f′(x) = −1/(x(ln x)²), so x·f′(x) = −1/(ln x)².
2. So f + x·f′ = 1/ln x − 1/(ln x)², exactly the integrand.
3. Answer is x·f(x) + C.

quickChecks.q: Evaluate ∫(ln x + 1)dx using the same form.
steps: 1. Take f(x) = ln x. Then f′(x) = 1/x, so x·f′(x) = 1.
2. The integrand is f + x·f′ = ln x + 1.
3. Answer is x·f(x) + C.

concepts.title: Manipulating e^{tan x} Problems into the General Form
concepts.oneLine: When the power of e is tan x, force a sec²x into the integrand by multiplying and dividing by sec x — then the integral is just f·e^g.
notes: The shape is ∫e^g(f·g′ + f′)dx = f·e^g + C. So the first thing to do is look at the power of e. Here the power is tan x, which means g′ must be sec²x.

Now look at the question: sec x and sin x are sitting there, but sec²x is nowhere. So make it appear: multiply by sec x and divide by sec x in the same term — that is always allowed, because nothing has been changed.

One sec was already given in the problem. The extra sec comes in from above, and the 1/sec brought in from below becomes cos x. That turns sec x into cos x · sec²x, which is exactly f·g′ with f = cos x.

And the moment f = cos x, f′ = −sin x — which is the other term, already waiting in the question with a minus sign. The sign matching is your proof that you picked the right f. Answer: cos x · e^{tan x}.

quickChecks.q: Evaluate ∫e^(cot x)(cos x − cosec x) dx.
steps: 1. Power of e is cot x, so g = cot x and g′ = −cosec²x.
2. Force the cosec²x: cosec x = cosec²x · sin x, so −cosec x = sin x · (−cosec²x) = f·g′ with f = sin x.
3. Then f′ = cos x, which is the first term. Shape matched.
4. Answer = f·e^g = sin x · e^(cot x) + C.

quickChecks.q: Evaluate ∫e^(tan x)(x sec²x + 1) dx.
steps: 1. g = tan x, g′ = sec²x. Here sec²x is already given, no manipulation needed.
2. f·g′ = x sec²x gives f = x, and f′ = 1, which is the second term.
3. Answer = x · e^(tan x) + C.

quickChecks.q: Evaluate ∫e^(tan x)(sec³x + sec x tan x) dx.
steps: 1. g = tan x, so sec²x is what is needed. Split the first term: sec³x = sec x · sec²x.
2. So f·g′ = sec x · sec²x gives f = sec x, and f′ = sec x tan x, which is exactly the second term.
3. Answer = sec x · e^(tan x) + C.

concepts.title: Quiz Solutions: Three Problems on the eˣ Formulas
concepts.oneLine: All three quiz questions are the same pattern in disguise: make the derivative of the power (or of the inner function) appear, and the answer is just the outside function times that function.
notes: None of these three is solved by putting ln x = t, or anything else = t. In an objective question your job is to recognise a pattern, not to perform a substitution. That is the whole skill being built here.

The pattern is the one we built in the last section. If the bracket is f(x) + f′(x) sitting with eˣ, the answer is eˣ f(x). If x is sitting outside instead of eˣ, the same idea gives f + x f′ → x f(x). And if the power is not plain x but some g(x), then f′ + f g′ → f(x) e^g(x).

So before you write anything, differentiate the power or the inner function. For x + 1/x that is 1 − 1/x². Now hunt for that shape in the bracket — and if it is hiding, take something common until it appears.

One more habit for the third question. Your answer and the given option can be the same thing wearing different clothes. The working gives eˣ tan(x/2), which no option states directly; convert it with the half-angle identities and option C matches.

quickChecks.q: Evaluate ∫ [1/(1 + ln x) − 1/(1 + ln x)²] dx
steps: 1. Take f(x) = 1/(1 + ln x), so f′(x) = −1/[x(1 + ln x)²].
2. Then x f′(x) = −1/(1 + ln x)², which is the second term.
3. So the integrand is f(x) + x f′(x) = d/dx [x f(x)].

quickChecks.q: Evaluate ∫ e^(x + 1/x) (1 − 1/x²) dx
steps: 1. Differentiate the power: d/dx (x + 1/x) = 1 − 1/x².
2. So the bracket is exactly g′(x) sitting with e^g(x).
3. ∫ e^g g′ dx = e^g.

quickChecks.q: Evaluate ∫ eˣ (1 − sin x)/(1 − cos x) dx
steps: 1. Use 1 − cos x = 2sin²(x/2) and sin x = 2 sin(x/2) cos(x/2).
2. The fraction becomes [1 − 2 sin(x/2)cos(x/2)]/[2sin²(x/2)] = ½ cosec²(x/2) − cot(x/2).
3. Take f(x) = −cot(x/2). Then f′(x) = ½ cosec²(x/2), so the bracket is f + f′.
4. Hence the integral is eˣ f(x).

concepts.title: Revision: Trigonometric Integrals Done by Identity
concepts.oneLine: Before the harder trigonometric integrals, revise the four identity-first formats — cos A cos B, sin 3θ, 1 + cos 2x, and tan(a+b) cross-multiplication — because in each one the identity, not a substitution, is the whole solution.
notes: We are now in the better, harder part of trigonometric integration. But be honest about what is actually new here: only two or three formats. The rest are the same formats we started this topic with, four lectures ago. Old does not mean useless — it means you must give them respect.

Look at the four questions on the screen. In (a) you put the cos A cos B identity. In (b) you put the sin 3θ identity. In (c) it is the 1 + cos 2x over 2 format, the one we used again and again in today's class. In every one of these, the question is won the moment you pick the right identity — the integration after that is a one-line job.

Part (d) is pure trigonometry. There you cross multiply the tan(a + b) expansion, and the eye you need is this: instead of leaving 2x as 2x, write it as 5x − 3x. Once you see that, the whole thing collapses.

So yes, it feels like we have gone back to lecture number one. We have — on purpose, for continuity. Do this recall once, properly, and then you never spend fresh time on these again. The basic is the most important thing you carry into the new formats.

quickChecks.q: Integrate cos 5x · cos x with respect to x.
steps: 1. 2 cos 5x cos x = cos 6x + cos 4x, so cos 5x cos x = (cos 6x + cos 4x)/2.
2. Integral = ½ [ sin 6x/6 + sin 4x/4 ].

quickChecks.q: Integrate cos²3x with respect to x.
steps: 1. cos²3x = (1 + cos 6x)/2.
2. Integral = ½ ∫(1 + cos 6x) dx = ½ [ x + sin 6x/6 ].

quickChecks.q: Write tan 3x · tan 4x · tan 7x as a sum of single tangents.
steps: 1. The angles give 3x = 7x − 4x.
2. tan 3x = (tan 7x − tan 4x)/(1 + tan 7x tan 4x).
3. Cross multiply: tan 3x + tan 3x tan 4x tan 7x = tan 7x − tan 4x.
quickChecks.answer: tan 3x tan 4x tan 7x = tan 7x − tan 4x − tan 3x

concepts.title: Choosing the Substitution for tanⁿx secᵐx Integrals
concepts.oneLine: In ∫secⁿx tanᵐx dx, pick the substitution that leaves an even power of tan behind, because sec²x = 1 + tan²x turns that even power into a plain polynomial in t.
notes: Start with the easy one: ∫sec²x tan³x dx. Here sec²x is exactly the derivative of tan x, so t = tan x, dt = sec²x dx, and the whole thing becomes ∫t³ dt. Done in one line. This is the same substitution habit we built when we first learnt integration by substitution — nothing new, only dressed in trigonometry.

Now change one power: ∫sec³x tan⁵x dx. Try t = tan x. The sec²x dx becomes dt, but one sec x is left standing alone, and a single sec x cannot be written in terms of t = tan x without a square root. That lone odd power is the problem.

So here t is not tan x — put t = sec x, which gives dt = sec x tan x dx. One sec x goes into dt, one tan x goes into dt, dx goes too. What survives is sec²x tan⁴x, and tan is now sitting on an even power.

An even power of tan is friendly: tan⁴x = (sec²x − 1)². So sec²x = t² and tan⁴x = (t² − 1)², and the integral is ∫t²(t² − 1)² dt. Expand, integrate term by term, put sec x back — that is the full method. Choose the substitution that leaves tan on an even power, every time.

quickChecks.q: Integrate ∫sec x tan³x dx.
steps: 1. sec power is odd and tan power is odd, so take t = sec x, dt = sec x tan x dx.
2. One sec x and one tan x go into dt, leaving tan²x.
3. tan²x = sec²x − 1 = t² − 1.

quickChecks.q: Integrate ∫sec²x tan⁴x dx.
steps: 1. sec sits on power 2, exactly the derivative of tan x, so take t = tan x, dt = sec²x dx.
2. The integral becomes ∫t⁴ dt = t⁵/5 + C.

quickChecks.q: Integrate ∫sec³x tan³x dx.
steps: 1. Both powers are odd, so take t = sec x, dt = sec x tan x dx.
2. Pull one sec x and one tan x into dt; what remains is sec²x tan²x.
3. sec²x = t² and tan²x = t² − 1, so the integral is ∫t²(t² − 1) dt = ∫(t⁴ − t²) dt.

concepts.title: The Even-Power Rule for sin–cos and tan–sec Substitutions
concepts.oneLine: Never count the power of the function you call t — only the power left after the derivative matters, and it must be even.
notes: In every sin–cos and tan–sec substitution, one power goes away inside the derivative, and whatever is left has to convert into t. The power of the function you put equal to t never matters; what matters is the power left over after the derivative, and that one must be even.

Take tan⁵x sec³x and put t = sec x. Then dt = sec x tan x dx, so one sec and one tan are eaten by the derivative. What is left is tan⁴x — even — and tan²x = sec²x − 1, so it becomes (t² − 1)². If that 3 were 13, nothing changes: sec¹²x is just t¹². The sec power is free.

Now make the tan power 6 instead of 5. One tan goes into dt and tan⁵x is left. Write it as (sec²x − 1)^(5/2) and you are finished — a half power has infinitely many terms, you cannot expand it, you cannot integrate it. That is the disaster, and parity is the only thing that caused it.

Same logic in sine and cosine. For sin³x cos⁴x put t = cos x, because one sine is eaten by the derivative and sin²x survives — even, and sin²x = 1 − cos²x. The cos power can be 4 or 14; it never needs a second look. Nothing is memorised here — just check which leftover lands on an even power.

quickChecks.q: Integrate tan³x sec⁴x dx.
steps: 1. Put t = sec x, dt = sec x tan x dx.
2. Split: tan³x sec⁴x dx = sec³x · tan²x · (sec x tan x dx).
3. Leftover tan power is 2 — even, so tan²x = t² − 1.
4. ∫ t³(t² − 1) dt = ∫ (t⁵ − t³) dt = t⁶/6 − t⁴/4 + C.

quickChecks.q: Integrate sin⁵x cos²x dx.
steps: 1. Put t = cos x, so sin x dx = −dt.
2. Split: sin⁵x cos²x dx = cos²x · sin⁴x · (sin x dx).
3. Leftover sine power is 4 — even, so sin⁴x = (1 − t²)².
4. −∫ t²(1 − t²)² dt = −∫ (t² − 2t⁴ + t⁶) dt = −t³/3 + 2t⁵/5 − t⁷/7 + C.

quickChecks.q: Can you put t = tan x in ∫ tan⁴x sec⁶x dx? Decide first, then finish it.
steps: 1. t = tan x eats sec²x dx, and the tan power 4 is t's own power — ignore it.
2. Leftover sec power is 6 − 2 = 4, which is even, so it converts: sec⁴x = (1 + t²)². The substitution is valid.
3. ∫ t⁴(1 + t²)² dt = ∫ (t⁴ + 2t⁶ + t⁸) dt = t⁵/5 + 2t⁷/7 + t⁹/9 + C.
quickChecks.answer: Yes, it works: tan⁵x/5 + 2tan⁷x/7 + tan⁹x/9 + C

concepts.title: Quiz: Which Substitution Works?
concepts.oneLine: Pull one factor into dt, look at the power that is left: if it is even the substitution works, and in ∫ sin⁵x cos³x dx both t = sin x and t = cos x pass that test.
notes: Look at ∫ sin⁵x cos³x dx. The four options are: A) t = cos x, B) t = sin x, C) both, D) neither. Notice that the question is not asking you to integrate. Integration after a good substitution is routine — anybody can finish it.
Take t = cos x. Then dt = −sin x dx, so one sin x dx goes into dt and sin⁴x is left over. That is (1 − cos²x)², pure t. The cos³x sitting there becomes t³. Clean.
Now take t = sin x instead. Then dt = cos x dx, so one cos x dx goes into dt and cos²x is left over, which is 1 − sin²x. The sin⁵x becomes t⁵. Also clean. Both substitutions work, so the answer is C.

Keep the test in your head exactly like this. The power of the function you are calling t does not matter at all — what must be even is the power that is left after you pull one factor out for dt. Here sin⁵ leaves sin⁴ and cos³ leaves cos², both even, so neither road is blocked.

quickChecks.q: For ∫ sin³x cos⁴x dx, which works: t = sin x, t = cos x, both or neither?
steps: 1. t = cos x: dt = −sin x dx, one sin x leaves sin²x = 1 − t², even — works.
2. t = sin x: dt = cos x dx, one cos x leaves cos³x, odd — blocked.

quickChecks.q: For ∫ sin x cos⁵x dx, which works?
steps: 1. t = cos x: dt = −sin x dx, the only sin x goes into dt, leftover sin power is 0, even — works, giving −∫ t⁵ dt.
2. t = sin x: dt = cos x dx, one cos x leaves cos⁴x = (1 − t²)², even — works too.
quickChecks.answer: Both — and t = cos x is the shorter one here.

quickChecks.q: For ∫ sin²x cos²x dx, which works?
steps: 1. t = cos x: pull out one sin x for dt and sin x is left, odd — blocked.
2. t = sin x: pull out one cos x for dt and cos x is left, odd — blocked.
quickChecks.answer: Neither — both powers are even to start with, so no substitution fits.

concepts.title: When No Substitution Works: Fall Back on Identities
concepts.oneLine: When both sin and cos sit at even powers, no substitution survives — convert with sin x cos x = sin2x/2 and then kill every square with the 1−cos double-angle identity.
notes: Try t = sin x first. Then dt = cos x dx eats one cosine, and you are left with cos³x sitting there. You cannot write cos³x in terms of sin x, because for that you need an even power of cosine to pair up. So that door is shut.

Now try t = cos x. Same story from the other side: one sine goes into dt, and sin³x is left over. Again an odd power, again no conversion. When both powers are even, substitution is dead — this is not a substitution problem, it is an identity problem.
So use the identity instead. sin x cos x = sin2x/2, and here both are at power 4, so the whole thing becomes (sin2x/2)⁴ = sin⁴2x/16. Now there are only sines, at an even power, of a double angle.

From there it is exactly the ∫sin²x question you already know. Write sin⁴2x as (sin²2x)², replace sin²2x by (1−cos4x)/2, open the square, and when a cos²4x appears, hit it with the same identity once more. Nothing here is to be learnt by heart — you only keep halving powers until every term is a plain cosine.

quickChecks.q: Evaluate ∫sin²x cos²x dx.
steps: 1. Equal powers, so pair: sin²x cos²x = (sin x cos x)² = (sin2x/2)² = sin²2x/4.
2. Use sin²2x = (1−cos4x)/2, so the integrand is (1−cos4x)/8.
3. Integrate: x/8 − (sin4x)/32 + C.

quickChecks.q: Evaluate ∫sin²x dx.
steps: 1. No substitution needed, just the identity: sin²x = (1−cos2x)/2.
2. Integrate: x/2 − (sin2x)/4 + C.

quickChecks.q: For ∫sin³x cos⁴x dx, do you substitute or use an identity?
steps: 1. Check the powers: sine is at 3, which is odd.
2. An odd power means you can keep one sin x aside for dt and convert the rest, so put t = cos x, dt = −sin x dx.
3. The leftover sin²x becomes 1 − t², and the integral turns into a polynomial in t.
quickChecks.answer: Substitution, with t = cos x — no identity needed, because one power is odd.

concepts.title: Even Powers Convert Either Way, Plus Odd and Fractional Cases
concepts.oneLine: An even leftover power converts in both directions — tan↔sec and sin↔cos — so for an odd power of sin you peel off one sin x, put cos x = t, and the even rest becomes (1 − t²).
notes: Close this idea properly. If the power left over is even, it makes no difference whether it is 4, 6 or 10 — they are all the same dish. And it makes no difference whether that even power sits on sin or on cos.

An even power is convertible both ways: that is the whole freedom. Say sin⁴x is left over and you want to take cos x = t. Fine — write sin⁴x as (1 − cos²x)², and everything is in cos. Nothing stops you, because the power was even.

The same freedom works with tan and sec, and it does not care about fractional powers either. In sin^(14/9)x cos^(4/9)x sitting in the denominator, pull a tan out of the sin: you get tan^(−14/9)x, and the cos powers collect as 4/9 + 14/9 = 18/9 = 2, which is exactly sec²x. Now tan x = t finishes it.

For an odd power there is one extra move. Peel off a single sin x, keep it with dx, and what is left behind is even. That single sin x dx is precisely −dt when you set cos x = t, so the question solves itself.

quickChecks.q: Integrate cos³x dx.
steps: 1. Peel off one cos x: cos³x = cos x · cos²x.
2. Take sin x = t, so cos x dx = dt (no minus this time).
3. Leftover cos²x is even: cos²x = 1 − sin²x = 1 − t².
5. Put t = sin x.

quickChecks.q: Integrate cos⁵x dx.
steps: 1. cos⁵x = cos x · cos⁴x, and take sin x = t so cos x dx = dt.
2. cos⁴x = (1 − sin²x)² = (1 − t²)².
3. ∫ (1 − t²)² dt = ∫ (1 − 2t² + t⁴) dt = t − 2t³/3 + t⁵/5.
4. Put t = sin x.

quickChecks.q: Integrate 1 / (sin^(5/3)x · cos^(1/3)x) with respect to x.
steps: 1. Check the sum of powers: 5/3 + 1/3 = 6/3 = 2. So tan x = t will work.
2. 1/sin^(5/3)x = tan^(−5/3)x · cos^(−5/3)x, and collecting cos powers gives 5/3 + 1/3 = 2 in the denominator, that is sec²x.
3. Integrand = tan^(−5/3)x · sec²x, so with tan x = t it is ∫ t^(−5/3) dt.

concepts.title: Linear in sin x and cos x in the Denominator: tan(x/2) Substitution
concepts.oneLine: When the denominator is linear in sin x and cos x, write both in tan(x/2) form, lift the sec²(x/2) upstairs, and t = tan(x/2) turns the whole thing into a rational integral.
notes: Look at the denominator before anything else. If sin x and cos x appear only to the first power — a + b sin x + c cos x, nothing squared, nothing multiplied together — the denominator is linear in sin x and cos x. That single observation decides the whole solution.

In that case replace both by their half-angle forms: sin x = 2tan(x/2)/(1 + tan²(x/2)) and cos x = (1 − tan²(x/2))/(1 + tan²(x/2)). Look carefully at the denominators — it is sec²(x/2) sitting below in the first one, and sec²(x/2) sitting below in the second one too. Same bottom in both.

So multiply the top and the bottom of the whole fraction by sec²(x/2). The bottom clears into a polynomial in tan(x/2), and the top is left holding sec²(x/2) dx. That leftover sec²(x/2) is exactly the derivative piece of tan(x/2), which is why putting t = tan(x/2) makes the substitution work so cleanly.

What you land on is 1/quadratic in t — and if the top also carried sin x and cos x, linear upon quadratic in t. Both of those we have already finished in this chapter. So there is no new trick here, only a new doorway into an old room: spot linear, substitute, reduce, finish, put tan(x/2) back.

quickChecks.q: Find ∫ dx/(1 + cos x).
steps: 1. Denominator is linear in cos x, so put t = tan(x/2), dx = 2dt/(1 + t²).
3. Integral = ∫ [2dt/(1 + t²)] × [(1 + t²)/2] = ∫ dt = t + C.

quickChecks.q: Find ∫ dx/(1 + sin x).
steps: 1. t = tan(x/2), dx = 2dt/(1 + t²).

quickChecks.q: Reduce ∫ dx/(3 + 5 cos x) to a rational integral in t and finish it.
steps: 1. t = tan(x/2), dx = 2dt/(1 + t²).
3. Integral = ∫ 2dt/(8 − 2t²) = ∫ dt/(4 − t²), a standard 1/quadratic.
4. ∫ dt/(2² − t²) = (1/4) ln |(2 + t)/(2 − t)| + C. Put t = tan(x/2) back.

concepts.title: Quadratic in sin x and cos x: Divide by cos²x and Use tan–sec
concepts.quote: Last time the denominator was linear in sin x and cos x, and tan(x/2) saved us. Now the denominator is quadratic — and the hero changes: tan x and sec x walk in together.
concepts.oneLine: When sin x and cos x sit in the denominator as a quadratic, divide top and bottom by cos²x so dx becomes sec²x dx, and then t = tan x turns the whole thing into a quadratic in t.
notes: Look at the denominator. If every term is degree two — sin²x, sin x cos x, cos²x — don't look for any new formula. Divide the numerator and the denominator by cos²x.

What happens? The numerator 1 becomes sec²x, and the denominator becomes a plain quadratic in tan x. Now sec²x dx is exactly dt for t = tan x. So the integral collapses to ∫dt over a quadratic in t, and you finish by completing the square — the same thing you have done a hundred times.

Now the same thought process at a higher level. If the powers are four, like sin⁴x + cos⁴x, divide by cos⁴x instead. Below you get 1 + tan⁴x, above you get sec⁴x. And sec⁴x is convertible into tan: write it as (1 + tan²x)·sec²x, because one sec²x must always be saved for dx.

After t = tan x you land on ∫(1 + t²)/(1 + t⁴) dt. Here is the second move: divide top and bottom by t². Now only even powers of t are left, t² + 1/t² below and 1 + 1/t² above, and the substitution u = t − 1/t finishes it.

quickChecks.q: Integrate dx/(4sin²x + 5cos²x).
steps: 1. Degree 2 denominator → divide the numerator and the denominator by cos²x.
2. Get ∫sec²x dx/(4tan²x + 5).
3. t = tan x, sec²x dx = dt → ∫dt/(4t² + 5).
4. Use ∫dt/(a²t² + b²) = (1/(ab)) tan⁻¹(at/b) with a = 2, b = √5.

quickChecks.q: Integrate dx/(2sin²x + 3 sin x cos x + 2cos²x).
steps: 1. Divide the numerator and the denominator by cos²x → ∫sec²x dx/(2tan²x + 3tan x + 2).
3. Complete the square: t² + 3t/2 + 1 = (t + 3/4)² + 7/16.

quickChecks.q: Integrate dx/(1 + 3cos²x).
steps: 1. Write 1 = sin²x + cos²x, so the denominator is sin²x + 4cos²x — degree 2.
2. Divide the numerator and the denominator by cos²x → ∫sec²x dx/(tan²x + 4).
3. t = tan x → ∫dt/(t² + 4) = ½ tan⁻¹(t/2).

concepts.title: ∫sin2x/(sin⁴x + cos⁴x)dx by Substituting tan²x
concepts.oneLine: For ∫sin2x/(sin⁴x + cos⁴x)dx, divide top and bottom by cos⁴x, see 2 tan x sec²x dx as d(tan²x), and the integral becomes tan⁻¹(tan²x) + c.
notes: The denominator is sin⁴x + cos⁴x. The highest power here is 4, so the dividing power is also 4. Divide the top and the bottom by cos⁴x — both, not one.

Below, sin⁴x/cos⁴x + cos⁴x/cos⁴x gives 1 + tan⁴x. Above, sin2x is 2 sin x cos x, so 2 sin x cos x/cos⁴x splits as 2 · (sin x/cos x) · (1/cos²x) = 2 tan x sec²x. So the integral is ∫2 tan x sec²x dx/(1 + tan⁴x).
Now look at the top carefully: 2 tan x sec²x dx is exactly d(tan²x). So put t = tan²x. Then dt = 2 tan x sec²x dx, and tan⁴x below is t². The question becomes ∫dt/(1 + t²).
That is a formula you already know: tan⁻¹t + c. Put t back and the answer is tan⁻¹(tan²x) + c. With practice this goes in a single shot — you see the numerator and write d(tan²x) straight away.

quickChecks.q: Evaluate ∫2 tan x sec²x dx/(1 + tan⁴x)
steps: 1. Put t = tan²x, so dt = 2 tan x sec²x dx and tan⁴x = t².
2. Integral = ∫dt/(1 + t²) = tan⁻¹t + c.

quickChecks.q: Evaluate ∫sin2x/(sin⁴x + 4cos⁴x) dx
steps: 1. Divide top and bottom by cos⁴x: denominator becomes tan⁴x + 4, numerator becomes 2 tan x sec²x.
2. Put t = tan²x, dt = 2 tan x sec²x dx.
3. Integral = ∫dt/(t² + 4) = ½ tan⁻¹(t/2) + c.

quickChecks.q: Evaluate ∫tan x sec²x dx/(1 + tan⁴x)
steps: 1. Here the 2 is missing, so write the integral as ½ ∫2 tan x sec²x dx/(1 + tan⁴x).
2. Put t = tan²x, dt = 2 tan x sec²x dx.
3. Integral = ½ ∫dt/(1 + t²) = ½ tan⁻¹t + c.

concepts.title: One Idea Behind All These Formats: The tan–sec Relation
concepts.oneLine: Every format in this chapter — board or competition — is the same single move: turn the integrand into a relation between tan and sec, then let t = tan x.
notes: Stop for a minute and look back at everything we just did. The competition question, the board question, the sin⁴x + cos⁴x one — they looked like different species of animal.

They are not. In every single one, I was only exploring the relation between tan and sec. Divide top and bottom by cos²x, let sec²x become 1 + tan²x, and the whole integral collapses into one variable: t = tan x.
That is the point of checking "yes or no" after each one. You are not learning five formats. You are learning one move, wearing five different costumes.

And notice what the paper setters do with this. One format gave you sin and cos appearing linearly, another gave sin and cos appearing quadratically — and a question came that mixed both together. Even in that mixed question, the escape route was the same: get to a tan and sec relation.

quickChecks.q: Evaluate ∫ dx/(1 + sin²x).
steps: 1. Divide numerator and denominator by cos²x: ∫ sec²x dx/(sec²x + tan²x).
2. Use sec²x = 1 + tan²x in the denominator: sec²x + tan²x = 1 + 2tan²x.
3. Put t = tan x, so sec²x dx = dt: ∫ dt/(1 + 2t²).

quickChecks.q: Evaluate ∫ dx/(4cos²x + 9sin²x).
steps: 1. Divide numerator and denominator by cos²x: ∫ sec²x dx/(4 + 9tan²x).
2. Put t = tan x, so sec²x dx = dt: ∫ dt/(9t² + 4).

quickChecks.q: Evaluate ∫ dx/(1 + 3cos²x).
steps: 1. Divide numerator and denominator by cos²x: ∫ sec²x dx/(sec²x + 3).
2. Use sec²x = 1 + tan²x: denominator becomes tan²x + 4.
3. Put t = tan x, so sec²x dx = dt: ∫ dt/(t² + 4) = (1/2) tan⁻¹(t/2).

concepts.title: Numerator = λ·Denominator + μ·(Derivative of Denominator) [+ γ]
concepts.oneLine: When the numerator is the troublemaker, write it as λ(denominator) + μ(derivative of denominator) + γ, and the integral falls apart into λx + μ ln|denominator| + γ∫dx/denominator.
notes: Look at a question like (2 sin x − cos x + 1)/(7 sin x + 2 cos x + 2). If the numerator were not there at all, our story is already done — ∫dx/(a sin x + b cos x + c) is a standard question we have already solved with t = tan(x/2). So the denominator is not the problem. The numerator is.

So stop fighting the numerator and write it in the denominator's language: numerator = λ(denominator) + μ(derivative of the denominator). Now divide by the denominator. The first piece becomes plain λ, and the second piece becomes μ times (derivative of denominator)/(denominator).

Both of those are free. ∫λ dx is λx, and ∫D′/D dx is ln|D| — the derivative is sitting right on top. So the answer is λx + μ ln|denominator| + C. To find λ and μ, compare the coefficient of sin x and the coefficient of cos x; or faster, put x = 0 and then x = 90° and read off two relations.

One extra case. If the denominator carries a constant, then λ(denominator) brings a constant along with it, and the numerator's constant will not match. So keep one more unknown: + γ. Now you get three relations — sin x, cos x, and the constant term — and the leftover γ∫dx/denominator is exactly that standard question. A little long, nothing difficult.

quickChecks.q: Integrate (3 sin x + 2 cos x)/(2 sin x + 3 cos x) dx.
steps: 1. D = 2 sin x + 3 cos x, D′ = 2 cos x − 3 sin x.
2. Write 3 sin x + 2 cos x = λ(2 sin x + 3 cos x) + μ(2 cos x − 3 sin x).
3. sin x: 2λ − 3μ = 3. cos x: 3λ + 2μ = 2.
6. Integral = λx + μ ln|D|.

quickChecks.q: Integrate (2 sin x + cos x + 3)/(3 sin x + 4 cos x + 5) dx.
steps: 1. D = 3 sin x + 4 cos x + 5, D′ = 3 cos x − 4 sin x. Constant present, so keep γ.
2. 2 sin x + cos x + 3 = λ(3 sin x + 4 cos x + 5) + μ(3 cos x − 4 sin x) + γ.
3. sin x: 3λ − 4μ = 2. cos x: 4λ + 3μ = 1. constant: 5λ + γ = 3.
5. For the γ piece put t = tan(x/2): denominator becomes (6t + 4(1 − t²) + 5(1 + t²))/(1 + t²) = (t² + 6t + 9)/(1 + t²) = (t + 3)²/(1 + t²).

quickChecks.q: Write 3 sin x + cos x + 2 as λ(sin x + cos x + 1) + μ(cos x − sin x) + γ and hence integrate (3 sin x + cos x + 2)/(sin x + cos x + 1) dx.
steps: 1. sin x: λ − μ = 3. cos x: λ + μ = 1. constant: λ + γ = 2.
2. Adding the first two: 2λ = 4, so λ = 2, and then μ = −1.
3. γ = 2 − 2 = 0, so the leftover piece vanishes — no tan(x/2) work needed here.
4. Integral = λx + μ ln|sin x + cos x + 1|.
quickChecks.answer: λ = 2, μ = −1, γ = 0; integral = 2x − ln|sin x + cos x + 1| + C

flashcards.q: Why must every indefinite integral carry a constant of integration?
flashcards.a: Because a function, that function plus five and that function plus two hundred all have the same derivative. One integrand therefore has infinitely many antiderivatives, differing only by a constant.

flashcards.q: Write the four algebraic formulas of the standard list.
flashcards.a: $$\int x^n\,dx = \frac{x^{n+1}}{n+1} + C,\quad n \neq -1$$Powers go up by one and divide by the new power, except at the power minus one, which gives the log of the modulus. The two exponentials give themselves back, divided by the log of the base.

flashcards.q: Why do tan, cot, sec and cosec sit in a separate block from sin and cos?
flashcards.a: $$\int \tan x\, dx = \ln|\sec x| + C$$Because the integrals of sine and cosine come straight from derivative knowledge, while the other four do not. Nothing you differentiate gives tan x directly, so they are a separate group proved later by substitution.

flashcards.q: In the inverse-trig pair, which formula carries a factor of one over a and which does not?
flashcards.a: $$\int \frac{dx}{a^2 + x^2} = \frac{1}{a}\tan^{-1}\frac{x}{a} + C$$The inverse sine formula carries no extra factor; the inverse tangent formula does.

flashcards.q: State the linear change rule.
flashcards.a: $$\int f(x)\,dx = F(x) + C \;\Rightarrow\; \int f(ax+b)\,dx = \frac{1}{a}F(ax+b) + C$$In any standard formula you may replace x by a linear expression and the formula stays valid, provided you multiply the answer by the reciprocal of the coefficient of x.

flashcards.q: Prove the linear change rule.
flashcards.a: $$\int f(ax+b)\,dx = \frac{1}{a}\,g(ax+b) + c$$Put the linear expression equal to t, so dx becomes dt over a. The integral becomes one over a times the known integral in t, and converting back gives the rule.

flashcards.q: You have written the log of the modulus of two minus three x. What is still missing?
flashcards.a: $$\int \frac{dx}{a + bx} = \frac{1}{b}\ln|a + bx| + C$$The division by the coefficient of x. The coefficient is minus three, so the answer carries a factor of minus one third.

flashcards.q: How do you integrate sin squared x, cos squared x, sin cubed x and cos cubed x?
flashcards.a: $$\sin^2 x = \frac{1-\cos 2x}{2}, \qquad \cos^2 x = \frac{1+\cos 2x}{2}$$Reduce each to linear form with the double-angle and triple-angle identities, then integrate term by term, dividing by the coefficient of x each time.

flashcards.q: What are the integrals of tan squared x and cot squared x?
flashcards.a: $$\int \tan^2 x\, dx = \int (\sec^2 x - 1)\, dx = \tan x - x + c$$Tan x minus x, and minus cot x minus x. The stray minus one has to be integrated too, and half the marks sit in that term.

flashcards.q: What is the integral of the square of tan x plus cot x?
flashcards.a: $$\int (\sec^2 x + \operatorname{cosec}^2 x)\,dx = \tan x - \cot x + C$$Tan x minus cot x. Expanding gives sec squared x plus cosec squared x, either by the Pythagorean identities or by writing one as sin squared plus cos squared on top.

flashcards.q: How do you handle a sin x plus b cos x sitting in the denominator?
flashcards.a: $$a\sin\theta + b\cos\theta = \sqrt{a^2+b^2}\,\sin(\theta + \phi)$$Take the root of a squared plus b squared common and compress the bracket into a single sine or cosine. What is left is a cosecant or secant with a linear change, so two separate factors appear outside.

flashcards.q: What is the integral of one over the product of cosine of x minus a and cosine of x minus b?
flashcards.a: $$\int\frac{dx}{\cos(x-a)\cos(x-b)}=\frac{1}{\sin(b-a)}\ln\left|\frac{\cos(x-b)}{\cos(x-a)}\right|+C$$Multiply and divide by the sine of b minus a, and use that sine of a difference over the product of cosines is a difference of tangents.

flashcards.q: What is the first thought process of substitution?
flashcards.a: $$\int f(g(x))\,g'(x)\,dx = \int f(t)\,dt, \quad t = g(x)$$Look for a function whose own derivative is written somewhere in the problem. Call that function t and the integrand collapses to a standard form.

flashcards.q: What is the second thought process of substitution?
flashcards.a: $$x - 5 = t^2 \;\Rightarrow\; dx = 2t\,dt,\quad \sqrt{x-5} = t$$Remove the radical. Put the inside of the root equal to the power that kills it, then differentiate your substitution and convert dx as well.

flashcards.q: What is the third thought process of substitution?
flashcards.a: $$\left(x^{n} + 1\right)^{p} = x^{np}\left(1 + x^{-n}\right)^{p}$$Take the highest power of x common from the bracket so that a derivative is manufactured. Remember that the bracket's power travels with whatever you take out.

flashcards.q: Write down the patterns you should integrate by eye.
flashcards.a: $$\int \frac{f'(x)}{f(x)}\, dx = \ln|f(x)| + C$$f prime over f gives the log of the modulus of f; f to the n times f prime gives f to the n plus one over n plus one; f prime over root f gives twice root f; and f times f prime gives f squared over two.

flashcards.q: How many kinds of quadratic actually matter in integration, and what are they?
flashcards.a: $$x^2 + a^2$$Three, once you complete the square: x squared plus a squared, x squared minus a squared, and a squared minus x squared. The fourth shape is negative for every x, so it is never real under a root.

flashcards.q: Write the three formulas for one over the root of a quadratic.
flashcards.a: $$\int \frac{dx}{\sqrt{a^2+x^2}} \;=\; \ln\left|x+\sqrt{x^2+a^2}\right| + c$$The two with a difference or sum of squares under the root give the log of x plus the root; the one with a squared minus x squared gives the inverse sine of x over a.

flashcards.q: What are the integrals of one over x squared minus a squared and one over a squared minus x squared?
flashcards.a: $$\int \frac{dx}{a^2-x^2} \;=\; \frac{1}{2a}\,\ln\left|\frac{a+x}{a-x}\right| + C$$Each is a log of a ratio divided by two a, and the two differ only in what sits on top. Remember one of the pair; taking minus one common converts it into the other.

flashcards.q: What is the shortcut for the integral of the root of a quadratic?
flashcards.a: $$\int \sqrt{a^2+x^2}\,dx = \frac{x}{2}\sqrt{a^2+x^2} + \frac{a^2}{2}\ln\left|x+\sqrt{a^2+x^2}\right| + c$$x over two times the same expression, plus or minus a squared over two times the integral of its reciprocal, the sign following the sign in front of a squared. It is a squared over two, not a over two.

flashcards.q: How do you integrate a linear function over a quadratic?
flashcards.a: $$px+q = \frac{p}{2a}\,(2ax+b) + \left(q - \frac{pb}{2a}\right)$$Write the linear as A times the derivative of the quadratic plus B and compare coefficients. The first piece is f prime over f and gives a log; the second is a constant over the quadratic, finished by completing the square.

flashcards.q: A quadratic over a quadratic. What is the first move?
flashcards.a: $$\frac{P(x)}{Q(x)} = q(x) + \frac{r(x)}{Q(x)}, \qquad \deg r < \deg Q$$Long division. The derivative of a quadratic is linear, so it can never build an x squared on top; after dividing you are left with a constant plus a linear over a quadratic.

flashcards.q: Only even powers of x appear. What do you do?
flashcards.a: $$t = x + \frac{a^2}{x} \;\Rightarrow\; x^2 + \frac{a^4}{x^2} = t^2 - 2a^2$$Divide the numerator and the denominator by x squared, then look for the derivative of x plus or minus a constant over x on top. Square the substitution on paper to rebuild the denominator in t.

flashcards.q: Which substitution do the two board classics with a fourth power below want?
flashcards.a: $$t = x + \frac{1}{x} \;\Rightarrow\; dt = \left(1 - \frac{1}{x^{2}}\right)dx, \quad x^{2} + \frac{1}{x^{2}} = t^{2} - 2$$Read the numerator after dividing by x squared. One minus one over x squared on top means x plus one over x; one plus one over x squared means x minus one over x. The other two are the half-sum and half-difference of these.

flashcards.q: When do you put x equal to one over t?
flashcards.a: $$\int \frac{dx}{(ax+b)\sqrt{cx^{2}+dx+e}}$$When a linear or a quadratic sits outside the root and another quadratic sits under it. After the substitution and a lowest common multiple it usually becomes a linear under a root linear, finished by one more substitution.

flashcards.q: What are the partial-fraction forms for a repeated linear factor and for an irreducible quadratic factor?
flashcards.a: $$\frac{N(x)}{(x-a_1)^2(x-a_2)} = \frac{A}{x-a_1} + \frac{B}{(x-a_1)^2} + \frac{C}{x-a_2}$$A repeated linear factor needs every power from one up to its own, each with a constant on top. A quadratic factor carries a full linear numerator, because the numerator is always one power less than the factor under it.

flashcards.q: What is the fastest way to get the constants in a partial fraction?
flashcards.a: $$x^2+1=A(x-1)(x+3)+B(x+3)+C(x-1)^2$$Clear the denominators and treat the result as an identity valid for every x. Substitute the roots one at a time to kill terms, then compare any one coefficient for the constant that remains.

flashcards.q: The integrand is in x squared throughout. What do you do?
flashcards.a: $$\frac{x^{2}-2}{(x^{2}+2)(2x^{2}+1)} = \frac{4}{3}\cdot\frac{1}{x^{2}+2} - \frac{5}{3}\cdot\frac{1}{2x^{2}+1}$$Do the partial fraction in t equal to x squared as pure algebra, then put x squared back and integrate. Two unknowns instead of four, and you have only rewritten the integrand.

flashcards.q: State integration by parts in words.
flashcards.a: $$\int f(x)\,g(x)\,dx = f(x)\int g(x)\,dx \; - \; \int\left[\left(\int g(x)\,dx\right)\frac{d}{dx}f(x)\right]dx$$Stop one function and integrate the other; then a minus sign, a big integral, and inside it the integral you just found times the derivative of the function you stopped.

flashcards.q: Which function do you stop, and which do you integrate?
flashcards.a: $$\int u\,v\,dx = u\int v\,dx - \int\left(\frac{du}{dx}\int v\,dx\right)dx$$Step one: integrate the one whose integral you actually know, so the log and the inverse functions get stopped. Step two, if both are integrable: stop the one whose derivative is easier. Common sense, not ILATE.

flashcards.q: What is the integral of log x?
flashcards.a: $$\int \ln x\,dx = x\ln x - x + C$$x log x minus x. Stop the log, integrate the one to get x, then subtract the integral of x times one over x.

flashcards.q: What is the integral of x times inverse sine of x over the root of one minus x squared?
flashcards.a: $$\int \frac{x\,\sin^{-1}x}{\sqrt{1-x^{2}}}\,dx=x-\sqrt{1-x^{2}}\,\sin^{-1}x+C$$x minus the root of one minus x squared times the inverse sine of x. Keep x as the first function, because the rest is a ready-made f times f prime.

flashcards.q: What is the integral of the square of inverse sine of x?
flashcards.a: $$\int (\sin^{-1}x)^{2}\,dx=x\left[(\sin^{-1}x)^{2}-2\right]+2\sqrt{1-x^{2}}\,\sin^{-1}x+C$$Substitute inverse sine of x equal to t, so the integral becomes t squared cos t, and two applications of by parts finish it.

flashcards.q: What is the integral of sec cubed x?
flashcards.a: $$\int \sec^3 x\,dx = \frac{1}{2}\left(\sec x\tan x + \ln\left|\sec x + \tan x\right|\right) + C$$Split it as sec x times sec squared x, always stopping the sec x. The original integral returns, so solve for it like an equation.

flashcards.q: What is the integral of an exponential times a cosine?
flashcards.a: $$\int e^{ax}\cos bx\,dx = \frac{e^{ax}\,(b\sin bx + a\cos bx)}{a^{2}+b^{2}} + C$$Apply by parts twice keeping the same choice both times; the original integral comes back, so shift it to the left and divide. Flip your choice and every step undoes itself.

flashcards.q: What is the integral of the log of x plus the root of x squared plus one?
flashcards.a: $$\int \ln\!\left(x+\sqrt{1+x^{2}}\right)dx=x\,\ln\!\left(x+\sqrt{1+x^{2}}\right)-\sqrt{1+x^{2}}+C$$Stop the log and integrate the one. The derivative of the log is one over the root, which cancels neatly against the x.

flashcards.q: State the exponential formula and its x f prime twin.
flashcards.a: $$\int e^{x}\left(f(x)+f'(x)\right)\,dx = e^{x}f(x)+c$$An exponential multiplied by a function plus its own derivative integrates to the exponential times that function. A function plus x times its derivative integrates to x times the function.

flashcards.q: What is the general version of the exponential f plus f prime formula?
flashcards.a: $$\int e^{g(x)}\left(f(x)\,g'(x) + f'(x)\right)dx = e^{g(x)}f(x) + c$$With an exponential of g of x, the function f must come multiplied by the derivative of g, and the answer carries the same exponential times f.

flashcards.q: What is the integral of the log of the log of x plus one over the log of x?
flashcards.a: $$\int \big( f(x) + x\,f'(x) \big)\,dx = x\,f(x) + C$$x times the log of the log of x. Take the log of the log as f; x times its derivative is exactly one over the log of x, so the integrand is f plus x f prime.

flashcards.q: In an integral of a power of tan times a power of sec, how do you choose the substitution?
flashcards.a: $$\sec^2 x = 1 + \tan^2 x \;\Rightarrow\; \tan^2 x = \sec^2 x - 1$$The power of the function you call t does not matter. What must be left over after the derivative is an even power of the other one, because the identities convert only even powers. An odd sec power strands a lonely sec x, so there t is sec x.

flashcards.q: For sin cubed x times cos to the fourth x, do you put t equal to sin x or cos x?
flashcards.a: $$\sin^2 x = 1 - \cos^2 x$$Cos x. One sine goes into dt and an even power of sine is left, which converts. The power of cosine is then irrelevant, four or fourteen makes no difference.

flashcards.q: Both leftover powers come out odd. What now?
flashcards.a: $$\int \sin^4 x \cos^4 x\, dx = \frac{3x}{128} - \frac{\sin 4x}{128} + \frac{\sin 8x}{1024} + C$$No substitution works, as in sin^4 x cos^4 x and sin^2 x cos^4 x, so fall back on identities: the double angle, one minus cosine and one plus cosine. Count the powers in five seconds and the decision is made.

flashcards.q: The denominator is linear in sin x and cos x. Which substitution?
flashcards.a: $$t=\tan\frac{x}{2}\ \Rightarrow\ dt=\tfrac{1}{2}\sec^{2}\frac{x}{2}\,dx\ \Rightarrow\ \sec^{2}\frac{x}{2}\,dx=2\,dt,\qquad dx=\frac{2\,dt}{1+t^{2}}$$The tangent of x over two. Everything in this format is half angle, so both sine and cosine carry the secant squared of x over two that becomes dt.

flashcards.q: The denominator is quadratic in sin x and cos x. Which move?
flashcards.a: $$\int \frac{dx}{a\sin^2 x + b\sin x\cos x + c\cos^2 x} = \int \frac{\sec^2 x\,dx}{a\tan^2 x + b\tan x + c}$$Divide the numerator and the denominator by cos squared x and work in tan and sec. The secant squared on top is your differential, and the denominator becomes a quadratic in tan x.

flashcards.q: A trigonometric function over a trigonometric function, with nothing cancelling. What is the last resort?
flashcards.a: $$\int \frac{\lambda D(x) + \mu D'(x) + \gamma}{D(x)}\, dx = \lambda x + \mu \ln|D(x)| + \gamma \int \frac{dx}{D(x)} + C$$Write the numerator as lambda times the denominator plus mu times its derivative, plus gamma if a stray constant is in the way. Compare coefficients, and the answer is lambda x plus mu times the log of the denominator plus the gamma piece.

flashcards.q: Write the statement that turns a derivative result into an integration formula.
flashcards.a: $$\frac{d}{dx}\big(F(x)\big) = f(x) \iff \int f(x)\,dx = F(x) + c$$If the derivative of F is f, then the integral of f is F plus a constant — the same line read in either direction.

flashcards.q: Which single line generates the whole standard list of integrals?
flashcards.a: $$\frac{d}{dx}\,F(x) = f(x) \;\Longleftrightarrow\; \int f(x)\,dx = F(x) + c$$The flip itself: a derivative result read from right to left is already an integration formula.

flashcards.q: How is the standard list built, and why recall it rather than re-derive it?
flashcards.a: It is built by flipping derivative results — four from the basic derivatives, six more from trigonometry, the rest from logs and inverse trigonometry. Re-deriving an integral in the exam is what keeps integration weak.

flashcards.q: Which functions make up the core list, the one to be memorised like your own phone number?
flashcards.a: Powers, the reciprocal, the two exponentials, sine and cosine, and the two secant and cosecant logs with their half-angle alternatives.

flashcards.q: Write the linear change rule.
flashcards.a: $$\int f(x)\,dx = F(x) + C \;\Rightarrow\; \int f(ax+b)\,dx = \frac{1}{a}F(ax+b) + C$$Any standard formula survives when x is replaced by a linear expression, provided the answer is multiplied by the reciprocal of the coefficient of x.

flashcards.q: Why does one rule stretch the whole standard list?
flashcards.a: Because ax plus b may be written wherever x used to sit and the formula still holds, so no second list of formulas is needed for linear arguments.

flashcards.q: What is the integral of one over a linear expression?
flashcards.a: $$\int \frac{dx}{ax+b} = \frac{1}{a}\ln|ax+b| + C$$The log of the modulus of that expression, divided once by the coefficient of x.

flashcards.q: Two integrals, two different formulas — what is the same last step in both?
flashcards.a: Dividing once by the coefficient of x. Miss that step and a correct-looking answer scores nothing.

flashcards.q: What is the integral of sin squared x?
flashcards.a: $$\int \sin^2 x\, dx = \frac{x}{2} - \frac{\sin 2x}{4} + c$$Half of x minus a quarter of sine two x, once the square has been reduced to linear form.

flashcards.q: Why can a power of sine or cosine never be integrated as it stands?
flashcards.a: There is no formula for a power. Convert it to linear form with the double-angle or triple-angle identity first, then integrate term by term with the one over a factor.

flashcards.q: Where does the term in x come from when tan squared x is integrated?
flashcards.a: From the stray minus one. Tan squared x becomes sec squared x minus one, and the minus one has to be integrated too.

flashcards.q: Which identity compresses a sine term and a cosine term into one?
flashcards.a: $$a\sin\theta + b\cos\theta = \sqrt{a^2+b^2}\,\sin(\theta + \phi)$$The root of a squared plus b squared comes out common and the two terms become a single sine, with a phase added to the angle.

flashcards.q: Once a sin x plus b cos x has been compressed, what is left to integrate?
flashcards.a: A cosecant or a secant with a linear change inside, so two separate halves appear in the answer.

flashcards.q: Write the inverse tangent formula used when the bracket inside is linear.
flashcards.a: $$\int \frac{dx}{a^2+x^2} = \frac{1}{a}\tan^{-1}\frac{x}{a} + c$$One over a times inverse tangent of x over a. The formula carries its own one over a, and the reciprocal of the coefficient of x multiplies it as well, so two factors appear.

flashcards.q: What are the two reads that finish an inverse sine or inverse tangent question?
flashcards.a: Read a from the constant, then read the linear expression sitting in the x slot — and multiply by the reciprocal of the coefficient of x.

flashcards.q: Which identity turns cot squared x into something standard?
flashcards.a: $$\cot^2 x = \mathrm{cosec}^2 x - 1$$Cot squared x is cosec squared x minus one, and both of those pieces are on the standard list.

flashcards.q: What has to happen before anything on this slide is integrated?
flashcards.a: It must be broken into pieces you already know — one identity, or one opened bracket, and each becomes a standard form.

flashcards.q: Which factorisation often cancels the denominator outright in a splitting question?
flashcards.a: $$a^3 + b^3 = (a+b)(a^2 - ab + b^2)$$The sum of cubes: a plus b, times a squared minus ab plus b squared.

flashcards.q: In a splitting question, what comes first and what comes last?
flashcards.a: The algebra first and the integration last — expand, divide or factorise until what remains is standard.

flashcards.q: What does tan x plus cot x collapse to, and why?
flashcards.a: One over the product of sine and cosine, because writing both over sine and cosine makes the numerator sine squared plus cosine squared, which is one.

flashcards.q: Which replacement manufactures the cancelling factor in the add-and-subtract trick?
flashcards.a: $$\cos^2 x = 1 - \sin^2 x$$Writing cos squared x as one minus sin squared x, which puts the denominator's own factor upstairs.

flashcards.q: Why must every factor of the denominator appear in the numerator before a fraction is split?
flashcards.a: Because only then can it cancel. Split it any earlier and nothing cancels, leaving a messier integral than the one you started with.

flashcards.q: How is an angle given in degrees prepared for integration?
flashcards.a: $$x^{\circ} = \frac{\pi x}{180}\ \text{radians}$$It is converted to radians first, by multiplying by pi over one hundred and eighty. No calculus formula is valid in degrees.

flashcards.q: What single habit runs through this bonus set?
flashcards.a: Integrate as though the bracket were a single x, then divide once by the coefficient of x — and convert degrees to radians before any calculus formula is used.

flashcards.q: With a product of two cosines below, what is manufactured in the numerator?
flashcards.a: The sine of the difference of the two angles, because sine of a difference over the product of the cosines splits into a difference of two tangents.

flashcards.q: What is the integral of an exponential with a linear power?
flashcards.a: $$\int e^{a + bx}\,dx = \frac{1}{b}e^{a + bx} + C$$The same exponential, divided by the coefficient of x, sign included.

flashcards.q: In these fifteen-second questions, where are the only marks at stake?
flashcards.a: In the division by the coefficient of x, sign included, since the standard result is already known.

flashcards.q: In the proof of the linear change rule, what does the substitution give for dx?
flashcards.a: $$t = ax + b \;\Rightarrow\; \frac{dt}{dx} = a \;\Rightarrow\; dx = \frac{dt}{a}$$Differentiating the substitution gives the coefficient of x, so dx becomes dt divided by that coefficient.

flashcards.q: How long is the proof of the linear change rule, and what does it rest on?
