flashcards.a: Three lines: put the linear expression equal to t, so dx becomes dt over a, and the one over a drops out on its own.

flashcards.q: Write the substitution rule for an inner function whose own derivative is present.
flashcards.a: $$\int f(g(x))\,g'(x)\,dx = \int f(t)\,dt, \quad t = g(x)$$The inner function becomes t, and the whole integral collapses into a basic integral in t.

flashcards.q: How is a substitution question built, and how is that read backwards?
flashcards.a: A known integral is taken, x is replaced by some function, and the maker is forced to plant that function's derivative beside it. Spotting that derivative is the whole of thought process one.

flashcards.q: Write an integral that shows a substitution landing back on a basic form.
flashcards.a: $$\int \sin(2x-3)\,dx = -\frac{\cos(2x-3)}{2} + C$$Minus the cosine of the linear expression, divided by the coefficient of x.

flashcards.q: What is the only job of a substitution?
flashcards.a: To convert the question into a basic form you already own. Substitution adds no new integral to the list, so a substitution that does not land on a standard integral was the wrong one.

flashcards.q: What is the integral of one over x log x?
flashcards.a: $$\int \frac{dx}{x\ln x}=\ln|\ln x|+C$$The log of the modulus of log x, because the derivative of log x is already sitting beside it.

flashcards.q: What is the one skill these five substitution questions train?
flashcards.a: Finding the function that already has its own derivative written beside it. Once the right t clicks there is nothing left in the question.

flashcards.q: After the substitution, what is done with a squared cosine?
flashcards.a: $$\cos^2 t = \frac{1+\cos 2t}{2}$$It is reduced to linear form: cos squared t is half of one plus cosine two t.

flashcards.q: Why does the cubic inside the cosine choose its own substitution here?
flashcards.a: Because the derivative of the inner cubic is three x squared, and an x squared is already standing in the integrand.

flashcards.q: What is the derivative of a cos squared x plus b sin squared x?
flashcards.a: $$\frac{d}{dx}\left(a\cos^{2}x+b\sin^{2}x\right)=(b-a)\sin 2x$$b minus a, times sine two x — which is why the whole denominator becomes t the moment sine two x appears.

flashcards.q: If no formula picks the substitution, what does?
flashcards.a: Looking for the function whose derivative is already present somewhere in the question, and then differentiating that choice honestly so no constant goes missing.

flashcards.q: When may one of the three direct patterns be written down by eye?
flashcards.a: Only when the derivative is present exactly, up to a constant. In those three shapes t need not be written at all.

flashcards.q: Which substitution removes a cube root, and what happens to dx?
flashcards.a: $$2 + x = t^3 \;\Rightarrow\; dx = 3t^2\,dt,\quad (2+x)^{1/3} = t$$The inside of the root is put equal to t cubed, and differentiating turns dx into three t squared dt.

flashcards.q: How is the power in a radical substitution chosen?
flashcards.a: It is the power that kills the root — t squared for a square root, t cubed for a cube root — and then every piece, dx included, is converted.

flashcards.q: Two different roots of the same bracket appear. Write the substitution.
flashcards.a: $$x+1=t^{6},\qquad dx=6t^{5}\,dt$$The bracket is put equal to t raised to the lowest common multiple of the two root orders, and dx follows by differentiating.

flashcards.q: Which power kills both roots when two different root orders sit on one bracket?
flashcards.a: The lowest common multiple of the two root orders. What is left afterwards is pure splitting.

flashcards.q: When the highest power of x leaves a bracket that carries a power, what happens to that power?
flashcards.a: $$\left(x^{n} + 1\right)^{p} = x^{np}\left(1 + x^{-n}\right)^{p}$$It travels with whatever is taken out, so the common factor leaves raised to the same power as the bracket.

flashcards.q: What do you do when no derivative is visible in the integrand?
flashcards.a: Pull the biggest power of x out of the bracket and a derivative is manufactured on its own. Taking common means every term inside is divided.

flashcards.q: What does the quotient rule give for one linear over another?
flashcards.a: $$\frac{d}{dx}\left(\frac{ax+b}{cx+d}\right)=\frac{ad-bc}{(cx+d)^2}$$A constant on top and the square of the lower linear below — exactly the square needed for dt.

flashcards.q: In a linear upon linear question, how are the two powers handled?
flashcards.a: They are balanced so that one linear over the other sits inside the bracket and the rest comes out cleanly, and either linear may be the one called t.

flashcards.q: Write the substitution and its derivative for the first of these quiz integrals.
flashcards.a: $$t = 1+\frac{1}{x^2} \;\Rightarrow\; dt = -\frac{2}{x^3}\,dx$$One plus one over x squared is called t, and its derivative supplies the power of x left in the denominator.

flashcards.q: Where does the power you take common come from?
flashcards.a: From inside the bracket, not from what is sitting outside it. One glance at the root decides whether it is x squared or x cubed.

flashcards.q: Write the format that is a linear over the root of a quadratic.
flashcards.a: $$\int \frac{ax+b}{\sqrt{px^2+qx+r}}\, dx$$It is one of the six closing formats: three quadratic shapes, each also allowed a linear factor.

flashcards.q: What are the six quadratic formats that close the formula work of the chapter?
flashcards.a: A quadratic below, its root below, and its root on top — and each of those three again with a linear attached. Nothing new comes after them.

flashcards.q: Why is there no fourth quadratic shape in integration?
flashcards.a: $$-(x^2 + a^2)$$That shape is negative for every x, so it is never real under a root and no question can be built on it.

flashcards.q: Where does the count of nine standard formulas come from?
flashcards.a: Each of the three quadratics is paired with the quadratic below, its root below, and its root on top — three times three.

flashcards.q: How is the shortcut for the integral of a root of a quadratic read as one sentence?
flashcards.a: x over two times the same expression, plus or minus a squared over two times the integral of its reciprocal — with the sign copied from the sign in front of a squared.

flashcards.q: Why is it enough to memorise only one of the two log formulas?
flashcards.a: Taking minus one common turns each into the other and the modulus hides the rest, so the pair comes free. These two are the ones swapped in the exam.

flashcards.q: Write the rule applied once the square is completed and a linear sits in the x slot.
flashcards.a: $$\int f(px+q)\,dx = \frac{1}{p}F(px+q) + c$$The formula is written unchanged with the linear expression in place of x, and the whole answer is divided by the coefficient of x.

flashcards.q: What order do these three examples follow?
flashcards.a: Complete the square, read off a and the linear expression sitting in the x slot, then write the reciprocal of the coefficient of x before writing anything else.

flashcards.q: Write the shortcut used when the root of a quadratic carries a linear inside.
flashcards.a: $$\int \sqrt{x^2+a^2}\,dx = \frac{x}{2}\sqrt{x^2+a^2} + \frac{a^2}{2}\ln\left|x+\sqrt{x^2+a^2}\right| + C$$Half the bracket times the same quadratic under the root, then a squared over two times the log form, with the bracket standing everywhere x used to stand.

flashcards.q: What does same thing mean in this shortcut, and what if the bracket makes you nervous?
flashcards.a: Exactly the same expression, bracket included, in both terms. If the bracket feels slippery, spend one extra line putting the linear equal to t.

flashcards.q: Write the split of a linear numerator in terms of the derivative of the quadratic.
flashcards.a: $$px+q = \frac{p}{2a}\,(2ax+b) + \left(q - \frac{pb}{2a}\right)$$The linear becomes a multiple of the derivative of the quadratic plus a constant, and both are fixed by comparing coefficients.

flashcards.q: What do the two pieces become after a linear over quadratic is split?
flashcards.a: The first piece is a log, and the second is a standard format once the square is completed.

flashcards.q: Nothing fits a formula. What is the move?
flashcards.a: $$\int f(\text{linear})\,dx \;\longrightarrow\; t = \text{linear},\quad dt = (\text{linear})'\,dx$$Put the linear part equal to t; the expression then opens up into a standard form.

flashcards.q: In what order should this class be revised?
flashcards.a: In the order the techniques were built: the common substitutions first, then the formats, then the questions written out by hand.

flashcards.q: Write the pattern that tells you a homework problem wants a substitution.
flashcards.a: $$\int f(g(x))\, g'(x)\, dx = F(g(x)) + c$$An inner function with its own derivative beside it — the answer is then the outer function evaluated at that inner function.

flashcards.q: What is the real practice in this homework set?
flashcards.a: Not the solving but the choosing: deciding in two seconds which of the three doors a question wants, and not substituting at all when it is already a standard form.

flashcards.q: Which questions are already finished business, and how do they both go?
flashcards.a: Any quadratic, and a quadratic multiplied by a linear. Both go the same way: make the perfect square, then apply whichever of the nine formulas fits.

flashcards.q: Write the one line that kills the whole linear upon quadratic family.
flashcards.a: $$\frac{px+q}{ax^2+bx+c} = \lambda\cdot\frac{2ax+b}{ax^2+bx+c} + \frac{\mu}{ax^2+bx+c}$$The linear numerator becomes lambda times the derivative of the quadratic plus mu, each over the same quadratic.

flashcards.q: The numerator is a sine. What should you notice?
flashcards.a: That it is already the derivative of something sitting downstairs, so the same eye for whose derivative the top is finishes the question.

flashcards.q: Which pair of identities clears a root carrying one plus x and one minus x together?
flashcards.a: $$1+\cos 2\theta = 2\cos^{2}\theta, \qquad 1-\cos 2\theta = 2\sin^{2}\theta$$One plus the cosine of a double angle is twice the cosine squared, and one minus it is twice the sine squared.

flashcards.q: Which substitution clears that root in one line, and what is the safer exam road?
flashcards.a: Putting x equal to the cosine of two theta clears it in one line. Rationalising also works, and in an exam that is the safer road.

flashcards.q: Write what long division does to an improper rational integrand.
flashcards.a: $$\frac{P(x)}{Q(x)} = q(x) + \frac{r(x)}{Q(x)}, \qquad \deg r < \deg Q$$It leaves a quotient plus a remainder over the same denominator, with the remainder of lower degree than the denominator.

flashcards.q: Why can a quadratic numerator never be written as a multiple of the derivative of the quadratic below?
flashcards.a: Because the derivative of a quadratic is linear, so it can never build an x squared on top. Divide first, and a constant or a polynomial plus a linear over a quadratic is left.

flashcards.q: Which format sits at the heavy end of the chapter flow?
flashcards.a: $$\int \frac{dx}{(px+q)\sqrt{ax^{2}+bx+c}}$$A linear outside the root of a quadratic — reached only after the earlier stages have been tested.

flashcards.q: What is the flow of the chapter so far?
flashcards.a: Linear change first, then a hidden derivative, then the quadratic formats, and only then the harder dressings — walked down from the top rather than reaching for the heaviest method.

flashcards.q: What is the derivative of x minus a squared over x?
flashcards.a: $$\frac{d}{dx}\left(x - \frac{a^2}{x}\right) = 1 + \frac{a^2}{x^2}$$One plus a squared over x squared — so a numerator of that shape picks this substitution.

flashcards.q: After dividing by x squared, why must the substitution be squared on paper?
flashcards.a: Because the substitution alone cannot reach the denominator. Squaring it rebuilds the denominator in t.

flashcards.q: Which standard formula finishes the x minus one over x branch?
flashcards.a: $$\int \frac{dt}{t^{2} + a^{2}} = \frac{1}{a}\tan^{-1}\frac{t}{a} + C$$One over a times inverse tangent of t over a, since that branch lands on a sum of squares.

flashcards.q: How do the four most asked integrals of this family travel together?
flashcards.a: After dividing by x squared the numerator decides everything, and the other two are the half-sum and half-difference of the first two.

flashcards.q: A bare number sits on top. How is it split?
flashcards.a: $$2 = (1 + x^2) + (1 - x^2)$$As the sum of one plus x squared and one minus x squared, which hands one piece to each substitution.

flashcards.q: What are the three questions that make up the even-power method?
flashcards.a: Divide by x squared; ask whose derivative the new numerator is; then check whether the denominator can be written in that same variable. Learn the process, not the answer.

flashcards.q: Which substitution does this practice integral want, and what is its derivative?
flashcards.a: $$t = x + \frac{5}{x} \;\Rightarrow\; dt = \left(1 - \frac{5}{x^2}\right)dx$$x plus five over x, whose derivative is one minus five over x squared — exactly the numerator left after dividing by x squared.

flashcards.q: What is the signal here, and what must be done before comparing?
flashcards.a: An even power on top with a constant, and a fourth-degree denominator below. Square t on paper before comparing, or the constant inside the denominator comes out wrong.

flashcards.q: What is the derivative of x to the minus n?
flashcards.a: $$\frac{d}{dx}\left(x^{-n}\right) = -\,n\,x^{-n-1}$$Minus n times x to the minus n minus one — the sign that is easiest to lose when a negative power is differentiated.

flashcards.q: How is this kind of question hidden, and how is it undone?
flashcards.a: The setter starts from the answer, differentiates it, then multiplies up and down by a power of x. If the powers look reversed or ugly, divide by that power and test whether the new numerator is the derivative of the new denominator.

flashcards.q: A linear sits under the root. What is the substitution?
flashcards.a: $$ax+b=t^{2}\;\Rightarrow\;x=\frac{t^{2}-b}{a}$$The linear is put equal to t squared, because x can then be written back in terms of t.

flashcards.q: Why does that move collapse the moment a quadratic walks under the root?
flashcards.a: Because x can no longer be recovered from t. Put the linear part, or x itself, equal to one over t instead.

flashcards.q: Write the substitution that turns this root in the denominator into a polynomial.
flashcards.a: $$x + 1 = t^2 \;\Rightarrow\; x = t^2 - 1,\quad \sqrt{x+1} = t,\quad dx = 2t\,dt$$x plus one is put equal to t squared, so the root becomes t and dx brings the factor of t that cancels it.

flashcards.q: The denominator jumps to degree four after substituting. Why is that good news?
flashcards.a: Because degree four in t with only even powers is far friendlier than a root in x, and the even-power method then takes over.

flashcards.q: What does x equal to one over t give for dx?
flashcards.a: $$x=\frac{1}{t}\ \Rightarrow\ dx=-\frac{dt}{t^{2}}$$Minus dt over t squared, and that minus one over t squared is what cancels the mess the lowest common multiple throws up.

flashcards.q: Which shape should be recognised here rather than derived?
flashcards.a: A linear or a quadratic outside the root with another quadratic under it. That shape is the signal for x equal to one over t.

flashcards.q: After x equals one over t and the lowest common multiple, which second substitution finishes it?
flashcards.a: $$-\frac{1}{2}\int\frac{du}{(u+1)\sqrt{u-1}},\qquad u-1=v^{2}$$A linear under the root of a linear is left, so that linear is put equal to a square in a new variable.

flashcards.q: What decides the move here, and what comes afterwards?
flashcards.a: The degree check: a quadratic outside and a quadratic under the root means x equals one over t. Take the lowest common multiple everywhere afterwards, and a second substitution finishes it.

flashcards.q: Write the partial-fraction split for three distinct linear factors.
flashcards.a: $$\frac{p(x)}{(x-a_1)(x-a_2)(x-a_3)} = \frac{A}{x-a_1} + \frac{B}{x-a_2} + \frac{C}{x-a_3}$$One constant over each factor. Cross-multiply, then put each root in turn to read the constants off.

flashcards.q: Is partial fractions an integration technique, and what must be checked first?
flashcards.a: It is pure algebra, not an integration technique — an ugly fraction becomes small fractions that integrate on sight. The fraction must be proper first, so compare the degrees before splitting.

flashcards.q: What goes on top of an irreducible quadratic factor?
flashcards.a: $$\frac{N(x)}{(x-a)(ax^2+bx+c)} = \frac{A}{x-a} + \frac{px+q}{ax^2+bx+c}$$A linear expression — always one power less than the factor sitting below it.

flashcards.q: What is the integral of one over the square of a linear factor?
flashcards.a: $$\int\frac{dx}{(x-a)^2}=-\frac{1}{x-a}+K$$Minus the reciprocal of that linear factor.

flashcards.q: How are the constants read off once the denominators are cleared?
flashcards.a: The result is treated as an identity true for every x: substitute the roots one at a time to kill terms, then compare any one coefficient for whatever constant is left over.

flashcards.q: Write the split that is done in t when every term is in x squared.
flashcards.a: $$\frac{t-2}{(t+2)(2t+1)} = \frac{A}{t+2} + \frac{B}{2t+1}$$A constant over each linear factor in t — a linear upon linear split, so two unknowns instead of four.

flashcards.q: When is the x squared equal to t move allowed?
flashcards.a: Only when there is no single x anywhere. The split is done in t as pure algebra and x squared is put back, so the integrand has been rewritten rather than substituted inside the integral.

flashcards.q: Write the split for a linear over two distinct linear factors.
flashcards.a: $$\frac{px+q}{(x-a)(x-b)} = \frac{A}{x-a}+\frac{B}{x-b}$$One constant over each factor, after which the integration is routine.

flashcards.q: What is the map of the chapter so far, and where should the effort go?
flashcards.a: Basics, then substitution, then the algebraic formats, then partial fractions. Knowing where you are in that map is half the battle, and once the constants are out the integration is routine.

flashcards.q: Write the split for one over the product of two linear factors.
flashcards.a: $$\frac{1}{(x+a)(x+b)} = \frac{1}{b-a}\left(\frac{1}{x+a} - \frac{1}{x+b}\right)$$One over the gap between the factors, times the difference of the two reciprocals.

flashcards.q: The two brackets below differ by a constant. How is the numerator written?
flashcards.a: As that difference itself, bigger bracket first, or the sign flips — and the fraction splits in one line with no substitution at all.

flashcards.q: Which rule is integration by parts the reverse of?
flashcards.a: $$\frac{d}{dx}\big[f(x)\,g(x)\big] = f(x)\,\frac{d}{dx}g(x) + g(x)\,\frac{d}{dx}f(x)$$The product rule: the derivative of a product is each function times the derivative of the other.

flashcards.q: Inside the second integral of by parts, what exactly is copied?
flashcards.a: The integration of the second function — never the function itself — multiplied by the derivative of the one that was stopped.

flashcards.q: What is the integral of x times sine x?
flashcards.a: $$\int x\sin x\,dx = -x\cos x + \sin x + C$$Minus x cosine x plus sine x, from stopping x and integrating the sine.

flashcards.q: What are the two steps that decide what to stop?
flashcards.a: First integrate the function whose integral you actually know, so the log and the inverse functions get stopped. Then, if both are integrable, stop the one whose derivative is easier.

flashcards.q: A single function sits under the integral sign. How does by parts start?
flashcards.a: Read it as one times that function, and stop the function that cannot be integrated yet.

flashcards.q: Why is x kept as the first function in the by-parts route here?
flashcards.a: Because the rest is a ready-made function times its own derivative. The clumsier route then hands you the integral of inverse sine squared, which is the real prize of the question.

flashcards.q: Which substitution kills the root inside a cosine?
flashcards.a: $$\sqrt{x} = t \;\Rightarrow\; x = t^2,\; dx = 2t\,dt$$The root itself is put equal to t, so x becomes t squared and dx brings a factor of two t.

flashcards.q: What should be asked before reaching for by parts?
flashcards.a: What should be substituted. Kill the root or introduce the angle first, and the by-parts step that follows is one line.

flashcards.q: What is the integral of a power of a linear expression?
flashcards.a: $$\int (ax+b)^{n}\,dx=\frac{(ax+b)^{n+1}}{a\,(n+1)}+C$$The power goes up by one, divided by the new power and by the coefficient of x.

flashcards.q: A linear times the root of a linear. Which route is shorter?
flashcards.a: By parts, stopping the bracket whose derivative is a constant. Substitution reaches the answer too, but remember to divide by the coefficient of x when the root is integrated.

flashcards.q: Neither piece gets simpler either way. What is the plan?
flashcards.a: Apply by parts twice keeping the same choice both times. The original integral returns, and it is solved for like an equation.

flashcards.q: How is an odd power of secant split for by parts?
flashcards.a: $$\sec^{3}x = \sec x\cdot\sec^{2}x$$One secant is peeled off and the secant squared stays with the dx.

flashcards.q: What is the only thinking left in this practice set?
flashcards.a: Which factor to differentiate — and whether a rationalisation or a substitution should come first, before by parts is used at all.

flashcards.q: What does one over one plus sine x become after rationalising?
flashcards.a: $$\frac{1}{1+\sin x}=\frac{1-\sin x}{\cos^2 x}=\sec^2 x-\sec x\tan x$$Secant squared x minus secant x tangent x, because the conjugate turns the denominator into a cosine squared.

flashcards.q: What is the problem with the plus sign downstairs, and what is left once it is cleared?
flashcards.a: It blocks the split, so multiply top and bottom by the conjugate. What is left is two by-parts questions you already know, and the second term carries a minus.

flashcards.q: Which function is stopped in the sec cubed x split, and what happens next?
flashcards.a: The single secant is always the one stopped. The original integral walks back in, so the line is treated as an equation and solved for it.

flashcards.q: What is the derivative of inverse cosine of x?
flashcards.a: $$\frac{d}{dx}\left(\cos^{-1}x\right) = -\frac{1}{\sqrt{1-x^{2}}}$$Minus one over the root of one minus x squared — which is why the inverse function is the one differentiated.

flashcards.q: Where does by parts drop you in this question, and what clears it?
flashcards.a: On a root integral, which the highest-power-common move clears at once. The inverse function is always the one differentiated, so the power is the one integrated.

flashcards.q: What does taking the highest power common do to the root of one minus x squared?
flashcards.a: $$\sqrt{1-x^2} = x\sqrt{\frac{1}{x^2}-1}$$It leaves x times the root of one over x squared minus one, which finishes the integral in one shot.

flashcards.q: Three substitutions give three answers that look nothing alike. What follows?
flashcards.a: All three are right. Take a common factor out and compare term by term before calling an answer wrong.

flashcards.q: With t equal to x plus the root, which two combinations are worth writing down first?
flashcards.a: $$t-\frac{1}{t} = 2x, \qquad t+\frac{1}{t} = 2\sqrt{x^2+1}$$t minus its reciprocal gives twice x, and t plus its reciprocal gives twice the root.

flashcards.q: Where does the factor go missing in this substitution?
flashcards.a: In dx, which carries a one half. Drop it and it is carried wrong all the way to the end.

flashcards.q: A log stands alone under the integral sign. What is the second function?
flashcards.a: A one, supplied by you. The log stays as the first function, and its derivative is exactly the root that cancels.

flashcards.q: What is the derivative of x sine x plus cosine x?
flashcards.a: $$\frac{d}{dx}\left(x\sin x+\cos x\right)=x\cos x$$x cosine x — the piece that has to be manufactured in the numerator before by parts has anything to work with.

flashcards.q: Which is the hardest pattern to spot here, and how is it handled?
flashcards.a: Look at the denominator, find its derivative, and manufacture that derivative in the numerator by multiplying and dividing in the same breath.

flashcards.q: Why must both choices of f be tested in the exponential formula?
flashcards.a: Because the obvious piece is often the wrong f. Once the right half is found, the derivative term vanishes from the answer altogether.

flashcards.q: Write the by-parts line that proves the exponential formula.
flashcards.a: $$\int e^{x}f(x)\,dx = e^{x}f(x) - \int e^{x}f'(x)\,dx$$The exponential times f, minus the integral of the exponential times the derivative of f — and that leftover integral is exactly what cancels.

flashcards.q: How are both exponential formulas proved?
flashcards.a: Split the integral in two and apply by parts to one piece, always differentiating f and integrating the exponential. The leftover integrals cancel and both formulas drop out.

flashcards.q: Why is the plain exponential formula rarely enough in an exam?
flashcards.a: Because the power is almost never x. The moment it is not, f must come multiplied by the derivative of that power, and the answer carries the same exponential.

flashcards.q: Which two double-angle expansions open this fraction?
flashcards.a: $$\sin 4x = 2\sin 2x\cos 2x,\qquad 1-\cos 4x = 2\sin^{2} 2x$$The sine of the angle as twice the sine times the cosine of half it, and one minus the cosine of the angle as twice the sine squared of half it.

flashcards.q: What is the halving habit that must be kept?
flashcards.a: One minus the cosine of an angle is twice the sine squared of half that angle. The angle halves every time.

flashcards.q: What is the derivative of one over a bracket raised to the power n?
flashcards.a: $$\frac{d}{dx}\left(\frac{1}{(x+a)^{n}}\right)=\frac{-n}{(x+a)^{n+1}}$$Minus n over the bracket raised to one higher power. Negative powers bring a minus.

flashcards.q: How is the numerator forced into shape here?
flashcards.a: Whatever bracket sits in the denominator, the numerator is made into that same bracket minus a number, and the constant is fixed by the denominator rather than chosen.

flashcards.q: Write the first of the two splits in this question.
flashcards.a: $$x^2+1=(x+1)^2-2x$$The numerator is rebuilt out of the bracket below, which leaves a term in x to be split a second time.

flashcards.q: How is the plus-one-minus-one trick actually found?
flashcards.a: Not by staring. Build the denominator in the numerator step by step, twice if needed, and the split shows up on its own.

flashcards.q: Before comparing with the x f prime form, what must be done to the derivative?
flashcards.a: Multiply it by x, because x times f prime is what the form actually asks for. Take the first written piece as f and build its partner.

flashcards.q: How is a secant squared forced into an exponential-of-tangent integrand?
flashcards.a: $$\sec x = \sec^2 x \cdot \cos x$$A secant is written as secant squared times cosine, so the multiplying and the dividing happen in the same breath.

flashcards.q: What does the power of the exponential tell you, and what becomes your f?
flashcards.a: It tells you what the derivative of g must be, which you then manufacture by multiplying and dividing in the same breath — and the price you pay becomes your f.

flashcards.q: Which two expressions are the same thing in this quiz?
flashcards.a: $$\tan\frac{x}{2} = \frac{\sin x}{1 + \cos x}$$The tangent of half the angle, and sine x over one plus cosine x.

flashcards.q: In an objective question on these formulas, what is the job?
flashcards.a: To recognise the pattern, not to perform a substitution. A log, an exponential of x plus one over x, and a half-angle tangent all fall to the same two forms.

flashcards.q: Write the product-to-sum identity for two cosines.
flashcards.a: $$2\cos A\cos B = \cos(A+B) + \cos(A-B)$$Twice the product is the cosine of the sum plus the cosine of the difference.

flashcards.q: How much of this last part is genuinely new?
flashcards.a: Only two or three formats. The rest is the identity work from the first lecture, so the product-to-sum and power-reduction identities deserve their respect.

flashcards.q: What is the derivative of secant x?
flashcards.a: $$\frac{d}{dx}(\sec x) = \sec x \tan x$$Secant x times tangent x — which is what gets pulled into dt when secant is the substitution.

flashcards.q: Why does an odd power of secant force the substitution to be secant?
flashcards.a: Because otherwise a lonely secant x is stranded. Count the powers before choosing.

flashcards.q: Which identity converts the leftover even power in a tangent-secant integral?
flashcards.a: $$\tan^2 x = \sec^2 x - 1$$Tangent squared x is secant squared x minus one, so an even power of tangent becomes a plain polynomial in t.

flashcards.q: Which power matters when the substitution is chosen, and which does not?
flashcards.a: The power of the function you call t never matters. What matters is the power left over after the derivative has eaten one factor, and that leftover must be even so the identity can convert it.

flashcards.q: Write the derivative line when cosine x is called t.
flashcards.a: $$t = \cos x \;\Rightarrow\; dt = -\sin x \, dx$$dt is minus sine x dx, so that minus has to be carried into the new integral.

flashcards.q: How is the choice of substitution tested every time?
flashcards.a: Pull one factor into dt and check the parity of what is left. That single decision is where most students lose the question, so it should not be learnt by rote.

flashcards.q: Which identity starts the fallback when no substitution survives?
flashcards.a: $$\sin x \cos x = \frac{\sin 2x}{2}$$The product of sine and cosine is half the sine of the double angle, and every square that follows is killed by the double-angle identity.

flashcards.q: How do you know in advance that no substitution will work?
flashcards.a: Count the powers first: odd anywhere means substitution, both even means identity.

flashcards.q: How is an even leftover power of sine converted?
flashcards.a: $$\sin^4 x = (1-\cos^2 x)^2$$It is written in cosine. An even leftover converts in both directions, so which function carries it makes no difference.

flashcards.q: An odd power of sine stands alone. Is substitution possible?
flashcards.a: Yes. Peel off one factor into dt and the even rest converts, so even a fifth power becomes a one-line substitution.

flashcards.q: What does the half-angle tangent substitution turn a linear trigonometric denominator into?
flashcards.a: $$\int\frac{dx}{a+b\sin x+c\cos x}=\int\frac{2\,dt}{(a-c)t^{2}+2bt+(a+c)},\qquad t=\tan\frac{x}{2}$$A rational integral in t, with a quadratic in the denominator.

flashcards.q: Why the tangent of half the angle rather than the tangent of the angle?
flashcards.a: Because everything in this format is half angle: both sine and cosine carry the secant squared of half the angle that becomes dt.

flashcards.q: Write the substitution that follows dividing by cosine squared x.
flashcards.a: $$t = \tan x \;\Rightarrow\; dt = \sec^2 x\,dx,\qquad \sec^2 x = 1 + \tan^2 x$$Tangent x is called t, its derivative is the secant squared that carries dx, and secant squared is one plus tangent squared.

flashcards.q: What does a denominator with every term of degree two mean?
flashcards.a: One move: divide the numerator and the denominator by cosine squared x. The numerator becomes the secant squared that carries dx, and the denominator a plain quadratic in tangent x.

flashcards.q: Which derivative is hiding in the numerator here?
flashcards.a: $$d(\tan^2 x) = 2\tan x \sec^2 x\,dx$$The derivative of tangent squared x, which is twice tangent x times secant squared x dx.

flashcards.q: Which power do you divide by, and what does the denominator become?
flashcards.a: The highest power below is four, so the dividing power is four as well. After dividing, tangent squared x is the substitution and the denominator becomes one plus t squared, not one plus t to the fourth.

flashcards.q: Which single relation sits behind all these formats?
flashcards.a: $$\sec^2 x = 1 + \tan^2 x$$Secant squared x is one plus tangent squared x.

flashcards.q: Are the competition question, the examination classic and the fourth-power one different species?
flashcards.a: No. Every one of them is only an exploration of the relation between tangent and secant.

flashcards.q: Write the numerator split for a trigonometric fraction over a trigonometric denominator.
flashcards.a: $$p\sin x + q\cos x + r = \lambda\,(a\sin x + b\cos x + c) + \mu\,(a\cos x - b\sin x) + \gamma$$The numerator becomes lambda times the denominator, plus mu times its derivative, plus gamma.

flashcards.q: What must be checked before comparing in this last format?
flashcards.a: The derivative of the denominator, written out separately with its sign. If the numerator is the troublemaker, build the numerator out of the denominator.

ladder.tier: L1 Drill — one formula applied directly
ladder.q: Evaluate integral of (2x + 3)^5 dx.
steps: 1. This is the x^n formula with x replaced by the linear 2x + 3, so the formula still holds.
2. integral of x^5 dx = x^6/6, so you get (2x + 3)^6/6.
3. The coefficient of x is 2, so multiply by 1/2.

ladder.tier: L1 Drill — one formula applied directly
ladder.q: Evaluate integral of dx/(7 - 3x).
steps: 1. This is the 1/x formula with x replaced by 7 - 3x, giving ln|7 - 3x|.
2. The coefficient of x is -3, so multiply by -1/3.

ladder.tier: L1 Drill — one formula applied directly
ladder.q: Evaluate integral of tan^2 x dx.
steps: 1. There is no formula for tan^2 x, so reduce it: tan^2 x = sec^2 x - 1.
2. integral of sec^2 x dx = tan x and integral of 1 dx = x.

ladder.tier: L1 Drill — one formula applied directly
ladder.q: Evaluate integral of (x^4 - 1)/(x^2 + 1) dx.
steps: 1. Factorise first: x^4 - 1 = (x^2 - 1)(x^2 + 1), so the x^2 + 1 cancels.
2. You are left with integral of (x^2 - 1) dx.

ladder.tier: L2 JEE Main standard — two or three steps, one main idea
ladder.q: Evaluate integral of sin^3 x dx.
steps: 1. Reduce the cube to linear form using sin 3x = 3 sin x - 4 sin^3 x, i.e. 4 sin^3 x = 3 sin x - sin 3x.
2. So the integral is (1/4) integral of (3 sin x - sin 3x) dx.
3. integral of sin x dx = -cos x, and integral of sin 3x dx = -cos 3x/3 after dividing by the coefficient 3.
4. This gives (1/4)[-3 cos x + (1/3) cos 3x].

ladder.tier: L2 JEE Main standard — two or three steps, one main idea
ladder.q: Evaluate integral of (tan x + cot x)^2 dx.
steps: 1. Expand: tan^2 x + cot^2 x + 2 tan x cot x, and tan x cot x = 1.
2. So the integrand is (sec^2 x - 1) + (cosec^2 x - 1) + 2 = sec^2 x + cosec^2 x, the constants cancelling.
3. integral of sec^2 x dx = tan x and integral of cosec^2 x dx = -cot x.

ladder.tier: L2 JEE Main standard — two or three steps, one main idea
ladder.q: Evaluate integral of dx/sqrt(16 - (5x - 2)^2).
steps: 1. This is the a^2 - x^2 format under a root, with a = 4 and x replaced by the linear 5x - 2.
2. The base formula gives sin inverse ((5x - 2)/4).
3. The coefficient of x is 5, so multiply by 1/5.

ladder.tier: L2 JEE Main standard — two or three steps, one main idea
ladder.q: Evaluate integral of x e^(3x) dx.
steps: 1. Both functions are integrable, so stop the one with the easier derivative, namely x, and integrate e^(3x) to e^(3x)/3.
2. By parts: x e^(3x)/3 - integral of (e^(3x)/3)(1) dx.
3. The remaining integral is e^(3x)/9.

ladder.tier: L3 Harder Main — two concepts combined, or a case split
ladder.q: Evaluate integral of dx/(sin 2x - sqrt3 cos 2x).
steps: 1. The denominator is of the form a sin t + b cos t with sqrt(a^2 + b^2) = 2, so take 2 common: 2[(1/2) sin 2x - (sqrt3/2) cos 2x].
2. That bracket is sin 2x cos(pi/3) - cos 2x sin(pi/3) = sin(2x - pi/3), so the denominator is 2 sin(2x - pi/3).
3. The integral is (1/2) integral of cosec(2x - pi/3) dx, and integral of cosec t dt = ln|tan(t/2)|.
4. A linear change with coefficient 2 brings in another 1/2, so you get (1/4) ln|tan((2x - pi/3)/2)|.

ladder.tier: L3 Harder Main — two concepts combined, or a case split
ladder.q: Evaluate integral of x^2 tan inverse x dx.
steps: 1. You cannot integrate tan inverse x yet, so stop it and integrate x^2 to x^3/3.
2. By parts: (x^3/3) tan inverse x - (1/3) integral of x^3/(1 + x^2) dx.
3. For the remaining integral use long division: x^3/(1 + x^2) = x - x/(1 + x^2), so it equals x^2/2 - (1/2) ln(1 + x^2).
4. Hence the answer is (x^3/3) tan inverse x - x^2/6 + (1/6) ln(1 + x^2) + C.
ladder.answer: (x^3/3) tan inverse x - x^2/6 + (1/6) ln(1 + x^2) + C

ladder.tier: L3 Harder Main — two concepts combined, or a case split
ladder.q: Evaluate integral of dx/(x^3 + x).
steps: 1. Factorise: x^3 + x = x(x^2 + 1), a proper fraction, so split it.
2. 1/(x(x^2 + 1)) = 1/x - x/(x^2 + 1), which you can see by writing 1 = (1 + x^2) - x^2 on top.
3. integral of dx/x = ln|x| and integral of x dx/(x^2 + 1) = (1/2) ln(1 + x^2).
4. So the answer is ln|x| - (1/2) ln(1 + x^2) + C, which can be written as (1/2) ln(x^2/(1 + x^2)) + C.

ladder.tier: L3 Harder Main — two concepts combined, or a case split
ladder.q: Evaluate integral of e^x (1/x - 1/x^2) dx.
steps: 1. Look for the e^x(f + f') pattern: take f = 1/x.
2. Then f' = -1/x^2, so the bracket is exactly f + f'.
3. Hence the integral is e^x f = e^x/x.

ladder.tier: L4 JEE Advanced — multi-concept, a non-obvious first move
ladder.q: Evaluate integral of (x^2 + 1)/(x^4 - x^2 + 1) dx.
steps: 1. Only even powers appear, so divide numerator and denominator by x^2: (1 + 1/x^2)/(x^2 - 1 + 1/x^2).
2. The numerator is the derivative of x - 1/x, so put t = x - 1/x.
3. Then x^2 + 1/x^2 = t^2 + 2, so the denominator becomes t^2 + 2 - 1 = t^2 + 1.
4. The integral is integral of dt/(t^2 + 1) = tan inverse t = tan inverse ((x^2 - 1)/x).

ladder.tier: L4 JEE Advanced — multi-concept, a non-obvious first move
ladder.q: Evaluate integral of dx/(x^2 (x^7 + 1)^(6/7)).
steps: 1. Take the highest power common inside the bracket: (x^7 + 1)^(6/7) = x^6 (1 + x^(-7))^(6/7).
2. So the denominator is x^8 (1 + x^(-7))^(6/7) and the integrand is x^(-8) dx/(1 + x^(-7))^(6/7).
4. The integral becomes -(1/7) integral of t^(-6/7) dt = -(1/7) t^(1/7)/(1/7) = -t^(1/7).

ladder.tier: L4 JEE Advanced — multi-concept, a non-obvious first move
ladder.q: Evaluate integral of e^x (x - 1)/(x + 1)^3 dx.
steps: 1. Try to build the e^x(f + f') pattern. Guess f = 1/(x + 1)^2.
2. Then f' = -2/(x + 1)^3, so f + f' = [(x + 1) - 2]/(x + 1)^3 = (x - 1)/(x + 1)^3, exactly the given bracket.
3. Hence the integral is e^x/(x + 1)^2 + C.
4. If you prefer the mechanical route, write x - 1 = (x + 1) - 2 and split, which gives e^x[1/(x + 1)^2 - 2/(x + 1)^3] and the same answer.

ladder.tier: L4 JEE Advanced — multi-concept, a non-obvious first move
ladder.q: Evaluate integral of tan inverse (sqrt x) dx.
steps: 1. Stop tan inverse (sqrt x) and integrate the 1 to get x.
2. Its derivative is (1/(1 + x)) times 1/(2 sqrt x), so I = x tan inverse (sqrt x) - (1/2) integral of sqrt x dx/(1 + x).
3. For the remaining integral put x = u^2: integral of sqrt x dx/(1 + x) = 2 integral of u^2 du/(1 + u^2) = 2[u - tan inverse u] = 2 sqrt x - 2 tan inverse (sqrt x).
4. So I = x tan inverse (sqrt x) - sqrt x + tan inverse (sqrt x) + C = (x + 1) tan inverse (sqrt x) - sqrt x + C.
ladder.answer: (x + 1) tan inverse (sqrt x) - sqrt x + C

ladder.tier: L4 JEE Advanced — multi-concept, a non-obvious first move
ladder.q: Evaluate integral of sqrt((1 + x)/(1 - x)) dx for |x| < 1.
steps: 1. Rationalise: multiply inside the root by (1 + x)/(1 + x) to get (1 + x)/sqrt(1 - x^2).
2. Split: integral of dx/sqrt(1 - x^2) + integral of x dx/sqrt(1 - x^2).
3. The first is sin inverse x. For the second, the derivative of 1 - x^2 is -2x, so it equals -sqrt(1 - x^2).
4. Hence the answer is sin inverse x - sqrt(1 - x^2) + C. The route x = cos 2theta gives the same answer in the form -2theta - sin 2theta.
ladder.answer: sin inverse x - sqrt(1 - x^2) + C

ladder.tier: L5 Advanced hardest — the toughest this chapter justifies
ladder.q: Evaluate integral of (x^2 - 5)/(x^4 + x^2 + 25) dx.
steps: 1. Only even powers appear, so divide numerator and denominator by x^2: (1 - 5/x^2)/(x^2 + 1 + 25/x^2).
2. The numerator is the derivative of x + 5/x, so put t = x + 5/x.
3. Then t^2 = x^2 + 10 + 25/x^2, so x^2 + 25/x^2 = t^2 - 10 and the denominator becomes t^2 - 9.

ladder.tier: L5 Advanced hardest — the toughest this chapter justifies
ladder.q: Evaluate integral of cos inverse x/x^3 dx for 0 < x < 1.
steps: 1. Stop cos inverse x and integrate x^(-3) to x^(-2)/(-2) = -1/(2x^2).
2. By parts: I = -cos inverse x/(2x^2) - integral of (-1/(2x^2))(-1/sqrt(1 - x^2)) dx = -cos inverse x/(2x^2) - (1/2) integral of dx/(x^2 sqrt(1 - x^2)).
3. For that integral take the highest power common: sqrt(1 - x^2) = x sqrt(x^(-2) - 1), so it is integral of x^(-3) dx/sqrt(x^(-2) - 1).
4. Put t = x^(-2) - 1, dt = -2 x^(-3) dx, giving -(1/2) integral of dt/sqrt t = -sqrt t = -sqrt(1 - x^2)/x.
5. So I = -cos inverse x/(2x^2) + sqrt(1 - x^2)/(2x) + C, which differentiates back to cos inverse x/x^3.
ladder.answer: sqrt(1 - x^2)/(2x) - cos inverse x/(2x^2) + C

ladder.tier: L5 Advanced hardest — the toughest this chapter justifies
ladder.q: Evaluate integral of dx/(sin^4 x + cos^4 x).
steps: 1. The denominator is quadratic in sin^2 x and cos^2 x, so divide numerator and denominator by cos^4 x: the integral becomes integral of sec^4 x dx/(1 + tan^4 x).
2. Put t = tan x, dt = sec^2 x dx, and sec^4 x dx = sec^2 x (sec^2 x dx) = (1 + t^2) dt, so the integral is integral of (1 + t^2) dt/(1 + t^4).
3. Only even powers of t appear, so divide above and below by t^2: (1/t^2 + 1)/(t^2 + 1/t^2).
4. Put u = t - 1/t, whose derivative 1 + 1/t^2 is on top, and t^2 + 1/t^2 = u^2 + 2.
5. So the integral is integral of du/(u^2 + 2) = (1/sqrt2) tan inverse (u/sqrt2) with u = (tan^2 x - 1)/tan x.
ladder.answer: (1/sqrt2) tan inverse ((tan^2 x - 1)/(sqrt2 tan x)) + C

ladder.tier: L5 Advanced hardest — the toughest this chapter justifies
ladder.q: Evaluate integral of e^(tan x)(sec x - sin x) dx.
steps: 1. This is the general form integral of e^g(x)(f g' + f') dx = e^g(x) f, with g = tan x and g' = sec^2 x.
2. So you need the bracket as f sec^2 x + f'. Try f = cos x.
3. Then f sec^2 x + f' = cos x sec^2 x - sin x = sec x - sin x, which is exactly the given bracket.
4. Hence the integral is e^(tan x) cos x + C. Differentiating confirms it: e^(tan x) sec^2 x cos x - e^(tan x) sin x = e^(tan x)(sec x - sin x).

testBank.q: integral of (x^2 - 1)/(x^4 + 3x^2 + 1) dx equals
opts: (1/sqrt5) ln|(x^2 - sqrt5 x + 1)/(x^2 + sqrt5 x + 1)| + C
steps: 1. Only even powers of x appear, so divide numerator and denominator by x^2: the integrand becomes (1 - 1/x^2)/(x^2 + 3 + 1/x^2).
2. The numerator 1 - 1/x^2 is the derivative of x + 1/x, so put t = x + 1/x, dt = (1 - 1/x^2) dx.
3. Then x^2 + 1/x^2 = t^2 - 2, so the denominator becomes t^2 - 2 + 3 = t^2 + 1.
4. The integral is integral of dt/(t^2 + 1) = tan inverse t + C = tan inverse (x + 1/x) + C = tan inverse ((x^2 + 1)/x) + C.

testBank.q: integral of dx/(cos(x - a) cos(x - b)) equals
steps: 1. Put alpha = x - a and beta = x - b, so alpha - beta = b - a, a constant.
2. Multiply and divide by sin(b - a): the integrand is (1/sin(b - a)) times sin(alpha - beta)/(cos alpha cos beta).
3. Expand sin(alpha - beta) = sin alpha cos beta - cos alpha sin beta and divide by cos alpha cos beta to get tan alpha - tan beta.
4. So the integral is (1/sin(b - a)) [ln|sec(x - a)| - ln|sec(x - b)|] + C = (1/sin(b - a)) ln|cos(x - b)/cos(x - a)| + C.

testBank.q: integral of (2x + 5) sqrt(3x - 8) dx equals
steps: 1. Both factors are integrable, so stop the one with the easier derivative, namely 2x + 5, and integrate sqrt(3x - 8): its integral is (2/9)(3x - 8)^(3/2).

testBank.q: The integral of cosec^3 x dx equals
opts: -(1/2) cosec x cot x + (1/2) ln|cosec x + cot x| + C
(1/2) cosec x cot x + (1/2) ln|tan(x/2)| + C
-(1/2) cosec x cot x - (1/2) ln|tan(x/2)| + C
-(1/2) cosec x cot x + (1/2) ln|tan(x/2)| + C
steps: 1. Write cosec^3 x as cosec x times cosec^2 x and integrate by parts, stopping cosec x.
2. The integral returns on the right-hand side, exactly as it does for sec^3 x.
3. Collecting the returning integral on the left gives 2I = -cosec x cot x + the integral of cosec x dx.
4. Since the integral of cosec x dx = ln|tan(x/2)| + C, divide by 2.
5. I = -(1/2) cosec x cot x + (1/2) ln|tan(x/2)| + C.
testBank.answer: (D) -(1/2) cosec x cot x + (1/2) ln|tan(x/2)| + C

testBank.q: integral of e^x (1 + x)/(2 + x)^2 dx equals
steps: 1. Build the denominator inside the numerator: 1 + x = (2 + x) - 1.
2. So the integrand is e^x[1/(2 + x) - 1/(2 + x)^2].
3. Take f = 1/(2 + x); then f' = -1/(2 + x)^2, so the bracket is exactly f + f'.
4. By integral of e^x(f + f') dx = e^x f + C, the answer is e^x/(x + 2) + C.

testBank.q: integral of e^x (x^2 + 1)/(x + 1)^2 dx equals
steps: 2. So the integrand is e^x[1 - 2/(x + 1) + 2/(x + 1)^2].
4. Hence the integral is e^x (x - 1)/(x + 1) + C.

testBank.q: integral of sin 2x/(sin^4 x + cos^4 x) dx equals
steps: 1. The denominator is quadratic in sin^2 x and cos^2 x, so divide numerator and denominator by cos^4 x.
2. Numerator: 2 sin x cos x/cos^4 x = 2 tan x sec^2 x. Denominator: tan^4 x + 1.
3. Now 2 tan x sec^2 x is exactly the derivative of tan^2 x, so put t = tan^2 x.
4. The integral becomes integral of dt/(1 + t^2) = tan inverse t + C = tan inverse (tan^2 x) + C.

testBank.q: integral of dx/(x^6 + x) equals
opts: ln|x| - (1/5) ln|x^5 + 1| + C only when x > 0
steps: 1. Take the highest power common in the denominator: x^6 + x = x^6(1 + x^(-5)).
2. So the integrand is x^(-6) dx/(1 + x^(-5)).
5. Check by differentiating: 1/x - x^4/(x^5 + 1) = [(x^5 + 1) - x^5]/(x(x^5 + 1)) = 1/(x^6 + x).

testBank.q: integral of (3x + 1)/sqrt(x^2 + 4x + 5) dx equals
steps: 1. Linear over root quadratic: write 3x + 1 = A(2x + 4) + B, the bracket being the derivative of x^2 + 4x + 5.
2. Comparing x: 2A = 3, so A = 3/2. Comparing constants: 4A + B = 1 gives B = 1 - 6 = -5.
3. First piece: (3/2) integral of (2x + 4)/sqrt(x^2 + 4x + 5) dx = (3/2)(2 sqrt(x^2 + 4x + 5)) = 3 sqrt(x^2 + 4x + 5), using integral of f'/sqrt f = 2 sqrt f.
4. Second piece: -5 integral of dx/sqrt((x + 2)^2 + 1) = -5 ln|x + 2 + sqrt(x^2 + 4x + 5)|.
5. Add the two pieces.

testBank.q: integral of dx/(5 + 4 cos x) equals
steps: 1. The denominator is linear in cos x, so put t = tan(x/2), with cos x = (1 - t^2)/(1 + t^2) and dx = 2 dt/(1 + t^2).
3. The integral becomes integral of 2 dt/(t^2 + 9) = (2/3) tan inverse (t/3) + C.
4. Put t back: (2/3) tan inverse ((1/3) tan(x/2)) + C.

testBank.q: Let I = integral of (x^2 + 1)/(x^4 + 1) dx. Which of the following are correct?
opts: The substitution t = x + 1/x reduces I to integral of dt/(t^2 - 2)
I = (1/(2 sqrt2)) ln|(x^2 - sqrt2 x + 1)/(x^2 + sqrt2 x + 1)| + C
The substitution t = x - 1/x reduces I to integral of dt/(t^2 + 2)
steps: 1. Divide numerator and denominator by x^2: the integrand is (1 + 1/x^2)/(x^2 + 1/x^2).
2. The numerator 1 + 1/x^2 is the derivative of x - 1/x, so t = x - 1/x is the right choice, and x^2 + 1/x^2 = t^2 + 2. Hence A is correct.
3. integral of dt/(t^2 + 2) = (1/sqrt2) tan inverse (t/sqrt2) + C, and t = (x^2 - 1)/x, so B is correct.
4. Option C is the answer to integral of (x^2 - 1)/(x^4 + 1) dx, which needs t = x + 1/x; and t = x + 1/x does not fit this numerator, so C and D are both wrong for this I.

testBank.q: Which of the following statements are correct?
opts: integral of (sec x + x sec x tan x) dx = x sec x + C
integral of e^x (tan x + sec^2 x) dx = e^x tan x + C
integral of (ln(ln x) + 1/ln x) dx = x ln(ln x) + C
integral of e^(x^3) (tan x + 3x^2 sec^2 x) dx = e^(x^3) tan x + C
steps: 1. A: with f = ln(ln x), x f' = x (1/ln x)(1/x) = 1/ln x, so the integrand is f + x f' and the integral is x f = x ln(ln x). Correct.
2. B: with f = sec x, x f' = x sec x tan x, so again f + x f', giving x sec x. Correct.
3. C: with f = tan x, f' = sec^2 x, so integral of e^x(f + f') = e^x tan x. Correct.
4. D: the general version needs e^g(f g' + f') with g = x^3, i.e. e^(x^3)(3x^2 tan x + sec^2 x). The pairing in D is the wrong way round, so D is incorrect.

testBank.q: For I = integral of tan^5 x sec^4 x dx, which substitutions reduce I to the integral of a polynomial in t?
steps: 1. t = tan x: dt = sec^2 x dx, and sec^4 x dx = sec^2 x (sec^2 x dx), with the leftover sec^2 x = 1 + t^2. I becomes integral of t^5(1 + t^2) dt, a polynomial. Correct.
2. t = sec x: dt = sec x tan x dx, and tan^5 x sec^4 x dx = tan^4 x sec^3 x (sec x tan x dx), with tan^4 x = (sec^2 x - 1)^2. I becomes integral of (t^2 - 1)^2 t^3 dt, a polynomial. Correct.
3. t = sin x: the integrand is sin^5 x/cos^9 x, and dt = cos x dx gives integral of t^5/(1 - t^2)^5 dt, a proper rational function, not a polynomial.
4. t = cos x: dt = -sin x dx gives -integral of (1 - t^2)^2/t^9 dt, which has negative powers of t, again not a polynomial.

testBank.q: Let I = integral of sqrt(x^2 + 4) dx. Which of the following are correct?
opts: The substitution x = 2 tan theta reduces I to 4 integral of sec^3 theta d theta
steps: 1. Use the shortcut integral of sqrt(x^2 + a^2) dx = (x/2) sqrt(x^2 + a^2) + (a^2/2) integral of dx/sqrt(x^2 + a^2). With a = 2, a^2/2 = 2 and the reciprocal integral is ln|x + sqrt(x^2 + 4)|. So A is correct and C has the wrong sign.
2. x = 2 tan theta gives dx = 2 sec^2 theta d theta and sqrt(x^2 + 4) = 2 sec theta, so I = integral of 4 sec^3 theta d theta. B is correct.
3. D differs from A by the constant -2 ln 2, which is absorbed into C. So D is also a correct form of the same answer.

testBank.q: Let x^2/((x - 1)(x - 2)(x - 3)) = A/(x - 1) + B/(x - 2) + C/(x - 3). Which of the following are correct?
steps: 1. The fraction is proper (degree 2 over degree 3), so the given split is legal. Clear denominators: x^2 = A(x - 2)(x - 3) + B(x - 1)(x - 3) + C(x - 1)(x - 2).
3. Comparing the coefficient of x^2 gives A + B + C = 1, and indeed 1/2 - 4 + 9/2 = 1.
4. The integral is (1/2) ln|x - 1| - 4 ln|x - 2| + (9/2) ln|x - 3| + k, so option D has the wrong sign on the middle term.

testBank.q: Let I = integral of x sin inverse x/sqrt(1 - x^2) dx. Which of the following are correct?
opts: The substitution x = sin theta reduces I to integral of theta sin theta d theta
I = sqrt(1 - x^2) sin inverse x - x + C
I = x - sqrt(1 - x^2) sin inverse x + C
integral of theta sin theta d theta = -theta cos theta + sin theta + C
steps: 1. By parts, stopping sin inverse x and integrating x/sqrt(1 - x^2) to -sqrt(1 - x^2): I = -sqrt(1 - x^2) sin inverse x + integral of sqrt(1 - x^2)/sqrt(1 - x^2) dx = -sqrt(1 - x^2) sin inverse x + x + C. So A is correct and C has both signs flipped.
2. With x = sin theta, dx = cos theta d theta and sqrt(1 - x^2) = cos theta, so the integrand becomes sin theta times theta/cos theta times cos theta = theta sin theta. B is correct.
3. By parts on theta sin theta: stop theta, integrate sin theta to -cos theta, giving -theta cos theta + integral of cos theta d theta = -theta cos theta + sin theta + C. D is correct.
4. Both routes agree, since -theta cos theta + sin theta = -sin inverse x sqrt(1 - x^2) + x.

testBank.q: If integral of e^(2x) cos 3x dx = e^(2x)(p sin 3x + q cos 3x)/13 + C, find the value of p + q.
steps: 1. Apply by parts twice. Stop e^(2x) and integrate cos 3x first: I = e^(2x) sin 3x/3 - (2/3) integral of e^(2x) sin 3x dx.
2. Apply by parts again on integral of e^(2x) sin 3x dx = -e^(2x) cos 3x/3 + (2/3) integral of e^(2x) cos 3x dx = -e^(2x) cos 3x/3 + (2/3) I.
4. Hence I = e^(2x)(3 sin 3x + 2 cos 3x)/13, so p = 3, q = 2 and p + q = 5. This matches the general result e^(ax)(b sin bx + a cos bx)/(a^2 + b^2).

testBank.q: If integral of (sin inverse x)^2 dx = x(sin inverse x)^2 + alpha sqrt(1 - x^2) sin inverse x + beta x + C, find alpha - beta.
steps: 1. Put x = sin t, dx = cos t dt, so the integral becomes integral of t^2 cos t dt.
2. By parts: integral of t^2 cos t dt = t^2 sin t - 2 integral of t sin t dt = t^2 sin t - 2[-t cos t + sin t].
3. So the integral is t^2 sin t + 2t cos t - 2 sin t + C.
4. Back-substitute t = sin inverse x, sin t = x, cos t = sqrt(1 - x^2): the answer is x(sin inverse x)^2 + 2 sqrt(1 - x^2) sin inverse x - 2x + C.
5. Hence alpha = 2, beta = -2 and alpha - beta = 4.
1. Clear denominators: 3x + 2 = A(x - 1)(x + 1) + B(x + 1) + C(x - 1)^2.
3. Compare the coefficient of x^2: 0 = A + C, so A = 1/4. (Check with the constant term: -A + B + C = -1/4 + 5/2 - 1/4 = 2.)

testBank.q: If integral of (x^4 + 1)/(x^6 + 1) dx = tan inverse x + (1/k) tan inverse (x^3) + C, find k.
steps: 1. Factorise the denominator: x^6 + 1 = (x^2 + 1)(x^4 - x^2 + 1).
2. Split the numerator to match: x^4 + 1 = (x^4 - x^2 + 1) + x^2.
4. The first piece gives tan inverse x. For the second, put t = x^3, dt = 3x^2 dx, giving (1/3) integral of dt/(1 + t^2) = (1/3) tan inverse (x^3).
5. Hence k = 3.

testBank.q: If integral of (5x + 3)/(x^2 + 4x + 10) dx = (5/2) ln(x^2 + 4x + 10) - (p/sqrt6) tan inverse ((x + 2)/sqrt6) + C, find p.
steps: 1. Write the linear as A(2x + 4) + B, since 2x + 4 is the derivative of the quadratic.
2. Comparing x: 2A = 5, so A = 5/2. Comparing constants: 4A + B = 3 gives B = 3 - 10 = -7.
3. First piece: (5/2) integral of (2x + 4) dx/(x^2 + 4x + 10) = (5/2) ln(x^2 + 4x + 10).
4. Second piece: -7 integral of dx/((x + 2)^2 + 6) = -(7/sqrt6) tan inverse ((x + 2)/sqrt6).
5. Hence p = 7.

testBank.q: If integral of tan^3 x sec^3 x dx = sec^5 x/a - sec^3 x/b + C, where a and b are positive integers, find a + b.
steps: 1. An even power of tan (namely tan^2 x) will be left if you substitute t = sec x, so that is the right choice.
2. Write tan^3 x sec^3 x dx = tan^2 x sec^2 x (sec x tan x dx), and dt = sec x tan x dx.
3. With tan^2 x = sec^2 x - 1 = t^2 - 1, the integral becomes integral of (t^2 - 1) t^2 dt = integral of (t^4 - t^2) dt.
4. That is t^5/5 - t^3/3 = sec^5 x/5 - sec^3 x/3 + C, so a = 5, b = 3 and a + b = 8.

testBank.q: integral of (20x^7 + x^4 - 9)/(5x^8 + x^5 + 5x^4 + 3x) dx equals
steps: 1. The powers are large and lopsided, which is the signature of a problem built by multiplying up and down by x^n. Divide numerator and denominator by x^4.
2. Numerator: 20x^3 + 1 - 9/x^4. Denominator: 5x^4 + x + 5 + 3/x^3.
3. Now notice that the derivative of 5x^4 + 3x^(-3) + x + 5 is 20x^3 - 9x^(-4) + 1, which is exactly the new numerator.
4. So the integral is of the form f'/f and equals ln|5x^4 + 3/x^3 + x + 5| + C.
5. Writing it over x^3: ln|(5x^7 + x^4 + 5x^3 + 3)/x^3| + C. Option B is the trap: the given numerator is not the derivative of the given denominator.

testBank.q: integral of ln(x + sqrt(x^2 + 1)) dx equals
steps: 1. There is no formula for the log, so stop the log and integrate the invisible 1 to get x.
2. The derivative of ln(x + sqrt(x^2 + 1)) is (1/(x + sqrt(x^2 + 1))) times (1 + x/sqrt(x^2 + 1)) = (1/(x + sqrt(x^2 + 1))) times (x + sqrt(x^2 + 1))/sqrt(x^2 + 1) = 1/sqrt(x^2 + 1).
3. So I = x ln(x + sqrt(x^2 + 1)) - integral of x dx/sqrt(x^2 + 1).
4. The remaining integral is of f'/sqrt f apart from a factor: integral of x dx/sqrt(x^2 + 1) = sqrt(x^2 + 1).
5. Hence I = x ln(x + sqrt(x^2 + 1)) - sqrt(x^2 + 1) + C. (The substitution t = x + sqrt(x^2 + 1) gives the same answer but takes far longer, and you must then remember to halve the t + 1/t piece.)

testBank.q: integral of x dx/(1 + sin x) equals
opts: x(sec x - tan x) + ln|1 + sin x| + C
x(tan x - sec x) + ln|1 + sin x| + C
x tan x - ln|sec x| + C
x(tan x - sec x) - ln|1 + sin x| + C
steps: 1. Rationalise: multiply numerator and denominator by 1 - sin x, so the integrand becomes x(1 - sin x)/cos^2 x = x sec^2 x - x sec x tan x.
2. First piece by parts: integral of x sec^2 x dx = x tan x - integral of tan x dx = x tan x - ln|sec x|.
3. Second piece by parts: integral of x sec x tan x dx = x sec x - integral of sec x dx = x sec x - ln|sec x + tan x|.
4. Subtract: I = x tan x - ln|sec x| - x sec x + ln|sec x + tan x| = x(tan x - sec x) + ln|(sec x + tan x)/sec x|.
5. Since (sec x + tan x)/sec x = 1 + sin x, I = x(tan x - sec x) + ln|1 + sin x| + C. Differentiating back confirms it: the two non-x terms cancel and x sec x(sec x - tan x) = x/(1 + sin x).
testBank.answer: x(tan x - sec x) + ln|1 + sin x| + C

testBank.q: integral of dx/(sqrt(x + 1) - (x + 1)^(1/3)) equals
steps: 1. Two different roots appear, of index 2 and 3, so kill both at once: put x + 1 = t^6, giving dx = 6t^5 dt.
2. Then sqrt(x + 1) = t^3 and (x + 1)^(1/3) = t^2, so the integrand is 6t^5 dt/(t^3 - t^2) = 6t^3 dt/(t - 1).
3. Split by division: t^3/(t - 1) = t^2 + t + 1 + 1/(t - 1), since t^3 = (t - 1)(t^2 + t + 1) + 1.
4. So the integral is 6[t^3/3 + t^2/2 + t + ln|t - 1|] = 2t^3 + 3t^2 + 6t + 6 ln|t - 1| + C.

testBank.q: integral of (3 sin x + 2 cos x)/(3 cos x + 2 sin x) dx equals
opts: ln|3 cos x + 2 sin x| + C
steps: 1. Write the numerator as lambda(denominator) + mu(derivative of the denominator). Here the denominator is 3 cos x + 2 sin x and its derivative is -3 sin x + 2 cos x.
2. So 3 sin x + 2 cos x = lambda(3 cos x + 2 sin x) + mu(-3 sin x + 2 cos x).
3. Compare sin x: 3 = 2 lambda - 3 mu. Compare cos x: 2 = 3 lambda + 2 mu. Solving gives mu = -5/13 and lambda = 12/13.
4. Then the integral splits into lambda integral of dx + mu integral of (derivative of denominator)/denominator dx = lambda x + mu ln|denominator|.
5. So the answer is (12/13)x - (5/13) ln|3 cos x + 2 sin x| + C. Differentiating back gives (26 cos x + 39 sin x)/(13(3 cos x + 2 sin x)) = (2 cos x + 3 sin x)/(3 cos x + 2 sin x), as required.

commonMistakes: 1. Leaving out + c.
Fix: A constant dies on differentiating, so an indefinite integral is a whole family — write + c in the same stroke as the answer, every single time.
▶ where this comes up in the lecture
2. Forgetting the 1/a factor when x is replaced by ax + b, or losing the minus sign when a is negative.
Fix: After applying any formula, immediately divide by the coefficient of x and carry its sign: ∫dx/(2 − 3x) = −(1/3)ln|2 − 3x| + c.
▶ where this comes up in the lecture
3. Writing ∫dx/x = ln x without the modulus, and the same inside every log answer.
Fix: It is ln|x| + c. Keep the modulus on ln|f|, ln|sec x + tan x|, ln|x + √(quadratic)| — marks are cut for the bare log.
▶ where this comes up in the lecture
4. Expecting tan x, cot x, sec x, cosec x to integrate as directly as sin x and cos x.
Fix: Those four are not derivative-reversals; they come from separate work (sec x needs the sec x + tan x manipulation). Learn those four results as their own line on the sheet.
▶ where this comes up in the lecture
5. Substituting t but not converting dx, or finishing the answer in t.
Fix: Every substitution has two halves — the function and its differential. Write dt = f′(x)dx on the same line, and put x back at the end.
▶ where this comes up in the lecture
6. Mixing up the nine quadratic formulas — sin⁻¹ used for x² − a², or 1/(x² − a²) given a tan⁻¹ answer.
Fix: Decide the shape first (x² + a², x² − a², a² − x²), then read the matching formula. Remember the pairs: 1/(x² − a²) → (1/2a)ln|(x − a)/(x + a)|, 1/(a² − x²) → (1/2a)ln|(a + x)/(a − x)|.
▶ where this comes up in the lecture
7. Doing partial fractions on an improper fraction, or using the wrong form for a repeated or quadratic factor.

Fix: Divide first until the top is of lower degree. Then: repeated factor needs B/(x − a) and C/(x − a)², a quadratic factor needs px + q on top, a linear factor only a constant — always one power less above than below.
▶ where this comes up in the lecture
8. In by parts, losing the minus sign on the second integral or stopping the wrong function.
Fix: The formula is (stopped)·(integral of other) − ∫(integral of other)·(derivative of stopped). If the derivative of your stopped function is getting worse, you stopped the wrong one — swap.
▶ where this comes up in the lecture
9. Reaching for by parts when a substitution would clear the question first.
Fix: ∫cos√x dx is not a by-parts question until √x = t makes it ∫2t cos t dt. Always substitute away the awkward inside before you split a product.
▶ where this comes up in the lecture
10. Integrating a degree angle as if it were radians, like ∫cos(x°)dx.
Fix: Convert inside first: x° = πx/180, so ∫cos(x°)dx = (180/π)sin(πx/180) + c.
▶ where this comes up in the lecture
shortcuts: The 1/a rule for ax + b Any standard formula stays true when x is replaced by ax + b — just multiply the whole result by 1/(coefficient of x). ∫(7x − 5)⁻³dx uses the power formula, then divides by 7. Watch the sign: 1/(2 − 3x) gives −(1/3)ln|2 − 3x|. Lecture 15
▶ watch Ankit Sir explain it

Ask whose derivative is sitting in the question Before any method, scan for an inner function whose derivative is already there. x²/(1 + x⁶) has x² under x³. dx/(x ln x) has 1/x under ln x. Put that function = t and the question collapses into a basic form. Substitution never creates a new integral; it only converts. Lecture 15
▶ watch Ankit Sir explain it

Three answers you can write without substituting ∫f′/f dx = ln|f| + c, ∫fⁿf′ dx = f^(n+1)/(n + 1) + c, ∫f′/√f dx = 2√f + c. Use them only as far as you can go without an error — the moment you are unsure, write t = f and do it properly. Lecture 16
▶ watch Ankit Sir explain it

Highest power common, and the even-power divide If the bracket resists, pull the highest power of x out of it — a negative power of x appears whose derivative is already outside. And when every power of x is even, divide top and bottom by x² and take t = x + a/x or t = x − a/x; squaring the substitution rebuilds the denominator as t² ∓ 2a. Lecture 16
▶ watch Ankit Sir explain it

Complete the square — only three quadratics exist After a perfect square every quadratic is x² + a², x² − a² or a² − x². That is why nine formulas cover the whole family, and why ∫√(quadratic) is just (x/2)·(the same root) ± (a²/2)·∫(its reciprocal). If the linear part inside scares you, substitute t for it first — one extra line, no sign errors. Lecture 16
▶ watch Ankit Sir explain it

Linear with a quadratic: split as a·(quadratic)′ + b For any (linear)/(quadratic) or (linear)/√(quadratic), write 5x + 3 = a(2x + 4) + b and compare coefficients. The a part gives a log (or 2√Q), the b part gives a standard formula. If the top is a quadratic or cubic, divide first and you are back to this same case. Lecture 16
▶ watch Ankit Sir explain it

By parts: integrate what you can, stop what differentiates easily Forget chanting ILATE. First integrate the function whose integral you know; if both are integrable, stop the one whose derivative is simpler. ln x and sin⁻¹x are products with 1. If the original integral reappears after two rounds (e^(ax)cos bx, sec³x), call it I and solve algebraically. Lecture 18
▶ watch Ankit Sir explain it

The two eˣ results, and how to force them ∫eˣ(f + f′)dx = eˣf + c and ∫(f + x f′)dx = x f + c, with the general form ∫e^g(f g′ + f′)dx = e^g f + c. Most JEE questions hide them: add and subtract to make the pattern — write x² + 1 as (x² − 1) + 2, or multiply and divide by sec x so sec²x appears next to e^(tan x). Lecture 19
▶ watch Ankit Sir explain it

chapters.title: Definite Integration

concepts.title: Newton–Leibniz rule: differentiating without integrating
concepts.oneLine: To differentiate a definite integral whose limits are functions of x, put the upper limit into the function and multiply by its derivative, then subtract the same thing done with the lower limit — no integration needed.
notes: Think about why differentiation keeps coming back in calculus. It is there in L'Hôpital's rule for limits, it is there in the whole of AOD, it is there in substitution in indefinite integration, it is there when we form differential equations. So a technique that lets you differentiate a new kind of object is worth a lot.

Here is the object. When you integrate f(t)·dt and then put in the upper limit and the lower limit, the t vanishes. Whatever is left depends only on the limits. So if the limits are functions of x, the whole definite integral is just a function of x, and we can differentiate it with respect to x.

Now the technique, in two steps. Put the upper limit into f, multiply by the derivative of the upper limit; then do exactly the same with the lower limit and put a minus in front. That is the whole rule. The t, the u, the y inside — the dummy letter makes no difference at all.

The special case is the one you will see most. If the lower limit is a constant a, then f(a) is some number but the derivative of a is 0, so that whole second term dies. The upper limit x gives derivative 1. You are left with just f(x).

quickChecks.q: Differentiate with respect to x: the integral of t² dt from 1 to x³.
steps: 1. Lower limit is the constant 1, so that term is f(1)·0 = 0.
2. Upper limit: put t = x³ into t², giving (x³)² = x⁶.
3. Multiply by the derivative of x³, which is 3x².
4. So the answer is x⁶·3x² = 3x⁸.

quickChecks.q: Differentiate with respect to x: the integral of sin t dt from 0 to x.
steps: 1. This is the special case: constant lower limit, upper limit x.
2. The lower term is sin 0 · 0 = 0.
3. Just put t = x into sin t, and the derivative of x is 1.
4. Answer is sin x.

quickChecks.q: Differentiate with respect to x: the integral of t dt from x to x².
steps: 1. f(t) = t, upper limit x², lower limit x.
2. Upper: put t = x² into t, giving x². Times derivative of x², which is 2x, gives 2x³.
3. Lower: put t = x into t, giving x. Times derivative of x, which is 1, gives x.
4. Subtract: 2x³ − x.

concepts.title: Variable in the limit? Differentiate first
concepts.oneLine: The moment a variable sits in the limit of a definite integral, differentiate both sides first — only then read what is being asked.
notes: In the last part you learnt the Newton–Leibniz rule. Now for why the questioner loves it. He hides a variable inside the limit of a definite integral and then asks you something that looks completely unrelated.

Variable in a definite-integral limit? Differentiate first, then read the problem. This is my cardinal rule — universal, no exceptions. Do not sit and try to integrate f(t)·sin√t. You cannot, and you are not supposed to.

Differentiating is mechanical. On the left, put the upper limit in place of t and multiply by the derivative of that upper limit. On the right, differentiate the ordinary function sitting there. Keep one eye on the domain — here ln x forces x > 0, so √(x²) is simply x.

What comes after differentiation is totally the questioner's choice. A plain f(x²) term and he asks a value. A y written inside and dy/dx appears — that is a differential equation. Set that dy/dx = 0 and the same question becomes a maximum–minimum question. Your job stops at differentiating.

quickChecks.q: If the integral of f(t) dt from 0 to x² equals x⁴ + x², find f(4).
steps: 1. Variable in the limit, so differentiate both sides: f(x²)·2x = 4x³ + 2x.
2. Divide by 2x: f(x²) = 2x² + 1.
3. For f(4) you need x² = 4, so x = 2.

quickChecks.q: If the integral of f(t) dt from 0 to 2x equals x³, find f(2).
steps: 1. Differentiate both sides: f(2x)·2 = 3x².
3. For f(2) you need 2x = 2, so x = 1.

quickChecks.q: If y is the integral of (t² − 3t + 2) dt from 0 to x, find the point of local maximum and the point of local minimum.
steps: 1. Differentiate: dy/dx = x² − 3x + 2.
2. Set dy/dx = 0: (x − 1)(x − 2) = 0, so x = 1 and x = 2 are the critical points.
3. Second derivative: d²y/dx² = 2x − 3.
4. At x = 1 it is −1, negative, so local maximum. At x = 2 it is +1, positive, so local minimum.
quickChecks.answer: Local maximum at x = 1, local minimum at x = 2

concepts.title: Newton–Leibniz inside a 0/0 limit
concepts.oneLine: In a 0/0 limit, apply L'Hôpital and differentiate the integral by Newton–Leibniz: d/dx ∫₀ˣ cos²t dt = cos²x, nothing more.
notes: First thing, always: put x = 0 and see the form. On top, x becomes 0 and ∫₀⁰ cos²t dt is 0, because the lower and upper limits are the same. On the bottom, x³ − 6x becomes 0. So it is 0/0, and L'Hôpital is allowed.

Now differentiate top and bottom separately. The bottom is easy, 3x² − 6. On top, the derivative of x is 1, and for ∫₀ˣ cos²t dt use Newton–Leibniz: put the upper limit into the function. That gives cos²x, multiplied by the derivative of x, which is 1.

Here you have no choice: the derivative of ∫₀ˣ cos²t dt is cos²x, period — you do not get to decide what to differentiate. So the top is 1 − cos²x, which is sin²x. Check the form of the new limit before you touch it again: top 0, bottom −6. Not 0/0 any more, so just substitute and the answer is 0.

One more thing, and this is the real lesson. Newton–Leibniz is not a question type, it is a differentiation technique — so it shows up inside limits, inside maxima-minima, inside anything. Do not call it "a limit rule". You differentiated; where you differentiated is the questioner's choice, not yours.

quickChecks.q: Evaluate lim x→0 (∫₀ˣ cos t dt)/(x² + 2x).
steps: 1. At x = 0: top is ∫₀⁰ cos t dt = 0, bottom is 0 + 0 = 0. It is 0/0.
2. Apply L'Hôpital. Top by Newton–Leibniz: cos x. Bottom: 2x + 2.
3. Substitute x = 0: cos 0 / (0 + 2) = 1/2.

quickChecks.q: Evaluate lim x→0 (∫₀ˣ (1 + cos t) dt)/(x² − 4x).
steps: 1. At x = 0: top is 0, bottom is 0 − 0 = 0. So 0/0.
2. Differentiate: top becomes 1 + cos x, bottom becomes 2x − 4.

quickChecks.q: Evaluate lim x→0 (x − ∫₀ˣ cos²t dt)/(x² − 5x).
steps: 1. At x = 0 both top and bottom are 0, so 0/0.
2. Differentiate the top: 1 − cos²x = sin²x. Differentiate the bottom: 2x − 5.
3. Substitute x = 0: 0/(0 − 5) = 0.

concepts.title: Fundamental 1: upper limit minus lower limit
concepts.oneLine: A definite integral is just upper limit minus lower limit: ∫ₐᵇ f(x) dx = F(b) − F(a), and the constant of integration always cancels.
notes: Start with what you already know. You integrate a function f(x) and you get F(x) + C. That capital F is the antiderivative, the small f is what you were given.

Now put limits on it, a at the bottom and b at the top. Put the upper limit in: you get F(b) + C. Put the lower limit in: you get F(a) + C. Subtract. The C sits in both terms, so it cancels, and the answer is simply F(b) − F(a).

A fair question at this point: how is C cancelling? Look at it once more: value at the upper limit is F(b) + C, value at the lower limit is F(a) + C. Same C in both. Subtraction eats it. That is why a definite integral never carries a constant.

One more piece and this fundamental is complete. Sometimes F is not defined exactly at a or at b. Then you do not panic, you take the limiting value. x is travelling from a to b, so at the lower limit you take the limit as x → a⁺, and at the upper limit you take the limit as x → b⁻. Approach the bad point from inside the interval, with a slightly larger number at the bottom and a slightly smaller number at the top.

quickChecks.q: Evaluate ∫₁³ 2x dx, and show that the constant of integration does not matter.
steps: 1. Antiderivative of 2x is x² + C, so F(x) = x² + C.
2. Upper limit: F(3) = 9 + C.
3. Lower limit: F(1) = 1 + C.
4. Subtract: (9 + C) − (1 + C) = 8.
quickChecks.answer: 8 — the C cancelled on its own

quickChecks.q: Evaluate ∫₁^e (1/x) dx.
steps: 1. F(x) = ln x.
2. Upper minus lower: ln e − ln 1.
3. ln e = 1 and ln 1 = 0.

quickChecks.q: Evaluate ∫₀¹ (1/x) dx using the fundamental, being careful at the lower limit.
steps: 1. F(x) = ln x, so the answer should be ln 1 − ln 0.
2. But ln x is not defined at x = 0, so take the limiting value from inside: limit as x → 0⁺ of ln x = −∞.
3. Upper limit value: ln 1 = 0.
4. So the value is 0 − (−∞).
quickChecks.answer: It does not come out to a finite number — the integral diverges (→ ∞)

concepts.title: Applying fundamental 1 when a limit misbehaves
concepts.oneLine: Upper limit minus lower limit still rules — but if the function has no value at a limit, you put the limiting value there instead, and 0×∞ is cracked by turning it into ∞/∞ and using L'Hopital.
notes: Four integrals, same single rule: integrate, put the upper limit, put the lower limit, subtract. And in a definite integral you never write + C — it cancels in the subtraction, so stop writing it.

The first two are pure plug-in. The third one, ∫ln x from 0 to 1, is where it gets interesting. The antiderivative is x(ln x − 1). At the upper limit 1 it behaves nicely and gives −1. At the lower limit 0 it does not: ln 0 is not defined.

When the function has no value at a limit, you do not stop — you take its limiting value as x approaches that limit. So instead of the value at 0, I take the limit as x → 0⁺ of x(ln x − 1). That is a 0 × ∞ form, and 0 × ∞ is not something L'Hopital eats directly.

So flip it: keep ln x − 1 on top and write x as 1 upon x below. Now top is −∞, bottom is ∞, it is an ∞/∞ form, and L'Hopital applies. Differentiate: (1/x) upon (−1/x²) = −x, which goes to 0. Lower limit contributes nothing, so the answer is −1. The fourth one plays the same game and the limiting value turns out to be infinite — that integral simply does not converge.

quickChecks.q: Evaluate ∫cos x dx from 0 to π/2.
steps: 1. Antiderivative is sin x, no + C.
2. Upper: sin(π/2) = 1. Lower: sin 0 = 0.

quickChecks.q: Find lim x → 0⁺ of x ln x.
steps: 1. It is a 0 × ∞ form, so convert it.
2. Write it as (ln x) upon (1/x): top → −∞, bottom → ∞, an ∞/∞ form.
3. L'Hopital: (1/x) ÷ (−1/x²) = −x.

quickChecks.q: Does ∫tan x dx from 0 to π/2 have a finite value?
steps: 1. Antiderivative is ln sec x.
2. Lower limit x = 0: ln sec 0 = ln 1 = 0.
3. Upper limit x = π/2: sec x → ∞, so ln sec x → ∞.
4. ∞ − 0 = ∞, so no finite value.

concepts.title: Fundamental 2: you are forced to break where the definition changes
concepts.oneLine: If the function changes its definition at a point c inside [a, b], you have no choice — split the integral at c and integrate each piece with its own formula.
notes: Fundamental 1 was simple: find the antiderivative, put upper limit minus lower limit. Fundamental 2 is about the case where you cannot do that in one shot.

Suppose you are integrating from a to b, and somewhere between them there is a point c where the definition of the function changes. Then you must break the integral at c — this is not a choice, it is compulsion. Walk from a to c with one definition, then from c to b with the other.
Think of mod x. Its definition changes at 0: for x negative, |x| = −x, and for x positive, |x| = x. So any integral whose limits cross 0 has to be cut at 0.

Same story for |x² − 1|. Inside dies at x = ±1, so if your journey is 0 to 2, the break sits at x = 1. Before 1 the inside is negative and the mod opens with an extra minus sign; after 1 the inside is positive and the mod opens directly. Find the point where the definition changes, then cut there — the rest is ordinary integration.

quickChecks.q: Evaluate the integral of |x|/x dx from x = −2 to x = 3.
steps: 1. Break at x = 0, since that is where |x| changes definition and it lies between −2 and 3.
2. On −2 to 0 the integrand is −1: value = −1 × (0 − (−2)) = −2.
3. On 0 to 3 the integrand is 1: value = 1 × (3 − 0) = 3.

quickChecks.q: Evaluate the integral of |x − 1| dx from x = 0 to x = 3.
steps: 1. Inside is zero at x = 1, which lies between 0 and 3, so break at x = 1.
2. On 0 to 1, x − 1 is negative, so |x − 1| = 1 − x. Integral = [x − x²/2] from 0 to 1 = 1 − ½ = ½.
3. On 1 to 3, x − 1 is positive, so |x − 1| = x − 1. Integral = [x²/2 − x] from 1 to 3 = (9/2 − 3) − (½ − 1) = 3/2 + ½ = 2.
4. Add: ½ + 2.

quickChecks.q: Evaluate the integral of |x² − 4| dx from x = 0 to x = 3.
steps: 1. Inside is zero at x = ±2; only x = 2 lies between 0 and 3, so break at x = 2.
2. On 0 to 2, x² − 4 is negative, so the mod gives 4 − x². Integral = [4x − x³/3] from 0 to 2 = 8 − 8/3 = 16/3.
3. On 2 to 3, x² − 4 is positive, so the mod opens directly. Integral = [x³/3 − 4x] from 2 to 3 = (9 − 12) − (8/3 − 8) = −3 + 16/3 = 7/3.

concepts.title: Greatest-integer integrals: locating every break point
concepts.oneLine: When a greatest-integer function sits inside a definite integral, you have no choice: break the integral at every point where the step jumps.
notes: If x is greater than 1, then x² − 1 is positive, so the modulus opens directly. That part is simple. But the greatest-integer function is a helpless case — you are forced to break.
The rule is this: if you are integrating from a to b and the definition of the function changes at some point inside, you must break the integral at that point. There is no choice.
Take [x] from 0 to 3. For x between 0 and 1, [x] = 0. Between 1 and 2, [x] = 1. Between 2 and 3, [x] = 2. So you break at 1 and at 2, and on each piece the function is just a constant.

And remember the one rule that runs through every chapter — continuity, differentiability, limits, differentiation, definite integration, it does not matter — [x] is a constant on each interval; only the ordinary x part stays variable. So in ∫[x]·x³ dx from 0 to 2, x³ keeps changing, but [x] is fixed at 0 on (0, 1) and fixed at 1 on (1, 2).

quickChecks.q: Where must you break the integral of [x] from 0 to 4, and what is [x] on each piece?
steps: 1. [x] jumps at every integer inside 0 to 4, so break at 1, 2 and 3.

quickChecks.q: Find the break points for [x²] when x runs from 0 to √3.
steps: 1. x from 0 to √3 means x² goes from 0 to 3.
2. Set x² = 1 and x² = 2, which gives x = 1 and x = √2.
3. So the pieces are 0 to 1, where [x²] = 0; 1 to √2, where [x²] = 1; and √2 to √3, where [x²] = 2.
quickChecks.answer: Break at x = 1 and x = √2; the values of [x²] are 0, 1, 2.

quickChecks.q: On the interval from 1 to 2, what does the integrand [x]·x³ become?
steps: 1. For x between 1 and 2, the greatest integer [x] = 1.
2. x³ stays variable, so pull out the constant 1.
quickChecks.answer: It becomes just x³, since [x] = 1 on that whole piece.

concepts.title: Fundamental 3: the integral is the algebraic sum of areas
concepts.oneLine: A definite integral is the algebraic sum of areas — plus where the graph is above the x-axis, minus where it is below — so its value can be positive, zero or negative.
notes: We have already fixed two things. Funda 1: for a constant function the integral is just upper limit minus lower limit. Funda 2: if the function is discontinuous at some point c lying between a and b, you have no choice — you must break the integral at c.

Now funda 3, the meaning of the whole thing. Definite integration from a to b is the algebraic sum of areas, not the total area. Wherever the graph sits above the x-axis, that piece of area goes in with a plus sign. Wherever it dips below the x-axis, that piece goes in with a minus sign.

So if the curve crosses the axis again and again between a and b, and the pieces of area are A₁, A₂, A₃, A₄, A₅ in order, then the integral from a to b is A₁ − A₂ + A₃ − A₄ + A₅. That word "algebraic" is doing all the work: it is telling you to carry the signs.

Because of this, a definite integral can come out positive, zero, or negative. A physical area can never be negative, but an integral is not a physical area. Keep the two words separate in your head and half the confusion in this chapter disappears.
