quickChecks.q: Between a and b a curve makes three regions: area 3 above the x-axis, area 8 below it, and area 5 above it. Find the definite integral from a to b.
steps: 1. Tag the pieces: +3, −8, +5.
2. Integral = 3 − 8 + 5.

quickChecks.q: Between a and b a curve makes two regions: area 6 above the x-axis and area 10 below it. Find the definite integral from a to b.
steps: 1. Tag the pieces: +6, −10.
2. Integral = 6 − 10.
quickChecks.answer: −4 (negative, and that is a correct answer, not an error)

quickChecks.q: A definite integral from a to b comes out 0.5, and you are told the regions below the x-axis have total area 4. What is the total area of the regions above the x-axis?
steps: 1. Let the area above be A. Then the algebraic sum is A − 4.

concepts.title: Why single points never matter
concepts.oneLine: One point has no width, so it has no area — include it or exclude it, the definite integral does not change.
notes: Look at any graph and pick one point on it. Now remove that point. Then remove another one. Has the area under the curve changed at all? Not even slightly. A single point has no width, so it carries no area, so it can never change a definite integral.

This matters because of the doubts you create for yourself while splitting. You write 0 to 1, and then you panic: but at exactly x = 1 the function jumps to a different value, so was 1 included or excluded? Then from 1 to √2 the same headache starts again — at exactly √2 the value changes, so is √2 in or out?

The answer is the same every time: it makes no difference. Include both ends, exclude both ends, include one and exclude the other — the area is identical. Read 0 to 1 as bigger than 0 and smaller than 1, and stop worrying about the two end points altogether.
So stop spending time there. Definite integration is the algebraic sum of area, and area does not notice single points. Clear your mind of this doubt and your splitting becomes fast.

quickChecks.q: You split an integral from 0 to 2 at x = 1, as a piece from 0 to 1 plus a piece from 1 to 2. Is x = 1 counted twice, and does that matter?
steps: 1. x = 1 sits at the end of the first piece and the start of the second.
2. A single point has no width, so it contributes zero area to each piece.
3. Zero plus zero is still zero.
quickChecks.answer: It makes no difference — the sum of the two pieces equals the integral from 0 to 2.

quickChecks.q: A function equals 1 everywhere on 0 to 2 except at the single point x = 1, where its value is 100. Find the integral from 0 to 2.
steps: 1. Away from x = 1 the height is 1, so the area is a rectangle of width 2 and height 1.
2. That gives 2.
3. The point x = 1 has no width, so the value 100 there adds no area.

quickChecks.q: On the stretch from 1 to √2 a function has the constant value 1, and you are unsure whether √2 is included. Find the integral from 1 to √2.
steps: 1. Width of the stretch = √2 − 1.
3. Including or excluding √2 changes nothing, since it is one point.

concepts.title: Breaking is a compulsion, and the integral of zero
concepts.oneLine: Integrate in one shot when you can; break only where the definition changes — and remember ∫ₐᵇ 0 dx = 0 while ∫0 dx = C.
notes: Keep one picture in your head: a definite integral is the algebraic sum of area. That one fundamental runs this whole chapter.

The ideal question is the one where the function keeps one definition from a to b. You integrate in one shot and do upper limit minus lower limit. If a function integrates directly, nothing is better than that.

The less ideal question is where the function changes its colour in between — 5 times between 0 and 100, say. Then you have no option. You must break at every point where the definition changes and integrate each piece by its own definition. Breaking is not a choice, it is a compulsion.

Now the silly one that costs marks. Asked for the integration of 0, the answer is C, because differentiating a constant gives 0. But if I ask for 0 dx from a to b, the answer is 0 — you put the constant at the upper limit, the constant at the lower limit, and they cancel. The definite integral of 0 over any interval is 0; the indefinite integral of 0 is C.

quickChecks.q: Evaluate ∫ from −3 to 7 of 0 dx.
steps: 1. The integrand is 0, so the antiderivative is the constant C.
2. Upper minus lower = C − C = 0.

quickChecks.q: Write both answers: ∫0 dx and ∫₀¹⁰⁰ 0 dx.
steps: 1. Indefinite: derivative of a constant is 0, so ∫0 dx = C.
2. Definite: the constant cancels between the two limits, so ∫₀¹⁰⁰ 0 dx = 0.

quickChecks.q: f(x) = 1 for 0 ≤ x < 1 and f(x) = 2 for 1 ≤ x ≤ 3. Find ∫₀³ f(x) dx.
steps: 1. The definition changes at x = 1, so the integral must be broken there.
2. ∫₀³ f dx = ∫₀¹ 1 dx + ∫₁³ 2 dx.
3. First piece: 1 × (1 − 0) = 1.
4. Second piece: 2 × (3 − 1) = 4.
5. Add the pieces: 1 + 4 = 5.

concepts.title: A zero definite integral forces a crossing of the x-axis
concepts.oneLine: If a continuous f(x) has ∫ from a to b equal to 0, the positive and negative areas have cancelled, so the graph must cross the x-axis at least once between a and b.
notes: Take a continuous function f(x), and suppose its definite integral from a to b comes out 0. Think logically about what that zero means. Definite integration gives you algebraic area — area above the x-axis counts as plus, area below counts as minus.

So a total of 0 means some positive area came, some negative area came, and the two balanced each other out perfectly. For a continuous function, to collect both positive and negative area it must have been above the axis somewhere and below the axis somewhere — and to go from above to below it has to cross the x-axis.
That is the whole interpretation. There is some point c between a and b where f(c) = 0. Notice the claim is at least once; it can cross many times, but zero crossings is impossible.
Continuity is what does the work here. A continuous graph cannot jump from the plus side to the minus side without touching the axis in between — it has no choice but to pass through zero.

quickChecks.q: The definite integral of sin x from 0 to 2π is 0, and sin x is continuous. Where does the graph cross the x-axis inside (0, 2π)?
steps: 1. Integral of sin x from 0 to π = 2 (area above the axis).
2. Integral of sin x from π to 2π = −2 (area below the axis).
3. Total = 2 + (−2) = 0, so plus and minus cancelled.
4. The changeover point is where sin x = 0 inside (0, 2π), that is x = π.

quickChecks.q: The definite integral of x³ from −1 to 1 is 0. Use the interpretation to find the crossing point.
steps: 1. Integral of x³ from −1 to 0 = −1/4 (area below the axis).
2. Integral of x³ from 0 to 1 = 1/4 (area above the axis).
4. x³ is continuous, so it must pass through zero where the sign changes, that is at x = 0.

quickChecks.q: f(x) is continuous on [a, b], f(x) > 0 for every x in [a, b], and someone claims the definite integral of f from a to b is 0. Can this be true?
steps: 1. A zero integral forces the graph to cross the x-axis at least once, so f(c) = 0 for some c in (a, b).
2. But f(x) > 0 everywhere on [a, b], so f is never 0 there.
3. The two statements fight each other.
quickChecks.answer: No, it cannot be true. With f > 0 throughout, the integral is strictly positive.

concepts.title: Opening the mod inside a definite integral
concepts.oneLine: A square root is a mod, so split the limits where the inside changes sign and open the mod separately on each piece.
notes: Remember one line: √(f²) is |f|, never just f. The moment a square root appears, the function's definition changes inside your limits, and in a definite integral you must incorporate that change.

So the work is always in two steps. First convert the root into a mod. Then ask where the inside is positive and where it is negative between your two limits, and break the integral at exactly those points.

Finding the break point is easy if you shift to the inner angle. For 2 sin(x/2) − 1, set sin(x/2) = ½. If x runs 0 to π, then x/2 runs 0 to π/2, so x/2 = π/6, which means x = π/3. That single number splits the question.
Before π/3 the sine is smaller than ½, so the bracket is negative and the mod opens with a minus. After π/3 it is bigger than ½, so the mod opens directly as it is. Same thinking, every time.

quickChecks.q: Evaluate the integral of √(1 + cos 2x) dx from 0 to π/2.
steps: 2. From 0 to π/2 cos x is positive, so no break and no minus sign: |cos x| = cos x.

quickChecks.q: Evaluate the integral of √(1 − cos 2x) dx from 0 to π.
steps: 1. 1 − cos 2x = 2sin²x, so the integrand is √2 |sin x|.
2. From 0 to π sin x is never negative, so |sin x| = sin x throughout — no break needed.

quickChecks.q: For the integral of |2 cos(x/2) − 1| dx from 0 to π, find the break point and say how the mod opens on each side.
steps: 1. Set 2 cos(x/2) − 1 = 0, so cos(x/2) = ½.
2. x from 0 to π means x/2 from 0 to π/2, so x/2 = π/3 and x = 2π/3.
3. For x from 0 to 2π/3, x/2 is below 60°, so cos(x/2) > ½ and the bracket is positive.
4. For x from 2π/3 to π the bracket is negative.
quickChecks.answer: Break at x = 2π/3: mod opens as 2 cos(x/2) − 1 on (0, 2π/3) and as 1 − 2 cos(x/2) on (2π/3, π)

concepts.title: Definite integrals that are really indefinite technique
concepts.oneLine: Definite integrals with ugly limits are often just indefinite integrals in disguise — spot the indefinite technique first, then put the limits in.
notes: In a paper they can set a trap here and you will not survive it. The reason is simple: before the limits do anything, a small indefinite integral has to come out. If you cannot see the indefinite technique, the limits are useless to you.

So train your eye on three things. One, the by-parts and substitution forms you already know. Two, the classical form f(x) + x·f'(x) — the moment you see it, you integrate it directly instead of hunting for a substitution. Three, the 1 ± sin 2x pair, where the choice of square decides everything.

For 1 ± sin 2x you have two honest options. (sin x + cos x)² = 1 + sin 2x, and (sin x − cos x)² = 1 − sin 2x. Both are correct identities, so the identity does not choose itself — the numerator chooses it for you.

Look at which derivative is sitting on top. If cos x − sin x is up there, that is the derivative of sin x + cos x, so take t = sin x + cos x and write sin 2x through the first square. If cos x + sin x is up there, that is the derivative of sin x − cos x, so take t = sin x − cos x and use the second square. That is the only decision in the question.

quickChecks.q: Which substitution would you take for an integral where cos x − sin x sits in the numerator and 1 + sin 2x in the denominator?
steps: 1. 1 + sin 2x = (sin x + cos x)².
2. d/dx (sin x + cos x) = cos x − sin x, which is exactly the numerator.
3. So t = sin x + cos x, dt = (cos x − sin x) dx.
quickChecks.answer: t = sin x + cos x, turning the integral into ∫ dt/t².

quickChecks.q: Integrate ln x + 1 using the classical form.
steps: 1. Take f(x) = ln x, so f'(x) = 1/x.
2. Then x·f'(x) = 1, and f(x) + x·f'(x) = ln x + 1.
3. The classical form integrates to x·f(x).

quickChecks.q: If cos x + sin x is in the numerator, which of 1 + sin 2x or 1 − sin 2x should you write as a perfect square, and why?
steps: 1. cos x + sin x is the derivative of sin x − cos x.
2. And (sin x − cos x)² = 1 − sin 2x.
3. So write 1 − sin 2x as that square and take t = sin x − cos x.
quickChecks.answer: 1 − sin 2x = (sin x − cos x)², with t = sin x − cos x.

concepts.title: Substitution: change the limits to match the new variable
concepts.oneLine: Whatever sits inside the d( ) owns the limits — the moment you turn d(ln x) into (1/x)dx, the limits must become limits of x.
notes: Before we enter the hardcore part of definite integration, one small thing has to be settled. Look at what is written inside the d( ). If the integral has d(ln x), then those limits written on the integral are the limits of ln x — not of x.

Now you do what you always do: you write d(ln x) as (1/x) dx, because the derivative of ln x is 1/x. Fine. But the variable has changed. The second you write dx, the limits must become the limits of x.

So if ln x was running from 0 to 1, then x runs from e⁰ to e¹, that is from 1 to e. Same story with d(sin x). Write it as cos x dx, and limits that belonged to sin x, say 0 to 1, now belong to x, so they become 0 to 90°.
That is the whole caution. In indefinite integration nobody asks you this, you just substitute and come back. Here the limits are sitting on the integral, so they have to travel with the variable.

quickChecks.q: An integral in d(ln x) has limits 1 to 2. You write it in dx form. New limits?
steps: 1. ln x = 1 gives x = e.
2. ln x = 2 gives x = e².

quickChecks.q: An integral in dx has x from 0 to 30°. You want to write it in d(sin x) form. What are the limits now?
steps: 1. Now the variable is sin x, so you need values of sin x.

quickChecks.q: An integral is written with d(x²) and limits 0 to 9. Convert to dx limits.
steps: 1. The limits belong to x², so x² goes from 0 to 9.
2. x² = 0 gives x = 0.
3. x² = 9 gives x = 3 (taking the positive value).

concepts.title: When a substitution hides a discontinuity
concepts.oneLine: A substitution is legal only if the new variable stays finite between the limits — wherever it blows up, break the integral there.
notes: Till now substitution meant one job: change the variable, change the limits. Here is the one place where that is not enough.

When you replace x by t, you must look at the function t(x) itself, not only at the new integrand. If t blows up at some point sitting between the old limits, that point has to become a break point. Otherwise your two limits pretend the journey of t was smooth, when it actually ran off to infinity and came back from the other side.
In the first example t = 1/x is fine to write, but it is discontinuous at x = 0 — and 0 sits right inside −1 to 1. In the second, t = tan x dies at π/2, which sits right inside 0 to π.

Nobody will feel the need to break anything by staring at 1 + t², because 1 + t² is defined for every t. The warning never comes from the new integrand. It comes from the substitution. That is the whole constraint of this topic.

quickChecks.q: You want to use t = 1/x in ∫ from 1 to 2 of dx/(1+x²). Is a break needed? Give the value.
steps: 1. The only bad point of t = 1/x is x = 0, and 0 is not inside 1 to 2.
2. So no break is needed. dx/(1+x²) = −dt/(1+t²), with t going from 1 to ½.
3. Value = −∫ from 1 to ½ of dt/(1+t²) = ∫ from ½ to 1 of dt/(1+t²) = π/4 − tan⁻¹(½).
quickChecks.answer: No break needed; the value is π/4 − tan⁻¹(½), which is the same as tan⁻¹2 − π/4.

quickChecks.q: Evaluate ∫ from 0 to π of dx/(1 + 2sin²x) by putting t = tan x.
steps: 1. Multiply numerator and denominator by sec²x: the numerator becomes dt and the denominator becomes sec²x + 2tan²x = 1 + 3t². So the integral is dt/(1+3t²).
2. t = tan x blows up at π/2, which lies inside 0 to π — so break there.
4. π/2 to π gives t from −∞ to 0, which gives the same π/(2√3).
quickChecks.answer: π/√3. Copying the limits as t = 0 to t = 0 would have given 0, which is impossible for a positive function.

quickChecks.q: For ∫ from −2 to 2 of dx/(1+x²) done by t = 1/x, where do you break and what is the value?
steps: 1. t = 1/x becomes infinite at x = 0, which is inside −2 to 2, so break at x = 0.
2. On 0 to 2, t runs from ∞ to ½, giving ∫ from ½ to ∞ of dt/(1+t²) = π/2 − tan⁻¹(½) = tan⁻¹2.
3. On −2 to 0, t runs from −½ to −∞, giving the same tan⁻¹2.
4. Add: 2tan⁻¹2, which matches the direct answer [tan⁻¹x] from −2 to 2.
quickChecks.answer: Break at x = 0; the value is 2tan⁻¹2.

concepts.title: Properties 1 and 2: change of variable and swapping the limits
concepts.oneLine: Renaming the variable changes nothing in a definite integral, and flipping the limits only flips the sign — which lets you glue neighbouring integrals into one.
notes: Start with the first one. The variable inside a definite integral is just a name — change it and the value does not change. Integrate x⁴ from 0 to 3, or t⁴ from 0 to 3, or u⁴ from 0 to 3: all three give you exactly the same number.

The logic is simple. Once you put the limits in, the variable is gone and only a number is left. So x, t, u are three names for the same dummy. This is why you may freely rename the variable while substituting.

The second one is even easier. Interchange the upper and the lower limit and the integral only picks up a minus sign. Think of upper minus lower: swap them and that difference flips in sign, so the whole value flips.

This second property is not just decoration — it is how you merge integrals. If a minus sign is sitting outside an integral, use the minus to turn the limits around, and suddenly the pieces sit end to end and become one integral.

quickChecks.q: Given ∫₂⁵ x dx = 10.5, what is ∫₅² x dx?
steps: 1. The limits are interchanged, so by Property 2 only the sign changes.
2. ∫₅² x dx = −∫₂⁵ x dx = −10.5.

quickChecks.q: Is ∫₁³ t³ dt the same as ∫₁³ x³ dx?
steps: 1. Same function, same limits 1 and 3; only the dummy letter differs.
2. Change of variable does not affect the value, so they are equal (both equal 20).

quickChecks.q: Write ∫₀¹ x² dx − ∫₃¹ x² dx as a single definite integral and evaluate it.
steps: 1. Use the minus to turn the limits: −∫₃¹ x² dx = ∫₁³ x² dx.
2. Now you have ∫₀¹ x² dx + ∫₁³ x² dx, and the pieces meet at x = 1 with x² continuous.
3. So the sum is ∫₀³ x² dx = [x³/3]₀³ = 27/3 = 9.

concepts.title: Property 3: split at any real number, even outside the interval
concepts.oneLine: ∫ₐᵇ f dx = ∫ₐᶜ f dx + ∫ᶜᵇ f dx for every real c — the breaking point does not have to sit inside [a, b].
notes: Property 3 says ∫ₐᵇ f dx = ∫ₐᶜ f dx + ∫ᶜᵇ f dx. Read the condition carefully: c is any real number. Nobody said c has to lie between a and b.

So if you are going from 1 to 5, the honest break is at some point inside, like 3. But you are also allowed to go from 1 to −3 first and then from −3 to 5. The answer is the same. Going from 10 to 50 through 0 is allowed too, and no one can stop you.

Why does it still work? Because the backward piece carries a minus sign with it (that is Property 2), and the extra distance you travelled cancels itself out. The two pieces always add back to the original integral.

Now the practical side. In a real question you break where the definition of the function changes — where a modulus opens, where a greatest integer jumps. With |x sin πx²| on [−2, 2] you break at every point where x sin πx² changes sign, and on each piece the mod opens with one fixed sign. The freedom of a c outside the interval is good to know conceptually; you will rarely need it.

quickChecks.q: Write ∫₂⁷ f(x) dx as a sum of two integrals using c = −5.
steps: 1. Property 3 with c = −5, which is outside [2, 7]: ∫₂⁷ f dx = ∫₂⁻⁵ f dx + ∫₋₅⁷ f dx.
2. Legal, because c can be any real number.
quickChecks.answer: ∫₂⁷ f(x) dx = ∫₂⁻⁵ f(x) dx + ∫₋₅⁷ f(x) dx

quickChecks.q: Is ∫₀¹⁰ f dx = ∫₀²⁰ f dx + ∫₂₀¹⁰ f dx correct?
steps: 1. Here c = 20, which sits outside [0, 10]. Property 3 still allows it.
2. Check it: ∫₂₀¹⁰ f dx = −∫₁₀²⁰ f dx by swapping the limits.
3. So the right side is ∫₀²⁰ f dx − ∫₁₀²⁰ f dx = ∫₀¹⁰ f dx.

quickChecks.q: Where do you break ∫₀^√2 |x sin πx²| dx, and how does the mod open on each piece?
steps: 1. Inside the mod, x ≥ 0 throughout, so only sin πx² can change sign.
2. sin πx² = 0 gives x² = 1 in (0, √2), so x = 1 is the only break point.
3. On [0, 1]: x² lies in [0, 1], so sin πx² ≥ 0 and the mod just drops.
4. On [1, √2]: x² lies in [1, 2], so sin πx² ≤ 0 and the mod flips the sign.
quickChecks.answer: Break at x = 1: ∫₀^√2 |x sin πx²| dx = ∫₀¹ x sin πx² dx − ∫₁^√2 x sin πx² dx

concepts.title: The King rule
concepts.quote: Rules 4, 5 and 6 are the King, the Queen and the Jack — and this trio is the reason the whole chapter of definite integration exists. Today only the King. Learn him properly and the hardcore questions stop being hardcore.
concepts.oneLine: King rule: in a definite integral from a to b you may replace x by (a + b − x) and the value does not change.
notes: Look at the integral from a to b of f(x) dx. The King says: wherever you see x inside the function, write (upper limit + lower limit − x) instead. Keep the same limits, keep the dx, change nothing else — and the value of the definite integral stays exactly the same.

So ∫ from a to b of f(x) dx equals ∫ from a to b of f(a + b − x) dx. The commonest version is with lower limit 0: then a + b − x becomes just a − x. Both forms are the same rule; remember the general one and the rest follows.

Why give this one so much time? Because every hardcore definite-integration question is built on the King. Jack and Queen come after, and all three deliberately do not come in one shot — do that and you learn nothing. One at a time, starting here.
The next one shows the King at work on the most common question of this type.

quickChecks.q: Apply the King rule to ∫ from 0 to 1 of f(x) dx.
steps: 1. Upper limit + lower limit = 1 + 0 = 1.
2. Replace x by 1 − x, keep the limits 0 and 1.
quickChecks.answer: ∫ from 0 to 1 of f(1 − x) dx

quickChecks.q: Apply the King rule to ∫ from 2 to 5 of f(x) dx.
steps: 1. Upper limit + lower limit = 5 + 2 = 7.
2. Replace x by 7 − x, limits stay 2 and 5.
quickChecks.answer: ∫ from 2 to 5 of f(7 − x) dx

quickChecks.q: Use the King rule on ∫ from 0 to π/2 of sin x dx and check that the value does not change.
steps: 1. Upper limit + lower limit = π/2 + 0 = π/2.
2. Replace x by π/2 − x: the integral becomes ∫ from 0 to π/2 of sin(π/2 − x) dx = ∫ from 0 to π/2 of cos x dx.
3. Original: ∫ from 0 to π/2 of sin x dx = [−cos x] from 0 to π/2 = 0 − (−1) = 1.
4. New form: ∫ from 0 to π/2 of cos x dx = [sin x] from 0 to π/2 = 1 − 0 = 1.
quickChecks.answer: Both equal 1 — the King leaves the value unchanged.

concepts.title: Laila–Majnu: the most common King-rule question
concepts.quote: There is one question in definite integration that comes back again and again, and you can finish it in two lines without integrating anything. I call it the Laila–Majnu question, and once you see the pattern you will never solve it the long way again.
concepts.oneLine: If the integrand is f(x)/(f(x) + f(a+b−x)) from a to b, add the King version to the original, the numerator becomes 1, and the answer is simply (b − a)/2.
notes: Look at I = ∫ from a to b of f(x)/(f(x) + f(a+b−x)) dx. The numerator is one person, and sitting next to it in the denominator is the other person. Call the numerator Laila and its partner Majnu.

Now put the King rule: replace x by a + b − x everywhere. The limits stay a to b, dx stays dx. On top, f(x) becomes f(a+b−x) — Laila has turned into Majnu. Below, f(a+b−x) becomes f(a + b − (a+b−x)) = f(x), so the denominator is f(a+b−x) + f(x) — the same two people, only the order changed.

Because the denominator is untouched, you can add the original and the King version straight away: 2I = ∫ from a to b of [f(x) + f(a+b−x)]/[f(x) + f(a+b−x)] dx = ∫ from a to b of 1 dx = b − a. So I = (b − a)/2, which is just (upper limit − lower limit)/2.

That is the whole trick. You never touch the function. The moment you check that the numerator and its King partner are the two terms sitting in the denominator, write the answer. In any Laila–Majnu story, the answer is (b − a)/2.

quickChecks.q: Evaluate ∫ from 0 to π/2 of cos x/(cos x + sin x) dx.
steps: 1. Partner of x is π/2 − x, and cos(π/2 − x) = sin x, so cos and sin swap on top while the denominator stays cos + sin.
2. Laila–Majnu, so answer = (upper − lower)/2 = (π/2 − 0)/2.

quickChecks.q: Evaluate ∫ from 1 to 3 of x²/(x² + (4 − x)²) dx.
steps: 1. Here a + b = 1 + 3 = 4, so the partner is 4 − x. The denominator is exactly f(x) + f(4−x) with f(x) = x².
2. Pattern confirmed, so answer = (3 − 1)/2.

quickChecks.q: Evaluate ∫ from 0 to π/2 of √(tan x)/(√(tan x) + √(cot x)) dx.
steps: 1. Put King: √(tan x) becomes √(cot x) and √(cot x) becomes √(tan x). Denominator unchanged.
2. Add both: 2I = ∫ from 0 to π/2 of 1 dx = π/2, so I = π/4.

concepts.title: King rule where indefinite integration is impossible
concepts.oneLine: Even when the integrand has no antiderivative at all, if the denominator is f(x) + f(a+b−x) the King rule hands you (b−a)/2.
notes: Look at the power. 2026 on top, 2026 below. There is no substitution, no by-parts, no identity that will give you the indefinite integral of cos²⁰²⁶x. It simply does not exist in any form you can write.

So the indefinite integration is impossible, but the definite integration is finished in two lines — thanks to the King rule. That is the beauty of this chapter. You never needed the antiderivative; you only needed the structure.

The structure is the same Laila–Majnu structure from the last part. Numerator f(x), denominator f(x) + f(a+b−x). The moment you see it, the power is irrelevant. Stop reading the function and start reading the structure.

Four such questions are worth attempting before reading on. The answer in every one is the same: upper limit minus lower limit, divided by 2. The answer was never the point — knowing why you wrote it is.

quickChecks.q: Evaluate ∫₀^(π/2) sin²⁰²⁶x / (sin²⁰²⁶x + cos²⁰²⁶x) dx
steps: 1. f(x) = sin²⁰²⁶x, a = 0, b = π/2, so a + b − x = π/2 − x.
2. f(π/2 − x) = cos²⁰²⁶x — the other term. Structure confirmed.

quickChecks.q: Evaluate ∫₀^(π/2) √(tan x) / (√(tan x) + √(cot x)) dx
steps: 1. f(x) = √(tan x), a = 0, b = π/2, so a + b − x = π/2 − x.
2. f(π/2 − x) = √(tan(π/2 − x)) = √(cot x) — exactly the second term.

quickChecks.q: For any function f, evaluate ∫₁^3 f(x) / (f(x) + f(4 − x)) dx
steps: 1. Here a = 1, b = 3, so a + b − x = 4 − x — which is what the denominator already uses.
2. Pure Laila–Majnu, no need to know f at all.

concepts.title: Discussion of the Laila–Majnu practice set
concepts.oneLine: When f(x) and its partner f(a+b−x) add up to 1, the definite integral is just (upper − lower)/2 — even when the partner is hidden inside something like (6 − x)².
notes: In this practice set every question had the same skeleton. Add the two limits, call that sum a + b, and the partner of x is a + b − x. Apply King rule, add the two integrals, and the whole mess cancels to 1.
The moment f(x) + f(a+b−x) = 1, you can write the answer as (upper − lower)/2 and move on. That is the only condition. Check it once by adding the pair, nothing more.

The one that confused people had (6 − x)² printed in the denominator. Limits were 2 and 4, so a + b = 6, and 6 − x was already sitting there looking at you. Once you spot that, the question is over in one line.
The solutions may show the full working for this one and the next one, but solving it that way is a waste of your time. Train your eye to see the pairing, not your hand to grind the integral.

quickChecks.q: Evaluate the integral of x²/(x² + (6 − x)²) from x = 1 to x = 5.
steps: 1. 1 + 5 = 6, so the partner is 6 − x — same structure as class.
3. So the answer is (5 − 1)/2 = 2.

quickChecks.q: Evaluate the integral of (10 − x)²/(x² + (10 − x)²) from x = 3 to x = 7.
steps: 1. 3 + 7 = 10, so the partner is 10 − x. The disguise is that the numerator is the partner's square this time, not x².
3. Answer is (7 − 3)/2 = 2.

quickChecks.q: Evaluate the integral of √x/(√x + √(6 − x)) from x = 2 to x = 4.
steps: 1. 2 + 4 = 6, partner is 6 − x, and √(6 − x) is already in the denominator.
3. Answer is (4 − 2)/2 = 1.

concepts.title: King rule for removal of useless terms
concepts.oneLine: If f(x) = f(a − x), then adding the King version to ∫₀ᵃ x·f(x) dx kills the x and leaves I = (a/2)∫₀ᵃ f(x) dx.
notes: This is my second standard law of definite integration: removal of useless terms. Learn the first two laws properly and the rest of the chapter follows.

Take I = ∫₀ᵃ x·f(x) dx, and you are also given f(x) = f(a − x). Apply King rule: the limits stay 0 to a, and every x becomes a − x. So I = ∫₀ᵃ (a − x)·f(a − x) dx, and because of the given condition f(a − x) is just f(x). So I = ∫₀ᵃ (a − x)·f(x) dx.

Now do the same thing as in the Laila–Majnu set: add the two forms. Same limits, so add the functions. 2I = ∫₀ᵃ [x + (a − x)]·f(x) dx. Look at the bracket: x + a − x = a. The useless x has disappeared, and that is the whole point of this law. So 2I = a∫₀ᵃ f(x) dx.

After this, no new theory is needed. What happens next depends entirely on which f(x) the question gives you — that integral you solve with your old knowledge. Don't ask what is next; the question answers that. Your job is only to remove the useless term.

quickChecks.q: Evaluate ∫₀^π x sin x dx.
steps: 1. Here a = π and f(x) = sin x. Check the condition: sin(π − x) = sin x, so f(x) = f(a − x). ✓
2. Use the law: I = (π/2)∫₀^π sin x dx.
3. ∫₀^π sin x dx = [−cos x]₀^π = −cos π + cos 0 = 1 + 1 = 2.

quickChecks.q: Evaluate ∫₀² x²(2 − x) dx using this law.
steps: 1. Write it as ∫₀² x·f(x) dx with f(x) = x(2 − x) and a = 2.
3. So I = (2/2)∫₀² x(2 − x) dx = ∫₀² (2x − x²) dx.

quickChecks.q: It is given that f(x) = f(4 − x) and ∫₀⁴ f(x) dx = 10. Find ∫₀⁴ x·f(x) dx.
steps: 1. The condition matches with a = 4.

concepts.title: Removing x from ∫₀^π x sin x/(1 + cos²x) dx
concepts.oneLine: King rule turns ∫₀^π x sin x/(1 + cos²x) dx into (π/2)∫₀^π sin x/(1 + cos²x) dx, and then t = cos x finishes it to π²/4.
notes: Look at the question first: ∫₀^π x sin x/(1 + cos²x) dx. Forget the x for a second. What is left is sin x/(1 + cos²x), and on top you have sin x, which is exactly what the derivative of cos x gives you. So without the x this is a plain substitution question.
That x is the only thing standing between you and an easy integral — so use King only to delete it. Write I = ∫₀^π x sin x/(1 + cos²x) dx, then replace x by π − x everywhere.

Check the leftover part. sin(π − x) = sin x, and cos(π − x) = −cos x, but it is squared, so cos²(π − x) = cos²x. Nothing changes. Only the x in front becomes π − x. So I = ∫₀^π (π − x) sin x/(1 + cos²x) dx.

Now add the two forms. The x and the −x kill each other and you get 2I = π∫₀^π sin x/(1 + cos²x) dx, that is I = (π/2)∫₀^π sin x/(1 + cos²x) dx. After this step King has no role left — put t = cos x and it is ordinary integration. If x had not disappeared, this question would have been very hard, maybe not doable at all by hand.

quickChecks.q: Evaluate ∫₀^π x sin x dx.
steps: 1. I = ∫₀^π x sin x dx; apply King: I = ∫₀^π (π − x) sin x dx.
2. Add: 2I = π∫₀^π sin x dx.
3. ∫₀^π sin x dx = [−cos x]₀^π = 1 + 1 = 2, so 2I = 2π.

quickChecks.q: Evaluate ∫₀^π x cos²x dx.
steps: 1. King gives I = ∫₀^π (π − x) cos²x dx, since cos²(π − x) = cos²x.
2. Add: 2I = π∫₀^π cos²x dx.
3. ∫₀^π cos²x dx = ∫₀^π (1 + cos 2x)/2 dx = π/2 + 0 = π/2.
4. So 2I = π²/2, giving I = π²/4.

quickChecks.q: Evaluate ∫₀^π x sin x cos²x dx.
steps: 1. The leftover sin x cos²x is unchanged under x → π − x (sin stays, cos is squared), so King gives 2I = π∫₀^π sin x cos²x dx.
2. Put t = cos x, dt = −sin x dx; limits 1 to −1, and the minus flips them: ∫₋₁^1 t² dt.
4. So 2I = 2π/3 and I = π/3.

concepts.title: Killing the 1 + aˣ denominator
concepts.oneLine: On symmetric limits the King rule turns aˣ into a⁻ˣ, and adding the two integrals kills the whole 1 + aˣ denominator, leaving only ∫cos²x dx.
notes: Look at ∫ cos²x/(1 + aˣ) dx on limits −π to π. Alone, cos²x is nothing — you write (1 + cos2x)/2 and you are done in one step. But nobody will give you that in the paper.
They put aˣ downstairs. Now indefinite integration is finished — there is no antiderivative for this. That aˣ is not there to be integrated, it is there to be killed.

King rule: replace x by (lower limit + upper limit − x). Here that is −π + π − x = −x. So aˣ becomes a⁻ˣ, and cos²x does not care at all, because cos²(−x) = cos²x. Write a⁻ˣ as 1/aˣ, take LCM, and the denominator becomes (1 + aˣ)/aˣ — so the new integrand is aˣ·cos²x/(1 + aˣ).
Now add the original I and the new I. On top you get 1 + aˣ, below you have 1 + aˣ. The entire thing that was blocking you cancels, and 2I = ∫cos²x dx. From there it is pure school-level work.

quickChecks.q: Evaluate ∫ from −1 to 1 of x²/(1 + 5ˣ) dx.
steps: 1. Limits are −1 to 1, so a + b − x = −x.

quickChecks.q: Evaluate ∫ from −π/2 to π/2 of sin²x/(1 + eˣ) dx.
steps: 1. Here a + b − x = −x again, and sin²(−x) = sin²x, so the numerator is safe.
2. Adding the two forms: 2I = ∫(−π/2 to π/2) sin²x dx.
3. sin²x = (1 − cos2x)/2, so 2I = ½[x − (sin2x)/2] from −π/2 to π/2 = ½(π/2 − (−π/2)) = π/2.
4. So I = π/4.

quickChecks.q: Evaluate ∫ from −2 to 2 of 1/(1 + 3ˣ) dx.
steps: 1. The numerator is just 1, which is even, so the same trick applies.

concepts.title: King rule first: the working strategy
concepts.oneLine: In any hardcore definite-integration question, apply the King rule first — replace x by a+b−x, keep the limits as they are — and let the change in the question decide your next step.
notes: King rule in one line: in place of x write a+b−x, do not touch the limits, and the value of the integral stays the same. That is the whole statement, nothing more.

The rule has two faces. One is the pairing idea, where the original and the King form add up to 1 and the answer simply becomes (upper − lower)/2. The other is the one where x itself disappears and the useless terms die. Both are the same rule seen from two sides.

But as a mathematician you must learn something simpler than a trick. First separate the two kinds of question. A fake definite question is just an indefinite integral with an upper and a lower limit stuck on it — you integrate, you substitute, done. A hardcore definite question is one that can only be cracked using the properties of definite integration. In any hardcore definite-integration question, put the King rule first, see what changes, and decide the next step from that change.

So the moment the indefinite click is not coming, or you can already see that the indefinite is not possible, stop staring at it. Apply King once. Either the variable dies, or the terms simplify, or you get a relation between I₁ and I₂ — and whichever of those happens is itself your instruction for step two.

quickChecks.q: Evaluate ∫ from −1 to 1 of dx/(1 + 2ˣ).
steps: 1. Indefinite is ugly, so it is a hardcore question — apply King with a + b = −1 + 1 = 0.
3. Add both forms: 1/(1 + 2ˣ) + 2ˣ/(1 + 2ˣ) = 1.
4. So 2I = ∫ from −1 to 1 of 1 dx = 2, giving I = 1.

quickChecks.q: Evaluate ∫ from 0 to π/2 of dx/(1 + √(tan x)).
steps: 1. Apply King with a + b = π/2, so tan x becomes cot x.
2. I = ∫ from 0 to π/2 of dx/(1 + √(cot x)) = ∫ from 0 to π/2 of √(tan x)/(1 + √(tan x)) dx.
3. Adding the two forms gives (1 + √(tan x))/(1 + √(tan x)) = 1.
4. So 2I = π/2, giving I = π/4.

quickChecks.q: Evaluate ∫ from −2 to 2 of dx/(1 + eˣ).
steps: 1. a + b = 0, so King replaces x by −x.
2. I = ∫ from −2 to 2 of dx/(1 + e⁻ˣ) = ∫ from −2 to 2 of eˣ/(1 + eˣ) dx.
3. The two forms add to 1, so 2I = ∫ from −2 to 2 of 1 dx = 4.
4. I = 2, which is also (upper − lower)/2 = 4/2.

concepts.title: Making x disappear with King rule
concepts.oneLine: If f(a−x) = f(x), then adding I to its King-rule image kills the x in front: ∫₀ᵃ x·f(x) dx = (a/2)·∫₀ᵃ f(x) dx.
notes: Look at I₁ = ∫₀² x·f(x) dx. The limits add up to 0 + 2 = 2, so the King rule says replace every x by 2 − x. The limits do not move.
Now check the inside. Here f(2 − x) comes back as f(x) itself — that is exactly what cos²θ + sin²θ = 1 was doing for us. So only the x in front actually changes: I₁ = ∫₀² (2 − x)·f(x) dx.
Add the two forms of I₁. On the left that gives 2I₁, and on the right x·f(x) + (2 − x)·f(x) = 2·f(x) — the x is gone. So 2I₁ = 2∫₀² f(x) dx, which means I₁ = ∫₀² f(x) dx.

That is the whole move. An x·f(x) integral becomes a plain f(x) integral, and the two integrals are now tied by one clean relation. Nothing was integrated, nothing was substituted — the integral was only added to its own mirror image.

quickChecks.q: Find ∫₀^π x·sin x dx.
steps: 1. Here a = 0, b = π, so a + b = π, and f(x) = sin x.
2. Check the inside: sin(π − x) = sin x, so f(π − x) = f(x). The trick applies.
3. So ∫₀^π x·sin x dx = (π/2)∫₀^π sin x dx.

quickChecks.q: Find ∫₀^π x·sin²x dx.
steps: 1. a + b = π and f(x) = sin²x. Check: sin²(π − x) = sin²x, so f(π − x) = f(x).
2. So the integral = (π/2)∫₀^π sin²x dx.
3. ∫₀^π sin²x dx = ∫₀^π (1 − cos 2x)/2 dx = ½[x − (sin 2x)/2]₀^π = ½(π) = π/2.
4. Answer = (π/2)(π/2).

quickChecks.q: Find ∫₀¹ x·g(x) dx where g(x) = x(1 − x).
steps: 1. a + b = 1. Check the inside: g(1 − x) = (1 − x)(1 − (1 − x)) = (1 − x)x = g(x). It passes.
2. So ∫₀¹ x·g(x) dx = (1/2)∫₀¹ x(1 − x) dx.
3. ∫₀¹ (x − x²) dx = ½ − ⅓ = 1/6.
4. Answer = (1/2)(1/6) = 1/12. (Check directly: ∫₀¹ (x² − x³) dx = ⅓ − ¼ = 1/12 ✓)

concepts.title: Answer in terms of ∫ sin x / x: King plus substitution
concepts.oneLine: When King rule hands the same question back, substitute t = 2x, split 1/(t(π−t)) by partial fractions, and both halves turn into the same ∫₀^π sin x/x — so the answer is (2/π)∫₀^π sin x/x dx.
notes: The question: I = ∫₀^{π/2} (sin x · cos x)/(x(π/2 − x)) dx, and the answer has to be written in terms of ∫₀^π (sin x)/x dx. So the goal here is not a number but a shape.

Put King in a definite integral first. Replace x by π/2 − x: sin x becomes cos x, cos x becomes sin x, and x(π/2 − x) stays exactly the same. The question has not changed at all. King giving you back the same question is not a failure — it means the symmetry is already used up, so now think substitution.

The top sin x · cos x is just (sin 2x)/2. Take LCM below and x(π/2 − x) becomes x(π − 2x)/2. The two halves cancel, and now every x sits inside a 2x. So put t = 2x — that is the only way the answer will come out in a single angle. Limits 0 and π/2 become 0 and π, x = t/2, dx = dt/2, and the 2s cancel once more: I = ∫₀^π sin t/(t(π − t)) dt.

King still does nothing to this. So split the bottom: 1/(t(π − t)) = (1/π)(1/t + 1/(π − t)). Now both pieces are the same integral — King on the second one turns sin t/(π − t) into sin t/t. Two copies of ∫₀^π sin t/t, divided by π, and I = (2/π)∫₀^π sin x/x dx.

quickChecks.q: Show that ∫₀^π (sin x)/(π − x) dx = ∫₀^π (sin x)/x dx.
steps: 1. Apply King on 0 to π: replace x by π − x.
2. Top: sin(π − x) = sin x.
3. Bottom: π − (π − x) = x.
4. So the integral becomes ∫₀^π (sin x)/x dx.
quickChecks.answer: They are equal — each is ∫₀^π (sin x)/x dx.

quickChecks.q: Split 1/(x(π − x)) into partial fractions.
steps: 1. Write it as A/x + B/(π − x).
2. Take LCM: [A(π − x) + Bx]/(x(π − x)) = 1/(x(π − x)).
3. Compare: A(π − x) + Bx = 1. Put x = 0 → Aπ = 1 → A = 1/π. Put x = π → Bπ = 1 → B = 1/π.

quickChecks.q: Write I = ∫₀^{π/2} (2 sin x · cos x)/(x(π/2 − x)) dx in terms of ∫₀^π (sin x)/x dx.
steps: 1. 2 sin x cos x = sin 2x, and x(π/2 − x) = x(π − 2x)/2, so I = 2∫₀^{π/2} sin 2x/(x(π − 2x)) dx.
2. Put t = 2x: dx = dt/2, limits 0 to π, and the integral becomes 2∫₀^π sin t/(t(π − t)) dt.
3. Split: 1/(t(π − t)) = (1/π)(1/t + 1/(π − t)), and by King both pieces equal ∫₀^π (sin t)/t dt.
4. So I = 2 × (2/π)∫₀^π (sin t)/t dt.

concepts.title: Two classic log integrals
concepts.quote: This one integral has come in your board paper almost ten times, and it started life as an IIT question. Nobody who knows the trick loses these marks — and the trick is just King rule.
concepts.oneLine: ∫₀^{π/4} ln(1+tan x)dx = (π/8)ln2 by King rule, and ∫₀^1 ln(1+x)/(1+x²)dx becomes the same integral the moment you put x = tan θ.
notes: Look at ∫₀^{π/4} ln(1+tan x)dx and your hand itches to integrate ln(1+tan x). Don't. The limits are 0 to π/4, so you put King rule and stop being clever.

King rule replaces x by π/4 − x. Do that small side work: 1 + tan(π/4 − x) = 1 + (1 − tan x)/(1 + tan x), take LCM, the numerator becomes 1 + tan x + 1 − tan x = 2. So the whole thing is 2/(1 + tan x).

Now add the original and the King version. ln m + ln n = ln(mn), the product is (1 + tan x) · 2/(1 + tan x), and 1 + tan x cancels. You are left with a constant: 2I = ∫₀^{π/4} ln2 dx = (π/4)ln2, so I = (π/8)ln2.

The second question, ∫₀^1 ln(1+x)/(1+x²)dx, has the same answer — and that is the clue. Whenever you see 1 + x² downstairs with limits 0 to 1, put x = tan θ: dx = sec²θ dθ, the sec²θ cancels, and 0 to 1 becomes 0 to π/4. You land exactly on the first integral.

quickChecks.q: Simplify 1 + tan(π/4 − x).
steps: 1. tan(π/4 − x) = (1 − tan x)/(1 + tan x).
2. Add 1 with LCM 1 + tan x: numerator = (1 + tan x) + (1 − tan x) = 2.

quickChecks.q: Find ∫₀^{π/4} ln(2/(1 + tan x)) dx.
steps: 1. Split it: ∫₀^{π/4} ln2 dx − ∫₀^{π/4} ln(1 + tan x) dx.
2. First piece = (π/4)ln2. Second piece = (π/8)ln2.

quickChecks.q: In ∫₀^1 ln(1 + x)/(1 + x²) dx you put x = tan θ. What do the limits become, and what does dx/(1 + x²) turn into?
steps: 1. x = 0 gives tan θ = 0, so θ = 0. x = 1 gives tan θ = 1, so θ = π/4.
2. dx = sec²θ dθ and 1 + x² = 1 + tan²θ = sec²θ, so the sec²θ cancels.
quickChecks.answer: Limits 0 to π/4, and dx/(1 + x²) = dθ

concepts.title: A log-ratio integral that comes out zero
concepts.oneLine: When the limits add up to π/2 and the lecture swaps cos and sin, King rule turns the two logs into ln 1, so ∫ from π/8 to 3π/8 of ln((4+3cos x)/(4+3sin x)) dx is 0.
notes: Before you touch anything, add the limits. π/8 + 3π/8 = 4π/8 = π/2. That is 90°, and the moment you see 90° with a cos and a sin sitting inside, you know what is coming.

Apply King rule: replace x by (a + b − x), which here is (π/2 − x). Now cos(π/2 − x) becomes sin x, and sin(π/2 − x) becomes cos x. So the numerator and the denominator simply trade places — the same integral comes back, just flipped upside down inside the log.

Now add the original and the new form. Two logs added become the log of their product, and that product is ((4+3cos x)/(4+3sin x)) × ((4+3sin x)/(4+3cos x)) = 1. So 2I = ∫ ln 1 dx = 0, which gives I = 0.
Notice that nothing was expanded, nothing substituted, not a single log integrated. The limits did all the work. That is the whole point of King rule in a definite integral.

quickChecks.q: Evaluate ∫ from π/8 to 3π/8 of ln((2 + 5sin x)/(2 + 5cos x)) dx.
steps: 1. a + b = π/8 + 3π/8 = π/2, so King rule will swap sin and cos.
2. By King rule, I = ∫ from π/8 to 3π/8 of ln((2 + 5cos x)/(2 + 5sin x)) dx.
3. Add both forms: 2I = ∫ ln of the product = ∫ ln 1 dx = 0.

quickChecks.q: Evaluate ∫ from 0 to π/2 of ln(tan x) dx.
steps: 2. By King rule, I = ∫ from 0 to π/2 of ln(tan(π/2 − x)) dx = ∫ from 0 to π/2 of ln(cot x) dx.
3. Add: 2I = ∫ ln(tan x · cot x) dx = ∫ ln 1 dx = 0, so I = 0.

quickChecks.q: Evaluate ∫ from π/6 to π/3 of ln((1 + tan x)/(1 + cot x)) dx.
steps: 1. a + b = π/6 + π/3 = π/2, so tan and cot will swap.
2. By King rule, I = ∫ from π/6 to π/3 of ln((1 + cot x)/(1 + tan x)) dx.
3. Add the two forms: 2I = ∫ ln 1 dx = 0, so I = 0.

concepts.title: √(sin 2θ) problem: King rule, then substitution
concepts.oneLine: King rule on ∫₀^(π/2) √(sin 2θ) sin θ dθ gives 2I = ∫₀^(π/2) √(sin 2θ)(sin θ + cos θ)dθ, then sin 2θ = 1 − (sin θ − cos θ)² with t = sin θ − cos θ turns it into ∫₋₁¹ √(1 − t²)dt = π/2, so I = π/4.
notes: Take I₁ = ∫₀^(π/2) √(sin 2θ) sin θ dθ. There is no harm in trying the King rule: if it gives you nothing, you find out in one line. So replace θ by 90° − θ. Then 2θ becomes 180° − 2θ, and sin(180° − 2θ) = sin 2θ, so the root is completely untouched. Only sin θ changes, into cos θ.

Add the old form and the new form. The √(sin 2θ) is common, so 2I₁ = ∫₀^(π/2) √(sin 2θ)(sin θ + cos θ)dθ. Now look at what King has handed you: a bracket (sin θ + cos θ) standing outside the root. That is a derivative waiting to be used.

From the indefinite class we had two ways to write sin 2θ: (sin θ + cos θ)² − 1, and 1 − (sin θ − cos θ)². Which one you pick is decided by the derivative sitting outside, not by taste. Here the outside factor is (sin θ + cos θ), which is the derivative of (sin θ − cos θ). So take sin 2θ = 1 − (sin θ − cos θ)² and put t = sin θ − cos θ, dt = (cos θ + sin θ)dθ.

Change the limits, because we are in a definite integral now. θ = 0 gives t = 0 − 1 = −1; θ = 90° gives t = 1 − 0 = 1. So 2I₁ = ∫₋₁¹ √(1 − t²)dt, the standard √(a² − x²) form with a = 1. Put the limits in and you get π/2, so I₁ = π/4.

quickChecks.q: Evaluate ∫₀^(π/2) √(sin 2θ) · cos θ dθ.
steps: 1. Apply King: θ → 90° − θ. The root is unchanged and cos θ becomes sin θ.
2. So this integral equals ∫₀^(π/2) √(sin 2θ) sin θ dθ, which is the I₁ we just did.
3. Hence its value is the same, π/4.

quickChecks.q: Evaluate ∫₀¹ √(1 − t²)dt using the standard form.
steps: 1. Use ∫√(a² − x²)dx = (x/2)√(a² − x²) + (a²/2)sin⁻¹(x/a) with a = 1.
2. Antiderivative: (t/2)√(1 − t²) + ½ sin⁻¹t.
4. Value = π/4.

quickChecks.q: Evaluate ∫₀^(π/2) (sin θ − cos θ)√(1 + sin 2θ) dθ.
steps: 1. Here 1 + sin 2θ = (sin θ + cos θ)², and sin θ + cos θ ≥ 0 on 0 to 90°, so the root is (sin θ + cos θ).
2. Integrand = (sin θ − cos θ)(sin θ + cos θ) = sin²θ − cos²θ = −cos 2θ.

concepts.title: Jack rule: odd and even functions over −a to a
concepts.oneLine: Between −a and +a, an odd function integrates to 0 and an even function to twice its 0-to-a integral — that is Jack rule, and it falls straight out of King.
notes: After King, the next rule is its own son. Take I = ∫ from −a to +a of f(x)dx. King says replace x by (upper limit + lower limit − x), which here is a + (−a) − x, that is simply −x. So I is also equal to ∫ from −a to +a of f(−x)dx.

Now assume f(x) is an odd function, so f(−x) = −f(x). Add the two forms of I, exactly the way we always add after applying King: 2I = ∫ from −a to +a of [f(x) − f(x)]dx = ∫ from −a to +a of 0 dx = 0. So for any odd function in the world, its definite integral from −a to +a is 0.

The graph says the same thing. An odd function is symmetric about the origin — picture y = x³ — so whatever shape sits above the axis on the right sits exactly as deep below the axis on the left. Definite integration is the algebraic sum of area, so the positive area and the negative area cancel and you get 0. For an even function the graph is symmetric about the y-axis, the area from −a to 0 equals the area from 0 to a, so you integrate from 0 to a and double it.

Be clear about which half is the gift. In the odd case the answer is directly 0 — that is powerful. In the even case, frankly, nothing much happened: only the limit changed, the integration is still standing there waiting for you. A 0 as the lower limit is nicer to work with than a negative number, that is all you gained. And notice this topic has almost no integration in it — it is your odd-even work from the functions chapter, so revise that and these questions become free marks.

quickChecks.q: Evaluate ∫ from −π/4 to +π/4 of sin³x · cos²x dx.
steps: 1. Limits are −a to +a with a = π/4.
2. sin³(−x) = −sin³x (odd power of sin), cos²(−x) = cos²x.
3. So f(−x) = −f(x): odd function.
4. Jack rule gives 0.

quickChecks.q: Evaluate ∫ from −3 to +3 of x² dx.
steps: 1. f(−x) = (−x)² = x² = f(x), so the function is even.
2. Jack rule: integral = 2∫ from 0 to 3 of x² dx.

quickChecks.q: Evaluate ∫ from −1 to +1 of (eˣ − 1)/(eˣ + 1) dx.
steps: 1. Symmetric limits, a = 1.
2. f(−x) = (e⁻ˣ − 1)/(e⁻ˣ + 1); multiply top and bottom by eˣ to get (1 − eˣ)/(1 + eˣ).
3. That is −f(x), so the function is odd.
4. Integral = 0.

concepts.title: Jack rule on the practice set
concepts.oneLine: On every symmetric-limit integral, first split the integrand into odd and even parts, strike out the odd part, and rewrite the even part as 2∫₀^a — only then start integrating.
notes: Look at the first one. The integrand is an x³ type function on −a to a, so f(−x) = −f(x). Odd function, symmetric limits — the answer is 0 and you write it in one line.

The second one is even, so the Jack rule cannot kill it. Here it only drops the lower limit to 0 — and that is still a big help, because ∫₀^{π/2} is where all your standard results live. After that you use sin²x = (1 − cos2x)/2 like always.

The third and fourth ones are the real pattern of the paper: one messy integrand that is part odd, part even. Split it. The odd part vanishes between −1 and 1, and only the even part survives as 2∫₀^a. Remember the denominator too — x² + 2 and 1 + cos²x are both even, so the parity of each term is decided by its numerator.

And notice where the fourth one goes. The Jack rule kills one term, the King rule then kills the x in the term that is left, and only after that do you do the actual integration with a substitution. That is what a complete question looks like — three tools stacked in one problem.

quickChecks.q: Evaluate ∫ from −2 to 2 of (x⁵ + 3x²) dx.
steps: 1. x⁵ is an odd power, so that term gives 0 on −2 to 2.
2. 3x² is even, so it becomes 2∫₀² 3x² dx = 2[x³]₀² = 2(8) = 16.

quickChecks.q: Evaluate ∫ from −π/2 to π/2 of (x cos x + sin²x) dx.
steps: 1. x is odd, cos x is even, so x cos x is odd — that term is 0.
2. sin²x is even, so it becomes 2∫₀^{π/2} sin²x dx = ∫₀^{π/2}(1 − cos2x) dx = [x − (sin2x)/2]₀^{π/2} = π/2.

quickChecks.q: Reduce ∫ from −1 to 1 of (x⁷ − 4x⁴ + 5x)/(x² + 3) dx as far as the Jack rule allows.
steps: 1. x² + 3 is even, so parity comes from the numerator.
2. x⁷ and 5x are odd powers, so those terms are odd and integrate to 0 on −1 to 1.
3. Only −4x⁴ survives, and it is even: 2∫₀¹ (−4x⁴)/(x² + 3) dx = −8∫₀¹ x⁴/(x² + 3) dx.

concepts.title: Inverse-trig integral from −1 to 3
concepts.oneLine: When the two inputs inside tan⁻¹ are reciprocals of each other, the integrand collapses to the constant π/2 for x > 0 and −π/2 for x < 0, so ∫ from −1 to 3 splits at 0 and gives π.
notes: Look at the two inputs first, not at the integral. One is x/(1+x²) and the other is (1+x²)/x. They are reciprocals of each other, so the integrand is tan⁻¹u + tan⁻¹(1/u) with u = x/(1+x²).

Now the one line that students write blindly: tan⁻¹(1/x) = cot⁻¹x. That is only true when x is positive; when the input is negative the value drops to the fourth quadrant, and then tan⁻¹(1/x) = cot⁻¹x − π. So check the sign of u before touching anything.

The second tool is free of sign: tan⁻¹u + cot⁻¹u = π/2 for every real u — 10 lakh, minus 10 lakh, 50 thousand, it does not matter. So on the positive side the integrand is exactly π/2, and on the negative side it is π/2 − π = −π/2.

That is why the split is at 0 and not anywhere else. Two constants, two lengths, done: −π/2 over a length of 1, plus π/2 over a length of 3, which is π. There is a shorter road as well — both terms are odd functions, so −1 to 1 dies on its own and only 1 to 3 survives. Same π, half the writing. The long road is worth walking once, because it revises the old inverse-trig conversion.

quickChecks.q: Write tan⁻¹(1/(−3)) in terms of cot⁻¹.
steps: 1. The input −3 is negative, so the plain conversion is not allowed.
2. Use tan⁻¹(1/x) = cot⁻¹x − π for x < 0 with x = −3.

quickChecks.q: Evaluate ∫ from −2 to 0 of [ tan⁻¹(x/(1+x²)) + tan⁻¹((1+x²)/x) ] dx.
steps: 1. On −2 to 0, x is negative, so u = x/(1+x²) is negative throughout.
2. So tan⁻¹(1/u) = cot⁻¹u − π and the integrand = π/2 − π = −π/2, a constant.

quickChecks.q: Evaluate ∫ from −2 to 6 of the same integrand.
steps: 1. Split at 0, where the sign of the input changes.
2. On −2 to 0 the integrand is −π/2, length 2, giving −π.
3. On 0 to 6 the integrand is π/2, length 6, giving 3π.
4. Add: −π + 3π.

concepts.title: The first Queen statement is really King
concepts.oneLine: The first line of the Queen rule is nothing new: if f(2a−x) = −f(x), King alone forces ∫f dx from 0 to 2a to be 0.
notes: King on the limits 0 to 2a says this: ∫ f(x) dx from 0 to 2a = ∫ f(2a−x) dx from 0 to 2a. That is all. Nothing extra, nothing new.
Now suppose the question is set up so that putting 2a−x in place of x simply pulls a minus sign out, that is f(2a−x) = −f(x). Then King gives you I = −I, so 2I = 0 and I = 0.

So the Queen's first statement is not a separate rule at all — it is King, plus one minus sign that the question itself hands you. That is why I tell my students: don't store it. Apply King, and if a clean negative falls out, the answer is 0 automatically.
Keep your head free for the real Queen rule, which is coming next. There the two halves don't cancel — something is left to join after King — and that is where Queen actually earns her name.

quickChecks.q: Evaluate ∫ (sin 6x / sin 5x) dx from 0 to π.
steps: 1. Apply King with 2a = π: replace x by π − x.
2. Top: sin(6π − 6x) = −sin 6x, as 6 is even. Bottom: sin(5π − 5x) = sin 5x, as 5 is odd.
3. Integrand becomes −sin 6x / sin 5x = −f(x), so I = −I and 2I = 0.

quickChecks.q: Evaluate ∫ (sin 4x / sin 3x) dx from 0 to π.
steps: 1. King: x goes to π − x.
2. Top: sin(4π − 4x) = −sin 4x (4 even). Bottom: sin(3π − 3x) = sin 3x (3 odd).
3. Integrand flips to −f(x), hence 2I = 0.

quickChecks.q: Can you call ∫ (sin 9x / sin 7x) dx from 0 to π equal to 0 by the same argument?
steps: 1. Apply King: top becomes sin(9π − 9x) = sin 9x (9 odd, sign kept), bottom becomes sin(7π − 7x) = sin 7x (7 odd, sign kept).
2. So f(π − x) = f(x), and King only gives I = I.
3. No negative came out, so nothing cancels and no zero is forced.
quickChecks.answer: No. King returns the same integral, so this one is not 0 by this argument — it needs the actual Queen rule.

concepts.title: Queen rule: its two conditions and the halving step
concepts.oneLine: If King changes nothing and the lower limit is 0, Queen halves the upper limit and doubles the integral: ∫₀^{2a} f(x) dx = 2∫₀^{a} f(x) dx.
notes: Take I = ∫₀^{2a} f(x) dx. Put King on it: the limits stay 0 to 2a and the integrand becomes f(2a − x). Now suppose it turns out that f(2a − x) = f(x).
That means King did nothing. The question after King is the same question you started with. King is completely ineffective here — no gain, no simplification.

Queen has two conditions: first King must be ineffective, and second the lower limit must be 0. Queen is strict about the order. She will not step in before King has tried; you fight with King first, and only when he fails does she come.

When both conditions hold, Queen does one simple thing. Halve the upper limit and multiply the integral by 2: ∫₀^{2a} f(x) dx = 2∫₀^{a} f(x) dx. That is her whole move — the 2a becomes a, and a 2 comes out in front.

quickChecks.q: I = ∫₀^{2a} f(x) dx and you are told f(2a − x) = f(x). Write I in Queen's form.
steps: 1. King gives I = ∫₀^{2a} f(2a − x) dx, which is the same as I — King is ineffective.
2. Lower limit is 0, so both Queen conditions are satisfied.
3. Halve the upper limit, multiply by 2.

quickChecks.q: For I = ∫₀^{π} f(x) dx, what exactly must you check before writing I = 2∫₀^{π/2} f(x) dx?
steps: 1. Here 2a = π, so a = π/2.
2. Condition 1: put King and check f(π − x) = f(x).
3. Condition 2: lower limit is 0. ✓
4. Only if f(π − x) = f(x) is the halving step valid.
quickChecks.answer: You must check f(π − x) = f(x); if it holds, then I = 2∫₀^{π/2} f(x) dx.

quickChecks.q: I = ∫₁^{2a} f(x) dx with f(2a + 1 − x) = f(x). Can Queen halve the upper limit here?
steps: 1. King on 1 to 2a replaces x by (1 + 2a − x), and the given condition makes the question unchanged — so King is indeed ineffective.
2. Now check Queen's second condition: the lower limit is 1, not 0.
3. Condition 2 fails.
quickChecks.answer: No. King being ineffective is not enough — Queen needs the lower limit to be 0, so she does not apply.

concepts.title: Ratio of two sin¹⁶ integrals, and the mistake to avoid
concepts.oneLine: On ∫sin¹⁶x dx from 0 to 4π, every time King turns out ineffective Queen halves the upper limit and doubles the number in front, so after four rounds I₁ = 8∫cos¹⁶x dx from 0 to π/2 and I₁/I₂ = 8 — but you may never halve a limit unless King is truly ineffective and the lower limit is 0.
notes: Take I₁ = integral of sin¹⁶x dx from 0 to 4π, and I₂ = integral of cos¹⁶x dx from 0 to π/2. The question does not ask for I₁ and I₂ separately, only for I₁/I₂ — so the whole job is to push I₁ into the shape of I₂.

Start on I₁ and put King. sin(4π − x) = −sin x, and the power is 16, so the minus dies and the question comes back exactly as it was. King gives nothing here — he is ineffective. And that is precisely Queen's green signal: she halves the upper limit and writes a 2 in front, so I₁ = 2∫sin¹⁶x dx from 0 to 2π.

Now just repeat the loop. King on 0 to 2π: sin(2π − x) = −sin x, power 16, no change, ineffective — so Queen halves again and I₁ = 4∫sin¹⁶x dx from 0 to π. King on 0 to π: sin(π − x) = sin x, again no change — Queen halves once more and I₁ = 8∫sin¹⁶x dx from 0 to π/2.

On 0 to π/2 King finally earns his money. sin(π/2 − x) = cos x, so I₁ = 8∫cos¹⁶x dx from 0 to π/2 = 8I₂, and I₁/I₂ = 8. Queen has attitude: she only goes to war when King cannot do the job, so you may halve the upper limit only when King is genuinely ineffective and the lower limit is 0. Halving a limit is not a free move you can play on any integral you like.
This is why King is King and Queen is Queen. King never changes the value, he only rewrites the question; Queen refuses to touch anything until King has already failed.

quickChecks.q: I₁ = integral of sin¹⁰x dx from 0 to 2π and I₂ = integral of sin¹⁰x dx from 0 to π/2. Find I₁/I₂.
steps: 1. King on 0 to 2π: sin(2π − x) = −sin x, power 10 is even, so no change. Ineffective.
2. Queen with 2a = 2π, a = π: I₁ = 2∫ sin¹⁰x dx from 0 to π.
3. King on 0 to π: sin(π − x) = sin x, no change. Ineffective.
4. Queen with 2a = π, a = π/2: I₁ = 4∫ sin¹⁰x dx from 0 to π/2 = 4I₂.

quickChecks.q: I₁ = integral of cos⁸x dx from 0 to 4π and I₂ = integral of cos⁸x dx from 0 to π/2. Find I₁/I₂.
steps: 1. King on 0 to 4π: cos(4π − x) = cos x, no change. Ineffective, so Queen comes: I₁ = 2∫ cos⁸x dx from 0 to 2π.
2. King on 0 to 2π: cos(2π − x) = cos x, no change. Queen again: I₁ = 4∫ cos⁸x dx from 0 to π.
3. King on 0 to π: cos(π − x) = −cos x, but the power 8 is even, so cos⁸ is unchanged. Still ineffective.
4. Queen with 2a = π, a = π/2: I₁ = 8∫ cos⁸x dx from 0 to π/2 = 8I₂.

quickChecks.q: Is integral of sin¹⁵x dx from 0 to 2π equal to 2 × integral of sin¹⁵x dx from 0 to π?
steps: 1. Check Queen's condition: 2a = 2π, so a = π, and f(x) = sin¹⁵x.
2. f(2π − x) = (sin(2π − x))¹⁵ = (−sin x)¹⁵ = −sin¹⁵x, because the power 15 is odd.
3. So f(2a − x) = −f(x), not f(x). The condition fails — King is effective here, so Queen must not be used.
4. Sanity check on the numbers: the left side is actually 0 over the full period, while ∫ sin¹⁵x dx from 0 to π is positive. Clearly not equal.
quickChecks.answer: No. The odd power breaks Queen's condition, so the halving step is not allowed.

concepts.title: Jack, King and Queen used together
concepts.oneLine: On −2π to 2π, Jack opens the question, a dead King hands it to Queen twice, and King finally finishes it at 0 to π/2.
notes: Take that standard King question again, the one whose answer came out as 5/4. Rather than write the long function out once more, call it f(x). Now widen the limits: the integral of f(x) from −2π to 2π. It looks like a monster. It is the same question.

Try King first on −2π to 2π. He replaces x by (−2π) + (2π) − x, which is just −x, and f is even, so nothing changes. King is ineffective here. So the question has to open with Jack: f is even, so the integral equals 2 times the integral from 0 to 2π.

Now look what Jack has given us. The lower limit is 0, which is exactly what Queen demands. Check King on 0 to 2π: put 2π − x in place of x, and there is no difference. King is ineffective again. A King who does nothing is not a dead end; being ineffective is exactly Queen's condition, so a dead King hands the question straight to Queen. Queen halves the top limit and the 2 in front becomes 2 × 2, with limits 0 to π.

Do it once more on 0 to π. King puts π − x, no difference, so Queen comes again: the constant becomes 8 and the limits become 0 to π/2. And 0 to π/2 is our old standard question, which King himself had solved as 5/4. So the answer is 8 × 5/4 = 10. There is no elder rule and no younger rule here; without Jack the lower limit never becomes 0, and Queen could never even start.

quickChecks.q: A function g is even, g(2π − x) = g(x), g(π − x) = g(x), and the integral of g from 0 to π/2 is 3. Find the integral of g from −2π to 2π.
steps: 1. Jack (g even): the integral equals 2 × (0 to 2π).
2. Queen on 0 to 2π, since g(2π − x) = g(x): it becomes 4 × (0 to π).
3. Queen on 0 to π, since g(π − x) = g(x): it becomes 8 × (0 to π/2).

quickChecks.q: h is even and h(2π − x) = h(x), but h(π − x) = −h(x). Find the integral of h from −2π to 2π.
steps: 1. Jack: the integral equals 2 × (0 to 2π).
2. Queen on 0 to 2π: h(2π − x) = h(x), so it becomes 4 × (0 to π).
3. On 0 to π, Queen's second case applies: h(π − x) = −h(x), so the integral from 0 to π is 0.

quickChecks.q: p is an odd function, p(−x) = −p(x). Find the integral of p from −2π to 2π.
steps: 1. Symmetric limits, so Jack speaks first.
2. p is odd, so the integral from −2π to 2π is 0.
3. No need to call King or Queen at all; the question is already finished.

concepts.title: King and Queen giving zero
concepts.oneLine: On 0 to 2π, Queen first halves the interval to 0 to π, then King turns cos(π−θ) into −cosθ, the integral becomes minus itself, and the whole thing collapses to zero.
notes: Look at the interval first. It runs from 0 to 2π, so the instinct is King: replace θ by 2π−θ. Do that and the integrand comes back exactly as it was. Nothing moved.

That looks like a wasted step, but it is not. The moment King gives you back the same function on 0 to 2π, you have just verified Queen's condition f(2a−θ) = f(θ) — so Queen lets you halve the interval to 0 to π. Give the credit for that line to Queen, not to King.

Now run King again, this time on 0 to π: θ becomes π−θ. And cos(π−θ) = −cosθ. The minus comes out of the whole integrand, so the integral equals minus itself. I = −I forces I = 0, and you stop writing.

Don't ask which property is the stronger one. That is like asking whether your hand matters more than your leg. Here King alone goes nowhere and Queen alone finishes nothing — together they kill the question in three lines.

quickChecks.q: Evaluate ∫₀^{2π} cos⁵θ dθ.
steps: 1. cos⁵(2π−θ) = cos⁵θ, so Queen applies: I = 2∫₀^{π} cos⁵θ dθ.
2. Let J = ∫₀^{π} cos⁵θ dθ. King gives J = ∫₀^{π} cos⁵(π−θ) dθ = −J, since cos(π−θ) = −cosθ and the power is odd.
3. So J = 0 and I = 0.

quickChecks.q: Evaluate ∫₀^{2π} cosθ · cos2θ dθ.
steps: 1. Check Queen: cos(2π−θ)·cos(4π−2θ) = cosθ·cos2θ, so I = 2∫₀^{π} cosθ cos2θ dθ.
2. Let J be that half-integral. King: cos(π−θ)·cos(2π−2θ) = (−cosθ)(cos2θ) = −cosθ cos2θ, so J = −J.
3. Hence J = 0 and I = 0.

quickChecks.q: Evaluate ∫₀^{2π} cos²θ dθ. Does the same trick give zero?
steps: 1. Queen applies, since cos²(2π−θ) = cos²θ: I = 2∫₀^{π} cos²θ dθ.
2. King on 0 to π: cos²(π−θ) = (−cosθ)² = +cos²θ. No minus comes out, so no zero.
3. Finish honestly: ∫₀^{π} cos²θ dθ = ∫₀^{π} (1 + cos2θ)/2 dθ = π/2. So I = 2 × π/2 = π.
quickChecks.answer: π (not zero — King gave a plus sign here)

concepts.title: Planning a longer King–Queen problem
concepts.oneLine: Before you integrate a long expression, plan the order: King first to kill the useless x, then Queen twice to come down to 0 to π/2, and call the inner thing f(x) so the whole solution fits in four lines.
notes: The first thing to spot in this question is a useless x sitting in front. It is not there to be integrated, it is there to be removed. So King goes first: replace x by a − x, add the two copies, and that x is gone.

Now look at what is left. The limits are still too wide. This is where Queen comes in, and in this question she is applied twice, so that we finally land on 0 to π/2. Only at 0 to π/2 does the expression become friendly.

One more habit, and it is the one that saves your page. The thing sitting inside is long, so do not write it again and again. Give it a name, f(x), and from then on only move f(x) around. The properties act on the name; the ugly expression just sits quietly.

Notice what was not done. We never tried to actually find the integral. Practically you cannot evaluate this one by force. The whole question is testing whether you know the right order: King, Queen, Queen, and a name.

quickChecks.q: For ∫ from 0 to π of x·f(sin x) dx, what is your first move and what do you get?
steps: 1. A lone x in front, so King first: replace x by π − x.
2. sin(π − x) = sin x, so the function part is unchanged.
3. Adding the two copies: 2I = π∫ from 0 to π of f(sin x) dx.
quickChecks.answer: King first; I = (π/2)·∫ from 0 to π of f(sin x) dx — the x is gone.

quickChecks.q: After King you are left with ∫ from 0 to π of f(sin x) dx. What next?
steps: 1. Here 2a = π, so a = π/2.
2. Check Queen's condition: f(sin(π − x)) = f(sin x). True.
3. So the integral equals 2∫ from 0 to π/2 of f(sin x) dx.
quickChecks.answer: Queen: it becomes 2∫ from 0 to π/2 of f(sin x) dx.

quickChecks.q: Why is it worth writing the inner expression as f(x) before touching the question?
steps: 1. King and Queen only need the name of the function, not its full form.
2. Writing f(x) means each property is one short line.
3. Fewer copies of a long expression means fewer sign and bracket mistakes.
quickChecks.answer: Because the properties act on the name, so the whole solution closes in about four clean lines.

concepts.title: f(sin 2x)·sin x: King, the √2 trick, then Jack
concepts.oneLine: King turns sin x into sin x + cos x, √2 turns that into one cosine, the shift t = x − π/4 makes the integrand even, and Jack closes it: ∫₀^{π/2} f(sin 2x) sin x dx = √2 ∫₀^{π/4} f(cos 2t) cos t dt.
notes: Start with I = ∫₀^{π/2} f(sin 2x) sin x dx and apply King, x → π/2 − x. Inside, sin 2(π/2 − x) = sin(π − 2x) = sin 2x, so f is untouched. Outside, sin(π/2 − x) = cos x.

Add the two forms, as we always do after King: 2I = ∫₀^{π/2} f(sin 2x) (sin x + cos x) dx. Here no king, no queen, nothing helps — sin x + cos x is the A sin x + B cos x form, so multiply and divide by √2 and make it a single angle.

You can write it as √2 sin(x + π/4) or as √2 cos(x − π/4). Both are correct, but think ahead: whatever you write, you will substitute t for the bracket, so pick the one that leaves a cos outside, because cos is what f will also need. Take sin x + cos x = √2 cos(x − π/4).

Now put t = x − π/4. Limits shift to −π/4 and π/4, and since x = t + π/4, 2x = 2t + π/2, so sin 2x = sin(π/2 + 2t) = cos 2t. The integrand becomes f(cos 2t) cos t, which is untouched when t → −t — a pure even function on a symmetric interval. Apply Jack, the 2 cancels with the 2 on the left, and the proof is finished.

quickChecks.q: Write sin x + cos x as a single cosine.
steps: 1. √(1² + 1²) = √2, so take √2 common: sin x + cos x = √2 [(1/√2) cos x + (1/√2) sin x].
2. 1/√2 = cos(π/4) = sin(π/4), so the bracket is cos x cos(π/4) + sin x sin(π/4) = cos(x − π/4).

quickChecks.q: In ∫₀^{π/2} f(sin 2x) cos(x − π/4) dx you put t = x − π/4. What are the new limits, and what does sin 2x become?
steps: 1. x = 0 gives t = −π/4; x = π/2 gives t = π/4.
2. x = t + π/4, so 2x = 2t + π/2 and sin 2x = sin(π/2 + 2t) = cos 2t.
quickChecks.answer: Limits −π/4 to π/4, and sin 2x becomes cos 2t

quickChecks.q: Use the proved result with f(u) = u to evaluate ∫₀^{π/2} sin 2x · sin x dx.
steps: 1. By the result, the value is √2 ∫₀^{π/4} cos 2t · cos t dt.
2. Write cos 2t = 1 − 2sin²t: √2 ∫₀^{π/4} (1 − 2sin²t) cos t dt.
3. Integrating, √2 [sin t − (2/3) sin³t] from 0 to π/4.
5. Direct check: ∫₀^{π/2} 2 sin²x cos x dx = 2[sin³x/3]₀^{π/2} = 2/3. Same.

concepts.title: Proving ∫₀^{π/2} ln sin x dx = −(π/2) ln 2
concepts.oneLine: Add the King copy to I, write sin x cos x as sin 2x / 2, then put t = 2x so the doubled angle folds straight back into I and gives I = −(π/2) ln 2.
notes: Start with I = ∫₀^{π/2} ln sin x dx. Apply the King rule, x → π/2 − x, and sin becomes cos, so I = ∫₀^{π/2} ln cos x dx as well. As always after King, I add the two copies: 2I = ∫₀^{π/2} ln(sin x cos x) dx.

Now ln of a product splits, but do the opposite here — keep it joined and use sin x cos x = sin 2x / 2. So 2I = ∫₀^{π/2} ln(sin 2x) dx + ∫₀^{π/2} ln(1/2) dx. The second piece is a constant, nothing to integrate: it is (π/2) · ln(1/2) = −(π/2) ln 2.

The first piece is the whole game. It can only be related to I when the angle inside is the same single angle — here it is 2x, in I it is x, so force it: put t = 2x. Then dx = dt/2 and the limits stretch from 0 → π/2 to 0 → π, giving ½ ∫₀^{π} ln sin t dt.

On 0 to π, King does nothing: sin(π − t) = sin t, the function comes back unchanged. When King fails like that, the symmetry itself is the gift — ∫₀^{2a} f = 2∫₀^{a} f, so the halves cancel and ½ · 2∫₀^{π/2} ln sin t dt = I. So 2I = I − (π/2) ln 2, which means I = −(π/2) ln 2. Proved, without ever finding an antiderivative.

quickChecks.q: Find ∫₀^{π/2} ln cos x dx.
steps: 1. Apply King, x → π/2 − x: cos x becomes sin x.
2. So ∫₀^{π/2} ln cos x dx = ∫₀^{π/2} ln sin x dx = I.
3. And that proves I = −(π/2) ln 2.

quickChecks.q: Find ∫₀^{π} ln sin x dx.
steps: 1. Here 2a = π, and sin(π − x) = sin x, so the function satisfies f(2a − x) = f(x).
2. Therefore ∫₀^{π} ln sin x dx = 2 ∫₀^{π/2} ln sin x dx = 2I.
3. Put I = −(π/2) ln 2.

quickChecks.q: Find ∫₀^{π/2} ln(sin 2x) dx.
steps: 1. Put t = 2x, so dx = dt/2 and the limits become t: 0 → π.
2. The integral is ½ ∫₀^{π} ln sin t dt = ½ · 2 ∫₀^{π/2} ln sin t dt = I.
3. So it equals I = −(π/2) ln 2.

concepts.title: Periodic functions in definite integration
concepts.oneLine: If f has period T, every block of length T contributes the same integral — so count how many periods the interval is worth, integrate over one period, and multiply.
notes: Periodic with period T means the same graph repeats after every interval of length T. Whatever the curve does between 0 and T, it does exactly that again between T and 2T, and again between 2T and 3T.

Area does not care where the block sits, only that the shape is the same. So ∫ from 0 to T, ∫ from T to 2T and ∫ from 2T to 3T are all the same number. Once the shape repeats, the integral over every period is identical, so you only ever compute one period.

Now the properties write themselves. From 0 to nT you are sitting on n identical blocks, so you integrate over one period and multiply by n. From mT to nT the length is (n − m)T, which is (n − m) blocks, so multiply by (n − m). Say the limits are 50T to 53T — that is just 3 periods of length, so it is 3 times the integral over a single period.

The last one shifts instead of stretching. From a + nT to b + nT the length is still b − a, and it is the same stretch of graph pushed forward by a whole number of periods, so it equals ∫ from a to b. So the whole method is: look at the length of the interval, ask how many periods that length is, integrate over one period and multiply.

quickChecks.q: f has period T and ∫ from 0 to T of f(x) dx = 5. Find ∫ from 0 to 4T of f(x) dx.
steps: 1. Length = 4T − 0 = 4T, which is 4 periods.
2. Answer = 4 × 5.

quickChecks.q: f has period T and ∫ from 0 to T of f(x) dx = 7. Find ∫ from 50T to 53T of f(x) dx.
steps: 1. Length = 53T − 50T = 3T, so 3 periods.
2. Answer = 3 × 7.

quickChecks.q: f has period 2 and ∫ from 1 to 3 of f(x) dx = 4. Find ∫ from 7 to 9 of f(x) dx.
steps: 1. Write 7 = 1 + 3(2) and 9 = 3 + 3(2), so both limits are shifted by n = 3 periods.
2. Length is still 9 − 7 = 2 = 3 − 1, so it is the same stretch of graph.
3. Shift back: ∫ from 7 to 9 = ∫ from 1 to 3 = 4.

concepts.title: Using periodicity on |cos x| and |sin x| + |cos x|
concepts.oneLine: On a huge interval, don't split signs quadrant by quadrant — find the function's own period (a mod halves it), count how many periods fit the length, and integrate over one period.
notes: Look at ∫₀^{100π}|cos x| dx. The silly road is to start opening cos²x as (1 + cos2x)/2, or to break the interval quadrant by quadrant — positive from 0 to π/2, negative from π/2 to 3π/2, positive again after 3π/2. On an interval this long nobody is sitting and writing fifty pieces.

So switch to periodicity. Period of cos x is 2π — old news. Put a mod on sin or cos and the period becomes half, so |cos x| has period π. Now 0 to 100π is exactly 100 such periods, so integrate over one period and multiply by 100.

That is the whole recipe, and it has only two steps. Find the total length of the interval, then divide it by the period of the function to get how many periods sit inside. Integrate over a single period, multiply by that count, done.

One warning worth repeating: you cannot pick the period to suit yourself. The period belongs to the function, not to your convenience. |sin x| + |cos x| repeats every π/2 — that is its period, whether you like the number or not.

quickChecks.q: Evaluate ∫₀^{10π} |sin x| dx.
steps: 1. |sin x| has period π.
2. Length = 10π, so number of periods = 10π ÷ π = 10.
3. ∫₀^{π} |sin x| dx = ∫₀^{π} sin x dx = [−cos x]₀^{π} = 1 + 1 = 2.

quickChecks.q: Evaluate ∫_{−π}^{5π} |cos x| dx.
steps: 1. |cos x| has period π.
2. Length = 5π − (−π) = 6π, so number of periods = 6π ÷ π = 6.
3. One period gives ∫₀^{π} |cos x| dx = 2.

quickChecks.q: Evaluate ∫₀^{6π} (|sin x| + |cos x|) dx.
steps: 1. Period of |sin x| + |cos x| is π/2.
2. Length = 6π, so number of periods = 6π ÷ (π/2) = 12.
3. One period gives ∫₀^{π/2} (sin x + cos x) dx = 2.

concepts.title: Fractional part {x} as a period-1 function
concepts.oneLine: x − [x] is the fractional part {x}, it repeats with period 1, so ∫₀¹⁰⁰ 2^{x−[x]} dx is just 100 × ∫₀¹ 2^x dx.
notes: Start with the identity. x − [x] is exactly the fractional part of x, written {x}. For any x at all, strip off the integer part and what is left over is {x}.

This fractional part is the most unique periodic function in the whole chapter: {x} is periodic with period 1. On 0 to 1 it climbs from 0 to 1, then it drops back to 0 and climbs again. Same shape, over and over.

Now see what happens without that idea. From 0 to 1 you say [x] = 0, so you integrate 2^x. From 1 to 2 you say [x] = 1, so you integrate 2^{x−1}. From 2 to 3 you integrate 2^{x−2}. This story goes on and on — a hundred pieces, and your hand gives up before the question does.

Because the function has period 1, the whole stretch 0 to 100 is one hundred copies of 0 to 1. So ∫₀¹⁰⁰ 2^{x−[x]} dx = 100 ∫₀¹ 2^{x−[x]} dx. And inside 0 to 1 the greatest integer is 0, so x − [x] is simply x. One easy integral, done.

quickChecks.q: Evaluate ∫₀¹⁰ 2^(x − [x]) dx.
steps: 1. Period of the integrand is 1, and 10 is a whole number of periods, so ∫₀¹⁰ = 10 ∫₀¹.
2. On 0 to 1, x − [x] = x, giving 10 ∫₀¹ 2^x dx = 10 × (2 − 1)/ln 2.

quickChecks.q: Evaluate ∫₀⁵ e^(x − [x]) dx.
steps: 1. Same period 1, five whole periods: 5 ∫₀¹ e^(x−[x]) dx.
2. On 0 to 1 it is 5 ∫₀¹ e^x dx = 5[e^x]₀¹ = 5(e − 1).

quickChecks.q: Evaluate ∫₀¹⁰⁰ {x} dx, where {x} is the fractional part of x.
steps: 1. {x} has period 1, so ∫₀¹⁰⁰ {x} dx = 100 ∫₀¹ {x} dx.
2. On 0 to 1, {x} = x, so ∫₀¹ x dx = ½.
3. Total = 100 × ½.

concepts.title: ∫₀^{nπ+v} |sin x| dx — periods plus a leftover piece
concepts.oneLine: ∫₀^{nπ+v} |sin x| dx = 2n + 1 − cos v: n full periods give 2 each, and the leftover piece slides down to 0 to v where sin x is positive.
notes: Start with the easy half. From 0 to nπ you have exactly n full periods of |sin x|, and in one period, 0 to π, sin x is positive, so the modulus opens as sin x and the integral is 2. n periods, so that part is just 2n.

Now the leftover. The remaining stretch is nπ to nπ + v, length v. Do not integrate it there. On that interval the sign of sin x depends on whether n is even or odd, and you do not want your answer to depend on n's parity.

So slide the leftover piece down to 0 to v — the function has period π, so shifting by a whole number of periods changes nothing. Now v lies between 0 and π, sin x is positive there, the modulus opens cleanly as sin x, and you integrate without thinking about n at all.
That gives ∫₀^v sin x dx = −cos x from 0 to v = −cos v + cos 0 = 1 − cos v. Add it to the 2n you already had: the whole answer is 2n + 1 − cos v. One formula, any upper limit.

quickChecks.q: Evaluate ∫₀^{3π + π/2} |sin x| dx.
steps: 2. Periods: 2n = 6.

quickChecks.q: Evaluate ∫₀^{4π + π/3} |sin x| dx.
steps: 2. Periods: 2n = 8.
3. Tail: 1 − cos(π/3) = 1 − ½ = ½.

quickChecks.q: Evaluate ∫₀^{7π} |sin x| dx.
steps: 1. Here the limit is an exact multiple of π, so n = 7 and v = 0.
2. Periods: 2n = 14.
4. Total = 14.

concepts.title: Inequalities and bounds for definite integrals
concepts.oneLine: If f(x) ≤ g(x) on [a,b] then ∫f ≤ ∫g, and for any f with minimum m and maximum M on [a,b], m(b−a) ≤ ∫f ≤ M(b−a).
notes: Draw two curves on the same axes between x = a and x = b. The blue one, g(x), stays above the black one, f(x), everywhere in that interval.

Now ask: does that same relation survive integration? Yes. Whatever inequality the graphs follow on [a,b], the definite integrals follow the same inequality. Area under the higher curve cannot be smaller than area under the lower one.

Use this on a single function and you get the bound. Suppose on [a,b] the smallest value of f is m and the largest is M. Then m ≤ f(x) ≤ M for every x in [a,b]. Integrate all three pieces from a to b: ∫m dx is just m(b−a), and ∫M dx is M(b−a). So m(b−a) ≤ ∫ₐᵇ f(x) dx ≤ M(b−a).

See it as a picture too. The width of the strip is b−a, the short height is m, the tall height is M. The small rectangle fits inside the region under the curve, the big rectangle swallows it — so the integral is squeezed between the two areas. And notice, the graph never needed to be increasing. Non-monotonic is fine; just read off its minimum and maximum on [a,b] and the same logic runs.

quickChecks.q: Find bounds for ∫₁³ x² dx without evaluating it.
steps: 1. x² is increasing on [1,3], so the minimum is m = 1² = 1 and the maximum is M = 3² = 9.
2. Width b−a = 3 − 1 = 2.
3. Apply the squeeze: 1 × 2 ≤ ∫₁³ x² dx ≤ 9 × 2.
quickChecks.answer: 2 ≤ ∫₁³ x² dx ≤ 18 (the true value 26/3 ≈ 8.67 does sit inside).

quickChecks.q: Find bounds for ∫₀¹ dx/(1+x²).
steps: 1. On [0,1] the denominator 1+x² grows from 1 to 2, so the function falls from 1 to ½.
2. So m = ½ and M = 1, and the width b−a = 1.
3. Squeeze: ½ × 1 ≤ ∫₀¹ dx/(1+x²) ≤ 1 × 1.
quickChecks.answer: ½ ≤ ∫₀¹ dx/(1+x²) ≤ 1 (the true value π/4 ≈ 0.785 lies inside).

quickChecks.q: Which is larger: ∫₀¹ x² dx or ∫₀¹ x³ dx?
steps: 1. For 0 < x < 1, multiply x² by x (positive, less than 1): x³ < x².
2. The inequality holds on the whole interval [0,1], so it passes to the integrals.
3. Therefore ∫₀¹ x³ dx ≤ ∫₀¹ x² dx — and indeed ¼ < ⅓.

concepts.title: Proving an inequality by building it from x < x² on (0,1)
concepts.oneLine: On (0,1) start from x² < x, carry that inequality through −1, e-power and a positive multiplier like cos²x, and integrate only at the very last step.
notes: Take any x between 0 and 1. Which is bigger, x or x²? When the number is less than 1, raising the power makes it smaller — so x² < x on (0,1). Put x = ½ and see it: ½² = ¼, and ¼ is less than ½.
Now build on top of that one line. Multiply by −1 and the sign flips: −x < −x². Put both as e-powers — e is increasing, so the direction stays — and you get e⁻ˣ < e⁻ˣ².
Next multiply both sides by cos²x. That is a positive quantity for x in (0,1), so again the direction stays: e⁻ˣ·cos²x < e⁻ˣ²·cos²x.

Only now integrate from 0 to 1. If one function stays below another on an interval, its definite integral over that interval is the smaller one — that is the whole weapon. So the proof is finished, without ever integrating e⁻ˣ² , which is just as well, because you cannot.

quickChecks.q: Prove that ∫₀¹ e⁻ˣ sin²x dx < ∫₀¹ e⁻ˣ² sin²x dx.
steps: 1. For x in (0,1): x² < x, so −x < −x², so e⁻ˣ < e⁻ˣ².
2. sin²x > 0 for x in (0,1), so multiplying keeps the direction: e⁻ˣ sin²x < e⁻ˣ² sin²x.
3. Integrate both sides from 0 to 1.
quickChecks.answer: ∫₀¹ e⁻ˣ sin²x dx < ∫₀¹ e⁻ˣ² sin²x dx. Only the positive multiplier changed; every step is the same.
