2. So y² − y − 2 = 0, which factorises as (y − 2)(y + 1) = 0.

quickChecks.q: y² = 4x meets the line 4x = 3y − 2. Find the y-limits.
steps: 1. Substitute: y² = 3y − 2.
2. So y² − 3y + 2 = 0, which factorises as (y − 1)(y − 2) = 0.

quickChecks.q: y² = 6x meets the line 6x = y + 6. Find the y-limits, then the two points.
steps: 1. Substitute: y² = y + 6, so y² − y − 6 = 0.
2. Factorise: (y − 3)(y + 2) = 0, so y = 3 and y = −2.
3. For the points: y = 3 gives 6x = 9, x = 3/2; y = −2 gives 6x = 4, x = 2/3.
quickChecks.answer: y = −2 and y = 3; the points are (2/3, −2) and (3/2, 3)

concepts.title: The same region by vertical stripes: rectangle minus integral
concepts.oneLine: The same eˣ/ln x region can be found as (area of the enclosing rectangle) − (vertical-stripe integral of ln x − 1 from x = e to x = e²), and it gives the same e² − e.
notes: Remember the region: on the right it is bounded by y = ln x, which is the same curve as x = e^y. On the left it sits on the y-axis, and it is trapped between y = 1 and y = 2. Horizontally it was a one-line job: x = e^y, integrate from y = 1 to y = 2, answer e² − e.

Now go vertical. First, the joke of the question — the rectangle. Take the point P where y = 2 meets the curve: put y = 2 in x = e^y and you get P = (e², 2). Straight below it, on y = 1, sits P′ = (e², 1). So the rectangle on the y-axis has width e² and height 2 − 1 = 1, area e² × 1 = e².

But rectangle area is not the answer. The curve has bitten a piece out of that rectangle, and that piece is exactly a vertical-stripe region: top boundary y = ln x, bottom boundary y = 1. So the second route is: rectangle area minus the integral of (ln x − 1), and the limits must now be x values, not y values. Where does that piece start? y = 1 on the curve gives x = e. Where does it end? At P, x = e². So subtract the integral of (ln x − 1) dx from x = e to x = e², and you land back on e² − e.

Was this harder? Yes, a little. But we are not here only to integrate, we are here to learn how to look at a figure. A smart student is not the one who is comfortable in vertical or comfortable in horizontal — he is the one who knows both, because only he can choose the easier one by looking. Some questions are half vertical, half horizontal. Some are a plain shape where you write the rectangle's area by eye and finish with one tiny integral.

quickChecks.q: Find the area bounded by y = ln x, the y-axis, y = 0 and y = 1 by the rectangle-minus-stripe route.
steps: 1. Top corner: y = 1 gives x = e¹ = e. Rectangle has width e and height 1 − 0 = 1, so its area is e.
2. Eaten piece: vertical stripe with top y = ln x, bottom y = 0, from x = 1 (where ln x = 0) to x = e.
3. ∫ln x dx from 1 to e = [x ln x − x] = (e − e) − (0 − 1) = 1.
4. Area = e − 1. Cross-check horizontally: ∫e^y dy from 0 to 1 = e − 1. ✓

quickChecks.q: For the same region, switch to vertical stripes. What are the x-limits, and what is the stripe height?
steps: 1. y = 1 on y = ln x gives x = e; y = 2 gives x = e².
2. Top boundary of the stripe is y = ln x, bottom boundary is the line y = 1.
quickChecks.answer: x goes from e to e², and the stripe height is (ln x − 1)

quickChecks.q: Same curve y = ln x with the y-axis, but now between y = 1 and y = 3. Do it as rectangle minus vertical stripes.
steps: 1. Corner: y = 3 gives x = e³. Rectangle width = e³, height = 3 − 1 = 2, so area = 2e³.
2. Eaten piece: ∫(ln x − 1) dx from x = e to x = e³.
3. ∫ln x dx = [x ln x − x] from e to e³ = (3e³ − e³) − (e − e) = 2e³.
4. ∫1 dx from e to e³ = e³ − e. So the piece = 2e³ − (e³ − e) = e³ + e.
5. Area = 2e³ − (e³ + e) = e³ − e. Cross-check: ∫e^y dy from 1 to 3 = e³ − e. ✓

concepts.title: Rectangle-minus-stripe on y = eˣ with y = 1/e²
concepts.oneLine: The region under y = eˣ and above y = 1/e² from x = −2 to x = −1 is one vertical stripe of height (eˣ − 1/e²), so the area is ∫ from −2 to −1 of (eˣ − 1/e²) dx = 1/e − 2/e².
notes: Look at the picture. The curve y = eˣ is rising, and at x = −2 it is sitting exactly at 1/e². So at the left end the curve and the line y = 1/e² touch, and as x moves to −1 the curve climbs away to 1/e.

Now take a thin vertical stripe inside the region. Its top head is on y = eˣ and its foot is on y = 1/e², so its height is (eˣ − 1/e²) and its width is dx. Slide that stripe from x = −2 to x = −1 and you have swept the whole region.

That is the entire setup: area = ∫ from −2 to −1 of (eˣ − 1/e²) dx. Split it if you like and it becomes ∫eˣ dx minus a flat rectangle of base 1 and height 1/e² — which is exactly the rectangle-minus-integral story from before, written in one line instead of two.

Before you write the answer, use the box. The region sits inside a rectangle of base 1 (from −2 to −1) and height 1/e − 1/e² ≈ 0.232. That box area is easy but it is not the answer; it is only the ceiling. The answer must come out below it.

quickChecks.q: Find the area bounded by y = eˣ, y = 1/e, x = −1 and x = 0.
steps: 1. They meet at x = −1 (eˣ = 1/e there), and for −1 ≤ x ≤ 0 the curve is above the line.
2. Area = ∫ from −1 to 0 of (eˣ − 1/e) dx.
3. ∫eˣ dx from −1 to 0 = e⁰ − e⁻¹ = 1 − 1/e.
4. Rectangle under the line: (1/e)(width 1) = 1/e.

quickChecks.q: Find the area bounded by y = eˣ, y = 1, x = 0 and x = 1.
steps: 1. On 0 ≤ x ≤ 1 the curve eˣ rises from 1 to e, so eˣ is on top and y = 1 is the floor.
2. Area = ∫ from 0 to 1 of (eˣ − 1) dx.
3. ∫eˣ dx from 0 to 1 = e − 1; rectangle under the line = (1)(1) = 1.

quickChecks.q: Shift the worked question one unit left: find the area bounded by y = eˣ, y = 1/e³, x = −3 and x = −2.
steps: 1. Same shape: curve on top, flat line 1/e³ at the bottom, and they touch at x = −3.
2. Area = ∫ from −3 to −2 of (eˣ − 1/e³) dx.
3. ∫eˣ dx from −3 to −2 = 1/e² − 1/e³.
4. Rectangle = (1/e³)(1) = 1/e³.

concepts.title: Plotting regions: the four parabola orientations
concepts.oneLine: In y² = ±4ax and x² = ±4ay the 4a is always positive, so the variable that is not squared names the axis of symmetry and its sign tells you which half-axis the parabola opens along.
notes: Area under curves is a very small chapter, but the plotting work around it is huge. So before any integration, your hand should draw the curve the moment you see the equation.

Start with y² = 4ax. In a parabola 4a is always positive, and y² on the left is never negative, so x itself must be positive — the whole graph lives on the positive x side. That is why it opens to the right, and because only y is squared, the curve is symmetric about the x-axis.
Now flip the sign. y² = −4ax forces x to be negative, so the same shape sits on the negative x side and opens left. Still symmetric about the x-axis, just mirrored.

Swap the roles for the other pair. x² = 4ay needs y positive, so it opens up along the positive y-axis and is symmetric about the y-axis; x² = −4ay needs y negative, so it opens down. Read the variable that is not squared: that variable's axis is the axis of symmetry, and its sign tells you which half of that axis the curve uses.

quickChecks.q: Which way does y² = −12x open, and about which axis is it symmetric?
steps: 1. Compare with y² = −4ax: 4a = 12, so a = 3.
2. y² ≥ 0 forces −12x ≥ 0, so x ≤ 0.
3. Only y is squared, so symmetry is about the x-axis.
quickChecks.answer: Opens left along the negative x-axis, symmetric about the x-axis, vertex at the origin, a = 3.

quickChecks.q: For x² = 8y, give a and describe the plot.
steps: 1. Compare with x² = 4ay: 4a = 8, so a = 2.
2. x² ≥ 0 forces 8y ≥ 0, so y ≥ 0.
3. Only x is squared, so symmetry is about the y-axis.
quickChecks.answer: a = 2; opens up along the positive y-axis, symmetric about the y-axis, vertex at the origin.

quickChecks.q: A parabola has its vertex at the origin, opens downward and is symmetric about the y-axis. Write its standard form and the form if it opened to the right instead.
steps: 1. Symmetric about the y-axis means x is the squared variable.
2. Downward means y must be ≤ 0, so the sign is minus: x² = −4ay.
3. Opening right means the lonely variable is x with a plus sign, and y is squared: y² = 4ax.
quickChecks.answer: Downward: x² = −4ay. Opening right: y² = 4ax (with a > 0 in both).

concepts.title: Shade the region bounded by x² = y, x² = −y and y = 4x − 3
concepts.oneLine: Draw x² = y and its mirror x² = −y, cut them with y = 4x − 3 to get (1,1), (3,9) and x = −2 ± √7, then shade the small middle region with horizontal stripes so one leg always stays on the line.
notes: Start with x² = y. That is the parabola opening upwards, vertex at the origin. Now replace y by −y and nothing about the shape changes — it just flips. x² = −y is the same parabola taken below the x-axis: it opens downwards, not sideways. The two are mirror images in the x-axis, so you get a neat bow-tie around the origin.
For the line y = 4x − 3 there is no need to plot points. x = 0 gives y = −3, y = 0 gives x = 3/4. Pass a straight line through (0, −3) and (3/4, 0) and the idea of the line is already on your page.

Then the intersections. Eliminate y every time: the line into x² = y gives x² − 4x + 3 = 0, so x = 1 and 3, and the y values come from the line — (1,1) and (3,9). The line into x² = −y gives x² + 4x − 3 = 0, which refuses to factorise, so the quadratic formula hands you x = −2 ± √7. Only the one near the origin, x = −2 + √7 ≈ 0.65, touches our region.

Now look at what you must shade: the small closed patch near the origin, upward parabola on top, downward parabola below, line closing it on the right. Walk a vertical stripe through it and watch the legs. Near the y-axis both legs sit on the two parabolas; past x = −2 + √7 the bottom leg jumps onto the line. A horizontal stripe is kinder — its right leg is on the line the whole way, and only the left leg swaps from one parabola to the other.

quickChecks.q: Where do x² = y and x² = −y meet?
steps: 1. Both equal x², so y = −y.
2. That gives 2y = 0, so y = 0.
3. Then x² = 0, so x = 0.

quickChecks.q: Write all three boundary curves of the worked example in x = form (right half), ready for a horizontal stripe.
steps: 1. x² = y gives x = √y, used for y ≥ 0.
2. x² = −y gives x = √(−y), used for y ≤ 0.
3. y = 4x − 3 gives 4x = y + 3, so x = (y + 3)/4.

quickChecks.q: In that shaded region, how long is the horizontal stripe at y = ¼?
steps: 1. Left leg on x² = y: x = √(1/4) = 1/2.

concepts.title: Sketching y = 2/(1 + x²) and shading it against x² = y
concepts.oneLine: Read f(−x) = f(x) as symmetry about the y-axis, squeeze the denominator for y_max = 2, check the x → ±∞ tail — then sketch y = 2/(1 + x²), drop x² = y on top of it and shade the lens between them.
notes: Look at y = 2/(1 + x²). Replace x by −x and nothing changes, so f(−x) = f(x). In a graph question that word "even" is useless to you; what you actually use is that the curve is symmetric about the y-axis — so sketch the right half and mirror it.

Its twin is worth writing down beside it. If replacing y by −y changes nothing, f(−y) = f(y), that is symmetry about the x-axis — and such a relation is not a function of x at all. Two lines, two symmetries — keep both in your head together.

Now the maximum, with no calculus. The numerator 2 is fixed, so y is big exactly when 1 + x² is small, and the smallest 1 + x² can ever be is 1, at x = 0. So y ≤ 2, and y_max = 2 at x = 0. Also 1 + x² > 0 always, so y stays positive — the curve never touches or crosses the x-axis.

Then the tail: as x → +∞ or x → −∞, the denominator blows up and y → 0. If you want it the calculus way, y′ = −4x/(1 + x²)², which is negative for x > 0 and positive for x < 0 — increasing to the left of 0, decreasing to the right of 0. Peak 2 at the origin, falling to 0 on both sides: that is the whole bell shape. Drop x² = y on the same axes and shade the region trapped between them, because the integral is coming next.

quickChecks.q: What is the maximum value of y = 6/(2 + x²), and where does it occur?
steps: 1. Numerator is fixed, so y is largest when 2 + x² is smallest.
2. 2 + x² ≥ 2, with equality at x = 0.
quickChecks.answer: y_max = 3, at x = 0 (and the graph is symmetric about the y-axis, with y → 0 as x → ±∞).

quickChecks.q: At which points does y = 2/(1 + x²) cross the line y = 1?
steps: 2. So 1 + x² = 2, giving x² = 1.
3. Hence x = ±1.
quickChecks.answer: At (−1, 1) and (1, 1) — the same two points where it meets x² = y.

quickChecks.q: The relation y² = x satisfies f(−y) = f(y). What does that tell you about its graph, and is it a function of x?
steps: 1. Replacing y by −y leaves y² = x unchanged.
2. That is the f(−y) = f(y) test, so the graph is symmetric about the x-axis.
3. For x = 4 you get y = 2 and y = −2, two outputs for one input.
quickChecks.answer: Symmetric about the x-axis, and it is not a function of x.

concepts.title: Full curve analysis of y = (x² − 1)/(x² + 1)
concepts.oneLine: For any unfamiliar curve, run one fixed checklist — even/odd, roots, value at 0, limit at infinity, sign of dy/dx — and ignore curvature, because area never depends on it.
notes: Come to the side of the page and do the analysis properly. Always put the even-odd idea first. If the function is even, half the graph is already made for you — sketch it for x ≥ 0 and mirror it across the y-axis. Replace x by −x here and nothing changes, so this one is even.
Next, roots. Put y = 0 and solve: x² − 1 = 0, so x = ±1. That is two points of the x-axis pinned down. Then the value at x = 0, which is very useful information: y = (0 − 1)/(0 + 1) = −1.

Now the limit. As x → ∞ the ratio is an ∞/∞ form and it goes to 1. So the line y = 1 is an asymptote — the curve gets closer and closer but you will never touch this line, you have to keep a distance from it forever.

Last, increasing or decreasing, and for that differentiation. dy/dx = 4x/(x² + 1)². The denominator is always positive, so the sign is just the sign of x: x = 0 is the critical point, the curve decreases before 0 and increases after 0. Start at (0, −1), rise through (1, 0), and climb towards 1 without reaching it. Mirror it on the left and the graph is done.

quickChecks.q: Run the checklist on y = (x² − 4)/(x² + 1). Give symmetry, roots, value at 0, asymptote, and where it increases.
steps: 1. Replace x by −x: the function is unchanged, so it is even — symmetric about the y-axis.
2. y = 0 gives x² − 4 = 0, so x = ±2.
4. As x → ∞ the value tends to 1, so y = 1 is the asymptote; setting the function equal to 1 gives −4 = 1, impossible, so it is never touched.
5. dy/dx = [(x² + 1)(2x) − (x² − 4)(2x)]/(x² + 1)² = 2x[x² + 1 − x² + 4]/(x² + 1)² = 10x/(x² + 1)², which has the sign of x.
quickChecks.answer: Even; roots x = ±2; minimum point (0, −4); asymptote y = 1 never touched; decreasing for x < 0 and increasing for x > 0.

quickChecks.q: For y = (1 − x²)/(1 + x²), find the asymptote and say whether x = 0 is a maximum or a minimum.
steps: 1. As x → ∞, the ∞/∞ form gives −1, so y = −1 is the asymptote.
3. So dy/dx is positive for x < 0 and negative for x > 0 — the curve rises up to x = 0 and falls after it.
quickChecks.answer: Asymptote y = −1; x = 0 is a maximum with value 1.

quickChecks.q: Write the range of y = (x² − 1)/(x² + 1) using only the checklist answers.
steps: 1. The minimum is at the critical point x = 0, where y = −1, so y ≥ −1.
2. The curve rises towards the asymptote y = 1 as x → ∞ but never reaches it, since the function equal to 1 gives the impossible −1 = 1.
3. So the values run from −1 up to, but not including, 1.

concepts.title: Translated graphs by tracking the key point
concepts.oneLine: Any shifted graph is the same old graph moved to one new point — find where the bracket inside becomes zero, read the y there, and draw the usual shape from that point.
notes: Start with what you already know. y = |x| is a V with its corner at (0, 0). y = x² is an upward parabola with its lowest point at (0, 0). That corner, that lowest point — that is the critical point, the one place where the shape turns.

Now for any shifted version there is only one thing to do: make the bracket inside zero, and read the y value there. For y = |x − 2|, inside is zero at x = 2, and y there is 0, so the corner sits at (2, 0). For y = |x + 3|, inside is zero at x = −3, so the corner is at (−3, 0). Same V, new corner.

This scales up straight away. y = |x − 2| − 5: inside zero at x = 2, and there y = 0 − 5 = −5. Corner at (2, −5), then draw the same V. y = (x + 3)² − 5: the perfect square is zero at x = −3, and y = −5 there. Lowest point (−3, −5), then the same upward parabola. Never ask whether it moved left or right. Ask only where the critical point went.

For a log graph, the turning point is replaced by the vertical asymptote — the line the curve runs along without ever touching it. y = ln x is defined for x > 0 and dives to −∞ as x approaches 0. So y = ln(x − e) is defined for x > e, and it dives to −∞ as x approaches e. The asymptote has simply moved to x = e. Track that one line and the shape follows.

quickChecks.q: Draw y = |x + 4| − 1 and find where it meets the x-axis.
steps: 1. Inside zero: x + 4 = 0 gives x = −4.
2. At x = −4, y = 0 − 1 = −1, so the corner is (−4, −1).
3. Draw the V from there. For the x-axis, |x + 4| = 1 gives x + 4 = 1 or x + 4 = −1.
4. So x = −3 or x = −5.
quickChecks.answer: V with corner (−4, −1), cutting the x-axis at x = −5 and x = −3.

quickChecks.q: What is the minimum value of y = (x − 2)² + 3, and how many times does the graph cut the x-axis?
steps: 1. Perfect square zero: x − 2 = 0 gives x = 2.
2. At x = 2, y = 0 + 3 = 3. Lowest point is (2, 3).
3. It is an upward parabola with its lowest point above the x-axis.
4. So y is never zero.
quickChecks.answer: Minimum value 3 at x = 2; it never cuts the x-axis.

quickChecks.q: For y = ln(x + 5), write the domain, the vertical asymptote and the x-intercept.
steps: 1. Argument positive: x + 5 > 0 gives x > −5.
2. As x → −5 from the right, y → −∞, so the asymptote is the line x = −5.
3. y = 0 needs x + 5 = 1, so x = −4.
quickChecks.answer: Domain x > −5, asymptote x = −5, cuts the x-axis at x = −4.

concepts.title: sin(ax) graphs by rescaling the period
concepts.oneLine: To plot sin(ax), don't stretch or squeeze the picture — keep the same sine shape and divide every marked x-value by |a|, because period = T/|a|.
notes: Start with what you already know: y = sin x, period 2π. Zeros at 0, π, 2π, peak at π/2, trough at 3π/2. That picture must be in your hand without thinking.

Now take sin 2x. The usual advice is: pinch the graph, deflate it, squeeze it to half. That is an art problem, not a maths problem. So do not touch the shape — only rewrite the x-values, because if the period of f(x) is T, then the period of f(ax) is T/|a|.

For sin 2x the period is 2π/2 = π. So every marked x gets divided by 2: π/2 becomes π/4, π becomes π/2, 3π/2 becomes 3π/4, 2π becomes π. Same sine curve, same up-down order, new labels. One full wave now finishes at π — exactly the period calculated above, which is the check that it is right.

The same move handles a < 1. For sin(x/2) the period is 2π ÷ ½ = 4π, and dividing by ½ just means multiplying by 2: π → 2π, 2π → 4π, 3π → 6π. Divide the coordinates, not the drawing — and then check that one complete wave ends exactly at the period you computed.

quickChecks.q: Where does one full wave of y = sin 4x finish, and where is its first peak?
steps: 1. Period = 2π/4 = π/2.
2. Divide the sin x marks by 4: peak π/2 → π/8, zero π → π/4.
quickChecks.answer: One full wave ends at π/2; first peak at x = π/8.

quickChecks.q: Mark the zeros of y = sin(x/3) in one period.
steps: 2. Multiply every mark by 3: 0 → 0, π → 3π, 2π → 6π.
quickChecks.answer: Zeros at 0, 3π and 6π, with the peak at 3π/2 — period 6π.

quickChecks.q: Find the period of y = sin(2x/5) and the x-value of its trough in the first period.
steps: 2. Multiply the marks by 5/2: trough 3π/2 → 15π/4.

concepts.title: Drawing y = f(|x|) from y = f(x)
concepts.oneLine: y = f(|x|) is always even, so keep only the x ≥ 0 part of y = f(x) and mirror it across the y-axis.
notes: Start from the blue graph. That is y = f(x). Now draw y = f(|x|) — and do not start by panicking about the formula.

Don't. Before you draw anything, notice that f(|x|) is an even function, and after that the story is over. Even means: put 1 or put −1, the value is the same. Put 2 or put −2, the value is the same. Yes or no?

So here is what we do. The part of the old graph sitting on the negative x side is of no use to us — throw it away. Keep the graph only for positive x, because for x ≥ 0 the mod does nothing: |x| = x.

Now the left side has to carry the same values as the right side, since the function is even. So just put a mirror on the y-axis and copy the right half across. That image of the right half is your whole left half — that is y = f(|x|).

quickChecks.q: If f(3) = 5, what is the value of y = f(|x|) at x = −3?
steps: 2. So the value is f(3) = 5.

quickChecks.q: The graph of y = f(x) passes through (−4, 7) and (4, 1). Which point on y = f(|x|) has x = −4?
steps: 1. At x = −4, |x| = 4, so we need f(4) = 1.
2. The old point (−4, 7) belongs to the discarded left part, so it is not used.

quickChecks.q: To get y = f(|x|), which half of y = f(x) do you keep, and in which axis do you mirror it?
steps: 1. The mod changes nothing for x ≥ 0, so keep the right half.
2. f(|x|) is even, so the graph is symmetric about the y-axis.
quickChecks.answer: Keep the x ≥ 0 half and mirror it in the y-axis.

concepts.title: Drawing y = |f(x)|
concepts.quote: This is the easiest of all the mod graphs. One line decides everything: y can never be negative.
concepts.oneLine: For y = |f(x)|, keep whatever is already above the x-axis exactly as it is, and reflect whatever lies below the x-axis up above it — because y can never be negative here.
notes: Start from the graph of y = f(x). Now put a mod on the whole thing: y = |f(x)|. Mod of f(x) means y is never negative, so no part of this graph can ever sit below the x-axis.
Remember where the sign lives. Above the x-axis, y is positive. Below the x-axis, y is negative. So in y = |f(x)|, the whole region below the x-axis is simply not allowed.

So what do you do with the portion that was below? You do not erase it. You take the mod of the whole graph: every piece above the x-axis stays as it is, and every piece below the x-axis is reflected straight up. The x-axis acts like a mirror.
The points where the graph was already touching the x-axis do not move at all. There f(x) = 0, and mod of 0 is 0. That is why those points become the sharp corners you see in a mod graph.

quickChecks.q: Starting from y = x − 3, draw y = |x − 3|. Which part changes?
steps: 1. The line y = x − 3 cuts the x-axis at x = 3.
2. For x > 3 the line is above the x-axis, so that part stays as it is.
3. For x < 3 the line is below the x-axis, so reflect it up: that piece becomes y = 3 − x.
4. At x = 3 the value is 0, so the point (3, 0) does not move.
quickChecks.answer: Only the part left of x = 3 changes. You get a V shape with its corner at (3, 0): y = 3 − x for x < 3 and y = x − 3 for x ≥ 3.

quickChecks.q: From y = x² − 4, draw y = |x² − 4|. Where are the corners and how high is the new hump?
steps: 1. x² − 4 = 0 gives x = −2 and x = 2, so the graph meets the x-axis at those two points.
2. For −2 < x < 2 the parabola is below the x-axis, so that arc is reflected up.
3. The lowest point was (0, −4); after reflection it becomes the highest point of the hump, (0, 4).
4. Outside −2 < x < 2 the parabola is already above the x-axis, so it stays unchanged.
quickChecks.answer: Corners at (−2, 0) and (2, 0), with a hump in between peaking at (0, 4); the two outer arms stay exactly as they were.

quickChecks.q: Can the graph of y = |f(x)| ever lie below the x-axis for some f?
steps: 1. Mod of any real number is either positive or zero.
2. So |f(x)| ≥ 0 for every x in the domain.
3. A point below the x-axis would need y < 0, which is impossible here.
quickChecks.answer: No. The graph can touch the x-axis where f(x) = 0, but it can never go below it.

concepts.title: Why |y| = f(x) is not a function
concepts.oneLine: In |y| = f(x), every x where f(x) ≥ 0 gives two y-values, y = ±f(x), so the curve is symmetric about the x-axis and has no graph at all wherever f(x) is negative.
notes: Take a curve y = f(x). Suppose it passes through the point (2, 7), so f(2) = 7. Now put x = 2 into the new equation |y| = f(x). You get |y| = 7, which means y = 7 or y = −7.
One x has given you two y-values, so |y| = f(x) is not a function — it is only a relation. A function is allowed one output for one input, and here 2 is sending you to both 7 and −7.

Second thing. Replace y by −y in |y| = f(x) and nothing changes, because |−y| = |y|. So whatever you draw above the x-axis, exactly the same thing appears below it. This curve is symmetric about the x-axis, not about the y-axis.

Third thing, and this is the one students forget. Suppose the curve passes through (4, −5), so f(4) = −5. Then |y| = −5, and a modulus can never be negative. Wherever f(x) is negative, no y exists, so there is simply no graph there. So the drawing is two steps: first erase the portion of y = f(x) that lies below the x-axis, then mirror whatever is left about the x-axis.

quickChecks.q: The graph of y = f(x) passes through (3, 4). Which points lie on |y| = f(x) at x = 3?
For the same f, f(−1) = −2. What does the graph of |y| = f(x) look like at x = −1?
steps: 2. A modulus can never be negative, so no y exists.
quickChecks.answer: Nothing at all — the graph does not exist at x = −1.

quickChecks.q: Is |y| = f(x) symmetric about the x-axis or the y-axis?
steps: 1. Replace y by −y: |−y| = |y|, so the equation is unchanged.
2. Replacing x by −x changes f(x) to f(−x), so nothing is guaranteed there.

concepts.title: Graphing y = ln(x + e) and its inverse for area
concepts.oneLine: Fix the log graph by its asymptote x = −e, flip it to x = e^y − e, and the area it bounds with y = e^(−x) collapses into one dy integral from y = 0 to 1.
notes: Start with y = ln(x + e). A log blows up where its inside becomes 0, so the asymptote is x + e = 0, that is x = −e. It is not x = 0 — that is the usual slip.
Now take two honest points. ln(x + e) = 0 when x + e = 1, so the curve cuts the x-axis at x = 1 − e. And at x = 0 the value is ln e = 1, so it passes through (0, 1).

The other curve in the question is given as x = ln(1/y). Don't be scared of the form, just free y: 1/y = e^x, so y = e^(−x). That is the ordinary falling exponential, and at x = 0 it is also 1. So both curves pass through the same point (0, 1) — that is your meeting point.

Now choose the strip. If you go vertically with dx, the top boundary swaps at x = 0 (log on the left, exponential on the right), so you are stuck with two integrals. Go horizontally instead: y runs from 0 to 1, and every strip starts on x = e^y − e and ends on x = −ln y — one integral, done in one shot.

quickChecks.q: Where is the asymptote and the x-intercept of y = ln(x + 2)?
steps: 1. Inside = 0: x + 2 = 0, so the asymptote is x = −2.
2. Inside = 1: x + 2 = 1, so x = −1.
quickChecks.answer: Asymptote x = −2; cuts the x-axis at (−1, 0).

quickChecks.q: Show that y = ln(x + e) and y = e^(−x) meet at (0, 1).
steps: 1. Put x = 0 in the log: y = ln(0 + e) = ln e = 1.
2. Put x = 0 in the exponential: y = e^0 = 1.
3. Both give y = 1 at the same x, so (0, 1) lies on both curves.

quickChecks.q: Evaluate the area you set up: A = ∫₀¹ (−ln y − e^y + e) dy.
steps: 1. Split it: A = ∫₀¹ (−ln y) dy − ∫₀¹ (e^y − e) dy.
2. First part: [y − y ln y] from 0 to 1 = (1 − 0) − 0 = 1.
3. Second part: [e^y − e y] from 0 to 1 = (e − e) − (1 − 0) = −1.

concepts.title: Graphs of sin x + cos x and |cos x − sin x| on [0°, 90°]
concepts.oneLine: On 0 to π/2, differentiate to see sin x + cos x rise to a peak √2 at π/4 and cos x − sin x fall from 1 to −1, then open the modulus as cos x − sin x before π/4 and sin x − cos x after it.
notes: Start with y = sin x + cos x on 0 to π/2. Differentiate: y′ = cos x − sin x. Put y′ = 0 and you get tan x = 1, so the only critical point inside the interval is x = π/4.

Now read the sign of y′ on either side. Before π/4 cos x is the bigger one and sin x is smaller, so y′ is positive and the curve rises. After π/4 sin x has grown past cos x, so y′ turns negative and the curve falls. So sin x + cos x is an arch: it starts at 1 when x = 0, climbs to a local maximum √2 at π/4, and comes back down to 1 at π/2.

Next curve: take cos x − sin x first and only then put the modulus on it. Differentiate: y′ = −sin x − cos x = −(sin x + cos x). On 0 to π/2 both sin x and cos x are positive, so y′ is always negative. That means cos x − sin x is a strictly decreasing function here — it starts at 1, cuts the x-axis at π/4, and ends at −1 at x = π/2.

The modulus is no big deal. Whatever part of the graph went below the axis, flip it up. So |cos x − sin x| opens as cos x − sin x on 0 to π/4 and as sin x − cos x on π/4 to π/2. That is why the next step cuts the area into two strips at π/4 — the upper curve stays sin x + cos x throughout, but the lower one changes its formula at π/4.

quickChecks.q: On 0 ≤ x ≤ π/2, where does sin x + cos x attain its maximum and what is the maximum value?
steps: 1. y′ = cos x − sin x = 0 gives tan x = 1, so x = π/4.
2. y′ > 0 before π/4 and y′ < 0 after it, so π/4 is a maximum.

quickChecks.q: At x = π/3, which expression does |cos x − sin x| open as, and what is its value?
steps: 1. π/3 is greater than π/4, so sin x is the bigger term there.
2. So the modulus opens as sin x − cos x.
quickChecks.answer: It opens as sin x − cos x, and the value is (√3 − 1)/2.

quickChecks.q: Show that cos x − sin x has no turning point in 0 < x < π/2.
steps: 1. Differentiate: y′ = −sin x − cos x = −(sin x + cos x).
2. On 0 < x < π/2 both sin x and cos x are positive, so sin x + cos x > 0.
3. Hence y′ < 0 everywhere in the interval and never becomes zero.
quickChecks.answer: y′ is strictly negative throughout, so the function only decreases — no turning point.

concepts.title: Area between the two curves: splitting the integral at π/4
concepts.oneLine: On [0°, 90°] the gap between sin x + cos x and |cos x − sin x| is 2 sin x before π/4 and 2 cos x after it, so the area splits into two integrals and comes to 4 − 2√2.
notes: Look at the picture we just drew. The top graph everywhere on [0°, 90°] is sin x + cos x. The bottom one is the mod graph, and the mod opens in two different ways.

Before π/4, cos x is bigger, so |cos x − sin x| = cos x − sin x. Subtract: (sin x + cos x) − (cos x − sin x) = 2 sin x. After π/4, sin x takes over, so the mod opens as sin x − cos x, and the gap becomes (sin x + cos x) − (sin x − cos x) = 2 cos x.
So the strip height changes at π/4, and that is exactly where the integral breaks: 2 sin x from 0 to π/4, then 2 cos x from π/4 to 90°. Nothing else about the question is hard.

Remember why the mod graph looks like that. Differentiate cos x − sin x and you get −(sin x + cos x), which is negative all through 0° to 90°, so that graph only falls — from +1 at 0° down to −1 at 90°. Taking mod lifts the part below the axis, and the corner sits at π/4 where the value is 0.

quickChecks.q: Evaluate ∫ 2 sin x dx from 0 to π/4.
steps: 1. Integral of 2 sin x is −2 cos x.
2. Put limits: −2 cos(π/4) − (−2 cos 0) = −2/√2 + 2.
3. −2/√2 = −√2, so the value is 2 − √2.

quickChecks.q: Evaluate ∫ 2 cos x dx from π/4 to π/2.
steps: 1. Integral of 2 cos x is 2 sin x.
2. Put limits: 2 sin(π/2) − 2 sin(π/4) = 2 − 2/√2.
3. 2/√2 = √2, so the value is 2 − √2.

quickChecks.q: What is the height of the vertical strip between the two curves at x = 60°?
steps: 1. 60° is after π/4, so the mod opens as sin x − cos x.
2. Height = (sin x + cos x) − (sin x − cos x) = 2 cos x.

concepts.title: Area enclosed by 2|x| + 3|y| ≤ 6 using symmetry
concepts.oneLine: When a region has |x| and |y| in it, it is symmetric about both axes — so draw it in the first quadrant only, find that area, and multiply by 4.
notes: Take the region 2|x| + 3|y| ≤ 6. Before drawing anything, test it. Replace x by −x — nothing changes. Replace y by −y — nothing changes.
So the region is symmetric about the x-axis and about the y-axis both. That one observation does all the work. Whatever shape appears in the first quadrant repeats in the other three quadrants.

In the first quadrant x ≥ 0 and y ≥ 0, so both mods open up as they are: 2x + 3y ≤ 6. Put y = 0, you get x = 3. Put x = 0, you get y = 2. Draw that line and keep only the piece sitting in the first quadrant — the rest of the line is going outside, so delete it.

Now reflect that piece in the y-axis, then reflect the whole thing in the x-axis. You end up with a four-sided region, a rhombus, made of four identical right triangles with legs 3 and 2. One triangle is ½ × 3 × 2 = 3, so the full area is 4 × 3 = 12. Nothing to do with integration.

quickChecks.q: Find the area of the region 3|x| + 4|y| ≤ 12.
steps: 1. Both −x and −y leave it unchanged, so it is symmetric about both axes.
2. First quadrant: 3x + 4y ≤ 12, with x-intercept 4 and y-intercept 3.
3. Triangle area = ½ × 4 × 3 = 6.

quickChecks.q: Find the area of the region |x| + |y| ≤ 5.
steps: 1. Symmetric about both axes.
2. First quadrant: x + y ≤ 5, intercepts 5 and 5.
3. Triangle area = ½ × 5 × 5 = 12.5.

quickChecks.q: Find the area of the region 3|x| + 2|y| ≤ 6.
steps: 1. Symmetric about both axes.
2. First quadrant: 3x + 2y ≤ 6, so x-intercept 2 and y-intercept 3.
3. Triangle area = ½ × 2 × 3 = 3.

concepts.title: Which side of a curve an inequality shades
concepts.oneLine: To find which side of a curve an inequality shades, either put (0, 0) in and see if it is satisfied, or stand at a point P on the curve, step straight up to P′, and check whether the expression grows.
notes: Take a line, say 2x + 3y = 6. The line itself is where 2x + 3y is exactly 6. The inequality 2x + 3y ≤ 6 is asking for one of the two sides. Which one?
Easiest way: put (0, 0) in. You get 0 ≤ 6, which is true. So the side of the line on which the origin sits is your region. That is the whole test.

Now the common sense way, and this is the one worth owning: stand at a point P on the curve, then go straight up to P′ — same x, bigger y — and ask whether the expression became bigger or smaller. At P, 2x + 3y = 6. At P′, x is unchanged and y has grown, so 3y has grown, so 2x + 3y is now greater than 6. But the requirement was ≤ 6. So going up was the wrong direction. Come down. The region is the part of the plane below the line.

Notice that nothing above used the fact that it was a straight line. The same step-up test works for a parabola, an ellipse or a hyperbola — put P on the curve, lift it to P′, see which way the expression moves. That is why it is worth owning this one test instead of memorising a rule for each shape.

quickChecks.q: Which side of x + y = 4 is the region x + y ≤ 4?
steps: 1. At P on the line, x + y = 4.
2. Step up to P′: x same, y bigger, so x + y becomes greater than 4.
3. I wanted ≤ 4, so up is the wrong direction — come down.
4. Origin check: 0 + 0 = 0 ≤ 4, true, and the origin is below the line.
quickChecks.answer: The side below the line x + y = 4, containing the origin.

quickChecks.q: Which side of 2x − y = 2 is the region 2x − y ≤ 2?
steps: 1. At P on the line, 2x − y = 2.
2. Step up to P′: x is unchanged, y increases, so −y decreases.
3. So the value at P′ is less than 2.
4. You want ≤ 2, and going up gave smaller, so up is the correct direction this time.
5. Origin check: 0 − 0 = 0 ≤ 2, true, and the origin does lie above this line.
quickChecks.answer: The side above the line 2x − y = 2, containing the origin.

quickChecks.q: Which side of x + 2y = 4 is the region x + 2y ≥ 4?
steps: 1. At P on the line, x + 2y = 4.
2. Step up to P′: x same, y bigger, so the value becomes greater than 4.
3. You want ≥ 4, so up is exactly the direction needed.
4. Origin check: 0 + 0 = 0 ≥ 4 is false, so the origin side is rejected — and the origin is below the line.
quickChecks.answer: The side above the line x + 2y = 4, the side away from the origin.

concepts.title: Region of a parabolic inequality x² + 3y ≤ 0
concepts.oneLine: Write the inequality as its curve, stand at a point P on that curve, step up or down, and the sign you get there is the sign of the whole region on that side.
notes: First, plot the curve. x² + 3y = 0 is just x² = −3y. The right side is negative when y is negative, so this parabola opens downward, with its vertex at the origin.
Now take any point P on the parabola. At P the expression x² + 3y is exactly 0 — that is what being on the curve means. Write that down every single time: at P, x² + 3y = 0.
From P, step straight down to a new point P′. Here is the only thing you have to notice: x² has not changed, because x is the same. Only y changed, and y got smaller.

So at P′ you are adding a smaller 3y to the same x². Earlier the total was 0, now it is less than 0. So the whole region below the parabola satisfies x² + 3y ≤ 0 — one point, one step, done. And nothing in that argument cared that it was a parabola. Do the same on an ellipse or a hyperbola and it works the same way.

quickChecks.q: Which side of x² = 2y satisfies x² − 2y ≤ 0?
steps: 1. Boundary: x² − 2y = 0, so x² = 2y, a parabola opening upward through the origin.
2. At a point P on it, x² − 2y = 0.
3. Step up to P′: x² is unchanged, y increases, so 2y increases and x² − 2y becomes less than 0.
4. So the side above the parabola works.
quickChecks.answer: The region above (inside) the upward parabola x² = 2y, boundary included.

quickChecks.q: Which side of the parabola x² = −3y satisfies x² + 3y ≥ 0?
steps: 1. Same boundary as in the worked example, where x² + 3y = 0 at every point P.
2. This time step up from P: x² is unchanged, y increases, so 3y increases.
3. The total becomes greater than 0.
4. So the region above (outside) the downward parabola is the answer.
quickChecks.answer: The region above the parabola x² = −3y, boundary included — exactly the other side of the worked answer.

quickChecks.q: Which side of the ellipse x²/4 + y²/9 = 1 satisfies x²/4 + y²/9 ≤ 1?
steps: 1. Take P = (0, 3), which lies on the ellipse. There x²/4 + y²/9 = 0 + 1 = 1.
2. Step down to P′ = (0, 2): x² is unchanged, and y²/9 becomes 4/9.
3. Now the value is 0 + 4/9 = 4/9, which is less than 1.
4. P′ is the point towards the centre, so the inequality holds on the inside.
quickChecks.answer: The region inside the ellipse, boundary included.

concepts.title: Area Common to a Circle and a Parabola
concepts.oneLine: For the region inside both y² = 3x and x² + y² = 4, slice it with a horizontal strip: the right leg comes off the circle, the left leg off the parabola, y runs 0 to √3, and you double for symmetry.
notes: First the picture, always. x² + y² ≤ 4 is the inside of the circle of radius 2 at the origin. y² ≤ 3x is the inside of the parabola that opens to the right. The region we want is the overlap — inside the circle and inside the parabola at the same time.

Now, which strip? If you go vertical, the top of your strip changes: up to the meeting point it is the parabola, after that it is the circle. That is two integrals for one small region. Take a horizontal strip instead and the whole region is covered by one integral: the right leg is on the circle, the left leg is on the parabola.

So at a height y, read the right end off the circle, x = √(4 − y²), and the left end off the parabola, x = y²/3. The strip length is right minus left. Both curves are symmetric about the x-axis, so work only with y from 0 up to the meeting height √3, and then double it.

That is the entire idea of this question — there is nothing new after it. In some very particular cases a shortcut exists and the answer drops out in seconds, but the strip method above never fails you.

quickChecks.q: Find the area of the region y² ≤ 2x, x² + y² ≤ 8.
steps: 1. Meeting point: x² + 2x − 8 = 0, (x + 4)(x − 2) = 0, so x = 2 and y = ±2.
2. Horizontal strip: right leg x = √(8 − y²), left leg x = y²/2, y from 0 to 2, doubled.

quickChecks.q: Find the area of the region y² ≤ x, x² + y² ≤ 2.
steps: 1. Meeting point: x² + x − 2 = 0, (x + 2)(x − 1) = 0, so x = 1 and y = ±1.
2. Strip: right leg x = √(2 − y²), left leg x = y², y from 0 to 1, doubled.

quickChecks.q: For the region y² ≤ 3x, x² + y² ≤ 4, write down the two legs of the horizontal strip at height y and the limits of integration, without integrating.
steps: 1. Right leg is on the circle: x = √(4 − y²).
2. Left leg is on the parabola: x = y²/3.
3. Curves meet at y = ±√3, and the region is symmetric about the x-axis.
quickChecks.answer: Length = √(4 − y²) − y²/3, with y from 0 to √3, and the integral multiplied by 2.

concepts.title: Parabola and Rectangle: the 1/3 – 2/3 Split
concepts.oneLine: For y² = 4ax cut by x = c, the area between the curve and the axis is (4/3)√a·c√c, and the parabola always splits the circumscribing rectangle into 2/3 (the axis side) and 1/3 (the vertex-tangent side).
notes: Take the parabola y² = 4ax and cut it with the vertical line x = c. The area A wanted here is the one between the curve and the x-axis, from the vertex up to that line. Vertical strip, as always: y = √(4ax) = 2√a·√x, and x runs 0 to c.

So A = ∫₀^c 2√a·√x dx = 2√a · (x^3/2)/(3/2) from 0 to c, which gives A = (4/3)√a·c√c. If the question asks for the total area bounded — both sides of the axis — the region is symmetric, so just double it: 8/3 · √a·c√c.

Now the nice part. Draw the rectangle on this piece: length c along the axis, and height up to the curve. At x = c the curve gives y = √(4ac) = 2√(ac), so the corner point is (c, 2√(ac)) and the rectangle's area is c × 2√(ac) = 2√a·c√c. Compare that with A. A is exactly 2/3 of the rectangle, and the leftover piece above the curve is exactly 1/3.

This is not special to one parabola. Any parabola of this family, whole rectangle or half rectangle, same answer: the parabola cuts its circumscribing rectangle into 2/3 and 1/3, with the 2/3 piece lying along the axis of the parabola. One figure, and the whole conclusion is in your hand.

quickChecks.q: Find the area bounded by y² = 4x, the x-axis and the line x = 4, using the rectangle trick.
steps: 1. Here 4a = 4, so a = 1 and c = 4.
2. At x = 4: y² = 16, y = 4. Corner is (4, 4).
3. Rectangle = 4 × 4 = 16.
4. Required area = (2/3) × 16 = 32/3.
quickChecks.answer: 32/3 square units (and the total area bounded by the parabola and x = 4 is 64/3).

quickChecks.q: For y² = 8x and the line x = 2, find the area between the parabola and the line x = 2, above the x-axis — that is, the piece above the curve inside the rectangle.
steps: 1. 4a = 8, so a = 2 and c = 2.
2. At x = 2: y² = 16, y = 4. Corner is (2, 4).
3. Rectangle = 2 × 4 = 8.
4. The piece above the curve is the 1/3 piece: (1/3) × 8 = 8/3.
5. Cross-check: the piece under the curve is (2/3) × 8 = 16/3, and 16/3 + 8/3 = 8.

quickChecks.q: The rectangle formed by y² = 16x, the x-axis, the y-axis and the line x = 1 is cut by the parabola. Write both pieces.
steps: 1. 4a = 16, so a = 4 and c = 1.
2. At x = 1: y² = 16, y = 4. Rectangle = 1 × 4 = 4.
3. Piece along the axis = (2/3) × 4 = 8/3.
4. Piece along the y-axis = (1/3) × 4 = 4/3.

concepts.title: Area Between Two Perpendicular Parabolas: 16ab/3
concepts.oneLine: For the region trapped between y² = 4ax and x² = 4by, the area is 16ab/3 — the product of the two latus recta divided by 3.
notes: Take the standard right-hand parabola y² = 4ax and the standard upward parabola x² = 4by. They meet at the origin and at one more point, and between them sits the leaf-shaped region.
The area of that region is 16ab/3. Nothing else is needed — no limits, no solving for the intersection point, no integration.

Now look at where 16ab comes from. The latus rectum of the first parabola is 4a, the latus rectum of the second is 4b, and 4a × 4b = 16ab. So the result is simply (LR of parabola 1) × (LR of parabola 2) ÷ 3.

Keep it in exactly that form in your notes. In revision you do not want to be scared of parabolas again — you want to glance at the two equations, pick off the two latus recta, multiply, divide by 3, and move on.

quickChecks.q: Find the area bounded by y² = 8x and x² = 12y.
steps: 1. y² = 4ax with 4a = 8, so a = 2.
2. x² = 4by with 4b = 12, so b = 3.

quickChecks.q: Find the area bounded by y² = 4x and x² = 4y.
steps: 1. Here 4a = 4 and 4b = 4, so a = 1 and b = 1.

quickChecks.q: Find the area bounded by y² = 16x and x² = 2y.
steps: 1. 4a = 16 gives a = 4; 4b = 2 gives b = ½.
2. Or straight from the latus recta: (16 × 2)/3.

concepts.title: Using 16ab/3 on an Exam Question
concepts.oneLine: Before using 16ab/3, force the coefficient of x² and y² to be 1 — then area = (LR₁ × LR₂)/3.
notes: Remember where 16ab/3 came from: y² = 4ax and x² = 4by. Both of those have the coefficient of y² and x² equal to 1. So in any question, first make the coefficient of x² (or y²) exactly 1, then read the latus rectum, then put it in the formula. Standard form first, LR second, formula third.
Here the curves are ax² = y and ay² = x. Divide the first by a and you get x² = (1/a)y. Divide the second by a and you get y² = (1/a)x. Now you can read it off: the latus rectum of each one is 1/a.

And the shortcut in LR language is simply: multiply the two latus recta and divide by 3. So the area here is (1/a)(1/a)/3 = 1/(3a²). The question says the area is 1, so 1/a² = 3, which gives a = 1/√3.

Do not feel that the formula is the only way. Both parabolas pass through (0, 0) and meet once more, so normal integration gives the same answer — it is not a big deal. The formula only saves you the two minutes you will want later in the paper.

quickChecks.q: Find the area bounded by y² = 4x and x² = 4y.
steps: 1. Both are already in standard form, so LR₁ = 4 and LR₂ = 4.

quickChecks.q: Find the area bounded by 2x² = y and 2y² = x.
steps: 1. 2x² = y → x² = y/2, so LR = 1/2.
2. 2y² = x → y² = x/2, so LR = 1/2.

quickChecks.q: If the area bounded by ax² = y and ay² = x (a > 0) is 4/3 square units, find a.
steps: 1. Standard forms: x² = (1/a)y and y² = (1/a)x, so both latus recta are 1/a.
3. So 1/a² = 4, giving a² = 1/4 and a = 1/2.

concepts.title: Parabola Cut by a Line: the (Δ)³ / 6·LR Shortcut
concepts.oneLine: A line cutting a parabola always leaves area |Δ|³ ⁄ (6 × LR), where Δ is the difference of the squared variable at the two meeting points and LR = 1/|coefficient of the square term|.
notes: Take a parabola of the y² = 4ax type and cut it with any line. The area trapped between the line and the curve is (y₂−y₁)³ divided by 6 times the latus rectum. For an x² = 4ay type parabola the same thing happens with x: (x₂−x₁)³ divided by 6 times the latus rectum.

Whichever variable is squared, that is the variable whose difference you take. Parabola is quadratic in y → use y₂−y₁. Parabola is quadratic in x → use x₂−x₁. A parabola can never be quadratic in both, so there is never a choice to agonise over.
Now note this down: this works for a shifted parabola too. y = x²+x+1, x = 2y²−y+3, anything. The shift does not touch the shortcut; you only have to read the latus rectum off the new form.

And reading LR is easy. Write the parabola as the plain variable equal to the quadratic one: y = ax²+bx+c gives LR = 1/a, and x = ay²+by+c gives LR = 1/a. Check it on y² = 4ax — divide across and you get x = (1/4a)y², coefficient 1/4a, so LR = 4a. Exactly what you already know. The deeper reason will be obvious to you in about ten days; for now the rule is enough.

quickChecks.q: For the parabola y = 2x²+3x+5, what is the latus rectum, and which difference would you use in the shortcut?
steps: 1. It is quadratic in x, coefficient of x² is 2.
3. Quadratic in x means the difference to use is x₂ − x₁.

quickChecks.q: Find the area enclosed between y = x² and the line y = 4.
steps: 1. Quadratic in x, so you need x₂ − x₁.
2. x² = 4 gives x = −2 and x = 2, so Δ = 4.
3. Coefficient of x² is 1, so LR = 1.

quickChecks.q: Find the area cut off from y² = 4x by the line y = x.
steps: 1. Quadratic in y, so you need y₂ − y₁.
2. Put x = y: y² = 4y, so y = 0 and y = 4, giving Δ = 4.
3. LR: x = (1/4)y², coefficient 1/4, so LR = 4.

concepts.title: Choosing x or y, and the Difference of Roots
concepts.oneLine: Whichever variable the parabola is quadratic in, kill the other one, cube that variable's difference of roots (√D/|a| — never solve), and divide by 6 times the latus rectum.
notes: Last part gave you the shortcut: area = (difference of roots)³ divided by 6 times the LR. Now the only doubt left is which difference — x₂ − x₁ or y₂ − y₁. Look at the parabola: whichever variable it is quadratic in, make your quadratic in that same variable.

If the parabola is quadratic in x, solve it with the line and let y disappear. If it is quadratic in y, solve it with the line and let x disappear. Either way you end up with one clean quadratic, and its two roots are exactly the two intersection points.
Second doubt: the roots come out ugly. Don't touch them. The difference of roots of any quadratic is √D/|a|, so you get Δ without ever solving. Cube that, divide by 6·LR, done.

And one small thing people overthink — take the LR of the parabola or read 1/|a| off the final quadratic, it is the same number. Removing the linear term never changes the coefficient of the squared variable, so a never changes.

quickChecks.q: Area bounded by y = 3x² − 2x + 4 and y = 4x + 4.
steps: 1. Quadratic in x, so eliminate y: 3x² − 2x + 4 = 4x + 4.
2. 3x² − 6x = 0, so x = 0 and x = 2, giving Δ = 2.

quickChecks.q: Area bounded by x = 2y² − 3y + 1 and x = y + 1.
steps: 1. Parabola is quadratic in y, so eliminate x: y + 1 = 2y² − 3y + 1.
2. 2y² − 4y = 0, so y = 0 and y = 2, giving Δ = 2.

quickChecks.q: Area bounded by x = 2y² − 5y + 1 and x = y + 2 (roots are ugly — use √D/|a|).
steps: 1. Quadratic in y: y + 2 = 2y² − 5y + 1, so 2y² − 6y − 1 = 0.

flashcards.q: What is the length of a vertical segment, in any quadrant?
flashcards.a: $$L = y_{upper} - y_{lower}$$Always y upper minus y lower, taken with signs. Minus 1 minus minus 7 gives 6 exactly as 7 minus 2 gives 5, so the rule never needs a quadrant check.

flashcards.q: Why is a definite integral not the same thing as an area?
flashcards.a: The integral is signed: wherever the curve lies below the axis it contributes a negative amount. An area is always positive, so you split at every crossing and take upper minus lower on each piece.

flashcards.q: Write the vertical stripe formula and say what the limits are.
flashcards.a: $$A=\int_{a}^{b}\big(y_{\text{upper}}-y_{\text{lower}}\big)\,dx=\int_{a}^{b}\big(f(x)-g(x)\big)\,dx$$Upper curve minus lower curve, integrated in x. Every y has to be written as a function of x, so the limits are x-values taken from the intersections.

flashcards.q: A curve crosses the x-axis at x = c inside your interval. What has to happen to the integral?
flashcards.a: $$A=\int_{a}^{c}\big(f(x)-0\big)\,dx+\int_{c}^{b}\big(0-f(x)\big)\,dx$$Split it at c. Up to c the stripe is f of x minus zero; after c the axis is the upper leg, so it is zero minus f of x. Write one integral across the crossing and the two parts cancel.

flashcards.q: Is the case where the x-axis forms one boundary a separate formula to learn?
flashcards.a: No. On the x-axis every y is zero, so putting that zero into upper minus lower reduces the stripe to f of x, or to zero minus f of x where the curve lies below the axis. One subtraction covers every case, and the sign comes out right by itself.

flashcards.q: Write the vertical-stripe set-up for the region between y = x squared, the x-axis and the walls x = minus 1 and x = 2.
flashcards.a: $$A = \int_{-1}^{2} \left( x^{2} - 0 \right) dx = \left[ \frac{x^{3}}{3} \right]_{-1}^{2} = 3$$The parabola is the upper boundary and the x-axis the lower one, so the integrand is x squared minus zero across the whole interval. The closing value 3 is this book's arithmetic on that set-up, not a number the lecture produced.

flashcards.q: Is x = minus 1 a horizontal or a vertical boundary, and does this region need splitting at the origin?
flashcards.a: Vertical. x equal to a number is always a vertical line and y equal to a number is always horizontal, so x = minus 1 and x = 2 are the left and right walls. No split is needed, because x squared is never negative and the curve stays above the axis throughout.

flashcards.q: What is the quickest way to sketch a line, with no slope work at all?
flashcards.a: $$\frac{x}{a} + \frac{y}{b} = 1$$Put x equal to zero for the y-intercept and y equal to zero for the x-intercept, then join the two points. You cannot plot the line wrongly that way.

flashcards.q: How do you find where y = x squared minus 4 meets y = minus x plus 2?
flashcards.a: $$x^2 - 4 = -x + 2 \;\Rightarrow\; x^2 + x - 6 = 0$$Eliminate y and solve the two equations together. The quadratic factorises and gives x equal to minus 3 and x equal to 2, and putting each x back into the line gives the points minus 3 comma 5 and 2 comma 0.

flashcards.q: Why is it not enough to name the upper curve once and start integrating?
flashcards.a: Because the upper curve can swap inside the interval. Test a point inside first: at the origin the line gives 2 and the parabola gives minus 4, so the line really is on top from minus 3 to 2 and one integral finishes it. Say that sentence out loud and check it holds right across the interval.

flashcards.q: The integral of sin x from zero to twice pi is zero. So what is the area between the curve and the axis there?
flashcards.a: $$A = \int_{0}^{\pi} \sin x \, dx + \int_{\pi}^{2\pi} (-\sin x) \, dx = 4$$It is 4, not zero. Split at pi: the stripe is sin x minus zero on the first half and zero minus sin x on the second. The zero is the lecture's point; the 4 is this book's arithmetic.

flashcards.q: How do you write a cubic down from its roots, and what else does the sketch need?
flashcards.a: $$y = x(x-1)(x-2)$$Multiply the factors: a cubic with roots 0, 1 and 2 is x times x minus 1 times x minus 2. Then fix the behaviour at the two ends, and check the sign in each gap by multiplying the signs of the factors.

flashcards.q: What is the least you need in order to sketch a cubic?
flashcards.a: Its three roots and its behaviour at the two ends. Plot the roots, fix the far-left and far-right directions, then read the sign in each gap from the signs of the factors. The sign must flip at every root, so the curve has nowhere else to go.

flashcards.q: For y = x squared and y = minus x squared plus 9 on the region from x = 0 to x = 3, is one integral enough?
flashcards.a: $$A = \int_{0}^{3/\sqrt{2}} \left[ (9 - x^2) - x^2 \right] dx \; + \; \int_{3/\sqrt{2}}^{3} \left[ x^2 - (9 - x^2) \right] dx$$No. The curves cross at x = 3 over root 2, and the legs trade places there: the height is 9 minus 2x squared before the crossing and 2x squared minus 9 after it. One crossing inside the limits means two integrals, so the integral must be broken.

flashcards.q: Where do the two parabolas y = x squared and y = minus x squared plus 9 cross, and what is that point for?
flashcards.a: $$x^2 = -x^2 + 9 \;\Rightarrow\; 2x^2 = 9 \;\Rightarrow\; x = \pm \frac{3}{\sqrt{2}}$$Set the two y's equal: 2x squared equals 9, so x is plus or minus 3 over root 2, with y equal to four and a half. That is the break point for the stripe, and it is not the same as x = 3, which is only where the downward parabola meets the axis.

flashcards.q: Over what stretch may the vertical-stripe formula be used as it stands?
flashcards.a: $$A = \int_a^b \left( y_{\text{top}} - y_{\text{bottom}} \right) dx$$Only over a stretch where neither boundary changes. Upper curve minus lower curve holds while the same two curves stay above and below; the moment they trade places that stretch ends and a fresh integral begins.

flashcards.q: Write the horizontal stripe formula and say why dy appears.
flashcards.a: $$A = \int_{c}^{d} \left( x_{\text{right}} - x_{\text{left}} \right)\, dy$$Right curve minus left curve, integrated in y. The stripe sweeps up and down, so y is what changes, and every x must be written as a function of y, which makes the limits y-values.

flashcards.q: Why does a horizontal stripe carry dy rather than dx?
flashcards.a: Because the stripe sweeps the region by moving up or down, so y is what changes, and the length itself is written in y. The integrand and the differential must speak the same language, so the limits are the smallest and largest y of the region.

flashcards.q: One leg of a horizontal stripe sits on the y-axis. What goes into the formula?
flashcards.a: $$A = \int_{c}^{d} \left( 0 - g(y) \right) dy$$That leg contributes x equal to zero, so the length is f of y minus zero if the curve is on the right, or zero minus g of y if it is on the left. If the curve crosses the axis inside the region, split at that y and add.

flashcards.q: Write the horizontal-stripe area for a region whose curve crosses the y-axis inside it.
flashcards.a: $$A = A_{1} + A_{2} = \int_{e}^{d} f(y)\, dy + \int_{c}^{e} \left( 0 - g(y) \right) dy$$Two integrals added, split at the switch point. Above it the curve lies to the right, so the stripe is f of y minus zero; below it the curve has gone to the left, so the stripe is zero minus g of y. One formula cannot be carried across the switch point.

flashcards.q: What does a leg of a stripe landing on the y-axis contribute?
flashcards.a: Zero, because on the y-axis x is always zero. The width then collapses to f of y minus zero, or to zero minus g of y when the curve sits on the left, and keeping that order is what makes the answer come out positive.

flashcards.q: The limits of a region are given in y. Which stripe do you take, and what does it give you here?
flashcards.a: $$A = \int_{1/2}^{2} \left( e^{y} - \ln y \right) dy$$A horizontal one. For the region between the exponential and the logarithm with y running from a half to 2, the stripe is the exponential's x minus the logarithm's x, and the whole region becomes one integral in y; vertical stripes would need splitting. The lecture stops at this set-up, so any number for it is supplied by this book.

flashcards.q: Rewrite y = ln x and y = e to the x with x as the subject.
flashcards.a: $$y = \ln x \iff x = e^{y} \qquad y = e^{x} \iff x = \ln y$$They become x equal to e to the y, and x equal to ln y. Same curves, different packaging, so rewrite rather than re-derive. It is the general logarithm-to-index flip doing the work.

flashcards.q: Which antiderivative do you need the moment a logarithm forms one end of a horizontal stripe?
flashcards.a: $$\int \ln y \, dy = y \ln y - y + C$$The integral of ln y, which is y ln y minus y plus a constant. It is wanted as soon as a log boundary has been rewritten as x in terms of y.

flashcards.q: Set up the same parabola-and-line region as a horizontal stripe.
flashcards.a: $$A=\int_{y_P}^{y_Q}\left(\frac{2y+3}{4}-\frac{y^{2}}{4}\right)dy$$Write both boundaries as x in terms of y: the line gives x equal to 2y plus 3 all over 4, the parabola gives x equal to y squared over 4. The stripe is the line's x minus the parabola's x, integrated in y between the two intersection points.

flashcards.q: Write the line 4x minus 2y = 3 in the form a horizontal stripe needs.
flashcards.a: $$4x-2y=3\ \Rightarrow\ x=\frac{2y+3}{4}$$Make x the subject: x equals 2y plus 3, all over 4. A thickness of dy forces every boundary into x as a function of y, and leaving a single x on the wrong side makes the integral impossible to evaluate.

flashcards.q: What is the fastest way to put a line on the page, and what is left once the stripe is set up?
flashcards.a: Two intercepts: put x equal to zero for one point and y equal to zero for the other, then join them, with no slope work. After that the only step left is the two y-coordinates of the intersection points, which become the limits.

flashcards.q: What are the three practice regions in this chapter actually asking for?
flashcards.a: Only the set-up. Plot the region, pick the stripe, write the integral and stop there; the stated reason is that the focus has come off integration. Do not treat any number you have seen for those three as a lectured result.

flashcards.q: How many of this chapter's areas are carried through to a number in the lectures?
flashcards.a: Two. The doubly symmetric modulus region is carried all the way to a number, and so is the exam question on the two-parabola shortcut; each of those values is stated in its own topic. Everywhere else the work stops at the stripe on purpose, the focus having come off integration. Any other value in this kit was supplied by the book, and each topic that carries one says so.

flashcards.q: Which stripe formula closes a region bounded above and below by curves?
flashcards.a: $$A = \int_{x_1}^{x_2} \left( y_{\text{top}} - y_{\text{bottom}} \right) dx$$The vertical one: top curve minus bottom curve, integrated in x between the x-limits. Use the horizontal one instead when the region is closed on its left and right. Fix the stripe direction first and the differential and the limits are then decided for you.

flashcards.q: For the region bounded by y squared = 4x and the line 4x minus 2y minus 3 = 0, how do you get the y-limits?
flashcards.a: $$y^2 - 2y - 3 = 0 \;\Rightarrow\; (y-3)(y+1) = 0 \;\Rightarrow\; y = -1,\; 3$$Eliminate x. Push the line's value of 4x into the parabola to get a quadratic in y, factorise it, and read y equal to minus 1 and y equal to 3. Limits always come from the intersections, never from the picture.

flashcards.q: Show the one-step elimination of x for a parabola written as y squared = 4x.
flashcards.a: $$y^2 = 4x, \quad 4x = 2y + 3 \;\Rightarrow\; y^2 = 2y + 3$$The parabola already carries 4x, so push the line's value of 4x in as one block and x disappears at once, leaving a plain quadratic in y. No fractions and no square roots appear on the way.

flashcards.q: Which variable do you eliminate, and where do the limits come from?
flashcards.a: Match the elimination to the variable you will integrate in: integrating in dy means eliminating x. The limits come from the intersections of the two given curves, never from the vertex or from the sketch — here the lower one is minus 1, which sits below the x-axis.

flashcards.q: An area is awkward with a vertical stripe and awkward with a horizontal one. What is the third route?
flashcards.a: $$A=\underbrace{e^{2}\cdot 1}_{\text{rectangle}}-\int_{e}^{e^{2}}\left(\ln x-1\right)dx$$Box the region inside a rectangle whose area you can read off, and subtract the easy stripe integral. Knowing both routes is what lets you pick the shorter one.

flashcards.q: Which antiderivative finishes the rectangle-minus-stripe route on a log boundary?
flashcards.a: $$\int \ln x\,dx = x\ln x - x + C$$The integral of ln x, which is x ln x minus x plus a constant. It is the only antiderivative the vertical route needs.

flashcards.q: Why learn the rectangle-minus-stripe route at all, when a stripe already works?
flashcards.a: Because some regions are half vertical and half horizontal, and some are a plain box with one small piece bitten out of it. Knowing both routes is what lets you look at a figure and choose the shorter one, and that choice costs nothing.

flashcards.q: Set up the area between y = e to the x, the line y = 1 over e squared and the line x = minus 1.
flashcards.a: $$\int_{-2}^{-1}\left(e^{x}-\frac{1}{e^{2}}\right)dx=\frac{1}{e}-\frac{2}{e^{2}}=\frac{e-2}{e^{2}}$$The curve meets the horizontal line at x = minus 2, so one vertical stripe runs from minus 2 to minus 1 with the exponential on top and the constant below. Keep the answer in e-form rather than going decimal; the closing value here is this book's arithmetic on the lecture's set-up.

flashcards.q: What is the two-second check on an area answer before you believe it?
flashcards.a: Box the region: multiply its x-width by the biggest vertical gap. The answer must come out below that ceiling. Here the box has base 1, from minus 2 to minus 1, so any value above the box's area is wrong on sight.

flashcards.q: Name the four parabola orientations and the tell that gives them away.
flashcards.a: $$y^2 = 4ax,\ a>0$$The right-opening and left-opening ones are squared in y and symmetric about the x-axis; the upward and downward ones are squared in x and symmetric about the y-axis. The variable that is not squared names the axis of symmetry, and its sign says which half-axis the curve opens along.

flashcards.q: Which way does y squared = minus 4ax open, and about which axis is it symmetric?
flashcards.a: $$y^2 = -4ax,\ a>0$$Left, along the negative x-axis, and symmetric about the x-axis. The left side is never negative and 4a is taken positive, so x must be zero or negative; only y is squared, so replacing y by minus y changes nothing.

flashcards.q: Where do x squared = y and x squared = minus y meet the line y = 4x minus 3, and what do the answers tell you?
flashcards.a: $$y = 4x - 3 \Rightarrow x = \frac{y+3}{4}$$The upward parabola gives the points 1 comma 1 and 3 comma 9. The flipped one gives x equal to minus 2 plus or minus root 7. Those surds are the signal that a vertical stripe is the wrong choice here, because a horizontal one keeps one leg on the line throughout.

flashcards.q: An intersection quadratic refuses to factorise. What then?
flashcards.a: $$x = \frac{-b \pm \sqrt{b^2 - 4ac}}{2a}$$Stop hunting for factors and use the quadratic formula. For x squared plus 4x minus 3 = 0 it gives x equal to minus 2 plus or minus root 7, and only the root near the origin borders the shaded region. Ugly roots rarely reach the final answer; they only tell you where the picture changes.

flashcards.q: What does replacing y by minus y do to x squared = y, and which stripe suits the region it makes?
flashcards.a: The shape does not change at all: the same parabola is reflected in the x-axis, so it opens downwards with the same vertex and you get a bow-tie around the origin. A horizontal stripe suits the closed patch, because its right leg stays on the line throughout while only the left leg swaps from one parabola to the other.

flashcards.q: Describe the curve y = 2 over 1 plus x squared, and say where it meets y = x squared.
flashcards.a: $$\frac{2}{1+x^2} = x^2 \;\Rightarrow\; x^4 + x^2 - 2 = 0 \;\Rightarrow\; (x^2-1)(x^2+2) = 0$$It is even, so symmetric about the y-axis; the denominator is smallest at the origin, so the maximum value is 2 there; and it tends to zero at both infinities. Against the parabola it meets at x equal to plus or minus 1. Any number quoted for the lens between them is supplied by this book.

flashcards.q: Find the maximum of y = 2 over 1 plus x squared without differentiating.
flashcards.a: $$y = \frac{2}{1+x^2}, \quad 1+x^2 \ge 1 \;\Rightarrow\; 0 < y \le 2$$The numerator is fixed, so y is largest where the denominator is smallest. The denominator is never below 1 and never zero, so y stays positive and reaches its maximum 2 at the origin.

flashcards.q: What is the usable form of the statement that a function is even?
flashcards.a: That the curve is symmetric about the y-axis, so you work out only the right half — the peak, the tail, the shape — and mirror it. The partner statement, that replacing y by minus y changes nothing, is symmetry about the x-axis, and such a relation is not a function of x.

flashcards.q: Run the full checklist on an unfamiliar curve, taking the quotient of x squared minus 1 and x squared plus 1 as the example.
flashcards.a: $$y=\frac{x^{2}-1}{x^{2}+1}\ \Rightarrow\ \frac{dy}{dx}=\frac{4x}{(x^{2}+1)^{2}}$$Even, so symmetric about the y-axis. Roots at plus and minus 1. Value minus 1 at the origin. It tends to 1 at both infinities without reaching it, so that is a horizontal asymptote. The derivative's denominator is a perfect square, so the sign of the derivative is the sign of x: decreasing then increasing. Curvature does not matter, because it never changes the area.

flashcards.q: What does a finite limit at infinity tell you about a curve?
flashcards.a: $$\lim_{x\to\pm\infty}\frac{x^{2}-1}{x^{2}+1}=1$$That the line at that value is a horizontal asymptote. For the quotient of x squared minus 1 and x squared plus 1 the limit at both infinities is 1, and setting the function equal to 1 has no solution, so the curve approaches that line without ever touching it.

flashcards.q: What is the fixed checklist for an unfamiliar curve?
flashcards.a: Even or odd, then the roots, then the value at the origin, then the limit at infinity for an asymptote, then the sign of the first derivative. Five answers and the shape is forced. Here the derivative's denominator is a perfect square, so the sign of the derivative is the sign of x alone.

flashcards.q: How do you draw a translated parabola or a translated V without memorising shift rules?
flashcards.a: $$y = (x - h)^2 + k$$Track the one key point. Set the squared bracket or the modulus to zero, read the y there, and draw the usual shape from that point. For a logarithm the same move gives the vertical asymptote and the domain.

flashcards.q: Where is the vertical asymptote and the domain of a shifted logarithm?
flashcards.a: $$y = \ln(x - a)$$Set the inside to zero for the asymptote and keep it positive for the domain. For a log of x minus a the asymptote stands at x equal to a and the domain is x greater than a. Copying the domain of the plain log is the usual slip.

flashcards.q: How do you avoid the shift-left and shift-right rules altogether?
flashcards.a: Solve instead of remembering. Set whatever sits inside the modulus, the square or the log to zero, put that x back into the whole expression to get the y, and draw the parent shape from that point. Sign mistakes vanish because you solved for x rather than recalling a direction.

flashcards.q: What is the period of f of ax, and how do you use it to draw a rescaled sine?
flashcards.a: $$\text{if period of } f(x) = T \text{ then period of } f(ax) = \frac{T}{|a|}$$The old period divided by the modulus of a. So keep the sine shape untouched and divide every marked x-value by the modulus of a: halve them for sin 2x, double them for sin of x over 2, multiply by two-thirds for sin of 3x over 2. Rescale the numbers, never squash the picture.

flashcards.q: What verifies a rescaled sine graph once you have relabelled it?
flashcards.a: One complete wave must end exactly at the period you computed. Divide every marked x-value by the modulus of a, then check the closing point: if it does not match the period, you divided the wrong way round.

flashcards.q: How do you draw f of mod x from f of x?
flashcards.a: $$f(|x|)=\begin{cases} f(x), & x\ge 0 \\ f(-x), & x<0 \end{cases}$$Throw away the part left of the y-axis, keep the part to the right, and mirror that right half across the y-axis. The function is even by construction, so the two halves have to agree.

flashcards.q: What is the one-line check that f of mod x must be even?
flashcards.a: $$f(|-x|)=f(|x|)$$The modulus of minus x equals the modulus of x, so the value at minus x is the same as the value at x. An even function can only be symmetric about the y-axis, and that single fact draws the curve for you.

flashcards.q: What happens to the original negative-x part of the graph when you draw f of mod x?
flashcards.a: It is discarded. Keep the graph only for x at least zero, where the modulus does nothing, then mirror that right half across the y-axis. Leaving the old left branch in place gives a graph with two different left halves.

flashcards.q: How do you draw the modulus of f of x?
flashcards.a: $$|f(x)| = \begin{cases} f(x), & f(x) \ge 0 \\ -f(x), & f(x) < 0 \end{cases}$$Keep every piece already above the x-axis as it is, and reflect every piece below the axis up above it. Nothing may stay negative, so a drawing that dips below the axis is wrong.

flashcards.q: What is the one-line check on a finished drawing of the modulus of f of x?
flashcards.a: $$|f(x)| \ge 0 \quad \text{for all } x$$No part of it may sit below the x-axis, because a modulus is never negative. The points where the original graph already touched the axis do not move, and those become the sharp corners.

flashcards.q: In the modulus of f of x, what happens to the part that was below the axis?
flashcards.a: It is reflected straight up, not erased. The x-axis acts as a mirror: everything already above it stays untouched and nothing is shifted sideways. The modulus sits on the output, which is why the mirror is the x-axis and not the y-axis.

flashcards.q: Why is mod y = f of x not a function, and how do you draw it?
flashcards.a: $$|y| = f(x) \iff y = \pm f(x), \quad f(x) \ge 0$$One x gives two y-values, plus and minus f of x. To draw it, delete every x where f of x is negative, because a modulus cannot equal a negative number, then keep what is left and mirror it across the x-axis, since replacing y by minus y changes nothing.

flashcards.q: Why is mod y = f of x symmetric about the x-axis?
flashcards.a: $$|-y| = |y|$$Because replacing y by minus y leaves the equation unchanged. So whatever is drawn above the axis appears identically below it, and every point you keep comes with its mirror image.

flashcards.q: In which two steps, and in which order, do you draw mod y = f of x?
flashcards.a: Erase first, then mirror. Erase every part of the curve lying below the x-axis, because a modulus cannot match a negative value and there is no graph there at all. Then reflect what survives about the x-axis. Mirror first and you reflect a piece that should not exist.

flashcards.q: Set up the area bounded by y = ln of x plus e, the curve y = e to the minus x and the x-axis. Does the lecture finish it?
flashcards.a: $$A = \int_{0}^{1}\left(x_{\text{right}} - x_{\text{left}}\right)dy = \int_{0}^{1}\left(-\ln y - e^{y} + e\right)dy$$No. The asymptote is fixed first, the log is inverted to x equal to e to the y minus e, and the other curve is written as minus ln y. Horizontal strips from y = 0 to y = 1 then give a single integral, and the lecture goes no further than that integral. The value 2 often quoted for it is supplied by this book, not produced in the lecture.

flashcards.q: Invert y = ln of x plus e, and say where its asymptote stands.
flashcards.a: $$y = \ln(x+e) \;\Longleftrightarrow\; x = e^{y} - e$$It becomes x equal to e to the y minus e. The asymptote follows the inside of the log: set x plus e to zero and it stands at x equal to minus e, not at the origin. Setting the inside to 1 instead gives the x-intercept at x equal to 1 minus e.

flashcards.q: How does sin x plus cos x behave between zero and a right angle, and how do you open the companion modulus?
flashcards.a: $$|\cos x - \sin x| = \begin{cases} \cos x - \sin x, & 0 \le x \le \frac{\pi}{4} \\ \sin x - \cos x, & \frac{\pi}{4} \le x \le \frac{\pi}{2} \end{cases}$$Differentiate: the derivative is cos x minus sin x, zero at a quarter of pi, positive before and negative after, so the curve rises from 1 to a peak of root 2 and comes back to 1. The companion curve cos x minus sin x decreases across the whole interval, so it crosses the axis once, and the modulus opens as cos x minus sin x before the corner and sin x minus cos x after it.

flashcards.q: How do you place the peak of sin x plus cos x between zero and a right angle?
flashcards.a: $$\frac{d}{dx}(\sin x + \cos x) = \cos x - \sin x$$Differentiate rather than guess. The derivative is cos x minus sin x, which vanishes where tan x equals 1, so the only critical point inside the interval is a quarter of pi. The derivative is positive before it and negative after it, so the curve rises from 1 to root 2 and falls back to 1.

flashcards.q: Why must cos x minus sin x be drawn before the modulus is put on it?
flashcards.a: Because the modulus has to be opened piecewise, and that needs the crossing. Its derivative is minus the sum of sin x and cos x, which is negative across the whole interval, so the curve falls steadily from 1 to minus 1 and crosses the axis exactly once. Only then do you lift the negative piece.

flashcards.q: Set up the area between sin x plus cos x and the modulus of cos x minus sin x. How much of this comes from the lecture?
flashcards.a: $$A=\int_{0}^{\pi/4}2\sin x\,dx+\int_{\pi/4}^{\pi/2}2\cos x\,dx$$The two integrals come from the lecture: split at a quarter of pi, with stripe height 2 sin x before it and 2 cos x after it. The closing number does not. Treat 4 minus 2 root 2 as this book's figure, supplied here rather than produced in the lecture, and do not quote it as a lectured result.

flashcards.q: What do the lectures for this chapter leave unfinished?
flashcards.a: Two regions are set up and never evaluated: the log pair and the trigonometric pair. The circle-and-parabola area is only quoted rather than worked, and most of a lettered run of plotting-region questions is left undone. Treat every value attached to those as supplied by this book, not as a lectured result.

flashcards.q: Open the modulus of cos x minus sin x on zero to a right angle.
flashcards.a: $$|\cos x-\sin x|=\begin{cases}\cos x-\sin x, & 0\le x\le \pi/4\\ \sin x-\cos x, & \pi/4\le x\le \pi/2\end{cases}$$Ask which term is bigger on each piece and write that one first. Before a quarter of pi cos x is bigger, so it opens as cos x minus sin x; after it sin x is bigger, so it opens as sin x minus cos x. The corner sits where the two are equal.

flashcards.q: Find the area enclosed by 2 mod x plus 3 mod y = 6 without integrating.
flashcards.a: $$\text{Area} = 4 \times \frac{1}{2} \times 3 \times 2 = 12$$It is 12, and this one really is a lectured result. The relation is unchanged when x or y changes sign, so it is symmetric about both axes: draw the line in the first quadrant only, from intercepts 3 and 2, take that right triangle's area of 3, and multiply by 4.

flashcards.q: When may you work one quadrant and multiply by 4?
flashcards.a: $$\text{Area}_{\text{total}} = 4 \times \text{Area in first quadrant}$$The moment both minus x and minus y leave the relation unchanged. A modulus in both variables does exactly that, so whatever shape appears in the first quadrant repeats in the other three.

flashcards.q: Why is there no integration in this region at all?
flashcards.a: Because the boundary is made only of straight lines. Once symmetry reduces the work to the first quadrant, the piece there is a right triangle read off the two intercepts, and the four copies make a rhombus. Checking symmetry and reading the shape is the whole method.

flashcards.q: Give the two ways of deciding which side of a boundary an inequality shades.
flashcards.a: $$P(x_0, y_0) \to P'(x_0, y_0 + h),\quad h > 0$$Test a convenient point, usually the origin: the side containing a point that satisfies the inequality is the shaded one. Or step off the boundary, where the expression equals the constant exactly, straight upwards so that y increases, and see whether the expression grows or shrinks. The second test is claimed for ellipses and hyperbolas too, though no worked example on either appears.

flashcards.q: Which side of the line 2x plus 3y = 6 does the inequality 2x plus 3y at most 6 shade?
flashcards.a: $$2x + 3y \le 6$$The side below it, which is the side containing the origin. Putting the origin in gives 0, which is at most 6, so that settles it; and stepping up from a point on the line makes the expression grow past 6, so up is the wrong direction.

flashcards.q: When does the origin test fail you, and what replaces it?
flashcards.a: It fails when the boundary passes through the origin, because there is then no side to read. Stand on the curve instead, where the expression equals its constant exactly, step straight up so that y increases, and see whether the value grows: if it grows and you wanted at most, come down.
