quickChecks.answer: x² + y² = 100, the circle of radius 10

concepts.title: Reducing a Question to Variable Separable Form
concepts.oneLine: Before you integrate, look for what is blocking separation — a 10ʸ sitting with dx, an e^(ax+ay) that is really a product, a right side that factorises — divide or factorise it away, then integrate.
notes: First order, first degree differential equations are in your syllabus, and variable separable is the base form of all of them. Base form means this is the shape you try to convert every other question into.
Integration has only one demand: every x must sit with dx, and every y must sit with dy. Nothing else. If that demand is met, the question is already done.

So when you open a question, don't start solving. Ask one line first: what is in the way here? In one question a 10ʸ is sitting with dx — 10ʸ cannot travel with dx. So divide the whole equation by 10ˣ·10ʸ and watch the troublemaker cancel.

Same idea, three costumes. Sometimes you cross multiply, sometimes you split a power of e into a product, sometimes you factorise the right side. In every case the function of y that was sitting with dx collapses, and the function of x that was sitting with dy collapses with it.

quickChecks.q: Solve 2ʸ dx + 2ˣ dy = 0.
steps: 1. Blockers: 2ʸ with dx, 2ˣ with dy. Divide the whole equation by 2ˣ·2ʸ.
2. You get dx/2ˣ + dy/2ʸ = 0.
3. Integrate: −(1/2ˣ)/ln 2 − (1/2ʸ)/ln 2 = constant.
4. Multiply by −ln 2.

quickChecks.q: Solve dy/dx = e^(2x + 2y).
steps: 1. Split the power: dy/dx = e²ˣ · e²ʸ.
2. Separate: (1/e²ʸ) dy = e²ˣ dx.
3. Integrate: −(1/e²ʸ)/2 = e²ˣ/2 + C.
4. Multiply by 2 and shift.

quickChecks.q: Solve dy/dx = (1 + x²)(1 + y²).
steps: 1. The right side is already factorised — one x-part, one y-part. The blocker is (1 + y²).
2. Divide by it: dy/(1 + y²) = (1 + x²) dx.
3. Integrate: tan⁻¹y = x + x³/3 + C.

concepts.title: Recap: variable separable form and particular solutions
concepts.oneLine: A differential equation can only be integrated once every x sits with dx and every y sits with dy, and a given point on the curve kills the constant C to give the particular solution.
notes: Look at it honestly. We have no machine that integrates a mixed-up equation. If the function of x is not sitting with dx and the function of y is not sitting with dy, integration simply cannot start. That is our helplessness, and that helplessness is the whole subject.

So variable separable is not really a "form" to memorise. It is the only state in which an equation becomes integrable. The terms start out scattered here and there, and the whole job is to push the x-part to the dx side and the y-part to the dy side. After that, integrate both sides and you are done.

When you integrate, a constant of integration appears. That answer, with the C still in it, is the general solution — it is a whole family of curves. In a particular solution question, some extra data is given to you, and that data exists only to remove C.

Usually that data is a point lying on the curve. Put the point in, solve for C, and the family collapses to one member. That single member is the particular solution. So from here on, there are only two roads: either the equation is directly variable separable, or we do some honest work and convert it into variable separable. Nothing else is possible. The forms we study next are nothing but that conversion work.

quickChecks.q: Solve dy/dx = 2x, given that y = 3 when x = 1.
steps: 1. Separate: dy = 2x dx.
2. Integrate both sides: y = x² + C.
3. This is the general solution. Now use the given point (1, 3): 3 = 1² + C, so C = 2.

quickChecks.q: Solve dy/dx = y/x for the curve passing through (1, 2).
steps: 1. Separate: dy/y = dx/x.
2. Integrate: ln|y| = ln|x| + ln k, so y = kx.

quickChecks.q: Solve dy/dx = (1 + y²)/(1 + x²) for the curve through the origin.
steps: 1. Separate: dy/(1 + y²) = dx/(1 + x²).
2. Integrate: tan⁻¹y = tan⁻¹x + C.
3. Put (0, 0): tan⁻¹0 = tan⁻¹0 + C, so C = 0.
4. Hence tan⁻¹y = tan⁻¹x, which gives y = x.

concepts.title: Form dy/dx = f(ax + by + c): substitute t
concepts.oneLine: If dy/dx = f(ax + by + c), put t = ax + by + c and the equation turns variable separable.
notes: Look at the right side of the equation. If the whole thing is some function of one linear bundle ax + by + c — squared, under a root, inside sin, inside a fraction, it does not matter — then you are in this form.
The moment you see dy/dx = f(ax + by + c), put t = ax + by + c and the equation becomes variable separable. That bundle is now one single letter, and the function on the right is just f(t).

Now differentiate the substitution with respect to x. From t = ax + by + c you get dt/dx = a + b·dy/dx, because a x gives a, b y gives b·dy/dx, and c is a constant. Replace dy/dx by f(t) and you have dt/dx = a + b·f(t).

That equation has only t on one side and only x on the other: dt/(a + b·f(t)) = dx. Integrate both sides, and at the very end put the bundle back in place of t. This is the whole method — it is not a new chapter, it is one line of effort to reach a form you already solved.

quickChecks.q: For dy/dx = (2x + 3y + 1)⁵, what substitution do you make and what does the equation become?
steps: 1. The right side is a function of the bundle 2x + 3y + 1, so put t = 2x + 3y + 1.
2. Differentiate: dt/dx = 2 + 3·dy/dx.
3. Replace dy/dx by t⁵: dt/dx = 2 + 3t⁵.
4. Separate: dt/(2 + 3t⁵) = dx.
quickChecks.answer: t = 2x + 3y + 1, and the separated form is dt/(2 + 3t⁵) = dx.

quickChecks.q: Separate dy/dx = 1/(x + y).
steps: 1. Put t = x + y, so here a = 1, b = 1, c = 0.
2. Differentiate: dt/dx = 1 + dy/dx.
4. Separate: t/(t + 1) dt = dx.
quickChecks.answer: t = x + y gives t/(t + 1) dt = dx, which is variable separable.

quickChecks.q: Separate dy/dx = x − y + 2.
steps: 2. Differentiate: dt/dx = 1 − dy/dx.
3. The equation says dy/dx = t, so dt/dx = 1 − t.
4. Separate: dt/(1 − t) = dx.
quickChecks.answer: t = x − y + 2 gives dt/(1 − t) = dx.

concepts.title: Worked example: dy/dx with (x + y)² and a²
concepts.quote: A student stopped me here and said, "Sir, x + y is not a linear function, how do I even integrate this?" Watch — one substitution and the whole thing collapses into variable separable.
concepts.oneLine: For dy/dx = a²/(x + y)², put t = x + y, use dy/dx = dt/dx − 1, split t²/(t² + a²) as 1 − a²/(t² + a²), and integrate to y = c + a·tan⁻¹((x + y)/a).
notes: Look at dy/dx = a²/(x + y)². The right side is not a function of x alone or y alone, so you cannot separate anything yet. But it only ever sees x + y as one block, and that is your signal.
Put t = x + y. Differentiate with respect to x: derivative of x is 1, derivative of y is dy/dx, derivative of t is dt/dx. So dt/dx = 1 + dy/dx, which means dy/dx = dt/dx − 1.

Feed both into the equation. dt/dx − 1 = a²/t², so dt/dx = 1 + a²/t² = (t² + a²)/t². Cross multiply and every t sits on one side, every x on the other: t²/(t² + a²) dt = dx. The substitution t = x + y is the entire chapter here — after it, whatever is left is only an integration question.

Now t²/(t² + a²) is quadratic upon quadratic, so you never integrate it as it stands. Make the same quadratic appear on top: add and subtract a². That gives 1 − a²/(t² + a²), and both pieces are standard. Integrate, put t = x + y back, cancel the x on both sides, and you are done.

quickChecks.q: Solve dy/dx = 1/(x + y)².
steps: 1. This is the same form with a = 1.
2. Put t = x + y, so dy/dx = dt/dx − 1, giving dt/dx − 1 = 1/t².
3. dt/dx = (t² + 1)/t², so t²/(t² + 1) dt = dx.
4. Split: 1 − 1/(t² + 1). Integrate: t − tan⁻¹t = x + c.
5. Put t = x + y: (x + y) − tan⁻¹(x + y) = x + c, and x cancels.

quickChecks.q: Solve dy/dx = 4/(x + y)².
steps: 1. Here a² = 4, so a = 2.
2. Put t = x + y: dt/dx − 1 = 4/t², so dt/dx = (t² + 4)/t².
3. Separate: t²/(t² + 4) dt = dx, and split as 1 − 4/(t² + 4).
4. Integrate: t − 4·(1/2)tan⁻¹(t/2) = x + c, i.e. t − 2tan⁻¹(t/2) = x + c.
5. Put t = x + y and cancel x from both sides.

quickChecks.q: In dy/dx = a²/(x + y)², after putting t = x + y, what does dy/dx become, and what is dt/dx equal to?
steps: 1. Differentiate t = x + y with respect to x: dt/dx = 1 + dy/dx.
2. So dy/dx = dt/dx − 1.
3. Substituting: dt/dx − 1 = a²/t², hence dt/dx = 1 + a²/t².

concepts.title: Practice solutions: choosing the substitution and surviving the integration
concepts.oneLine: t may be x + y, x + y + 1 or x + y − 1 without any harm; once t is in, kill the root with u² = 1 + t and cut quadratic-upon-quadratic down to linear-upon-quadratic.
notes: In the solution you will see t = x + y. You may well have put t = x + y + 1, or t = x + y − 1. It makes no difference: the extra constant dies the moment you differentiate, so dt/dx = 1 + dy/dx in every one of the three.

Usually the student picks the plain t = x + y, and that is fine. Whatever you pick, after you separate the variables the real question begins — the integral. If the integration goes well the question is only long; if it does not, it is madness.
Here the root has to disappear first. Put u² = 1 + t, so t = u² − 1 and dt = 2u du. The radical sign is gone and what is sitting in front of you is quadratic upon quadratic.

Split that numerator quadratic against the denominator so you are left with a constant plus linear upon quadratic — that is the boundary of this topic, and it does come in the exam. After integrating, put u = √(1 + t) back, then t = x + y back. Two substitutions in, two substitutions out.

quickChecks.q: If t = x + y − 1, write dy/dx in terms of dt/dx.
steps: 1. Differentiate both sides with respect to x: dt/dx = 1 + dy/dx − 0.
2. So dy/dx = dt/dx − 1.
quickChecks.answer: dy/dx = dt/dx − 1 — exactly the same as for t = x + y.

quickChecks.q: Evaluate ∫ dt/(1 + √(1 + t)).
steps: 1. Put u² = 1 + t, so t = u² − 1 and dt = 2u du.
2. The integral becomes ∫ 2u du/(1 + u).
4. Integrate: 2u − 2 ln|1 + u| + C.
5. Put u = √(1 + t) back.

quickChecks.q: Reduce (u² + 3)/(u² + 1) and integrate it with respect to u.
steps: 1. Split the numerator: u² + 3 = (u² + 1) + 2.
2. So the integrand is 1 + 2/(u² + 1).
3. Integrate: u + 2 tan⁻¹u + C.

concepts.title: Substituting t = 2x + 3y
concepts.oneLine: If dy/dx is a function of 2x + 3y, put t = 2x + 3y, use dt/dx = 2 + 3·dy/dx, and the equation turns into linear upon linear in t, which you integrate by splitting.
notes: Earlier the same thing was done with x + y. Now the question comes with 2x + 3y. Nothing changes, brother. Whatever sits inside the function — x + y, 2x + 3y, any ax + by + c — you call that whole thing t.

The only care is the differentiation. t = 2x + 3y gives dt/dx = 2 + 3·dy/dx. The 2 comes free, and the dy/dx carries a 3 with it. Replace dy/dx by the given function of t and the variables are separated in one step.

After separation you will almost always get something like t dt/(5t + 3) = dx. This is linear upon linear. Never cancel in linear upon linear — make the numerator look like the denominator, then split into two easy pieces.
Then integrate both sides, put t = 2x + 3y back, and clean the answer. The whole thing takes about three lines.

quickChecks.q: Solve dy/dx = 1/(2x + 3y).
steps: 2. Separate: t dt/(2t + 3) = dx.
4. Integrate: t/2 − (3/4)·ln|2t + 3| = x + C.
5. Put t = 2x + 3y and multiply by 4: 2(2x + 3y) − 3·ln|4x + 6y + 3| = 4x + C, i.e. 6y − 3·ln|4x + 6y + 3| = C.

quickChecks.q: For t = 2x + 3y, write dt/dx when dy/dx = (2x + 3y)².
steps: 1. dt/dx = 2 + 3·dy/dx.
2. dy/dx = t², so dt/dx = 2 + 3t².
quickChecks.answer: dt/dx = 2 + 3t², which separates as dt/(2 + 3t²) = dx

quickChecks.q: Integrate ∫ t dt/(3t + 1) by splitting.

concepts.title: Homogeneous equations: dy/dx = f(y/x) or f(x/y)
concepts.oneLine: If the sum of the powers is the same in the numerator and the denominator, the equation is homogeneous — write it as a function of y/x and put y = tx, so dy/dx = t + x·dt/dx.
notes: Look at the right side of your equation. If the whole thing can be written using only y/x, then put y/x = t. If it comes out nicely as x/y instead, put x/y = t. Either way, one new variable replaces two old ones.

Take y/x = t. That means y = tx. Now differentiate with respect to x, and remember both t and x are changing — so it is a product. Hold t and differentiate x, you get t·1. Hold x and differentiate t, you get x·dt/dx. So dy/dx = t + x·dt/dx. For the other case, x = ty gives dx/dy = t + y·dt/dy.

Now the real question: when can an equation be written purely in y/x or x/y? Only when it is homogeneous — the sum of the powers of x and y in the numerator equals the sum of the powers in the denominator. Add the powers term by term; every term must give the same total.

Check (x³ + y³)/(3x²y). In the numerator, x³ is degree 3 and y³ is degree 3. In the denominator, x²y is 2 + 1 = 3. Same degree, so it is homogeneous of degree 3. Divide the top and the bottom by x³ and it turns into (1 + (y/x)³) / (3(y/x)) — pure y/x, exactly what the substitution wants. If the degrees had not matched, no amount of dividing would have given you that.

quickChecks.q: Is dy/dx = (x² + y²)/(xy) homogeneous? If yes, write it in y/x form.
steps: 1. Numerator: x² gives 2, y² gives 2.
2. Denominator: xy gives 1 + 1 = 2.
3. All totals are 2, so it is homogeneous of degree 2.
4. Divide top and bottom by x²: (1 + (y/x)²) / (y/x).
quickChecks.answer: Yes, degree 2; dy/dx = (1 + (y/x)²)/(y/x), so put y = tx.

quickChecks.q: Is dy/dx = (x³ + y²)/(x²y) homogeneous?
steps: 1. Numerator: x³ gives 3, but y² gives only 2.
2. The two terms in the numerator do not even match each other.
3. Denominator: x²y gives 3.
quickChecks.answer: No. The powers do not add up to the same total, so it cannot be written as a function of y/x.

quickChecks.q: In dy/dx = (y² − x²)/(2xy) you substitute y = tx. Write what the left side becomes and what the right side becomes.
steps: 1. y = tx, so dy/dx = t + x·dt/dx.
2. Degrees: numerator 2 and 2, denominator 1 + 1 = 2 — homogeneous of degree 2.
3. Divide top and bottom by x²: ((y/x)² − 1) / (2(y/x)) = (t² − 1)/(2t).

concepts.title: Reducing questions to f(y/x) form
concepts.oneLine: Check that every term has the same total power, divide by that power of x to expose y/x — and when dy/dx comes squared, the quadratic formula splits one question into two differential equations and two families of solutions.
notes: Before you divide anything, do the power check. Add the powers of x and y in every single term: if the total is the same on top and at the bottom, the question will convert to y/x form — otherwise it will not. That one look decides whether this method is even allowed.

Once the check passes, divide by that power of x. If every term is power 2, divide top and bottom by x². If every term is power 1, divide by x only — not x². Then each piece becomes y/x, you put y/x = t, and the question is a standard homogeneous one.
Watch the root carefully. When you take an outside x inside a square root, it goes in as x². So √(x² − y²) divided by x is √(1 − (y/x)²), not √(1 − y/x). Same single rule, every time.

Now the one students fear: dy/dx sitting squared. Treat dy/dx as the unknown of a quadratic and use the quadratic formula — the ± then gives you two differential equations, and each one is solved separately to give its own family of solutions. Nothing new is happening. It is just the earlier question written twice.

quickChecks.q: Reduce dy/dx = (x² + y²)/(xy) to a function of y/x.
steps: 1. Power check: x², y² and xy are all of power 2 — top and bottom match.
2. Divide the numerator and the denominator by x²: top becomes 1 + (y/x)², bottom becomes y/x.
3. So dy/dx = (1 + (y/x)²)/(y/x). Put y/x = t.

quickChecks.q: Reduce x dy/dx = y − √(x² + y²) to a function of y/x.
steps: 1. Divide throughout by x, since every term is of power 1: dy/dx = y/x − √(x² + y²)/x.
2. The x enters the root as x²: √(x² + y²)/x = √(1 + (y/x)²).
3. So dy/dx = y/x − √(1 + (y/x)²).
quickChecks.answer: dy/dx = t − √(1 + t²), where t = y/x.

quickChecks.q: Reduce x(dy/dx)² + 2y(dy/dx) − x = 0. How many families of solutions will it give?
steps: 1. dy/dx is squared, so use the quadratic formula with a = x, b = 2y, c = −x.
2. dy/dx = (−2y ± √(4y² + 4x²))/(2x). Cancel the 2: dy/dx = (−y ± √(x² + y²))/x.
3. Take x into the root: dy/dx = −y/x ± √(1 + (y/x)²).
4. Two signs means two differential equations, each homogeneous in y/x.
quickChecks.answer: dy/dx = −y/x ± √(1 + (y/x)²); two differential equations, so two families of solutions.

concepts.title: Solving a homogeneous equation with a tan inverse term
concepts.oneLine: Divide by x to get dy/dx − y/x = (y/x)·tan⁻¹(y/x), put t = y/x, let the free t's cancel, and separate into dt/(t·tan⁻¹t) = dx/x.
notes: Start with x·dy/dx − y = y·tan⁻¹(y/x). Don't touch the tan⁻¹ yet. Just divide every single term by x.
You get dy/dx − y/x = (y/x)·tan⁻¹(y/x). Look at it now — the only thing living in this equation is y/x. The moment every term is a function of y/x, the substitution t = y/x is forced on you.
So put y = tx. Then dy/dx = t + x·dt/dx, by the product rule. The left side becomes t + x·dt/dx − t, and that lone t cancels straight away. The right side is t·tan⁻¹t.

What's left is x·dt/dx = t·tan⁻¹t. Now t goes with dt, and x goes with dx: dt/(t·tan⁻¹t) = dx/x. That's it, it's separated. The whole difficulty of the question was in two steps — divide by x, cancel the free t. Integrating this is the next job, and the right side of it is just an f′/f pattern waiting for you.

quickChecks.q: Reduce x·dy/dx − y = x·tan(y/x) to a separated form.
steps: 1. Divide by x: dy/dx − y/x = tan(y/x).
2. Put y = tx, so dy/dx = t + x·dt/dx.
3. t + x·dt/dx − t = tan t, so x·dt/dx = tan t.
4. Separate: cot t dt = dx/x.
quickChecks.answer: cot t dt = dx/x, with t = y/x.

quickChecks.q: Separate dy/dx − y/x = (y/x)·log(y/x).
steps: 1. Put y = tx, so dy/dx = t + x·dt/dx.
2. t + x·dt/dx − t = t·log t, so x·dt/dx = t·log t.
3. Separate: dt/(t·log t) = dx/x.
quickChecks.answer: dt/(t·log t) = dx/x, with t = y/x.

quickChecks.q: In x·dy/dx − y = y·tan⁻¹(y/x), after putting y = tx, which term cancels and what is left?
steps: 1. After dividing by x and substituting: t + x·dt/dx − t = t·tan⁻¹t.
2. The standalone t cancels with −t (that −t came from −y/x).
3. Nothing on the right cancels — the t multiplying tan⁻¹t stays.
quickChecks.answer: The free t cancels, leaving x·dt/dx = t·tan⁻¹t.

concepts.title: Finding the constant and spotting the f'/f integral
concepts.oneLine: Use the extra data in the question to kill the constant, and before you start splitting anything, check whether the integral is already f'(x)/f(x).
notes: There are two versions of the same problem. In one you have to find an extra constant, in the other you do not. That is the only reason the first one looks longer — the extra data is there so that the constant can be removed, nothing more.

Then comes the part where time leaks. After separating the variables you reach an integral that looks like one linear expression divided by another, and the hand automatically starts splitting it or hunting for a method.

Stop there and look up: very often the derivative of the denominator is already sitting in the numerator, written by you, one line above. The moment you see that, the whole thing is just f'(x)/f(x), and it closes in one step as a log.

So the problem was never long. What goes wrong is the clicking. After a page of algebra, with e raised to something and the right side split into pieces, your decision making gets tired and you stop noticing the obvious. That happens to everyone — the fix is to make this check a habit, not a flash of insight.

quickChecks.q: Integrate (2x + 3)/(x² + 3x + 5) with respect to x.
steps: 1. Differentiate the denominator: d/dx (x² + 3x + 5) = 2x + 3.
2. That is exactly the numerator, so this is f'(x)/f(x).
3. Write the log directly.

quickChecks.q: Integrate 2/(2x + 7) with respect to x. Do not split anything.
steps: 1. Denominator is f(x) = 2x + 7, so f'(x) = 2.
2. Numerator is 2, which is f'(x).
3. So the integral is ln|f(x)|.

quickChecks.q: Solve dy/dx = 2x/(x² + 1) given that y = 3 when x = 0.
steps: 1. Derivative of x² + 1 is 2x, which is the numerator — so it is f'/f.
2. Integrating: y = ln|x² + 1| + C.

concepts.title: Substitution that turns an equation into a homogeneous one
concepts.oneLine: Expand sin 2y, call sin y = t, and a strange-looking equation becomes a plain homogeneous equation in t and x — which u = t/x then separates.
notes: Substitution in differential equations works exactly the way it works in indefinite integration. You are not solving the equation yet — you are only renaming things until a known shape shows up.

Here the denominator has sin 2y. Write it as 2 sin y cos y, and now both terms of the denominator carry a cos y, so pull it out: cos y (2 sin y − x). Shift that cos y to the left and the left side is cos y · dy/dx.

The moment you see cos y · dy/dx sitting next to sin y, the equation is telling you to put t = sin y. Differentiate t = sin y and you get dt/dx = cos y · dy/dx, which is precisely the left side. The whole equation collapses to dt/dx = (t + x)/(2t − x) — homogeneous in t and x, and a very simple one.

From there it is the usual story. Divide top and bottom by x, put u = t/x, remember dt/dx = u + x du/dx, and separate. Most students happily substitute in a linear differential equation but never think of substituting in a homogeneous one — that is the new idea in this question.

quickChecks.q: Solve cos y · dy/dx = (2 sin y + x)/(sin y − 2x).
steps: 1. Put t = sin y, so dt/dx = cos y · dy/dx and the equation becomes dt/dx = (2t + x)/(t − 2x), homogeneous in t and x.
2. Put u = t/x, so dt/dx = u + x du/dx: u + x du/dx = (2u + 1)/(u − 2).
4. Separate: (u − 2)/(1 + 4u − u²) du = dx/x. Derivative of the bottom is 4 − 2u = −2(u − 2), so the left side is −½ · f'/f.
5. −½ ln|1 + 4u − u²| = ln|x| + c, so x²(1 + 4u − u²) = C.
6. Put u = sin y / x: x² + 4x sin y − sin²y = C.

quickChecks.q: Integrate ∫ (2u − 1)/(1 + 2u − 2u²) du.
steps: 1. Derivative of the denominator: 2 − 4u = −2(2u − 1).
2. So the numerator is −½ of that derivative, and the integrand is −½ · f'/f.

quickChecks.q: Which of these is ready for the substitution u = t/x: (i) dt/dx = (t + x)/(2t − x), (ii) dt/dx = (t² + x)/(2t − x)?
steps: 1. In (i) every term on the top and the bottom is of degree one in t and x, so dividing by x leaves a function of t/x alone — homogeneous.
2. In (ii) the top mixes degree two (t²) with degree one (x), so dividing by x does not give a function of t/x only.
quickChecks.answer: Only (i); u = t/x works there. (ii) is not homogeneous.

concepts.title: Linear upon linear: shifting the origin
concepts.oneLine: When dy/dx is linear upon linear, shift the origin to where the two lines meet — the constants die, the equation turns homogeneous, and you substitute back with X = x − a, Y = y − b.
notes: Look at dy/dx = (x − 2y + 5)/(2x + y − 1). Cover the +5 and the −1 with your thumb. What is left is (x − 2y)/(2x + y), which is homogeneous — divide top and bottom by x and everything becomes a function of y/x. So the only thing standing between you and a method you already know is two constants.

Now think like a straight-line question. x − 2y + 5 = 0 and 2x + y − 1 = 0 are two lines, and they meet at one point. Shift the origin to that intersection point, and in the new coordinate system both lines pass through the origin — which means their constant terms disappear. That is the whole trick.

Call the new world capital X and capital Y. If the origin moves to (a, b), then X = x − a and Y = y − b. In the X–Y world the equation is clean and homogeneous, so you put Y = vX and integrate as usual. Since a shift is just a translation, dY/dX = dy/dx — nothing changes on the left side.

One last step, and this is where marks leak: the question was asked in small x and small y, so the answer must come back in small x and small y. Put X = x − a and Y = y − b into your solution at the end. And this only works because the two lines actually meet — if they are parallel there is no intersection point to shift to, which is exactly the next case I take up.

quickChecks.q: For dy/dx = (x + y − 3)/(x − y − 1), write the shift you would use and the equation you get.
steps: 1. Solve x + y − 3 = 0 and x − y − 1 = 0 together: adding gives 2x = 4, so x = 2 and then y = 1.
2. Intersection is (2, 1), so shift with X = x − 2 and Y = y − 1.
3. Both constants die and the equation becomes dY/dX = (X + Y)/(X − Y), which is homogeneous — put Y = vX.
quickChecks.answer: X = x − 2, Y = y − 1, giving dY/dX = (X + Y)/(X − Y).

quickChecks.q: Why can you not use shifting of origin on dy/dx = (x − 2y + 5)/(2x − 4y − 1)?
steps: 1. Check the coefficients: 1 : −2 and 2 : −4 are proportional, since 1×(−4) = (−2)×2.
2. So the two lines are parallel and never intersect.
3. There is no intersection point to shift the origin to, so this method has nothing to stand on.
quickChecks.answer: The lines are parallel, so there is no intersection point — this needs the parallel-line method instead.

quickChecks.q: The answer above is written as (x + A)² − 4(x + A)(y + B) − (y + B)² = C. Find A and B.
steps: 1. The shift was X = x + 3/5 and Y = y − 11/5.
2. Compare: x + A = x + 3/5 gives A = 3/5, and y + B = y − 11/5 gives B = −11/5.
3. Both come straight from the intersection point (−3/5, 11/5).

concepts.title: When the two lines are parallel
concepts.oneLine: If the two linear expressions are parallel (a₁/a₂ = b₁/b₂), there is no meeting point to shift the origin to, so that trick is dead and the question is solved directly.
notes: Remember what the shift was doing. For dy/dx = (a₁x + b₁y + c₁)/(a₂x + b₂y + c₂), the numerator and the denominator are treated as two straight lines; you find where they meet and move the origin to that point. The constants die there and the equation becomes homogeneous.

That whole idea stands on one thing: the two lines must meet somewhere. If a₁/a₂ = b₁/b₂, the two lines are parallel — they never intersect, so there is no point (h, k) to shift to, and the method simply does not apply.

So in a parallel case, do not go hunting for h and k. Such a question is solved directly, straight away, with the substitution that suits it. The parallel look is itself the hint that this is a different form.

A fair question here is whether such an equation can be cross multiplied. For cross multiplication you need a particular type of setting in the expressions — the previous question had it, this one does not. Cross multiplying here is just not possible; that technique belongs to a different setting.

quickChecks.q: Can the origin be shifted for dy/dx = (2x + 3y − 1)/(4x + 6y + 5)?
steps: 3. Equal, so the lines are parallel.
quickChecks.answer: No. The lines are parallel, there is no intersection point, so this one is solved directly.

quickChecks.q: Can the origin be shifted for dy/dx = (x − 2y + 4)/(3x + y − 7)?
steps: 3. Unequal, so the two lines meet at exactly one point.
quickChecks.answer: Yes. Find the meeting point, shift the origin there, and the equation becomes homogeneous.

quickChecks.q: Which form is dy/dx = (x + y + 1)/(2x + 2y + 3)?
steps: 1. a₁/a₂ = 1/2 and b₁/b₂ = 1/2.
2. Equal ratios, so numerator and denominator are parallel lines.
quickChecks.answer: The parallel case — no shifting, solve it directly.

concepts.title: The three forms so far
concepts.oneLine: Three forms so far: variable separable, dy/dx = f(ax + by + c), and homogeneous dy/dx = f(y/x) or f(x/y) — each with its own fixed substitution.
notes: Start from where we began the chapter: variable separable. All the y stuff on one side with dy, all the x stuff on the other side with dx, then integrate both sides. That is form number one.

Then came the second one. dy/dx = function of (ax + by + c). The whole right side depends on that one single bundle ax + by + c, so you give that bundle a new name and the equation collapses into a separable one.

Third is the homogeneous type. Call it homogeneous, call it anything you like — the name is not the point; the form is: dy/dx = f(y/x) or dy/dx = f(x/y). If the right side can be written purely in terms of y/x, put y = vx. If it comes out purely in terms of x/y, put x = vy.

So the checklist on any new equation is short. Can it be separated? No — can the right side be squeezed into one bundle ax + by + c? No — can it be squeezed into y/x or x/y? Every one of these three ends the same way: a substitution that turns the equation back into variable separable. And one more big form is still left to come.

quickChecks.q: Which form is dy/dx = (1 + y²)/(1 + x²), and how do you start?
steps: 1. The right side is an x part divided by a y part, and they come apart cleanly.
2. Write dy/(1 + y²) = dx/(1 + x²).
3. Integrate both sides: tan⁻¹y = tan⁻¹x + C.
quickChecks.answer: Form 1, variable separable — separate and integrate.

quickChecks.q: Which form is dy/dx = (x + y + 1)², and what substitution do you use?
steps: 1. The whole right side depends only on the bundle x + y + 1.
2. So this is dy/dx = f(ax + by + c) with a = 1, b = 1, c = 1.
3. Put v = x + y + 1, so dv/dx = 1 + dy/dx = 1 + v², which is now separable: dv/(1 + v²) = dx.

quickChecks.q: Which form is dy/dx = (x² + y²)/(xy), and what substitution do you use?
steps: 1. Divide numerator and denominator by x²: dy/dx = (1 + (y/x)²)/(y/x).
2. The right side is now purely a function of y/x, so it is homogeneous.
3. Put y = vx, dy/dx = v + x dv/dx, giving v + x dv/dx = (1 + v²)/v, so x dv/dx = 1/v — separable.

concepts.title: Recognising a linear differential equation
concepts.oneLine: An equation is linear in y when y and dy/dx both sit at power one, are added and not multiplied, no other function of y appears, and any function of x is allowed — and the same four checks work with the variables swapped.
notes: Start with the equation being linear in y. Then dy/dx must be there, and with it y must sit at power one — y¹, not y², not √y, not sin y. The derivative and the y are added, never multiplied — the moment you see y·dy/dx, it is not linear.
Next, no other function of y is allowed anywhere in the equation. Only y to the power one, and only added on. And the derivative itself is written just once, to the first power.
Now the generous part. Any function of x can appear — any function at all. x², sin x, e^x, log x, all of it is fine, because x is the independent variable here and the test never looks at it.

Here is the part that is missed most often. The same four checks apply with the roles swapped. If the equation is linear in t and the other variable is y, you need dt/dy, t to the power one, no other term containing t — and then anything can happen to y. The structure is identical; only the names change.

quickChecks.q: Is dy/dx + y = x² linear in y?
steps: 1. dy/dx is present and y is at power one.
2. They are added, not multiplied.
3. No other function of y appears; x² is a function of x, which is allowed.

quickChecks.q: Is y·dy/dx + y = x linear in y?
steps: 1. y and dy/dx are both at power one, so the powers look fine.
2. But they are multiplied together in the first term.
3. Multiplication of the unknown with its derivative breaks the test.
quickChecks.answer: No — dy/dx is multiplied by y.

quickChecks.q: Is dt/dy + t = y³ + sin y linear in t?
steps: 1. The derivative dt/dy is present and t sits at power one.
2. The two t terms are added, not multiplied, and no other term contains t.
3. y³ and sin y are functions of the independent variable y, so they are allowed.

concepts.title: Is it linear in y or linear in x?
concepts.oneLine: Check the y side only: if y and dy/dx both sit at power 1 it is linear in y; if a ln y or y² spoils that, flip to dx/dy and see whether it is linear in x instead.
notes: Here is the only test that matters. Look at y and dy/dx. Both must be power 1, and y must not be sitting inside anything — no y², no ln y, no y multiplying dy/dx. Whatever is written in x does not matter at all: 3, 1/x, sin x, x³ — all of it is allowed as a coefficient.
So the breakers are always on the y side. A second y in a product, like y·dy/dx, breaks it. A y² breaks it. A ln y breaks it. The moment you see one of those, stop calling it linear in y.

But do not throw the equation away yet. Take the reciprocal of both sides and look at it as dx/dy — many equations that are not linear in y are perfectly linear in x. Now the roles swap: x and dx/dy must be power 1, and anything in y is allowed as a coefficient.
That is how the sixth type of question is built. dy/dx = −(ln y)/x looks hopeless. Flip it and you get dx/dy = −x/ln y, which is dx/dy + (1/ln y)x = 0. Linear in x, and solvable.

quickChecks.q: Classify dy/dx = 1/(x + y).
steps: 1. y sits in the denominator, so it is not linear in y.
2. Take the reciprocal: dx/dy = x + y.
3. Standard form: dx/dy − x = y, so P(y) = −1 and Q(y) = y.

quickChecks.q: Classify dy/dx + (sin x)y = x⁵.
steps: 1. y is power 1 and dy/dx is power 1.
2. sin x and x⁵ are functions of x only, which is allowed.
3. Matches dy/dx + P(x)y = Q(x) with P(x) = sin x.

quickChecks.q: Classify dy/dx + y² tan x = x.
steps: 1. y appears as y², so it is not linear in y.
2. Flip it: dx/dy = 1/(x − y² tan x); x still appears mixed with y² inside the denominator.
3. So the dx/dy form is not of the type dx/dy + P(y)x = Q(y) either.
quickChecks.answer: Neither — not linear in y, not linear in x.

concepts.title: Standard form and the integrating factor
concepts.oneLine: First make the coefficient of dy/dx (or dx/dy) equal to 1, then the integrating factor is e raised to the integral of the coefficient of y — and for an equation linear in x, of the coefficient of x, integrated with respect to y.
notes: After recognising that the equation is linear, write it in the standard form. Standard form means only one thing: the coefficient of dy/dx must be 1. Whatever sits with y, and whatever sits on the right hand side, does not matter — P and Q can be functions of x or plain constants.

Once it is in standard form, we solve in two steps. The first step is to find a quantity called the integrating factor. Why that name? I will show you in the derivation; it is a very easy one. For now, learn to build it.
The rule is simple. Take the coefficient of y, integrate it, and put the answer on top of e. That is your integrating factor. So for dy/dx + Py = Q, the I.F. is e raised to ∫P dx.

And if the equation is linear in x instead of y, nothing changes in spirit. Write it as dx/dy with coefficient 1, then take the coefficient of x, integrate it with respect to y, and put that on top of e. Same story, roles of x and y swapped — the four worked equations here do exactly this.

quickChecks.q: Find the integrating factor of dy/dx + (3/x)y = x².
steps: 1. Coefficient of dy/dx is already 1.
2. Coefficient of y is 3/x; ∫(3/x) dx = 3 ln x = ln x³.
3. I.F. = e^(ln x³) = x³.

quickChecks.q: Find the integrating factor of x dy/dx + 2y = x⁴.
steps: 1. Not in standard form, so divide by x: dy/dx + (2/x)y = x³.
2. ∫(2/x) dx = 2 ln x = ln x².
3. I.F. = e^(ln x²) = x².

quickChecks.q: Find the integrating factor of y dx/dy − x = y³.
steps: 1. This is linear in x, so make the coefficient of dx/dy equal to 1: divide by y.
2. dx/dy − x/y = y². Coefficient of x is −1/y.
3. ∫(−1/y) dy = −ln y, so I.F. = e^(−ln y) = 1/y.

concepts.title: What the solution of a linear equation looks like
concepts.oneLine: In an equation linear in y, y shows up exactly once and only to the power one — every other piece is a function of x, because the coefficient of y only builds the integrating factor and the right-hand side Q gets integrated along with it.
notes: Look at the standard form again: dy/dx + P y = Q, where P and Q are functions of x. Now ask a simple question before you write a single line of solution — where can y possibly appear in the answer? In a linear differential equation in y, y comes only once in the whole solution, and only as y to the power one. Everything else you write is a function of x.

The reason is in the structure itself. The integrating factor is e raised to ∫P dx, and P is a function of x, so the integrating factor is a function of x. Q is a function of x. So the only y in the entire line is the one y sitting next to the integrating factor.

That gives each piece one clear job. The coefficient of y, that is P, has exactly one job — to build the integrating factor. The right-hand side Q has exactly one job — to get integrated together with the integrating factor and hand you the answer. P never gets integrated with Q; it gets integrated and lifted on top of e.

The same logic flips cleanly when the equation is linear in x: dx/dy + P x = Q with P and Q functions of y. Here the integrating factor comes from ∫P dy, so it is a function of y, and x appears once in the whole answer, as x to the power one. Even if P is just a constant, you still integrate it and raise it on e. Have clarity at this level and the next step writes itself.

quickChecks.q: For dy/dx + (1/x)y = x², write the shape of the solution without solving the final integral. Where does y appear, and is the integrating factor a function of x or of y?
steps: 1. It is linear in y, so P = 1/x and Q = x², both functions of x.
2. P's job is only to build the integrating factor: IF = e^(∫(1/x)dx) = e^(ln x) = x, a function of x.
3. Q's job is to be integrated with the integrating factor.
4. Shape: y·x = ∫ x²·x dx + C = ∫ x³ dx + C.
quickChecks.answer: y appears exactly once, at power one; IF = x, a function of x. Shape: y·x = ∫x³ dx + C, that is yx = x⁴/4 + C.

quickChecks.q: The equation (x + y)dy/dx = 1 is not linear in y. Rearrange it and say which variable it is linear in, what the integrating factor is, and where that variable appears in the answer.
steps: 1. Flip it: dx/dy = x + y.
2. Bring it to standard form: dx/dy − x = y. So it is linear in x, with P = −1 and Q = y, both functions of y.
3. IF = e^(∫(−1)dy) = e^(−y), a function of y — a constant P still gets integrated and lifted on e.
4. Shape: x·e^(−y) = ∫ y·e^(−y) dy + C.
quickChecks.answer: Linear in x; IF = e^(−y); x appears exactly once, at power one, and everything else is a function of y.

quickChecks.q: Which of these is linear in y, and why is the other one not? (i) dy/dx + y² = x (ii) dy/dx + xy = x
steps: 1. Test: does y appear exactly once and only to the power one?
2. In (i), y sits at power 2, so it fails the test — it is not linear in y.
3. In (ii), y appears once at power one, its coefficient x is a function of x, and the right side x is a function of x.
quickChecks.answer: (ii) is linear in y, with P = x and Q = x. (i) is not, because of the y² term.

concepts.title: The solution formula y·(IF) = ∫(IF)·Q dx
concepts.oneLine: Once the IF is in your hand, the answer is one line: y·(IF) = ∫(IF)·Q dx + c — multiply, cancel, integrate.
notes: The formula is the whole method. For dy/dx + Py = Q, once you have the integrating factor, you write y·(IF) = ∫(IF)·Q dx + c. Nothing else is left to think about.

Always multiply (IF) into Q first, simplify, and only then integrate. Students who integrate in a hurry make it look like a monster. If you cancel first, the integral is usually something you already know by heart.
In both worked examples the IF came from the same place — P was of the form 2x/(something), so the IF turned out to be that something itself. The moment it sits next to Q, the denominator collapses.
And don't forget the + c. It is not decoration; it is the family of solutions. One mark gone for nothing is the cheapest mark to lose.

quickChecks.q: Solve dy/dx + (2x/(1 + x²))y = 1/(1 + x²).
steps: 1. IF = 1 + x².

quickChecks.q: Solve dy/dx + (2x/(x² − 1))y = x/(x² − 1).
steps: 1. IF = x² − 1.

quickChecks.q: Solve dy/dx + (2x/(1 + x²))y = 2x/(1 + x²).
steps: 1. IF = 1 + x².

concepts.title: Solutions when the equation is linear in x
concepts.oneLine: When the equation is linear in x, the solution line becomes x·(IF) = ∫(IF)·Q dy + C — same formula, roles swapped.
notes: Look at what we have. We already found the integrating factor for both of these, so the thinking part is over. Now we only write the solution line.

When the equation is linear in x, every single thing changes partner: x sits where y used to sit, and dy sits where dx used to sit. So the line is x·(IF) = ∫(IF)·Q dy + C. Nothing new to remember, just a swap.

In the first one the product inside is y(2 ln y + 1), and that needs by parts. In the second one the product collapses to 1/y², which is a plain power integral. Always multiply IF and Q first and look at what you are left with — many times a scary Q becomes a one-step integral.

About the by-parts: there are two ways to break y(2 ln y + 1), and neither is worth an argument. Take the whole bracket as the first function, because its derivative is 2/y and that kills the y beautifully.

quickChecks.q: An equation linear in x gives IF = y and Q = 1/y². Find the solution.
steps: 1. x·y = ∫ y·(1/y²) dy + C
2. y/y² = 1/y, so x·y = ∫ (1/y) dy + C = ln y + C

quickChecks.q: An equation linear in x gives IF = y and Q = ln y. Find the solution.
steps: 1. x·y = ∫ y ln y dy + C
2. By parts with ln y as first function: (ln y)·y²/2 − ∫ (1/y)·(y²/2) dy
3. = (y²/2) ln y − ∫ (y/2) dy = (y²/2) ln y − y²/4

quickChecks.q: An equation linear in x gives IF = y and Q = 1/y⁴. Find the solution.
steps: 1. x·y = ∫ y·(1/y⁴) dy + C = ∫ y⁻³ dy + C

concepts.title: Quiz review: integrating factor e^(−sin y) and a JEE Advanced 2014 question
concepts.oneLine: When the equation is linear in x, the integrating factor is e^(∫P(y)dy) — so with P(y) = −cos y you get e^(−sin y), minus sign and all.
notes: Look at your quiz work again. The equation was linear in x, not in y, so it is written as dx/dy + P(y)x = Q(y) and the integrating factor becomes e raised to ∫P(y)dy.

Here P(y) came out as −cos y. Now integrate: ∫cos y dy = sin y, so ∫P(y)dy = −sin y. That is why the integrating factor is e^(−sin y). The minus does not sit outside the e, it goes up into the power with the integral.

That is the only place the error crept in. Everything before it — spotting that the equation was linear in x, swapping the roles of x and y, picking out P(y) — all of that was correct. So fix one line and your solution is full marks.

Then comes the next one: a very popular JEE Advanced 2014 linear differential equation, built on exactly this idea. Before solving it, ask yourself why this thing is called an "integrating factor" at all — that is where the next section starts.

quickChecks.q: Find the integrating factor of dx/dy + (sin y)x = y.
steps: 1. P(y) = sin y.
2. ∫sin y dy = −cos y.
3. I.F. = e^(−cos y).

quickChecks.q: Find the integrating factor of dx/dy + x/y = y², for y > 0.
steps: 2. ∫(1/y)dy = ln y.
3. I.F. = e^(ln y) = y.

quickChecks.q: Find the integrating factor of dx/dy − (sec² y)x = tan y.
steps: 1. P(y) = −sec² y, minus sign included.
2. ∫(−sec² y)dy = −tan y.
3. I.F. = e^(−tan y).

concepts.title: Why the Integrating Factor Works
concepts.oneLine: Multiply dy/dx + Py = Q by e^(∫P dx) and the left side collapses into d(y·IF)/dx — that single fact is the whole integrating factor method.
notes: Start with the standard linear equation: dy/dx + Py = Q, where P and Q are functions of x. Now multiply every single term by the integrating factor e^(∫P dx). Left side gives e^(∫P dx)·dy/dx plus e^(∫P dx)·Py, and the right side gives Q·e^(∫P dx).

Look carefully at those two terms on the left, and ask one question: what is d/dx of y·e^(∫P dx)? Product rule — derivative of y times e^(∫P dx), plus y times the derivative of e^(∫P dx), and that derivative is e^(∫P dx)·P, because the derivative of ∫P dx is just P again.

That is exactly the two terms we got. So after multiplying by the integrating factor, the whole left side is nothing but the derivative of one product: d/dx(y·IF). Nothing has to be done to the right side; it is already Q·IF.

Now take the dx across: d(y·IF) = Q·IF dx. Integrate both sides and the left side integrates in one step to y·IF, while the right side becomes ∫Q·IF dx plus the constant. The integrating factor is called that because it is the one multiplier which makes the left side exactly integrable.

quickChecks.q: For dy/dx + y/x = x², find the integrating factor and write the left side as a single derivative.
steps: 1. Here P = 1/x, so ∫P dx = ln x and IF = e^(ln x) = x.
2. Multiply throughout by x: x·dy/dx + y = x³.
3. Left side is exactly d/dx(y·x), since the derivative of xy is x·dy/dx + y.
quickChecks.answer: IF = x, and the equation becomes d(xy)/dx = x³.

quickChecks.q: Find d/dx of y·e^(2x), and from it say which linear equation has IF = e^(2x).
steps: 1. Product rule: e^(2x)·dy/dx + y·2e^(2x) = e^(2x)(dy/dx + 2y).
2. Compare with e^(∫P dx)(dy/dx + Py): here P = 2.
quickChecks.answer: d/dx(y·e^(2x)) = e^(2x)(dy/dx + 2y); so IF = e^(2x) belongs to dy/dx + 2y = Q.

quickChecks.q: For dy/dx + y·tan x = sec x, build the integrating factor and show the left side becomes an exact derivative.
steps: 1. P = tan x, so ∫tan x dx = ln(sec x) and IF = e^(ln sec x) = sec x.
2. Multiply throughout: sec x·dy/dx + y·sec x·tan x = sec²x.
3. Left side is d/dx(y·sec x), because the derivative of sec x is sec x·tan x.
quickChecks.answer: IF = sec x, and the equation becomes d(y·sec x)/dx = sec²x.

concepts.title: Integrating Factor on an Inequality: Proving p(x) > 0
concepts.oneLine: Multiply an inequality by the integrating factor e^(−x): the left side becomes d/dx(p(x)e^(−x)), so p(x)e^(−x) is increasing, and comparing it with its value at x = 1 proves p(x) > 0.
notes: Read the given line carefully. It says p'(x) − p(x) > 0, with a greater-than sign, not an equal-to sign. So this is not a linear differential equation — nobody knows that better than me. But look at the shape of it: it is exactly the shape of a linear equation.

So do what you would have done if it were one. To write less, call p(x) simply y. The coefficient of y is −1, so the integrating factor would be e^(∫−1 dx) = e^(−x). Multiply the whole inequality by e^(−x).
The inequality direction does not flip, because e^(−x) is positive for every x — and the left side collapses into one single derivative, d/dx(y·e^(−x)). So we get d/dx(p(x)e^(−x)) > 0.

Now it is pure application of derivatives. A function whose derivative is positive is increasing. So u(x) = p(x)e^(−x) is increasing, which means for x > 1 we get u(x) > u(1). Put the values in and the result falls out.

quickChecks.q: A differentiable function f satisfies f'(x) > 2f(x) for all x > 0 and f(0) = 0. Show that f(x) > 0 for x > 0.
steps: 1. Write it as f'(x) − 2f(x) > 0. Coefficient of f is −2, so the multiplier is e^(∫−2 dx) = e^(−2x).
2. Multiply by e^(−2x), which is positive, so the sign stays: e^(−2x)f'(x) − 2e^(−2x)f(x) > 0.
3. The left side is d/dx(f(x)e^(−2x)), so f(x)e^(−2x) is increasing on x > 0.
4. Hence f(x)e^(−2x) > f(0)·e^0 = 0, and since e^(−2x) > 0, we get f(x) > 0.

quickChecks.q: A differentiable function h satisfies h'(x) + h(x) < 0 for all x > 0 and h(0) = 0. What can you say about the sign of h(x) for x > 0?
steps: 1. Coefficient of h is +1, so the multiplier is e^(∫1 dx) = e^x, which is positive.
2. Multiplying: e^x h'(x) + e^x h(x) < 0, that is d/dx(h(x)e^x) < 0.
3. So h(x)e^x is a decreasing function on x > 0, giving h(x)e^x < h(0)·e^0 = 0.
4. Divide by e^x > 0.

quickChecks.q: In the inequality g'(x) − 3g(x) > 0, what function should you multiply throughout by, and what does the left side become?
steps: 1. Coefficient of g is −3, so the integrating factor is e^(∫−3 dx) = e^(−3x).
2. After multiplying, the left side packs into a single derivative.
quickChecks.answer: Multiply by e^(−3x); the left side becomes d/dx(g(x)e^(−3x)), so g(x)e^(−3x) is increasing.

concepts.title: Reducible to Linear: Substitution and Bernoulli's Equation
concepts.quote: Your eye is trained to see dy/dx with a lonely y. So the moment sec²y shows up next to dy/dx, the question looks new. It is not — one substitution and you are back on the linear differential equation you already know.
concepts.oneLine: If an equation shows f′(y)·dy/dx sitting with f(y), put t = f(y) and it becomes a plain linear DE in t — and Bernoulli's equation is only this same trick after dividing by yⁿ.
notes: Till now every linear equation you solved had dy/dx and a plain y. That is a habit of the eye. Many questions hide the same equation behind a function of y.

Look at the shape f′(y)·dy/dx + P(x)·f(y) = Q(x). Here f′(y) is sitting right beside dy/dx, and f(y) is standing alone in the next term. Put t = f(y); then f′(y)·dy/dx is exactly dt/dx, and the whole thing turns into dt/dx + P(x)·t = Q(x) — a linear differential equation in t. After that it is the same old story: integrating factor, integrate, done.

Bernoulli's equation is this and nothing more. It is written as dy/dx + P(x)·y = Q(x)·yⁿ. Divide the whole equation by yⁿ and you get (1/yⁿ)·dy/dx + P(x)·y¹⁻ⁿ = Q(x). Now y¹⁻ⁿ is your f(y), its derivative is sitting with dy/dx, so take t = y¹⁻ⁿ.

Honestly, I cannot teach you anything new here. The only skill is getting the substitution — after that you are back in known territory. And one more thing: finish in t, then put f(y) back so your answer is in y.

quickChecks.q: Reduce e^y · dy/dx + e^y = x to a linear differential equation and write its integrating factor.
steps: 1. e^y sits with dy/dx and e^y also appears alone, so take t = e^y.
2. Differentiate: e^y · dy/dx = dt/dx.
3. The equation becomes dt/dx + t = x.
4. Here P(x) = 1, so I.F. = e^(∫1 dx) = eˣ.
quickChecks.answer: t = e^y gives dt/dx + t = x, with I.F. = eˣ

quickChecks.q: Reduce the Bernoulli equation dy/dx + y = y² to a linear differential equation in t.
steps: 1. n = 2, so divide throughout by y²: (1/y²)·dy/dx + (1/y) = 1.
2. Take t = −1/y, so dt/dx = (1/y²)·dy/dx and (1/y) = −t.
3. Substitute: dt/dx − t = 1.
quickChecks.answer: t = −1/y gives dt/dx − t = 1, with I.F. = e^(−x)

quickChecks.q: For cos y · dy/dx + (sin y)/x = x², what is the substitution and the integrating factor?
steps: 1. cos y is the derivative of sin y, and sin y stands alone, so take t = sin y.
2. Then cos y · dy/dx = dt/dx, and the equation becomes dt/dx + t/x = x².
3. P(x) = 1/x, so ∫(1/x) dx = ln x and I.F. = e^(ln x) = x.
quickChecks.answer: t = sin y gives dt/dx + t/x = x², with I.F. = x

concepts.title: Practice: Reducing Four Equations to Standard LDE
concepts.oneLine: Four reducible equations, one routine: match the y-group to a derivative (tan y, ln y, y², 1/y), put t there, force the derivative's coefficient to 1, then read P and write IF = e^∫P dx.
notes: In every one of these four, only two things have to happen. First, convert it to a standard LDE in t — and standard means the coefficient of the derivative is 1. Second, find the integrating factor. You do not have to finish the solving here; leave that for your own practice.

The substitution is never a guess: look at the y-group and ask which function's derivative is already sitting in front of dy/dx. sec²y in front means t = tan y. A 1/y after dividing means t = ln y. A 2y means t = y². A 1/y² means t = 1/y.

One more thing that saves you every time. Here dy/dx is written, not dx/dy. So the linear equation has to come out in x as the independent variable, which means t must be a function of y only. That is why dividing by x or by tan x to "simplify" leads nowhere; you divide by whatever makes the y-part match a derivative.
After that the integration is usually tiny, because the derivative you need is already in the question — 2x with e^(x²), cos x with sin x. Look for that before you start grinding.

quickChecks.q: Reduce to standard linear form and find the IF: sec²y (dy/dx) + tan y = x³.
steps: 1. sec²y in front of dy/dx, tan y elsewhere, so t = tan y and dt/dx = sec²y (dy/dx).
2. Equation becomes dt/dx + t = x³, so P = 1.
quickChecks.answer: t = tan y, dt/dx + t = x³, IF = e^x.

quickChecks.q: Reduce to standard linear form and find the IF: x (dy/dx) + y ln y = x y e^x.
steps: 1. Divide by y: (x/y)(dy/dx) + ln y = x e^x.
2. Divide by x to make the derivative's coefficient 1: (1/y)(dy/dx) + (ln y)/x = e^x.
3. Put t = ln y: dt/dx + t/x = e^x, so P = 1/x.
4. IF = e^(∫dx/x) = x.
quickChecks.answer: t = ln y, dt/dx + t/x = e^x, IF = x.

quickChecks.q: Reduce to standard linear form and find the IF: dy/dx + y/x = y².
steps: 1. Highest power of y on the right is y², so divide by y²: (1/y²)(dy/dx) + 1/(xy) = 1.
2. Put t = 1/y, so dt/dx = −(1/y²)(dy/dx). This gives −dt/dx + t/x = 1.
3. Multiply by −1: dt/dx − t/x = −1, so P = −1/x.

concepts.title: When an Equation Already Looks Linear: the y^(−2) Substitution
concepts.oneLine: If a question is already linear in y but carries a block like (y − 2), just call that block t — since dt/dx = dy/dx, the equation stays linear and the integrating factor here is 1/(x+1).
notes: Look at the equation first, before you obey the instruction. dy/dx is sitting there, y comes with power 1, so this is already a linear differential equation. Only one thing disturbs you: y does not come alone, it comes as the block (y − 2) divided by (x+1).

So clean that block. Put t = y − 2. Differentiate: dt/dx = dy/dx, because the 2 is a constant and dies. The substitution costs you nothing — dy/dx becomes dt/dx directly, so the equation stays linear, just in t instead of y.

Now it is the standard shape: dt/dx − t/(x+1) = (x+1)². Here P = −1/(x+1), so ∫P dx = −ln(x+1), and the integrating factor is e^(−ln(x+1)) = 1/(x+1). The minus in front of the log flips it, nothing more.

After that it is the same two lines you do every day: t × IF = ∫ (IF × Q) dx. The 1/(x+1) eats one power of (x+1)² and you are integrating (x+1) — that is it. These dressed-up substitution questions are rare in Mains and common in Advanced, but the maths inside them is always easier than the wrapping.

quickChecks.q: Solve dy/dx − (y − 3)/(x + 2) = (x + 2)².
steps: 1. Put t = y − 3, so dt/dx = dy/dx.
2. Equation: dt/dx − t/(x + 2) = (x + 2)², with P = −1/(x + 2).

quickChecks.q: What is the integrating factor of dt/dx − t/(x + 1) = x + 1?
Solve dy/dx + (y + 5)/x = x.
steps: 1. Put t = y + 5, so dt/dx = dy/dx.
2. Equation: dt/dx + t/x = x, with P = 1/x.
3. ∫P dx = ln x, so I.F. = x.
4. t·x = ∫ x·x dx = x³/3 + C.
5. t = x²/3 + C/x, and t = y + 5.

concepts.title: Practice: A Creative Substitution Problem
concepts.oneLine: When the same bundle 2y + x keeps repeating in an equation, call it v — the frightening question collapses into a plain variable-separable one.
notes: Look at the question before you start solving. The same combination 2y + x is sitting in the numerator and in the denominator. That repetition is the hint.

When one bundle repeats, give it one new name: v = 2y + x. Now differentiate carefully. dv/dx = 1 + 2·dy/dx, so dy/dx = (dv/dx − 1)/2. Notice the 2 — it comes from the 2y, and most students lose it right here.

Put that into the equation and every x and y disappears. You are left with only v on one side and x on the other — variable separable, the very first form you learnt. After that it is only an integration, and even that splits into a constant plus a log.

So the whole difficulty of the question was in its looks, not in its work. In competition the paper is designed to look dangerous and turn out small. Spend ten seconds hunting for the repeating bundle before you panic.

quickChecks.q: Solve dy/dx = x + 2y using the same substitution.
steps: 1. Put v = 2y + x, so dv/dx = 1 + 2·dy/dx.
2. Then dv/dx = 1 + 2(x + 2y) = 1 + 2v.
3. Separate: dv/(1 + 2v) = dx.
4. Integrate: ½ ln|1 + 2v| = x + C.
5. So ln|1 + 2v| = 2x + C, and v = 2y + x gives ln|1 + 2x + 4y| = 2x + C.

quickChecks.q: Solve dy/dx = 1/(x + 2y).
steps: 1. Put v = 2y + x, so dv/dx = 1 + 2·dy/dx = 1 + 2/v = (v + 2)/v.
2. Separate: v/(v + 2) dv = dx.
4. Integrate: v − 2 ln|v + 2| = x + C.
5. Put v = 2y + x back: x + 2y − 2 ln|x + 2y + 2| = x + C, so 2y − 2 ln|x + 2y + 2| = C.

concepts.title: Exact Form: Standard Partial Differentials to Recognise
concepts.oneLine: Exact form means you spot a known differential like d(xy), d(y/x), d(x/y) or d(eˣ/y) sitting inside the equation, and integrate it straight back.
notes: The exact form is also called the partial derivative method. The idea is simple: you look at the equation, apply a little wisdom, and realise that the terms in front of you are already somebody's derivative. Once you see whose derivative it is, you just integrate it back.
You have already used this without naming it. In the earlier proof the derivative was made by observation and then integrated back — that was exactly this method at work.

So you need to recognise a few standard differentials. d(xy) by product rule gives x dy + y dx. d(y/x) by quotient rule gives (x dy − y dx) divided by x². d(x/y) gives (y dx − x dy) divided by y². Notice the pattern: the denominator gets squared, and the numerator starts with the derivative of the top with the bottom held still.

Do not memorise the whole list — learn to derive any of them with the product or quotient rule, and keep only d(xy), d(y/x) and d(x/y) in your head. Those three are the common ones and the easy ones. For the rest, the moment you need d(eˣ/y) or anything like it, you write the quotient rule and it appears.

quickChecks.q: You see the terms y dx + x dy in a differential equation. What is this the differential of?
steps: 1. Compare with the product rule: x dy + y dx.
2. Addition order does not matter, so it is the same expression.

quickChecks.q: The expression (y dx − x dy)/y² appears in a question. Which exact differential is it?
steps: 1. The denominator is y², so the function has y at the bottom.
2. The numerator starts with y dx, that is the derivative of x with y held still.
3. So the function is x/y.

quickChecks.q: Derive d(x/eʸ) using the quotient rule.
steps: 1. Denominator is eʸ, so eʸ squared, that is e²ʸ, goes below.
2. Hold eʸ still and differentiate x: that gives eʸ dx.
3. Minus: hold x still and differentiate eʸ: that gives x eʸ dy.
4. So d(x/eʸ) = (eʸ dx − x eʸ dy)/e²ʸ, and one eʸ cancels.

concepts.title: Finding the Exact Differential from the Problem Terms
concepts.oneLine: Split the equation into harmless terms (x-stuff with dx, y-stuff with dy) and problem terms, then force the problem terms into d(xy) and integrate.
notes: Look at every term one at a time and ask one question only: can this be integrated as it stands? x² dx is a function of x sitting with dx, so it is harmless. y² dy is a function of y sitting with dy, also harmless.
Now the troublemakers. −ay dx has a y sitting with dx. −ax dy has an x sitting with dy. Neither one can be integrated alone, so these are the problem terms.

Alone those two terms are useless; together they are exactly d(xy). Pull out the common −a and look inside: y dx + x dy. That is the standard differential of the product xy, so the whole bracket becomes d(xy).
Once every term is a d(something), integration is just one line. x³/3 + y³/3 − axy = c. The tension terms are the ones you force into a known differential — the rest you never worry about.

quickChecks.q: Solve x dx + y dy + y dx + x dy = 0.
steps: 1. Harmless terms: x dx and y dy.
2. Problem terms: y dx + x dy = d(xy).
3. Integrate: x²/2 + y²/2 + xy = c.
4. Multiply by 2: x² + y² + 2xy = 2c, which is (x + y)² = constant.
quickChecks.answer: x²/2 + y²/2 + xy = c, i.e. (x + y)² = constant

quickChecks.q: Solve 3x² dx + 2y dy − 5(x dy + y dx) = 0.
steps: 1. 3x² dx is harmless: ∫3x² dx = x³.
2. 2y dy is harmless: ∫2y dy = y².
3. The bracket x dy + y dx is d(xy), with −5 outside.
4. So x³ + y² − 5xy = c.

quickChecks.q: Solve x³ dx + y dy − b(y dx + x dy) = 0.
steps: 1. ∫x³ dx = x⁴/4.
2. ∫y dy = y²/2.
3. y dx + x dy = d(xy), so −b∫d(xy) = −bxy.
4. Add the constant: x⁴/4 + y²/2 − bxy = c.

concepts.title: Integrating After the Substitution Without Slips
concepts.oneLine: Once you spot the exact differential, put t for that whole combination and the integral becomes a plain t-integral — then switch back to y/x at the very end.
notes: Keep the order of priorities straight: the observation is the skill, the integration is just hygiene. Once the problem has collapsed into something like d(y/x) divided by 1 + (y/x)², there is nothing left to discover. Put t = y/x, and the whole thing becomes a standard integral you have done many times.
So ∫ d(y/x)/(1 + (y/x)²) is simply ∫ dt/(1 + t²), and that is tan⁻¹t. Write t back as y/x and you are done. No brain needed here — that is the point.
The second one is where students slip. ∫ (x/y)³ d(y/x): if t = y/x, then x/y is 1/t, so (x/y)³ is t⁻³, not t³. Convert the bracket into t first, read the power carefully, and only then integrate.
Now t⁻³ integrates as t⁻³⁺¹/(−3+1) = −1/(2t²), and putting t = y/x gives −x²/(2y²) + c. Different-looking expressions, same two-step habit: name it t, integrate, rename it y/x.

quickChecks.q: Integrate (x/y)² d(y/x).
steps: 1. t = y/x, so x/y = 1/t and (x/y)² = t⁻².

quickChecks.q: Integrate d(y/x) ÷ (y/x).
steps: 1. t = y/x gives ∫ dt/t.
2. That is ln|t| + c.
3. Replace t by y/x.

quickChecks.q: Integrate (y/x)⁴ d(y/x).
steps: 1. t = y/x gives ∫ t⁴ dt.
3. Replace t by y/x.

concepts.title: The Odd-Term Trick: Pairing Mismatched Terms
concepts.oneLine: When a function of y sits with dx and a function of x sits with dy, those two odd terms are partners — they add up to one exact differential, and the equation is solved by just writing it back.
notes: Look at any equation of the form M dx + N dy = 0. A function of x sitting with dx is no problem at all, and a function of y sitting with dy is no problem either. Those are the matched, comfortable pieces.

The trouble-makers are the mismatched ones: a function of y sitting with dx, and a function of x sitting with dy. In 2x ln y dx + (x²/y) dy, the odd term on the first side is ln y and the odd term on the second side is x². Join those two odd terms together and you get the function whose exact differential this is — here x² ln y.

Check it this way. Hold ln y fixed and differentiate x²: you get 2x dx, so that piece is 2x ln y dx. Now hold x² fixed and differentiate ln y: you get (1/y) dy, so that piece is (x²/y) dy. Both terms of the question come back exactly.

Once you see that, there is nothing left to integrate the long way. d(x² ln y) = 0 means x² ln y = C, and you are done. Same logic with y dx + x dy: the odd term with dx is y, the odd term with dy is x, their product xy is the answer, so xy = C.

quickChecks.q: Solve 3x² ln y dx + (x³/y) dy = 0.
steps: 1. Odd term with dx is ln y; odd term with dy is x³.
2. Pair them: the function is x³ ln y.
3. Check: freeze ln y, d(x³) = 3x² dx, giving 3x² ln y dx; freeze x³, d(ln y) = (1/y) dy, giving (x³/y) dy.
4. Both terms match, so d(x³ ln y) = 0.

quickChecks.q: Solve 2xy dx + x² dy = 0.
steps: 1. Odd term with dx is y; odd term with dy is x².
2. Pair them: try x²y.
3. d(x²y) = 2xy dx + x² dy, exactly the given left side.
4. So d(x²y) = 0.

quickChecks.q: In y² dx + 2xy dy = 0, name the two odd terms and solve.
steps: 1. With dx the odd term is y²; with dy the odd term is x (the 2y is the natural y-part).
2. Pair them: try xy².
3. d(xy²) = y² dx + 2xy dy, which is the given left side.
4. So d(xy²) = 0.
quickChecks.answer: Odd terms y² and x; solution xy² = C

concepts.title: Practice: Two Exact-Form Questions
concepts.oneLine: Two exact-form questions, twelve to thirteen minutes on your clock, pen moving before you look at any solution.
notes: The pairing idea is now in place. The next thing is what your hands do with it: two questions, labelled C and D, and the clock is yours.
Twelve to thirteen minutes for both. Pen down, solution hidden, no peeking. That is the whole instruction. Pause the clip right here and actually do them.

One more thing, worth saying before you start. D may look very simple — but that is only one pair of eyes. Everyone has their own view of which question is the easy one, so start with whichever one your eye likes and come back to the other.
When you are done, or when the time is up, come back and go through them line by line. Looking at the solution before you have struggled is the one way to waste this section.

quickChecks.q: Solve x dy + y dx = 0.
steps: 1. Look at the pair: x with dy, y with dx. That is exactly d(xy).
2. So the equation is d(xy) = 0.
3. Integrate both sides: xy = c.

quickChecks.q: Solve x dy − y dx = 0 for x ≠ 0.
steps: 1. Same two terms, but with a minus sign, so think of y/x.
2. Divide through by x²: (x dy − y dx)/x² = 0, which is d(y/x) = 0.
3. Integrate: y/x = c, so y = cx.

quickChecks.q: Solve 2x dx + 2y dy = 0.
steps: 1. 2x dx is d(x²) and 2y dy is d(y²).
2. So the equation is d(x² + y²) = 0.
3. Integrate: x² + y² = c.

concepts.title: Exact Form with d(xy) and sin(xy)
concepts.oneLine: Both terms carry x dy + y dx, so call it d(xy), put t = xy, and sin t dt + t cos t dt is nothing but d(t sin t) — giving xy·sin(xy) = c.
notes: Look at the equation first: sin(xy)·(x dy + y dx) + xy cos(xy)·(x dy + y dx) = 0. The bracket x dy + y dx is sitting in both terms. That bracket is d(xy), so the equation is sin(xy) d(xy) + xy cos(xy) d(xy) = 0.
Now don't strain your brain with xy written everywhere. Put t = xy. Then d(xy) becomes dt and the equation reads sin t dt + t cos t dt = 0. Suddenly it is a one-letter question.

Read that left side out loud: sin t dt plus t cos t dt. Differentiate t·sin t and you get exactly this — sin t from the derivative of t, and t cos t from the derivative of sin t. So the whole left side is d(t sin t).

d(t sin t) = 0 means t sin t = c. Put t back as xy and you are done: xy·sin(xy) = c. Some students instead integrate the two pieces separately, by parts on the second one — that works too and lands on the same answer, but it is the long road.

quickChecks.q: Solve cos(xy)·(x dy + y dx) − xy sin(xy)·(x dy + y dx) = 0.
steps: 1. Common bracket is d(xy); put t = xy.
2. Equation becomes cos t dt − t sin t dt = 0.
3. Differentiate t·cos t: you get cos t dt − t sin t dt. Exact match.
4. So d(t cos t) = 0, giving t cos t = c.

quickChecks.q: Solve (x dy + y dx)·e^(xy) + xy e^(xy)·(x dy + y dx) = 0.
steps: 1. Put t = xy, so d(xy) = dt.
2. Equation becomes e^t dt + t e^t dt = 0.
3. Differentiate t·e^t: you get e^t dt + t e^t dt. Same two terms.
4. So d(t e^t) = 0, giving t e^t = c.

quickChecks.q: Solve (x dy + y dx)·(1 + ln(xy)) = 0, for xy > 0.
steps: 1. Put t = xy, so the equation is (1 + ln t) dt = 0.
2. Differentiate t·ln t: you get ln t dt + t·(1/t) dt = (ln t + 1) dt.
3. So d(t ln t) = 0, giving t ln t = c.

concepts.title: Forcing a Common Factor: d(xy)/(xy)² with d(y/x)
concepts.oneLine: When one group is already d(xy) and the other needs x² underneath, divide the whole equation by (xy)² instead of xy — the forced extra xy turns both groups into clean differentials and gives −1/(xy) + ln(y/x) = c.
notes: Open the brackets and there are four terms. Two of them, y dx + x dy, are honestly d(xy). The other two have xy sitting in both, so pull xy out and what is left is xy(x dy − y dx).

Now the trouble starts. That second bracket wants x² below it, because (x dy − y dx)/x² is exactly d(y/x). But the moment you divide by xy and then stick x² under the first group as well, the first group becomes d(xy) over xy·x², and xy·x² is not a function of xy alone. The substitution t = xy then dies.

So do not divide by xy. Divide by (xy)² — force one more xy into both groups on purpose. The first group becomes d(xy)/(xy)², perfectly in t = xy. The second becomes (x dy − y dx)/(xy), and that extra x/y is exactly what converts d(y/x) into d(y/x) divided by (y/x), which is a log.

After that the integration is nothing. t⁻² gives −1/t, and du/u gives ln u. The skill in this whole question is not integration, it is choosing the denominator that keeps both groups recognisable at the same time.

quickChecks.q: Solve y dx + x dy = xy(y dx − x dy).
steps: 1. Left side is d(xy). Bring everything to one side: d(xy) − xy(y dx − x dy) = 0.
2. Divide by (xy)²: d(xy)/(xy)² = (y dx − x dy)/(xy).
3. Right side = −(x dy − y dx)/(xy) = −d(y/x) ÷ (y/x).
4. Integrate: −1/(xy) = −ln(y/x) + c.

quickChecks.q: Divide (x dy − y dx) by xy. Which exact differential do you get?
steps: 1. (x dy − y dx)/(xy) = (x/y)·(x dy − y dx)/x².
2. (x dy − y dx)/x² is d(y/x), and x/y is 1/(y/x).

quickChecks.q: Integrate ∫ d(xy)/(xy)³.
steps: 1. Put t = xy, so the integral is ∫ t⁻³ dt.

concepts.title: Linear upon Linear Solved by Exact Differentials
concepts.oneLine: Cross multiply a (ax + by + c)/(px + qy + d) equation and only two terms misbehave — the y sitting with dx and the x sitting with dy — and those two are exactly b·d(xy).
notes: Linear upon linear means dy/dx = (ax + by + c)/(px + qy + d). Most students see this shape and immediately reach for the long substitution route. Cross multiply first and a shorter door opens.

Bring everything to one side and read the terms one by one. ax dx is pure x. c dx is pure x. qy dy and d dy are pure y. Every one of those has a single variable sitting with its own differential, so each integrates on its own — not a problem.

Only two terms misbehave: the y that is stuck with dx, and the x that is stuck with dy. And those two disliked terms are exactly the ones that pair up: b(y dx + x dy) = b d(xy). The thing you were unhappy about is the thing that finishes the question.

That is the whole trick, and the same match is the exactness test too — the ∂/∂y of the dx bracket and the ∂/∂x of the dy bracket both come out b. So check in one glance that the coefficient of y in one bracket equals the coefficient of x in the other. If the setting is there, write the answer. Don't memorise the final line; memorise this reading.

quickChecks.q: Solve (2x + 3y + 1) dx + (3x + 4y + 5) dy = 0.
steps: 1. Coefficient of y in the first bracket is 3, coefficient of x in the second is 3 — the setting is there.
2. Open up: 2x dx + dx + 4y dy + 5 dy + 3(y dx + x dy) = 0.
3. The last bracket is 3 d(xy); integrate the rest term by term: x² + x + 2y² + 5y + 3xy = C.

quickChecks.q: Solve dy/dx = −(x + 2y + 3)/(2x + y + 1).
steps: 1. Cross multiply: (2x + y + 1) dy + (x + 2y + 3) dx = 0.
2. Coefficient of y in the dx bracket is 2, coefficient of x in the dy bracket is 2 — pair confirmed.
3. x dx + 3 dx + y dy + dy + 2(y dx + x dy) = 0, so x²/2 + 3x + y²/2 + y + 2xy = C.
4. Multiply right through by 2 to clear the halves.

quickChecks.q: In (3x + 5y + 2) dx + (5x + 7y + 4) dy = 0, which two terms are the problem, what do they become, and what is the solution?
steps: 1. The two problem terms are 5y dx and 5x dy; together they are 5(y dx + x dy) = 5 d(xy).
2. Everything else is a single variable with its own differential: 3x dx, 2 dx, 7y dy, 4 dy.
3. Integrate: 3x²/2 + 2x + 7y²/2 + 4y + 5xy = C, then multiply by 2.
quickChecks.answer: The pair is 5y dx + 5x dy = 5 d(xy), and the solution is 3x² + 10xy + 7y² + 4x + 8y = C

concepts.title: Orthogonal Trajectory: The Three-Step Method
concepts.quote: This concept shows up once in a blue moon — but when it does, it is a free mark, because the whole thing is three fixed steps. Learn the steps today and you never have to think again.
concepts.oneLine: Orthogonal trajectory in three steps: differentiate the given family until dy/dx has no arbitrary constant in it, replace that dy/dx by −1/(dy/dx), and solve the new differential equation.
notes: A family of curves has an arbitrary constant in it. The orthogonal trajectory is the family that cuts every curve of that family at 90°. So the slope you want at every point is the negative reciprocal of the slope the given family already has there.

Step 1: differentiate the given curve and get dy/dx. The dy/dx you get must be free of the arbitrary constant — if the constant is still sitting there, eliminate it using the original equation. That is the only place students slip.
Step 2: write the differential equation of the orthogonal trajectory as dy/dx = −1 upon the derivative you found in step 1. Nothing clever here, just flip and put a minus.

Step 3: solve that differential equation. Whatever family you get is the orthogonal trajectory. Variable separable, homogeneous, linear — it is one of the types you already know, so step 3 is old work.

quickChecks.q: Find the orthogonal trajectory of the family y = cx².
steps: 1. Differentiate: dy/dx = 2cx.
2. Constant is still there, so kill it: c = y/x², giving dy/dx = 2y/x.
3. Replace: dy/dx = −x/(2y).
4. Separate: 2y dy = −x dx, so y² = −x²/2 + k.
5. Tidy up: x² + 2y² = constant.

quickChecks.q: Find the orthogonal trajectory of the family xy = c.
steps: 1. Differentiate: y + x dy/dx = 0, so dy/dx = −y/x. No constant left, good.
2. Replace: dy/dx = x/y.
3. Separate: y dy = x dx, so y²/2 = x²/2 + k.
4. Tidy up: y² − x² = constant.

quickChecks.q: Find the orthogonal trajectory of the family of circles x² + y² = c².
steps: 1. Differentiate: 2x + 2y dy/dx = 0, so dy/dx = −x/y. The constant is already gone.
2. Replace: dy/dx = y/x.
3. Separate: dy/y = dx/x, so ln|y| = ln|x| + ln|k|.
4. So y = kx.
quickChecks.answer: y = kx — all straight lines through the centre, which is exactly what you expect to cut a circle at 90°

concepts.title: Practice: Quiz and Bonus Orthogonal Trajectory Problems
concepts.oneLine: Attempt both orthogonal trajectory questions yourself — one quiz, one bonus — using the same three steps.
notes: Two families, and both of them are orthogonal trajectory questions. The first is the quiz problem, the second is the bonus. Commit to an answer on each before you open the solution.
Do the same here. Attempt both before you read the next section — a solution you watch feels easy, a solution you fight for is the one you remember in the exam.

One hint: start by finding the derivative. Differentiate the given family, kill the arbitrary constant, and only then flip dy/dx to −dx/dy. That is the whole job; nothing new is needed beyond the three steps already set out.
And honestly, these two are easy. Both are one differentiation and one small variable-separable integration. If you have the three-step method, you already have everything.

quickChecks.q: Find the orthogonal trajectories of the family y = cx.
steps: 1. Differentiate: dy/dx = c.
2. Eliminate c using y = cx, so c = y/x, giving dy/dx = y/x.
3. Replace dy/dx by −dx/dy: −dx/dy = y/x, so x dx = −y dy.
4. Integrate: x²/2 = −y²/2 + C, so x² + y² = k.
quickChecks.answer: x² + y² = k — circles centred at the origin.

quickChecks.q: Find the orthogonal trajectories of the family x² + y² = c².
steps: 1. Differentiate: 2x + 2y(dy/dx) = 0, so dy/dx = −x/y. The constant is already gone.
2. Replace dy/dx by −dx/dy: −dx/dy = −x/y, so dx/dy = x/y.
3. Separate: dx/x = dy/y.
4. Integrate: ln|x| = ln|y| + ln|k|, so y = kx.
quickChecks.answer: y = kx — straight lines through the origin.

quickChecks.q: Find the orthogonal trajectories of the family y² = 4ax.
steps: 1. Differentiate: 2y(dy/dx) = 4a, so a = y(dy/dx)/2.
2. From the family, a = y²/(4x). Equate: y(dy/dx)/2 = y²/(4x), so dy/dx = y/(2x).
3. Replace dy/dx by −dx/dy: −dx/dy = y/(2x), so 2x dx = −y dy.
4. Integrate: x² = −y²/2 + C, so 2x² + y² = k.
quickChecks.answer: 2x² + y² = k — a family of ellipses.

concepts.title: Orthogonal Trajectory of xy = c
concepts.oneLine: For the family xy = c you get dy/dx = −y/x, so the orthogonal trajectory satisfies dy/dx = x/y and comes out as the rectangular hyperbola y² − x² = λ.
notes: Start with the family xy = c. Here c is an arbitrary constant, so one differentiation kills it. Product rule on the left: x(dy/dx) + y = 0, which gives dy/dx = −y/x. That is the slope of the given family at any point (x, y).
Now the orthogonal trajectory must cut this family at right angles. Perpendicular means the product of slopes is −1. So for the trajectory, dy/dx = −1 divided by the slope of the given curve.
Put it in: −1 ÷ (−y/x) = x/y. So the trajectory satisfies dy/dx = x/y. This is variable separable, the easiest kind. Cross-multiply: y dy = x dx.

Integrate both sides: y²/2 = x²/2 + constant. Multiply by 2 and shift: y² − x² = λ, where λ is just a new arbitrary constant. That is again a rectangular hyperbola — xy = c is cut at right angles everywhere by y² − x² = λ.

quickChecks.q: Find the orthogonal trajectory of the family x² − y² = c.
steps: 1. Differentiate: 2x − 2y(dy/dx) = 0, so dy/dx = x/y.
2. Trajectory slope = −1 ÷ (x/y) = −y/x.
3. Separate: dy/y = −dx/x.
4. Integrate: ln|y| = −ln|x| + k, so ln|xy| = k.
5. Hence xy = λ.
quickChecks.answer: xy = λ (so xy = c and x² − y² = c are orthogonal families — exactly the pair from the worked example, read backwards)

quickChecks.q: Find the orthogonal trajectory of the family of circles x² + y² = c.
steps: 1. Differentiate: 2x + 2y(dy/dx) = 0, so dy/dx = −x/y.
2. Trajectory slope = −1 ÷ (−x/y) = y/x.
3. Separate: dy/y = dx/x.
4. Integrate: ln|y| = ln|x| + k, so y = λx.
quickChecks.answer: y = λx, the straight lines through the origin

quickChecks.q: A family of curves satisfies dy/dx = y/x. Find the differential equation and the equation of its orthogonal trajectory.
steps: 1. Trajectory slope = −1 ÷ (y/x) = −x/y.
2. So the required differential equation is dy/dx = −x/y.
3. Separate: y dy = −x dx.
4. Integrate: y²/2 = −x²/2 + k, so x² + y² = λ.
quickChecks.answer: dy/dx = −x/y, giving x² + y² = λ — circles centred at the origin

concepts.title: What Orthogonal Trajectory Means Geometrically
concepts.oneLine: Two families are orthogonal trajectories of each other when every member of one cuts every member of the other at 90°, as the circles x² + y² = a² and the lines y = Cx do.
notes: Start with x² + y² = a². That is not one circle, it is a family of circles about the origin. Put a = 1, you get one circle; a = 1.5 gives the next; a = √3, then a = 4 — same centre, growing radius.
Now take y = Cx. Again a family, this time of straight lines through the origin. C = 1, C = 2, C = 3 — each value gives you one more line through the centre.

Look at where a line crosses a circle. The line passes through the centre, so at that point it is lying along the radius — it is the normal to the circle there. And the normal is at 90° to the circle's own direction. So every line of y = Cx cuts every circle of x² + y² = a² at a right angle.

That is all orthogonal trajectory means. Say it carefully: not "this is the orthogonal trajectory of that" — both families are orthogonal trajectories of each other. And since the 90° has to hold for every member against every member, the differential equation we work with must belong to the whole family, which is exactly why we kill the arbitrary constant before touching it.

quickChecks.q: At what angle does the line y = 2x cut the circle x² + y² = 25?
steps: 1. y = 2x passes through the origin, which is the centre of the circle.
2. So the line lies along a radius, i.e. it is the normal to the circle at the crossing point.
3. Normal is perpendicular to the curve there.

quickChecks.q: True or false: only the line y = x cuts the circle x² + y² = 1 at a right angle.
steps: 1. Every member of y = Cx passes through the origin, the centre.
2. So every such line is a normal to that circle at its crossing point.
3. C = 1 is in no way special.
quickChecks.answer: False — every line of the family y = Cx cuts it at 90°.

quickChecks.q: Why must dy/dx of the family x² + y² = a² come out free of a before we use it for orthogonal trajectories?
steps: 1. Differentiate: 2x + 2y·dy/dx = 0, so dy/dx = −x/y.
2. This slope is written only in x and y, so it gives the direction of whichever member passes through that point.
3. If a were still sitting in it, the equation would describe one single circle, not the family — and the 90° condition has to hold for every member.
