quickChecks.answer: Because the differential equation must represent the whole family; dy/dx must depend only on x and y, giving dy/dx = −x/y.

concepts.title: Eliminating the Arbitrary Constant: OT of y² = 4ax
concepts.oneLine: To find the orthogonal trajectory of y² = 4ax, first make dy/dx free of a by putting 4a = y²/x, which gives dy/dx = y/(2x), then solve dy/dx = −2x/y to get 2x² + y² = c.
notes: Orthogonal trajectory means every member of the second family cuts every member of the first family at 90°. The word "every" is the whole story. That is exactly why the derivative of the given family must be free of the arbitrary constant.

Take y² = 4ax. Differentiate: 2y · dy/dx = 4a, so dy/dx = 4a/(2y) = 2a/y. Look at it carefully — a is still sitting there. This is not the derivative of the family, this is the derivative of one curve of the family, and it changes as a changes.

So kill the constant using the original equation itself. From y² = 4ax we get 4a = y²/x. Put that back: dy/dx = (y²/x)/(2y) = y/(2x). Now the slope depends only on where you are, not on which parabola you are standing on. This is the derivative of the parabolic family.
For the orthogonal family, slopes multiply to −1, so replace dy/dx by −1 divided by y/(2x): dy/dx = −2x/y. Separate and solve, and the parabolas are gone — you get a family of ellipses.

quickChecks.q: Find the orthogonal trajectory of the family y = ax².
steps: 1. Differentiate: dy/dx = 2ax.
2. From the family, a = y/x², so dy/dx = 2x · y/x² = 2y/x.
3. OT slope: dy/dx = −x/(2y).
4. Separate: 2y dy = −x dx.
5. Integrate: y² = −x²/2 + C, i.e. x² + 2y² = c.

quickChecks.q: Find the orthogonal trajectory of the family xy = k.
steps: 1. Differentiate: y + x · dy/dx = 0, so dy/dx = −y/x (the constant is already gone).
2. OT slope: dy/dx = x/y.
3. Separate: y dy = x dx.
4. Integrate: y²/2 = x²/2 + C, i.e. y² − x² = c.
quickChecks.answer: y² − x² = c — the rectangular hyperbolas with the axes as asymptotes are cut at 90° by these.

quickChecks.q: Find the orthogonal trajectory of the family of circles x² + y² = a².
steps: 1. Differentiate: 2x + 2y · dy/dx = 0, so dy/dx = −x/y (no constant left).
2. OT slope: dy/dx = y/x.
3. Separate: dy/y = dx/x.
4. Integrate: ln|y| = ln|x| + ln|c|, so y = cx.
quickChecks.answer: y = cx — the straight lines through the centre, exactly as the picture tells you.

concepts.title: Forming a DE from Geometry: Length of Normal = Radius Vector
concepts.oneLine: Write length of normal = radius vector as y√(1 + (dy/dx)²) = √(x² + y²); squaring gives dy/dx = ±x/y, so you get a circle and a rectangular hyperbola.
notes: Application of differential equations feels like a new chapter, but there is nothing new in it. The only new work is forming the equation yourself; after that it is the same old solving you already know.

So read the question slowly. Find a curve, not passing through the origin, such that at any point the length of the normal equals the magnitude of the radius vector. Radius vector is just OP — origin O to your point P(x, y) — so its length is √(x² + y²). Nothing vector-like to fear.

The other half is a formula students always forget, and they mix it up with subnormal. Length of the normal at P(x, y) is y√(1 + (dy/dx)²). Put the two equal and your differential equation is already made.

Now square both sides. The y² cancels and you are left with y²(dy/dx)² = x², which gives dy/dx = ±x/y. Two values means two easy equations, so two curves come out: one is a circle, the other a rectangular hyperbola. That is the whole method — mix what is old with what is new and use it.

quickChecks.q: For the same condition (length of normal = radius vector), find the curve of the circle family that passes through (3, 4).
steps: 1. Circle branch comes from dy/dx = −x/y.
2. y dy = −x dx gives x² + y² = c.

quickChecks.q: For the same condition, find the curve of the rectangular hyperbola family that passes through (5, 3).
steps: 1. Hyperbola branch comes from dy/dx = x/y.
2. y dy = x dx gives y² − x² = c.
4. So y² − x² = −16, which is x² − y² = 16.

quickChecks.q: At any point of a curve the length of the normal is twice the magnitude of the radius vector. Form the differential equation and get dy/dx.
steps: 1. Condition: y√(1 + (dy/dx)²) = 2√(x² + y²).
2. Square: y²(1 + (dy/dx)²) = 4(x² + y²).
3. So y² + y²(dy/dx)² = 4x² + 4y², giving y²(dy/dx)² = 4x² + 3y².
4. Hence dy/dx = ±√(4x² + 3y²)/y.

concepts.title: Tangent Segment Bisected on an Axis: Finding the Curve
concepts.quote: This is the last question of the whole chapter, and it is pure geometry turned into one line of calculus. Take a random point, write the tangent, read off its two intercepts — the answer falls out.
concepts.oneLine: If the point of tangency is the midpoint of the tangent's piece between the axes, then m = −y/x, and solving dy/dx = −y/x gives the curve xy = c.
notes: Picture a curve with a tangent drawn at some random point P. That tangent meets the x-axis at T and the y-axis at A. The data says P is the midpoint of TA — the piece of the tangent between the axes is bisected at the point of tangency.

So the curve's equation is never touched. Call the point P(α, β), call the slope there m, and write the tangent as y − β = m(x − α). Put y = 0 to get T, put x = 0 to get A. Two intercepts, two coordinates, nothing clever.

Now the midpoint condition. Match the x-coordinates of the midpoint of TA with α, and m comes out as −β/α. Match the y-coordinates instead and you get the same m — and it must, otherwise the question itself is wrong.

Last step is the generalisation that makes it a differential equation. P was any point, so replace α, β by x, y and replace m by dy/dx. dy/dx = −y/x, separate the variables, and the curve is xy = c. Do not forget the constant of integration — without it the whole exercise means nothing.

quickChecks.q: The tangent to a curve at P(α, β) has slope m. Write the coordinates of its x-intercept T and its y-intercept A.
steps: 1. Tangent: y − β = m(x − α).
2. Put y = 0: x = α − β/m.
3. Put x = 0: y = β − mα.
quickChecks.answer: T is (α − β/m, 0) and A is (0, β − mα).

quickChecks.q: Solve dy/dx = −y/x for the curve passing through (2, 3).
steps: 1. Separate: dy/y = −dx/x.
2. Integrate: ln|y| = −ln|x| + ln c, so xy = c.

quickChecks.q: Find the curve through (1, 4) for which the point of contact of the tangent is always the midpoint of the part of the tangent cut off between the axes.
steps: 1. At P(α, β) the midpoint condition gives m = −β/α, so dy/dx = −y/x.
2. Separate and integrate: ln|y| = −ln|x| + ln c, giving xy = c.

flashcards.q: How do you read off the order of a differential equation?
flashcards.a: $$\frac{d^{n}y}{dx^{n}}$$It is the order of the highest order derivative appearing in it. Nothing else in the equation matters.

flashcards.q: What exactly is the degree, and what must you do before reading it?
flashcards.a: $$\text{degree} = \text{power of the highest order derivative, in polynomial-in-derivatives form}$$The power of the highest order derivative, but only after the equation has been written as a polynomial in its derivatives, that is with every derivative carrying a whole-number power.

flashcards.q: When is the degree of a differential equation not defined?
flashcards.a: $$e^{\,dy/dx} = \frac{d^2y}{dx^2} \;\Rightarrow\; \text{degree undefined}$$When no amount of algebra will make it polynomial in the derivatives, typically when a derivative is trapped inside an exponential, a log or a trigonometric function. The order is still perfectly well defined.

flashcards.q: What is an arbitrary constant in a family of curves?
flashcards.a: $$y = a\sin(x + b)$$A constant whose value is frozen for one particular member but which you were free to choose in the first place. It is exactly what distinguishes one member of the family from another.

flashcards.q: State the formation algorithm.
flashcards.a: $$F\left(x,\ y,\ \frac{dy}{dx},\ \dots,\ \frac{d^ny}{dx^n}\right) = 0$$If the family carries n independent arbitrary constants, differentiate it n times and eliminate the constants from those n equations together with the original one. What survives has order n and no constants in it.

flashcards.q: You have differentiated the allowed number of times and a constant still survives. What now?
flashcards.a: $$2\frac{dy}{dx} = \frac{y}{x}$$Make that constant the subject of the original equation and substitute it in. You are not allowed an extra differentiation, which is how 4a becomes y squared over x.

flashcards.q: One arbitrary constant multiplies a bracket and also sits inside it. What do you do?
flashcards.a: $$y = c(x-c)^{2} \;\Longrightarrow\; (y')^{3} - 4xy\,y' + 8y^{2} = 0$$Do not solve for the constant. Divide the differentiated equation into the original: the outside copy cancels along with one power of the bracket, leaving the bracket alone to substitute back.

flashcards.q: What is the segregate-then-differentiate idea, and what does it give for a sum of two exponentials?
flashcards.a: $$y'' - 3y' + 2y = 0$$If one differentiation will not remove a constant, multiply the whole equation by the reciprocal of the exponential attached to it so that the constant stands bare, and only then differentiate. Repeat for the second constant.

flashcards.q: What is the differential equation of the family of ellipses centred at the origin with both semi-axes arbitrary?
flashcards.a: $$xy\,\frac{d^2y}{dx^2}+x\left(\frac{dy}{dx}\right)^2-y\,\frac{dy}{dx}=0$$Rename the two reciprocal squares as single constants, strand one of them by multiplying by y to the power minus two, and differentiate twice. Order two, degree one.

flashcards.q: How do you state the order of a family's differential equation without forming it?
flashcards.a: $$\text{order} = \text{number of independent arbitrary constants}$$The order equals the number of independent arbitrary constants in the family. Merge every combination that collapses into a single number, then count what is left.

flashcards.q: What is the order for a family whose only x-dependence is an exponential multiplied by a string of constants?
flashcards.a: $$C_1 C_2 C_3 e^{C_4} = C$$One. A product of constants, including e raised to a constant, is just one constant, so the whole family collapses to a single constant times the exponential.

flashcards.q: What does it mean for something to be a solution, and how far does the syllabus go?
flashcards.a: $$\frac{dy}{dx} = f(x,y)$$A solution is any relation between x and y that satisfies the equation identically; to verify one, substitute y and its derivative and the left side must vanish. Everything inside the syllabus here is first order and first degree.

flashcards.q: General solution against particular solution, and what shape should the constant take?
flashcards.a: $$\ln y = \ln x + \ln C \;\Rightarrow\; y = Cx$$The general solution still carries the constant of integration and is the whole family; a particular solution fixes that constant and picks out one member. If both sides integrate to logs, write the constant as log C so the answer collapses in one line.

flashcards.q: A question gives the condition x(2) = 5. What point is that, and when do you use it?
flashcards.a: $$(x^2+1)(y^2+1) = 130$$Whatever is inside the bracket is the input, so this is x as a function of y: when y is 2, x is 5, and the point is (5, 2). Use it only at the very end, after you already hold the general solution.

flashcards.q: How do you separate an equation in which a power of ten in y sits with dx and a power of ten in x sits with dy?
flashcards.a: $$\int a^{x}\,dx=\frac{a^{x}}{\ln a}+C$$Name the blocker and divide the whole equation by the product of the two powers in one move. Each variable then goes to its own side and integrating gives the reciprocal of each power adding to a constant.

flashcards.q: What substitution handles an equation whose right-hand side depends only on the bundle ax + by + c?
flashcards.a: $$t = ax + by + c \;\Rightarrow\; \frac{dt}{dx} = a + b\,\frac{dy}{dx}$$Set t equal to that bundle, whatever is wrapped around it. Differentiate the substitution first, and the equation always becomes separable in t and x.

flashcards.q: Solve the equation whose right-hand side is a squared over (x + y) squared.
flashcards.a: $$y = c + a\,\tan^{-1}\!\left(\frac{x+y}{a}\right)$$Put t equal to x plus y, so the derivative becomes dt/dx minus one. The result is quadratic upon quadratic, which you split by adding and subtracting a squared on top; one piece gives t and the other a tan inverse.

flashcards.q: The bundle is 2x + 3y. What is the first line, and what does the integral look like?
flashcards.a: $$t=2x+3y\ \Rightarrow\ \frac{dt}{dx}=2+3\frac{dy}{dx}$$Write the derivative of the substitution straight from memory: two comes free and only the derivative picks up three. The equation then lands on linear upon linear, which you split into a constant plus a log rather than cancelling.

flashcards.q: When is an equation homogeneous, and what do you substitute?
flashcards.a: $$\frac{y}{x} = t \;\Rightarrow\; y = tx \;\Rightarrow\; \frac{dy}{dx} = t + x\frac{dt}{dx}$$When the powers of x and y add to the same total in every term, top and bottom. Divide by that power of x to expose y over x, then substitute y = tx so the derivative becomes t plus x times dt/dx.

flashcards.q: The derivative appears squared. What do you do?
flashcards.a: $$y\left(\frac{dy}{dx}\right)^{2}+2x\frac{dy}{dx}-y=0\;\Longrightarrow\;\frac{dy}{dx}=-\frac{x}{y}\pm\sqrt{1+\left(\frac{x}{y}\right)^{2}}$$Fire the quadratic formula on the derivative itself. The plus root and the minus root are two separate differential equations giving two separate families, and both belong in the answer.

flashcards.q: How does naming sin y help when sin 2y sits beside cos y?
flashcards.a: $$t=\sin y\;\Rightarrow\;\frac{dt}{dx}=\cos y\,\frac{dy}{dx}$$Expand sin 2y as twice sin y cos y so that cos y times the derivative appears as one block, then set t equal to sin y. The equation becomes an ordinary homogeneous one in t and x.

flashcards.q: How do you handle an equation that is one linear expression over another?
flashcards.a: $$X=x-a,\quad Y=y-b$$Cover the constants with your thumb; if what is left is homogeneous, find where the two lines meet and move the origin there. The constants vanish, the equation turns homogeneous, and you restore x and y at the end.

flashcards.q: What if the two lines in a linear-upon-linear equation are parallel?
flashcards.a: $$\frac{a_1}{a_2}=\frac{b_1}{b_2}$$Then there is no intersection point and nothing to shift to, so that method is dead. Both parts are built from the same bundle, so solve it directly with the bundle substitution instead.

flashcards.q: How do you recognise a linear differential equation in y?
flashcards.a: $$\frac{dy}{dx} + P(x)\,y = Q(x)$$The derivative at power one, y at power one, the two added rather than multiplied, and no other function of y anywhere. Any function of x is allowed to sit wherever it likes.

flashcards.q: The equation is ugly in y but clean in x. What do you try?
flashcards.a: $$\frac{dx}{dy} + P(y)\,x = Q(y)$$Take reciprocals and read it as linear in x, with y as the independent variable. A log y or a y squared that kills linearity in y very often leaves a perfectly linear equation in x.

flashcards.q: What is the standard form of a linear equation, and what is the integrating factor?
flashcards.a: $$\text{I.F.} = e^{\int P\,dx}$$First make the coefficient of the derivative equal to one; only then is the coefficient of the unknown P. The integrating factor is e raised to the integral of P, and when that integral is a log the exponential simply cancels it.

flashcards.q: State the solution formula for a linear differential equation.
flashcards.a: $$y \cdot (\mathrm{IF}) = \int (\mathrm{IF}) \cdot Q \, dx + c$$The unknown times the integrating factor equals the integral of the integrating factor times Q, plus a constant. Simplify that product before the integral sign does any work, and keep the integrating factor on the left beside the unknown only.

flashcards.q: Write the solution when the equation is linear in x.
flashcards.a: $$x \cdot (\mathrm{IF}) = \int (\mathrm{IF}) \cdot Q \, dy + C$$Exactly the same line with the roles swapped: x times the integrating factor equals the integral of the integrating factor times Q with respect to y, plus a constant.

flashcards.q: The coefficient in standard form comes out as minus cos y. What is the integrating factor?
flashcards.a: $$\text{I.F.} = e^{\int P(y)\,dy}$$e to the minus sin y. Whatever sign sits with the coefficient travels up into the exponent along with the integral, and you must read that sign off the standard form, never off the equation as printed.

flashcards.q: Why is the integrating factor called an integrating factor?
flashcards.a: $$\frac{d}{dx}\left(y\,e^{\int P\,dx}\right) = e^{\int P\,dx}\left(\frac{dy}{dx} + Py\right)$$Because multiplying through by it makes the left side exactly the derivative of the unknown times that factor, which is the product rule read backwards. One integration then finishes the problem, and e is the only function that behaves this way.

flashcards.q: A function p is differentiable with p(1) = 0 and its derivative minus itself is positive beyond 1. Show that p is positive beyond 1.
flashcards.a: $$e^{-x}\left(\frac{dy}{dx} - y\right) = \frac{d}{dx}\left(y\,e^{-x}\right)$$Multiply the inequality by the integrating factor e to the minus x: the left side becomes the derivative of p times that factor, so the product is increasing. Comparing it with its value zero at x equal to one makes the product positive, and since the exponential is positive, so is p.

flashcards.q: What is the reducible-to-linear pattern, and what do you substitute?
flashcards.a: $$f'(y)\frac{dy}{dx} + P(x)\,f(y) = Q(x) \;\Rightarrow\; t = f(y)$$When the derivative of a function of y sits beside dy/dx while the function itself stands alone elsewhere, put t equal to that function. The equation becomes a plain linear one in t, which the integrating factor then settles.

flashcards.q: What is Bernoulli's equation and how is it reduced?
flashcards.a: $$\frac{dy}{dx} + P(x)\,y = Q(x)\,y^{n} \;\Rightarrow\; \frac{1}{y^{n}}\frac{dy}{dx} + P(x)\,y^{1-n} = Q(x),\; t = y^{1-n}$$A linear-looking equation with a power of y on the right. Divide throughout by that power and substitute t equal to y to the power one minus n; the result is linear in t. It is the reducible-to-linear idea with a famous name attached.

flashcards.q: Which four substitutions cover almost every reducible question?
flashcards.a: $$t = \tan y \;\Rightarrow\; \frac{dt}{dx} = \sec^2 y\,\frac{dy}{dx}$$Secant squared y in front of the derivative calls for tan y; dividing by y calls for log y; a y or a 2y multiplying the derivative calls for y squared; and dividing by y squared calls for one over y. Whatever multiplies the derivative is the derivative of your t.

flashcards.q: The equation is already linear but y appears only inside a shifted block. What is the shortcut?
flashcards.a: $$e^{-\ln (x+1)}=\frac{1}{x+1}$$Name the whole block t. A constant shift leaves the derivative unchanged, so the equation stays linear with no Bernoulli and no extra factor. And when the integral of P comes out as a negative log, the integrating factor is simply a reciprocal.

flashcards.q: List the exact differentials worth keeping in memory.
flashcards.a: $$d\left(\frac{y}{x}\right) = \frac{x\,dy - y\,dx}{x^{2}}$$Only three really recur: d of xy is x dy plus y dx, d of y over x is x dy minus y dx all over x squared, and d of x over y is y dx minus x dy all over y squared. Anything else you derive on the spot with the quotient rule.

flashcards.q: What is the practical rule for spotting an exact form?
flashcards.a: $$x^{2}dx + y^{2}dy - a(y\,dx + x\,dy) = 0 \;\Rightarrow\; \frac{x^{3}}{3} + \frac{y^{3}}{3} - axy = c$$Tag each term. A function of x with dx or a function of y with dy is harmless and integrates alone; anything mixed is a problem term. Look only at the problem terms and ask which standard differential they make.

flashcards.q: A function of y sits with dx and a function of x sits with dy. What does that tell you?
flashcards.a: $$d(x^2 \ln y) = 2x \ln y \, dx + \frac{x^2}{y} \, dy$$They are partners, not two separate terms. Multiply them and you have the function whose differential the equation is, so set that product equal to a constant. Confirm it in five seconds by freezing one part and differentiating the other.

flashcards.q: The exact pairing will not close: one group wants xy underneath and the other wants x squared. What is the trick?
flashcards.a: $$\frac{x\,dy - y\,dx}{xy} = \frac{d(y/x)}{y/x}$$Divide the whole equation by the square of xy rather than by xy. One group then becomes d of xy over the square of xy, which integrates to a reciprocal, and the other becomes d of y over x divided by y over x, which integrates to a log.

flashcards.q: Can a linear-upon-linear equation be done without shifting the origin?
flashcards.a: $$\frac{a x^{2}}{2} + c x + \frac{q y^{2}}{2} + d y + b\,xy = C$$Often yes. Cross-multiply and glance at whether the coefficient of y upstairs matches the coefficient of x downstairs; if it does, those two awkward terms close into that coefficient times d of xy while every other term integrates on its own.

flashcards.q: State the three-step method for an orthogonal trajectory.
flashcards.a: $$\left(\frac{dy}{dx}\right)_{\text{OT}} = -\frac{1}{\left(\frac{dy}{dx}\right)_{\text{given family}}}$$Differentiate the family and eliminate the arbitrary constant, so the slope depends on x and y alone. Replace that slope by its negative reciprocal. Solve the resulting equation. Kill the constant, flip, solve.

flashcards.q: Find the orthogonal trajectories of the family xy = c.
flashcards.a: $$y\,dy = x\,dx \;\Rightarrow\; \frac{y^2}{2} = \frac{x^2}{2} + k \;\Rightarrow\; y^2 - x^2 = \lambda$$Differentiating gives slope minus y over x, so the trajectories have slope x over y. Separating and integrating gives y squared minus x squared equal to a fresh constant, a family of rectangular hyperbolas.

flashcards.q: Find the orthogonal trajectories of the family of right-opening parabolas.
flashcards.a: $$2x^2 + y^2 = c$$Differentiate, then replace the surviving constant from the original equation so the slope is y over twice x with no constant in it. Flip it to minus twice x over y, separate, and the trajectories are a family of ellipses.

flashcards.q: Find the curves for which the length of the normal equals the radius vector at every point.
flashcards.a: $$\frac{dy}{dx}=\pm\frac{x}{y}$$Write both lengths in symbols and square the condition; the y squared on the left cancels the y squared on the right and leaves the slope as plus or minus x over y. The plus sign gives rectangular hyperbolas and the minus sign gives circles centred at the origin.

flashcards.q: What is the standing of the last problem of the chapter, the tangent segment bisected on an axis?
flashcards.a: $$m = -\frac{\beta}{\alpha} \;\Rightarrow\; \frac{dy}{dx} = -\frac{y}{x}$$The lecture sets it up and does not finish it. The set-up goes from the tangent at a named general point to both intercepts, imposes the midpoint condition on each coordinate and reaches the slope as minus y over x; the final step is never reconciled, so treat the set-up as the lesson and do not quote a finished answer.

flashcards.q: Which single feature decides that an equation is a differential equation?
flashcards.a: $$\frac{dy}{dx} + 2y = x$$The presence of a derivative. Scan for any derivative at all — if one is there the equation is a differential equation, and if none is there it is not.

flashcards.q: How does this chapter split, and where should the bulk of the practice time go?
flashcards.a: A small new part — order, degree and formation — sits beside a much larger part that is really indefinite integration wearing a new shirt. Order and degree are the minor piece, so most of the time belongs to solving.

flashcards.q: What does the nth order differential coefficient tell you about the order of an equation?
flashcards.a: $$\frac{d^{n}y}{dx^{n}}$$The order of the equation is the largest n that actually appears in it. Hunt for the biggest number sitting on top of the d and write that down.

flashcards.q: The second derivative appears to the fifth power and the first derivative to a fractional power. How is the degree read?
flashcards.a: $$(y'')^{5} = (y')^{2/3} \;\Longrightarrow\; (y'')^{15} = (y')^{2} \;\Rightarrow\; \text{degree } 15$$Raise both sides until every derivative carries a whole-number power, and only then read the power of the highest order derivative — which gives 15 here. Reading the power straight off the printed equation gives 5, and that is wrong.

flashcards.q: A fourth root sits over the first derivative. What is the first move before the degree is read?
flashcards.a: $$\frac{d^2y}{dx^2} = \sqrt[4]{1 + \frac{dy}{dx}}$$Raise both sides to the fourth power so the root disappears, then read the power of the highest order derivative. A degree read before the cleaning is almost always the wrong one.

flashcards.q: Which single sight tells you the degree is undefined rather than merely large?
flashcards.a: $$\frac{d^2y}{dx^2} + e^{\frac{dy}{dx}} = 0$$A derivative sitting as a power of e. It sticks there and no algebra removes it, so state the order, write undefined for the degree and move on.

flashcards.q: Why is the relation y equals mx a family of curves rather than one line?
flashcards.a: $$y = mx$$Because m is free to take any real value, and the moment a letter is free you are looking at a whole family rather than one curve. Each value of m freezes one member.

flashcards.q: What is the differential equation of the family of circles centred at the origin with arbitrary radius?
flashcards.a: $$x + y\frac{dy}{dx} = 0$$One arbitrary constant buys exactly one differentiation, and the radius squared differentiates away, leaving x plus y times the derivative equal to zero.

flashcards.q: A family carries three arbitrary constants. How many differentiations may you take, and what order results?
flashcards.a: $$\frac{d^3y}{dx^3} = 0$$Three — one for each constant and not one more — so the resulting equation is of order three.

flashcards.q: What does the opening line of a formation problem look like, and how are the constants treated?
flashcards.a: $$f(x,\ y,\ c_1,\ c_2,\ \dots,\ c_n) = 0$$The family is written out with its arbitrary constants still in it, and those constants are treated as unknowns to be eliminated rather than as part of the answer.

flashcards.q: With n arbitrary constants, how many equations are you holding, and what order is the answer?
flashcards.a: $$\frac{dy}{dx},\ \frac{d^2y}{dx^2},\ \dots,\ \frac{d^ny}{dx^n}$$n plus one — the curve itself together with n differentiations — and what survives has order n with not one arbitrary constant left inside it.

flashcards.q: One constant multiplies a bracket and also sits inside it. Which equation is divided by which?
flashcards.a: $$\frac{y}{y'} = \frac{x-c}{2}$$Divide the original by the differentiated equation, so the bracket survives on top. The outside copy of the constant cancels along with one power of the bracket.

flashcards.q: Once the division has handed you the bracket, what happens next?
flashcards.a: $$c = x - \frac{2y}{y'}$$Make the constant the subject and substitute it back into the original equation. There is no second differentiation, because one constant is worth exactly one differentiation.

flashcards.q: What is the differential equation of the family built from one linear expression over another?
flashcards.a: $$(y-1)y'' - 2(y')^2 = 0$$Cross-multiply first so that one constant stands alone, differentiate, segregate the second constant, then differentiate again. Two constants give an equation of order two.

flashcards.q: For a sum of two exponentials, how is the multiplying factor chosen?
flashcards.a: $$e^{-2x}y = A + Be^{-x}$$By the constant you are targeting: multiply by the reciprocal of the exponential attached to it so that constant stands bare, then differentiate. The wrong factor kills the other constant instead.

flashcards.q: Why is the renamed ellipse equation multiplied by y to the power minus two?
flashcards.a: $$A\,\frac{x^2}{y^2}+B=\frac{1}{y^2}$$To strand one of the two constants with nothing attached to it. A stranded constant dies in one differentiation, and the second one goes on the next differentiation.

flashcards.q: A combination of three constants appears in a family. How much does it count for?
flashcards.a: $$\frac{y}{x} = \frac{m_1+m_2}{m_3} = C$$One constant, because the whole combination collapses into a single free number. Merge first and count second, since only independent constants decide the order.

flashcards.q: Two arbitrary constants are added together in a family. How many are they?
flashcards.a: $$C_1 + C_2 = C$$One. Their sum is a single free number, so replace it by one letter and the family looks exactly the same.

flashcards.q: What happens to a string of constant factors multiplying an exponential in x?
flashcards.a: $$C_3 e^{C_4} e^{C_5} e^{x} = C e^{x}$$They collapse into one constant in front of the exponential, because e raised to a constant is just a positive number. Only the part carrying x survives as a function.

flashcards.q: What is the verification form of a solution, and what must happen on substituting?
flashcards.a: $$y' - f(x,y) \equiv 0$$Substitute y and its derivative from the expression you were handed; if the left side vanishes for every x, that expression is a solution. Verification is a two-line job, not a fresh solve.

flashcards.q: What does the separation step look like when the right-hand side factorises?
flashcards.a: $$\frac{dy}{dx} = f(x)\,g(y) \;\Rightarrow\; \frac{dy}{g(y)} = f(x)\,dx$$Every y goes with dy on one side and every x with dx on the other. Only a fully separated equation can be integrated at all.

flashcards.q: A general solution carries an arbitrary radius. What does a given point turn it into?
flashcards.a: $$x^2 + y^2 = 25$$One particular member: the constant becomes a fixed number, so the family of circles collapses to the single circle of radius 5.

flashcards.q: When is the given point substituted, however early the question mentions it?
flashcards.a: $$(x^2+1)(y^2+1) = C$$At the very end. Separate, integrate, write the general solution with its constant, and only then put the point in to kill that constant.

flashcards.q: A sum sits in an exponent and blocks separation. What is it really?
flashcards.a: $$e^{ax+ay}=e^{ax}\cdot e^{ay}$$A product — e raised to a sum is the product of the two separate exponentials. That one split sends one factor to the dy side on its own, and it is often the whole question.

flashcards.q: An exponential with a base other than e has to be integrated. What does that base cost you?
flashcards.a: $$\int a^{x}\,dx=\frac{a^{x}}{\ln a}+C$$A division by the natural log of the base, so that log must appear in the working. Treating it like e and skipping the log is the standard slip.

flashcards.q: What is the separated state, and what appears the moment you integrate?
flashcards.a: $$f(y)\,dy = g(x)\,dx \;\Rightarrow\; \int f(y)\,dy = \int g(x)\,dx + C$$Every y with dy on one side and every x with dx on the other, and one constant of integration on one side only. That constant is what makes the answer the general solution.

flashcards.q: What does a given point on the curve do to the general solution?
flashcards.a: $$y(x_0) = y_0 \;\Rightarrow\; C = \text{a fixed number}$$It fixes the constant as one definite number, turning the general solution into the particular solution — one member of the family instead of all of them.

flashcards.q: What must the right-hand side look like before the bundle substitution applies?
flashcards.a: $$\frac{dy}{dx} = f(ax + by + c)$$It must depend on x and y only through a single bundle ax plus by plus c, whatever is wrapped around that bundle. If an x or a y survives after substituting, the form does not apply.

flashcards.q: The substitution leaves a quadratic over a quadratic. How is that split?
flashcards.a: $$\frac{t^2}{t^2+a^2} = 1 - \frac{a^2}{t^2+a^2}$$Build the same quadratic on top by adding and subtracting the constant from the bottom. One piece then integrates to the new variable and the other to a tan inverse.

flashcards.q: After putting t equal to x plus y, what replaces the derivative?
flashcards.a: $$t = x + y \;\Rightarrow\; \frac{dt}{dx} = 1 + \frac{dy}{dx} \;\Rightarrow\; \frac{dy}{dx} = \frac{dt}{dx} - 1$$The derivative of t with respect to x, minus one — because differentiating the substitution gives one plus the derivative. That extra minus one is exactly what makes the question separate.

flashcards.q: A root appears in the integral after the substitution. What clears it?
flashcards.a: $$u^2 = 1 + t \;\Rightarrow\; t = u^2 - 1,\; dt = 2u\,du$$Set whatever sits under the root equal to a square. The differential then picks up the factor that comes from differentiating that substitution, and the radical sign is gone in one line.

flashcards.q: Does a constant added inside the bundle change anything?
flashcards.a: $$t = x + y \;\Rightarrow\; \frac{dt}{dx} = 1 + \frac{dy}{dx}$$No. A constant inside the bundle vanishes on differentiating, so the relation between the derivatives is the same whichever shift you pick, and the constant only moves into the answer's constant.

flashcards.q: Linear over linear turns up after the substitution. How is it handled?
flashcards.a: $$\frac{t}{5t+3}=\frac{1}{5}-\frac{3}{5}\cdot\frac{1}{5t+3}$$Split it, never cancel. Force the numerator to be a multiple of the denominator and correct with a constant; one piece becomes a plain number and the other a log.

flashcards.q: For a bundle ax plus by, which part of the derivative picks up a coefficient?
flashcards.a: $$\frac{dy}{dx}=f(ax+by+c)\ \Rightarrow\ t=ax+by+c,\ \frac{dt}{dx}=a+b\,f(t)$$Only the derivative picks up the coefficient of y; the coefficient of x comes free as a constant. Dropping that free constant destroys the separation.

flashcards.q: Once the common total power is known, what do you divide by?
flashcards.a: $$\frac{dy}{dx} = \frac{x^3 + y^3}{3x^2 y} = \frac{1 + \left(\frac{y}{x}\right)^3}{3\left(\frac{y}{x}\right)}$$The numerator and the denominator both by x raised to that power. The function of y over x then falls out by itself, so the substitution is never a guess.

flashcards.q: An x is taken inside a square root while reducing to the y over x form. What happens to it?
flashcards.a: $$x\frac{dy}{dx}=y+\sqrt{x^{2}-y^{2}}\;\Longrightarrow\;\frac{dy}{dx}=\frac{y}{x}+\sqrt{1-\left(\frac{y}{x}\right)^{2}}$$It enters as its square, so the bracket under the root carries y over x squared. Divide every term by exactly the total power you counted, nothing more and nothing less.

flashcards.q: How do you check that an equation reduces to a function of y over x?
flashcards.a: $$\frac{dy}{dx}=\frac{y^{2}-2xy-x^{2}}{y^{2}+2xy-x^{2}}\;\Longrightarrow\;\frac{(y/x)^{2}-2(y/x)-1}{(y/x)^{2}+2(y/x)-1}$$Add the powers of x and y in every term, top and bottom. Matching totals mean it converts, and that common total tells you which power of x to divide by; one different total means the method is not for that question.

flashcards.q: Dividing a homogeneous equation by x puts it in which shape?
flashcards.a: $$x\frac{dy}{dx} - y = y\tan^{-1}\frac{y}{x} \;\Longleftrightarrow\; \frac{dy}{dx} - \frac{y}{x} = \frac{y}{x}\tan^{-1}\frac{y}{x}$$The derivative minus y over x on the left, and a function of y over x on the right. Every term must be divided, including the one carrying the tan inverse.

flashcards.q: What names the substitution in an equation with a tan inverse term?
flashcards.a: $$\frac{dy}{dx} = f\!\left(\frac{y}{x}\right) \;\Rightarrow\; y = tx, \quad \frac{dy}{dx} = t + x\frac{dt}{dx}$$Whatever is sitting inside the tan inverse. The bracket then becomes a plain tan inverse of the new variable, the free copy of that variable cancels against the y over x term, and you go straight to separating.

flashcards.q: Before splitting any quotient integral, what do you check?
flashcards.a: $$\int \frac{f'(x)}{f(x)}\,dx = \ln|f(x)| + C$$Cover the numerator and differentiate the denominator. If they match, even up to a constant you can pull out, the integral is a single log and there is nothing else to do.

flashcards.q: What is the extra data in a question there for?
flashcards.a: For one job only — fixing the constant. Finish the general solution first and put the data in last, so the problem never feels bigger than it is.

flashcards.q: Which expansion opens an equation carrying sin 2y beside cos y?
flashcards.a: $$\sin 2y = 2\sin y\cos y$$Write sin 2y as twice sin y times cos y. Only then can the cos y be taken out and moved across to sit with the derivative.

flashcards.q: After sin y has been named t, what is the next substitution?
flashcards.a: $$u=\frac{t}{x}\;\Rightarrow\;t=ux,\quad \frac{dt}{dx}=u+x\frac{du}{dx}$$The ratio of t to x, exactly as in any homogeneous equation, so the derivative of t becomes that ratio plus x times its derivative. Dropping the second piece stops the equation separating.

flashcards.q: What does a linear-upon-linear equation look like after the origin has been shifted?
flashcards.a: $$\frac{dY}{dX}=\frac{a_1X+b_1Y}{a_2X+b_2Y},\quad Y=vX$$Homogeneous in the new variables, with both constants gone, so the usual ratio substitution solves it — and the old variables are restored in the last line.

flashcards.q: Which check guarantees that a shift of origin exists?
flashcards.a: $$\frac{dy}{dx}=\frac{a_1x+b_1y+c_1}{a_2x+b_2y+c_2}$$That the two lines actually meet. Compare the coefficients and make sure they are not in the same ratio; with no meeting point there is nothing to shift to.

flashcards.q: Unequal coefficient ratios in a linear-upon-linear equation mean what?
flashcards.a: $$\frac{a_1}{a_2}\neq\frac{b_1}{b_2}$$The two lines meet at one point, so shift the origin to it and the equation turns homogeneous.

flashcards.q: Which check comes first in every linear-upon-linear question?
flashcards.a: $$\frac{dy}{dx}=\frac{a_1x+b_1y+c_1}{a_2x+b_2y+c_2}$$The ratio of the coefficients, before a single line is written. Unequal means the lines meet and the origin can be shifted; equal means parallel, so the shift is put away and the equation is solved directly.

flashcards.q: Which substitution belongs to a right-hand side built from one bundle?
flashcards.a: $$\frac{dy}{dx} = f(ax + by + c), \quad v = ax + by + c \;\Rightarrow\; \frac{dv}{dx} = a + b\,f(v)$$Name the bundle with one letter. Its derivative is then the coefficient of x plus the coefficient of y times the function of that bundle, and the equation separates.

flashcards.q: The right-hand side comes out purely in terms of x over y. What changes?
flashcards.a: $$\frac{dy}{dx} = f\!\left(\frac{x}{y}\right), \quad x = vy \;\Rightarrow\; v + y\frac{dv}{dy} = \frac{1}{f(v)}$$The substitution flips: write x as the new variable times y and differentiate with respect to y. Match the substitution to the ratio you actually see instead of forcing the other one.

flashcards.q: The linearity test is applied with the roles swapped. What is the standard form then?
flashcards.a: $$\frac{dt}{dy} + P(y)\,t = Q(y)$$The unknown at power one with its derivative taken with respect to the other variable, the two added and not multiplied, and the coefficients free to be any function of that other variable.

flashcards.q: What is the standard form of an equation linear in y?
flashcards.a: $$\frac{dy}{dx} + P(x)\,y = Q(x)$$The derivative plus a function of x times y on the left, and a function of x on the right. Coefficients in x are free; only the y side decides linearity.

flashcards.q: The y test fails. What must you always try before writing non-linear?
flashcards.a: $$\frac{dx}{dy} + P(y)\,x = Q(y)$$One flip. Take the reciprocal and read the equation with y as the independent variable; if x and its derivative come out at power one, the integrating factor method still works.

flashcards.q: Which step has to come before the integrating factor, every single time?
flashcards.a: $$\frac{dy}{dx} + Py = Q$$Making the coefficient of the derivative equal to one. Read the coefficient of the unknown only after that, or the integrating factor comes out wrong.

flashcards.q: What shape does the solution of an equation linear in y always take?
flashcards.a: $$y \cdot e^{\int P\,dx} = \int Q\,e^{\int P\,dx}\,dx + C$$The unknown times the integrating factor on the left, and the integral of the right-hand side with that same factor on the other side, plus a constant. One y, at power one, and everything else a function of x.

flashcards.q: What are the two separate jobs inside a linear equation?
flashcards.a: $$\text{IF} = e^{\int P(x)\,dx}$$The coefficient of the unknown builds the integrating factor and does nothing else; the right-hand side gets integrated together with that factor. Nothing else happens.

flashcards.q: What has to be in your hand before the one-line solution is any use?
flashcards.a: $$\mathrm{IF} = e^{\int P \, dx}$$The integrating factor, built from the coefficient of the unknown. Write it on its own line first, then multiply it into the right-hand side and simplify before integrating.

flashcards.q: When the equation is linear in x, which variable do you integrate with respect to?
flashcards.a: $$\mathrm{IF} = e^{\int P \, dy}$$y. The variable follows the form, so every differential in the formula becomes dy and the integrating factor is built by integrating the coefficient with respect to y.

flashcards.q: Which standard form is P read from when the equation is linear in x?
flashcards.a: $$\frac{dx}{dy} + P(y)\,x = Q(y)$$The one carrying the derivative of x with respect to y plus a function of y times x. Reading it off the equation as printed is how the sign gets lost.

flashcards.q: Why does a minus sign survive into the integrating factor?
flashcards.a: $$\int \cos y\,dy = \sin y + C$$Because the whole integral, sign and all, sits in the exponent. Integrating a cosine gives a sine, so a minus in front of the coefficient leaves a minus in the exponent.

flashcards.q: What does the solution look like once both sides have been integrated?
flashcards.a: $$y\,e^{\int P\,dx} = \int Q\,e^{\int P\,dx}\,dx + C$$The unknown times the integrating factor equals the integral of the right-hand side carrying that factor, plus a constant. The factor multiplies throughout, so the right-hand side must carry it too.

flashcards.q: Why is e the only function that can serve as the integrating factor?
flashcards.a: $$\text{IF} = e^{\int P\,dx}$$Because it is the only one that differentiates back into itself times the coefficient, and that extra coefficient is exactly what the second term on the left needs.

flashcards.q: The coefficient of the unknown is minus one. What is the integrating factor?
flashcards.a: $$\text{I.F.} = e^{\int -1\,dx} = e^{-x}$$e to the minus x. The coefficient is integrated with its sign, and the whole integral goes up into the exponent.

flashcards.q: Once the product has been shown to be increasing, how is the result finished?
flashcards.a: $$u'(x) > 0 \text{ on } (1,\infty) \;\Rightarrow\; u(x) > u(1) \text{ for } x > 1$$Compare it with its value at the left end point. The value given there is what makes the whole argument collapse to the answer, so that data point is not decoration.

flashcards.q: What does the equation become after the substitution, and what must not survive?
flashcards.a: $$\frac{dt}{dx} + P(x)\,t = Q(x)$$A plain linear equation in the new variable, with no trace of the old one left in it. If any of the old variable survives, the substitution is incomplete and the integrating factor has to wait.

flashcards.q: What is the only target when reducing an equation to a standard linear one?
flashcards.a: $$\frac{dt}{dx} + P(x)\,t = Q(x), \quad \text{IF} = e^{\int P\,dx}$$The derivative of the new variable plus a function of x times that variable, with the coefficient of the derivative equal to one. From there the integrating factor is automatic.

flashcards.q: The unknown appears only inside a block shifted by a constant. What does naming that block cost?
flashcards.a: $$t=y-2\quad\Rightarrow\quad \frac{dt}{dx}=\frac{dy}{dx}$$Nothing. A constant shift leaves the derivative untouched, so the equation stays linear in the new variable with no extra work at all.

flashcards.q: When a substitution is involved, when do you read off P and Q?
flashcards.a: $$\frac{dy}{dx}+P(x)\,y=Q(x)\quad\Rightarrow\quad \text{I.F.}=e^{\int P\,dx}$$Only after the substitution is in place and the coefficient of the derivative has been forced to one. The integrating factor is then e raised to the integral of P.

flashcards.q: The same bundle keeps repeating in an equation. What is the substitution, and what is easy to drop?
flashcards.a: $$v = 2y + x \Rightarrow \frac{dv}{dx} = 1 + 2\frac{dy}{dx}$$Name the bundle with one letter and differentiate it term by term. The coefficient sitting on the y part must come through into the derivative; one missing coefficient changes the whole answer.

flashcards.q: What is done with a linear-over-linear fraction before integrating?
flashcards.a: $$\frac{v+1}{3v-1} = \frac{1}{3} + \frac{4}{3}\cdot\frac{1}{3v-1}$$Split it into a constant plus a multiple of the reciprocal of the denominator, which integrates to a log. Nothing is ever cancelled across a sum.

flashcards.q: Which exact differential comes up most often, and what does it look like?
flashcards.a: $$d(xy) = x\,dy + y\,dx$$The differential of the product xy — x with dy plus y with dx. Spot that pair anywhere and replace it by the single differential.

flashcards.q: Two mixed terms appear with the same number in front. What are they?
flashcards.a: $$d(xy) = x\,dy + y\,dx$$One differential of the product xy. Take the common factor out first; if nothing common comes out, the pair is not that differential.

flashcards.q: How are the terms sorted when hunting for an exact form?
flashcards.a: Tag each one. A function of x with dx, or a function of y with dy, is harmless and integrates alone; anything mixed is a problem term, and only the problem terms are asked which standard differential they make.

flashcards.q: The named combination appears raised to a power. Which integral finishes it?
flashcards.a: $$\int t^{n}\,dt = \frac{t^{n+1}}{n+1} + c,\ n \neq -1$$The plain power integral in the new variable, valid for every power except minus one, negative powers included.

flashcards.q: The bracket is the reciprocal of the name you chose. What must be written first?
flashcards.a: $$t = \frac{y}{x} \;\Rightarrow\; \frac{x}{y} = t^{-1}$$The reciprocal as a negative power, on paper and as its own line, before anything is integrated. Deciding the power in your head is where the minus sign disappears.

flashcards.q: The odd term with dx carries a y and the odd term with dy is x squared. Which differential is it?
flashcards.a: $$d(x^2 y) = 2xy \, dx + x^2 \, dy$$The differential of x squared times y. Multiply the two odd parts together and that product is the function whose differential the equation is.

flashcards.q: What is the smallest case of the odd-term pairing?
flashcards.a: $$d(xy) = y \, dx + x \, dy$$y standing with dx and x standing with dy. Those two always come from the product xy, and that is the pairing to look for first.

flashcards.q: The two mismatched terms come with a minus between them. Which differential is that?
flashcards.a: $$d\!\left(\frac{y}{x}\right) = \frac{x\,dy - y\,dx}{x^{2}}$$The differential of y over x, which wants x squared underneath it. A plus between the terms points to the product xy instead.

flashcards.q: What pairing are you hunting for in an exact-form question?
flashcards.a: $$d(xy) = x\,dy + y\,dx$$One term carrying x with dy and one carrying y with dx. Write the two terms out and physically try to pair them, because these questions crack on paper rather than in your head.

flashcards.q: A function of the new variable sits beside that variable times the derivative of the function. What is the pair?
flashcards.a: $$\sin t\,dt + t\cos t\,dt = d(t\sin t)$$The differential of the variable times the function. Training your eye on that pair saves an integration by parts every time.

flashcards.q: Every term carries the same bracket of x with dy plus y with dx. What is the move?
flashcards.a: $$d(xy) = x\,dy + y\,dx$$Pull it out as one object, the differential of the product xy, and give that product a single letter. The two-variable monster then becomes a plain equation in one variable.

flashcards.q: One group has become the differential of xy over the square of xy. What does it integrate to?
flashcards.a: $$\int \frac{d(xy)}{(xy)^{2}} = -\frac{1}{xy} + c$$A reciprocal — minus one over xy, plus a constant — which is why dividing by the square is worth forcing.

flashcards.q: Which denominator does the mismatched pair with a minus sign want?
flashcards.a: $$d\left(\frac{y}{x}\right) = \frac{x\,dy - y\,dx}{x^{2}}$$x squared, which turns it into the differential of y over x. Dividing by the product instead leaves an extra factor behind and the piece integrates to a log.

flashcards.q: What is the exactness check for an equation written as M with dx plus N with dy?
flashcards.a: $$\frac{\partial M}{\partial y} = \frac{\partial N}{\partial x} = b$$The partial derivative of M with respect to y must equal the partial derivative of N with respect to x. It is the same thing as comparing the two coefficients by eye.

flashcards.q: After cross-multiplying a linear-upon-linear equation, how many terms misbehave?
flashcards.a: $$(ax + by + c)\,dx + (bx + qy + d)\,dy = 0$$Exactly two — the y sitting with dx and the x sitting with dy. When their coefficients match, those two close into the differential of the product xy and every other term integrates on its own.

flashcards.q: Why is the slope of the trajectory the negative reciprocal?
flashcards.a: $$m_1 m_2 = -1$$Because the two curves have to meet at right angles, so the product of the two slopes at the meeting point is minus one.

flashcards.q: What is the only replacement made in an orthogonal trajectory question?
flashcards.a: $$\frac{dy}{dx} \longrightarrow -\frac{dx}{dy}$$The derivative is replaced by minus its reciprocal, and only once the arbitrary constant has already been eliminated from the differential equation.

flashcards.q: In which order do the three steps have to be done?
flashcards.a: $$m_1 m_2 = -1$$Differentiate, eliminate the constant, then flip. In that order the work is mechanical; out of order it becomes a mess.

flashcards.q: What is the slope of the family xy equal to a constant?
flashcards.a: $$xy = c \;\Rightarrow\; x\frac{dy}{dx} + y = 0 \;\Rightarrow\; \frac{dy}{dx} = -\frac{y}{x}$$Minus y over x. Differentiate the family, remembering that the derivative of an arbitrary constant is zero, and the slope falls out with no constant left in it.

flashcards.q: What is the single step that turns any family into its orthogonal trajectory?
flashcards.a: $$\left(\frac{dy}{dx}\right)_{OT} = -\frac{1}{\left(\frac{dy}{dx}\right)_{\text{given}}}$$Taking the negative reciprocal of the slope — upside down, with a minus in front. No new theory is needed beyond that one step.

flashcards.q: Which family do the lines through the origin cut at right angles?
flashcards.a: $$x^2 + y^2 = a^2$$The circles centred at the origin, one member for each radius. A line through the centre is the normal to such a circle where they cross, so the right angle comes free with no differentiation.

flashcards.q: What makes two families orthogonal trajectories of each other?
flashcards.a: $$m_1 m_2 = -1$$Every member of one cutting every member of the other at right angles, so the product of the slopes at each crossing point is minus one. The relation is mutual, so state it both ways.

flashcards.q: The derivative still carries the arbitrary constant. How is it removed?
flashcards.a: $$4a = \frac{y^2}{x} \implies \frac{dy}{dx} = \frac{y}{2x}$$By substituting the constant out from the original family, so the slope depends on x and y alone. A second differentiation is not allowed, because it raises the order and changes the problem.

flashcards.q: How is the negative reciprocal taken correctly?
flashcards.a: $$\left(\frac{dy}{dx}\right)_{OT} = -\frac{1}{\left(\frac{dy}{dx}\right)} = -\frac{2x}{y}$$Turn the whole fraction upside down and then put the minus in front. Changing only the sign, or only inverting, is the usual slip.

flashcards.q: What is the length of the normal at a point?
flashcards.a: $$y\sqrt{1+\left(\frac{dy}{dx}\right)^{2}}$$y times the square root of one plus the derivative squared. Keep it apart from the subnormal, because questions deliberately alternate between the two.

flashcards.q: What does radius vector mean in these questions?
flashcards.a: $$\sqrt{x^{2}+y^{2}}$$Nothing more than the distance of the point from the origin: join the origin to the point and that length is the radius vector. No vectors are involved.

flashcards.q: Where does the working for a tangent condition always start?
flashcards.a: $$y - \beta = m(x - \alpha)$$From the tangent at a named general point with the slope kept as a plain letter. The named point and the letter are swapped for x, y and the derivative only at the very end. The lecture sets this problem up and does not finish it.

flashcards.q: The point of contact is the midpoint of the tangent's piece between the axes. How many conditions must be checked?
flashcards.a: $$\frac{\left(\alpha - \frac{\beta}{m}\right) + 0}{2} = \alpha$$Both of them — the x coordinates and the y coordinates must give the same relation for the slope, and two different relations would mean the data is inconsistent. The lecture sets this problem up and does not finish it, so the final step has to be checked rather than quoted.

ladder.tier: L1 Drill — one formula applied directly
ladder.q: Write down the order and the degree of (d^3y/dx^3)^2 + (d^2y/dx^2)^3 + dy/dx + y = 0.
steps: 1. The highest order derivative present is d^3y/dx^3, so the order is 3.
2. Every derivative already carries a whole-number power, so the equation is already a polynomial in the derivatives and no manipulation is needed.
3. The degree is the power of the HIGHEST order derivative, not the largest power in sight.
4. The power of d^3y/dx^3 is 2, so the degree is 2. The cube on d^2y/dx^2 is a distractor.

ladder.tier: L1 Drill — one formula applied directly
ladder.q: Solve dy/dx = e^(x + y).
steps: 1. Split the exponential: e^(x + y) = e^x e^y, so dy/dx = e^x e^y.
2. Separate the variables: e^(-y) dy = e^x dx.
3. Integrate both sides: -e^(-y) = e^x + c.
4. Rearranging and renaming the constant, e^x + e^(-y) = C.

ladder.tier: L1 Drill — one formula applied directly
ladder.q: Form the differential equation of the family of straight lines through the origin, y = mx, m an arbitrary constant.
steps: 1. There is one arbitrary constant m, so you are allowed exactly one differentiation.
2. Differentiating, dy/dx = m.
3. That is not an acceptable answer because the arbitrary constant m has survived.
4. Use the original equation: m = y/x. Substituting gives dy/dx = y/x, that is x dy/dx - y = 0.

ladder.tier: L1 Drill — one formula applied directly
ladder.q: Find the integrating factor of dy/dx + (2/x) y = x^2, x > 0.
steps: 1. The equation is already in standard form, since the coefficient of dy/dx is 1.
2. Read off P = 2/x, the coefficient of y.
3. Integrating factor = e^(integral of P dx) = e^(integral of (2/x) dx) = e^(2 ln x).
4. Since e^(2 ln x) = e^(ln x^2) = x^2, the integrating factor is x^2.

ladder.tier: L2 JEE Main standard — two or three steps, one main idea
ladder.q: Solve dy/dx = 10^(x + y).
steps: 1. Write 10^(x + y) = 10^x . 10^y, so the trouble is that 10^y cannot travel with dx.
2. Divide through by 10^y: 10^(-y) dy = 10^x dx.
3. Integrate: -10^(-y)/ln 10 = 10^x/ln 10 + c.
4. Multiply by ln 10 and rename the constant: 10^x + 10^(-y) = C.

ladder.tier: L2 JEE Main standard — two or three steps, one main idea
ladder.q: Solve (x^2 + y^2) dx = 2xy dy.
steps: 1. Write dy/dx = (x^2 + y^2)/(2xy). Numerator and denominator are both of degree 2, so the equation is homogeneous.
2. Put y = vx, so dy/dx = v + x dv/dx, giving v + x dv/dx = (1 + v^2)/(2v).
3. The v cancels partly: x dv/dx = (1 + v^2 - 2v^2)/(2v) = (1 - v^2)/(2v).
4. Separate: 2v dv/(1 - v^2) = dx/x. Integrating, -ln|1 - v^2| = ln x + c, so 1/(1 - v^2) = Cx.
5. With v = y/x this is x^2/(x^2 - y^2) = Cx, hence x^2 - y^2 = kx on renaming the constant.

ladder.tier: L2 JEE Main standard — two or three steps, one main idea
ladder.q: Solve dy/dx + y cot x = 2 cos x on (0, pi).
steps: 1. The equation is linear in y and already in standard form, with P = cot x and Q = 2 cos x.
2. Integrating factor = e^(integral of cot x dx) = e^(ln sin x) = sin x.
3. Multiplying through, d/dx [y sin x] = 2 cos x . sin x = sin 2x.
4. Integrate: y sin x = -cos(2x)/2 + c. Since -cos(2x)/2 = sin^2 x - 1/2, absorb the 1/2 into the constant.
5. So y sin x = sin^2 x + C.
ladder.answer: y sin x = sin^2 x + C

ladder.tier: L2 JEE Main standard — two or three steps, one main idea
ladder.q: Solve dy/dx = (x + y - 1)/(x + y + 1).
steps: 1. Both numerator and denominator involve x and y only through the bundle x + y, so this is the form dy/dx = f(ax + by + c).
2. Put t = x + y, so dt/dx = 1 + dy/dx and dy/dx = dt/dx - 1.
3. The equation becomes dt/dx - 1 = (t - 1)/(t + 1), so dt/dx = (t - 1 + t + 1)/(t + 1) = 2t/(t + 1).
4. Separate: ((t + 1)/(2t)) dt = dx, that is (1/2)(1 + 1/t) dt = dx.
5. Integrate: (1/2)(t + ln|t|) = x + c, so t + ln|t| = 2x + c'.
6. Restore t = x + y: x + y + ln|x + y| = 2x + c', that is y - x + ln|x + y| = C.

ladder.tier: L2 JEE Main standard — two or three steps, one main idea
ladder.q: Solve x(1 + y^2) dx + y(1 + x^2) dy = 0 given x(2) = 5.
steps: 1. First read the condition correctly. x(2) = 5 means x is written as a function of y, so y = 2 and x = 5. Keep it aside until the end.
2. Separate: x dx/(1 + x^2) = -y dy/(1 + y^2).
4. Hence the general solution is (1 + x^2)(1 + y^2) = C.
5. Now use the point: at x = 5, y = 2 we get (1 + 25)(1 + 4) = 26 . 5 = 130.

ladder.tier: L2 JEE Main standard — two or three steps, one main idea
ladder.q: Solve dy/dx + y = y^2.
steps: 1. This is Bernoulli with n = 2. Divide throughout by y^2: y^(-2) dy/dx + y^(-1) = 1.
2. Put t = y^(1 - n) = 1/y, so dt/dx = -y^(-2) dy/dx.
3. The equation becomes -dt/dx + t = 1, that is dt/dx - t = -1, linear in t.
4. Integrating factor = e^(-x), so d/dx [t e^(-x)] = -e^(-x), giving t e^(-x) = e^(-x) + c.
5. Hence t = 1 + C e^x, that is 1/y = 1 + C e^x, so y = 1/(1 + C e^x).

ladder.tier: L3 Harder Main — two concepts combined, or a case split
ladder.q: Solve dy/dx = a^2/(x + y)^2, where a is a non-zero constant.
steps: 1. The right-hand side depends on x and y only through x + y, so put t = x + y.
2. Then dy/dx = dt/dx - 1 and the equation becomes dt/dx - 1 = a^2/t^2, so dt/dx = (t^2 + a^2)/t^2.
3. Separate: t^2 dt/(t^2 + a^2) = dx. Write t^2/(t^2 + a^2) = 1 - a^2/(t^2 + a^2) so the integral is doable.
4. Integrate: t - a^2 . (1/a) tan inverse (t/a) = x + c, that is t - a tan inverse (t/a) = x + c.
5. Restore t = x + y: x + y - a tan inverse ((x + y)/a) = x + c.
6. The x cancels, leaving y = C + a tan inverse ((x + y)/a).
ladder.answer: y = C + a tan inverse ((x + y)/a)

ladder.tier: L3 Harder Main — two concepts combined, or a case split
ladder.q: Solve x dy/dx = y + x tan(y/x), x > 0.
steps: 1. Divide by x: dy/dx = y/x + tan(y/x), a function of y/x alone, so the equation is homogeneous.
2. Put y = vx, so dy/dx = v + x dv/dx. Then v + x dv/dx = v + tan v.
3. The v cancels: x dv/dx = tan v, which separates as cot v dv = dx/x.
4. Integrate: ln|sin v| = ln x + ln C.
5. So sin v = Cx, that is sin(y/x) = Cx.

ladder.tier: L3 Harder Main — two concepts combined, or a case split
ladder.q: Solve (x^2 - ay) dx + (y^2 - ax) dy = 0, where a is a constant.
steps: 1. Sort the terms. x^2 dx is a function of x with dx, so it integrates on its own. y^2 dy is a function of y with dy, so it too is harmless.
2. The odd terms are -ay dx (a function of y sitting with dx) and -ax dy (a function of x sitting with dy). Pair them.
3. -ay dx - ax dy = -a(y dx + x dy) = -a d(xy), a standard exact differential.
4. So the equation reads x^2 dx + y^2 dy - a d(xy) = 0.
5. Integrating term by term: x^3/3 + y^3/3 - a xy = c.
6. Multiplying by 3, x^3 + y^3 - 3axy = C.

ladder.tier: L3 Harder Main — two concepts combined, or a case split
ladder.q: Solve (x + 2y^3) dy/dx = y, y > 0.
steps: 1. As it stands y appears cubed, so the equation is not linear in y. But x appears only to the first power, so try reading it as linear in x.
2. Take reciprocals: dx/dy = (x + 2y^3)/y = x/y + 2y^2.
3. Rearrange into standard form: dx/dy - x/y = 2y^2, with P = -1/y.
4. Integrating factor = e^(integral of (-1/y) dy) = 1/y, so d/dy (x/y) = 2y.
5. Integrate: x/y = y^2 + C, hence x = y^3 + Cy.

ladder.tier: L3 Harder Main — two concepts combined, or a case split
ladder.q: Find the orthogonal trajectories of the family of parabolas y^2 = 4ax.
steps: 1. Step 1: differentiate the family. 2y dy/dx = 4a, so dy/dx = 2a/y - but the arbitrary constant a is still there.
2. Eliminate it using the original equation, 4a = y^2/x. Then dy/dx = (y^2/x)/(2y) = y/(2x), which is free of a.
3. Step 2: replace dy/dx by -1/(y/(2x)) = -2x/y.
4. Step 3: solve y dy = -2x dx, which gives y^2/2 = -x^2 + c.
5. Multiplying by 2 and renaming the constant, 2x^2 + y^2 = k - a family of ellipses.
ladder.answer: 2x^2 + y^2 = k, a family of ellipses

ladder.tier: L4 JEE Advanced — multi-concept, a non-obvious first move
ladder.q: Solve x dy - y dx = (x^2 + y^2) dx, x > 0.
steps: 1. The combination x dy - y dx with x^2 + y^2 underneath is the signature of d(tan inverse (y/x)).
2. Divide the whole equation by x^2 + y^2: (x dy - y dx)/(x^2 + y^2) = dx.
3. The left side is exactly d(tan inverse (y/x)).
4. Integrate: tan inverse (y/x) = x + C.
5. Equivalently y = x tan(x + C).

ladder.tier: L4 JEE Advanced — multi-concept, a non-obvious first move
ladder.q: Solve dy/dx = (x + y - 2)/(x - y).
steps: 1. This is linear upon linear, so shift the origin to the intersection of x + y - 2 = 0 and x - y = 0. Solving gives x = 1, y = 1.
2. Put X = x - 1, Y = y - 1. Then dY/dX = (X + Y)/(X - Y), which is homogeneous.
4. Separate: (1 - v) dv/(1 + v^2) = dX/X. Integrating, tan inverse v - (1/2) ln(1 + v^2) = ln X + c.
5. With v = Y/X, (1/2) ln(1 + Y^2/X^2) = (1/2) ln(X^2 + Y^2) - ln X, so the ln X terms cancel.
6. This leaves tan inverse (Y/X) = (1/2) ln(X^2 + Y^2) + C.
7. Restoring X = x - 1 and Y = y - 1: tan inverse ((y - 1)/(x - 1)) = (1/2) ln((x - 1)^2 + (y - 1)^2) + C.

ladder.tier: L4 JEE Advanced — multi-concept, a non-obvious first move
ladder.q: Solve x dy/dx + y = y^2 ln x, x > 0.
steps: 1. Divide by x: dy/dx + y/x = (y^2 ln x)/x. This is Bernoulli with n = 2.
2. Divide throughout by y^2: y^(-2) dy/dx + (1/x) y^(-1) = (ln x)/x.
3. Put t = 1/y, so dt/dx = -y^(-2) dy/dx. The equation becomes -dt/dx + t/x = (ln x)/x, that is dt/dx - t/x = -(ln x)/x.
4. Integrating factor = 1/x, so d/dx (t/x) = -(ln x)/x^2.
5. Integrate by parts: integral of (ln x) x^(-2) dx = -(ln x)/x - 1/x, so integral of -(ln x)/x^2 dx = (ln x)/x + 1/x.
6. Hence t/x = (ln x + 1)/x + C, so t = ln x + 1 + Cx.
7. Since t = 1/y, the solution is y(1 + ln x + Cx) = 1.

ladder.tier: L4 JEE Advanced — multi-concept, a non-obvious first move
ladder.q: Solve (y sin(xy) + x y^2 cos(xy)) dx + (x sin(xy) + x^2 y cos(xy)) dy = 0.
steps: 1. Group the terms by the factor they share. The sin(xy) terms give sin(xy)(y dx + x dy).
2. The cosine terms give xy cos(xy)(y dx + x dy), after taking xy out of x y^2 cos(xy) and x^2 y cos(xy).
3. Both brackets are y dx + x dy = d(xy). So with t = xy the equation is (sin t + t cos t) dt = 0.
4. Integrate: integral of sin t dt = -cos t, and integral of t cos t dt = t sin t + cos t by parts.
5. Adding, the total is t sin t, so t sin t = C.
6. Restoring t = xy: xy sin(xy) = C.

ladder.tier: L5 Advanced hardest — the toughest this chapter justifies
ladder.q: Solve (1 + y^2) dx = (tan inverse y - x) dy.
steps: 1. The equation is not linear in y, but x appears only to the first power, so read it as linear in x.
2. Divide by (1 + y^2) dy: dx/dy = (tan inverse y - x)/(1 + y^2), so dx/dy + x/(1 + y^2) = (tan inverse y)/(1 + y^2).
3. Here P = 1/(1 + y^2), so the integrating factor is e^(integral of dy/(1 + y^2)) = e^(tan inverse y).
4. Multiplying through: d/dy [x e^(tan inverse y)] = (tan inverse y) e^(tan inverse y)/(1 + y^2).
5. Put u = tan inverse y, du = dy/(1 + y^2). The right side integrates to integral of u e^u du = (u - 1) e^u + C.
6. So x e^(tan inverse y) = (tan inverse y - 1) e^(tan inverse y) + C.
7. Therefore x = tan inverse y - 1 + C e^(-tan inverse y).
ladder.answer: x = tan inverse y - 1 + C e^(-tan inverse y)

ladder.tier: L5 Advanced hardest — the toughest this chapter justifies
ladder.q: Find all curves, not passing through the origin, for which the length of the normal at every point equals the length of the radius vector at that point.
steps: 1. At a point (x, y) the length of the normal is |y| sqrt(1 + (dy/dx)^2) and the radius vector, the distance from the origin, is sqrt(x^2 + y^2).
2. Equate and square: y^2 (1 + (dy/dx)^2) = x^2 + y^2.
3. Cancel y^2 on both sides: y^2 (dy/dx)^2 = x^2, so y dy/dx = x or y dy/dx = -x. There are two differential equations, so expect two families.
4. Take y dy/dx = x first: y dy = x dx, giving y^2/2 = x^2/2 + c, that is y^2 - x^2 = C. These are rectangular hyperbolas.
5. Take y dy/dx = -x next: y dy = -x dx, giving y^2/2 = -x^2/2 + c, that is x^2 + y^2 = C. These are circles centred at the origin.
6. The condition that the curve does not pass through the origin simply forces C to be non-zero.
ladder.answer: Two families: the circles x^2 + y^2 = C and the rectangular hyperbolas y^2 - x^2 = C, with C non-zero.

ladder.tier: L5 Advanced hardest — the toughest this chapter justifies
ladder.q: Let y = y(x) satisfy (x ln x) dy/dx + y = 2x ln x for x >= 1. Find y(e).
steps: 1. Substituting x = 1 in the equation gives (1 . 0) dy/dx + y(1) = 2 . 1 . 0, so the equation itself forces y(1) = 0. Keep that as the data point.
2. Divide by x ln x for the standard form: dy/dx + y/(x ln x) = 2.
3. Integrating factor = e^(integral of dx/(x ln x)). With u = ln x this integral is ln(ln x), so the integrating factor is ln x.
4. Multiplying through: d/dx [y ln x] = 2 ln x, so y ln x = 2(x ln x - x) + C by parts.
6. Hence y ln x = 2x ln x - 2x + 2. At x = e, ln e = 1, so y(e) = 2e - 2e + 2 = 2.

ladder.tier: L5 Advanced hardest — the toughest this chapter justifies
ladder.q: Solve dy/dx + x sin 2y = x^3 cos^2 y.
steps: 1. Divide throughout by cos^2 y: sec^2 y dy/dx + x . (sin 2y)/(cos^2 y) = x^3.
2. Since sin 2y = 2 sin y cos y, the middle term is 2x tan y. So sec^2 y dy/dx + 2x tan y = x^3.
3. The derivative of tan y is sec^2 y dy/dx, so put t = tan y. Then dt/dx + 2xt = x^3, linear in t.
4. Integrating factor = e^(integral of 2x dx) = e^(x^2), so d/dx [t e^(x^2)] = x^3 e^(x^2).
5. Put u = x^2 in the right side: integral of x^3 e^(x^2) dx = (1/2) integral of u e^u du = (1/2)(u - 1) e^u = (1/2)(x^2 - 1) e^(x^2).
7. Therefore tan y = (x^2 - 1)/2 + C e^(-x^2).

testBank.q: The order and the degree of the differential equation (1 + (dy/dx)^2)^(3/2) = 5 d^2y/dx^2 are respectively
steps: 1. The highest order derivative present is d^2y/dx^2, so the order is 2 straight away.
2. The equation is not yet a polynomial in the derivatives because of the power 3/2, so you may not read the degree off it as it stands.
3. Square both sides to clear the fractional power: (1 + (dy/dx)^2)^3 = 25 (d^2y/dx^2)^2.
4. Every derivative now carries a whole-number power, so this is a polynomial in the derivatives.
5. The power of the highest order derivative d^2y/dx^2 is 2, so the degree is 2.

testBank.q: The order and the degree of the differential equation d^2y/dx^2 + e^(dy/dx) = 0 are respectively
steps: 1. The highest order derivative is d^2y/dx^2, so the order is 2.
2. For the degree the equation must first be written as a polynomial in the derivatives, that is, with every derivative carrying a whole-number power.
3. Here dy/dx sits in the exponent. Expanding e^(dy/dx) gives an infinite series in dy/dx, which is not a polynomial.
4. Rearranging and taking logarithms gives dy/dx = ln(-d^2y/dx^2), which puts a derivative inside a logarithm - again not polynomial.
5. No manipulation clears it, so the degree is not defined, while the order remains 2.

testBank.q: The order of the differential equation of the family y = (c1 + c2) sin(x + c3) - c4 e^(x + c5), where c1, c2, c3, c4, c5 are arbitrary constants, is
steps: 1. The order equals the number of INDEPENDENT arbitrary constants, so first compress the family.
2. c1 + c2 is a single constant; call it A. Also c4 e^(c5) is a single constant; call it B.
3. So y = A sin(x + c3) - B e^x = A cos(c3) sin x + A sin(c3) cos x - B e^x.
4. Write P = A cos(c3), Q = A sin(c3), R = -B. Then y = P sin x + Q cos x + R e^x, and P, Q, R can be chosen freely and independently.
5. There are exactly three independent arbitrary constants, so the order is 3.

testBank.q: The differential equation of the family of all circles that touch the x-axis at the origin is
steps: 1. A circle touching the x-axis at the origin has its centre on the y-axis at (0, a) and radius |a|, so x^2 + (y - a)^2 = a^2, that is x^2 + y^2 = 2ay. There is one arbitrary constant a, so differentiate once.
2. Differentiating: 2x + 2y dy/dx = 2a dy/dx, so a = (x + y dy/dx)/(dy/dx).
3. The constant has survived, so substitute it back into the original: x^2 + y^2 = 2y (x + y dy/dx)/(dy/dx).
4. Cross-multiplying: (x^2 + y^2) dy/dx = 2xy + 2y^2 dy/dx, hence (x^2 + y^2 - 2y^2) dy/dx = 2xy.
5. Therefore (x^2 - y^2) dy/dx = 2xy, that is dy/dx = 2xy/(x^2 - y^2).

testBank.q: The general solution of dy/dx = cos(x + y) is
steps: 1. The right-hand side depends on x and y only through the bundle x + y, so put t = x + y.
2. Then dt/dx = 1 + dy/dx, so dy/dx = dt/dx - 1 and the equation becomes dt/dx - 1 = cos t, i.e. dt/dx = 1 + cos t.
3. Separate: dt/(1 + cos t) = dx. Use 1 + cos t = 2 cos^2(t/2), so (1/2) sec^2(t/2) dt = dx.
4. Integrate: (1/2) . 2 tan(t/2) = x + C, that is tan(t/2) = x + C.
5. Restore t = x + y to get tan((x + y)/2) = x + C.

testBank.q: For x > 0, the general solution of x dy/dx = y + sqrt(x^2 + y^2) is
steps: 1. Divide by x: dy/dx = y/x + sqrt(1 + (y/x)^2) for x > 0, which is a function of y/x alone, so the equation is homogeneous.
2. Put y = vx, so dy/dx = v + x dv/dx. The equation becomes v + x dv/dx = v + sqrt(1 + v^2).
3. The v cancels, leaving x dv/dx = sqrt(1 + v^2), which is separable: dv/sqrt(1 + v^2) = dx/x.
4. Integrating, ln|v + sqrt(1 + v^2)| = ln x + ln C, so v + sqrt(1 + v^2) = Cx.
5. Put v = y/x: y/x + sqrt(x^2 + y^2)/x = Cx, hence y + sqrt(x^2 + y^2) = Cx^2.

testBank.q: Let y = y(x) satisfy (1 + x^2) dy/dx + 2xy = 4x^2 with y(0) = 0. Then y(1) equals
steps: 1. Divide by 1 + x^2 to reach the standard form: dy/dx + (2x/(1 + x^2)) y = 4x^2/(1 + x^2).
2. Integrating factor = e^(integral of 2x/(1 + x^2) dx) = e^(ln(1 + x^2)) = 1 + x^2.
3. Multiplying through, the left side is d/dx [y(1 + x^2)], and the right side is 4x^2.
4. Integrate: y(1 + x^2) = 4x^3/3 + C. The condition y(0) = 0 gives C = 0.

testBank.q: Let y = y(x), x > 0, satisfy dy/dx + y/x = x y^2 with y(1) = 1. Then y(x) equals
steps: 1. This is Bernoulli's equation with n = 2. Divide throughout by y^2: y^(-2) dy/dx + (1/x) y^(-1) = x.
2. Put t = y^(1 - n) = y^(-1) = 1/y. Then dt/dx = -y^(-2) dy/dx, so y^(-2) dy/dx = -dt/dx.
3. The equation becomes -dt/dx + t/x = x, that is dt/dx - t/x = -x, linear in t.
4. Integrating factor = e^(integral of (-1/x) dx) = 1/x, so d/dx (t/x) = -1 and t/x = -x + C, i.e. t = Cx - x^2.
5. Since y(1) = 1, t(1) = 1, so 1 = C - 1 and C = 2. Hence 1/y = 2x - x^2 and y = 1/(2x - x^2).

testBank.q: The orthogonal trajectories of the family of parabolas y = a x^2 (a an arbitrary constant) form the family
steps: 1. Differentiate the family: dy/dx = 2ax. The arbitrary constant a is still present, so eliminate it using a = y/x^2.
2. This gives the slope of the family free of a: dy/dx = 2(y/x^2) x = 2y/x.
3. For the orthogonal trajectories replace dy/dx by -1/(2y/x) = -x/(2y).
4. Separate: 2y dy = -x dx, and integrate to get y^2 = -x^2/2 + c.
5. Multiplying by 2 and renaming the constant, x^2 + 2y^2 = k - a family of ellipses.

testBank.q: Let y : (-infinity, infinity) -> (0, infinity) be the solution of the differential equation dy/dx = (e^(5x) y^3 + y^3)/(e^x + e^x y^4), satisfying y(0) = 1/sqrt(2). Then the value of y(log_e 2) is
steps: 1. Factorise both sides of the fraction: the numerator is y^3 (e^(5x) + 1) and the denominator is e^x (1 + y^4).
2. So dy/dx = y^3 (e^(5x) + 1) / (e^x (1 + y^4)), which separates as ((1 + y^4)/y^3) dy = ((e^(5x) + 1)/e^x) dx.
3. Left side: integral of (y^(-3) + y) dy = -1/(2y^2) + y^2/2. Right side: integral of (e^(4x) + e^(-x)) dx = e^(4x)/4 - e^(-x).
4. So y^2/2 - 1/(2y^2) = e^(4x)/4 - e^(-x) + C. At x = 0, y^2 = 1/2, so the left side is 1/4 - 1 = -3/4 and the right side is 1/4 - 1 + C = -3/4 + C. Hence C = 0.
5. At x = log_e 2: e^(4x) = 16 and e^(-x) = 1/2, so the right side is 16/4 - 1/2 = 7/2.
6. Thus y^2/2 - 1/(2y^2) = 7/2. Writing u = y^2 > 0, u - 1/u = 7, so u^2 - 7u - 1 = 0 and u = (7 + sqrt(53))/2 (the negative root is rejected since u > 0).
7. Therefore y(log_e 2) = sqrt((7 + sqrt(53))/2).

testBank.q: Let y = f(x) be the real valued function defined on the interval (0, infinity), satisfying y(1) = 0 and the differential equation x dy/dx = y - x^3. Then which of the following statements is (are) TRUE?
opts: The function f has a local minimum at x = 1/sqrt(3)
The function f has a local maximum at x = 1/sqrt(3)
The function f is increasing in the interval (1, 2)
If g(x) = 4x^3 - 5x^2 + (3/2) x for x > 0, then the number of elements in the set {x in (0, infinity) : f(x) = g(x)} is 2
steps: 1. Write the equation in standard linear form: dy/dx - y/x = -x^2 on (0, infinity).
2. Integrating factor = e^(integral of (-1/x) dx) = 1/x, so d/dx (y/x) = -x, giving y/x = -x^2/2 + C and y = -x^3/2 + Cx.
3. The condition y(1) = 0 gives -1/2 + C = 0, so C = 1/2 and f(x) = (x - x^3)/2.

4. Then f'(x) = (1 - 3x^2)/2, which is zero only at x = 1/sqrt(3) on (0, infinity), positive for 0 < x < 1/sqrt(3) and negative for x > 1/sqrt(3). So f has a local MAXIMUM at x = 1/sqrt(3): (B) is true and (A) is false.
5. On (1, 2), 3x^2 > 1, so f'(x) < 0 and f is decreasing: (C) is false.
6. For (D): set (x - x^3)/2 = 4x^3 - 5x^2 + (3/2) x. Multiplying by 2 gives x - x^3 = 8x^3 - 10x^2 + 3x, so 9x^3 - 10x^2 + 2x = 0, that is x(9x^2 - 10x + 2) = 0.

7. On (0, infinity) discard x = 0. The quadratic 9x^2 - 10x + 2 has discriminant 100 - 72 = 28 > 0 and roots (5 +/- sqrt(7))/9, both positive since sqrt(7) < 5. So the set has exactly 2 elements and (D) is true.

testBank.q: Consider the family of curves y = c1 e^(3x) + c2 e^(-x), where c1 and c2 are arbitrary constants. Which of the following statements is (are) TRUE?
opts: The order of the differential equation of the family is 2
The differential equation of the family is d^2y/dx^2 + 2 dy/dx - 3y = 0
y = 7 e^(3x) is a member of the family
y = e^(3x) - 4 e^(-x) is a member of the family
steps: 1. There are two independent arbitrary constants, so the order is 2: (A) is true.
2. Find the equation: multiply by e^(-3x) to segregate c1, giving y e^(-3x) = c1 + c2 e^(-4x). Differentiating, e^(-3x)(y' - 3y) = -4 c2 e^(-4x), so e^(x)(y' - 3y) = -4c2.
3. Differentiate once more: e^(x)(y'' - 3y') + e^(x)(y' - 3y) = 0, and dividing by e^x gives y'' - 2y' - 3y = 0.
4. So the correct equation is d^2y/dx^2 - 2 dy/dx - 3y = 0, not the one in (B) (that one has characteristic roots 1 and -3): (B) is false.
5. y = 7 e^(3x) is the member with c1 = 7, c2 = 0, so (C) is true.
6. y = e^(3x) - 4 e^(-x) is the member with c1 = 1, c2 = -4, so (D) is true.

testBank.q: Let y = y(x), x > 0, satisfy dy/dx = y/x + tan(y/x) with y(1) = pi/2, and let the solution be taken on the branch through that point. Which of the following statements is (are) TRUE?
opts: The solution is defined for every x > 0
steps: 1. The right-hand side is a function of y/x alone, so the equation is homogeneous. Put y = vx, giving v + x dv/dx = v + tan v.
2. The v cancels: x dv/dx = tan v, so cot v dv = dx/x.
3. Integrating, ln|sin v| = ln x + ln C, so sin v = Cx, that is sin(y/x) = Cx.
4. At x = 1, y = pi/2, so sin(pi/2) = C, giving C = 1 and sin(y/x) = x: (A) is true.
5. On the branch through (1, pi/2) we have y/x = sin inverse x taken on the principal branch, since sin inverse 1 = pi/2. Hence y = x sin inverse x: (D) is true.
6. At x = 1/2, sin(y/x) = 1/2 gives y/x = pi/6, so y = (1/2)(pi/6) = pi/12: (B) is true.
7. Since sin(y/x) = x requires |x| <= 1, the solution cannot be continued beyond x = 1: (C) is false.

testBank.q: For the differential equation (x ln x) dy/dx + y = 2 ln x, x > 1, which of the following statements is (are) TRUE?
opts: An integrating factor of the equation is ln x
The general solution is y = ln x + C/ln x
steps: 1. Divide by x ln x to reach standard form: dy/dx + y/(x ln x) = 2/x.
2. Integrating factor = e^(integral of dx/(x ln x)). With u = ln x, the integral is integral of du/u = ln(ln x), so the integrating factor is e^(ln(ln x)) = ln x: (A) is true.
3. Multiplying through, d/dx [y ln x] = (ln x)(2/x), so y ln x = integral of (2 ln x)/x dx = (ln x)^2 + C.
4. Hence y = ln x + C/ln x: (B) is true.
5. If y(e) = 2, then y(e) ln e = (ln e)^2 + C gives 2 = 1 + C, so C = 1: (C) is true.
6. Then y(e^2) . 2 = 4 + 1 = 5, so y(e^2) = 5/2, not 3: (D) is false.

testBank.q: Let C1 be the family x^2 - y^2 = a^2 and C2 the family xy = k, where a and k are arbitrary constants. Which of the following statements is (are) TRUE?
opts: C2 is the family of orthogonal trajectories of C1
C1 is the family of orthogonal trajectories of C2
At every point where a member of C1 meets a member of C2 the two curves are perpendicular
C1 is self-orthogonal, that is, its orthogonal trajectories are again of the form x^2 - y^2 = constant
steps: 1. For C1: differentiate x^2 - y^2 = a^2 to get 2x - 2y dy/dx = 0, so dy/dx = x/y, which is already free of a.
2. Replacing dy/dx by -1/(x/y) = -y/x gives dy/y = -dx/x, hence ln|y| = -ln|x| + constant and xy = k. So (A) is true.
3. For C2: differentiate xy = k to get y + x dy/dx = 0, so dy/dx = -y/x, free of k.

4. Replacing it by -1/(-y/x) = x/y gives y dy = x dx, hence y^2 - x^2 = constant, that is x^2 - y^2 = constant. So (B) is true, and the two families are orthogonal trajectories of each other, giving (C).
5. Since the orthogonal trajectories of C1 are the rectangular hyperbolas xy = k and not members of C1, the family C1 is not self-orthogonal: (D) is false.

testBank.q: Consider the differential equation dy/dx + y tan x = y^2 sec x on (-pi/2, pi/2). Which of the following statements is (are) TRUE?
opts: The substitution t = 1/y reduces the equation to one that is linear in t
An integrating factor of the reduced linear equation is sec x
The general solution satisfies y(C - x) = cos x
The solution through the point (0, 1) is y = cos x/(1 - x)
steps: 1. This is Bernoulli with n = 2. Divide by y^2: y^(-2) dy/dx + y^(-1) tan x = sec x.
2. Put t = 1/y, so dt/dx = -y^(-2) dy/dx. The equation becomes -dt/dx + t tan x = sec x, that is dt/dx - t tan x = -sec x, which is linear in t: (A) is true.
